reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the lung and head and neck cancer conclusion as 'moderate evidence for no association'; the report's Conclusions 5-1 and 5-2 say 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' (and its Chapter 5 Summary 'no statistically significant association').
reporting_issues.consequence: The table drops the qualifier 'statistical', which changes the meaning from 'not statistically significant' to 'no association'.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the second COPD conclusion as insufficient evidence on 'COPD severity'; the report's Conclusion 7-2(b) concerns hospital admissions for COPD.
reporting_issues.consequence: Paraphrase changes the outcome graded; cite the report.

reporting_issues.issue: The final section lists 'aggravation of existing respiratory problems' among harms with substantial evidence, 'judging from Table 1'; the report's substantial grade for the lungs concerns worse symptoms and more frequent bronchitis episodes in people who have smoked cannabis long term, and it grades COPD in people who smoke cannabis occasionally limited, COPD admissions insufficient and asthma no or insufficient.
reporting_issues.consequence: The example overstates what the table supports.

reporting_issues.issue: The criticism that the report cut the literature to systematic reviews and studies of more than 500 participants (page 284 of the report) is not found in Chapter 5, Chapter 7 or Appendix B, and Chapter 7 describes studies of 12 and 110 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: It may apply to another chapter; unchecked here.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Animal and human experimental studies were omitted from the review'; Appendix B ranks randomised trials first, and Chapter 7 includes a 12-person before-and-after vaporizer study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement needs a qualifier (which kinds of experiment were left out).

reporting_issues.issue: The article says 10,700 abstracts were 'eventually considered'; Appendix B reports a master library of 10,759 unique articles, then 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews after filtering to the chosen endpoints.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the figure matches neither stage exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 'long volume' and 'long function' where 'lung' is meant (pulmonary function row).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no change in meaning.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9520128 (summary, introduction, report overview with Table 1, strengths and limitations, the urgent call and research agenda sections, footnotes and the reference list); compared with the National Academies text of Chapters 5 and 7 and Appendix B (see card sc_nasem_2017). The WHO report and the cited reviews were not read.

design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224) with random-effects meta-analysis of the association between smoked cannabis (called marijuana in the paper) and respiratory symptoms (cough, sputum production, wheezing, dyspnea), obstructive lung disease and pulmonary function, in people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime use. Five databases were searched from 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018. 22 studies were included (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional); 3 were rated high risk of bias. Prospective and cross-sectional studies were pooled separately and only when at least 2 studies of low or moderate risk of bias had usable data: 5 of 13 outcomes could be pooled. Strength of evidence was graded by the AHRQ method.
can_establish: The average size of the association between cannabis use and cough, sputum production, wheezing, dyspnea and chronic bronchitis in the published English-language studies up to April 2018, split by cohort and cross-sectional designs, and how thin the evidence is for lung-function tests and obstructive lung disease.
cannot_establish: Causation or the effect of cannabis apart from tobacco (the main text does not say whether the pooled ratios were adjusted, and several studies reported people who smoked both together); effects of heavy long-term use on lung function (few people had more than 20 joint-years and cohorts were young); dose-response; differences between smoking, vaping and eating cannabis (only smoking is described); and whether the published literature is affected by publication bias (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library, 1 January 1973 (the year Oregon decriminalised possession) to 30 April 2018, plus author and reference tracking. English-language observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) and interventional studies in people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use; studies reporting only short-term laboratory outcomes and studies with fewer than 10 people who used cannabis were excluded. 1265 abstracts were identified, 927 selected for further evaluation, 70 read in full and 3 added by reference tracking: 73 candidate articles, 22 included (Results › Literature Search; Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As above. The 30-day lifetime cut-off was chosen by the authors to ensure meaningful exposure. Route of use is not a stated inclusion criterion, but every exposure described in the text is smoking (joints, joint-years).
sample.demographics: Study-level tables are in the Supplement (a PDF, not opened). The text names the largest cohorts: CARDIA (5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed 20 years), the Dunedin birth cohort (1037 children born in 1972 and 1973; mean follow-up 15 years for symptoms, 10 years from age 18 to 32 for lung function), a random sample of the population of Tucson, Arizona (n = 1802, surveyed 1981 to 1988), a Los Angeles cohort (299 people at the start, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years) and SPIROMICS (1174 people currently or formerly smoking tobacco). The authors state that cohorts were young overall and cannabis exposure limited.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The one Los Angeles cohort that contributed to the pooled prospective symptom estimates and to the chronic-bronchitis result lost 49% of participants to follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: English language only; no registry, grey-literature or expert search described in the main text; the cut-off of 30 lifetime days and a lower limit of 10 people who used cannabis. The pooled prospective symptom estimates rest on two cohorts with very different exposure (about once a week for a year in Dunedin; about 3 joints a day for 9.8 years in Los Angeles). Two low-risk cross-sectional studies of symptoms (refs 26 and 27) are not among the 4 pooled; the text does not say why. Studies in people who smoke tobacco only (SPIROMICS) or with cannabis and tobacco smoking combined (NHANES, SPIROMICS) are hard to read as effects of cannabis alone. Heavy long-term exposure is thin: across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used: self-reported cannabis use, quantified in different ways (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years). The authors say this varied exposure measurement is a main source of heterogeneity. No biological verification is described in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Across all outcomes and studies, 1255 participants had more than 10 joint-years of exposure and 756 people who smoked cannabis only had more than 20 joint-years (Results › Study Characteristics); across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (Discussion, 4th paragraph). The authors note that 1 joint a day for 20 years is 7300 joints. Route: smoking, as described; vaping and eating are not covered.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is the key confounder. The authors rated a study low risk of bias only if tobacco use was assessed and adjusted for and people who smoked cannabis only could be told apart from people who smoked both. The symptom comparisons were of people who used cannabis against people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco (Methods › Data Synthesis and Analysis, 1st paragraph); whether the cannabis group in each pooled study included people who also smoked tobacco is not described in the main text. NHANES and SPIROMICS reported lung-function results for combined cannabis and tobacco smoking only.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the two pooled prospective studies each reported that stopping cannabis was followed by fewer respiratory symptoms (Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: People who did not use cannabis (for the symptom comparisons, people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco), as defined in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. The main text does not say whether the pooled ratios were adjusted; the methods say ratios were extracted when reported and calculated from counts otherwise (so some are probably crude).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed by the review. Cross-sectional studies (12 of 22) cannot separate pre-existing differences in airways from effects of smoking. CARDIA and Dunedin enrolled people when young, before most of their cannabis exposure.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparators were meant to be people who did not smoke tobacco for the symptom pools; other drug and alcohol use are not discussed.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported cough, sputum production, wheezing and dyspnea (definitions vary: the authors give 'most days for 3 consecutive months' against 'more than 6 times a day' for cough); chronic bronchitis and COPD; spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio); airway resistance and specific conductance of airways; other respiratory outcomes (outpatient visits, hospital admission, airway reactivity to methacholine).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised by the review beyond the risk-of-bias ratings. The authors state that tobacco-related FEV1 loss becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years (36,500 to 73,000 cigarettes), and that exposure in the included cannabis studies may be too low to show a comparable change.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory symptoms were pooled as risk ratios (and risk differences) of cough, sputum production, wheezing and dyspnea; lung function was kept as mean differences and narrative synthesis because most studies reported 1 or 2 indices.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 distinct outcomes were identified (Supplement Figure 1); 5 were pooled.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened all titles, abstracts and full texts independently (Cohen kappa 0.81 on 80 random abstracts); four reviewers extracted data and rated risk of bias independently; three reviewers graded the strength of evidence together.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects model (Paule-Mandel tau-squared, Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment, R package meta 3.3.3); numbers of participants in the pooled analyses are not given in the main text. Prospective cohorts, 2 studies (Dunedin and Los Angeles), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), risk difference 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); low heterogeneity; after the Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20; Figure 2 legend). Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias): cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13); chronic bronchitis (3 studies) RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16); Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01, chronic bronchitis 0.31 (Figure 3 legend). Lung function was not pooled; single-study results are in the key findings. I-squared values are in the forest plots (images, not read); the text calls heterogeneity low in the prospective pools and high for wheezing in the cross-sectional pools.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Ratios were extracted or calculated from counts; the text does not say whether adjusted estimates were preferred. Risk-of-bias ratings (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies) took account of tobacco adjustment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017059224. The protocol also covered respiratory tract neoplasms, which this paper says it does not report. The registry record was not read, so differences between record and paper were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-study estimates for most lung-function outcomes are in Supplement Tables 2 to 5 (PDF, not opened). The paper states that it reports complete data for all analyses. The paper does not say where the protocol's neoplasm outcomes are reported.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The prospective symptom pools contain 2 studies, so their intervals are those of two cohorts rather than a distribution of studies. The authors say the cohorts were young and cannabis exposure limited, which limits the ability to detect lung-function loss.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 22 studies of mostly young people with limited cannabis exposure (the authors' description), smoking cannabis was associated with more cough, sputum production and wheezing against not using cannabis or tobacco, in both cohort and cross-sectional pools (cross-sectional wheezing RR 2.83, cough RR 4.37). In the two prospective studies pooled for cough and sputum the intervals excluded 1, but the Knapp-Hartung adjusted P values were 0.10 and 0.20. Lung-function tests showed no clear fall in FEV1 in the low-risk cohorts at the low exposure they had (CARDIA: -18 mL, CI -42 to 6.1), a higher FVC in several studies, and one cross-sectional signal at more than 20 joint-years (FEV1-FVC ratio below 70%, OR 2.1, CI 1.1 to 3.9). Airway resistance was higher in all 4 studies that measured it. Chronic bronchitis and COPD could not be settled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Conclusion: "Low-strength evidence suggests that smoking marijuana is associated with cough, sputum production, and wheezing." The Discussion says use more than once a week for at least 1 year is associated with these symptoms, and says evidence on lung function and obstructive lung disease is insufficient. Gaps: (1) the pooled prospective ratios are presented in the abstract and Results with confidence intervals that exclude 1, while the figure legend shows the method the paper says it used (Knapp-Hartung) gave non-significant results; (2) the 'more than once a week for at least 1 year' threshold is not derived from any analysis shown (no analysis by frequency or duration of use appears in the text, and the inclusion cut-off was 30 lifetime days); (3) the Introduction states that cannabis smoke may contain particulate matter at 20 times the concentration of tobacco smoke, citing a 1975 book chapter, which the review does not test; (4) the Discussion's remark that lung function may not be among cannabis's most important long-term health outcomes is conjecture. Against this, the strength ratings are modest, 'insufficient' is used honestly for lung function (not 'no effect'), and the limitations name low exposure, young cohorts and non-uniform exposure measurement.

timeline.event: Systematic review of cannabis smoking, lung function and respiratory complications (Tetrault et al., cited as ref 38): found an association with symptoms and called for more lung-function data.
CARDIA 20-year cohort: contributes the FEV1 and FVC results of this review (Pletcher et al.)
Two further reviews (Ribeiro and Ind; Martinasek et al., refs 39 and 40): symptoms associated with cannabis smoking; conflicting lung-function results.

National Academies report (searches to August 2016): the committee graded as 'substantial' the association of long-term cannabis smoking with worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent bronchitis episodes and as 'moderate' the association with higher FVC, and found lung-function evidence otherwise inconclusive (committee's wording)
This review: first review to rate risk of bias, pool where possible and grade the strength of evidence, by the authors' account.
Population-based data-linkage cohort study of cannabis use and respiratory and all-cause illness and death (Ontario)

replication.where_it_stands: The symptom finding (more cough, sputum and wheeze in people who smoke cannabis) is consistent across designs but graded low strength here because few studies are at low risk of bias and tobacco co-use is hard to separate. Whether lung function falls with heavy long-term smoking was not answered: the cohorts were young and their exposure low. Studies in this review overlap with others read for this library (CARDIA is also appraised as pletcher_2012), so they do not count as independent replication.

funding.funder: No project funding (stated twice: Role of the Funding Source and Acknowledgments). Salomeh Keyhani was supported by NHLBI grant R01HL130484-01A1; Deborah Korenstein by a National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support Grant (P30 CA008748) to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
funding.declared_conflicts: Authors disclosed no conflicts of interest (ICMJE forms referenced).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of California San Francisco and the San Francisco VA Medical Center, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the Wright Center for Graduate Medical Education and the University of Toronto. No cannabis- or tobacco-industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts of adults followed into middle and older age, with repeated spirometry, measured lifetime cannabis exposure by route and amount, tobacco use recorded in detail and enough people who smoke cannabis only at heavy exposure (for example more than 20 joint-years); or an individual-participant pooling of the existing cohorts (CARDIA, Dunedin, Tucson, Los Angeles) with standardised exposure and symptom definitions.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (older than 12 years, at least 30 lifetime days), exposure (cannabis use), comparison (non-use) and outcomes (symptoms, obstructive lung disease, pulmonary function) are stated.
PROSPERO CRD42017059224 and a PRISMA statement; the protocol also covered neoplasms; deviations from the protocol are not discussed and the registry record was not read.
Cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and interventional designs are named but the choice is not explained.

Five databases with a stated date range (justified by Oregon's 1973 decriminalisation) and reference tracking, but English only without justification, and no registry, grey-literature or expert search described; the search was completed within a few months of publication.
Two reviewers screened all titles and abstracts independently and the same two reviewed full texts, with a third for disagreements; kappa 0.81 on 80 abstracts.
Four reviewers extracted data independently.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the main text gives the numbers screened and excluded (Figure 1 is an image) but no list of excluded full texts with reasons; the Supplement PDF was not opened and may contain one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The text describes the main cohorts, their sizes, exposures and risk-of-bias ratings; full study tables are in the Supplement (not opened).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale or Cochrane tool by four reviewers independently, with a low-risk definition built on tobacco adjustment, follow-up, exposure detail and quantified use, so confounding and selection were assessed; selective reporting was not.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Provisional: the methods say funding source was extracted, but it is not reported in the main text; the Supplement (not opened) may hold it.

Random-effects pooling by design (Paule-Mandel tau-squared, Knapp-Hartung adjustment) is appropriate, but ratios were extracted or calculated from counts without saying that adjusted estimates were preferred or justifying pooled crude ones, studies with very different exposure were pooled (two prospective studies), and the intervals reported in the abstract and text do not appear to be the Knapp-Hartung ones the figure legends refer to.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Only low and moderate risk-of-bias studies were pooled, but no analysis compares them or tests the pooled estimates for bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract names few low-risk studies, limited exposure, young cohorts and non-uniform exposure measurement as limits; strength of evidence is graded and the table comments give reasons.

Heterogeneity is described (low in the prospective pools, high for wheezing) and attributed to non-uniform exposure and outcome definitions, but it was not investigated by subgroup or meta-regression.
Not mentioned in the main text; pools of 2 to 4 studies.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No project funding and no conflicts, with personal grant support named.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails; here items 4 (English only, no registry or grey search), 11 (crude or mixed ratios pooled, intervals not the stated adjusted ones) and 15 (publication bias not examined) fail, item 7 could not be judged without the Supplement, and items 2 and 9 are only partly met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled ratios can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the review's value: it is registered, searched five databases, screened and extracted in duplicate, rated risk of bias, graded the evidence cautiously and called lung-function evidence insufficient. The pooled prospective ratios rest on two cohorts, one with a 49% loss to follow-up; the cross-sectional pools rest on four studies. It may be cited for the direction and rough size of the symptom association (low strength), for the list of what the cohorts could and could not show about lung function, and for the exposure limits; not for a size of effect adjusted for tobacco, for heavy long-term lung-function loss or for a causal effect.

key_findings.finding: 22 studies were included (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) of 73 candidate articles; 3 were rated high risk of bias. 13 distinct outcomes were found and 5 could be pooled. Participants were older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use; English only; five databases from 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Selection; Results › Literature Search; Results › Study Characteristics

key_findings.finding: Exposure was low in most studies: across all outcomes and studies 1255 participants had more than 10 joint-years of exposure and 756 people who smoked cannabis only had more than 20 joint-years; across all prospective lung-function evaluations 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (1 joint a day for 20 years = 7300 joints, the authors' arithmetic). Methods of quantifying use varied (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Characteristics; Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The two counts have different scopes (all studies and outcomes against prospective lung-function evaluations only) and should not be mixed.

key_findings.finding: Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The abstract reports the unadjusted-looking intervals as showing increased risk. The legend's P values come from the small-sample method the Methods say was used.

key_findings.finding: Single prospective studies not pooled: the Tucson random-sample cohort (n = 1802, four surveys 1981 to 1988, moderate risk of bias) found current cannabis smoking associated with chronic cough OR 1.73 (1.21 to 2.47), chronic sputum OR 1.53 (1.08 to 2.18) and wheezing OR 2.01 (1.50 to 2.70); the Dunedin study found wheezing OR 1.55 (1.23 to 1.94), P < 0.001, and a trend for dyspnea OR 1.23 (0.97 to 1.56), P = 0.086.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias; all included moderate to heavy use), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum production RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13). Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01. Heterogeneity was high for wheezing and is attributed to non-uniform exposure and symptom definitions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table (wheezing comment); Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic bronchitis and COPD: the Los Angeles cohort (3.0 joints a day, mean 9.8 years, 49% lost) found more bronchitis episodes, OR 2.3 (1.2 to 4.4), P = 0.011. Three cross-sectional studies pooled: RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16), not significant (Knapp-Hartung P = 0.31). SPIROMICS (n = 1174, people currently or formerly smoking tobacco only): current use OR 0.87 (0.59 to 1.31), former use OR 1.0 (0.79 to 1.26). A high-risk-of-bias study found COPD prevalence higher by 0.3% (0.0% to 0.5%) per joint-year, with people who used cannabis and tobacco combined.
key_findings.locator: Results › Obstructive Lung Disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: FEV1: CARDIA (low risk of bias; 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start; exposure minimal, 2 to 3 episodes a month): current use not associated with FEV1, adjusted mean difference -18 mL (-42 to 6.1), P = 0.32. A Los Angeles cohort (mean age 33, over 3.5 joints a day, 8 years): no significant fall in FEV1 in people who smoked cannabis continuously or intermittently against people who did not smoke it. Dunedin (10 years): no change. Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week, moderate risk of bias): significant FEV1 reductions after 1 year (P < 0.01). Six cross-sectional studies: NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking combined; the other four found no effect but were small and young.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: FVC: CARDIA current use (more than 20 episodes in the past 30 days) +20 mL (-5.2 to 49), P = 0.03; lifetime use over 10 joint-years +59 mL (12 to 107), P = 0.01; Dunedin cannabis dependence +17.5 mL (-2.5 to 37.4), P = 0.087. Cross-sectional: SPIROMICS higher FVC in current and former use (P < 0.001); NHANES (mean 15.8 joint-years) +0.07% (SD 0.02%) per joint-year, P = 0.004; two studies found no effect (one at mean 50.4 joint-years, SD 4.6; one small, n = 50, high risk of bias).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FVC, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The CARDIA current-use interval includes zero while P = 0.03.

key_findings.finding: FEV1-FVC ratio: Dunedin, 10 years, adjusted mean difference -0.19 (-0.42% to 0.04%), P = 0.100 (cumulative exposure not reported); Tucson significant reduction after 1 year. Cross-sectional: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (low risk of bias) over 20 joint-years against people who did not smoke cannabis, ratio below 70%: OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9), P = 0.02 after tobacco adjustment; the earlier NHANES study (moderate) no definite relationship; SPIROMICS (mean 30.1 joint-years, all with a tobacco-smoking history) positive association, P < 0.001; a Wellington study (n = 339, mean 54.2 joint-years, SD 75.3) marginally lower ratio, -1.1% (-2.6% to 0.1%); two further studies are described as showing no association (see reporting issues for one of them).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1-FVC Ratio, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Airway resistance and specific conductance of airways: all four studies (1 prospective, low risk of bias; 3 cross-sectional) reported higher resistance and lower conductance in people who smoked cannabis. Other respiratory outcomes: one prospective study found more outpatient visits for respiratory illness (colds, flu, sore throat) but no increase in hospital admission; a high-risk study found more respiratory problems; two cross-sectional studies found no difference in airway reactivity to methacholine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Airway Resistance and Specific Conductance of Airways; Results › Other Respiratory Outcomes

key_findings.finding: Strength of evidence (AHRQ method): low for cough, sputum production, wheezing and airway resistance; insufficient for dyspnea, obstructive lung disease, FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio and other respiratory outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Strength of Evidence; Table

key_findings.finding: The authors say the lung-function evidence is limited by low exposure and young cohorts: tobacco's effect on FEV1 becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years; obstructive lung disease develops in about a third of people who smoke tobacco long term and is usually identified after age 35 to 40; large cohorts of middle-aged to older people with heavier cannabis exposure may be needed. They add, as a conjecture, that few people may use enough cannabis to change lung function, so lung function may not be among its most important long-term health outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment was applied, and the Figure 2 legend says the pooled prospective ratios were not significant after it (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20), yet the abstract and Results report intervals that exclude 1 (cough 1.02 to 4.06; sputum 1.62 to 9.07) as showing an increased risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two-study prospective pools are weaker than the abstract suggests; cite the ratios with the adjusted P values or lean on the cross-sectional pools and the single-cohort results.

reporting_issues.issue: CARDIA current-use FVC difference is given as 20 mL (-5.2 to 49 mL) with P = 0.03; the interval includes zero. Checked against the primary CARDIA paper (card sc_pletcher_2012): the 20 mL (-5.2 to 49) contrast is the heaviest current category (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) and 0.030 is the P value for trend across all four current-intensity categories, not for that contrast; likewise P = 0.32 for the FEV1 difference of -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) is the trend P, and P = 0.01 for lifetime exposure over 10 joint-years is the trend P (0.013) across lifetime categories.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review attaches trend P values to single-category contrasts. Cite the CARDIA contrasts from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes the CARDIA FEV1 result (-18 mL, current use) as having minimal exposure, 2 to 3 episodes a month. In the primary paper 2 to 3 episodes a month is the median among people who smoked cannabis, while -18 mL is the contrast for over 20 episodes in 30 days (484 observations). The review also does not report the primary paper's spline result for current use (FEV1 slope -3.2 mL per episode a month at 20 episodes a month, 95% CI -5.8 to -0.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's 'no association' for CARDIA FEV1 understates the range of exposure the CARDIA contrast covers and omits a significant negative slope; the insufficient-evidence rating for lung function is unaffected, but the exposure wording should not be repeated.

reporting_issues.issue: In the cross-sectional pools the ratio and difference scales disagree: dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83) has a confidence interval excluding 1 while RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13) includes 0, and cough has a very narrow RD interval (0.15 to 0.21) beside a wide RR interval (1.71 to 11.19).
reporting_issues.consequence: Ratios and differences were pooled with different weights, so the absolute differences mostly reflect one or two large studies; the absolute figures should not be read as typical.

reporting_issues.issue: The text pools cross-sectional studies 'with low or moderate' risk of bias from a set of 7 (3 low, 3 moderate, 1 high), but the abstract and Table show 4 pooled studies (1 low and 3 moderate); two low-risk studies are not accounted for in the text, and the identity of the four is only in the forest-plot image.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which studies make up the cross-sectional pools could not be checked from the text; Figure 3 values were not extracted.

reporting_issues.issue: In the FEV1-FVC section the two remaining cross-sectional studies (refs 20 and 21) are said to show no association with a reduced ratio, but the next sentences say the study of ref 20 (38 people who used cannabis only) found significantly lower ratios (P < 0.05) in men who currently smoked cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text contradicts itself about one small study; the FEV1-FVC evidence is rated insufficient in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: The FEV1 row of the Table refers to 'the experimental study' limited by lack of adjustment for key confounders, but the Results describe no experimental study for FEV1 (4 prospective and 6 cross-sectional studies only).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor text-to-table mismatch; the FEV1 conclusion rests on the studies listed in the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: Two different counts of heavy exposure appear: Results give 756 people who smoked cannabis only with more than 20 joint-years across all outcomes and studies; the Discussion gives 243 people (131 cannabis-only) across prospective lung-function evaluations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error, but the scopes differ; a citation of 'few heavy smokers' must name the 243 (131) figure for lung function.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says cannabis smoke may contain particulate matter, toxic gases and aromatic hydrocarbons at 20 times the concentration of tobacco smoke, citing a 1975 book chapter; no included study tests this.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background framing only; it should not be cited as a finding of the review.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6231497 (author manuscript; abstract, introduction, methods, results, strength-of-evidence table as text, discussion, funding and disclosures read; Figures 1 to 3, including the flow chart and all forest plots, are images and their values were not extracted; the Supplement PDF was not opened)

design_detail: Consensus evidence review by a 16-member expert committee of the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (published 12 January 2017), covering 11 health-endpoint areas. This card covers Chapter 7 (Respiratory Disease: pulmonary function, COPD, respiratory symptoms including chronic bronchitis, asthma), the lung cancer and head and neck cancer sections of Chapter 5 (Cancer) and Appendix B (Study Approach). Appendix B says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review but adopted key features of one: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (and PsycINFO for one) for January 1999 to 2 August 2016, quality assessment by more than one person (systematic reviews rated good, fair or poor by at least two members; primary studies guided by the Cochrane tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), questions pre-specified before conclusions, standard wording for the strength of evidence (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, no or insufficient; Box B-3) and National Academies conflict-of-interest procedures. Existing systematic reviews were used first, then primary studies. In the chapters read the committee pools nothing itself.
can_establish: What an expert committee concluded in January 2017, from searches that closed on 2 August 2016, about the strength of published evidence on statistical associations between cannabis (mainly smoking) and lung function, COPD, respiratory symptoms and chronic bronchitis, asthma, lung cancer, and head and neck cancer; which studies it relied on, the limitations it named, and the research it asked for.
cannot_establish: Whether smoking cannabis causes any of these outcomes (every conclusion is worded as a statistical association and rests mostly on observational studies, many with self-reported use and without control for tobacco); the size of any effect (the grading hierarchy 'does not imply the magnitude of the observed effect' and the committee pools nothing); evidence published after 2 August 2016, including the 2018 meta-analysis and the 2022 Ontario cohort in this library; the effect of heavy daily smoking apart from tobacco; the effect of tobacco mixed into joints or of product strength; other forms of cannabis (vaping, edibles). For lung cancer it cannot settle the gap between its own wording and the Swedish cohort it describes (see reporting issues).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). Evidence base per Appendix B: Search 1 (Medline, Embase, Cochrane; January 1999 to June 2016) found 19,189 articles and was judged too broad; Searches 2 and 3 (2,092 and 7,198 articles) used narrower and then broader terms and excluded animal and 'spice' terms; Search 4 (PsycINFO, 1,396) covered mental health, Search 5 ('nabilone', 33) and Search 6 (389, extended to 2 August 2016) filled gaps; members also added articles from their own libraries. Articles were sorted into topic areas, then into 11 endpoint areas, and the committee chose the specific health endpoints to review.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Primary literature: peer-reviewed cross-sectional, case-control and cohort studies, randomised trials and non-systematic reviews; editorials, opinion pieces and grey literature were removed on reading abstracts. Weight by design: randomised trials first, then non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies and case-control studies, with case series and case studies only where nothing better existed (the list does not name cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7). Where a good or fair systematic review existed, primacy went to the most recent (since 2011) and only primary studies after its search date were added; where none existed all primary studies from 1 January 1999 to 2 August 2016 were reviewed. Chapter 7 found no fair- or good-quality systematic review since 2011 and 'elected to include' one from 2007 (literature through 2005).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The committee narrowed a very large literature to chosen endpoints and says some literature may have been missed and that 'very good research may not be reflected' in the report. The search listing for Search 2 limits to English-language human studies from 1999 (other listings not read). The respiratory chapter rests on a 2007 systematic review plus 14 primary articles; the lung cancer evidence on one pooled analysis of six case-control studies (four unpublished) and one cohort; the head and neck evidence on one meta-analysis of nine case-control studies with no newer good-quality study. A committee member named Stephen Sidney (Kaiser Permanente Northern California) shares a name and initial with the 'Sidney S' listed among the authors of the CARDIA cohort paper the lung-function section relies on (Pletcher et al., 2012); the report does not comment (name match only).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study. The chapters say most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking without objective confirmation; a few used joint-years (1 joint a day for 1 year) or frequency in the past year; many did not control dose or duration, and lung-toxic content may vary 'from joint to joint'. Smoking technique, depth of inhalation and product strength are largely not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco and other inhaled drugs and occupational and environmental exposures are the main confounders, and the report says many studies did not control for them. The Swedish cohort did not account for tobacco or cannabis use during its 40 years of follow-up, and its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis (as described in Chapter 5).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (observational studies of current and past use). Symptom studies compare people who stopped with people who continued.

comparison.controls: Varies: people who do not smoke, or who never used cannabis; low-use groups; groups smoking tobacco only in several lung and COPD studies; one study has no non-smoking group. The pooled lung-cancer analysis compares habitual with non-habitual cannabis smoking, the latter defined as under 1 joint-year including people who never used cannabis (Chapter 5, footnote 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not assessed by the committee beyond naming confounding. The report says cancer studies often lacked family history, occupational exposures and diet, and that cancer's long incubation needs long follow-up (Chapter 5, Summary, paragraph after Box 5-1).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly not controlled; the committee lists 'tobacco and other inhaled drugs' among unadjusted confounders (Chapter 7, pulmonary function, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC), lung volumes, airway conductance and resistance, diffusing capacity, CT lung density; COPD by FEV1/FVC below 0.7 or hospital readmission; symptoms (cough, phlegm, wheeze, chronic bronchitis, dyspnea) by questionnaire; asthma by self-report; lung cancer and head and neck cancer incidence from case-control and cohort data.
outcomes.operationalization: The committee's conclusions concern a 'statistical association' with each endpoint; they do not give a size of effect and do not claim causation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis by the committee). Nine graded conclusions (numbered 7-1 to 7-4 with sub-parts, and 5-1 and 5-2) fall in the parts read.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: The committee pools nothing. Figures it reports from cited studies: lung cancer, pooled analysis of six case-control studies, habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08); adenocarcinoma only, more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00) and more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56). Swedish conscripts followed 40 years, more than 50 occasions at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. Head and neck cancer, nine case-control studies pooled: OR 1.021 (0.912 to 1.143). Symptoms: 2007 review, long-term smoking cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0; Dunedin cohort, frequent use, morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; Tashkin 2012 cohort (299 people, 9.8 years), current against never use, cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4. COPD: tobacco only 24.3% against tobacco and cannabis 25.2% (p = 0.90); NHANES, more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9).
analysis.covariates: Varies by cited study; the committee often notes that tobacco and occupational and environmental exposures were not controlled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registered protocol is described; Appendix B says the questions of interest were pre-specified before conclusions were formulated.
analysis.selective_reporting: The committee chose which primary studies to describe (14 for the respiratory chapter; three primary articles for the whole cancer chapter) and shows no per-study quality ratings. The lung cancer text reports a positive cohort estimate while its conclusion points the other way (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable. The committee notes small numbers of people who smoked heavily in the cited studies (CARDIA; the pooled lung-cancer analysis).

interpretation_gap.results_show: What the chapters describe: cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes are more frequent in people who smoke cannabis than in people who do not, in cross-sectional studies and a few cohorts, mostly with self-reported use and incomplete control for tobacco, and fell after stopping in two cohorts, one with high loss to follow-up; lung-function results are inconsistent (short-term airway widening; higher lung volumes; no consistent loss of FEV1; a lower FEV1/FVC ratio at more than 20 joint-years in one national survey that is partly explained by the higher FVC); COPD and asthma studies are few, small or cross-sectional; for lung cancer a pooled analysis of case-control studies found no significant association, with an interval that includes a 38% rise and imprecise estimates at heavy use, while a Swedish cohort found a doubled hazard in those who reported using cannabis more than 50 times at conscription; for head and neck cancer a meta-analysis of case-control studies found no association in the pooled estimate, and its authors judged the evidence insufficient.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Graded conclusions (the committee's judgments): symptoms 'substantial' (7-3a) and stopping 'moderate' (7-3b); acute airway widening 'moderate' and higher FVC 'moderate' (7-1); COPD in people who smoke cannabis occasionally, controlled for tobacco 'limited' (7-2a) and COPD admissions 'insufficient' (7-2b); asthma 'no or insufficient' (7-4); lung cancer and head and neck cancer 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' (5-1, 5-2). Beyond these, the Chapter 5 highlight says the evidence suggests smoking cannabis 'does not increase the risk' of lung and head and neck cancer; the Chapter 7 highlight says 'Quitting cannabis smoking is likely to reduce chronic cough and phlegm production'; and the Chapter 7 Summary says respiratory risks 'appear to be relatively small' and 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking'. Gaps: (1) the cancer highlight is stronger than the graded wording, which is about statistical significance; the pooled lung-cancer interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the chapter reports a hazard ratio of 2.12 and says other reviewed studies 'indicate an increased risk', whereas Box B-3 asks for 'very few or no credible opposing findings' for 'moderate'; (2) for head and neck cancer the committee's grade is stronger than the review authors' own conclusion that evidence was insufficient; (3) the quitting highlight uses causal wording over an association graded on cohorts with loss to follow-up; (4) the tobacco comparison in the Summary is not a numbered conclusion, and the chapter holds pieces pointing both ways (per joint, a 339-person cross-sectional study estimated a lower FEV1/FVC equal to that of 2.5 to 5 cigarettes, an analysis the committee itself criticises, and 15 volunteers took in more carbon monoxide and tar per joint; per day, people who smoke cannabis usually smoke fewer cannabis cigarettes than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes) without showing how they were weighed; (5) Conclusion 7-2(a) says 'occasional' smoking while the Discussion calls the link unclear for regular use and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally.

timeline.event: Wu et al.: 15 volunteers, one joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of one cigarette (as described in this report's Chapter 7).

The Institute of Medicine's earlier report concluded that cannabis smoking was an important risk factor for respiratory disease and that bronchitis may result from chronic use (as described in this report's Chapter 7).
Tetrault et al. systematic review (literature through 2005): the respiratory chapter's main systematic review.
CARDIA cohort, 20 years: occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with lower lung function; used by this report.
Swedish military conscript cohort, 40 years: HR 2.12 for the highest cannabis group (as described in this report's Chapter 5; the paper itself is not yet read in this library).

Pooled analysis of six case-control studies of lung cancer (Zhang et al.), meta-analysis of head and neck cancer (de Carvalho et al.) and the American Thoracic Society position statement (Douglas et al.), all used by this report.
This report, searches to 2 August 2016.
Critical review of this report by Cousijn and colleagues
Systematic review and meta-analysis to April 2018: symptom evidence 'low' strength, lung-function evidence 'insufficient' on its own scale
Ontario linked-data cohort: no excess respiratory emergency visits or admissions over 12 months

replication.where_it_stands: A consensus review is not replicated as such. Later work in this library: the 2018 meta-analysis rated the same symptom evidence 'low' on the AHRQ scale and lung function 'insufficient' (different scales from the committee's, not a contradiction of direction); the 2022 Ontario cohort found no excess respiratory emergency visits; the Swedish cohort and the pooled lung-cancer analysis have not been replicated in the sources read. The committee itself asks for replication because 'many associations are based on single studies'.

funding.funder: Sponsors listed in the Acknowledgments: Alaska Mental Health Trust Authority; Arizona Department of Health Services; California Department of Public Health; CDC Foundation; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; The Colorado Health Foundation; Mat-Su Health Foundation; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration; National Institutes of Health (National Cancer Institute; National Institute on Drug Abuse); Oregon Health Authority; the Robert W. Woodruff Foundation; Truth Initiative; US Food and Drug Administration; Washington State Department of Health.
funding.declared_conflicts: Appendix B says conflicts of interest were declared under the National Academies conflict-of-interest policies; the individual declarations are not in the parts read.
funding.affiliations_note: A committee of 16 academics (Harvard, UCSF, Johns Hopkins, Columbia, Kaiser Permanente Northern California and others, as listed). No cannabis- or tobacco-industry sponsor is listed in the Acknowledgments. One committee member's name matches a co-author of a cohort the lung-function section relies on (see selection effects). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the report.

what_would_settle_it: Cohorts of people who smoke cannabis with objective and repeated measures of use, product content and tobacco mixing, followed for decades with spirometry, imaging and cancer-registry linkage, large enough in heavy use and compared with people who smoke tobacco only and people who use neither. The committee itself asks for better observational studies with self-reported and quantitative measures of dose and duration, longitudinal studies for asthma and allergy, and trials of other inhaled forms against smoking.

domains.note: A documented multi-database search and an explicit hierarchy, with systematic reviews first; but the report says it was not a systematic review, narrowed the literature to committee-chosen endpoints, may have missed literature, and shows only the studies it judged best (14 primary respiratory articles; three primary articles in the whole cancer chapter). The respiratory chapter rests on a 2007 review.

Methods named (Box B-2 questions rated by at least two members; Cochrane tool and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), and the text names limitations of most studies and catches a labelling error in one; but no per-study ratings are shown, so 'good- to fair-quality' cannot be traced to a study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No sign that the committee relied on its own work; one committee member's name matches a co-author of one cited cohort (CARDIA).

Graded conclusions are separate from discussion, but the chapter highlights and the respiratory Summary go beyond them: a causal 'likely to reduce' over an association, a cancer highlight stronger than 'no statistical association', and a comparison with tobacco that is not a numbered conclusion.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: Both sides are described, including the Swedish cohort and the symptom studies, but the lung cancer grade sits uneasily with the contrary evidence described in the same chapter and with the committee's own definition of 'moderate'; the head and neck grade is stronger than the review authors' own conclusion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a consensus review (METHODS section 5.3 lists none), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. This is a documented, multi-database, cautiously worded committee review whose respiratory conclusions follow the studies it describes. Its weaker points for this library are the cancer wording (a grade of 'no statistical association' over a pooled estimate that does not exclude a rise and a cohort that points up) and highlights that go beyond the numbered conclusions. It may be cited for the committee's graded wording as the committee's, for the list of studies under each conclusion with their sizes and limitations, and for its research gaps; claims should cite the primary studies and later reviews it summarises, not use its highlights as findings.

key_findings.finding: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), sorted into 11 endpoint areas; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st to 6th paragraphs (from 'A professional research librarian' to 'After filtering the original search results'); Search Strategies (Search 2)

key_findings.finding: Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then rated good, fair or poor on five attributes adapted from the Cochrane group by at least two members independently (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 7th to 9th paragraphs; Box B-2; Primary Literature: Identification and Quality Review, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines 'substantial' (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), 'moderate' (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), 'limited' (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and 'no or insufficient' (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied). The hierarchy 'does not imply the magnitude of the observed effect'.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-3

key_findings.finding: Respiratory symptoms (Conclusion 7-3): 'substantial evidence of a statistical association' (7-3a) between long-term cannabis smoking and worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent chronic bronchitis episodes, and 'moderate evidence' (7-3b) of an association between stopping and improvement. Under it: a 2007 systematic review of 14 symptom studies (nine cross-sectional, three case series, one case-control, one cohort; cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0); a Wellington cross-sectional study (cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%, people who smoked cannabis against people who did not); the Dunedin cohort of 1,037 followed to age 38 (frequent use, defined as 52 or more times in the past year: morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; fewer symptoms after quitting); an internet survey of 5,987 adults recruited through drug-policy-reform organisations; a longitudinal cohort of 299 followed at least two visits over 9.8 years, with high or variable loss to follow-up (current against never use: cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4; current against former use: cough 3.3, sputum 4.2, wheeze 2.1). The committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both cannabis and tobacco on symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms, Including Chronic Bronchitis › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Hancox 2015, Walden and Earleywine, Tashkin 2012); Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 7-3

key_findings.finding: Limits of the symptom evidence as the committee states them: most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking; many did not control for tobacco and occupational or environmental exposures, or for dose or duration; joint-years were rarely used and the THC content of a joint varies 'from joint to joint and from year to year'; Dunedin classed fewer than 52 uses a year as non-use and did not know whether cannabis was smoked; the internet survey recruited through organisations advocating drug-policy reform.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies (paragraphs after Figure 7-1 on Hancox 2015 limitations and on Walden and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lung function (Conclusion 7-1): 'moderate evidence' of an association between cannabis smoking and improved airway dynamics with acute use but not chronic use (7-1a) and with higher FVC (7-1b); the chapter highlight says it is unclear whether cannabis use is associated with worsened lung function. Under it: the 2007 review (34 publications; acute bronchodilation; regular smoking associated with lower specific airway conductance, about 16% on average, and a lower FEV1; inconsistent findings otherwise); CARDIA, 5,115 adults over 20 years, occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with adverse effects on lung function, with a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure (20 or more joint-years) and with few people at heavy exposure; Dunedin (1,037, spirometry at 32): cumulative cannabis associated with higher FVC, total lung capacity and residual volume but not lower FEV1 or FEV1/FVC; NHANES 2007 to 2012 (10,327 adults, cross-sectional): lower FEV1/FVC and higher FEV1 and FVC in people who had smoked cannabis recently; a 12-person vaporizer feasibility study with no control group.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Papatheodorou, Pletcher, Hancox 2010, Van Dam and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-1; Chapter Highlights

key_findings.finding: COPD (Conclusion 7-2): 'limited evidence' of an association between occasional cannabis smoking and developing COPD when controlled for tobacco (7-2a); 'insufficient evidence' for hospital admissions for COPD (7-2b). Under it: a 339-person Wellington CT study with inconsistent results; Vancouver cross-sectional study of 878 adults (at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco history: not at significantly greater risk of COPD or more respiratory symptoms; tobacco plus cannabis not clearly different from tobacco only); a 709-person readmission study (cannabis 0.22 against tobacco 0.26, unit not specified); a 500-person cross-sectional study with no non-smoking group (COPD 24.3% tobacco only against 25.2% tobacco plus cannabis, p = 0.90; more cough, phlegm and wheeze with both, no adjusted comparison); NHANES (more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.9, but higher FVC and no FEV1 association, and pre-bronchodilator spirometry). The Discussion says it is unclear whether regular use is associated with developing or worsening COPD and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally once tobacco is controlled for.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Tan 2009, Yadavilli, Macleod, Kempker); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-2

key_findings.finding: Asthma (Conclusion 7-4): 'no or insufficient evidence' to support or refute an association between cannabis smoking and asthma development or exacerbation, from a 506-boy cohort that found no link to self-reported asthma symptoms, a cohort of 110 adolescents with asthma that found no association with asthma concern, severity or symptoms, and one case-control letter of 100 emergency department patients that found no association with THC. The Discussion adds that wheeze appears common among people who use cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Asthma › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies; Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-4

key_findings.finding: Chapter 7 Summary and gaps: the committee writes that the risks of respiratory complications of cannabis smoking 'appear to be relatively small' and 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking', that people who smoke heavily may be at higher risk of chronic bronchitis and COPD but 'current studies do not provide sufficient evidence for a link', and names the limitations (cannabis and tobacco hard to separate; self-reported exposure; few cohorts of people who smoke regularly or daily; inadequate control of environmental factors; generalisability). Unknown, it says: whether long-term cannabis smoking above tobacco causes faster lung-function decline, chronic bronchitis or COPD; whether it raises the risk of allergic disease or asthma; whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Summary, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps, 1st paragraph and bullets

key_findings.finding: Background given for smoke exposure: in 15 volunteers one cannabis joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of a single cigarette, with deeper inhalation, longer breath-holding and no filters; against this, cannabis cigarettes are less densely packed and people who use cannabis usually smoke fewer of them per day than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › opening text (before Pulmonary Function), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lung cancer (Conclusion 5-1): 'moderate evidence of no statistical association between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer'. Under it: a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (four unpublished) with 2,159 cases and 2,985 controls found habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38), and OR 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08) in people who did not smoke tobacco; risk rose with duration and intensity but not significantly; in adenocarcinoma alone, more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00) and more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56), 'suggestive' but not significant. An epidemiologic review (no meta-analysis) is said to include studies that 'indicate an increased risk'; its one cohort, 49,321 Swedish military conscripts followed 40 years (44,257 in the cannabis analysis), found HR 2.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 uses at conscription against never, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. Habitual smoking was defined as at least 1 joint-year; non-habitual as under 1 joint-year, including people who never used cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Systematic Reviews; Primary Literature; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 5-1; Footnotes 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Limits of the lung cancer evidence as the committee states them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had too few people with heavy long-term smoking for precise estimates, and relied on self-report without biological validation; in the Swedish cohort detailed cannabis and tobacco use before and after baseline was lacking, tobacco and cannabis were not accounted for during the 40-year follow-up, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and self-reports were not anonymous.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Head and neck cancer (Conclusion 5-2): 'moderate evidence of no statistical association'. Under it: one meta-analysis of nine case-control studies (13,931 people; 5,732 cases, 8,199 controls) adjusted for tobacco, age, gender and race, OR 1.021 (0.912 to 1.143), whose authors concluded there was 'insufficient epidemiological evidence' to support a positive or negative association; no newer good-quality primary study; a null grouped result does not exclude associations with specific cancer types, and differences in methods prevented analysis of frequency, duration or method of use.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Head and Neck Cancers › Systematic Reviews; Primary Literature; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 5-2

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 gaps and summary: the committee judged the evidence on lung and head and neck cancer 'moderate' for 'no statistically significant association', lists small samples, low participation, unverifiable self-reported use and difficulty controlling confounders (family history, occupational exposures and diet often not accounted for) as common problems, says the long incubation of cancer needs long observation, and asks for studies that 'confirm existing evidence on lung and head and neck cancers' and for replication because exposures are changing and 'many associations are based on single studies'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Research Gaps, bullets; Summary, 1st paragraph; paragraphs after Box 5-1

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 5, head and neck Discussion: 'The systematic review also relied on cohort studies', although the same section describes the review (de Carvalho et al.) as nine case-control studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated limitation (cohort studies may miss smaller or later-emerging risks) does not match the designs described; it is unclear which limitation was meant.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-2 (head and neck) grades the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association', while the review it rests on, quoted in the same section, concluded there was insufficient epidemiological evidence to support a positive or negative association.
reporting_issues.consequence: The committee's grade and the review authors' conclusion are not equivalent; cite each as its holder's.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-1 (lung cancer) is graded 'moderate evidence of no statistical association', yet Box B-3 asks for very few or no credible opposing findings for 'moderate', and the chapter reports a cohort with HR 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), says studies in the epidemiologic review but not in the pooled analysis 'indicate an increased risk', and gives adenocarcinoma estimates of about 1.7 that were not significant. The chapter does not explain how these were weighed.
reporting_issues.consequence: 'No statistical association' here means not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 5 highlight (the evidence 'suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk' of lung and head and neck cancer) is stronger than Conclusions 5-1 and 5-2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not use the highlight as a finding; cite the numbered conclusion and the studies under it.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 7 highlight 'Quitting cannabis smoking is likely to reduce chronic cough and phlegm production' uses causal wording, while Conclusion 7-3(b) grades only a statistical association between stopping and improvement, from cohorts with substantial loss to follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 7-3(b) and the cohorts, not the highlight.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 7-2(a) refers to 'occasional' cannabis smoking and 'limited evidence' of an increased risk of developing COPD when tobacco is controlled for; the Discussion calls the link unclear for regular use, and the position statement it cites found minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally. The studies described do not show an association in people who smoke cannabis occasionally (the Vancouver study found no significantly greater risk; the 500-person study found no difference; the NHANES association was at more than 20 joint-years).
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis for the word 'occasional' in 7-2(a) is not apparent in the text read; use with care.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 7 Summary states the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking are 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking'. This is not a numbered conclusion, and the sections read give no study that compares the two with the same measures at matched exposure; they give fewer joints per day, a position statement, and, pointing the other way, per-joint smoke exposure in 15 volunteers and an estimate (from an analysis the committee criticises) of a lower FEV1/FVC per joint equal to 2.5 to 5 cigarettes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite as the committee's overall judgment, not as a measured comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: NHANES paragraph (Papatheodorou et al.): the group sizes (never 4,794; past 4,084; 5 to 30 days 555; 0 to 4 days 891) add to 10,324, not the 10,327 stated; and the effects given 'respectively' (FEV1/FVC -0.01 and -0.02; FEV1 49 and 89 mL; FVC 159 and 204 mL) are said to compare 'current smokers' with 'never smokers' without naming which two current groups the pairs belong to.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the pairs cannot be assigned to groups from the text; check the primary paper before quoting.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix B lists the order of evidence as randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies and case-control studies, but does not place cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7, and a chapter-7 conclusion of 'substantial' rests largely on cross-sectional data (nine of 14 studies in the 2007 review).
reporting_issues.consequence: How cross-sectional evidence was weighted for the grade is not stated.

design_detail: Prospective community cohort (CARDIA: Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults), 5115 Black and White women and men aged 18 to 30 recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities (Oakland, Chicago, Minneapolis, Birmingham) without selection for smoking, followed 20 years with spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20. Self-reported cannabis and tobacco smoking (current intensity at every exam; lifetime exposure in joint-years and pack-years) were modelled together in mixed linear models with individual age trajectories, first as four-level categories and then as flexible cubic splines. Tobacco was analysed in parallel as a positive control. Secondary analysis of a cohort designed for heart disease risk factors.
can_establish: How forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) tracked with self-reported cannabis smoking, current and cumulative and mostly at light levels, in young adults over 20 years, with tobacco smoking modelled at the same time and shown to produce the expected dose-related loss.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis smoking causes or prevents any change in lung function (self-reported exposure, no measure of physical fitness, residual confounding possible); effects of heavy long-term smoking without tobacco (91 people had more than 10 joint-years and no tobacco, 40 more than 20); anything about respiratory symptoms, bronchitis, COPD, the FEV1-FVC ratio, lung volumes, gas transfer or emphysema (not reported or not measured); differences between joints, pipes and bongs (not recorded); effects of product strength or of vaping or eating.

sample.recruitment: Community sample from four US cities, recruited 1985 to 1986 to be balanced by race (Black, White), sex and age, not selected for smoking; healthy at enrolment; baseline plus 6 follow-up exams, 69% retention at year 20 (Methods › Study Design and Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All visits with spirometry, smoking behaviour, second-hand smoke exposure, height and waist circumference. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 959 were excluded for incomplete smoking information, 114 for missing height or waist and 1 for an unknown date, leaving 19,703 visits (95%) from 5016 participants (98%).
sample.demographics: Mean age 25 (SD 4) at baseline; Black and White women and men were sampled in roughly equal numbers by design. 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams. Black women were most likely to smoke tobacco only, White men cannabis only and Black men both. People who smoked cannabis tended to be taller and more active than people who did not smoke; people who smoked tobacco had lower education and income (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: 69% retention at year 20; attrition more common in people who smoked tobacco but not associated with cannabis use (Results, 1st paragraph). Mixed models use every available visit.
sample.selection_effects: Participants were Black and White adults from four cities, mostly people who smoked cannabis lightly (median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days); very heavy cumulative exposure is rare and mostly combined with tobacco, which limits estimates above about 10 joint-years. Attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each exam. Cannabis: episodes in the last 30 days (current intensity) and lifetime joint-years (365 joints or pipe-fulls = 1 joint-year), built from baseline lifetime use, current intensity and a question on joints or pipe-fulls per episode, using assumptions given in an online appendix (not read). Tobacco: cigarettes per day and pack-years (1 pack-year = 7300 cigarettes); the authors cite a comparison with serum cotinine showing little misclassification of tobacco status.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cannabis exposure was mostly light: median 2 episodes (interquartile range 1 to 6) in the past 30 days in the cannabis-only group and 3 (1 to 9) in the group using both; median lifetime exposure 0.9 joint-years (0.2 to 2.8) and 1.5 (0.6 to 4.3). Tobacco medians 8 to 9 cigarettes a day and 7 to 9 pack-years. Route and method of smoking (joint, pipe, bong) were not recorded; strength and tobacco mixed into joints were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco was the main co-exposure and was modelled in the same model (current and lifetime, together with cannabis); the two exposures were strongly correlated. No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis was found for FEV1 or FVC. Other drugs and alcohol were not adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; current use was whatever the participant reported at each exam. The authors note that any acute widening of the airways after cannabis lasts about an hour and is unlikely to explain higher volumes unless many smoked just before testing.

comparison.controls: People with no reported exposure to the substance in question: the models compare each level of cannabis (or tobacco) exposure with zero, with tobacco and cannabis in the same model.
comparison.matching: No matching; covariate adjustment for year, centre and centre-by-year, race-sex group, education (a proxy for socio-economic status), baseline asthma, and flexible splines of age, height, waist circumference, second-hand smoke exposure (hours a week) and city-level particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Spirometry at year 0 gives a baseline for the cohort, but baseline use of cannabis by then was already present in some. Not among the adjustment variables: physical activity (the authors say people who smoked cannabis tended to be more active), income (Table 1 shows it differs by group), occupational exposures, other drug use and respiratory infections.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported or adjusted, apart from tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: Forced spirometry (FEV1 and FVC) with a Collins Survey 8-litre water-sealed spirometer and Eagle II Microprocessor at years 0, 2, 5 and 10, and an OMI rolling-seal spirometer at year 20 (average difference under 1% in a comparability test of 25 participants); standard quality control to published guidelines.
outcomes.validity_norms: Spirometry is a standard test; no comparison with predicted values is reported. The positive control (tobacco) shows the design can detect smoking-related loss.
outcomes.operationalization: Mean FEV1 and FVC differences in millilitres against zero exposure ('net association') and incremental differences per unit of exposure ('slope'), from models that follow each person's own age trajectory.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two outcomes against four smoking variables, in categories and in splines, with several slopes and net associations at chosen exposure levels; two-sided tests at 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.
