analysis.effect_sizes: Four-level categories (Table 2), against zero exposure, all four smoking variables in one model: tobacco more than 20 cigarettes a day FEV1 -63 mL (95% CI -89 to -36), FVC -69 mL (-97 to -41); lifetime tobacco over 20 pack-years FEV1 -101 mL (-136 to -65). Cannabis only (current status) FEV1 +0.7 mL (-12 to 13), FVC +8.2 mL (-5 to 22). Lifetime cannabis 1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL (15 to 62), FVC +41 mL (14 to 67); 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL (32 to 100), FVC +54 mL (16 to 91); over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL (-6.5 to 79), FVC +59 mL (12 to 107). Current cannabis more than 20 episodes in 30 days FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1), FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); P for trend across the four current-intensity categories 0.32 (FEV1) and 0.030 (FVC). Splines (Table 3): lifetime cannabis non-linear (P < 0.001 for both); slope at 2 joint-years FEV1 +13 mL per joint-year (6.4 to 20), FVC +20 (12 to 27); at 7 joint-years -0.4 (-2.6 to 1.8) and 0.0 (-2.4 to 2.5); at 20 and 50 joint-years FEV1 -2.2 (-4.6 to 0.3), P = 0.079, FVC +1.0 (-1.8 to 3.7). Net association at 7 joint-years FEV1 +53 mL (28 to 79), FVC +64 (36 to 92); at 20 joint-years FEV1 +27 (-10 to 64), FVC +76 (34 to 117); at 50 joint-years FEV1 -39 (-141 to 64), FVC +104 (-12 to 220). Current cannabis non-linear (P = 0.025 FEV1, 0.035 FVC); slope at 20 episodes a month FEV1 -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6), P = 0.017, FVC -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); no data at 40 episodes a month. Tobacco, linear: slope -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years; net FEV1 -332 mL (-401 to -263) and FVC -229 mL (-310 to -147) at 50 pack-years.
analysis.covariates: Year, centre, centre-by-year, race-sex group, education, baseline asthma, splines of age, height, waist circumference, second-hand smoke hours a week, PM10 and PM2.5, and interactions of age splines with race-sex, asthma, waist and height; random intercept and random 3-knot age spline per person, unstructured covariance; tobacco and cannabis, current and lifetime, in the same model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned. The authors state an a priori hypothesis that cannabis smoking should damage the airways like tobacco (Comment, 7th paragraph). Spline models were added to explore non-linear associations after the categorical models.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only FEV1 and FVC are reported; the FEV1-FVC ratio, the usual marker of airway obstruction, and respiratory symptoms are not, although the Comment discusses the ratio in earlier studies. The online appendix (assumptions for joint-years, spline details) was not read.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The authors state that the sample had too few people who smoked heavily to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use and that estimates at high exposure are imprecise (Comment, 1st and 8th paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a community cohort followed 20 years, tobacco smoking showed the expected linear loss of FEV1 and FVC (about 7 mL per pack-year), while cannabis smoking at the light levels typical of the cohort showed slightly higher FEV1 and FVC: at 7 joint-years net +53 mL (FEV1) and +64 mL (FVC). Above about 7 joint-years the cannabis curve levelled off for FEV1 and turned slightly down (slope -2.2 mL per joint-year, not significant), net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years were not significantly different from zero, and FVC stayed higher at 20 joint-years (and, not significantly, at 50). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes a month) showed a significant negative FEV1 slope (-3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017) with no significant net difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract conclusion: "Occasional and low cumulative marijuana use was not associated with adverse effects on pulmonary function." The final paragraph says the findings 'suggest an accelerated decline in pulmonary function with heavy use' and a need for caution. Gaps: (1) the final sentence is stronger than the results, since no net FEV1 difference at high exposure was significant and the authors themselves say the sample was too small to confirm harm; (2) the higher FEV1 and FVC at low exposure are explained by a speculative stretch or training effect without a test, and residual confounding by physical activity or fitness is not considered; (3) the abstract says the association 'leveled off or even reversed', which describes a curve whose reversal is not statistically significant; (4) the abstract opens by calling cannabis smoke very similar to tobacco smoke, which frames the question, but the data show a different pattern from tobacco.

timeline.event: Los Angeles cohort of people who smoked cannabis heavily and habitually (Tashkin et al., cited as ref 35; its title reports no accelerated FEV1 decline with age; the paper was not read here).
Dunedin birth cohort (Hancox et al., cited as ref 20): higher FVC and total lung capacity with cannabis exposure, as described in this paper's Comment.
This study: CARDIA, 20 years, cannabis and tobacco modelled together, non-linear association.

National Academies report describes this study as showing no adverse effect of occasional and low cumulative cannabis smoking on lung function and a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure, with few people at heavy exposure (committee's description)
Systematic review and meta-analysis that includes CARDIA (rated low risk of bias) among its studies of FEV1 and FVC and grades the lung-function evidence insufficient

replication.where_it_stands: The higher volumes and the absence of a clear FEV1 loss at light cumulative cannabis exposure fit the Dunedin cohort (higher FVC) and the Los Angeles cohort (no significant FEV1 fall), as the 2018 review describes them, whereas the Tucson cohort reported FEV1 reductions after one year; all rest on young, mostly light-exposure samples; the signal of a possible FEV1 loss at heavy exposure is single-study, not significant in net terms and from a sample with few people who smoked cannabis heavily without tobacco. CARDIA is also inside the pooled evidence of the 2018 review, so the two are not independent.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse (R01-DA-025067) funded this analysis; the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (N01-HC-95095, N01-HC-48047) funds CARDIA data collection and supports the committee that reviews all CARDIA publications. NIDA did not participate in CARDIA or review the manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: R. Kalhan: consultant for Boehringer-Ingelheim, Forest Laboratories and AstraZeneca; honoraria from GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca, Quantia Communications and Medscape Education; industry-sponsored grants from GlaxoSmithKline and Boehringer-Ingelheim (respiratory-drug companies). S. Kertesz chaired a committee advising the Drug Treatment Task Force for the Chief Justice of Alabama and is employed by the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Otherwise none beyond federal funding.
funding.affiliations_note: No cannabis- or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared. Author affiliations appear only as symbols in the extracted text.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort with many people who smoke cannabis heavily and no tobacco (for example more than 20 joint-years), recruited young and followed into their 40s and 50s with repeated spirometry including the FEV1-FVC ratio, plethysmography and gas transfer or low-dose CT, with physical activity, other drugs and the method and product of cannabis smoking recorded, and exposure checked against biomarkers.

domains.note: Extensive measured adjustment (race, sex, education, asthma, height, waist, second-hand smoke, particulate matter) and tobacco modelled at the same time, with tobacco as a positive control; but physical activity (which the authors say differs by cannabis use), income, other drug use and occupational dust were not adjusted, and tobacco and cannabis exposure were strongly correlated, so tobacco misclassification could leak into heavy-cannabis estimates.

Self-reported at each exam; lifetime joint-years built on assumptions in an appendix; no route, method, strength or tobacco-in-joints data; recall error acknowledged (the authors argue it is non-differential).
Community sample not selected for smoking; 98% of participants and 95% of visits had complete data.
No intervention after exposure is described that would differ by cannabis use.
69% retention at year 20; attrition associated with tobacco (included in the model) and not with cannabis; mixed models use all visits.

Standardised spirometry with quality control and a device comparison (under 1% difference); assessor blinding not reported; spirometry depends on effort, and recent cannabis smoking could widen the airways for about an hour.
No registered plan; spline analyses added to explore non-linearity; only FEV1 and FVC reported (not the FEV1-FVC ratio or symptoms); several exposure levels and slopes tested without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns rather than high because the design is strong for this question (20 years, repeated measures, individual age trajectories, tobacco modelled alongside as a positive control that behaves as expected), but physical activity and other co-exposures were not measured, cannabis exposure is self-reported and mostly light, and heavy cannabis-only exposure is rare. The study may be cited for the adjusted pattern of FEV1 and FVC against self-reported cannabis exposure at light and moderate cumulative levels in young adults, and for the parallel tobacco finding; not for a causal effect, for a benefit, for lung function after heavy long-term smoking or for any respiratory symptom or disease outcome.

key_findings.finding: 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 were recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20 with 69% retention at year 20. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 19,703 (95%) from 5016 participants (98%) were used, 3.9 visits each on average; attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco and not associated with cannabis use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Sample; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams (neither 2305, tobacco only 851, cannabis only 795, both 1065). Cannabis exposure was nearly as common as tobacco but mostly light: median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days against 8 to 9 cigarettes a day for tobacco; 91 participants had no tobacco exposure and more than 10 joint-years of cannabis (153 spirometry observations), 40 of them more than 20 joint-years (56 observations).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Tobacco (positive control): current smoking of more than 20 cigarettes a day was associated with FEV1 63 mL lower (95% CI -89 to -36) and FVC 69 mL lower (-97 to -41); lifetime exposure over 20 pack-years with FEV1 101 mL lower (-136 to -65). In spline models the association was linear and dose-related, with a slope of -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years and net differences at 50 pack-years of -332 mL (-401 to -263) for FEV1 and -229 mL (-310 to -147) for FVC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Table 3 (lifetime tobacco rows)

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, four-level categories, tobacco in the same model: lifetime exposure was associated with higher FVC and FEV1 than zero exposure (1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL, 15 to 62; FVC +41 mL, 14 to 67; 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL, 32 to 100; FVC +54 mL, 16 to 91; over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL, -6.5 to 79; FVC +59 mL, 12 to 107). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) was FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) and FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); people who used cannabis only differed little from people using neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, -12 to 13; FVC +8.2 mL, -5 to 22), while tobacco only was -24 mL (-38 to -11) for FEV1.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: The Results text gives the lifetime category as 'more than 20' joint-years while Table 2 labels it 'more than 10'. P for trend across current-intensity categories 0.32 (FEV1) and 0.030 (FVC); across lifetime categories 0.049 and 0.013.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, spline models: the association with lifetime exposure was non-linear (P < 0.001 for FEV1 and FVC). The slope was +13 mL per joint-year for FEV1 (6.4 to 20) and +20 mL for FVC (12 to 27) at 2 joint-years, about zero at 7 joint-years (FEV1 -0.4, -2.6 to 1.8; FVC 0.0, -2.4 to 2.5), and for FEV1 -2.2 mL per joint-year (-4.6 to 0.3, P = 0.079) at 20 and 50 joint-years. Net FEV1 difference against no exposure: +53 mL (28 to 79) at 7 joint-years, +27 mL (-10 to 64) at 20 and -39 mL (-141 to 64) at 50; net FVC +64 (36 to 92), +76 (34 to 117) and +104 (-12 to 220).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (lifetime marijuana rows); Abstract (Results)
key_findings.note: The Results text gives the confidence interval of the -2.2 slope as -4.9 to 0.36 against -4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Current intensity, spline models: non-linear for both outcomes (FEV1 P = 0.025, FVC P = 0.035). At 20 episodes a month the FEV1 slope was -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6, P = 0.017) and the FVC slope -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); net differences at 20 episodes a month were FEV1 +14 mL (-4.7 to 32) and FVC +43 mL (23 to 63). No data at 40 episodes a month. The authors state the net FEV1 association became negative only at very high exposure (over 40 joint-years or 25 episodes a month) and not significantly.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (current marijuana rows)

key_findings.finding: No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis exposure was found for FEV1 or FVC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that up to about 7 joint-years of lifetime exposure (for example 1 joint a day for 7 years or 1 joint a week for 49 years) gave no evidence that more exposure harms lung function, that at higher exposure the pattern levelled off or reversed especially for FEV1, and that the sample contained too few people with heavy use to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use. They propose a stretch or training effect (one version called a speculative possibility) and a short-lived airway widening, which they consider unlikely to explain the higher volumes.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph; Comment, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: no plethysmography, diffusing capacity or imaging of emphysema; only a minority with very high cannabis exposure, fewer still without tobacco, so estimates at high exposure are imprecise; self-reported exposure with recall error and no record of smoking method; unmeasured confounding possible.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 8th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives the lifetime category with FVC +59 mL (12 to 107) and FEV1 +36 mL (-6.5 to 79) as 'more than 20 joint-years'; Table 2 labels it 'more than 10 joint-years' (the four lifetime categories are 0, 1 to 5, 6 to 10 and over 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use Table 2's definition (over 10 joint-years). The 2018 meta-analysis also cites it as over 10.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% interval of the FEV1 slope of -2.2 mL per joint-year is -4.9 to 0.36 in the Results text and -4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3; the abstract says the slope applies 'at more than 10 joint-years' while Table 3 gives it at 20 and 50 joint-years (the slope at 7 joint-years is -0.4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the slope is not significant in either version (P = 0.079).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2, FEV1 for 11 to 20 pack-years of lifetime tobacco: the estimate -41 mL lies outside its printed interval (-38 to -14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the tobacco rows; the surrounding rows and the spline results are consistent. Not used for the cannabis claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample counts differ between places: 19,703 visits from 5016 participants (Results), 19,704 observations (Table 2), 19,705 measurements from 5017 participants (Figure 1 legend). The 'Overall' FEV1 mean in Table 2 is printed as 3420 in a column headed liters while the rows are in liters.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; none changes an estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The final paragraph says the findings 'suggest an accelerated decline in pulmonary function with heavy use', while the results show non-significant net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years (+27 mL, -10 to 64; -39 mL, -141 to 64) and a non-significant spline slope (-2.2 mL per joint-year, P = 0.079). Only the slope for current use at 20 episodes a month was significant (-3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstatement in the discussion; the data allow 'possible' at most. Claims should cite the numbers, not that sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2018 meta-analysis reports the CARDIA FEV1 result '-18 mL' as current cannabis use with minimal exposure (2 to 3 episodes a month), and gives P = 0.32 and P = 0.03 for the FEV1 and FVC contrasts; in the primary paper -18 mL is the contrast for the heaviest current category (over 20 episodes in 30 days, 484 observations), 2 to 3 episodes a month is the median among people who smoked cannabis, and 0.32 and 0.030 are P values for trend across the four categories, not for that contrast (whose FVC interval -5.2 to 49 includes zero).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review understates the CARDIA exposure for this contrast and passes over the significant negative spline slope at 20 episodes a month; cite CARDIA from the primary paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3840897 (author manuscript; abstract, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1 to 3 as text, figure legends, comment, funding and conflict statements read; Figures 1 and 2 are images and were not extracted; the online appendix was not read)

design_detail: Retrospective population-based cohort: Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 who answered the 2009-2010 or 2011-2012 Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), linked at ICES to hospital, emergency department, physician-claims, mental-health and death records (data window 1 January 2009 to 31 December 2015). Exposure was any self-reported cannabis use in the 12 months before the interview; controls reported never using cannabis, or using it only once and more than 12 months earlier. Cannabis and control groups were matched up to 1 to 3 on a propensity score from 31 variables (including tobacco history and amount, problem drinking, other substance use, comorbidities and previous respiratory emergency visits) and exactly on sex, previous-year respiratory visit, tobacco smoking history and pre-existing asthma or COPD. Outcomes within 12 months of the interview: respiratory-related emergency room (ER) visit or hospital admission (primary), all-cause ER visit or admission, and all-cause death. Odds ratios by logistic regression with generalised estimating equations.
can_establish: Whether Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 who reported any cannabis use in the past year, matched to controls on 31 characteristics, differed in the odds of an emergency visit or hospital admission for a respiratory reason, for any reason, or of death, over the following 12 months.
cannot_establish: The lung effect of smoked cannabis specifically (route, amount, strength and mixing with tobacco were not asked; 42.5% of the cannabis group used less than once a month); chronic lung outcomes (symptoms, lung function, COPD) or events beyond 12 months in the main analysis; causation (observational, residual confounding possible); dose-response; results after 2015 (end of the data window) or after October 2018 (the paper says cannabis was decriminalised in Canada then); results for people under 20 or aged 50 to 65 separately (too few).

sample.recruitment: Respondents to the CCHS, a national cross-sectional survey of community-dwelling people aged 12 and over, in two cycles (2009-2010, 2011-2012); linked by coded identifiers to Ontario administrative databases held at ICES. If someone answered both cycles (about 0.2%), only the later one was used. People aged 66 and over were excluded (about 1% of the cannabis group). Survey response rate not reported in the text.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: Ontario residents aged 12 to 65. Excluded: people who had used cannabis several times but not in the past year (to keep an uncontaminated control group), and people over 65. Routes: inhalation is described as by far the most common but was not asked. Medicinal and recreational use were not distinguished.
sample.demographics: After matching, mean age 34.4 (SD 14.6) in the cannabis group and 35.2 (15.4) in controls; 42.0% women in both; 73.9% currently or formerly smoking tobacco in both (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (administrative follow-up of everyone linked). About a quarter of the cannabis group (1618 of 6425, 25.2%) found no match and was left out of the main analysis.
sample.selection_effects: Matching kept 4807 of 6425 people in the cannabis group (74.8%). Before matching, 10.3% of the cannabis group reported illicit substance use in the past year and 25.1% problem drinking, against 0.1% and 6.7% of controls; after matching both groups were at 0.7% illicit use and 17.1% to 18.3% problem drinking, so the matched cannabis group is probably one with less other drug use than the whole group (an inference; not stated by the authors). The matched controls are also unusual: 73.9% were currently or formerly smoking tobacco, against 41.3% of all controls. Survey respondents only; pre-legalisation data.

exposure.measurement: Two survey questions asked once at the interview: ever used or tried marijuana, cannabis or hashish (no; once; more than once) and, if yes, used in the past 12 months. Exposure was not updated afterwards. Route, medicinal against recreational use, quantity and potency were not collected.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, not available 8.0%. The authors could not run a dose-response analysis because the frequency categories were too small. Route not collected.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco history and cigarettes per day, problem drinking and illicit substance use in the past year were in the propensity score; tobacco history was also matched exactly. Before matching, 79.1% of the cannabis group and 41.3% of controls were currently or formerly smoking tobacco; after matching 73.9% of each. 'Never or not available' is one tobacco category, so missing tobacco status is counted with never-smoking. Whether tobacco was mixed into cannabis was not asked.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The authors followed outcomes for 12 months only, to limit changes in cannabis use after the interview (a 3-year analysis is in the supplement, not read).

comparison.controls: People who reported never using cannabis, or using it once and more than 12 months before the interview; people with earlier repeated use were excluded on purpose.
comparison.matching: Propensity score (31 variables: demographics, comorbidities, general health-care use, previous respiratory ER visit or admission, tobacco history and amount, problem drinking and other substance use, respirologist visits, spirometry, respiratory medicines, influenza vaccine, survey year), caliper 0.2 SD of the logit, 1 to up to 3 controls; exact matching on sex, previous-year respiratory ER visit or admission, tobacco smoking history and pre-existing asthma or COPD. All standardised differences below 0.10 after matching (largest 0.05).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the model: cannabis use before the past year (except for defining controls), risk-taking, injury history, secondhand smoke, occupational exposures, exercise and diet, deprivation beyond income quintile, details of other substances. Pre-exposure health care use was measured for one year.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: After matching, illicit substance use in the past year was 0.7% in both groups and problem drinking 17.1% (cannabis) against 18.3% (controls). The authors could not adjust for secondhand cannabis smoke exposure in controls.

outcomes.instruments: Administrative records: ICD-10 diagnosis codes at ER visits (NACRS) and hospital discharges (CIHI-DAD) and deaths (Registered Persons Database). Primary outcome: respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission, with a diagnosis of upper or lower respiratory tract infection, respiratory failure, asthma or COPD (code list in the supplement, not read). Secondary: all-cause ER visit or admission, and all-cause death. All within 12 months of the interview or until death.
outcomes.validity_norms: Asthma and COPD diagnoses for matching came from validated algorithms (asthma sensitivity 84%, specificity 76%; COPD 85.0% and 78.4%). The respiratory outcome definition is the authors' own and was not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory harm is defined as an ER visit or hospital admission coded to a respiratory diagnosis within 12 months; chronic symptoms, lung function and milder illness that does not reach the ER are not captured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three outcomes in the main analysis, then four stratified sensitivity analyses (sex, previous respiratory visit, tobacco history, asthma or COPD) of two outcomes each (mortality too few to stratify).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (administrative data).

analysis.effect_sizes: Propensity-matched cohort (4807 against 10,395). Respiratory-related ER visit or admission: 175 events (3.6%) against 410 (3.9%), OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), p < 0.0001, number needed to harm 25 (the authors' calculation). All-cause death: 11 (0.2%) against 24 (0.2%), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02). Respiratory outcome by subgroup: men OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31), women 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10); no previous respiratory visit 0.94 (0.77 to 1.14), previous visit 0.82 (0.53 to 1.26); people currently or formerly smoking tobacco 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04, people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70); pre-existing asthma or COPD 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11), none 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20). All-cause outcome by subgroup: men 1.23 (1.11 to 1.36), women 1.23 (1.10 to 1.37); people currently or formerly smoking tobacco 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26), people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56); asthma or COPD 1.16 (1.00 to 1.35), none 1.24 (1.13 to 1.35).
analysis.covariates: Propensity score (31 variables) plus exact matching on four; no further model adjustment described.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is cited. The sensitivity analyses are described as planned. The supplement (PDF: variable definitions, ICD-10 code list, 3-year follow-up) was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: The conclusions rest on the secondary all-cause outcome after a null primary outcome; the 3-year analysis is reported only in the supplement. Subgroup results are given for both outcomes.
analysis.power: Not calculated. The authors say the study might be insufficiently powered for the primary outcome; the interval for the respiratory outcome runs from a 23% lower to a 9% higher odds. Deaths were too few to analyse in subgroups (11 and 24), and frequency categories too small for dose-response.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In matched adults aged 12 to 65, with a mostly infrequent-use cannabis group (42.5% less than monthly) and 12 months of follow-up, respiratory ER visits and admissions were no more frequent than in controls (3.6% against 3.9%; OR 0.91, 0.77 to 1.09), while ER visits or admissions for any reason were more frequent (30.0% against 26.0%; OR 1.22, 1.13 to 1.31). In the cannabis group's top-100-diagnosis list, trauma accounted for 15.1% of all-cause events and respiratory reasons for 14.2%; the matching list for controls is not given. Among people currently or formerly smoking tobacco the respiratory odds were lower (OR 0.80, 0.65 to 0.99), and among people who had never smoked tobacco or whose status was unknown not significantly higher (OR 1.23, 0.89 to 1.70).
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: cannabis use 'is associated with increased risk for serious adverse health events' and "its recreational consumption is not benign". Main text: use "should be discouraged" and, in the key-messages box, the rising recreational use 'needs to be curtailed'. Gaps: (1) the designated primary respiratory outcome was null, and the policy statements rest on a secondary all-cause composite that includes any emergency visit, with trauma its largest category; (2) 'serious adverse health events' describes visits of any severity, and Table 3's footnote lists attention to dressings or sutures, repeat prescriptions and follow-up of test results among the 11.3% 'miscellaneous' reasons; (3) respiratory reasons being the second most common category among the cannabis group says nothing about excess, because the categories are not shown for controls; (4) the authors themselves say causation should not be inferred and unmeasured confounding may account for the positive finding; (5) the box describes the comparison group as people who never used cannabis, but controls included people who had tried cannabis once; (6) the recommendations (discouraged, curtailed) are not results of the study; (7) the authors write that the null respiratory result 'may certainly be real' but list factors that could hide an effect (low exposure, non-inhaled use, secondhand smoke in controls, low power), none of which the study can test, and the conclusions are drawn from the all-cause result.

timeline.event: Tashkin et al. (cited as ref 16): small study reporting more frequent protracted acute bronchitis episodes in people who smoked cannabis, as described in this paper's Introduction.

Polen et al. (cited as ref 17): more outpatient visits for respiratory illness but not more hospital admissions in people who smoked cannabis frequently and not tobacco, as described in this paper's Introduction.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of respiratory symptoms and lung function (cited as ref 4)

This study: population-based linked-data analysis of respiratory emergency and hospital use by past-year cannabis use; the authors describe the published literature on acute respiratory illness and cannabis smoking as extremely limited.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, well-linked but crude-exposure study. The authors describe the null respiratory result as somewhat at odds with the two older small studies they cite (more bronchitis episodes in one; more outpatient respiratory visits but not more hospital admissions in the other). The exposure was mostly infrequent use of unknown route. No replication is cited in the paper, and the authors say further research is needed to confirm their findings.

funding.funder: Research award grant from The Lung Association - Ontario, which received unrestricted funding from Tetra-Bio Pharma to administer the grant competition independently; ICES, funded by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Ministry of Long-Term Care; data from MOH, CIHI and Cancer Care Ontario. The paper states the funding sources had no role in the research or writing.
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations appear as numbers only in the extracted text. Tetra-Bio Pharma, the source of the grant competition's money, is described in a newswire press release about the partnership with the Lung Association (editors' lookup, not part of the paper) as a biopharmaceutical company focused on cannabinoid-based drug discovery and development; the release says the research is administered at arm's length from the funder. Funding from a cannabinoid-drug company is a reason to read the interpretation closely, not a reason to drop the findings.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort in which route, frequency, amount, product strength and tobacco co-use are recorded, with respiratory symptoms, spirometry and imaging as well as hospital use, following people who smoke cannabis without tobacco for years against people who smoke tobacco and people who use neither; plus an analysis of why the cannabis group attends emergency departments (trauma, mental health, respiratory), with the same breakdown for controls.

domains.note: Propensity matching on 31 variables including tobacco history and amount, other substances and previous respiratory visits, with exact matching on four and stratified checks; residual confounding by risk-taking, deprivation, secondhand smoke and the detail of other substances remains, and the authors say it may explain the positive finding.

One survey question on any use in the past 12 months, asked once; 42.5% used less than monthly; route, amount, strength and tobacco mixing not collected, so the exposure is only loosely related to smoking cannabis; exposure could change after the interview. The rating is for the question of smoked cannabis and lungs.

Survey respondents (response rate not given); a quarter of the cannabis group unmatched; the matched cannabis group has much less illicit drug use than the whole group, and the matched controls are unusual (73.9% with a tobacco-smoking history).
No intervention after exposure is described; the 12-month window limits drift in exposure.

The administrative databases cover all Ontario residents (single-payer plan), but the share of survey respondents who could be linked is not given in the text (Figure 1 was not extracted), item non-response in the survey is not described, and missing tobacco status is grouped with never-smoking.

Objective administrative records of ER visits, admissions and deaths, with diagnoses from ICD-10 coding; the respiratory definition was not validated, and differences between the groups in whether they seek emergency care were not examined.
No registered protocol; the headline messages come from the secondary all-cause outcome after a null primary; 3-year results are only in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, set by the exposure domain: the exposure is a single self-reported question about any use in the past year, which says little about smoking, amount or product, and the two groups were built by matching in a way that changed the cannabis group (less illicit drug use) and produced unusual controls. The other domains raise some concerns. The study may be cited for the odds of respiratory and all-cause emergency and hospital use over 12 months in a matched, mostly infrequent-use group, the null respiratory result with its interval, the breakdown of the cannabis group's visits and the tobacco-stratified results; not for the lung effect of smoking cannabis, for long-term or heavy use, for causation, or for the policy statements in its conclusions.

key_findings.finding: Of 35,114 Ontario residents aged 12 to 65 in the CCHS who either used cannabis in the past year or were controls, 6425 (18.3%) used cannabis in the past year; 4807 of them (74.8%) were matched to 10,395 controls (15,202 people). After matching, 73.9% of both groups currently or formerly smoked tobacco and standardised differences were below 0.10 for all variables.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cohort derivation, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Cannabis use frequency in the matched cannabis group: less than once a month 42.5%, 1 to 3 times a month 18.1%, once a week 9.4%, more than once a week 11.4%, every day 10.5%, unknown 8.0%. Route, amount and potency were not collected; the authors say inhalation is by far the most common route (citing a scoping review).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cohort derivation, 1st paragraph; Methods › Data sources; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, respiratory-related ER visit or hospital admission within 12 months: 175 events (3.6%) in the cannabis group against 410 (3.9%) in controls, OR 0.91 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.09), p = 0.32. All-cause ER visit or admission: 1443 (30.0%) against 2699 (26.0%), OR 1.22 (1.13 to 1.31), number needed to harm 25. All-cause death: 11 against 24 (0.2% each), OR 0.99 (0.49 to 2.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among the cannabis group's all-cause events (top 100 diagnosis codes), acute trauma was 15.1%, respiratory reasons 14.2%, gastrointestinal 13.3%, genitourinary 11.0%, muscle or joint pain 8.0%, infection 6.8%, mental health 5.4% and cardiovascular 5.4%. The same breakdown for controls is not given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overall cohort analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: The Discussion gives acute trauma as about 18%.

key_findings.finding: Respiratory outcome by tobacco history: people currently or formerly smoking tobacco OR 0.80 (0.65 to 0.99), p = 0.04 (123 events, 3.5%, against 290, 4.2%); people who had never smoked tobacco or had no record OR 1.23 (0.89 to 1.70). All-cause outcome: 1.16 (1.06 to 1.26) and 1.35 (1.16 to 1.56). By sex, respiratory OR 1.00 (0.77 to 1.31) in men and 0.86 (0.68 to 1.10) in women; by pre-existing asthma or COPD, respiratory OR 0.82 (0.61 to 1.11) with and 0.96 (0.77 to 1.20) without.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses › By sex; By tobacco smoking history; By pre-existing asthma or COPD; Table 4
key_findings.note: The authors call the lower respiratory odds in people with a tobacco-smoking history surprising; it is one of several uncorrected subgroup tests.

key_findings.finding: The authors give reasons the null respiratory result may understate an effect (not adjustable): too little cannabis smoke exposure among people in the study (citing research that lung-function decline occurs only above 20 'joints per year'), some non-inhaled use, secondhand cannabis smoke in controls, and low power. They also say the large share of people in the cannabis group who used it infrequently may have contributed to the null result, that causation should not be inferred, and that unmeasured confounding might explain the positive findings.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: self-report (recall and social-desirability bias); no dose-response (frequency categories too small); no quantity or potency data; about 25% of the cannabis group unmatched; data only before October 2018; no secondhand-smoke adjustment; too few people under 20 and aged 50 to 65 for age-group analyses; a single province.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4, respiratory outcome by previous respiratory ER visit or admission: events in the cannabis group are 149 (no previous visit) and 33 (previous visit), which sum to 182, not the 175 of Table 2; the other splits add up (sex 81 + 94, tobacco 123 + 52, asthma or COPD 62 + 113) and so do all the control counts. In the same rows the printed percentages (3.0% and 3.5%) do not fit the counts divided by the group sizes implied by the all-cause row (our calculation: about 3.2% and 3.3%).
reporting_issues.consequence: One row of a sensitivity table is internally inconsistent and cannot be reconstructed from the text; the main result and the other subgroups are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says acute trauma was about 18% of the all-cause events in the cannabis group; Table 3 gives 15.1% (respiratory 14.2%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Table 3 figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The key-messages box ('What this study adds') describes the comparison group as people who never used cannabis, but the controls also included people who had used cannabis once and more than 12 months earlier (the Methods and abstract state this correctly).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misdescription of the comparison group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says previous research has shown lung-function decline only above 20 'joints per year' of exposure, citing Tan et al. (2019) and Pletcher et al. (2012). In CARDIA the unit is joint-years (1 joint-year = 365 joints), net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years were not significant, and the authors say the sample was too small to confirm harm (card sc_pletcher_2012).
reporting_issues.consequence: Wrong unit and a threshold the cited cohort did not establish; do not repeat it. Tan et al. (2019) was not read here.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Never/not available' is one tobacco category in Table 1 and in the subgroup analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: People with missing tobacco status are analysed as if they had never smoked tobacco, which weakens the 'never smokers' stratum.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9240874 (abstract, key-messages boxes, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1 to 4 as text, figure 1 legend, discussion, funding and competing interests read; Figure 1 is an image and was not extracted; the supplementary PDF was not opened)

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA cited as a guide; no protocol or registration stated) of cardiovascular and respiratory effects of cannabis by route of administration in articles from 2009 to 2023: 42 sources (6 case reports or case series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies), summarised in three tables and narrative text, with no pooled estimates and no risk-of-bias appraisal of the included studies reported.
can_establish: Which studies, among those its search found, reported heart or breathing effects of cannabis by route (smoking, vaping, eating, dabbing), and what each reported, as the review relays it.
cannot_establish: Whether heart or breathing risks differ between routes, or how large any risk is: routes were compared within one study only in a small laboratory crossover and a perceived-harm survey, most sources are cross-sectional, retrospective, case reports or other reviews, nothing was pooled, and no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies is reported (the authors graded the overall strength of evidence for each outcome by group discussion, using AHRQ methods), the search string excluded the term tobacco, some included cases involved synthetic cannabinoids or other drugs, and some oral-route data come from poison-centre reports about young children.

sample.recruitment: Database search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Methods; the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus the reference lists of retrieved articles; peer-reviewed English-language articles published January 2009 to December 2023 (p. 1332–1333).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English articles presenting data on humans exposed to cannabis or cannabis-based products, with cannabis confirmed through drug screening and the route of administration reported. Excluded: opinion pieces, studies including other illicit drugs, and patients with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. Of 110 full texts, 68 were excluded: route not indicated 15, effects not reported 7, other illicit drugs 20, no confirmation of cannabis use 18, published before 2009 8 (Figure 1).
sample.demographics: The primary studies range from children younger than 6 (poison-centre and hospital records) to adults aged 40 or more (Vancouver), college students, Canadian medical cannabis patients and laboratory volunteers; settings in the US, Canada, New Zealand and Italy (Table 4).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: In Table 1 the cannabis search terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco, which would drop records that mention tobacco, the main co-exposure of smoked cannabis; the Embase string required both cardiovascular and respiratory terms; English only, from 2009. Several studies within the window and topic, read for this library, are not among the 42 (editors' observation): Monte 2019 (emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis), Braymiller 2020 (vaping cannabis and bronchitic symptoms), Spindle 2018 (smoked against vaporised cannabis in the laboratory) and Ghasemiesfe 2018 (systematic review of respiratory outcomes). The criteria were applied unevenly: included case reports involve synthetic cannabinoids, LSD and mushrooms, and most included empirical studies did not confirm cannabis by drug screening. Literature reviews are counted beside the primary studies they summarise, so the same studies appear more than once.

exposure.measurement: As in each source: controlled administration in the two laboratory studies, self-report in surveys and cohorts, poison-centre coding, hospital records and tweets.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Routes as the review groups them: smoking (joints, blunts, pipes), vaping (a vaporizer for dried cannabis in the laboratory study; devices not described elsewhere), oral (edibles, brownies) and dabbing. Amounts, frequency and potency are rarely comparable across sources; doses appear only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is handled only as each primary study handled it, and the search excluded the term tobacco. Synthetic cannabinoids (spice, K2, AM-2201) appear in included case reports and reviews and are discussed beside cannabis; one included case also took LSD and mushrooms.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: No common comparator: placebo or inactive cannabis (laboratory studies), people who did not use cannabis (cohorts, NHANES, Vancouver), people treated for pneumothorax who did not smoke cannabis, most of whom smoked tobacco (Fiorelli), other routes (Newmeyer; perceived harm in Shiplo), before against after (Van Dam and Earleywine), or none (case reports, poison-centre and hospital series, tweets).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed by the review.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed by the review beyond its exclusion criterion, which was not applied to all included cases.

outcomes.instruments: Whatever each source used: heart rate, blood pressure, chest pain, ECG and troponin in cases; respiratory symptoms, spirometry, expired carbon monoxide, CT and histology, need for respiratory support.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed by the review.
outcomes.operationalization: Any cardiovascular or respiratory effect reported by a source.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; abstract selection was done independently by reviewers (kappa 0.89).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. The numbers are those relayed from single studies (see the key findings).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA is cited as a guide.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods say the strength of evidence was discussed and graded for each outcome (as insufficient, low, moderate or high, using AHRQ methods), but no grade is reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The two randomised laboratory studies had 24 and 20 participants (Table 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among the 15 empirical studies, routes were compared within the same study only in one laboratory crossover (heart-rate rises similar after smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis against placebo; more expired carbon monoxide after smoking than vaporising; no route effect on breathing rate or blood pressure) and in one perceived-harm survey. The other studies examined one route each, mostly smoking, with cross-sectional, retrospective or case designs. The oral-route breathing data come mostly from records of young children (respiratory depression, need for respiratory support, severe effects at higher doses by body weight).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract concludes that "Cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects" and that edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects (p. 1331). The Discussion says severe cardiovascular effects, including myocardial infarction, arrhythmias and ischemic stroke, were associated with higher THC doses in all routes (p. 1346), and that each route was associated with effects of some kind, "suggesting the need to avoid cannabis use altogether", followed by harm-reduction recommendations (p. 1347). These go beyond the review's own tables: causal wording from designs that, as the authors write, cannot establish temporality (p. 1347); minimal respiratory effects for edibles against its children's data (pp. 1342–1345); and no included empirical study of myocardial infarction or stroke by dose across routes. The recommendations are not derived from a synthesis.

timeline.event: Cooper and Haney: laboratory comparison of cannabis smoked as blunts and as joints (heart rate, expired carbon monoxide, plasma THC); included in this review.
Van Dam and Earleywine: one-month switch to a vaporizer without a control group; included in this review.
Pletcher et al.: CARDIA, 20 years of lung function and cannabis exposure; included in this review.
Newmeyer et al.: double-blind crossover of smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis; Russell et al.: scoping review of routes of administration; both included in this review.
Ghasemiesfe et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of cannabis use and respiratory outcomes; not among this review's sources.
This review: 42 sources, no pooled estimates; conclusions by route described by its authors as tentative.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review read here that is organised by route. It maps what has been studied rather than measuring risk by route; its route-specific findings rest on a few small or uncontrolled studies and on records of children, and its text misreports several studies against its own tables. Cite it for what single studies report, as relayed, never for a pooled or appraised comparison.

funding.funder: There was no funding for developing this manuscript (as printed).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Illinois Chicago; University of Miami; University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. No industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts and controlled studies that measure heart and lung outcomes in the same people across routes (smoked flower, vaped dried cannabis, vaped oil, concentrates, edibles), with use recorded by route, amount and tobacco co-use and a comparison group of people who do not use cannabis, with adults and children analysed separately; and a registered systematic review with risk-of-bias appraisal and a search that does not exclude records mentioning tobacco.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans exposed to cannabis), exposure (route) and outcomes (cardiovascular and respiratory effects) are named, but no comparator is defined.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Case reports and reviews were included, with a stated reason, to make the review exhaustive alongside the empirical studies.

Five databases (six in the Abstract) with search strings and reference-list searching, but English only without justification, the cannabis terms combined with AND NOT Tobacco without justification, an Embase string requiring both cardiovascular and respiratory terms, and no grey literature or registries; several relevant studies from the window are missing.
Independent reviewers, discordance resolved by discussion; kappa 0.89 for abstract selection and inclusion.
The independent work described concerns selecting articles; the extraction of study type, route and effects into a matrix is not described as done by two reviewers.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only counts by reason in the flow diagram; no list of the 68 excluded full texts.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 gives design, sample, setting, measures and route for the empirical studies, but comparators, doses and follow-up are uneven; the reviews are described only by purpose and route.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool named and no appraisal of any study reported; 'quality indicators' are mentioned without description.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Design limitations are discussed in general, but no study-level risk of bias informs the conclusions; the Abstract states a causal conclusion and the Discussion gives recommendations.
The difference between minimal effects in the empirical studies and major effects in earlier reviews is noted but not investigated; the authors say it leaves the evidence unclear.
No quantitative synthesis.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, search; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk of bias) and a fifth (13) follows from the missing appraisal, so the confidence is critically low. The review is useful as a map of which route-specific studies exist and what they reported, and its tables are more reliable than its text; it may be cited for single studies as it relays them (second-hand), never for a comparison of risk between routes.

key_findings.finding: Search of five databases (Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase, Medline; the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; English-language peer-reviewed articles from January 2009 to December 2023. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco; the Embase and Medline strings were adapted to database requirements.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note

key_findings.finding: Inclusion required human data on cannabis or cannabis-based products, cannabis confirmed through drug screening and a reported route; opinion pieces, studies with other illicit drugs and patients with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory conditions were excluded. Selection was done independently (kappa 0.89); the strength of evidence was to be graded for each outcome with AHRQ methods, but no grades are reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 1,873 records (1,811 from databases, 62 from other sources), 990 after duplicates and title screening, 258 abstracts, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or case series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Full-text exclusions: route not indicated 15, effects not reported 7, other illicit drugs 20, no confirmation of cannabis use 18, published before 2009 8.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image without a text layer: the counts 1,811, 62, 990, 258 and the five exclusion reasons were read on the rendered page; 1,873, 110 and 42 are also in the text.

key_findings.finding: Smoking was the most common route in the reviews and the empirical studies. The reviews relate smoking to cough, sputum, chronic bronchitis, airway inflammation, dyspnea and COPD, with COPD only with heavy and not occasional or low cumulative use (Joshi 2014); they report vaporizing and edibles as reducing respiratory problems (Russell 2017; Van Dam and Earleywine 2010), and they did not conclusively link cannabis smoking and lung cancer.
key_findings.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Empirical studies by route as listed in the text: smoking (9 studies), vaping (Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016), oral (Cao 2016, Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016) and dabbing (Cavazos-Rehg 2016). Table 4 gives Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023 as edible studies in children and Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 as the vaping study, so the text's vaping list is wrong.
key_findings.locator: Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Table 4 (Kaczor, Pepin, Van Dam and Earleywine rows)

key_findings.finding: Laboratory comparison of routes (Newmeyer 2017; double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally): heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different between routes; no significant effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; smoking produced greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Newmeyer row)

key_findings.finding: Blunts against joints (Cooper and Haney 2009; 24 healthy volunteers; the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive, three puffs): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent for blunts and joints, and the highest strength raised heart rate against inactive cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 2nd paragraph; Respiratory effects, 3rd paragraph; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney row)

key_findings.finding: Smoking and breathing, single studies: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (Kempker 2015): cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days in 16.9%, 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of people who smoked cannabis on 0, 1–5, 6–20 and more than 20 of the past 30 days, wheeze in the past year in 12.4%, 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (as printed, unadjusted); more than 20 joint-years against none, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9). Vancouver (Tan 2009; random sample of 878 aged 40 or more): at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco, no significantly greater risk of COPD or symptoms; both tobacco and cannabis, COPD OR 2.90 (1.53 to 5.51) and symptoms OR 2.39 (1.58 to 3.62), adjusted for age, asthma and comorbidities.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory effects, 1st paragraph; Table 4 (Kempker and Tan rows)
key_findings.note: The review does not name Tan's comparison group.

key_findings.finding: Smoking and breathing, cohorts and cases: Dunedin (Hancox 2010; 1,037 followed to age 32): cumulative use associated with higher FVC, lung volumes and airway resistance but not with FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio or gas transfer. Los Angeles (Tashkin 2012; 299 followed 9.8 years): more chronic bronchitis at follow-up with continued cannabis smoking than in never or former smokers. Naples (Fiorelli 2013; people treated for spontaneous pneumothorax, 13 who smoked cannabis and 140 who did not, 135 of them tobacco smokers): bullae in 8 (62%) against 110 (78%) overall, and under age 35 in 7 of 10 against 3 of 10.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (Hancox, Tashkin and Fiorelli rows)

key_findings.finding: Vaping against smoking, other studies: Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22, p = 0.000065) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007), and FEV1 did not change significantly (t(11) = 1.77, p = 0.053); grams a day fell from 1.75 to 1.46 (t(18) = 1.34, p = 0.10).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (Shiplo and Van Dam and Earleywine rows)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-tailed p for t(11) = 2.90, t(11) = 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 is about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so three of the printed p values match one-tailed tests; the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups (for paired data about 1.8, 0.8 and 0.5); t(18) implies 19 people, while 22 enrolled and 12 are analysed.

key_findings.finding: Oral route, records mostly of young children: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, January 2013 to December 2015): tachycardia in 84, hypertension 7, chest pain 18, chest pain and hypotension 14; respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger. Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support. Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common; severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at doses above 2 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 4 (Cao, Kaczor and Pepin rows)
key_findings.note: Cao's printed percentages (tachycardia 31%, hypertension 8%) cannot be reproduced from 430 cases (19.5% and 1.6%; editors' arithmetic). Doses are the children's recorded exposures, reported only as study measures.

key_findings.finding: Dabbing: in a content analysis of tweets (Cavazos-Rehg 2016), coughing was the respiratory effect most often mentioned (807 of 1,179, 68%), followed by lung pain and difficulty breathing; one case report (Rickner 2017; a 17-year-old) describes hypertension, tachycardia, raised troponin and hyperthermia after dabbing.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case reports and case series, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (Rickner row); Respiratory effects, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (Cavazos-Rehg row)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: most studies cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; two small randomised trials (n = 24 and, as the Discussion gives it, n = 11); only 5 of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); English articles from 2009 to 2023 only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs beginning First, Second and Third; Strength and limitations

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the Abstract says cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects, that edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects and that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' limitations; the Discussion says severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes, that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, and adds harm-reduction recommendations from a clinical reference.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraph beginning Nevertheless

key_findings.finding: Funding: there was no funding for developing the manuscript; no potential conflict of interest was reported.
key_findings.locator: Disclosure statement; Funding

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract lists six databases including Scopus; the Methods list five, without Scopus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis search terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco (Table 1) without a stated reason.
reporting_issues.consequence: Records that mention tobacco, which covers much of the literature on smoked cannabis, may have been lost; this may explain why relevant studies from the window are missing.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grade appears in the text or tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: No appraisal of the evidence can be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says no other substance was implicated in any case report, but Table 2 lists a case with synthetic cannabinoids, LSD and mushrooms (Abouchedid 2016), one with several synthetic cannabinoids plus tobacco (Alhadi 2013) and a case series of brownies laced with the synthetic cannabinoid AM-2201 (Obafemi 2015), against the exclusion criterion for other drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The case evidence for oral and smoked routes partly concerns synthetic cannabinoids, not cannabis.

reporting_issues.issue: The case series is described as eleven patients, seven men and six women aged 19 to 57 in the text, but as 20–57, five men and six women in Table 2; the text first counts four case reports and one case series, then describes a fifth case report.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting errors.

reporting_issues.issue: The text lists Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023 as vaping studies, while Table 4 gives both as edible studies in children; Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (vaping in Table 4) is missing from the text's vaping list and Tashkin 2012 (smoking in Table 4) from its smoking list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The vaping evidence is three studies (Newmeyer, Shiplo, Van Dam and Earleywine), not the four the text names.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the Newmeyer 2017 sample as n = 11; Table 4 lists 11 frequent and 9 occasional cannabis smokers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the crossover had 20 participants by Table 4 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: In the Cao 2016 row, tachycardia 84 is printed as 31% and hypertension 7 as 8% of 430 cases (19.5% and 1.6%; editors' arithmetic), and chest pain appears twice.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages cannot be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports Tan 2009 as smoking cannabis in a joint combined with tobacco, while Table 4 describes people who had smoked both tobacco and cannabis (concurrent use).
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding concerns smoking both, not mixing tobacco into joints.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Fiorelli 2013 found that cannabis smoking predisposed to bullous lung disease, but Table 4 reports bullae in 62% of people who smoked cannabis against 78% of the comparison group overall, higher only under age 35 (7 of 10 against 3 of 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text overstates a small, mixed finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says vaping reduced the grams of cannabis smoked a day (Van Dam and Earleywine 2010); Table 4 shows a marginal, non-significant fall (p = 0.10). The printed statistics mix one- and two-tailed p values and give d values from a formula for independent groups (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The vaporizer findings are weaker than the text says; they come from 12 of 22 people, with no control group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says only one review (Russell 2017) reported an association between inhaled cannabis and lung cancer, but Table 3 attributes that report to Martinasek 2016 and shows none for Russell 2017.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the lung cancer statements cannot be traced reliably.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1331–1351 after an unnumbered Taylor & Francis cover page (PDFs/Cannabis/MuheriwaMatemba_2024_CardioRespiratoryByRoute.pdf); text extracted once with pdftotext -layout: all text, Tables 1 to 4 (the rotated Table 4 page, p. 1346, checked on a rendered image), the Figure 1 flow diagram (rendered page), disclosure and funding statements and the reference list. No supplementary material is mentioned.

design_detail: Retrospective, repeated annual analysis of aggregate data from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), the database of the American Association of Poison Control Centers that records potentially toxic exposures reported to the 55 regional poison control centres serving the United States and its territories (Pediatrics 2023;151(2):e2022057761; article pages 1 to 7). Cases: calls coded with the generic code for edible cannabis in children younger than 6 years, 2017 to 2021 (2021 data preliminary). Reported: counts by year; age, sex, place of exposure, management site and caller site; the NPDS medical outcome (no, minor, moderate or major effect); level of care; the top 30 clinical effects and top 20 treatments among the 4,827 cases followed to a known outcome; and chi-squared comparisons of 2017 to 2019 (before the COVID-19 pandemic) with 2020 to 2021. No denominator of children exposed and no comparison group. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as for the surveillance series sc_jones_2015.
can_establish: How many calls about children younger than 6 who ate cannabis edibles reached US poison centres each year from 2017 to 2021, and what share of all calls about children of that age they were; the ages, sex and place of exposure of those children; how the reported cases were graded (no, minor, moderate or major effect), which clinical effects and treatments were recorded among those followed up, and what level of care they received, year by year.
cannot_establish: How many children ate edibles (only reported calls reach the data, which the authors call an underestimate) or the rate per child in the population; why the calls rose (no state-level data, so the link the authors draw with legalization of adult use is not tested here, and more reporting or less stigma could contribute, as they say); whether the pandemic itself made cases more severe (the 2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021 comparison sets earlier against later years of a series already rising, with a coding change in 2019 and changing choices of where children were treated); what was eaten, how much THC, from what source or in what packaging (not in these data); outcomes for the 30% not followed to a known outcome; and any effect after the acute episode.

sample.recruitment: All cases in the NPDS data portal with the generic code for edible cannabis in children younger than 6, 2017 to 2021: calls to US poison centres from homes, health care facilities and other places (Methods › Data Source and Case Selection Criteria, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age under 6 years; edible cannabis code; years 2017 to 2021. The code is not named, and the paper does not say whether cases were limited to unintentional exposures or to exposures to cannabis alone, though it describes them as unintentional ingestions. The 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome were left out of the analysis of clinical effects and treatments (Methods › Clinical Effects and Therapies, pp. 2-3).
sample.demographics: Median age 3 years (interquartile range 2 to 4): under 1 year 136 (1.9%), 1 year 1,046 (14.9%), 2 years 1,954 (27.7%), 3 years 1,734 (24.6%), 4 years 1,265 (18.0%), 5 years 891 (12.7%), unknown 17 (0.2%). Female 3,450 (49.0%), male 3,495 (49.6%), unknown 98 (1.4%) (Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph, p. 3; Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Not followed to a known outcome: 2,141 (30.4%) in Table 1; the Methods leave 2,216 out of the clinical analyses, apparently counting the 74 confirmed non-exposures with them (see reporting issues). Level of care: 2,268 (32.2%) lost to follow-up or other, 625 (8.9%) refused referral or did not arrive at a health care facility.
sample.selection_effects: Passive surveillance: only exposures someone reported to a poison centre, and reporting may have changed over the years (the authors name more reporting and less stigma as possible contributors). 43.6% of calls came from a health care facility, so cases already seen by clinicians are well represented, while mild cases handled at home may be missed. No state is identified.

exposure.measurement: A child's eating of a cannabis edible as reported by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff with the NPDS generic code; 74 cases were coded as confirmed non-exposures. No laboratory confirmation is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not in the data analysed: product, amount and THC content are unknown. The Introduction's background on adult servings and multi-serving packages is cited from other sources, not measured here.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: the paper does not say whether calls involving other substances were included or left out.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. Comparisons are between years and between 2017 to 2019 and 2020 to 2021; the yearly share uses all calls about children under 6 as its denominator (956,871 in 2017 and 846,296 in 2021, Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 5).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No child-level data beyond age and sex; state, product type, amount eaten, time to care and other substances are not available; changes in reporting over time were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: NPDS coding by poison-centre staff: the medical outcome categories defined in the NPDS coding manual (cited, not read; not defined in the paper), clinical-effect and treatment codes, and level of health care facility.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard national coding, but in 2019 the codes for decreased mental status (drowsiness or lethargy, coma) were replaced by graded CNS depression; the authors combined the codes into one CNS depression category. The data depend on what callers and clinicians report (Methods, p. 3; limitations, p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: Severity as the NPDS medical outcome (no, minor, moderate or major effect), as a share of all 7,043 cases; level of care as admitted to critical care, admitted to noncritical care, treated and released, refused referral or did not arrive, lost to follow-up or other; clinical effects and treatments as shares of the 4,827 cases followed to a known outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 12 chi-squared comparisons are reported (yearly share; four outcome grades; three levels of care; CNS depression, tachycardia, vomiting, respiratory depression), each only as P < .05 or P > .05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; coding by poison-centre staff at the time of the call.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only; no confidence intervals, test statistics or exact P values. Rise 2017 to 2021: 207 to 3,054 calls (printed 1375.0%; editors' arithmetic 1375.4%, 14.75 times), and 0.2 to 3.6 per 1,000 calls about children under 6 (Figure 1 data labels 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.5 and 3.6 for 2017 to 2021). 2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021: major effect 1.6% against 2.4%; moderate 15.9% against 23.8%; minor 33.4% against 30.1%; no effect 17% against 11.8%; critical care 6.6% against 8.6%; noncritical admission 12.7% against 15.7% (the yearly shares in Table 2 give 11.2% for 2017 to 2019, editors' arithmetic); treated and released 41.2% against 34.5%; CNS depression 61.6% against 72.9%; vomiting 7.5% against 10.0% (each P < .05); tachycardia 10.3% against 11.6% and respiratory depression 2.5% against 3.3% (P > .05).
analysis.covariates: None; no adjustment of any kind.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the institutional review board judged the study exempt (deidentified data that the paper calls publicly available).
analysis.selective_reporting: Clinical effects limited to the top 30 codes (with codes of the 'other' organ systems removed) and treatments to the top 20; denominators of cases followed up in each period are not given; counts by state were not available.
analysis.power: Not addressed; counts are large in the pandemic years and small in 2017 (207).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Calls about young children who ate cannabis edibles rose every year from 2017 to 2021, in number and as a share of all calls about children under 6, while those calls overall fell. Most children were 1 to 4 years old and had eaten the product at home. About a quarter of all cases (about a third of those followed up) were graded moderate or major, 22.7% were admitted, 35 were intubated and no deaths were reported. Severity and admission shares were higher in 2020 to 2021 than in 2017 to 2019.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the exposures 'can cause significant toxicity' and are responsible for an increasing number of hospitalizations, which the counts support for reported cases. The Discussion links the rise to more states allowing adult recreational use, as a belief, which cannot be tested without state data, as the authors acknowledge, and names the pandemic as a possible part. The period comparison is presented as rising severity during the pandemic, but compares later with earlier years of a rising series, across a coding change and changing choices of where children were treated; the authors themselves say it is unknown why disposition changed. The abstract has three errors (97.7% residential for 97.1%; the number treated and released is said to have decreased when the share fell and the number rose; the sentence on major and moderate effects reverses the periods). The prevention measures in the Conclusions are recommendations, not tested here.

timeline.event: RTI Press overview of edibles reports second-hand that US poison-centre calls about cannabis in young children rose from 2005 to 2011, with similar rises in edible calls in 2013 to 2015, and says emergency visits for children remained relatively low.
Cao et al., Clinical Toxicology: edible cannabis exposures reported to US poison centres (cited as this paper's reference 3; not read).
American College of Medical Toxicology position statement on paediatric cannabis exposure (cited as reference 16; not read); the authors note that calls kept rising after it.
This national analysis, 2017 to 2021.

replication.where_it_stands: National data in the same direction as the earlier state-level reports the paper cites (not read here). None of these sources can separate legal sales, product changes, the pandemic and reporting as causes of the rise.

funding.funder: No external funding (p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have indicated they have no potential conflicts of interest to disclose (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are affiliated with the Illinois Poison Center; also Southern Illinois University School of Medicine (Tweet), Rush University Medical Center (Nemanich) and NorthShore University HealthSystem (Wahl). Dr Wahl conceived the study, obtained the NPDS data and did the statistical analyses (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: State-level poison-centre and emergency-department data with child population denominators, dates of legal retail sales, product type and amount, and measures of reporting behaviour, analysed as interrupted time series, would show how much of the rise follows legal sales or product changes rather than reporting or the pandemic.
