domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NPDS covers calls to all 55 US poison centres, the right frame for reported exposures; it misses exposures never reported, which the authors call an underestimate.
A census of coded cases, but the code is not named, and whether only unintentional or only cannabis-alone exposures were taken is not stated.
7,043 cases; 4,827 followed to a known outcome.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, place of exposure, management and caller site; no state, product, amount or other substances.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 30.4% not followed to a known outcome; clinical effects and treatments analysed only among those followed, while the severity grades in Table 1 are shares of all cases; whether follow-up differed by year is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Exposure from the caller's account, coded by poison-centre staff; no laboratory confirmation reported; 74 confirmed non-exposures recorded.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: National coding manual; the 2019 change in the CNS depression codes was handled by combining categories; outcome grades depend on follow-up.

Only P < .05 or P > .05 reported, with no test statistics or intervals and no correction across at least 12 comparisons; the before-and-during-pandemic split confounds a rising trend with the pandemic; the Discussion's 295.7% is the ratio of the two periods' counts, not the increase (195.7%), and the periods differ in length (three years against two).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Reporting to poison centres is voluntary; the share of exposures reported, and whether it changed over the years, is unknown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of reported calls about young children who ate cannabis edibles, the counts, ages, places and graded outcomes are national and internally consistent in the tables, but they are floors, and part of the rise may reflect reporting. The statistical comparisons are thinly reported and the pandemic contrast cannot isolate the pandemic. Citable for the yearly counts and shares, ages, place of exposure, level of care and graded outcomes among reported cases; not for incidence per child, for the causes of the rise (legal sales, the pandemic or reporting), or for a pandemic effect on severity.

key_findings.finding: 7,043 calls, 2017 to 2021: 207 in 2017, 590 in 2018, 983 in 2019, 2,209 in 2020 and 3,054 in 2021 (an increase the paper gives as 1375.0%). Edible calls were 0.02% of all calls about children under 6 in 2017 (0.2 per 1,000) and 0.36% in 2021 (3.6 per 1,000; P < .05); the data labels of Figure 1 give 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.5 and 3.6 per 1,000 for 2017 to 2021.
key_findings.locator: Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1, data labels (p. 3); Table 1, Number of cases per year (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: (3,054 - 207)/207 = 1375.4%, 14.75 times. The largest rise in number was 2019 to 2020 (+1,226, printed as +124.7%, which the Discussion calls the biggest increase); the largest relative rise was 2017 to 2018 (+185.0%).

key_findings.finding: Over the same five years, all calls about children aged 0 to 5 to poison centres fell from 956,871 to 846,296.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ages: median 3 years (interquartile range 2 to 4); 2-year-olds were the largest group (1,954, 27.7%), then 3-year-olds (1,734, 24.6%), 4-year-olds (1,265, 18.0%), 1-year-olds (1,046, 14.9%), 5-year-olds (891, 12.7%) and under 1 year (136, 1.9%). Female 3,450 (49.0%), male 3,495 (49.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Age and Sex (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Place: own residence 6,391 (90.7%), another residence 451 (6.4%), other or unknown 201 (2.9%); residential in all 6,842 (97.1%; the abstract says 97.7%). Managed on site without referral 973 (13.8%); already in or on the way to a health care facility when the centre was called 3,405 (48.3%); referred by the centre 2,557 (36.3%). Callers: a health care facility 3,071 (43.6%), a residence 3,468 (49.2%), other places 7.2%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results › General Characteristics, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Exposure site and Management site (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Medical outcome of all 7,043: major effect 155 (2.2%), moderate 1,539 (21.9%), minor 2,211 (31.4%), no effect 923 (13.1%), confirmed non-exposure 74 (1.1%), not followed to a known outcome 2,141 (30.4%). No deaths were reported in the five years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Medical Outcome, paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Medical outcome (p. 4); Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System › Respiratory Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: moderate or major 1,694, 24.1% of all calls and 35.1% of the 4,827 followed to a known outcome; major 3.2% of those.

key_findings.finding: Level of care: admitted to critical care 573 (8.1%), to noncritical care 1,027 (14.6%), together 22.7% as in the abstract; treated and released 2,550 (36.2%); refused referral or did not arrive 625 (8.9%); lost to follow-up or other 2,268 (32.2%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results › Disposition, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Level of HCF (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Year by year (Table 2, % of each year's calls, 2017 to 2021): critical care 8.7, 4.7, 7.3, 8.2, 9.0; noncritical care 9.7, 10.5, 12.0, 14.9, 16.3; treated and released 44.9, 42.4, 39.7, 32.6, 35.9. Text: critical care 6.6% in 2017 to 2019 against 8.6% in 2020 to 2021 (a 30% increase), noncritical care 12.7% against 15.7%, treated and released 41.2% against 34.5% (each P < .05).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Disposition, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Weighting the yearly shares in Table 2 by the yearly counts gives 11.2% (not 12.7%) for noncritical care in 2017 to 2019, while reproducing the 1,027 total and the 15.7% for 2020 to 2021 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Severity by period, 2017 to 2019 (1,780 calls) against 2020 to 2021 (5,263): major effect 1.6% against 2.4%, moderate 15.9% against 23.8%, minor 33.4% against 30.1%, no effect 17% against 11.8% (each P < .05); CNS depression 61.6% against 72.9% (P < .05); vomiting 7.5% against 10.0% (P < .05); tachycardia 10.3% against 11.6% and respiratory depression 2.5% against 3.3% (both P > .05).
key_findings.locator: Results › Medical Outcome, paragraph (p. 3); Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System: Neurologic, Cardiovascular and Gastrointestinal Effects (p. 4), Respiratory Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Clinical effects among the 4,827 followed to a known outcome: CNS depression 3,381 (70.0%), major CNS depression or coma 90 (1.9%), tachycardia 548 (11.4%), vomiting 458 (9.5%), ataxia 359 (7.4%), agitation 342 (7.1%), confusion 294 (6.1%), mydriasis 284 (5.9%), respiratory depression 148 (3.1%), hypotension 123 (2.5%), seizure 79 (1.6%), bradycardia 68 (1.4%), hallucinations or delusions 47 (1.0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System (p. 4 and p. 5); Table 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Treatments among the 4,827: intravenous fluids 997 (20.7%), dilution or washing 525 (10.9%), food or snack 495 (10.3%), oxygen 193 (4.0%), benzodiazepines 107 (2.2%), single-dose charcoal 100 (2.1%), naloxone 68 (1.4%), intubation 35 (0.7%), ventilator 33 (0.7%), vasopressors 13 (0.3%); the authors put intubation at about 1 in 140 children.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 97.7% of exposures occurred in a residential setting; the Results give 6,842 cases (97.1%), which matches Table 1 (6,391 + 451 of 7,043 = 97.15%, editors' arithmetic).

The Discussion calls the change from 1,780 cases (2017 to 2019) to 5,263 (2020 to 2021) an increase of 295.7%; 5,263 is 295.7% of 1,780, an increase of 195.7%, and the periods are three years against two (per year, about 593 against 2,632, about 4.4 times; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite 295.7% as the increase; give the yearly counts instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives noncritical admissions as 12.7% of cases in 2017 to 2019 (a 24% rise to 15.7%), but the yearly shares in Table 2 weighted by the yearly counts give 11.2% (editors' arithmetic); the same weighting reproduces the 1,027 total in Table 1, the 15.7% for 2020 to 2021, and the text's critical-care (6.6%, 8.6%) and treated-and-released (41.2%, 34.5%) shares.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2017 to 2019 noncritical share is probably 11.2%, a relative rise of about 40%, not 24%.

reporting_issues.issue: Numbers and shares are mixed up in places: the abstract says the number of patients treated and released decreased between periods, but only the share fell (41.2% to 34.5%; the count implied by Table 2 rose from about 733 to about 1,817, editors' arithmetic); the text says the number admitted to noncritical care increased 68.0% from 9.7% in 2017 to 16.3% in 2021, which is the rise in the share (the count rose from about 20 to about 498). The abstract's sentence on major and moderate effects puts the periods the wrong way round.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite shares as shares; the absolute numbers rose in every category.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods exclude 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome and analyse 4,827; Table 1 has 2,141 not followed plus 74 confirmed non-exposures (2,215) and 4,828 cases in the four known-outcome grades.
reporting_issues.consequence: A difference of one case; the 4,827 evidently exclude the confirmed non-exposures as well.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor items: minor effects are 31.3% in the text and 31.4% in Table 1, and the period shares for minor effects (33.4% and 30.1%) imply about 2,179 cases against 2,211 (editors' arithmetic); flumazenil is 0.2% in the text and 0.1% in Table 4 (7 of 4,827); the text says Table 4 lists 23 treatments, and it lists 22; caller-site figures are attributed to Table 1, which does not show them; 1375.0% is 1375.4% by the editors' arithmetic.
reporting_issues.consequence: None changes a conclusion; they show the text was not checked against the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Statistical reporting: every comparison is given only as P < .05 or P > .05, with no test statistic, degrees of freedom or interval and no correction across at least 12 comparisons; the before-and-during-pandemic contrast compares three earlier with two later years of a series that was already rising (207, 590, 983).
reporting_issues.consequence: Period differences show that later years differed from earlier ones, not that the pandemic caused them.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Tweet_2023_PediatricEdibleExposures.pdf (article pages 1 to 7: abstract and boxes, all text, Tables 1 to 4, Figure 1 data labels read on the rendered page, references, funding and disclosures). Text extracted once with pdftotext -layout; every page was also checked on a rendered image, because the extraction turns some symbols into digits (the plus sign before 124.7% on p. 6 comes out as 1, the equals sign in table headings as 5).

design_detail: Systematic review with four-level random-effects meta-analyses and multiple meta-regressions (R, metafor; effect estimates nested in trials and studies) of placebo-controlled experimental trials that gave a single dose of THC and measured simulated or on-road driving, or a driving-related cognitive skill, within 12 hours. 80 studies, 155 trials, 3454 participants, 1534 outcomes, of which 1011 were eligible for quantitative synthesis. Peak-effect meta-analyses by performance domain (within 1.5 h of inhaled or intravenous THC, 1.5 to 3.5 h after oral THC); meta-regressions of inhaled THC (all, regular and other cannabis use) and oral THC to model how impairment varies with dose and time, and to predict a recovery time.
can_establish: The average size of THC-related impairment on laboratory driving and cognitive measures shortly after a single dose, and, in people who use cannabis less than weekly, how that impairment tends to grow with dose and fade with time in laboratory studies, as modelled across trials.
cannot_establish: A safe time to drive for any person (no crash outcome, averaged effect sizes, a recovery threshold chosen by the authors); how long impairment lasts in people who use cannabis weekly or more (their model explained nothing); impairment beyond the few studies that tested after about 4 to 6 hours (later predictions are extrapolations of a fixed recovery rate); effects of real-world products, repeated use or alcohol combined; effects in women (71% of participants were men).

sample.recruitment: Web of Science and Scopus, 2000 to April 2020, English-language articles only, with a secondary search using modified terms; reference lists of two earlier reviews hand-searched (pp. 176-177).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Placebo-controlled trials (within- or between-subject) giving a single acute dose of THC and testing driving or a driving-related skill within 12 h; excluded THC combined with another active treatment, more than one dose before testing, unreported dose or timing, duplicate reports and inadequate reporting; studies scoring below 50% on the Rosendal quality scale and studies of clinical populations were excluded from the quantitative synthesis (pp. 176-179).
sample.demographics: 71% men overall (Table 3, p. 180); mostly healthy adults; cannabis use grouped as regular (weekly or more in all participants) or other (mostly occasional) (Table 2, p. 178).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; 31% of outcomes from healthy-participant studies were ineligible for quantitative synthesis (p. 188).
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only, from 2000, no grey literature or trial registries; authors of 2010-2020 studies were contacted for data; values were digitized from graphs where needed. Regular-use trials were few and clustered at 20-60 min after one narrow band of doses (exposure field) (p. 186).

exposure.measurement: THC dose given in each trial, in absolute milligrams (body weight was rarely reported, so doses could not be made relative) (p. 187).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single doses; in the eligible trials mean doses were 20 mg oral, 14 mg vaporised, 32 mg smoked and 2.5 mg intravenous (Table 4, p. 180); in the meta-regressions doses ranged 3.7-94 mg inhaled (interquartile range 10-26 mg) and 2.5-50 mg oral (10-25 mg), and post-dose test times 1-480 min inhaled (45-240 min) and 60-720 min oral (120-360 min) (p. 182). Predictions in Table 9 are for a reference dose of 20 mg, and Figs. 2 and 3 also show 10 mg (pp. 186-187). In the other-use inhaled model doses were 3.7-69 mg (interquartile range 10-25) at 1-480 min (60-240); in the regular-use model 90% of outcomes were at 20-60 min and 71% at 21-26 mg (pp. 182, 186).
exposure.polysubstance: Trials combining THC with another active treatment were excluded; placebo treatments (such as placebo alcohol), tobacco and other cannabinoids were allowed (p. 176).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Regular-use studies standardized prior use differently: at least 24 h abstinence, overnight abstinence, usual use, or not stated (p. 186).

comparison.controls: Placebo, within or between subjects.
comparison.matching: Within-subject designs predominated; effect sizes standardized against the SD of the change, with the correlation imputed (R = 0.53) where not reported, or against the pooled SD for between-subject designs (p. 178).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; tolerance, recent use and body weight varied and were partly captured only by the regular-or-other grouping.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Driving simulator or on-road measures (lateral control including standard deviation of lane position, speed and its variability, car-following headway, reaction time) and cognitive tests grouped into domains: divided attention, tracking, information processing, conflict control, fluid intelligence, reaction time, fine and gross motor function, sensory discrimination, time perception, sustained attention, working memory (Table 1, p. 177).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality scored with the Rosendal scale (mean 62%, SD 10, range 43-93%) (p. 179); individual scores in a supplement not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment = negative Hedges' g against placebo; recovery = the predicted time at which g reaches -0.25, described as the level at which effects are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on performance (Table 9 footnote, p. 186); no external validation of this threshold is given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 17 peak meta-analyses were run (Table 7) plus four meta-regression models.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; screening by two investigators independently (p. 176); data extraction procedures are described against a Cochrane checklist without saying whether extraction was duplicated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Peak effects, Hedges' g (95% CI) (Table 7, p. 184): divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20); tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25); information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21); conflict control -0.34 (-0.42 to -0.25); fluid intelligence -0.37 (-0.46 to -0.27); reaction time -0.28 (-0.43 to -0.13); fine motor -0.36 (-0.60 to -0.12); sustained attention -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10); working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); sensory discrimination +0.09 and time perception -0.05, not significant. Driving: lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08); lane weaving (SDLP) -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11); driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29), speed variability -0.16, headway -0.03 and headway variability -0.24, not significant. Meta-regression (Table 8, p. 185): in the combined inhaled model regular use +0.17 (+0.06 to +0.28, p = 0.003) and vaporising -0.09 (-0.17 to -0.01) against smoking, but pseudo-R-squared 0.0; regular-use model, no covariate significant; other-use inhaled model, dose -0.0082 per mg (-0.0112 to -0.0053) and time +0.0005 per min (+0.0004 to +0.0007), pseudo-R-squared 0.64; oral model, dose -0.0087 per mg, curvilinear time term significant, pseudo-R-squared 0.28.
analysis.covariates: Performance domain, cannabis use (regular or other), route (smoked or vaporised), dose, post-dose time (plus a quadratic term for oral THC).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol registration is mentioned; methods are said to be reported according to PRISMA-P 2015 (p. 176).
analysis.selective_reporting: Robustness to the imputed correlation (R = 0.2 and 0.8) is reported only in Supplementary File 5, not read; no publication-bias assessment; predicted recovery times in Table 9 are given without intervals.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors note few studies of regular cannabis use and of longer post-dose intervals (4-6 h) (p. 188).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Shortly after THC, most driving-related measures were impaired by small to moderate amounts (g about -0.23 to -0.47), while speed was not (drivers tended to go slightly slower). In people who use cannabis less than weekly, impairment grew with dose and faded with time; at the reference dose (exposure field) the model's aggregate effect reached the authors' threshold at 300 min smoked, 350 min vaporised and 480 min oral, with domain predictions from under 60 min to 530 min after inhaling (lane weaving 427-472 min, information processing 486-530 min) and 415-665 min after oral THC. Regular use was associated with less impairment, but its duration could not be modelled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says most skills would recover within about 5 h and almost all within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose, and that individuals should wait at least 5 h after inhaled cannabis before safety-sensitive tasks (p. 175; repeated p. 188). Gaps: (1) Table 9 shows lane weaving and information processing beyond 7 h at that dose, and only 4 of 8 domains within 5 h when smoked (editors' count); (2) the waiting advice turns a dose-specific average into a rule for all inhaled use, while the Discussion itself says there is no universal answer and that dose matters (p. 184); (3) the recovery threshold is not linked to crash risk; (4) predictions past about 4 h rest on few data and assume steady recovery, as the Limitations concede (p. 188).

timeline.event: Hartman et al., simulator study of cannabis and lane weaving with and without alcohol, among the trials in this field.
This review: first meta-analytic estimate of the duration of THC impairment of driving-related skills, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The main quantitative synthesis of how long acute THC impairment lasts in laboratory studies. Its duration estimates are model predictions with no intervals, fitted mostly to tests within 4 hours, and apply to people who use cannabis occasionally.

funding.funder: No specific grant; three authors receive salary support from the Lambert Initiative for Cannabinoid Therapeutics, a philanthropically funded centre for medicinal cannabis research at the University of Sydney (p. 188).
funding.declared_conflicts: None (p. 188).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Sydney (Lambert Initiative, Brain and Mind Centre) and Griffith University; the review includes trials by its own authors' group (for example Arkell et al., 2019).

what_would_settle_it: Controlled studies that test driving repeatedly from 1 to 12 hours after realistic doses and products, in people who use cannabis daily as well as occasionally and in women, reporting individual recovery curves and crash-relevant outcomes rather than averaged standardized effects.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, single-dose THC, placebo comparison, driving and driving-related outcomes, and the 12-hour window are specified.
No registration or published protocol; PRISMA-P is cited only as a reporting standard.
Placebo-controlled experimental trials only, as required to isolate the acute drug effect.
Two databases from 2000, English only without justification, no grey literature or registries; reference lists of two reviews hand-searched.
Two investigators screened independently, with a third for discrepancies.
Extraction against a Cochrane checklist, but duplicate extraction or checking is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The main text gives only a shortened flow diagram; excluded tasks and outcomes with reasons and the full PRISMA flow are in Supplementary Files 1 and 2, not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Doses, routes, timing and use frequency summarized by domain (Tables 3 to 6); per-study details only in Supplementary File 4, not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The Rosendal scale (combining Jadad, PEDro and the Delphi list) covers randomization, blinding and reporting, but collapses them into a percentage; scores per study only in a supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Multilevel random-effects models handle dependent effect estimates; the imputed correlation was varied in sensitivity analyses. Caveats: peak analyses pool across doses, routes and use frequency, and recovery predictions extrapolate a linear fade.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Studies under 50% on the quality scale were dropped, but no analysis examined how quality affected the estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and conclusions do not consider the quality of the primary trials.
I-squared, Q and variance components reported; meta-regression used to explain heterogeneity; residual variance and its possible sources discussed (p. 187).
Not assessed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and salary support declared; no conflicts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 could only be judged from supplements that were not read. AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because several critical items are not met (no registration, a restricted search, no account of primary-study quality in the interpretation, no publication-bias assessment), whatever item 7 turns out to be. The statistical modelling is sophisticated and transparent, and the peak impairment estimates rest on many placebo-controlled trials; the weakness lies in the duration predictions, which have no intervals, depend on a chosen threshold and extend beyond most of the data. The review can be cited for the size of acute impairment and for the direction of dose, time, route and use-frequency effects; its recovery times can be cited only as model predictions for occasional use, not as safe waiting times.

key_findings.finding: Included: 155 trials from 80 studies, 3454 participants (71% men), 1534 outcomes, of which 1011 from 108 trials (2583 participants) were eligible for quantitative synthesis. Mean Rosendal quality score 62% (SD 10, range 43-93%); six studies scored under 50% and were excluded from quantitative synthesis.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1 (p. 179, right column); Table 3 (p. 180)

key_findings.finding: Peak effects (Hedges' g, 95% CI): divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20), tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25), information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21), conflict control -0.34 (-0.42 to -0.25), fluid intelligence -0.37 (-0.46 to -0.27), reaction time -0.28 (-0.43 to -0.13), fine motor -0.36 (-0.60 to -0.12), sustained attention -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10), working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); sensory discrimination +0.09 (-0.08 to +0.25) and time perception -0.05 (-0.30 to +0.20) not significant.

key_findings.finding: Peak effects on driving: lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08), lane weaving (SDLP) -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11), driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29), speed variability -0.16 (-0.35 to +0.02), car-following headway -0.03 and its variability -0.24, not significant. The authors read the speed trend as drivers widening their safety margins.
key_findings.locator: Table 7, Car Driving rows (p. 184); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 186, left column)

key_findings.finding: Inhaled THC, combined model (579 estimates): regular cannabis use (weekly or more) associated with less impairment (+0.17, +0.06 to +0.28, p = 0.003) and vaporising with more than smoking (-0.09, -0.17 to -0.01, p = 0.021), but the model left most heterogeneity unexplained (pseudo-R-squared 0.0). Regular-use model (59 estimates): no covariate related to effect size, so duration could not be predicted for regular use; 90% of these outcomes were measured 20-60 min after dosing, within one narrow band of doses (exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.1, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 182); Table 8, upper two panels (p. 185); Discussion (p. 186, right column)

key_findings.finding: Inhaled THC, other (mostly occasional) use, 481 estimates: impairment increased with dose (-0.0082 in g per mg, -0.0112 to -0.0053) and decreased with time (+0.0005 per min, +0.0004 to +0.0007), and differed by domain (information processing, lane weaving, tracking and divided attention most sensitive); pseudo-R-squared 0.64. Dose and time ranges are in the exposure field.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.1, 4th paragraph (p. 182, right column); Table 8, third panel (p. 185)

key_findings.finding: Oral THC (243 estimates, all from other use): impairment increased with dose (-0.0087 per mg) with a U-shaped time course (delayed peak, predicted at 283 min, then recovery); pseudo-R-squared 0.28, so the authors advise more caution.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.3.2 (p. 182); Table 8, lowest panel (p. 185); Table 9 footnote d (p. 186); Discussion (p. 187)

Predicted peak effects at that dose: aggregate -0.40 smoked, -0.42 vaporised, -0.32 oral.

key_findings.note: No intervals are given for any prediction; the footnote for the Aggregate row (f) is missing from the table.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion summarizes that most driving-related skills recover within about 3 and 5 h of inhaling the lower and the higher reference dose respectively, almost all within about 5 and 7 h, and that oral impairment of most skills takes about 8 h to subside after the higher reference dose (doses in the exposure field); the conclusion says individuals should wait at least 5 h after inhaled cannabis before safety-sensitive tasks, depending on dose, while also stating there is no universal answer to how long to wait.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 184, right column); Discussion (p. 187, left column, top and right column); final paragraph (p. 188)

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: English only; 31% of healthy-participant outcomes ineligible for synthesis; models assume a fixed rate of recovery; trials contributing many estimates weigh more; studies testing after 12 h excluded; few studies of regular use and of longer intervals (4-6 h); women underrepresented and doses absolute rather than per body weight.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs on residual variance (p. 187) and on further limitations (p. 188, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion say almost all skills recover within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose, but Table 9 predicts 427 min (smoked) and 472 min (vaporised) for lane weaving and 486 and 530 min for information processing at that dose; and only 4 of the 8 inhaled domains with values (smoked) fall within 5 h, so the 5-hour figure matches the aggregate row rather than most skills (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline durations are more favourable than the review's own table; the table's values should be cited, as predictions.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 9 has an Aggregate Effect row marked with footnote f, but no footnote f is printed; the aggregate is described only in the text as an average across domains graphed in a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: How the aggregate recovery time was computed cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The combined inhaled model is reported with significant covariates and also with a pseudo-R-squared of 0.0, that is, no improvement over a model without moderators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regular-against-other difference comes from a model that explains almost none of the variance; it is consistent in direction with the separate models but its size is uncertain.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis, written for the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine GRACE guideline programme, of direct evidence on topical capsaicin and dopamine antagonists (haloperidol, droperidol) for adults with cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) in emergency departments, against usual care or no active comparator. Seven studies, 492 patients: two randomized trials (59 patients), two retrospective cohort studies (244), two retrospective chart reviews (133) and one retrospective observational study (56); five on capsaicin (386) and two on dopamine antagonists (106). Narrative synthesis with study-level tables.
can_establish: What the few direct studies up to March 2022 report on capsaicin cream and on dopamine antagonists for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome treated in emergency departments, and how weak that evidence is.
cannot_establish: Pooled effect sizes (no meta-analysis), whether either treatment works better than standard antiemetics in a definitive trial, how CHS should be diagnosed, anything about treatment outside emergency departments, or about stopping cannabis, hot showers or other self-care measures (outside the review question).

sample.recruitment: Ovid MEDLINE to 24 March 2022, APA PsycInfo to March 2022, Cochrane CENTRAL (November 2021) and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and Scopus; search designed by a medical librarian (Appendix S1, not read); reference lists of relevant reviews screened (p. 494).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed original articles in English; adults 18 or older presenting to an urgent care or emergency department for CHS; pharmacological treatment with a control group (usual care, no active comparator or head-to-head drugs). Excluded: no published results, no control or comparison group, reviews and guidelines, inaccessible full texts, non-ED settings (Table 1, p. 495).
sample.demographics: Study-level only (Tables 2 and 3): median or mean ages around 27 to 35; one cohort included patients from age 16; one trial's sample was about 90% African American.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; both randomized trials were judged at high risk of bias because of loss to follow-up (p. 498).
sample.selection_effects: English only; no trial registries searched for unpublished results (registered trials without results were excluded); few studies, mostly single-centre retrospective chart reviews in North America, some during the COVID-19 pandemic (p. 502).

exposure.measurement: Treatments as recorded in charts or given in trials; CHS defined differently across studies (for example recurrent vomiting with cannabis use, a coded diagnosis, or criteria such as hot-shower relief) (Tables 2 and 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 496-500): capsaicin cream 0.025% to 0.1% (one study also 0.15%), applied to the abdomen, amount often not measured; intravenous droperidol, median 2.19 mg (interquartile range 1.25-4.69); intravenous haloperidol printed as 0.05 mg or 0.1 mg (pooled), against intravenous ondansetron 8 mg; capsaicin against placebo cream in the other trial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; patients often received several other antiemetics, opioids or benzodiazepines, not standardized (Tables 2 and 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Placebo cream (one trial), ondansetron (one trial), patients not given the study drug, the same patients' earlier visits, or pre-treatment pain scores.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity and duration of cannabis use and of symptoms often missing from charts (Table 2).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Nausea and pain visual analogue scales, need for rescue medicines, length of emergency department or hospital stay, admission, return visits, adverse events.
outcomes.validity_norms: Outcome definitions differed between studies; one cohort defined efficacy as needing at most one further drug.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit judged from each study's own outcomes and significance tests.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative synthesis of six outcome types).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Two independent reviewers for title and abstract screening; risk-of-bias disagreements resolved by discussion; extraction procedure not described as duplicate.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Capsaicin trial (Dean et al., 2020, about 30 patients): nausea at 30 min not different from placebo cream (difference -2.0 cm, 95% CI printed as 0.2 to -4.2); complete resolution 29.4% against 0% (risk ratio printed 3.4, 1.6 to 7.1); lower mean nausea at 60 min; no difference in disposition or rescue antiemetics. Capsaicin cohorts: efficacy 55% against 21% (p<0.001) and time to discharge 3.72 against 6.11 h (Kum et al.); no change in pain scores before and after (Lee and Coralic); no difference in length of stay, 179 against 201 min (Wagner et al.); no difference in stay, medicines or return within 72 h and admissions 8 against 1 (Yusuf et al.). Haloperidol trial (Ruberto et al., 2021, 30 patients): greater improvement in pain and nausea at 2 h than ondansetron (mean difference 2.3 cm, p = 0.01), treatment success 54% against 29%, rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%, time to discharge 3.1 against 5.6 h (p = 0.03). Droperidol chart review (Lee et al., 2019, 76 patients): hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014).
analysis.covariates: None at review level.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The review says it followed its protocol (p. 494), but no registration or published protocol is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: Risk-of-bias assessments only in an appendix (not read); no certainty-of-evidence rating, although the review was written for a guideline programme.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Capsaicin: one small placebo-controlled trial negative on its primary outcome with some secondary benefit, and four non-randomized studies split between modest benefit and no difference, one with more admissions after capsaicin. Dopamine antagonists: one small randomized trial against ondansetron and one chart review, both favouring the dopamine antagonist, with acute dystonia in three patients across the two. All evidence at moderate to high risk of bias.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion describe the evidence as limited, mixed for capsaicin and potentially beneficial (conclusion: positive support) for dopamine antagonists (pp. 493, 502), and call for rigorous trials; the Discussion adds that capsaicin's ease of use may justify a place in management (p. 501). The summary is broadly faithful; positive support for dopamine antagonists rests on two small studies, one non-randomized, and the haloperidol trial compared against ondansetron, an active usual-care drug.

timeline.event: Ruberto et al. (HaVOC), the randomized trial of haloperidol against ondansetron included in this review.
This review, for the SAEM GRACE guideline programme.

replication.where_it_stands: A small evidence base summarized carefully; the authors mention an ongoing randomized trial of capsaicin (NCT04283292) and an interim report comparing droperidol with haloperidol. Claims must not cite Ruberto et al. (2021) and this review as independent support.

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine to answer a question set by its GRACE writing team; one author supported by the Peter Boris Chair in Addictions Research and a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair (p. 502).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 502); the funding statement also says one author is a principal in Beam Diagnostics, Inc. and a consultant to Clairvoyant Therapeutics, Inc.
funding.affiliations_note: McMaster University and St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton (Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research; Michael G. DeGroote Centre for Medicinal Cannabis Research).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered randomized trials in emergency departments comparing capsaicin, haloperidol or droperidol with standard antiemetics, using an agreed CHS definition, prespecified symptom outcomes at fixed times, return visits and adverse events, and follow-up of cannabis use afterwards.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no registered protocol, a restricted search, no list of excluded studies), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review is nevertheless a clear, conservative description of a very small literature, and its tables let each study be traced. It can be cited for what the seven studies reported and for the weakness of the evidence; not for an effect size or as proof that either treatment works.

key_findings.finding: Included: 7 of 25 full texts (53 records): two randomized trials (59 patients), two retrospective cohort studies (244), two retrospective chart reviews (133) and one retrospective observational study (56), 492 patients in all; five studies of capsaicin (386 patients) and two of dopamine antagonists (106).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 493); Results, Study selection and characteristics (p. 495); Fig. 1

key_findings.finding: Capsaicin, randomized trial (Dean et al.): nausea 30 min after the cream did not differ from placebo cream (difference -2.0 cm, CI printed as 0.2 to -4.2); a higher proportion had complete resolution of nausea, 29.4% against 0% (risk ratio printed 3.4, 1.6 to 7.1); mean nausea was lower at 60 min; disposition and rescue antiemetics did not differ. The exclusion criteria were changed midway through recruitment.
key_findings.locator: Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (p. 498, right column); Table 3, Dean et al. row (p. 500)

key_findings.finding: Capsaicin, non-randomized studies: Kum et al. (201 patients) found more patients needing at most one further drug with capsaicin (55% against 21%, p<0.001) and a shorter time to discharge (3.72 against 6.11 h), with the review noting the capsaicin group had already received more drugs; Lee and Coralic (57, before-and-after) found no significant change in pain scores and no adverse drug events; Wagner et al. (43, compared with their own earlier visits) found no difference in length of stay (179 against 201 min, p = 0.33) but fewer additional medicines; Yusuf et al. (56, capsaicin available or not depending on the pharmacist on duty) found no difference in stay, medicines, 72-hour returns or admission rate, with 8 admissions after capsaicin against 1 without.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (pp. 496-499); Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (pp. 498-499)

key_findings.finding: Haloperidol trial (Ruberto et al., 30 patients, against ondansetron, the two haloperidol doses pooled): greater reduction in abdominal pain and nausea at 2 h (mean difference 2.3 cm, p = 0.01), treatment success 54% against 29%, rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%, benzodiazepines 8% against 41%, any medicine 31% against 76%, time to discharge 3.1 (SD 1.7) against 5.6 (SD 4.5) h (p = 0.03); two return visits for acute dystonia after haloperidol and none after ondansetron.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Ruberto et al. row (p. 500); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501, left column)

key_findings.finding: Droperidol chart review (Lee et al., 76 patients): total hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014) and time to discharge after the last antiemetic 137 against 185 min (p = 0.002); two patients drowsy, one acute dystonia that responded to benztropine, no cardiac events.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Lee et al. row (pp. 496-497); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: both randomized trials high, mainly because of loss to follow-up; retrospective studies low to high, most moderate to high.
key_findings.locator: Results, paragraph after Table 2 (left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors' conclusion: limited direct evidence, mixed support for capsaicin and positive but preliminary support for dopamine antagonists; capsaicin is not known to have serious side effects though application may be uncomfortable, while dystonia, arrhythmias and drowsiness are noted for dopamine antagonists.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 501); Conclusions (p. 502)

reporting_issues.issue: For Kum et al., Table 2 gives an odds ratio of 0.2881 (p = 0.0070) for efficacy with symptoms of a month or longer against under a week, that is, lower odds, while the text says symptoms over a month had a significantly higher likelihood of relief (p. 499); the nausea odds ratio is 2.478 (p = 0.0285) in Table 2 and 2.626 (p = 0.036) in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Who benefits from capsaicin in that cohort cannot be cited from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 reports for Dean et al. a significantly higher rate of complete resolution of nausea (29.4% against 0%) and, among secondary outcomes, no significant difference in complete relief of nausea; a risk ratio of 3.4 with a finite interval is printed for a comparison with zero events in one arm; the control group is printed as n = 1 although the trial had about 29 patients, 17 on capsaicin.
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial's secondary results should be taken from the primary paper, not the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria require a control group and the flow diagram excludes one study for having none (Fig. 1), yet a before-and-after study without a control group (Lee and Coralic) is included; the text calls the five non-randomized studies uncontrolled although four had comparison groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in how designs are described.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name RoB 2 for trials but cite the 2011 Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; the appendix holding the assessments is called S2 in the text and Table 2 and S3 in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which tool was used for the trials is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Haloperidol doses are printed without a per-kilogram unit (Table 3; p. 501).
reporting_issues.consequence: Doses should be checked against the primary trial before they are quoted anywhere.

design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42023462484) with random-effects meta-analyses of standardized mean differences for polysomnographic or EEG sleep measures (total sleep time, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, N1, N2, slow-wave sleep, REM sleep, REM latency) in studies of cannabis or cannabinoid administration, chronic use against no use, and withdrawal. 18 studies included (1972-1982 and 2004 onward); 9 entered meta-analyses: 6 of administration (all oral products: THC, dronabinol, CBD or combinations) and 3 of withdrawal.
can_establish: What sleep-laboratory studies have found, on average, for sleep measured during use of oral cannabis products (mostly modern trials of CBD or low-dose THC, mostly in people with sleep disorders), and for sleep in the first days after people stop regular cannabis use or daily high-dose THC.
cannot_establish: Effects of smoked or vaped cannabis on sleep architecture (no eligible modern study), effects of the doses and products most people use, effects in people who use cannabis daily while they continue, how long withdrawal sleep problems last beyond the first week, or effects on how rested people feel (subjective sleep was outside the review).

sample.recruitment: Embase, Medline and Web of Science searched on 2 September 2023 without restrictions; screening in Covidence by two reviewers with two others resolving conflicts (pp. 3, 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any form of cannabis (THC, CBD, nabilone, dronabinol, whole plant); sleep measured by EEG, polysomnography, polygraphy or actigraphy; at least one of nine sleep outcomes; a comparison (pre-post or control group). Excluded: cannabis only as a moderator, cannabis combined with other substances without isolating its effect, and non-English publications (p. 5).
sample.demographics: Early studies (1972-1982): samples of 2 to 11 (mean 5.6), all young adult men aged 21-29, healthy, given THC at doses up to far above modern trials (exposure field). Modern studies: 8 to 73 participants (mean 29.7), mean age 49.8, 55.5% men, four of six in sleep disorders (obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia, REM behaviour disorder in Parkinson's disease) (pp. 6-7; Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level.
sample.selection_effects: English only; three databases, no grey literature or registries; all early administration studies lacked the statistics needed for pooling, so the administration meta-analyses contain only modern trials of oral medicinal products, while two of the three withdrawal studies pooled are early high-dose studies (p. 9).

exposure.measurement: Cannabis or cannabinoid given by investigators (administration and early withdrawal studies) or self-reported use (comparisons of people who use cannabis with people who do not, and real-world withdrawal studies); purity of plant material not commonly reported (p. 13).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 1, p. 4; pp. 6, 11-12): pooled administration trials used oral THC and THC:CBD combinations (15:0, 5:5 and 15:15 mg), dronabinol titrated 2.5-10 mg, CBD 300 mg or titrated 75-300 mg, and a THC:CBN:CBD 10:1:0.5 mg product, over 4 to 84 days; early studies used oral THC up to 70-210 mg a day or 0.2-1.4 mg/kg. Withdrawal studies pooled: two early studies stopping 70-210 mg a day of oral THC in men with a history of daily use (n = 7 and 11) and one modern study of 20 people actively using cannabis who stopped (inhaled, real-world use).
exposure.polysubstance: Studies combining cannabis with other substances without isolating its effect were excluded; other drug use in the comparison and withdrawal samples is not summarized.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Administration studies: washouts of two weeks to two months in six, self-reported abstinence in two, urine confirmation in three; withdrawal data taken from the first three days in two studies and days four to six in one (pp. 8-9).

comparison.controls: Placebo (crossover or parallel), pre-post baselines, or non-using comparison groups, depending on the study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep disorders in most modern samples; prior cannabis use unspecified in two administration studies; in withdrawal, sleep before regular use began is unknown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not summarized.

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography or EEG in every included study; one study also used actigraphy, but its polysomnography data were pooled (p. 7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard sleep staging; no subjective sleep outcomes.
outcomes.operationalization: Standardized mean differences between cannabis and comparison conditions for each sleep measure.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 9 administration and 5 withdrawal meta-analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; risk of bias in primary studies rated with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I (Tables 2 and 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Administration, SMD (95% CI) as printed in the forest plots: total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17), 0%; wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34), 0%; sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27), 0%; N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%; REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1% (Figs. 2-10, pp. 6-11). Withdrawal: total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67), 6.4%; sleep efficiency -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46), 0% (two studies); REM 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66), 0%.
analysis.covariates: None; sensitivity analyses removing two studies without prior-use information and two CBD-only studies did not change significance (p. 11).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42023462484 (p. 3). Funnel plots and Egger tests were planned but not done because of the small number of studies (pp. 6, 9); a sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was planned (p. 6) and its results are not reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Text and figures disagree on the sign of four administration estimates (see reporting issues); the planned risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis is not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors stress the thin evidence base (six administration and three withdrawal studies in meta-analyses) (p. 12).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six modern trials of oral cannabis products (mostly CBD or low-dose THC medicines, four of six in people with sleep disorders, 178 participants), no sleep measure differed on average from the comparison condition, with narrow intervals for sleep time, onset, waking and efficiency but wide, inconsistent results for REM sleep. In three withdrawal studies (about 38 people), sleep in the first week after stopping was shorter, slower to start and less efficient, with more and earlier REM sleep, by large standardized amounts; two of the three withdrew high experimental oral THC doses in the 1970s.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and practice points say cannabis administration does not consistently alter sleep architecture and that withdrawal from chronic use significantly disrupts sleep (pp. 1, 13); the conclusion advises clinicians not to view cannabis as a reliable sleep aid and to prepare people who use regularly for transient insomnia when quitting (p. 13). The administration statement is accurate for the pooled oral products and populations but is phrased for cannabis in general, which was not studied in its common inhaled form; the withdrawal statement rests on three small studies, two of them withdrawals of experimental high doses, though the authors call the estimates tiny-cohort and cautious (p. 13). The authors rated an uncontrolled pre-post withdrawal study as low risk of bias.

timeline.event: Angarita et al., narrative review of sleep in alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioid use, describing withdrawal sleep problems second-hand.
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analysis of polysomnographic sleep architecture and cannabis.

replication.where_it_stands: The only quantitative synthesis of measured sleep architecture with cannabis identified by its authors. Its administration pools rest on modern oral medicinal trials and its withdrawal pools largely on 1970s high-dose studies plus one modern study (Vandrey et al., 2011), which narrative reviews such as Angarita et al. (2016) also cite, so the two are not independent.

funding.funder: No specific grant (p. 14).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 14).
funding.affiliations_note: First and last authors are affiliated with the clinical research department of Tranq Sleep Care, a sleep clinic in Kelowna, Canada, and with the University of British Columbia.

what_would_settle_it: Preregistered, adequately powered sleep-laboratory studies of inhaled cannabis at doses people use, in people who use it regularly and occasionally, including nights during use and repeated nights after stopping, with objective and subjective sleep measures and next-day functioning.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Cannabis exposures, comparisons (pre-post or control), polysomnographic outcomes and study types are specified.
Registered in PROSPERO; the registered content was not examined, and planned analyses (publication bias, risk-of-bias sensitivity) were not done or not reported.
Any design with a pre-post or control comparison was admitted without a stated reason for mixing randomized trials with uncontrolled designs.

Three databases without search restrictions, but non-English papers were excluded at eligibility without justification (three excluded for language), and no grey literature, registries or reference lists.
Two reviewers screened, with two others resolving conflicts.
Each charted study underwent double review (p. 6).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow diagram gives counts by reason only (supplement 41, outcome 15, method 6, review 4, language 3 and others); no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, blinding, control, duration, prior use, sex, age, condition, size, route, product, dose, direction of each outcome and risk of bias.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 for randomized and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies, with domain-level judgments shown (Tables 2 and 3); the ROBINS-I ratings use a three-level scheme and rate an uncontrolled pre-post study low.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

A non-randomized uncontrolled study (Farabi et al., 2014) is pooled with randomized trials in four administration analyses; CBD and THC products and different patient groups are combined in single pools; the handling of crossover and pre-post correlations is not described beyond pooling means and SDs.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was planned, but no result is reported, although two of three withdrawal studies pooled were rated high risk.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion repeatedly weighs the early studies' methodological limits and calls the withdrawal estimates tiny-cohort and cautious.
I-squared reported; heterogeneity in REM measures examined in sensitivity analyses and discussed in terms of dose, product, tolerance and sleep apnea.
Planned but not done because of the small number of studies.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: More than one critical item is not met (restricted search, inappropriate pooling of randomized and non-randomized designs, no list of excluded studies, no publication-bias assessment), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review is registered, transparent about its thin evidence base and careful in its discussion; its tables and forest plots allow each pooled result to be traced. It can be cited for what measured sleep looked like in the few pooled studies, with their populations and products named; not for effects of inhaled cannabis or for a precise size of withdrawal effects.

key_findings.finding: 18 studies included: 9 administration only, 2 chronic use only, 1 withdrawal only, 5 administration and withdrawal, 1 chronic use and withdrawal; 9 in meta-analyses (6 administration, 3 withdrawal). Studies came from 1972-1982 and from 2004 onward, none in between.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 flow diagram (p. 3); Results 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 (pp. 6-7)

key_findings.finding: Administration, pooled SMD (95% CI): total sleep time -0.02 (-0.25 to 0.21), 5 arms from 4 studies; sleep onset latency -0.06 (-0.28 to 0.17), 6 arms from 5 studies; wake after sleep onset 0.11 (-0.13 to 0.34); sleep efficiency 0.01 (-0.25 to 0.27); all I-squared 0-6%. Of 12 administration studies measuring total sleep time, one (n = 4) found an increase and 11 no change; of 12 measuring onset latency, one (n = 2) found an increase.
key_findings.locator: Figs. 2a, 3a, 4 and 5a (pp. 6-8); Results 3.2.1 to 3.2.4 (pp. 9-10)
key_findings.note: Signs as printed in the forest plots; the text prints +0.021, +0.056 and -0.009 for total sleep time, onset latency and efficiency (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Administration, sleep stages: N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5% (dronabinol in sleep apnea raised REM, 1.16 and 0.72; CBD in REM behaviour disorder lowered it, -0.98); REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%. Of 14 administration studies, six (mostly early high-dose THC studies of 4 to 11 people, and one CBD study) found less REM sleep and one more.

Withdrawal, pooled SMD (95% CI), three studies (Feinberg et al., 1975, n = 7; Feinberg et al., 1976, n = 11; Vandrey et al., 2011, n = 20): total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42); sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67); REM sleep 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), I-squared 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66); sleep efficiency (two studies) -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46). Individual studies all in the same direction (for example total sleep time -0.95, -0.89 and -0.70).
key_findings.locator: Figs. 2b, 3b, 5b, 9b and 10b (pp. 6-11); Results 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.4, 3.2.8 (pp. 10-11) and 3.2.9 (p. 12); Table 1 sample sizes (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered forest plots.

key_findings.finding: Across all seven withdrawal studies: total sleep time fell in 3 and did not change in 4; time to fall asleep rose in 5 of 7; REM rose in 3 of 7; wake after sleep onset rose in 3 of 7. Withdrawal data came from the first three nights in the two early studies and nights four to six in the modern one.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1.5, last paragraphs (p. 9, right column); 3.2.1 to 3.2.3 (p. 10); 3.2.8 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Two of the three withdrawal studies in the meta-analyses (Feinberg et al., 1975 and 1976) replaced high daily experimental doses of oral THC (exposure field) with placebo in men with a history of daily use; the third (Vandrey et al., 2011) compared sleep before and during abstinence in 20 people actively using cannabis, who knew they had stopped. ROBINS-I: the two early studies high risk overall, the modern study low.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 withdrawal rows (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5); Results 3.1.2 (p. 8); Discussion (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Comparisons of people who use cannabis with people who do not (three studies with inhaled cannabis, 1973-2008): no significant differences in most measures; one found shorter total sleep time and less slow-wave sleep, one more REM.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2.1 (p. 10, left column) and 3.2.7-3.2.8 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses removing the two administration studies that did not specify prior use, and the two CBD-only studies, did not change the significance of any administration result or reduce REM heterogeneity.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2.10 (left column)

key_findings.finding: Practice points: no consistent effect of administration on sleep parameters; REM suppression in high-dose 1970s trials and mixed findings in modern trials; withdrawal from chronic use reduces sleep time and lengthens sleep onset, though polysomnographic evidence is scarce.
key_findings.locator: Practice Points box

reporting_issues.issue: Four administration estimates have a different sign in the text than in the forest plots: total sleep time +0.021 in the text against -0.02 in Fig. 2a; sleep onset latency +0.056 against -0.06 (Fig. 3a); sleep efficiency -0.009 against 0.01 (Fig. 5a); REM +0.0356 against -0.04 (Fig. 9a). In each case the text's confidence interval is centred on the figure's sign.
reporting_issues.consequence: The point estimates are near zero, so conclusions do not change, but the figures are the values to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the administration REM latency result one with no heterogeneity while printing I-squared 76.12% (p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: Heterogeneity was high for REM latency as for REM.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says one study focused only on chronic use (p. 7), but the flow diagram and Table 1 show two (pp. 3-4); it says three withdrawal studies used pre-post measures, citing references 46-48 (p. 8), but reference 47 is not among the seven withdrawal studies in Table 1, so the stated design counts sum to eight.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 is the record to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 codes Vandrey et al. (2011) as double-blind, while the text says participants in the pre-post withdrawal studies were aware of cessation (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: The modern withdrawal study is better read as an open pre-post comparison, which affects its low risk-of-bias rating.

reporting_issues.issue: The search is described as having no restrictions (p. 5), but non-English publications were excluded at eligibility (p. 5; three excluded for language in Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: A language restriction applied in practice.
