Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that measures frequency and biologically verified potency (THC and CBD) of cannabis use from adolescence, records psychotic-like symptoms before first use, and has family-history and polygenic data, ideally with sibling or co-twin comparisons; and, for the population claim, repeated measurement within sites showing whether changes in daily and high-potency use are followed by changes in incidence.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drug use, but not for family history or genetic liability, childhood adversity or premorbid functioning; full adjustment roughly halved every odds ratio, which shows how sensitive the estimates are to measured confounders and makes residual confounding plausible. Use during a prodrome (reverse causation) is not addressed, and education and employment may be affected by the illness itself.

Retrospective self-report of a lifetime pattern after a first psychotic episode, without biological verification; potency assigned from national mean THC for the type named, dichotomized at 10%, without CBD; the timing of the pattern relative to onset is not stated in the main text. Recruitment materials did not mention cannabis, which limits but does not remove differential recall.

Incident cases from defined catchments, but 23% refused, and refusers differed by age, sex and ethnicity; control response is not reported; quota sampling with advertising top-ups and weights. The bias analysis that the authors cite is not applied to the main estimate (see reporting issues).
No intervention between exposure and outcome is relevant to this comparison.

Complete-case analysis; six of 17 sites excluded (five for at least 10% missing data), so 229 of 1130 cases and 262 of 1499 controls were not analysed; no comparison of included and excluded participants or imputation is reported in the main text.
First-episode psychosis with ICD-10 diagnoses harmonized by OPCRIT; the incidence rates come from a separate standardized study.
Six exposure measures, a combined measure built after seeing which measures had the largest odds ratios, many site-level estimates and attributable fractions, and no registered analysis plan.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large incident-case study with harmonized diagnoses and a population-based control strategy, so the reported associations are well documented as associations; but they remain open to residual confounding and reverse causation, which no part of the study addresses. The attributable fractions add the assumption that the adjusted odds ratios are causal, and the incidence analysis adds an ecological inference from 10 sites. The paper may be cited for the adjusted odds ratios with their reference groups, for the absence of an association with occasional use, and for the site differences in the prevalence of daily and high-potency use; it should not be cited for the share of cases caused by cannabis, or for cannabis use explaining variation in incidence.

key_findings.finding: Of 1519 people with first-episode psychosis approached between 1 May 2010 and 1 April 2015, 356 (23%) refused, 19 could not consent because of language and 14 were outside the age range; 1130 took part. Refusers were older, more often women and more often of white European origin; participants were younger than the full incidence sample (mean 31.2 vs 34.5 years). 1499 controls were recruited at 16 of the 17 sites.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: After excluding Maison Blanche (no controls) and five sites with at least 10% missing data on cannabis or main confounders (Verona, Santiago, Oviedo, Valencia, Cuenca), 901 cases and 1237 controls in 11 sites were analysed as complete cases.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 229 of 1130 cases (20%) and 262 of 1499 controls (17%) were not analysed.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime cannabis use was reported by 574 of 1237 controls (46.4%) and 585 of 901 cases (64.9%); smoking 10 or more cigarettes a day by 12.8% and 32.9%; ever use of stimulants by 12.0% and 21.8%, hallucinogens 9.0% and 14.5%, ketamine 2.8% and 6.1%, legal highs 2.4% and 4.3%. Cases were younger, more often men and from ethnic minorities, less educated and more often unemployed.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Lifetime use: odds ratio 2.45 (2.0 to 2.9) adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity, and 1.3 (1.1 to 1.6) fully adjusted (p = 0.0225). Current use: 2.7 (2.1 to 3.5) and 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) (p = 0.36). First use at 15 or younger: 3.9 (3.0 to 4.9) and 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1) (p = 0.0122).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 2 labels the first-stage estimates crude, but they are adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity; the full models add education, employment, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs and hallucinogens (Table 2 footnote).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime frequency (most consistent pattern), against never or occasional use: more than once a week 2.5 (1.9 to 3.5), fully adjusted 1.4 (1.0 to 2.0), p = 0.066; daily use 6.2 (4.8 to 8.2), fully adjusted 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1), p < 0.0001. Daily use was reported by 84 of 1237 controls (6.8%) and 266 of 901 cases (29.5%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: The reference group for frequency is never or occasional use (1061 controls, 528 cases), not never use as the abstract states; by the editors' arithmetic it includes about 411 controls and 225 cases who had used cannabis occasionally.

key_findings.finding: The daily-use odds ratio changed little when age at first use (3.1, 2.1 to 5.2), money spent (2.9, 1.9 to 4.4) or type of cannabis (2.6, 2.0 to 3.9) were added. Spending €20 or more a week (2.5, 1.6 to 3.8) fell to 1.3 (1.0 to 2.1) after adjustment for daily use and type; no interaction between daily use and spending (p = 0.67).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Potency, against never use: low-potency cannabis (THC below 10%) 2.0 (1.6 to 2.5), fully adjusted 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5), p = 0.38; high-potency cannabis (THC 10% or more) 3.2 (2.6 to 4.0), fully adjusted 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), p = 0.0032, and 1.5 (1.1 to 2.6) after also adjusting for daily use. Starting high-potency use by age 15: 2.3 (1.4 to 3.1), no interaction (p = 0.63). High-potency use was reported by 240 controls (19.4%) and 334 cases (37.1%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 8th paragraph
key_findings.note: The main text speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency, not of the type mainly used: in Table 2 every person who had used is in one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, potency missing for 3; 251 + 334 = 585 cases; editors' arithmetic), and how people who used both types were classed is described only in the appendix (not read).

key_findings.finding: Combined frequency and potency, fully adjusted odds ratios against never use: occasional use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (THC 10% or more); use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57; daily use 2.19 (1.4 to 3.6) and 4.78 (2.5 to 6.3). The corresponding age, gender and ethnicity adjusted values are 0.93, 1.11, 1.71, 2.12, 3.08 and 5.81. No interaction between frequency and type (p = 0.25).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph; Figure 1 (value labels, read on screen)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 labels the occasional categories 'rare use'. Intervals are printed in the text only for the two daily categories; the others are shown only as error bars.

key_findings.finding: Neither the daily-use nor the high-potency odds ratio varied significantly by site (p = 0.25 and 0.45). Fully adjusted daily-use odds ratios ranged from 7.1 (3.4 to 11.8) in Amsterdam to 1.1 (0.4 to 12.2) in Puy de Dôme, and high-potency odds ratios from 3.6 (1.5 to 7.7) in Amsterdam to 0.6 (0.1 to 2.5) in Palermo; London 3.6 (1.4 to 4.4) and 2.4 (1.4 to 4.0); Paris 2.8 (1.7 to 12.3) and 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6).
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: In the three sites with the most high-potency use, the fully adjusted odds ratio for daily high-potency use against never use was 5.16 in London (201 cases, 230 controls), 9.43 in Amsterdam (96 cases, 101 controls) and 4.28 in Paris (54 cases, 100 controls).
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph; Figure 2 (value labels and legend, read on screen)
key_findings.note: Intervals are not printed; read approximately from the error bars, they run from about 3.0 to 12 (London), 6 to 20 (Amsterdam) and 2.1 to 15 (Paris).

key_findings.finding: Attributable fractions assuming causality: whole sample, high-potency use 12.2% (3.0 to 16.1) and daily use 20.4% (17.6 to 22.0); London 30.3% (15.2 to 40.0) and 21.0% (11.1 to 31.2); Amsterdam 50.3% (27.4 to 66.0) and 43.8% (34.0 to 69.1); lowest for high-potency use 1.9% (Bologna and Ribeirão Preto) and for daily use 1.2% (Puy de Dôme); not calculated for high-potency use in Palermo, where there was no main effect.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 12th and 13th paragraphs; Summary › Findings
key_findings.note: Editors' check: the printed fractions match the case-based formula (prevalence of exposure in cases × [1 − 1/odds ratio]) within about one percentage point, using the case prevalences in Table 3 (for example Amsterdam, 69.6% × 2.6/3.6 = 50.3%).

key_findings.finding: Across sites, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder correlated with the prevalence of daily use in controls (r = 0.8, p = 0.0109) and of high-potency use (r = 0.7, p = 0.0286). London (daily use in 26 of 223 controls, 11.7%; high-potency 58 of 223) had 45.7 cases per 100,000 person-years, Amsterdam (13 of 100 daily; 54 of 100 high-potency) 37.9, Paris (21 of 100 high-potency) 46.1 and Bologna (3 of 65 daily, 4.6%) 21.0.
key_findings.locator: Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Figure 3 plots 10 sites (Puy de Dôme excluded for missing ethnicity data). The printed p-values correspond to r of about 0.76 and 0.69 with 10 sites (editors' calculation); with 11 sites, p = 0.0109 would correspond to r of about 0.73.

key_findings.finding: The probabilistic sensitivity analysis for selection bias gave a corrected odds ratio for daily use of 5.7 (3.5 to 9.4), against an original 5.7 (4.4 to 7.5); the authors conclude selection bias is unlikely to explain the findings.
key_findings.locator: Results, 14th paragraph
key_findings.note: Neither value matches the daily-use odds ratios in Table 2 (6.2 adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity; 3.2 fully adjusted); the details are in the appendix, not read.

key_findings.finding: Assuming causality, the authors estimate that without high-potency cannabis the adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder would fall from 37.9 to 18.8 cases per 100,000 person-years in Amsterdam and from 45.7 to 31.9 in London.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: no biological validation of self-report; potency based on official estimates of mean THC by type, without CBD (reliable data only for England and the Netherlands); a 10% cut-off that they call conservative and that may underestimate the effect of potency in the UK and the Netherlands; weights for oversampling, most sites having oversampled people aged 16 to 24.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th, 9th and 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors give THC contents of up to 67% for Nederhasj and 22% for Nederwiet in the Netherlands, and state that skunk-like cannabis with an average THC of 14% made up 94% of the London street market, while herbal types below 10% THC were still common in Italy, France and Spain.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures, from refs 17, 18 and 29 (EMCDDA 2016; Spanish national report; Potter et al., 2018), not measured in this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion compare daily use with people who never used cannabis, but the reference category for lifetime frequency in Table 2 is never or occasional use (1061 controls, 528 cases), which includes about 411 controls and 225 cases who had used cannabis occasionally (editors' arithmetic from Table 2).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) is daily use against never-or-occasional use; claims must state that reference group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results describe the incidence correlations as across 11 sites, but Figure 3 excludes Puy de Dôme, leaving 10; the printed p-values (0.0109 and 0.0286) fit r of about 0.76 and 0.69 with 10 sites, which the paper rounds to 0.8 and 0.7 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Summary › Findings; Results, 15th and 16th paragraphs; Figure 3 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Each ecological correlation rests on 10 points; the rounded r values overstate the daily-use correlation.

reporting_issues.issue: The prevalences of daily use and of high-potency use in controls are said to be only modestly correlated across sites (r = 0.2, p = 0.0413). A correlation of 0.2 gives p of about 0.56 to 0.58 with 10 or 11 sites (p = 0.04 would need about 100 observations), and the site prevalences in Table 3 give r of about 0.71 for the 10 plotted sites (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two site-level exposures are strongly collinear, so the two incidence correlations are not separate pieces of evidence, and the stated reason for reporting both does not hold.

reporting_issues.issue: The selection-bias analysis reports an original daily-use odds ratio of 5.7 (4.4 to 7.5), which matches neither the age, gender and ethnicity adjusted (6.2, 4.8 to 8.2) nor the fully adjusted (3.2, 2.2 to 4.1) estimates in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysis cited to show that selection bias is unlikely was not applied to the estimate the conclusions rest on.

reporting_issues.issue: The whole-sample attributable fraction for high-potency use is given as 12.2% (3.0 to 16.1) in the Summary and Table 3 but as 12.2% (3.0 to 6.1) in the Results.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 12th paragraph; Table 3; Summary › Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; use the Table 3 interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The same quantities differ between places: high-potency use in 19.4% of controls and 37.1% of cases in Table 2, but 19.1% and 35.1% in Table 3; daily use in Bologna controls 4.1% in Table 3 but 3 of 65 (4.6%) in the text; London controls 223 in the text but 230 in the Figure 2 legend, Amsterdam 100 and 101.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Table 3; Results, 15th paragraph; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Small differences, but they show that the site-level inputs to the attributable fractions and correlations cannot be reconciled exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3 does not match the text and Table 3 at some sites (approximate reading of the image): Paris's adjusted incidence is plotted at about 41 to 42 per 100,000 person-years, below London, while the text gives 46.1, above London's 45.7; daily-use prevalence in controls is plotted at about 6% for Barcelona and 10% for Paris against 8.3% and 11.6% in Table 3.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figure 3; Results, 16th paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The data behind the correlations are uncertain; the incidence values should be taken from the EU-GEI incidence paper rather than from this one.

reporting_issues.issue: The χ² p-value for current cannabis use (132 of 1237 controls, 10.7%, vs 198 of 901 cases, 22.0%) is printed as 0.00349; these proportions give p < 0.0001 (z about 7.1, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misprint; no effect on the odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol is reported as 5.2 drinks a day (SD 0.4) among controls and 4.8 (SD 0.4) among cases with p = 0.45, but with SDs of 0.4 in groups of this size the difference would give t of about 23; the p-value fits only if 0.4 is a standard error. Alcohol is also named among the confounders in the Methods but is absent from the Table 2 adjustment footnote.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 5th paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 footnote
reporting_issues.consequence: The alcohol figures and the adjustment set are reported inconsistently; claims should list the adjustment set from the Table 2 footnote.

reporting_issues.issue: Several fully adjusted intervals are not centred on their point estimates on the log scale, as Wald intervals from logistic regression would be: daily use 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1), geometric centre about 3.0; daily high-potency use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3), centre about 4.0; London daily use 3.6 (1.4 to 4.4), centre about 2.5; Madrid daily use 2.5 (2.1 to 7.3), centre about 3.9 (editors' calculation). The method for the intervals is not described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Table 3; Results, 9th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the intervals or some point estimates are misprinted, or a different method was used; the precision of the headline estimates cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: At sites where the odds-ratio interval includes 1, the attributable-fraction interval nevertheless excludes 0: Paris high-potency use 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6) with 18.9% (14.6 to 36.0), marked significant; Gouda and Voorhout 1.5 (0.8 to 3.1) with 12.2% (8.7 to 25.3), marked significant; Cambridge daily use 2.2 (0.8 to 6.5) with 10.4% (4.7 to 21.0), marked significant. The problem is general: every site-level fraction in Table 3 has an interval above zero, including 13 site estimates whose odds-ratio interval includes 1 (8 for high-potency use, 5 for daily use; editors' count), for example Madrid high-potency use 2.0 (0.7 to 5.7) with 17.2% (0.9 to 25.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: The attributable-fraction intervals understate uncertainty; site-level fractions marked significant should not be cited as such.

reporting_issues.issue: Text errors in the Discussion: daily use of high-potency cannabis is said to be associated with a doubling of the odds in the whole sample, but that odds ratio is 4.8 and the doubling (2.2) belongs to daily low-potency use (2nd paragraph); the attributable fraction for daily use is said to range from 44% in Amsterdam to 6% in Palermo, whereas the lowest in Table 3 is 1.2% in Puy de Dôme, and the London figure is called similar to one previously reported, citing reference 3, a review of cannabis legalization, rather than the team's 2015 study (6th paragraph).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should take figures from the tables, not from the Discussion text.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (1st paragraph) says that starting by 15 raised the odds modestly but not independently of frequency of use or of potency, but no estimate for first use at 15 or younger adjusted for daily use or potency is printed; only the reverse adjustment (daily use 3.1, 2.1 to 5.2, after adding age at first use) and starting high-potency use by 15 (2.3, 1.4 to 3.1) are given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that early first use adds nothing beyond frequency or potency is not shown by a printed estimate; claims should say that this was not shown, not that it was tested and found absent.

design_detail: Narrative review (Biological Psychiatry; read as the Author's Accepted Manuscript) of the epidemiological evidence on cannabis and psychotic outcomes: the longitudinal cohorts of Moore et al. (2007) plus three later ones, summarized in Table 1; reasons the cohorts might over- or underestimate a causal effect (residual confounding, misclassified outcomes from intoxication, reverse causation, misclassified exposure, attrition); candidate high-risk groups (age at first use, COMT and AKT1 genotypes, childhood trauma, cannabis strains); evidence for and against causation; complementary methods; and conditional public-health arithmetic. No search strategy or selection criteria; one informal re-pooling of the 2007 ever-use estimate.
can_establish: How three University of Bristol authors, one of them an author of Moore et al. (2007), weighed the cohort evidence up to 2015, which alternative explanations they considered and how they judged each, and pointers to the primary cohorts and to calculations of lifetime risk, attributable fraction and numbers needed to prevent that assume causality.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes psychosis, or the size of an effect: the review has no systematic search or formal appraisal, its updated pooled estimate is given without methods or inputs, and its risk and prevention figures are conditional calculations, several without stated inputs.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Table 1 gives each cohort's sample size and, in brackets, the number with the outcome: ECA 2295 (477), NEMESIS 4045 (38), Swedish conscripts 50087 (362), Dunedin 759 (25), Christchurch 1265 (not given), EDSP 2437 (424), NPMS 1795 (134), Zurich 591 with 2200 records (221), California 41670 (174), ALSPAC 1756 (97) (AM pp. 19-21).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria beyond scope: longitudinal cohort studies of cannabis and psychotic outcomes, with case-control and cross-sectional studies mentioned in one paragraph. Excluded, with reasons: randomized trials of cannabinoids or of interventions to reduce use (follow-up too short), case studies, and studies relying on a diagnosis of cannabis-induced psychotic disorder, which the authors say presupposes a causal role and has no robust distinguishing features (AM p. 3).
sample.demographics: Not reported beyond Table 1; the Swedish cohort is described as men only (Table 1 limitations, AM p. 19).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The review notes that CHDS, NEMESIS and ALSPAC modelled attrition and found no effect on the findings, under assumptions (AM p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the authors. The cohort list starts from Moore et al. (2007), which Zammit co-wrote, and adds three cohorts without saying how they were found. Several central sources are the authors' own: Moore et al. (2007), the Swedish conscript follow-up and the NPMS report (Zammit), ALSPAC (Gage, Hickman, Zammit), the numbers-needed-to-prevent paper (Hickman, Zammit), and papers by Gage or Zammit on potency, Mendelian randomization, specificity and gene-environment interaction.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited cohorts (Table 1): daily use (ECA); ever use and frequency (NEMESIS); cumulative use by conscription (Swedish conscripts); ever use by age 15 or 18 (Dunedin); use and dependence (Christchurch); use at least 5 times (EDSP); dependence on a 3-level measure (NPMS); heaviness of use on a 3-level measure (Zurich); hospitalisation with a diagnosis of cannabis abuse, as Table 1 labels it, or cannabis use disorder in the text (California); cumulative use on 4 levels (ALSPAC). All self-report except the California hospital diagnosis.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors argue that self-report misclassifies use, that the THC:CBD ratio of what people used is unknown in these cohorts, and that hair biomarkers index only recent heavy use (AM p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed for ALSPAC, where adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use attenuated the association to the null, with the authors noting the difficulty of separating confounding from mediation and the risk of over-adjustment (AM p. 5); and as specificity of exposure, found in some studies but not all (AM p. 10). Otherwise as adjusted in the primary studies.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; intoxication as a source of misclassified psychosis outcomes is discussed (AM p. 6).

comparison.controls: People in each cohort who did not use cannabis (people who had never used it, for the 2007 pooled estimates); in the California study, people hospitalised for appendicitis.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name early-life attachment, abuse and trauma as rarely adjusted for, and shared genetic effects as not adequately adjusted for; prodromal symptoms missed at baseline screening are considered and judged unlikely to explain the association (AM pp. 6-7).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited cohorts: psychotic experiences or symptoms by interview or self-report (ECA, NEMESIS, Christchurch, EDSP, NPMS, Zurich, ALSPAC), schizophreniform disorder (Dunedin), and hospital diagnosis of schizophrenia (Swedish conscripts, California) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Table 1 lists strengths and limitations of each cohort; no formal appraisal tool.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive psychotic symptoms and disorders only; the authors set aside cognitive features of schizophrenia (AM p. 11).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis apart from one informal re-pooling).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, with the primary source each comes from. Swedish conscripts (Zammit et al. 2002): about 3-fold risk of schizophrenia by 45 for use more than 50 times by 18 (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5); Table 1 gives a linear trend of 1.2 (1.1 to 1.4). Dunedin (Arseneault et al. 2002): schizophreniform disorder at 26 after use by 15, OR 11.4 (1.8 to 70.5); first use 15 to 18, 2.0 (0.8 to 5.0); Table 1 gives 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04) for ever use by 15/18. NEMESIS (van Os et al. 2002): 1.89 (1.25 to 2.85) in the text, 2.76 (1.18 to 6.47) in Table 1. California (Callaghan et al. 2012): HR 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12) against an appendicitis cohort. Table 1 also: ECA 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12); Christchurch 1.8 (1.2 to 2.6); EDSP 1.2 (1.1 to 1.3); NPMS 1.5 (0.6 to 3.9); Zurich unadjusted 1.77 (0.96 to 3.24), adjusted not reported; ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76 to 1.65). From Moore et al. (2007): 1.4 (1.20 to 1.65) ever use, 2.1 (1.5 to 2.8) heavier use, 2.6 (1.1 to 6.1) psychotic disorder. The authors' update adding Zurich and ALSPAC, California omitted: 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), p<0.001, I2 19%, no methods given. Attenuation of 60% to 80% of the unadjusted estimate in the three most comprehensively adjusted studies (figures that match Moore et al. 2007, Table 1). Conditional on causality: lifetime schizophrenia risk about 2% with regular use, about 20% with regular use and a first-degree relative (if regular use doubles risk and risks multiply), population attributable fraction 10% to 25%, about 5000 men with heavy use and 10,000 to 15,000 women to stop use to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (Hickman et al. 2009), and treatment efficacy about 20%, so these numbers would need multiplying by five.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The section on reverse causation cites a single cohort (Christchurch) for a weaker reverse association, while a 2005 Dutch study whose title reports prediction in both directions (ref. 7) appears only among case-control and cross-sectional studies supporting an association. Evidence against causation from incidence trends gets one paragraph. The authors do report their own ALSPAC result going to the null after full adjustment, and the co-relative study that points to overestimation.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review documents a consistent association across ten cohorts, mostly with psychotic experiences or symptoms; four cohorts had a disorder or hospital-diagnosis outcome (Swedish conscripts, Dunedin, California, and NEMESIS within Moore's pooled disorder estimate). Its own sections report that the most comprehensively adjusted studies lost 60% to 80% of the unadjusted association, that the only co-relative study found the association shrinking with genetic relatedness, and that the two newest general-population cohorts (Zurich, ALSPAC) were null after adjustment; the authors' re-pooled ever-use estimate barely changed (1.46).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the epidemiological evidence is strong enough to warrant a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (AM p. 2), and the conclusion that there is a "strong body of epidemiological evidence" that regular or heavy use increases the risk of psychotic disorders that persist beyond intoxication (AM p. 13). Gaps: (1) the review states that the usual causal criteria, specificity included, are all met (AM p. 11), one page after saying specificity of exposure and of outcome is found in some studies but not in others (AM p. 10); (2) the disorder evidence comes from few cohorts; (3) reverse causation through undetected prodromal symptoms is judged unlikely with one restricted analysis and one cohort's reverse-direction analysis as support; (4) the public-health message is called appropriate beyond doubt (AM p. 13). Otherwise the review is explicit about uncertainty, sets out reasons for both over- and underestimation, and frames its risk and attributable-fraction figures as conditional on causality.

timeline.event: Swedish conscript follow-up (Zammit et al.), Dunedin (Arseneault et al.) and NEMESIS (van Os et al.): the cohorts with disorder outcomes that the review describes first.

Christchurch analyses (Fergusson et al.): fixed-effects regression for stable unmeasured confounders changed little, and the reverse association (psychotic experiences predicting cannabis use) was weaker; Caspi et al. report COMT moderation in Dunedin, which the review says none of eight later studies replicated.
Moore et al. systematic review (Zammit co-author): the review's pooled estimates and the attenuation figures it cites.
Hickman et al.: numbers of people with heavy use who would need to stop to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (about 5000 men; 10,000 to 15,000 women), cited for the implications.
McGrath et al.: association of duration of cannabis use with psychotic symptoms within sibling pairs, cited against a purely genetic or shared-environment explanation.

Kuepper et al. (BMJ, 10-year follow-up): weak evidence of more psychotic experiences in people who had stopped using cannabis than in people who had never used it, which the review attributes to NEMESIS (see reporting issues); van Winkel et al. report a cannabis by AKT1 interaction, replicated once (Di Forti et al. 2012), judged not robust.
Zurich cohort (Rossler et al., 30 years; weak association lost after adjustment) and the California hospital cohort (Callaghan et al.; HR 8.16): two of the three cohorts added since 2007.

ALSPAC (Gage et al.; the third added cohort): association with psychotic experiences at 18 lost after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drugs. Power et al.: genetic risk for schizophrenia associated with cannabis use, explaining a small share of its variance.

Giordano et al.: Swedish co-relative design, association smaller with closer genetic relatedness (cousins to monozygotic twins), read by the review as overestimation from genetic and shared-environment effects. Di Forti et al.: high-potency (skunk) but not resin (hash) cannabis associated with first-episode psychosis in south London; Gage et al. (in press) on whether that reflects selection to extremes of use.

Ksir and Hart, critical overview of the same evidence period reaching the opposite reading (shared vulnerability); they cite a 2013 commentary by the same three authors (Gage, Zammit and Hickman, F1000 Medicine Reports) for a UK rise in cannabis use without a rise in first admissions for schizophrenia, a commentary this review does not cite.

Gillespie and Kendler, viewpoint: the Mendelian randomization studies this review called for (including Gage et al. 2017) found stronger evidence that liability to schizophrenia raises cannabis use than the reverse, and one (Vaucher et al. 2018) an effect of liability to cannabis use on schizophrenia.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited statement of the causal-leaning epidemiological reading, by authors of Moore et al. (2007). The Mendelian randomization studies it proposed have since been done, with results that Gillespie and Kendler (2021) read as mostly reverse causation and partial confounding. Its numbers are second-hand or conditional; claims should cite the primary cohorts, or Moore et al. (2007) for pooled estimates, and use this review for its arguments and its conditional public-health arithmetic, labelled as assuming causality.

funding.funder: As printed: SG is funded an UK Medical Research Council PhD scholarship (grant number SD1708) (Acknowledgements, AM p. 14). No other funding is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no biomedical financial interests or potential conflicts of interest (Financial Disclosures, AM p. 14).
funding.affiliations_note: MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit and School of Social and Community Medicine, University of Bristol. Zammit is an author of Moore et al. (2007), the Swedish conscript follow-up and the NPMS report; Gage, Hickman and Zammit of the ALSPAC report; Hickman and Zammit of the numbers-needed-to-prevent paper. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: As the authors propose: estimates free of residual confounding from large cluster-randomized prevention trials with registry follow-up for psychosis, comparisons across cohorts whose confounding structures differ, and Mendelian randomization with genetic instruments that predict heavy use; and cohorts that measure the THC and CBD content of what people use.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; three cohorts are added to Moore et al. (2007) without saying how they were found.

Table 1 lists strengths and limitations per cohort and the interpretation sections weigh each bias in turn, but there is no formal tool and the genetically informed and gene-environment studies are summarized without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The pooled estimates, the Swedish and NPMS cohorts, ALSPAC, the numbers-needed-to-prevent estimate and the gene-environment commentaries cited for non-replication of COMT are the authors' own; their null ALSPAC result is reported plainly.

The implications figures are labelled as conditional on causality, but inputs are not given (baseline risks behind 2% and 20%; methods of the 1.46 re-pooling; the 10% to 25% range, which is not in the cited source as read). Statements without data: people who use heavily are rarely un-intoxicated because of THC's long half-life; undetected prodrome unlikely; the causal criteria all met.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal effect of cannabis on psychosis
domains.note: Under-represented: the non-causal explanations. Reverse causation and incidence trends get one paragraph each and are argued against; shared genetic liability is dismissed on one polygenic-score study. The co-relative study pointing to overestimation and the null ALSPAC and Zurich results are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of a systematic search. The review is well structured and open about uncertainty, but selective, built largely on its authors' own work, and its few new numbers (the 1.46 re-pooling, the 2% and 20% lifetime risks, the 10% to 25% attributable fraction) come without methods or inputs. It may be cited for its arguments (directions of bias, the case for complementary designs, the conditional public-health arithmetic, labelled as such) and as a pointer to the cohorts in Table 1; every figure must be cited to its primary source.

key_findings.finding: Scope and update: a 2007 systematic review (Moore et al.) identified 7 cohorts; three more have been published since (Zurich, ALSPAC, California), and these 10 are described in the text and Table 1. The 2007 estimates are restated (any psychotic outcome, ever versus never use, 40% increase, 95% CI 20% to 65%; heavier or more regular use OR 2.1, 1.5 to 2.8; psychotic disorder 2.6, 1.1 to 6.1). Adding adjusted results from the Zurich study and ALSPAC, with California omitted for its extreme exposure measure, gives an updated pooled OR for any psychotic outcome of 1.46 (95% CI 1.24 to 1.72), p<0.001, I2 19%.
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies, 1st paragraph (AM p. 4) and last paragraph, before Interpretation of the findings (AM p. 5)
key_findings.note: No model or inputs are given for the update. Table 1 says adjusted Zurich results were not reported, and the Zurich and ALSPAC exposures are heaviness or cumulative use, not ever use (see reporting issues). AM p. is the PDF page, one more than the manuscript's own page number.

key_findings.finding: Cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome: Swedish conscripts, dose-response between cannabis use by 18 and schizophrenia by 45, about 3-fold risk for more than 50 times (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5); Dunedin, use by 15 and schizophreniform disorder at 26, OR 11.4 (1.8 to 70.5), first use between 15 and 18, 2.0 (0.8 to 5.0), intervals wide and overlapping; NEMESIS, cumulative use and incident psychotic outcomes 3 years later, OR 1.89 (1.25 to 2.85); California, hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder and later hospitalisation for schizophrenia against an appendicitis cohort, HR 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12).
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic disorder, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cohorts with psychotic experiences: Christchurch, cannabis dependence associated after adjustment for numerous confounders; EDSP, any use at baseline associated with psychotic symptoms 42 months later; ECA, daily use associated, little evidence for ever use; NPMS, dependence associated with incident symptoms 18 months later before but not after adjustment; Zurich (30-year follow-up), weak evidence for schizophrenia nuclear symptoms before but not after adjustment; ALSPAC, cumulative use at 16 associated with psychotic experiences at 18 after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood confounders, attenuated to the null after further adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use (the authors discuss confounding versus mediation and over-adjustment).
key_findings.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic experiences, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 4-5) and 2nd paragraph (AM p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Table 1, sample size (with outcome), exposure, outcome and result: ECA 2295 (477), daily use, psychotic experiences, OR 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12); NEMESIS 4045 (38), ever use and frequency, psychosis symptom severity, 2.76 (1.18 to 6.47); Swedish conscripts 50087 (362), cumulative use, schizophrenia diagnosis, linear trend 1.2 (1.1 to 1.4); Dunedin 759 (25), ever use by 15/18, schizophreniform diagnosis, 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04); Christchurch 1265, use or dependence, psychotic experiences, 1.8 (1.2 to 2.6); EDSP 2437 (424), use at least 5 times, psychotic symptoms, 1.2 (1.1 to 1.3); NPMS 1795 (134), dependence (3 levels), self-reported psychotic symptoms, 1.5 (0.6 to 3.9); Zurich 591 [2200 records] (221), heaviness of use (3 levels), self-reported schizophrenia nuclear symptoms, adjusted results not reported, unadjusted 1.77 (0.96 to 3.24); California 41670 (174), hospitalisation for cannabis abuse, hospitalisation for schizophrenia, 8.2 (5.1 to 13.1); ALSPAC 1756 (97), cumulative use (4 levels), psychotic experience severity (4 levels), 1.12 (0.76 to 1.65).
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: The column is headed adjusted OR but holds a hazard ratio (California), a per-category linear trend (Swedish) and an unadjusted estimate (Zurich).

key_findings.finding: Residual confounding, the authors argue, would most likely inflate the estimates: studies adjusting for more confounders showed more attenuation, 60% to 80% of the unadjusted estimate in the 3 most comprehensively adjusted studies, and few studies adjusted for early-life attachment, abuse and trauma. Shared genetic effects are judged unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little variance in cannabis use (Power et al., ref. 24); a sibling-pair study (McGrath et al., ref. 25) and fixed-effects regression in Christchurch argue against stable familial confounding; but a co-relative study (Giordano et al., ref. 26) found the association substantially smaller with closer genetic relatedness, from cousins to monozygotic twins, suggesting overestimation in population studies.
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Confounding, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 5-6) and 2nd paragraph (AM p. 6)
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for the genetic studies. The 60% to 80% figure is cited to ref. 9 (Miettunen et al., on prodromal symptoms in adolescence); by the editors' cross-check it matches Moore et al. (2007), Table 1: Swedish conscripts 60%, CHDS 65%, NPMS 80%.

key_findings.finding: Bias and reverse causation: outcomes based on hospitalisation for schizophrenia are unlikely to be misclassified intoxication; a cessation analysis found weak evidence of more psychotic experiences in people who had stopped using cannabis than in people who had never used it, with very few who had stopped. Most studies excluded or adjusted for baseline symptoms; undetected prodromal symptoms driving cannabis use are judged unlikely, especially where outcomes were restricted to after a likely prodrome; psychotic experiences predicting later cannabis use show much weaker and less consistent evidence than the reverse (Christchurch).
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › ii) Bias, 1st paragraph (AM p. 6); iii) Reverse causation, 1st paragraph (AM p. 7)
key_findings.note: The cessation analysis is cited to ref. 15 and described as NEMESIS (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Reasons for underestimation: random misclassification of self-reported use would bias towards the null, and differential misclassification could act either way; the THC:CBD ratio of what was used is unknown and CBD may have antipsychotic effects; drop-out of people who use drugs or develop mental-health problems would bias towards the null, though attrition modelling in Christchurch, NEMESIS and ALSPAC found no impact.
key_findings.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Misclassification bias (AM p. 7); ii) Attrition (AM p. 8)

key_findings.finding: High-risk groups: in Dunedin, use by 15 had a higher point estimate than later first use, but intervals overlapped substantially, were not formally compared, and the difference could reflect cumulative use; in the Swedish conscripts, allowing for cumulative use, risk did not differ by age at first use; the authors find no strong evidence that cannabis is more harmful to younger people, though it remains a concern. The COMT interaction in Dunedin appeared only in people who first used before 18 and was not replicated in any of eight later studies; an AKT1 interaction, replicated once, is not robust. Three studies found that childhood trauma and cannabis use together raised absolute risk more than the sum of the two, which the authors call the norm for multifactorial diseases.
key_findings.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Age of use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 8), 3rd paragraph (AM pp. 8-9); Genetic susceptibility and Childhood trauma (AM p. 9)
key_findings.note: The Swedish age-at-first-use result is cited to Moore et al. (ref. 10), which in turn cites a PhD thesis by Zammit; the eight non-replications are not individually cited.

key_findings.finding: Potency: several studies suggest strains with higher THC:CBD ratios carry greater risk; a south London case-control study (Di Forti et al., ref. 48) found skunk but not hash associated with a psychotic episode. Because studies from before skunk was widespread also found an association, the authors judge it too early to assume only high-potency cannabis carries risk, and say future studies must address selection of people to the extremes of use. Ecological evidence that psychosis risk rose in cohorts exposed to higher THC has not been examined. Evidence on synthetic cannabinoids comes from case reports.
key_findings.locator: Identifying high risk groups › Strains of cannabis, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 9-10), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (AM p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Evidence for causation, as the authors list it: consistent association after adjustment, dose-response where examined, transient psychotic experiences during experimental intoxication, consistent neurobiology; specificity of exposure in some studies but not all (refs 16, 23 against); specificity of outcome in some but not all. Evidence against: incidence of psychotic outcomes rose in some studies and was unchanged or fell in others, which the authors call very weak, ecological evidence. They state that the usual causal criteria are all met, while noting examples of criteria-meeting associations later shown by trials to be confounded.
key_findings.locator: Evidence in support of causation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 10); Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship (AM p. 11); Addressing the uncertainty, 1st paragraph (AM p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Methods proposed: large cluster-randomized trials of substance-use interventions with long-term psychosis outcomes (linked registers), cross-cohort comparisons in populations with different confounding structures (the UK and Brazil breastfeeding example), and Mendelian randomization, then limited because genetic variants robustly predicting cannabis use had not been identified.
key_findings.locator: Addressing the uncertainty, 2nd paragraph (AM pp. 11-12), 3rd and 4th paragraphs (AM p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Conditional implications: if the association is causal and of the size estimated, lifetime risk of schizophrenia with regular use would be about 2%, so about 98% of people who use regularly would not develop it; if regular use doubled risk and risks multiplied, lifetime risk with regular use and a first-degree relative with schizophrenia could be around 20%.
key_findings.locator: Implications, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No baseline risks are given or cited; the 20% implies a lifetime risk of about 10% without cannabis in people with a first-degree relative (editors' arithmetic: 20% halved).

key_findings.finding: Attributable fraction and prevention: assuming causality, 10% to 25% of schizophrenia depending on whether risk is confined to heavy use or extends to all use (cited to Moore et al., ref. 10); about 5000 men with heavy use, and 10,000 to 15,000 women, would need to stop to prevent one case of schizophrenia a year (Hickman et al., ref. 67); with treatment for cannabis dependence about 20% effective, these figures may need multiplying by five; preventing uptake or progression to heavier use is judged a better target than stopping current use.
key_findings.locator: Implications, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 10% to 25% range is not in the cited source as read, and the multiplied figures are not printed. Editors' cross-check and arithmetic: Moore et al. (2007, p. 326) print a single attributable fraction of about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) for ever use; multiplying by five gives about 25,000 men and 50,000 to 75,000 women.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that a public-health message that cannabis use is harmful is beyond doubt appropriate, but that harms should be neither understated nor overstated, since overstated warnings may be ignored when experience does not match them. Conclusion: a strong body of evidence supports the view that regular or heavy use increases the risk of psychotic disorders that persist beyond intoxication; psychosis remains rare while cannabis use among young people is common.
key_findings.locator: Implications, 3rd paragraph; Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: The attenuation of 60% to 80% in the 3 most comprehensively adjusted studies is cited to ref. 9, Miettunen et al. (2008), on prodromal symptoms of psychosis in adolescence; the figures match Table 1 of Moore et al. (2007), ref. 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; claims should cite Moore et al. (2007), Table 1 (p. 322), for the attenuation figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The NEMESIS estimate differs between the text (OR 1.89, 1.25 to 2.85, psychotic outcomes 3 years later) and Table 1 (2.76, 1.18 to 6.47, psychosis symptom severity), and neither matches the NEMESIS estimates in Moore et al.; editors' cross-check: Moore et al. (2007), Figures 1 and 2, give ever use 2.11 (0.78 to 5.71) and weekly use 6.81 (1.79 to 25.91).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least three NEMESIS estimates circulate for different exposure and outcome definitions; any claim must take the figure from the primary paper and name its exposure, outcome and adjustment.

reporting_issues.issue: The updated ever-use pool (1.46) is said to include adjusted results from the Zurich study, but Table 1 states that adjusted Zurich results were not reported and gives only an unadjusted 1.77; the Zurich and ALSPAC exposures in Table 1 are heaviness and cumulative use, not ever use; no model or input estimates are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The updated estimate cannot be reproduced or checked from the review; claims should use Moore et al.'s 1.41 with its stated methods, or label 1.46 as an informal update. Editors' recomputation (AI readers 211 and 242): DerSimonian-Laird pooling of Moore et al.'s seven estimates reproduces 1.41 (1.20 to 1.65), I2 19%; adding Table 1's Zurich (unadjusted 1.77, 0.96 to 3.24) and ALSPAC (1.12, 0.76 to 1.65) gives 1.38 (1.20 to 1.59), I2 13%, not 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), so the update used inputs the review does not print.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 15 (Kuepper et al. 2011, BMJ, a 10-year follow-up cohort study whose authors include Lieb and Wittchen, also authors of the EDSP report, ref. 19) is presented as an extension of NEMESIS and as a study using the NEMESIS cohort, while the review gives NEMESIS outcomes as measured 3 years later.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cohort behind the finding on people who stopped using may be misattributed; check the primary paper before citing it for either cohort.

reporting_issues.issue: The attributable fraction of 10% to 25% is cited to Moore et al. (ref. 10), whose discussion, by the editors' cross-check, gives about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) for ever use and no range by heaviness of use (Moore et al. 2007, p. 326).
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand figure that differs from its cited source; claims should cite Moore et al. (2007), p. 326, for 14%, and not attribute 10% to 25% to it.

reporting_issues.issue: A placeholder is left in the text: the neurobiology sentence ends with a reference to other articles in this issue followed by (refs), with no references given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, accepted-manuscript artefact; the version of record may differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the four references for trends in psychosis incidence do not concern incidence over time by their titles: ref. 58 (Ajdacic-Gross et al. 2009, adolescent versus adult onset of smoking and mood disorders) and ref. 60 (Breslau et al. 2006, race-ethnic differences in psychiatric disorder). Refs 59 and 61 are incidence-trend studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that some studies found rising and others unchanged or falling incidence rests, as cited, on one study each way (Boydell et al. 2003; Frisher et al. 2009).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 1 results column is headed adjusted OR but mixes metrics: a hazard ratio (California), a linear trend per category of use (Swedish conscripts) and an unadjusted OR (Zurich); exposure categories differ between rows.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 values are not comparable with one another or with Moore et al.'s ever-use estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the ECA daily-use estimate as 2.0 (1.25 to 3.12), while the same estimate in Moore et al. (2007), Figure 2, is 2.00 (1.27 to 3.16).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small transcription difference; cite the ECA estimate from Moore et al. (2007) or the primary paper, not from this review's Table 1.

design_detail: Two-page Viewpoint (JAMA Psychiatry; read as the online-first PDF, published online 4 November 2020, pages E1-E2) that sets three hypotheses for the cannabis-schizophrenia association (1, entirely causal; 2, partly causal and partly confounded by genetic or familial effects and/or reverse causation; 3, entirely non-causal), states in a Table what each of four genetically informed methods should show under each hypothesis (discordant-relative or co-relative designs, Mendelian randomization, linkage disequilibrium score regression, polygenic risk score regression) and compares the expectations with published results. Nine references; no search, no new data.
can_establish: How two authors from a psychiatric and behavioral genetics institute, one of whom co-wrote the only co-relative study they cite, read the genetically informed evidence available in 2020, and what pattern of results they expect each method to give under each hypothesis.
cannot_establish: What proportion of the association is causal: the quantitative statement (familial confounding accounting for more than half) rests on one co-relative study (a Swedish national registry study by its title as cited by Gage et al., 2016, and as Ksir and Hart, 2016, describe it; the viewpoint says neither) whose monozygotic-twin estimate is printed two ways and was not significance-tested, and the viewpoint has no systematic search.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (viewpoint). The co-relative study is a Swedish national co-relative registry analysis (Giordano et al. 2015; the viewpoint does not describe it, and its design is taken from the reference lists and text of Gage et al. 2016 and Ksir and Hart 2016); the other studies are genome-wide association analyses and polygenic-score studies in population samples, as cited.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the four methods; studies of the short-term psychiatric effects of administering cannabis are explicitly out of scope (p. E1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The authors know of only one discordant-relative analysis, co-written by Kendler; three of the four large population-based polygenic-score studies said to be positive are not cited; non-genetic designs (cohorts, dose-response, potency) are outside the question asked.

exposure.measurement: By method, as cited: cannabis misuse in the co-relative study, a national registry study by its title (cannabis abuse in its title); genetic instruments for lifetime cannabis use in the Mendelian randomization studies, which the authors note are not instruments for heavy use or misuse; lifetime cannabis use or misuse in the genetic-correlation studies; cannabis misuse and other cannabis phenotypes as outcomes of schizophrenia polygenic scores.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not addressed; the Mendelian randomization evidence concerns liability to lifetime use only.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that high schizophrenia polygenic scores are said to predict comorbid substance use or misuse as well as cannabis use (pp. E1-E2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Co-relative design: the association in unrelated pairs from the general population compared with that within full-sibling pairs and monozygotic twin pairs discordant for cannabis misuse. Mendelian randomization: people with higher versus lower genetic liability to the exposure.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within-pair comparisons remove familial factors shared by relatives, but not factors that differ between them (childhood adversity affecting one twin, prodromal symptoms before the first registry record of misuse); not discussed in the viewpoint.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Schizophrenia as a registry diagnosis (co-relative study) or as case status in genome-wide association studies; cannabis phenotypes as outcomes in polygenic-score and reverse-direction Mendelian randomization analyses.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: The hypotheses are defined by expected patterns (Table): under 1, equal odds ratios across levels of relatedness, a genetic correlation of zero and a schizophrenia polygenic-score coefficient of zero; under 2, odds ratios that fall with relatedness but stay significantly above 1 in monozygotic twins, and coefficients above zero; under 3, odds ratios falling to 1 in monozygotic twins and no effect of liability to cannabis use in Mendelian randomization.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, with the primary source of each. Co-relative (Giordano et al. 2015): OR 10.44 for unrelated pairs in the general population, 5.07 for full siblings, and for discordant monozygotic twins 3.52 in the text (a 66% decline) or 3.92 in the Table; tests of significance were unavailable for monozygotic pairs. Mendelian randomization: genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use increased schizophrenia risk by 37% (Vaucher et al. 2018); much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia increases lifetime cannabis use (Gage et al. 2017; Pasman et al. 2018); no evidence of pleiotropy for the instruments in all three. Genetic correlation between lifetime cannabis use or misuse and schizophrenia 0.22 to 0.25 (two studies). Polygenic scores: no association with cannabis misuse in one restricted sample (Hjorthoj et al. 2019); high schizophrenia scores predicted more cannabis and comorbid substance use in four large population-based studies, one cited (Verweij et al. 2017), effect sizes small and not given. Editors' calculation from the printed odds ratios: the 66% decline is on the odds-ratio scale; on the log scale the odds ratio falls by 46% (with 3.52) or 42% (with 3.92), and the excess odds (OR minus 1) by 73% or 69%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only one of the four positive population-based polygenic-score studies is cited; the effect sizes of the polygenic scores, the unit behind the 37% Mendelian randomization estimate and the numbers of discordant monozygotic pairs are not given.
analysis.power: Not addressed beyond the remark that the number of available studies is modest (p. E2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: One co-relative study (a Swedish national registry study by its cited title) shows the odds ratio for cannabis misuse and schizophrenia falling from 10.44 in unrelated pairs to 5.07 in full siblings and to about 3.5 to 3.9 in discordant monozygotic twins, without a significance test at that level. Of three Mendelian randomization studies, one estimates an effect of liability to lifetime cannabis use on schizophrenia and two find stronger evidence for the reverse direction. Genetic correlations are modest (0.22 to 0.25) and polygenic-score effects small.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusions say there is relatively reliable evidence across methods that the association stems partly from shared familial or genetic risk and/or reverse causation, good evidence against an entirely non-causal association, and that in the one co-relative study familial confounding "accounts for more than half of the observed association" (p. E2). Gaps: (1) the more-than-half statement rests on one co-relative study (a registry study by its cited title) co-written by Kendler, holds on the odds-ratio and excess-odds scales but not on the log scale on which odds ratios are modelled (a 46% or 42% fall; editors' calculation), and uses a monozygotic estimate printed as 3.52 in the text and 3.92 in the Table; (2) by the viewpoint's own criterion, separating hypothesis 2 from 3 in this design requires a monozygotic odds ratio significantly above 1, which was not tested (Table, footnote e), so the evidence against hypothesis 3 rests mainly on one Mendelian randomization estimate; (3) the Table expects a genetic correlation of zero under an entirely causal model, but a causal effect of cannabis use on schizophrenia would itself make variants that influence cannabis use associate with schizophrenia, so a correlation above zero does not by itself show confounding (editors' appraisal; the same applies, less strongly, to the polygenic-score expectation); (4) measurement error in the exposure attenuates within-pair estimates more than population estimates, which would make a co-relative decline overstate confounding; not discussed (editors' appraisal). The closing warning that claims about changing risk with changing use are very likely exaggerated is limited by the authors to estimates without control for confounders, and the prudent conclusion (some causal effect, an appreciable non-causal share) is in line with the evidence they present.

timeline.event: Giordano et al., Swedish national co-relative control study (Kendler co-author): the only discordant-relative analysis cited, the basis of the more-than-half estimate. Ksir and Hart (2016) cite the same study as showing that most of the association disappears after controlling for familial relationships; Gage et al. (2016) read it as showing that population estimates may be overestimated.
Marconi et al., meta-analysis of the association between level of cannabis use and psychosis, cited for the robust association.
Gage, Hickman and Zammit had proposed Mendelian randomization as a way to minimise confounding, then limited by the lack of genetic variants robustly predicting cannabis use.

Ksir and Hart argue for shared vulnerability, reading the same co-relative study, an Australian twin and polygenic-score study (Power et al. 2014) and a US family study as strong evidence for shared vulnerability over a causal contribution.

Gage et al., two-sample Mendelian randomization: much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia raises lifetime cannabis use than the reverse. Verweij et al.: genetic correlation and polygenic-score association between schizophrenia and cannabis use.

Vaucher et al., Mendelian randomization: genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use associated with a 37% increase in schizophrenia risk. Pasman et al., genome-wide study of lifetime cannabis use with genetic correlation and Mendelian randomization pointing to a causal influence of schizophrenia liability on cannabis use.

Di Forti et al., EU-GEI study of the contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe, cited for the robust association. Hjorthoj et al.: no association between genetic liability for schizophrenia and cannabis use disorder in a restricted sample.

This viewpoint, published online 4 November 2020 (print issue 2021); the authors call for further co-relative and Mendelian randomization designs and for controlled pre-post studies of schizophrenia incidence where cannabis use rose after decriminalization.

replication.where_it_stands: The clearest short statement of the partly-causal reading from genetically informed designs. Its quantitative core is one co-relative study; the Mendelian randomization results are mixed (one estimate of an effect of liability to cannabis use, two of the reverse direction, all with instruments for lifetime rather than heavy use). Claims citing it should name the primary studies, give the co-relative odds ratios with their scale, and not present more than half as a measured proportion.

funding.funder: Not reported (the viewpoint has no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of Interest Disclosures: none reported (Article Information, p. E2).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Virginia Institute for Psychiatric and Behavior Genetics, Department of Psychiatry, Virginia Commonwealth University; Gillespie also QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, Australia. Kendler is an author of the only co-relative study cited (Giordano et al. 2015), on which the more-than-half statement rests. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the viewpoint.

what_would_settle_it: Co-relative analyses in several registries with exposure recorded before any prodromal symptoms, reporting the numbers of discordant monozygotic and sibling pairs and confidence intervals at each level of relatedness, combined with Mendelian randomization that uses instruments for heavy use or cannabis use disorder and methods robust to pleiotropy; and the controlled pre-post studies of schizophrenia incidence the authors propose.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the authors cite the studies they know of, and three of the four positive polygenic-score studies are not cited.

Some limitations are named (Mendelian randomization instruments for lifetime use only; a restricted sample in the null polygenic-score study; no significance test for monozygotic pairs), but not the co-relative design's sensitivity to measurement error and to non-shared confounders, nor the number of discordant pairs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only co-relative study, which carries the quantitative conclusion, is co-written by Kendler.

The more-than-half statement is presented as what the study suggests but depends on the scale and on an untested, inconsistently printed estimate; the expectation of zero genetic correlation under causation is asserted without justification; good evidence against hypothesis 3 is stronger than the evidence shown.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for causal and non-causal explanations
domains.note: Results pointing both ways are reported (an effect of liability to cannabis use; a monozygotic odds ratio above 1), but limitations that would bias the genetically informed designs towards finding confounding are not discussed. Under-represented: the weaknesses of the designs favoured by the viewpoint.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a viewpoint or narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the overall judgment follows the worst domain, the absence of a systematic search. The viewpoint is short, explicit about its hypotheses and expectations, and hedged in its conclusion, but its single quantitative claim rests on one study by one of its authors, printed inconsistently and not significance-tested at the decisive level. It may be cited for the framework (what each design should show under each hypothesis) and as a pointer to the co-relative and Mendelian randomization studies; the numbers belong to those primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Framing: cohort studies and meta-analyses show a robust association of cannabis use, heavy use and misuse with later schizophrenia, but adjusted models cannot determine how much is causal; for prevention, the causal proportion is critical. Three hypotheses are tested against four genetic methods (two natural experiments, discordant-relative designs and Mendelian randomization, and two measures of genetic association, genetic correlation by LD score regression and polygenic risk scores). Confounding means genetic risks raising both cannabis use and schizophrenia; reverse causality means schizophrenia liability or symptoms raising cannabis use. Short-term effects of cannabis administration are out of scope.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Opening section (untitled), 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Co-relative evidence: only one analysis is known (Giordano et al.). Schizophrenia was significantly increased among people with cannabis misuse, but the odds ratio fell as genetic relatedness increased, from 10.44 in the general population to 3.52 for discordant monozygotic twin pairs, a 66% decline, which the authors read as consistent with hypothesis 2 (partly causal, partly confounded) and as suggesting substantial confounding.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Natural Experiments, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Exposure: cannabis misuse (the cited study's title says cannabis abuse); outcome: schizophrenia. The viewpoint does not say what the population estimate was adjusted for, or how many discordant pairs there were. The Table gives a different monozygotic value (see reporting issues). Editors' cross-check and calculation: the Table (p. E2) gives 3.92; 66% matches 3.52; the log odds ratio falls by 46% (3.52) or 42% (3.92), and the excess odds by 73% or 69%.

key_findings.finding: Table summary of published results: discordant pairs, OR 10.44 for unrelated pairs, 5.07 for full siblings and 3.92 for monozygotic twins, consistent with hypothesis 2; Mendelian randomization, stronger evidence of reverse causality, consistent with hypothesis 2; genetic correlation 0.22 to 0.25 (modest pleiotropy) and schizophrenia polygenic scores predicting several cannabis phenotypes, each consistent with hypotheses 2 and 3. Footnotes: tests of significance were unavailable for monozygotic twin pairs; all 3 Mendelian randomization studies found no evidence of pleiotropy for their instruments.
key_findings.page: p. E2 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table, Summary of published results and Results consistent with rows; footnotes e and f

key_findings.finding: Mendelian randomization: using genetic variants as instruments, Vaucher et al. found that genetic liability to lifetime cannabis use was associated with a 37% increase in schizophrenia risk; Gage et al. and Pasman et al. found much stronger evidence that genetic liability to schizophrenia increased lifetime cannabis use (reverse causality). The instruments are associated with lifetime use, not heavy use or misuse. In aggregate the authors judge the results most consistent with hypothesis 2.
key_findings.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Natural Experiments, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The viewpoint does not state the unit of genetic liability behind the 37%; take it from the primary study (ref. 1, Vaucher et al.).

key_findings.finding: Measures of genetic association: the authors state that a genetic correlation or schizophrenia polygenic-score coefficient above zero is incompatible with an entirely causal association, while neither method can distinguish hypothesis 2 from 3. Two LD score regression studies reported significant genetic correlations of 0.22 to 0.25 between lifetime cannabis use or misuse and schizophrenia. One polygenic-score study, in a restricted sample, found no effect on cannabis misuse; four large population-based studies, including Verweij et al., found that high schizophrenia scores predicted more cannabis and comorbid substance use or misuse. Despite modest correlations and small effects, the authors conclude these show significant confounding inconsistent with hypothesis 1.
key_findings.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Measures of Genetic Association, 1st paragraph (p. E1, continued on p. E2)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: across the 4 methods, with considerable but not complete consistency, the findings argue against an entirely causal association; despite a modest number of studies, the evidence that the association stems partly from shared familial or genetic risk and/or reverse causation is called relatively reliable, and the evidence against an entirely non-causal association good; the 1 co-relative study suggests familial confounding is substantial and accounts for more than half of the association; genetic correlation and polygenic-score results suggest more modest confounding and raise the possibility of reverse causation. Prudent conclusion: some causal effect of cannabis on schizophrenia risk is possible, while an appreciable part of the association is not causal; claims about changing schizophrenia risk with changing cannabis use that are based on population associations without control for confounders are very likely exaggerated. Further co-relative and Mendelian randomization studies are needed, and controlled pre-post designs of schizophrenia incidence in states where cannabis use rose with decriminalization.
key_findings.page: p. E2 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Conclusions (one paragraph across both columns)

reporting_issues.issue: The monozygotic-twin odds ratio from the co-relative study is 3.52 in the text (p. E1), where the 66% decline is computed, and 3.92 in the Table (p. E2).
reporting_issues.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is wrong; the decline would be 62.5% with 3.92 (editors' calculation). Take the value from Giordano et al. (2015) before quoting either.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's Mendelian randomization cell cites refs 5 to 7, but ref. 7 (Hjorthoj et al.) is described in the text as the polygenic-score study that found no effect; footnote f refers to all 3 Mendelian randomization studies, which in the text are refs 1, 5 and 6.
reporting_issues.page: pp. E1-E2 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error in the Table; the reverse-causation Mendelian randomization evidence is refs 5 and 6, and ref. 1 is the study supporting an effect of cannabis-use liability.

reporting_issues.issue: Of the four large population-based polygenic-score studies said to show that schizophrenia scores predict cannabis use, only one (Verweij et al., ref. 8) is cited.
reporting_issues.page: p. E1 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the studies behind the polygenic-score conclusion cannot be identified from the viewpoint.
