design_detail: Longitudinal co-twin control study in the E-Risk Longitudinal Twin Study, a nationally representative birth cohort of same-sex twins born in England and Wales in 1994-1995. IQ was measured at 5 and 12 (before almost anyone had used cannabis) and again at 18; executive functions (CANTAB) only at 18. Cannabis was measured once, at 18: DSM-IV past-year dependence and self-reported past-year frequency. Full-sample regressions with twins nested in pairs (SAS SURVEYREG), and within-pair comparisons: 57 pairs discordant for dependence, and twin differences in frequency across 977 complete pairs, monozygotic and dizygotic pairs analysed together. Version read: the author manuscript deposited in PubMed Central (NIHMS894998), not the version of record.
can_establish: Whether adolescents who report cannabis use or meet criteria for dependence at 18 already had lower IQ at 5 and 12, whether their IQ fell more than their peers' between 12 and 18, and how much of the IQ and executive-function differences seen at 18 remain when twins from the same family who differ in cannabis use are compared.
cannot_establish: Effects of heavy, prolonged or adult use (use was measured once, as past-year use at 18, and 3% used daily or more often); any change in executive functions (measured only at 18) or effects on memory (not tested); the absence of a small or moderate effect (57 discordant pairs and no confidence intervals); or confounding by factors that differ between twins of the same family, such as alcohol, tobacco and other drug use, which do not enter these analyses.

sample.recruitment: Birth-register sample (E-Risk): 1,116 families with same-sex twins (93% of those eligible), drawn from a register of twins born in England and Wales in 1994-1995 and first visited at home at age 5 in 1999-2000 (2,232 children). Teenage mothers were over-selected to replace high-risk families lost to non-response and older mothers of twins conceived by assisted reproduction under-selected, so that the families span British socioeconomic conditions; their neighbourhood distribution is compared with national figures, with urban-prosperity areas under-represented (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Analytic sample: all cohort members with IQ data at ages 5, 12 and 18 (n=1,989; 96% of the 2,066 seen at 18). No exclusions by psychiatric history, substance use or medical condition are described (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: 47.26% male; 43.99% dizygotic pairs (56% monozygotic at intake); mean family SES 2.00 (SD 0.82) on a 1 to 3 scale; IQ standardized to mean 100 (SD 15) in the cohort at each age. Boys had slightly higher IQ at 12 and 18 and more past-year use (45.96% vs 30.03%) and dependence (6.06% vs 2.57%) than girls (Table 1). Ethnicity is not reported.
sample.attrition: Participation was 98% at 7, 96% at 10, 96% at 12 and 93% at 18 (n=2,066). Those seen and not seen at 18 did not differ at age 5 in SES (chi-square 0.86, p = .65), IQ (t = 0.98, p = .33), internalizing problems (t = 0.40, p = .69) or externalizing problems (t = 0.41, p = .68). The 77 people seen at 18 who lacked IQ data at one of the three ages are not compared with the analytic sample (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: A population-representative cohort of same-sex twins with high retention; whether the results apply to singletons is not discussed. Exposure was mostly light: 63% reported no past-year use, 28% use less than monthly, 3% monthly, 3% weekly, 2% daily and 1% many times a day; dependence affected 84 people. Heavy and prolonged use is therefore barely represented, which the authors name as a limitation (Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Interview at 18 only: DSM-IV criteria for past-year cannabis dependence (the interview instrument is not named in the main text) and self-reported past-year frequency on a six-point scale (never, less than monthly, monthly, weekly, daily, many times a day). No biological verification; the authors name possible under-reporting as a limitation (Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Past-year frequency at 18 only (distribution under sample.selection_effects); the within-pair correlation for frequency was r = 0.55. Age at first use, duration, cumulative use, route and product strength were not reported. Only 19 participants had tried cannabis by age 12, the last IQ assessment before exposure (Methods › Measures › Intelligence Quotient (IQ), 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. No alcohol, tobacco or other drug variable enters any reported model: covariates were sex, plus age-5 IQ in the IQ-change analyses and age-12 IQ in the executive-function analyses (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph). The within-pair comparison removes only influences that twins share.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. The age-18 IQ and CANTAB testing and the cannabis interview were all part of the age-18 phase of the study; whether participants had used cannabis shortly before testing is not reported or analysed.

comparison.controls: Full sample: adolescents without dependence (n=1,905), or less frequent use (frequency treated as a continuous score). Co-twin analyses: the co-twin without dependence in 57 discordant pairs; for frequency, within-pair differences in outcomes regressed on within-pair differences in frequency in all 977 complete pairs (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Co-twins share family environment, age and sex (same-sex pairs only) and all (monozygotic) or about half (dizygotic) of their segregating genes. Monozygotic and dizygotic pairs were analysed together to preserve power; the authors report little evidence that associations differed by zygosity, without showing the results (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Unusually, IQ was measured before cannabis initiation (ages 5 and 12) and is used as a covariate. Executive functions have no pre-use baseline. Twin-specific premorbid differences (for example childhood conduct or attention problems, or mental health) are not adjusted for; family SES was measured (Table 1) but does not enter the models.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported.

outcomes.instruments: IQ: age 5, WPPSI-R short form (Vocabulary and Block Design, pro-rated); age 12, WISC-R, and age 18, WAIS-IV, each pro-rated from the same two subtests (Information and Matrix Reasoning) and standardized within the cohort to mean 100, SD 15. Executive functions at 18 only: CANTAB Rapid Visual Processing (A prime; total false alarms), Spatial Working Memory (total errors; strategy) and Spatial Span forward and reversed, each standardized to mean 0, SD 1 (Methods › Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scores are standardized within the cohort rather than against published norms, so IQ change is change in standing relative to peers. Full-scale IQ is pro-rated from two subtests, and the 12-to-18 change score spans two Wechsler editions; reliability of the change scores is not reported. Test descriptions are in Supplemental Table 2 (not read).
outcomes.operationalization: IQ decline: age-18 minus age-12 pro-rated IQ (change score), with and without adjustment for age-5 IQ; the authors focus on 12 to 18 because both scores use the same two subtests. Executive-function impairment: a lower standardized score at 18 than the comparison group, with and without adjustment for age-12 IQ. All models adjusted for sex.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten outcome measures (IQ at 5, 12 and 18, IQ change, six CANTAB scores), each analysed for two exposures, in the full sample and within pairs, with and without baseline adjustment. The authors say the single significant within-pair result might be a false positive (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Dependence and IQ (Table 2; sex-adjusted means): full sample, dependent vs not, age 5: 95.18 vs 100.41 (difference -5.23, t = -2.94, p = .003); age 12: 94.95 vs 100.56 (-5.61, t = -3.11, p = .002); age 18: 93.14 vs 100.48 (-7.34, t = -5.27, p < .001); change 12 to 18: -1.81 vs -0.08 (difference -1.73, t = -1.27, p = .20; after age-5 IQ -2.02, t = -1.49, p = .14). Discordant pairs (57): age 5: 94.26 vs 93.50 (+0.76, p = .70); age 12: 93.97 vs 95.47 (-1.50, p = .43); age 18: 92.86 vs 94.31 (-1.45, t = -0.81, p = .42); change 0.05 (t = 0.02, p = .98). Frequency and IQ (Table 3; standardized betas): full sample age 5 -0.05 (p = .07), age 12 -0.11, age 18 -0.15 (both p < .001), change -0.05 (p = .035; -0.05, p = .023 after age-5 IQ); within pairs 0.02, 0.03, 0.00 and change -0.02 (p = .46). Dependence and executive functions (Table 4; z-scores): full sample worse on RVP A prime (-0.22 vs 0.02, p = .024), SWM strategy (0.21 vs -0.01, p = .017), Spatial Span Forward (-0.48 vs 0.02, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.33 vs 0.01, p < .001); after age-12 IQ only Spatial Span Forward (-0.35 vs 0.01, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.20 vs 0.01, p = .030); no difference within discordant pairs (all p >= .20). Frequency and executive functions (Table 5): full sample worse on 5 of 6 tests after age-12 IQ (betas -0.05 to -0.09, or 0.06 where higher is worse); within pairs only Spatial Span Reversed, beta -0.07 (p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ). No confidence intervals are printed. Editors' approximations (SE = estimate / t, or from the two-sided p; normal approximation, t with 56 df for discordant pairs): full-sample dependence and IQ change -1.73, 95% CI about -4.4 to +0.9 points; discordant-pair age-18 IQ difference -1.45, about -5.0 to +2.1; within-pair frequency and IQ change beta -0.02, about -0.07 to +0.03 SD (full sample -0.05, about -0.10 to -0.004); Spatial Span Forward, discordant pairs -0.20 SD, about -0.51 to +0.11, against -0.50 (about -0.71 to -0.29) in the full sample.
analysis.covariates: Sex in all models; age-5 IQ (IQ change) or age-12 IQ (executive functions) in the adjusted models; non-independence of twins handled by Taylor linearization (SAS SURVEYREG). No adjustment for SES, other substance use or psychiatric problems (Methods › Statistical Analyses).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No pre-registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All ages, change scores and six executive-function scores are tabulated for both exposures, both samples and both levels of adjustment. The sensitivity analyses (excluding the 19 people who had used cannabis by 12; Information and Matrix Reasoning separately; at least weekly use versus none) are in Supplemental Tables 3 to 7 and are summarized in one sentence each; zygosity-specific results are not shown; no confidence intervals are reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors note the discordant-twin analyses may have been underpowered and that many estimates were close to zero (Discussion, 5th paragraph). See the editors' approximate intervals under effect_sizes: the data exclude large IQ declines between 12 and 18 more firmly than they exclude executive-function differences.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1,989 twins followed from 5 to 18, those with past-year cannabis dependence at 18 (n=84) had lower IQ than the rest at 5 (by 5.23 points), at 12 (5.61) and at 18 (7.34), but their IQ did not fall significantly more between 12 and 18 (difference -1.73 points, p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI -4.4 to +0.9). Within 57 pairs discordant for dependence the twins with dependence did not differ from their co-twins at any age (differences between +0.76 and -1.50 points) or in change (0.05), and both twins in these pairs scored below the cohort mean. More frequent past-year use went with slightly greater IQ decline in the full sample (beta -0.05 SD per SD of frequency, p = .035) but not within pairs (beta -0.02, p = .46). Executive-function scores at 18 were lower with dependence on 4 of 6 CANTAB measures (2 of 6 after age-12 IQ) and with more frequent use on 5 of 6, but not within pairs, except Spatial Span Reversed for frequency (beta -0.07, p = .036; .022 after age-12 IQ).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that short-term adolescent use "does not appear to cause IQ decline or impair executive functions", even at the level of dependence, and that family background factors explain the poorer test performance (Abstract › Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs). Gaps: (1) duration of use was never measured: use was assessed once, as past-year use at 18, so short-term is the authors' inference; (2) the within-pair nulls come from 57 discordant pairs and are printed without confidence intervals; the editors' approximations include IQ differences of a few points and executive-function differences up to about half a standard deviation (Spatial Span Forward -0.20 SD within pairs against -0.50 SD in the full sample), so the data rule out large short-term IQ declines more firmly than effects on executive functions; (3) executive functions were measured only at 18, so the study shows that cross-sectional differences shrink within families, not whether these functions changed after use; (4) family background combines shared environment with only part of genetic influence, because monozygotic and dizygotic pairs were pooled, and factors that differ between twins (alcohol, tobacco, other drugs) were not measured; (5) the abstract reports little evidence of IQ decline, although the full-sample frequency analysis found a small significant one, which the Results and Discussion do report. Against this, the Discussion states the limits plainly (self-report, no memory tests, possible lack of power, rare intensive use) and presents the result as compatible with harm that appears only after years of heavy use.

timeline.event: Fried et al. (2002, 2005; refs 12 and 11), a cohort compared with its own pre-drug test performance; the 2005 report is one of the three studies with the greatest exposure that, the authors say, showed the strongest evidence of decline.

Meier et al. (ref. 8), Dunedin: described here as an 8-point IQ decline with dependence that persisted through adulthood and no decline with dependence only at 18; the authors say their null result does not conflict with it.
Rogeberg (2013), critique of the Dunedin analysis (socioeconomic confounding), and the reply by Moffitt et al. (2013): both in the project's Tier A list; neither is cited by this paper.
Hall (ref. 3), cited with other reviews for the consensus that heavy use is associated with neuropsychological impairment.
Broyd et al. (ref. 5), cited for the consensus and for previously inconsistent findings on working memory, the authors' reason to doubt their one within-pair result.
Curran et al. (ref. 6), cited for the consensus that heavy use is associated with neuropsychological impairment.
Auer et al. (ref. 9), CARDIA: with Dunedin, the longest follow-up and greatest exposure, and the strongest evidence of decline, as characterized here.

Jackson et al. (ref. 14), two US longitudinal twin studies with a co-twin design, and Mokrysz et al. (ref. 15, ALSPAC) and Castellanos-Ryan et al. (ref. 16): adolescent cohorts described as finding no IQ decline; Jackson et al. and Castellanos-Ryan et al. are the two cohorts said to find some evidence that lower IQ or executive functions preceded use.
Boccio and Beaver (ref. 17), on adolescent use and adult intelligence, grouped with the adolescent cohorts described as finding no IQ decline; the paper gives no further detail.
This study, published online 5 September 2017 (issue February 2018).

Scott et al., meta-analysis of cognition in adolescents and young adults (read in this round): cites this study, with Jackson et al. (2016), as large-scale evidence questioning cannabis as a cause of cognitive change once confounding and familial factors are taken into account.
Later tests in the project's lists, not cited here: co-twin control analyses by Schaefer et al. (2021, 2022) and the Dunedin follow-up at 45 (Meier et al., 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: One of the few designs that combine IQ measured before use with a within-family comparison. Its null result for adolescent IQ decline agrees with the other adolescent cohorts it cites (Jackson et al., 2016; Mokrysz et al., 2016; Castellanos-Ryan et al., 2016; Boccio and Beaver, 2017, as described here), whereas cohorts with longer and heavier exposure (Dunedin; CARDIA) reported decline; whether lower IQ precedes use is mixed across cohorts (by the authors' count, four of six found no earlier difference, two some). Claims should cite it for the absence of a detectable IQ decline between 12 and 18 at the mostly light exposure levels of a British birth cohort, and for familial confounding of IQ differences at 18, with the approximate intervals; not for the absence of effects of sustained heavy use, of effects on memory, or of effects on executive functions.

funding.funder: The E-Risk Study is funded by the UK Medical Research Council (grant G1002190), with additional support from NICHD grant HD077482 and the Jacobs Foundation; H. L. Fisher is supported by an MQ: Transforming Mental Health Fellowship (MQ14F40) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the PMC author manuscript contains no declaration-of-interests statement; the version of record, which may carry one, was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Arizona State University; Duke University (psychology and neuroscience; psychiatry); King's College London (MRC Social, Genetic and Developmental Psychiatry Centre; child and adolescent psychiatry); a London foundation trust. Meier, Caspi and Houts are among the listed authors of the Dunedin IQ report (ref. 8) that the Discussion reconciles with this null result. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A large population cohort that tests cognition, including memory, before any cannabis use and repeatedly afterwards, records frequency, product strength and duration at every wave, follows people with sustained heavy use into adulthood, and compares twins or siblings who differ in use while adjusting for alcohol, tobacco and other between-twin differences, reporting within-family estimates with confidence intervals; the authors point to the ABCD study (about 10,000 children followed from age 9-10) as the kind of cohort needed.

domains.note: Judged for the within-pair estimates that carry the conclusions: they remove shared family environment and part of genetic influence (fully only in monozygotic pairs, which were pooled with dizygotic pairs), but nothing that differs between twins, such as alcohol, tobacco, other drug use or childhood behaviour problems, is measured or adjusted. The full-sample estimates, adjusted only for sex and baseline IQ, are at high risk of confounding, which is the paper's own point.

One self-report of past-year frequency and a DSM-IV past-year dependence assessment, both at 18, with no biological check, age at onset, duration, cumulative use or potency. The 12-to-18 IQ change is set against use measured only at its end. Misclassification is probably unrelated to IQ change and so biases toward no association, more strongly for within-pair differences (twin correlation for frequency 0.55), which matters for a null result.
Population-representative birth cohort; 93% seen at 18 with no age-5 differences between those seen and not seen; 96% of those seen are analysed.
None relevant reported; treatment for cannabis problems is not mentioned.
1,989 of 2,232 children (89%) analysed; a few CANTAB scores missing (Ns 1,895 to 1,902 non-dependent, 83 to 84 dependent). The 77 seen at 18 without complete IQ data are not compared.

Standard tests, but IQ at 12 and 18 is pro-rated from two subtests of different Wechsler editions and standardized within the cohort; executive functions were measured only at 18; blinding of testers to cannabis use and recent use or intoxication at testing are not reported.

No pre-registration, but every IQ age, the change score and all six CANTAB scores are reported for both exposures, both samples and both adjustment levels; sensitivity analyses are summarized from the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The co-twin design with IQ measured before use is one of the stronger observational tests of whether adolescent cannabis use lowers IQ, and selection, attrition and reporting are well handled. The concerns are twin-specific confounding (no alcohol, tobacco or other drug measures), an exposure measured once at 18, and outcomes standardized within the cohort, with executive functions measured only once. Beyond bias, imprecision limits what the null can show: the within-pair estimates rest on 57 discordant pairs, no intervals are printed, and heavy use was rare. Cite it for: lower childhood IQ predating dependence; no detectable IQ decline from 12 to 18 with dependence or frequency, in the full sample or within pairs; familial confounding of IQ differences at 18. Do not cite it for: the absence of effects of sustained heavy use, effects on memory, or a change in executive functions.

key_findings.finding: E-Risk cohort: 2,232 children from 1,116 families with same-sex twins (93% of those eligible) assessed at 5 in 1999-2000; participation 98% at 7, 96% at 10 and 12, 93% at 18 (n=2,066). Those seen and not seen at 18 did not differ at age 5 in SES, IQ, internalizing or externalizing problems (all p >= .33). 1,989 participants (96% of those seen at 18) had IQ at 5, 12 and 18: 47.26% male, 43.99% dizygotic.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Exposure at 18: 84 participants (4%; 4.22% in Table 1) met DSM-IV criteria for past-year cannabis dependence; of 977 complete pairs, 908 were concordant for no dependence, 12 concordant for dependence and 57 discordant. Past-year frequency: never 63%, less than monthly 28%, monthly 3%, weekly 3%, daily 2%, many times a day 1%; twin correlation for frequency r = 0.55. 37.56% had used in the past year (girls 30.03%, boys 45.96%). Only 19 participants had tried cannabis by age 12.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Measures › Intelligence Quotient (IQ), 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Exposure is past-year use at 18 only; no measure of age at onset, duration, cumulative use or potency.

key_findings.finding: Full sample, dependence (n=84) vs no dependence (n=1,905), sex-adjusted mean IQ: age 5, 95.18 vs 100.41 (difference -5.23, t = -2.94, p = .003); age 12, 94.95 vs 100.56 (-5.61, t = -3.11, p = .002); age 18, 93.14 vs 100.48 (-7.34, t = -5.27, p < .001). Change from 12 to 18: -1.81 vs -0.08 points (difference -1.73, t = -1.27, p = .20). After adjustment for age-5 IQ: age 12, -2.80 (p = .08); age 18, -4.82 (t = -3.88, p < .001); change, -2.02 (t = -1.49, p = .14).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 1st paragraph; Table 2, full-sample rows
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (SE = difference / t, normal approximation): 95% CI for the difference in change about -4.4 to +0.9 IQ points (-4.7 to +0.6 after age-5 IQ). IQ is standardized within the cohort at each age, so change means change relative to peers.

key_findings.finding: 57 pairs discordant for dependence, sex-adjusted mean IQ of the twin with dependence vs the co-twin without: age 5, 94.26 vs 93.50 (+0.76, t = 0.39, p = .70); age 12, 93.97 vs 95.47 (-1.50, t = -0.80, p = .43); age 18, 92.86 vs 94.31 (-1.45, t = -0.81, p = .42); change 12 to 18, -1.11 vs -1.16 (0.05, t = 0.02, p = .98); similar after age-5 IQ. Both twins in discordant pairs scored below the cohort mean, which the authors read as family factors confounding the full-sample association.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, Discordant Twins rows
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (t with 56 df): age-18 difference -1.45, 95% CI about -5.0 to +2.1 points; the interval for the change score cannot be computed reliably from the printed t of 0.02.

key_findings.finding: Results for the full sample and the discordant pairs were similar after excluding the 19 participants who had used cannabis by age 12, and for the Information and Matrix Reasoning subtests separately.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and IQ, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Values are in Supplemental Tables 3 to 5, not read.

key_findings.finding: Frequency of past-year use at 18 (standardized betas, sex-adjusted): full sample (n=1,989) age-5 IQ -0.05 (p = .07), age-12 IQ -0.11 (p < .001), age-18 IQ -0.15 (p < .001), IQ change 12 to 18 -0.05 (p = .035; -0.05, p = .023 after age-5 IQ), described as an additional decline of 0.05 SD per SD of frequency. Within pairs (977 pairs): 0.02 (p = .56), 0.03 (p = .32), 0.00 (p = .94) and change -0.02 (p = .46; .47 after age-5 IQ). At least weekly use versus none: little evidence of greater IQ decline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and IQ, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (SE from the two-sided p, normal approximation; betas rounded to two decimals): within-pair change beta about -0.07 to +0.03 SD; full sample about -0.10 to -0.004. The weekly-use comparison is in Supplemental Table 6, not read.

key_findings.finding: Dependence and executive functions at 18 (sex-adjusted z-scores, dependent vs not): full sample worse on RVP A prime (-0.22 vs 0.02, t = -2.26, p = .024), SWM strategy (0.21 vs -0.01, t = 2.40, p = .017; higher is worse), Spatial Span Forward (-0.48 vs 0.02, t = -4.57, p < .001) and Spatial Span Reversed (-0.33 vs 0.01, t = -3.37, p < .001); not on RVP false alarms (p = .83) or SWM errors (p = .07). After age-12 IQ, only Spatial Span Forward (-0.35 vs 0.01, t = -3.60, p < .001) and Reversed (-0.20 vs 0.01, t = -2.17, p = .030). Discordant pairs: no significant differences on any test (p = .20 to .72); for example Spatial Span Forward -0.38 vs -0.18 (t = -1.30, p = .20).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Executive functions were measured only at 18 (no pre-use baseline). Editors' calculation (t with 56 df): the discordant-pair Spatial Span Forward difference of -0.20 SD has a 95% CI of about -0.51 to +0.11, compatible with the full-sample difference of -0.50 (about -0.71 to -0.29).

key_findings.finding: Frequency and executive functions at 18 (standardized betas): in the full sample (n=1,978 to 1,985) more frequent use went with worse performance on every test except RVP false alarms, also after age-12 IQ (for example Spatial Span Forward -0.13, then -0.09; both p < .001). Within pairs (967 to 974 pairs) the associations were not significant except Spatial Span Reversed, beta -0.07 (p = .036; -0.07, p = .022 after age-12 IQ), which the authors call small and possibly a false positive. At least weekly use versus none gave similar findings.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and Executive Functions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5; Discussion, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The weekly-use comparison is in Supplemental Table 7, not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors place their result beside earlier cohorts: of six cohorts with tests before first use, four found no evidence that lower IQ preceded use and two found some; across nine cohorts with repeated testing, those with the longest follow-up (Dunedin; CARDIA) and greatest exposure showed the strongest evidence of decline, and adolescent cohorts with light use the weakest.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded, after the Abstract), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the per-study details are in Supplemental Table 1, not read.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion describes its own group's Dunedin report as showing an 8-point IQ decline in people with dependence persisting through adulthood and no decline in people dependent only at 18, and calls the adolescent null results consistent with it and with four recent cohorts, one using a co-twin design.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure from Meier et al. (2012); claim writers should take Dunedin numbers from that paper (see reporting issue 4: the Discussion's time frame and its single-wave statement are inaccurate).

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-reported use without biological tests; no tests of memory; discordant-twin analyses possibly underpowered, although many estimates were close to zero; intensive use (many times a day) at 1% prevalence was too rare to test, and very large cohorts such as ABCD (about 10,000 children followed from 9-10 for 10 years) are needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: short-term adolescent use does not appear to cause IQ decline or impair executive functions, even at the level of dependence; family background explains the poorer test performance of adolescents who use cannabis; neuropsychological functions should be tested before initiation; impairment may develop only with long-term persistent use, which needs further research.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: UK Medical Research Council (G1002190), NICHD (HD077482), the Jacobs Foundation and an MQ fellowship (MQ14F40). No declaration of interests in the author manuscript.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments

reporting_issues.issue: The within-pair association of frequency with Spatial Span Reversed is given as beta -0.07, p = .036 in the abstract and as p = .022 in the Results text; Table 5 shows these are the estimates before and after adjustment for age-12 IQ, and neither place says which model it reports.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Findings; Results › Associations between Frequency of Cannabis Use and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a claim should name the model (p = .036 sex-adjusted, p = .022 also adjusted for age-12 IQ).

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence interval is printed for any estimate, and the within-pair results (57 discordant pairs) are summarized as showing no differences.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see what size of effect the null results exclude; the editors' approximations under analysis.effect_sizes show intervals compatible with IQ differences of a few points and executive-function differences of up to about half a standard deviation within pairs.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 63% for no past-year use at 18, while Table 1 gives 37.56% with past-year use in the analytic sample, which implies 62.44% (editors' arithmetic); the frequency percentages may refer to all 2,066 seen at 18.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures › Cannabis Use, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote Table 1 for the analytic sample.

reporting_issues.issue: Within-pair estimates pool monozygotic and dizygotic pairs; the statement that associations differed little by zygosity is not supported by any reported estimate.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of the familial confounding that is genetic cannot be judged; family background in the conclusions means shared environment plus part of genetic influence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the Dunedin result as an 8-point IQ decline 'from age 18–38' in people whose dependence persisted through adulthood, and says that people dependent only at 18 did not show IQ decline. Meier et al. (2012) measured change from childhood IQ (mean of ages 7 to 13) to 38 and had no IQ test at 18; in its Fig. 2 the matching group (dependence before 18 at one wave, 17 people) changed by about −0.22 SD (about 3 points), not significantly different from adult onset (p = .44), with no test against no change; and the 8 points refer to the 23 people with adolescent-onset dependence at 3 or more waves, read from a figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion misstates the time frame and the single-wave result of the 2012 Dunedin paper; Dunedin figures should be taken from Meier et al. (2012) itself (this round's Broyd et al. and Curran et al. cards record that reviews give the decline as about 6 or about 8 points).

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC author manuscript has no declaration-of-interests statement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Conflicts cannot be recorded from the version read; the version of record should be checked when the reference record is built.

Read in the app's browser on 2026-10-27: all sections, Tables 1 to 5 (rendered as text) with their notes, acknowledgments, author information and the reference list. The supplement (one PDF: Supplemental Tables 1 to 7, with the overview of earlier cohorts, test descriptions, the analyses excluding the 19 people who had used cannabis by 12, the subtest analyses and the weekly-use sensitivity analyses) was not opened; the findings flagged in the key-finding notes depend on it, the main results do not.

design_detail: Systematic review of population-based longitudinal studies (cohorts, or case-control studies nested in cohorts) of cannabis use and later psychotic or affective outcomes, with DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis of adjusted odds ratios where studies were judged homogeneous enough, and narrative synthesis otherwise. Ten databases searched from inception to 5 September 2006 without language limits. 35 reports included: 11 on psychosis from 7 cohorts and 24 on affective outcomes (depression, depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation or attempts, anxiety) from 15 cohorts. Funded by the UK Department of Health.
can_establish: The average adjusted association, in general-population cohorts published up to 2006, between ever use or the most frequent use of cannabis and later psychotic outcomes (mostly self-reported or interview-rated psychotic symptoms; three cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome) and depression, and how much adjustment for measured confounders reduced each cohort's crude association.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes psychosis or depression (all included studies are observational, and the authors state that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out), the size of any causal effect, effects of potency or of age at first use (no robust data), or absolute risks (none are pooled; the lifetime risk of less than 3% in the conclusion is given without a source).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ISI Web of Knowledge, ISI Proceedings, ZETOC, BIOSIS, LILACS and MEDCARIB from inception to 5 September 2006, plus reference lists of included studies and other reviews, and letters to experts and study investigators for published and unpublished studies (pp. 319-320). Psychosis cohorts: five adult population cohorts (ECA, USA; EDSP, Germany; NEMESIS, Netherlands; NPMS, UK; 1969 Swedish conscripts) and two New Zealand birth cohorts (Dunedin; Christchurch, CHDS). Affective cohorts: the two birth cohorts, six adult population cohorts (Berkeley, ECA and New York state, USA; NPMS, UK; Northern Rivers, NoRMHS, Australia; Colombia) and seven school-based cohorts (Victoria, Australia; AddHealth, Baltimore, Chicago, LA schools, LAT and NY schools, USA) (pp. 320-321).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: population-based longitudinal studies or case-control studies nested within them. Excluded: cohorts of people with mental illness or substance-use problems, prison populations, and randomized trials of cannabis for medical use (different pharmacokinetics from recreational cannabis, short follow-up). Every psychosis outcome required delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder (schizophrenia and related disorders, affective or non-affective psychoses, psychotic symptoms); affective outcomes covered mood and bipolar disorders, depression, suicidal ideation or attempts, anxiety, neurosis and mania. Search restricted to human studies, not by language or design (pp. 319-320).
sample.demographics: Not given in the article: per-study sample sizes, ages, sex and follow-up are in webtables 1 and 2 (online supplement, not read). The main text gives country and cohort type only.
sample.attrition: Within the included cohorts: loss to follow-up 4% to 32% in the psychosis cohorts (no attrition data for the Swedish conscripts), and 4% to 70% (median 20%) in the affective cohorts, not reported for two. The authors judge from attrition modelling in CHDS, NEMESIS and NoRMHS that attrition had little effect on the findings (pp. 322, 324, 326).
sample.selection_effects: General-population cohorts by design, which avoids the clinical selection of case-control and cross-sectional samples. The psychosis evidence rests on seven cohorts, two of them (Dunedin, CHDS) with additional analyses supplied by the investigators and one Swedish analysis unpublished (Zammit S); the affective NPMS data come from a personal communication. Excluding treatment and psychiatric samples means the review says nothing about people already in services. Per-study data needed to reconstruct the pools are only in the webtables.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use measured before the outcome in each cohort; no biological verification. Psychosis analyses: ever use in all cohorts except NPMS, where the measure was use in the past year (Figure 1 legend); most frequent use was daily use in CHDS, ECA and EDSP, weekly use in NEMESIS, dependence in NPMS and use more than 50 times by conscription in the Swedish cohort (Figure 2). Affective analyses used ever use, current use, use less than weekly or at least monthly, at least weekly or heavy use, frequency trends, and cannabis misuse disorder (Figures 3 to 6 legends).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable as dose. The pooled most-frequent-use estimates combine categories ranging from more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use and dependence, so they describe the top category of each cohort, not one exposure level. Route not reported. The authors note large variation in the cannabinoid content people actually take in and error in self-reported frequency (p. 325).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled through each study's own adjustment. The discussion states that all psychosis studies reporting an association adjusted for other drug use (two not for alcohol), but Figure 2 marks three of the six most-frequent-use estimates (EDSP, NEMESIS, NPMS) as not adjusted for other drug use (see reporting issues). Roughly half the affective studies made no adjustment for alcohol or other drug use. The authors note that under-reporting of stimulant use, which is commoner in people who use cannabis, could inflate associations (p. 326).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Intoxication at outcome assessment was addressed only partly: the interview instruments used in ECA, NEMESIS, Dunedin and EDSP instruct the interviewer to exclude symptoms arising solely from drug use; the SCL-90 (CHDS) and the psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS) cannot separate intoxication; no affective study explicitly excluded intoxication or withdrawal effects (pp. 322, 324-325).

comparison.controls: People in the same cohorts who had never used cannabis (ever-use estimates) or did not use it (most-frequent-use estimates).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjusted estimates from each study's own models were pooled. About 60 confounders were adjusted for across the psychosis studies (other substance use, personality traits, sociodemographic markers, intellectual ability, other mental-health problems) and about 50 across the affective studies (family and peer relationships, adverse life events, criminality, mental-health problems, sociodemographic markers, other substance use); the set used by each study is in the webtables (not read).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychotic symptoms at baseline were excluded (ECA, NEMESIS, NPMS, Swedish conscripts) or adjusted for (EDSP, Dunedin, CHDS), but three psychosis studies (EDSP, NEMESIS, Dunedin) made no adjustment for other mental disorders at baseline, two (NEMESIS, Dunedin) none for alcohol, and the authors judge the baseline tools unlikely to capture all symptoms (p. 325). Family history of psychosis, genetic liability, childhood adversity and sub-threshold prodromal symptoms are not discussed as adjustment variables. For affective outcomes, only four studies excluded people with affective symptoms at baseline and seven neither excluded nor adjusted (p. 324).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported per study; comparison groups were defined by cannabis use only.

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis: SCL-90 (CHDS), Diagnostic Interview Schedule (Dunedin, ECA), Munich CIDI (EDSP), CIDI (NEMESIS), psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS), ICD clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia at hospital admission (Swedish conscripts) (Table 1). Affective: CES-D, DIS, DISC, CIDI, CIS-R, SCL-90, Hopkins symptom checklist, an NIMH interview, and DSM or ICD-10 diagnoses (Table 2; Figures 3 to 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was assessed descriptively: sampling, response rates, missing data, attrition, and how each study limited reverse causation, intoxication effects and confounding (Tables 1 and 2). No scored tool.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis outcomes were pooled on the stated assumption that they lie on a continuum from self-reported symptoms to a clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia. Six of the seven psychosis cohorts had a symptom outcome without any requirement for impaired functioning; three had a psychotic-disorder outcome with impaired functioning (Dunedin schizophreniform disorder, NEMESIS needs-based diagnosis, Swedish conscripts hospital admission for schizophrenia). Depression outcomes were diagnoses or above-threshold scale scores.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six pooled estimates: four main (any psychotic outcome by ever use and by most frequent use; psychotic disorder by ever use; depression by most frequent use) and two sensitivity analyses omitting NEMESIS. Depressive symptoms, suicidality and anxiety were synthesized narratively.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility was judged and data extracted independently and in duplicate, with disagreements resolved by consensus; screening of titles and abstracts is not described as duplicate (p. 320).

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian and Laird random-effects pooled adjusted odds ratios (Stata metan), with I-squared and a heterogeneity p value; no tau-squared or prediction intervals. Any psychotic outcome, ever use versus never: OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65), 7 cohorts, I2 19.2%, heterogeneity p=0.28. Most frequent use versus none: 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84), 6 cohorts, I2 44.1%, p=0.11; without NEMESIS 1.92 (1.50 to 2.47), I2 25.0%, p=0.26. Psychotic disorder, ever use: 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13), 3 cohorts, I2 66.9%, p=0.049; without NEMESIS 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30), I2 48.3%, p=0.16. Depression, most frequent use: 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), 8 estimates from 7 cohorts, I2 29.6%, p=0.192. Egger test: psychosis p=0.48 (7 studies), depression p=0.13 (10 studies). Adjustment reduced the crude psychosis associations by about 45% on average (range 10% to 80%), measured as the share of the crude excess odds removed. Population attributable fraction, assuming causality and 40% ever use: about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) of psychotic outcomes in young UK adults.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; the per-study adjustment sets are in the webtables. Because adjusted estimates from different models were pooled, no single adjustment set lies behind a pooled odds ratio.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. Full search details, eligibility record forms, the list of excluded studies and a MOOSE compliance summary are said to be on the authors' departmental website (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The review did not pool depression by ever use because exposure measures were too heterogeneous (p. 323), yet it pooled depression by most frequent use across at-least-weekly use, at-least-monthly use, heavy use, dependence and misuse disorder, including one unadjusted estimate (NoRMHS). The sensitivity analyses drop NEMESIS because it contributed most to heterogeneity, a data-driven choice. Per-study results behind the narrative syntheses are only in webtable 2.
analysis.power: The authors calculate that more than 230 events were needed for 80% power to detect a depression odds ratio of 1.5 and judge that about half the depression studies were underpowered (p. 323). The publication-bias tests rest on 7 and 10 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In seven general-population cohorts, ever use of cannabis was associated with 1.41 times the adjusted odds of a later psychotic outcome, mostly self-reported or interview-rated symptoms; the top use category of each cohort (from more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use or dependence) with 2.09 times the odds; and the three cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome gave 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13) with I2 67%, or 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30) without NEMESIS. Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort). Four of the seven adjusted ever-use estimates have intervals that exclude 1 (editors' count from Figure 1). Evidence for depression was weaker (most-frequent-use pool 1.49, 1.15 to 1.94) and less protected against reverse causation and confounding; suicidality and anxiety were not pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says the evidence is consistent with the view that cannabis increases the risk of psychotic outcomes independently of confounding and transient intoxication, that results restricted to psychotic disorders were similar, and that there is sufficient evidence to warn young people (p. 319); the conclusion repeats the warning and puts individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorder, even with regular use, at "likely to be low (less than 3%)" without a source (p. 327). Gaps: (1) the discussion itself says residual confounding can never be eliminated and that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out (pp. 325, 327), so independence from confounding holds only for the measured confounders; (2) intoxication was addressed in some cohorts only (Table 1); (3) the disorder estimate is nearly twice the any-outcome estimate, rests on three cohorts with substantial heterogeneity and has a lower limit near 1 without NEMESIS, which the word similar understates; (4) the dose-response wording rests on top-use categories that differ between cohorts and include three estimates not adjusted for other drug use. The authors are explicit that their attributable fraction assumes causality (p. 326) and present the warning as a policy judgment under uncertainty (p. 327).

timeline.event: Andreasson et al., Swedish conscript cohort (the review's ref. 28); with the 2002 follow-up by Zammit et al. (ref. 29) and a Zammit PhD thesis (ref. 30) it supplies the review's schizophrenia estimates (ever use 1.50, 1.11 to 2.02; more than 50 times 3.10, 1.72 to 5.58).
Dunedin (Arseneault et al., ref. 31) and NEMESIS (van Os et al., ref. 26) cohorts: the two other psychotic-disorder outcomes in the pooled disorder estimate.
Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (ref. 60): schizophrenia incidence has not tracked trends in cannabis use, used as an argument against a causal effect; the review cites it and the reply below.

Earlier syntheses compared in Table 3: Arseneault et al. 2004 (narrative review with meta-analysis), Macleod et al. 2004 (systematic review of psychosocial outcomes, no meta-analysis), Semple et al. 2005 (systematic review), Henquet et al. 2005 (narrative review); the meta-analyses among them included cross-sectional data, unadjusted results or combined ever use with dependence, and all reported larger effects.

Caspi et al. (ref. 32): COMT Val158Met moderation of the cannabis-psychosis association in Dunedin, and Henquet et al. 2006 (ref. 56), an experimental test; the review judges the evidence for this effect modification very weak (both seen only in subgroups).

Hickman et al. (ref. 61): model projections in which time lags and unreliable incidence data mean changes in schizophrenia incidence may not yet be visible; cited by the review against the trends argument.
This review, published with an editorial (p. 292) and a comment (p. 293) in the same Lancet issue (not read).

Gage, Hickman and Zammit (narrative review; Zammit is an author of both) restate this review's three pooled estimates and re-pool ever use with two later cohorts (Zurich, ALSPAC): 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), I2 19%, methods not given.
Ksir and Hart, critical overview arguing for shared vulnerability; it does not cite this review or the cohorts pooled in it.
Gillespie and Kendler, viewpoint triangulating genetically informed designs: the association is judged partly causal and partly confounded or reverse-causal.

replication.where_it_stands: The first systematic review restricted to longitudinal population studies, and the source of the most quoted pooled figures (1.41 for ever use; 2.09 for the most frequent use). Gage et al. (2016), with Zammit as a shared author, re-pooled with two later cohorts and obtained 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72). The estimates are observational: Gillespie and Kendler (2021) read genetically informed designs as showing an appreciable non-causal share of the association, and Ksir and Hart (2016) argue that the whole association reflects shared vulnerability; neither re-analyses these cohorts. Claims must not count this review and the cohorts pooled in it, or Gage et al.'s re-pooling, as independent support.

funding.funder: Department of Health, UK; Zammit funded through a Clinician Scientist Award from the National Assembly for Wales (Acknowledgments, p. 327). The paper states that the sponsor had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing, and that the corresponding author had full access to the data and final responsibility for submission (Role of the funding source, p. 320).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 327): Jones and Barnes were invited experts on the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs cannabis review in 2005. Zammit, Jones, TJ (initials that match no author), Lewis and Lingford-Hughes have received honoraria for lectures and talks or consultancy fees from pharmaceutical companies, for work unrelated to cannabis. Lingford-Hughes has received an honorarium from Sanofi-Aventis for attending a meeting about cannabinoid antagonists, consultancy fees from Bristol Myers Squibb and unrestricted research monies from Merck. Barnes has received consultancy fees from Servier, Johnson & Johnson and Bristol-Myers Squibb regarding antipsychotic medication. Moore and Burke have no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Universities of Bristol, Cardiff and Cambridge, and Imperial College London. Zammit and Lewis are authors of included reports (the 2002 Swedish conscript follow-up, ref. 29; the NPMS psychosis report, ref. 27), Zammit's PhD thesis (ref. 30) and an unpublished Zammit analysis are used, and the affective NPMS data are a personal communication from a Bristol colleague. Selection and extraction were in duplicate, but no procedure for appraising the authors' own studies is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis of general-population cohorts with repeated, biologically checked measures of cannabis use and potency taken before any psychotic symptoms, clinically diagnosed psychotic disorder as the outcome, a common adjustment set (family history, childhood adversity, other drug use, prodromal symptoms) and a sibling or other genetically informed comparison that estimates the part of the association that is familial.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population longitudinal studies; cannabis use (ever, frequency); comparison with no use; psychotic and affective outcomes defined (pp. 319-320).

No protocol or statement that methods were fixed in advance; eligibility forms and a MOOSE summary are said to be on a departmental website. The data-driven sensitivity analyses (omitting NEMESIS) are not justified against a plan.

Restriction to population-based longitudinal studies is explained: medical-cannabis trials differ in pharmacokinetics and follow-up, and earlier reviews were weakened by cross-sectional data (p. 319).

Ten databases including conference-proceedings indexes (ISI Proceedings, ZETOC), no language or design limit, reference lists, letters to experts and investigators for unpublished studies, two PhD theses included; search to September 2006 for a July 2007 publication. Full strategy on a departmental website (not read); the search format is given in the text (p. 320).

Eligibility was judged independently and in duplicate with consensus (p. 320). Title and abstract screening is not described as duplicate; if the item is read as requiring duplicate screening at every stage, it becomes no (non-critical; overall unchanged).
Data extracted independently and in duplicate (pp. 319-320).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 143 full texts excluded, with near misses, are said to be detailed on the senior author's departmental website (p. 320), which was not read; whether each exclusion is justified cannot be judged from the article.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article gives cohort type, country, exposure and outcome definitions (Figures 1 to 6 legends) and each study's handling of reverse causation, intoxication and confounding (Tables 1 and 2); sample sizes, ages, sex and follow-up are only in webtables 1 and 2 (not read), which may meet the item in full.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Confounding, reverse causation, intoxication, attrition and response were assessed per study (Tables 1 and 2), but measurement of the exposure was not appraised study by study and selection of the reported result was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of adjusted estimates with stated grounds for pooling (judged homogeneity; a stated continuum of psychosis measures), and no trials mixed in. A close call: the depression pool includes one unadjusted estimate (NoRMHS) without a stated reason, three of the six most-frequent-use psychosis estimates are not adjusted for other drug use, top-use categories differ between cohorts, and no tau-squared or prediction interval is given.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by study quality (for example excluding cohorts that could not separate intoxication or did not exclude baseline psychosis); the only sensitivity analyses omit NEMESIS for heterogeneity.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs reverse causation, intoxication, residual confounding, attrition and misclassification and states that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out (pp. 325-327).
Heterogeneity is reported for every pool and discussed (the SCL-90 outcome in CHDS; NEMESIS), with sensitivity analyses (pp. 321, 325).
Funnel plots and Egger tests: psychosis p=0.48 (7 studies), depression p=0.13 (10 studies); the authors note the psychosis test rests on only seven studies (pp. 321-322, 325).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, role of the funder and authors' interests are stated (pp. 320, 327); the statement does not flag that review authors wrote included reports.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 (list of excluded studies with reasons) can be judged only from the authors' departmental website, which was not read. With item 2 judged no (no protocol stated), the review has one critical flaw, which gives low confidence; if the excluded-studies list proves missing or unjustified, a second critical flaw would make it critically low. Items 9 (partial yes) and 10 and 12 (no) are further weaknesses. Strengths are real: a broad search without language limits that sought unpublished data, duplicate selection and extraction, restriction to longitudinal population studies, per-study appraisal of reverse causation, intoxication and confounding, random-effects pooling of adjusted estimates and publication-bias tests. The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries; the review remains a sound map of the cohort evidence to 2006, and its pooled odds ratios remain observational associations, as the authors say.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 10 databases from inception to 5 September 2006, no language limit, plus reference lists and contact with experts; 4804 references, of which 175 (3.6%) were read in full and 143 excluded. Included: 11 psychosis reports from 7 cohorts (ECA, EDSP, NEMESIS, NPMS, Swedish conscripts, Dunedin, CHDS) and 24 affective reports from 15 cohorts.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Methods; Methods › Study selection and data collection, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The summary's 35 studies count reports per outcome group (11 + 24); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Any psychotic outcome, ever use versus never use: pooled adjusted OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65), heterogeneity p=0.28, I2 19.2%, 7 cohorts. Adjusted ORs by cohort (Figure 1): CHDS 1.28 (1.04 to 1.57), Dunedin schizophreniform disorder 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04), ECA 1.30 (0.98 to 1.73), EDSP 1.67 (1.13 to 2.46), NEMESIS 2.11 (0.78 to 5.71), NPMS 0.72 (0.30 to 1.74), Swedish conscripts schizophrenia 1.50 (1.11 to 2.02). Egger test p=0.48. Unadjusted results of all studies showed increased risk, reduced but persisting after adjustment in six.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 320); Results, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 321)
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who had never used cannabis. Adjustment: each cohort's own confounder set (listed in webtable 1, not read). Exposure was past-year use in NPMS. Persisting in six refers to point estimates above 1; four of the seven adjusted intervals exclude 1 (editors' count). Psychosis outcomes range from self-reported symptoms to hospital diagnosis of schizophrenia.

key_findings.finding: Most frequent use versus no use: pooled adjusted OR 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84), heterogeneity p=0.11, I2 44.1%, 6 cohorts: CHDS daily 1.56 (1.20 to 2.03), ECA daily 2.00 (1.27 to 3.16), EDSP daily 2.23 (1.30 to 3.83), NEMESIS weekly 6.81 (1.79 to 25.91), NPMS dependence 1.47 (0.55 to 3.93), Swedish conscripts more than 50 times 3.10 (1.72 to 5.58). Without NEMESIS: 1.92 (1.50 to 2.47), p=0.26, I2 25.0%. All six studies that examined frequency reported results consistent with a dose-response effect.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th and 9th paragraphs; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who did not use cannabis. Adjustment: each cohort's own model, but Figure 2 marks the EDSP, NEMESIS and NPMS estimates as not adjusted for other drug use. The top category differs between cohorts (more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use or dependence).

key_findings.finding: Psychotic disorder (psychotic symptoms with impaired functioning) in three cohorts (Swedish conscripts, hospital admission for schizophrenia; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder from additional unstratified data supplied by the investigators; NEMESIS, needs-based diagnosis), ever use: pooled adjusted OR 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13), heterogeneity p=0.049, I2 66.9%. Without NEMESIS: 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30), p=0.16, I2 48.3%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th and 9th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Comparison: never use; adjustment as in each cohort's own model. The NEMESIS disorder estimate itself is not given in the main text (webtable 1, not read).

key_findings.finding: Age at first use: in Dunedin the effect on psychotic symptoms was stronger for first use before 16, with much weaker evidence for schizophreniform disorder (very wide intervals); in the Swedish conscripts, accounting for cumulative use, risk of schizophrenia did not differ by first use before or after 16. The authors conclude no robust evidence shows that earlier use is more harmful; the Dunedin pattern could reflect greater cumulative exposure.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (p. 321); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 325)

key_findings.finding: Putative interactions: in Dunedin, crude OR 10.9 (2.2 to 54.1) for schizophreniform disorder in valine homozygotes at COMT Val158Met versus 1.1 (0.21 to 5.4) in methionine homozygotes, seen only in people who first used before 18. In EDSP the association was stronger in psychosis-prone groups, but these already had psychotic features at baseline. The authors call the evidence for COMT effect modification very weak.
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 321); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 325)

key_findings.finding: Reverse causation and intoxication in the psychosis cohorts (Table 1): ECA, NEMESIS, NPMS and the Swedish conscripts excluded people with psychosis at baseline; EDSP, Dunedin and CHDS adjusted for baseline symptoms, which the authors note mixes incidence with persistence or relapse; a Swedish analysis restricted to admissions at least 5 years after conscription gave similar results; structural equation modelling in CHDS suggested cannabis predicted later symptoms rather than the reverse. The SCL-90 (CHDS) and the psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS) cannot identify symptoms caused by intoxication.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 14th and 15th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Confounding: the psychosis studies adjusted for about 60 different confounders; fully adjusted estimates were smaller than crude ones by an average of about 45% (range 10% to 80%), computed as (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1): CHDS 65%, Dunedin 10%, ECA 30%, EDSP 15%, NEMESIS 50%, NPMS 80%, Swedish conscripts 60%. Fixed-effects regression in CHDS for unmeasured stable confounders changed little; adjustment for other substance use attenuated ECA and NEMESIS substantially; in the Swedish conscripts the strongest confounders were IQ, urban upbringing and other mental disorders. Loss to follow-up 4% to 32%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (last column and footnote); Results, 16th and 17th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Consistent with the text by the editors' calculation: the mean of the seven Table 1 values is 44.3%.

key_findings.finding: Depression: 15 cohorts; Egger test p=0.13 (ten studies). Of ten studies with a diagnosis or an above-threshold score, five reported an association persisting after adjustment (two only in subgroups) and no ever-use pool was made because exposure measures differed. More than 230 events would be needed for 80% power to detect an OR of 1.5, so about half the studies were probably underpowered. Most frequent use versus none, pooled adjusted OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), heterogeneity p=0.192, I2 29.6%: CHDS at least weekly 1.70 (1.03 to 2.79), Colombia 1.31 (0.95 to 1.80), ECA 4.00 (1.23 to 12.99), NoRMHS 1.39 (0.32 to 6.02, unadjusted), NPMS dependence 0.90 (0.22 to 3.63), NY state heavy use 1.62 (1.11 to 2.36), Victoria at least weekly, men 0.47 (0.17 to 1.30) and women 1.90 (1.10 to 3.29).
key_findings.locator: Results, 18th paragraph (pp. 322-323) and 20th paragraph (p. 323); Figure 4 (p. 323)
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who did not use cannabis. Adjustment: each study's own model, except NoRMHS (unadjusted, calculated by the reviewers from published tables); outcomes were diagnoses or above-threshold scale scores.

key_findings.finding: Suicidality and anxiety, not pooled: of seven studies of suicidal ideation or attempts, four reported an association in adjusted analyses and one little evidence, and the LA schools cohort reported fewer attempts but more ideation (Figure 5: Baltimore 1.80, 1.02 to 3.17; CHDS 1.43, 1.22 to 1.67; ECA 4.55, 1.37 to 15.11; Chicago men 1.21 and women 0.64, unadjusted). Of seven anxiety studies, two reported an association persisting after adjustment (Figure 6: NY state 1.16, 1.00 to 1.35; Colombia 1.48, 1.10 to 2.00); the ECA obsessive-compulsive disorder association (2.90, 1.11 to 7.57) appeared in a matched sample but not in the whole sample with an unconditional analysis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 21st and 22nd paragraphs; Figures 5 and 6

key_findings.finding: Affective studies' handling of bias (Table 2): only four excluded people with affective symptoms at baseline, ten reports adjusted for the baseline outcome, and seven did neither; none explicitly excluded intoxication; five presented only unadjusted results. In six of eight studies with crude and adjusted results, adjustment reduced the association by 10% to 100%; in two (ECA obsessive-compulsive disorder; Baltimore suicidal ideation) it increased. Comprehensive adjustment in CHDS removed associations with depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation, although the depression association persisted at a longer follow-up. Attrition 4% to 70%, median 20%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 25th to 28th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors judge reverse causation an unlikely explanation for the psychosis associations, because most psychosis studies excluded people with psychosis at baseline, but not for the affective associations; residual confounding can never be eliminated from observational studies; and confounding seems more likely to explain the affective than the psychotic associations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Population impact and time trends: with about 40% of UK adolescents and young adults having ever used cannabis and a causal OR of 1.4, about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) of psychotic outcomes in young UK adults would not occur without cannabis; the authors stress that this assumes the association is causal and the pooled estimate accurate. Projected schizophrenia incidence has not followed cannabis trends (Degenhardt et al., ref. 60), but other projections suggest time lags and unreliable incidence data (Hickman et al., ref. 61).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th and 11th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The method behind the printed interval is not stated. By the editors' calculation, Levin's formula with the pooled interval (1.20 to 1.65) gives about 7% to 21%.

key_findings.finding: Previous syntheses (Table 3): the meta-analyses in Semple et al. (2005), Arseneault et al. (2004) and Henquet et al. (2005) included cross-sectional data, used unadjusted estimates or combined ever use with dependence, and all reported larger effects than this review.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and Discussion, 13th paragraph (p. 326); publication years from the reference list, refs 15, 17 and 19 (p. 327)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: a consistent association between cannabis use and psychotic symptoms, including disabling psychotic disorders, which may result from confounding or bias that cannot be ruled out; enough evidence to inform people that cannabis could increase their risk of a psychotic illness later in life; weaker evidence for affective outcomes. The authors suggest the more pertinent question is whether the evidence justifies policy such as public education. They put individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, even with regular use, at less than 3%.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 15th and 16th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The less-than-3% lifetime risk has no citation or calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that all psychosis studies reporting an association adjusted for other drug use (two not for alcohol), but the Figure 2 footnote marks the EDSP (2.23), NEMESIS (6.81) and NPMS (1.47) most-frequent-use estimates as not adjusted for other drug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Half the estimates behind the pooled most-frequent-use OR of 2.09 (the summary's dose-response figure) lack adjustment for other drugs; claims should not describe that figure as adjusted for other drug use.

reporting_issues.issue: Four of seven studies of suicidal ideation or attempts are cited as refs 10, 37, 47 and 49; ref. 10 is Renault et al. (1974), a laboratory study of repeated marihuana smoke administration, not a cohort. Figure 5 includes an ECA estimate, so an ECA report (ref. 40 or 41) may have been meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the cohorts behind the suicidality statement must be identified from Figure 5, not from the reference numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary reports 35 studies, whereas 175 full texts minus 143 exclusions leaves 32 references. The 35 are reports counted per outcome group (11 psychosis + 24 affective): two Dunedin reports (refs 31, 32) are counted in both groups and the affective NPMS data are a personal communication. The reports come from 18 distinct cohorts (7 + 15, with CHDS, Dunedin, ECA and NPMS in both; editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe the evidence as 7 cohorts for psychosis and 15 for affective outcomes, not 35 independent studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 3 to 6 are titled as adjusted odds ratios, but footnotes mark some estimates as unadjusted (NoRMHS and NY schools in Figure 3; NoRMHS in Figures 4 and 6; Chicago in Figure 5). The pooled depression OR of 1.49 includes the unadjusted NoRMHS estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled depression estimate is not wholly adjusted; NoRMHS's wide interval (0.32 to 6.02) gives it little weight, so the effect on the pooled value is probably small.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says depression odds ratios for the highest weekly or monthly exposure categories ranged from 1.3 to 1.6, the ECA misuse-disorder study excepted; Figure 4 shows CHDS at least weekly 1.70, Victoria at least weekly 1.90 in women and 0.47 in men, and NPMS dependence 0.90.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the spread of the depression estimates; Figure 4 values should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The population attributable fraction is printed as about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19), and the method for the interval is not stated. By the editors' calculation, Levin's formula with 40% exposure and the pooled interval 1.20 to 1.65 gives about 7% to 21%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point estimate reproduces, and the figure is conditional on causality in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts of affective studies differ between paragraphs: suicidal ideation or attempts in six studies and anxiety in five plus one (p. 321), but seven studies each later (p. 323). Figure 6 includes NPMS and Victoria (combined depression and anxiety outcomes), which are not among the seven anxiety references cited in the text, while the cited LA schools reports (refs 51, 52) are not in Figure 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reports and cohorts are counted interchangeably; study counts for suicidality and anxiety should be taken from the figures with their cohorts named.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflict-of-interest statement lists TJ among those who received honoraria; no author has these initials.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error; the declaration should be reported as printed with this noted.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's column of approximate change from crude to adjusted odds ratio, computed as (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1), does not say which exposure contrast each cohort's figure refers to. For NPMS the 80% cannot refer to the ever-use estimate pooled in Figure 1 (adjusted OR 0.72), for which the formula would exceed 100% for any crude OR above 1; it fits the dependence estimate of Figure 2 (1.47) with a crude OR of about 3.35 (editors' calculation). The average of about 45% (range 10% to 80%) given in the text may therefore mix ever-use and most-frequent-use contrasts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 45% (10% to 80%) describes how much adjustment shrank the cohorts' associations for unstated contrasts; claims should not attach it to the pooled ever-use odds ratio of 1.41 in particular.
