key_findings.locator: Abstract; introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (starts p. e1); Article Information, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. e19); Reviewer Disclosures table (p. e20)

key_findings.finding: The AHA's overall cardiovascular judgment: evidence on cannabis use and adverse cardiovascular outcomes is “still inconclusive”, with an urgent need for carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies and, ideally, controlled trials of different forms and routes, which the authors say remain hard to do for recreational drugs.
key_findings.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: No well-documented cardiovascular benefits of cannabis (summary of Table 2, refs 5, 12, 13, 17, 18); the abstract says cannabis may have therapeutic benefits but few are cardiovascular. For people with cardiac risk factors the statement judges the present evidence for a link between cannabis use and health outcomes insufficient, citing limited longitudinal data and recall bias in cross-sectional studies.
key_findings.page: pp. e1, e8, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. e1); Potential and Known Benefits, paragraph (p. e8); Considerations in Special Populations › Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)

key_findings.finding: Weaknesses of the cardiovascular literature as the statement names them (citing the DeFilippis et al. 2020 review, ref 20, and a NIDA web page, ref 25): most data are short-term, observational and retrospective; exposure is poorly determined and open to recall bias; exposure is minimal, with no dose or product standardisation; cohorts are typically low-risk; epidemiological studies may be confounded by access to health care and other behaviours such as tobacco use; older studies may not reflect current, higher THC concentrations; few data come from rigorous prospective cohorts. Studies restricted to hospitalised patients analyse only a fraction of the people with an outcome and carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; tobacco and other drug co-use is inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment.
key_findings.page: pp. e9–e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. e9), 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9) and 4th paragraph (p. e10)

key_findings.finding: Table 3 (“Seminal Studies”) lists 25 studies (refs 19 and 26–49) without a selection rule or quality rating: 7 National Inpatient Sample analyses (refs 27, 33–36, 41, 45), other hospital or health-record data (refs 31, 32, 40, 49), two surveys (NHANES, ref 28; PATH Through Life, ref 38), 4 papers from CARDIA (refs 29, 30, 46, 48), an HIV cohort (ref 42), two papers from the Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study (refs 37, 43), a pharmacovigilance series (ref 39), vital statistics around medical cannabis laws (ref 26), one ED chart review (ref 19) and two systematic reviews of case reports and studies (refs 44, 47). Confidence intervals are printed in 5 rows; three rows give no figures in the results column (Auer, Bancks, Lorenz).
key_findings.page: pp. e11–e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, all rows; Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9)

key_findings.finding: CARDIA, incident disease (Reis et al., 2017, ref 46): 5113 adults aged 18–30 at the 1985–1986 baseline, followed for more than 25 years; 84% reported a history of cannabis use. Cumulative lifetime and recent use (units not given) showed no association with incident cardiovascular disease, stroke or TIA, coronary heart disease or cardiac mortality. No estimates, intervals or adjustment set are printed.
key_findings.page: pp. e9–e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 3rd paragraph (starts p. e9); Table 3, row Reis et al (p. e12)
key_findings.note: The text cites this finding to ref 29 (Auer et al., 2018) and omits stroke or TIA; Table 3 and the reference list give it to ref 46 (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Other CARDIA papers as relayed: Auer et al., 2018 (ref 29; 3498 participants): among people who had ever smoked tobacco, marijuana exposure was associated with higher abdominal aortic and coronary artery calcium scores, and among people who had never smoked tobacco it was not (no numbers). Bancks et al., 2015 (ref 30; more than 3000): cannabis use in young adulthood associated with higher risk of prediabetes but not diabetes by middle adulthood (no numbers). Rodondi et al., 2006 (ref 48; 3617 with 15 years of data): 38% had ever used cannabis; use was associated with male sex, tobacco and other illicit drug use, higher caloric and alcohol intake, systolic blood pressure (113–117 mm Hg) and triglycerides, but not with BMI, lipids or glucose; after multivariable adjustment it was not associated with systolic pressure or triglycerides.
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e11, e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, rows Auer et al and Bancks et al (p. e11) and Rodondi et al (p. e13)
key_findings.note: The text cites the calcification finding to ref 46 instead of ref 29 (reporting issue). Ever-use is 84% in one CARDIA row and 38% in another, with no definitions.

key_findings.finding: Triggering (Mittleman et al., 2001, ref 43; Determinants of Myocardial Infarction Onset Study, case-crossover, 3882 people with AMI): risk of MI onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after cannabis use (no interval printed). 3% had smoked cannabis in the prior year; 37 within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of AMI presentation. People who used cannabis were more often men, cigarette smokers and obese. The statement adds that observational studies suggest cannabis may trigger AMI (refs 86, 87) and that the risk may be related to the timing of use.
key_findings.page: pp. e12, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, row Mittleman et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from the statement's own numbers: the 4.8-fold estimate rests on few exposed people; the statement says 9 had smoked within 1 hour of AMI presentation (the timing used in the primary paper should be taken from Mittleman et al., 2001). Ref 37 (Frost et al., 2013) follows the same study, so the two rows are not independent. The primary paper is on this project's Tier B list.

key_findings.finding: Outcomes after MI, as relayed: long-term mortality 29% higher in people who used cannabis than in those who did not, not significant (95% CI 0.81–2.05; P = 0.28) (Frost et al., 2013, ref 37; 3886 MI survivors, National Death Index). In young adults with MI at two academic hospitals 2000–2016 (DeFilippis et al., 2018, ref 32; n = 2097), adjusted HRs of 1.99 for all-cause and 2.22 for cardiovascular mortality among people who used cocaine and marijuana (no intervals; whether the two exposures were combined is not said); the text says cannabis use was present in 6% of patients aged 50 or under with AMI. In hospital records from 8 states 1994–2013 (Johnson-Sasso et al., 2018, ref 40; more than 1.2 million AMI patients, 3854 or about 0.3% reporting cannabis use), the composite outcome (death, intra-aortic balloon pump, mechanical ventilation, cardiac arrest, shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval; short-term outcomes by the reference title); Desai et al., 2017 (ref 34) also report lower mortality in AMI patients who used cannabis. Smaller studies are said to show a signal toward higher mortality in coronary disease, although many of these findings were not statistically significant (refs 37, 87).
key_findings.page: pp. e11, e12, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows DeFilippis et al, Desai et al (ref 34) and Frost et al (p. e11) and Johnson-Sasso et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17)

key_findings.finding: AMI in health-record and inpatient databases, as relayed (exposure is recorded cannabis use or diagnosis codes; comparators are other patients in the same database; adjustment mostly not stated): Chami and Kim, 2019 (ref 31; Explorys 2011–2016; 292,770 people with a history of cannabis use, labelled the “cannabis abuse group”, against more than 10 million controls): 3-year cumulative AMI incidence 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53 (95% CI 2.45–2.61). Desai et al., 2019 (ref 33; National Inpatient Sample 2007–2014, more than 52 million hospitalisations, cannabis without other substance use): AMI admissions in young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%; arrhythmia and stroke more frequent, venous thromboembolism less frequent. Desai et al., 2017 (ref 34; 2010–2014): adjusted OR for AMI 1.079 (1.065–1.093); 35,771 of more than 2.4 million patients with AMI had a history of cannabis use. Patel et al., 2018 (ref 45; 2010–2014, 379,843 primary AMI admissions): 3.3% had a cannabis-use-disorder codiagnosis; AMI admissions among people who used cannabis rose 32% over 5 years (P = 0.001), mean age 41, with a 38% rise in women. Desai et al., 2018 (ref 35; 465,959 hospitalisations with recreational cannabis use): 1.2% for AMI, 1% for heart failure, 0.8% for arrhythmia, AMI rising from 1.4% to 1.8% over 2010–2014.
key_findings.page: pp. e11–e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Chami and Kim and Desai et al (refs 33, 34, 35) (p. e11) and Patel et al (ref 45) (p. e12)
key_findings.note: Five of the inpatient analyses include the years 2010–2014 and four share a first author, so they are not independent replications. The ref 34 and ref 35 rows cannot be right as printed (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Heart failure, arrhythmia and stroke in inpatient data, as relayed: Kalla et al., 2018 (ref 41; National Inpatient Sample 2009–2010, more than 316,000 aged 18–55): in multivariable regression cannabis use predicted heart failure (OR 1.1) and stroke (OR 1.24), no intervals. Adegbala et al., 2018 (ref 27; about 4 million patients with heart failure): atrial fibrillation less frequent in people who used cannabis (19% vs 21%). Desai et al., 2018 (ref 36; 2010–2014): of 2,459,856 hospitalised people who used cannabis, 66,179 (2.7%) had arrhythmias, most often atrial fibrillation, rising from 2010 to 2014; in-hospital mortality in those with arrhythmia rose from 3.7% to 4.4%; no comparison group is reported. The text adds that case reports and observational studies support a temporal relationship with atrial fibrillation, though the evidence conflicts (refs 20, 22, 36).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e11, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, rows Adegbala et al and Desai et al (ref 36) (p. e11) and Kalla et al (p. e12)

key_findings.finding: Stroke, as relayed: PATH Through Life (Hemachandra et al., 2016, ref 38; age cohorts 20–24, 40–44 and 60–64 years, surveyed 1999–2002): people with past-year cannabis use (n = 1043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or TIA (95% CI 1.8–6.3; P < 0.001), IRR 2.3 (1.1–4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking; the excess was in people using weekly or more often (IRR 4.7, 2.1–10.7; adjustment not stated), with no elevation at lower frequency. BRFSS (Parekh et al., 2020, ref 68; adults aged 18–44): stroke adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08–3.10) for people who used marijuana against those who did not, 2.45 (1.31–4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40–6.97) for frequent use with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07–6.46) with e-cigarettes (adjustment set not stated). Against these, CARDIA found no association with stroke or TIA (ref 46).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e12, e14, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Hemachandra et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)
key_findings.note: Cohort sizes differ between text (2404, 2530, 2551) and Table 3 (2383, 2525, 2547), and the text gives only the 3.3 before adjustment for stroke-related covariates (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Population trends around legalisation, as relayed: cardiac death rates rose 2.3% in men and 1.3% in women after medical cannabis laws (Abouk and Adams, 2018, ref 26; US vital statistics 1990–2014; design not described). Colorado (Wang et al., 2017, ref 49; more than 7 million hospitalisations and ED visits 2000–2015, plus poison-centre data): 0.3% of hospitalisations had cannabis-related billing codes, rising from 274 to 593 per 100,000 hospitalisations between 2000 and 2015; cannabis-related ED visits rose from 313 to 478 per 100,000 between 2011 and 2015; poison-centre calls rose after medical and recreational legalisation. French addictovigilance 2006–2010 (Jouanjus et al., 2014, ref 39): 35 of 1979 cannabis-related reports were cardiovascular, their share rising from 1.1% to 3.6%.
key_findings.page: pp. e10–e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, rows Abouk and Adams (p. e11), Jouanjus et al (p. e12) and Wang et al (p. e13)
key_findings.note: The text says AMI hospitalisations and ED visits rose in states with legal cannabis (refs 26, 48), but none of these rows reports AMI-specific admissions (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Case-based and other studies, as relayed: a systematic review of published cases (Patel et al., ref 44; 62 patients with AMI and cannabis use): mean age 28, mostly men, AMI within 5 hours of last use, normal coronary angiograms in 37% and left anterior descending occlusion in 42% of angiograms. A systematic review of 85 studies, case reports and series (Richards et al., 2019, ref 47; 541,581 adults): 28 of 33 studies suggested higher risk of acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease; of 51 case reports or series with 62 people, 21 (34%) had cardiomyopathy and 14 deaths (23%) were attributed to acute coronary syndrome. HIV cohort (Lorenz et al., 2017, ref 42; 558 HIV-positive men, Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study 1990–2010): long-term heavy use independently associated with more cardiovascular events at ages 40–60 (no numbers). The text adds that AMI with cannabis occurs mostly in young men without ischaemic disease (refs 20, 22, 36).
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Lorenz et al, Patel et al (ref 44) and Richards et al (p. e12); Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (p. e10)
key_findings.note: Both reviews count 62 case patients; whether their case sets overlap cannot be checked from the statement. Table 3 dates ref 44 to 2019, the reference list to 2020.

key_findings.finding: Route (Monte et al., 2019, ref 19, as relayed in Table 3: one Colorado academic hospital 2012–2016, described as 9973 adult ED visits for cannabis use): people who had eaten cannabis more often had cardiovascular symptoms (8%) than people who had inhaled it (3%), and more often acute psychiatric symptoms and intoxication; inhaled cannabis was more often linked to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; cannabis-related visits rose 2012–2016. The text says eating cannabis “appears more likely” than smoking to cause adverse effects prompting acute care, particularly psychiatric and cardiovascular, citing Health Canada (ref 5) and attributing this to greater systemic absorption and a slower onset and peak.
key_findings.page: pp. e9, e12 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Acute Effects, 1st paragraph (starts p. e8; this passage on p. e9); Table 3, row Monte et al (p. e12)
key_findings.note: The library's card on the primary paper (sc_monte_2019) records 9,973 visits with a cannabis-related code, of which 2,567 were judged attributable to cannabis; the 8.0% vs 3.1% comparison is among 238 edible-attributed and 2,329 inhaled-attributed visits. Cite the primary card.

key_findings.finding: Acute effects and mechanisms, summarised from reviews (refs 5, 12, 13, 19 for acute effects; refs 20–22 for mechanisms and Figure 5): short-term use has been associated with tachycardia, premature ventricular contractions, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmia, bronchitis, blurred vision, altered judgment, dysphoria and anxiety, paranoia and psychosis at higher doses, and impaired motor coordination. THC stimulates the sympathetic and inhibits the parasympathetic nervous system, increases heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, supine blood pressure and platelet activation, and is associated with endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress; CBD may lower heart rate and blood pressure. Figure 5 lists cardiomyopathy, MI, arrhythmias and sudden death, cerebral vascular accidents, and a questioned anti-atherogenic effect of CB2 activation.
key_findings.page: pp. e8–e9 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Acute Effects, 1st paragraph (starts p. e8); Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 1st paragraph (p. e9); Figure 5 (p. e9)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: refs 20–22 are reviews (DeFilippis et al., 2020; Pacher et al., 2018; Rezkalla and Kloner, 2019, co-authored by a writing-group member).

key_findings.finding: Smoke and carbon monoxide: compared with tobacco, smoking cannabis “regardless of THC content” is said to raise blood carboxyhaemoglobin 5-fold with 3-fold more tar (ref 23, Wu et al., 1988). Carbon monoxide intoxication is associated with endothelial dysfunction, lipoprotein oxidation, impaired oxygen binding and presentations from angina and AMI to cardiogenic shock and sudden death (ref 24, Kaya et al., 2016, a study of carbon monoxide poisoning).
key_findings.page: p. e9 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The clinical presentations come from carbon monoxide poisoning, not from cannabis smoking. NASEM 2017 (sc_nasem_2017) gives about four times the carbon monoxide and three to five times the tar for a 15-volunteer comparison; whether it is the same study cannot be checked here. Read Wu et al. (1988) before citing a multiple.

key_findings.finding: People with heart disease: in chronic stable angina, smoking one cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo (ref 88, Aronow and Cassidy, 1974); in coronary disease with angina, cannabis use went with lower end-diastolic volume, stroke index and ejection fraction without change in end-systolic volume or cardiac index (ref 89, Prakash et al., 1975); sample sizes are not given. From NHANES 2005–2016, about 2 million (2.3%) of the 89.6 million US adults who reported marijuana use had cardiovascular disease (ref 20). The statement reasons that because cannabis raises myocardial oxygen demand and lowers supply, people with ischaemic disease could have more angina, particularly when it is smoked.
key_findings.page: p. e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Peripheral arteries: smoking cannabis has been associated, controversially, with a cannabis arteritis resembling thromboangiitis obliterans; more than 20% of lower-limb arteriopathy in young adults may be due to it, an estimate the statement says may be confounded because 97% of people who smoke cannabis also smoke tobacco (ref 50, Cottencin et al., 2010, a literature review; ref 51, a case report). It recommends considering cannabis arteritis in adults under 50 with peripheral vascular disease.
key_findings.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiometabolic risk factors, as relayed: NHANES 2005–2012 (Alshaarawy et al., 2016, ref 28; 12,426 adults): cannabis use associated with higher systolic but not diastolic blood pressure, β = 1.6 (95% CI 0.6–2.7; units and adjustment not stated). Cross-sectional data link long-term continual use with metabolic syndrome (ref 91), while other studies report similar or lower rates of hyperglycaemia, raised fasting glucose and diabetes, and lower BMI, total and LDL cholesterol, in people who use cannabis (refs 92–98); Table 2 lists an observational association of long-term use with an improved metabolic profile.
key_findings.page: pp. e8, e11, e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 2, row Metabolic syndrome, obesity, diabetes mellitus (p. e8); Table 3, row Alshaarawy et al (p. e11); Considerations in Special Populations › Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17)

key_findings.finding: Smoke and lungs, as summarised: cannabis smoke contains many of the carcinogens and mutagens of tobacco smoke (refs 5, 12, 20); limited and conflicting epidemiological evidence has not shown a robust and consistent association with cancers (ref 52, Ghasemiesfe et al., 2019, JAMA Network Open), with low-strength evidence for testicular cancer and mixed, confounded findings for lung cancer; the association of long-term heavy smoking without tobacco with COPD is unclear, though chronic bronchitis has been reported (refs 5, 12). For COVID-19 only tobacco figures are given (severe symptoms RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.98–2.00; ICU, ventilation or death RR 2.4, 1.43–4.04; ref 53); whether the risk extends to cannabis is said to be unknown.
key_findings.page: p. e10 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Smoking and Vaping Administration Concerns, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref 52 is the 2019 cancer review by Ghasemiesfe et al., not the 2018 respiratory review held as ghasemiesfe_2018.

key_findings.finding: Vaping and impurities: as of 18 February 2020, 2807 hospitalised patients with e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury and 68 confirmed deaths (29 states and DC) had been reported to CDC (ref 55, CDC web page); most patients reported THC-containing products; CDC linked THC products from informal sources to most cases without excluding nicotine products; vitamin E acetate was identified as a possible cause from a relatively small number of tissue samples (ref 56, Blount et al., 2019, MMWR). The statement nonetheless concludes that cannabis vaping should be avoided. It also cites an FDA warning (June 2018) about synthetic illicit cannabinoid products laced with brodifacoum (ref 54) and says unregulated over-the-counter topical CBD products may contain heavy metals, herbicides, pesticides and fungicides.
key_findings.page: pp. e10, e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Impurities, 1st paragraph (starts p. e10) and 2nd paragraph (p. e13)
key_findings.note: Ref 56 is the 2019 MMWR report, not the 2020 NEJM paper held as blount_2020. The brodifacoum source (ref 54) concerns synthetic cannabinoids, not cannabis.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis: the statement says significant preclinical, clinical and epidemiological evidence supports an association between cannabis, especially THC-predominant cannabis, and higher risk of psychosis and schizophrenia, particularly in people with a predisposition and those who start in early adolescence (refs 5, Health Canada, and 12, NASEM 2017; no primary study cited). From EU-GEI (ref 67, Di Forti et al., 2019; multicentre case-control): daily use against never use, adjusted OR 3.2 (95% CI 2.2–4.1) for psychotic disorder; daily use of high-potency cannabis (THC 10% or more) described as nearly 5 times the odds but printed as adjusted OR 3.2 (3.0–16.1) and described against low-potency cannabis (THC below 10%); the statement adds that the study did not account for genetic and environmental factors. It recommends that THC-predominant cannabis not be used by people with a personal history of psychiatric disorders (psychosis, schizophrenia, anxiety, mood disorders), a history of substance use problems, or a family history of schizophrenia.
key_findings.page: pp. e13, e14, e18 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph (p. e13); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patient Education and Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e17; this passage on p. e18)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the high-potency figures cannot all be right (reporting issue) and no adjustment set is given. Cite Di Forti et al. (2019) from its own card.

key_findings.finding: Cognition and brain, from Health Canada, NASEM 2017 and Volkow et al., 2014 (refs 5, 12, 13; no primary study): early-onset use, typically before age 16–18, has been associated with reports of poorer sustained attention, lower overall or verbal IQ and worse executive functioning; neuroimaging studies suggest regular adolescent use “may lead to” altered cortical grey-matter development and reduced white-matter myelination. No effect sizes, comparison groups, tests or abstinence periods are given.
key_findings.page: p. e14 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Depression and suicidality: a meta-analysis of 11 studies with 23,317 people assessed from adolescence to young adulthood (ref 66, Gobbi et al., 2019) found OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.16–1.62) for depression, 1.5 (1.11–2.03) for suicidal ideation and 3.46 (1.53–7.84) for suicide attempt in people who used cannabis against those who did not; the statement contrasts this with small observational reports of improved mood and anxiety in older adults. In US adults aged 50 or more (NESARC 2012–2013, ref 77), past-year cannabis use went with mental disorders in 33.2%, against 26.5% of people who had used cannabis only in the past and 19.4% of people who never had, possibly driven by self-medication (refs 78, 79).
key_findings.page: pp. e14, e16 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Geriatric Population, 1st paragraph (p. e16)

key_findings.finding: Dependence: the statement says “addiction” to cannabis has been reported in about 9% of people who use it, 17% of those who start in adolescence and 25% to 50% of those who use daily; this sentence carries no citation (the sentence before cites refs 57 and 58). From the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (ref 58, Hasin et al., 2016, whose title in the reference list names DSM-5 cannabis use disorder and NESARC-III, 2012–2013): 3 in 10 people who used cannabis in the past year met criteria for cannabis use disorder, a 30% prevalence the statement calls greater than that of alcohol use disorder (17.5%; denominator not stated). Named risk factors for use disorder: more edible use and vaping, higher THC and lower CBD content, younger age at first use (refs 59, 60). Prevalence may be underestimated, the statement says, because estimates rest on self-report and may use DSM-IV criteria without craving or withdrawal (ref 60). Tolerance develops with long-term use through reduced CB1 receptor availability (ref 20); withdrawal symptoms begin a few days after stopping or cutting down, peak at about 10 days and end after about 30 days (refs 5, 12).
key_findings.page: pp. e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph; Addiction Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e13); References, ref 58 (p. e21)
key_findings.note: Definitions differ: the uncited 9%, 17% and 25–50% figures have no stated definition or denominator; Hasin et al. counted DSM-5 use disorder among people who used in the past year; the DSM-IV caveat concerns other estimates (ref 60). Leung et al. (2020, sc_leung_2020) pools 22% for use disorder and 13% for dependence.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: in a state with legalised medical and recreational cannabis (ref 70, Crume et al., 2018; the statement does not name the state), self-reported cannabis use during pregnancy was 5.7% ± 0.5% and early postnatal use among breastfeeding women 5.0% (95% CI 4.1–6.2); prenatal use was associated with low birth weight, OR 1.5 (1.1–2.1; P = 0.02), independent of maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use. A meta-analysis (ref 71, Gunn et al., 2016) found anaemia in pregnancy OR 1.36 (1.10–1.69) and infant low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04–3.01), with a pooled mean difference in birth weight of 109.42 g (38.72–180.12; direction not stated). THC has been found in breast milk up to 6 days after the last recorded use (ref 69, US Surgeon General's 2019 advisory). The statement relays ACOG (2017) and AAP (2018) advice against use in pregnancy and discourages use while breastfeeding.
key_findings.page: pp. e14, e16 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph (p. e14) and 2nd paragraph (starts p. e14, continues p. e16)

key_findings.finding: Product strength and pharmacokinetics: newer commercial products are said to have a higher average THC content than products sold before 1996, 3.8% in the 1990s against 12.2% in 2014 (refs 13, Volkow et al., 2014, and 14, Klein, 2017, both secondary). Table 1 (no row-level sources; drawn from refs 5 and 7–11) gives for THC: inhaled onset seconds to minutes, bioavailability 2%–56%, duration 2–3 h; oral onset 30 min to 2 h, bioavailability 4%–20%, duration 5–8 h; half-life 20–30 h; protein binding 97%.
key_findings.page: pp. e3, e5 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Definitions and Cannabis Formulations, 3rd paragraph (p. e3); Table 1, THC row (p. e5)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; cite primary potency and pharmacokinetic sources on this project's lists instead. The DOSING section (pp. e4, e6, e8) is not extracted, by project rule.

key_findings.finding: Table 2 rows without row-level citations (footnote sources: Health Canada, NASEM 2017, Volkow et al., 2014, Segura et al., 2019, Wu et al., 2019): long-term (about 6–7 years) daily and weekly use has been associated with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, possibly through CB1 downregulation and slower gastric emptying; human experimental data suggest a dose-dependent effect on sleep (shorter sleep-onset latency and more slow-wave and total sleep at low doses, disturbed sleep at high doses); in a nationally representative US sample, use at least once a month, but not less often, was associated with incident social anxiety disorder; in a retrospective propensity-matched analysis of 161,000 patients with heart failure, cannabis use went with lower in-hospital mortality (OR 0.197, 0.046–0.833), shorter stay (4.2 vs 4.8 days; P = 0.004) and lower costs (US$43,800 vs US$50,900; P = 0.039), data the table says have not been peer reviewed.
key_findings.page: pp. e7–e8 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows Nausea and vomiting and Anxiety and depression (p. e7) and Heart failure and Sleep (p. e8)
key_findings.note: The heart failure figures match the title of ref 18 (Wu et al., 2019, J Card Fail 25:S158, a meeting-abstract supplement).

key_findings.finding: Advice and policy: smoked or vaporised cannabis is generally not recommended, especially with asthma or COPD, and black- or grey-market products should be avoided; driving should be avoided because blood THC concentrations of 2–5 ng/mL are said to be associated with substantial driving impairment (ref 100, Hartman and Huestis, 2013, a review). Policy (Table 5 and closing section): remove cannabis from Schedule 1, standardise THC and CBD labelling and a unit of consumption, regulate CBD products, fund research, integrate cannabis into tobacco control and prevent use by minors; clinicians should be alert that cannabis or potent synthetic analogues might underlie severe cardiovascular events. Patient education (p. e18, no citation): people with long-term heavy use should be advised not to stop suddenly because of the risk of cannabis withdrawal syndrome, and to contact their provider if signs of withdrawal or hyperemesis syndrome arise.
key_findings.page: pp. e17–e19 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Patient Education and Considerations, paragraph (starts p. e17); Table 5 (p. e18); Policy Considerations and Future Directions, paragraph (starts p. e18)
key_findings.note: The driving threshold is second-hand; Hartman and Huestis (2013) is on this project's Tier B list. The advice on stopping is the AHA's recommendation without cited evidence; it is recorded here as such, not as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Transplantation: at least 7 US states forbid denying transplant listing for medical cannabis use (refs 83, a news article, and 84); in a web survey of heart-transplant providers in 26 countries (ref 84), 64.4% supported listing patients who use legal medical cannabis, 68.3% required a documented period of abstinence and 27.5% supported listing patients using legal recreational cannabis; inhaled cannabis may expose immunocompromised patients to pulmonary infections, most often aspergillosis (ref 85).
key_findings.page: p. e17 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Transplantation Patients, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prevalence background: Figure 2, adapted from NSDUH 2018 (ref 1), shows 2016–2018 bars by substance, with a printed label of 43.5 million for marijuana in 2018 (read on the rendered page; the label is not in the text extraction); neither the figure nor its legend states the measure (for example past-year use) or the age base. The text says US use has risen particularly among people aged 18–25 and points to Figure 2, which has no age breakdown.
key_findings.page: pp. e1, e3 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (p. e1); Figure 2 and legend (p. e3)

key_findings.finding: Hyperemesis: the statement says long-term, heavy (THC-predominant) use is associated with a higher risk of hyperemesis syndrome, with prodromal abdominal discomfort and nausea leading to intractable vomiting; the sentence carries no citation.
key_findings.page: p. e13 of the online-first PDF
key_findings.locator: Safety Considerations › Chronic Side Effects, paragraph (left column, continued in the right column below Table 3)
key_findings.note: Second-hand and uncited; Table 2 also lists the syndrome (see the key finding on Table 2 rows without row-level citations).

reporting_issues.issue: The two CARDIA citations in the text are swapped: the no-association finding for incident cardiovascular disease is cited to ref 29 (Auer et al., 2018, subclinical atherosclerosis) and the calcification finding in people who smoked tobacco to ref 46 (Reis et al., 2017, incident cardiovascular disease). Table 3 and the reference list attribute them the other way round.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e9–e12, e20–e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim traced through the text's citations would cite the wrong CARDIA paper; use the Table 3 attribution (Reis 2017 for incident disease, Auer 2018 for calcification) and read the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence that AMI hospitalisations and ED visits rose in states with legal cannabis cites refs 26 and 48. Ref 48 is Rodondi et al. (2006), a CARDIA analysis of diet and risk factors with no bearing on legalisation; ref 26 (Abouk and Adams) reports cardiac death rates; and the Colorado study (ref 49), probably intended, reports cannabis-related billing codes overall, not AMI.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e10–e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: The AMI part of the sentence has no traceable support in the statement and should not be cited from it.

reporting_issues.issue: PATH Through Life (ref 38): the text gives cohort sizes of 2404, 2530 and 2551 and calls the study a retrospective evaluation; Table 3 gives 2383, 2525 and 2547 and calls it a population survey. The text reports only the 3.3-fold rate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates; Table 3 adds the adjusted IRR of 2.3 (1.1–4.5).
reporting_issues.page: pp. e10, e12 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the adjusted estimate and the sample sizes from the primary paper; the text alone overstates the association.

reporting_issues.issue: EU-GEI (ref 67): the text says daily use of high-potency cannabis gave nearly 5 times the odds of psychotic disorder but prints adjusted OR 3.2 (95% CI 3.0–16.1), the same 3.2 as the daily-use estimate before it and near the lower limit of its own interval; the comparator is given as low-potency cannabis, whereas the preceding estimate is against never use. Editors' calculation: the geometric midpoint of 3.0–16.1 is about 7.0, and that of the daily-use interval 2.2–4.1 about 3.0, so neither printed 3.2 is centred.
reporting_issues.page: p. e14 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one printed number is wrong; no EU-GEI figure should be cited from this statement (use Di Forti et al., 2019, Tier A).

reporting_issues.issue: Two Table 3 rows cannot be right as printed: Desai et al. 2017 (ref 34) is described as a sample of more than 2.4 million patients with AMI yet reports an adjusted OR for AMI with cannabis use (1.079), which cannot be estimated among people who all had AMI; Johnson-Sasso et al. (ref 40) report an incidence of AMI of 54% vs 20% in people under 50 who did and did not use cannabis within a sample of AMI patients, which reads as an age distribution rather than an incidence.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e11–e12 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: These rows misdescribe either the population or the measure; neither figure can be cited without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Desai et al. 2018 (ref 35): 1.2% of hospitalisations of people with recreational cannabis use were for AMI overall, yet the annual AMI share is said to have risen from 1.4% to 1.8% over the same 2010–2014 period.
reporting_issues.page: p. e11 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: An overall share cannot lie below every annual share unless the two figures measure different things, which the row does not say; neither figure is usable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: DeFilippis et al. 2018 (ref 32): Table 3 gives adjusted HRs of 1.99 (all-cause) and 2.22 (cardiovascular mortality) among people who used cocaine and marijuana, without intervals and without saying whether the exposures were combined, while the text (p. e17) attributes worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality to cannabis use; the 6% prevalence in the text is not in the table.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e11, e17 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot support a cannabis-specific mortality estimate after MI; read the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The text attributes the greater adverse-effect risk of edibles partly to increased systemic absorption compared with smoked cannabis, while Table 1 gives oral THC a bioavailability of 4%–20% against 2%–56% for inhalation.
reporting_issues.page: pp. e5, e9 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency; claims about edibles should rest on the primary studies (Monte et al., 2019, has a card) and pharmacokinetic sources, not on this statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The dependence figures (about 9% of people who use cannabis, 17% of those who start in adolescence, 25–50% of those who use daily) carry no citation; the comparison of 30% cannabis use disorder among people who used in the past year (ref 58) with 17.5% alcohol use disorder gives no denominator for the alcohol figure; and a caveat about DSM-IV criteria without craving or withdrawal (ref 60) follows a study titled as DSM-5 (ref 58).
reporting_issues.page: pp. e13, e21 of the online-first PDF
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these figures can be cited from this statement as evidence; claims on how many people become dependent should use the primary sources with their definitions (for example Leung et al., 2020, which has a card).

design_detail: Systematic review and two-level multivariate mixed-effects meta-analysis (GLLAMM, Stata 13; MOOSE reporting) of cross-sectional comparisons of neurocognitive test scores between adolescents and young adults (sample mean age 26 or younger) with frequent, heavy or problematic cannabis use and comparison participants with minimal use. 69 samples (the Table's rows, from 62 publications, 1973-2017) and 384 Hedges-corrected standardized mean differences classified into 10 cognitive domains; longitudinal studies contributed baseline data only. Searches 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017; English-language, peer-reviewed studies; no registered protocol. Predetermined moderators included age, age at first use and the abstinence required before testing.
can_establish: The average size and spread of reported cross-sectional differences in neurocognitive test scores between young people who use cannabis frequently and comparison groups up to May 2017, by cognitive domain, and whether those differences vary with study-level features such as the abstinence required before testing or treatment seeking.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes the differences (no pre-use baseline; raw scores not adjusted for confounders); whether deficits recover in any person who stops (the abstinence result compares different studies, not the same people over time); effects of years of use into adulthood (longitudinal follow-ups and IQ-only studies were excluded); or the clinical meaning of a group difference for individuals.

sample.recruitment: Database search (PubMed, PsycINFO, Academic Search Premier, Scopus) run independently by two authors from 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017, plus the bibliographies of four qualitative reviews; English-language, peer-reviewed studies from database inception (Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection; Abstract › Data Sources). Seven investigators supplied supplementary data from their studies (Article information, Additional Contributions). Participants came from the included studies, 12 of them treatment-seeking samples; median group size 23 with cannabis and 30 comparison participants, and 31 of 69 cannabis groups had 20 or fewer people (editors' count from the Table).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human adolescents or young adults with a sample mean age of 26 or younger; heavy, frequent or problematic cannabis use as the primary variable; cannabis not identified solely as a comorbidity of another substance use or mental disorder; not focused on acute effects; an appropriate comparison group; at least one standardized neurocognitive test; written in English; data sufficient for an effect size. Only cross-sectional data (baseline data from longitudinal studies). Full texts excluded (Figure 1): 67 no relevant neurocognitive testing, 48 no cannabis-only group, 35 outside the age range, 34 no appropriate comparison group, 29 measures only during neuroimaging, 19 reviews, 17 insufficient data, 16 participants with psychosis, 8 acute use, 7 prenatal exposure, 5 insufficient cannabis data, 3 IQ measures only, 1 intervention study; 5 articles removed for overlapping samples (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Cannabis groups: mean age 20.6 (SD 2.8) years, 68.4% male (abstract; 68.1% in the Results), mean age at first use 15.2 (SD 1.5). Comparison groups: mean age 20.8 (SD 3.4), 55.8% male. Studies mainly from the United States, United Kingdom, Europe and Australia, published 1973 to 2017 (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph). Age ranges in the Table run from 10-23 to 18-50.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the included studies.
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed literature only, without grey literature. Most groups were small, most included studies enrolled people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 3rd paragraph), and one study by the review's first author (Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort: 227 people who used cannabis, 3,401 comparison participants, no abstinence required) supplies 52% of the comparison participants (editors' arithmetic). By their titles, at least 18 of the 62 publications were designed around another drug or a disorder (ecstasy or polydrug use 9, inhalant use 4, schizophrenia 3, ADHD 1, ketamine and cocaine dependence 1); which subgroups entered the analysis is in the supplement (not read). Excluding studies with participants with psychosis (16) and studies reporting only IQ (3) shapes what the pool can say.

exposure.measurement: As defined by each included study: frequent, heavy or problematic use, most included studies enrolling people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder; how use was measured and defined is tabulated only in the supplement. The authors call heterogeneity in measuring cannabis use a substantial limitation of this literature (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable: studies measured use over different periods (past year, past month), frequency units (per week, per day) and quantities (grams, joints), and cannabinoid content was not characterized; the only exposure moderators tested were age at first use (study means; early versus late onset defined between 15 and 18 by each study) and required or reported abstinence.
exposure.polysubstance: Not adjusted: effect sizes came primarily from raw scores, so they do not account for other substance use (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph). Whether studies matched groups on alcohol use was tested as a moderator, with no significant difference (Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph). Several included studies came from research on ecstasy or polydrug use, inhalant use or combined alcohol and cannabis use (by their titles).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Required abstinence before testing varied from none to 2,160 hours (mean 152.7 hours, SD 335.2): 22 studies (32%) required none or did not say, 32 (46%) required 1 to 72 hours, 15 (22%) more than 72 hours; only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). So in up to a third of studies participants may have been tested soon after use.

comparison.controls: Comparison participants with minimal cannabis use, as each study defined it (n=6,575 as reported).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; matching varied by study. Whether studies matched groups on alcohol use was examined as a moderator.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use cognitive baseline in any pooled comparison (cross-sectional data only); premorbid IQ, attention or conduct problems, socioeconomic status and psychiatric comorbidity are not accounted for in raw-score effect sizes. The authors note that adolescents at risk of substance use problems may show cognitive vulnerabilities before use (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported in the main text; comparison groups' alcohol, tobacco and other drug use varied by study (details in the supplement, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Standardized neurocognitive tests from each study, assigned by construct validity to 10 domains: attention, learning, delayed memory, speed of information processing, verbal/language, visuospatial, motor, and three executive-function subdomains (abstraction/shifting, updating/working memory, inhibition); tests by domain are in the supplement (Methods › Data Extraction).
outcomes.validity_norms: Effect sizes were computed primarily from raw scores; some included studies used demographically adjusted normative data (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph). No appraisal of test quality or of the included studies.
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges-corrected standardized mean difference d per test, inverse-variance weighted, signed so that negative values mean worse performance in the cannabis group; measures selected for construct validity rather than significance, avoiding several indices from one test (Methods › Effect Size Calculation; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. 11 counts the overall estimate and the 10 domain estimates; differences between domains were tested with Bonferroni correction, but the moderator tests (treatment seeking P = .04; mean hours of abstinence P = .04) are uncorrected, and the abstinence subgroup test (P = .01) is one of several predetermined moderator analyses; the authors say the abstinence associations hold at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Searches, screening and extraction were each done independently by two researchers, with a third resolving extraction discrepancies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17), between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001); no I-squared or prediction interval reported. Editors' calculation (normal random effects, d plus or minus 1.96 times the square root of the variance plus SE squared): approximate 95% prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28. Domains: learning -0.33 (-0.42 to -0.24); executive abstraction/shifting -0.30 (-0.40 to -0.20); speed of processing -0.26 (-0.38 to -0.15); delayed memory -0.26 (-0.35 to -0.16); executive inhibition -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13); executive updating/working memory -0.22 (-0.31 to -0.12); attention -0.21 (-0.31 to -0.12); verbal/language -0.14 (-0.27 to 0.001; P = .05); visuospatial -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.08); motor -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.18); domains differ overall (chi-square 41.14, 9 df, P < .001), but learning, delayed memory, attention, speed and executive domains do not differ after Bonferroni correction. Abstinence: required more than 72 hours (k = 15; n = 928) d -0.08 (-0.22 to 0.07; P = .29) vs 72 hours or less (k = 54; n = 7,799) d -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22), difference chi-square 6.36, P = .01; mean reported hours of abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected. Treatment-seeking samples (k = 12; n = 581) d -0.43 (-0.62 to -0.24) vs others (k = 56; n = 8,146) -0.22 (-0.29 to -0.14), chi-square 4.32, uncorrected P = .04. No significant moderation by sample age group, early vs late onset, alcohol matching or publication period; mean age, mean age at first use and the group difference in depression not associated. Small-study effects: Egger t = 4.70, P < .001; trim-and-fill (univariate random effects, 44 effect sizes filled) d -0.206 (-0.24 to -0.16) to -0.128 (-0.17 to -0.09), about 37.9% smaller.
analysis.covariates: None at effect-size level (raw-score differences). Study-level moderators: sample age category, mean age, age at first use (mean, early vs late), sociodemographic and clinical characteristics (group difference in depression), publication year, mean reported abstinence hours, required abstinence over 72 hours, treatment seeking, alcohol matching (Results › Follow-up Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the inclusion criteria are described as defined a priori and the moderators as predetermined (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st paragraph; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Domain-level numbers of studies and effect sizes, domain heterogeneity and the moderator estimates for age, onset and alcohol matching are only in the supplement (eResults, eFigures 2 and 3). The 72-hours-or-less estimate (-0.30) appears only in the abstract; the separate estimates for 0-hour and 1-to-72-hour studies appear only as points in Figure 3 (its axis was not legible in the rendering; values not extracted).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Moderator analyses are study-level comparisons; the more-than-72-hours subgroup has 15 studies (n = 928), whose interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 69 mostly small cross-sectional samples (2,152 people who used cannabis frequently, 6,575 comparison participants, mean age about 21), cannabis groups scored on average a quarter of a standard deviation lower (d -0.25, -0.32 to -0.17), with substantial between-study spread (editors' approximate prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28) and significant small-study effects (trim-and-fill estimate about -0.13). Differences were similar across learning, memory, attention, speed and executive domains (-0.21 to -0.33) and absent for visuospatial and motor tests. Studies that required more than 72 hours of abstinence found a smaller difference (d -0.08, -0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies) than the others (-0.30), and treatment-seeking samples a larger one (-0.43); no moderation by age or age at first use was detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the associations are small and may be of questionable clinical importance for most individuals, that "abstinence of longer than 72 hours diminishes cognitive deficits associated with cannabis use", and that earlier studies may have overstated the magnitude and persistence of deficits; the Key Points say deficits are substantially diminished with abstinence, and the Conclusions speak of restored cognitive functioning. Gaps: (1) the abstinence result compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping, so it cannot show that deficits diminish or are restored; studies requiring longer abstinence also differ in other ways (7 of the 15 come from papers that list the same author, S. F. Tapert, and 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger), and two of the 15 rows apparently share their comparison group with a row in the other subgroup; (2) the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference but reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25, so it does not show that no deficit remains; (3) small and of questionable clinical importance is a statement about the mean, while the spread between studies is wide and treatment-seeking samples showed d -0.43; (4) no difference by age is a non-significant comparison between study means among samples whose mean age is 26 or less, so adolescents are compared with young adults, not with adults generally; (5) all estimates are unadjusted raw-score differences without pre-use baselines; the authors expect adjustment for confounders to shrink them, and differences that predate use would also mean the pooled values overstate any effect of cannabis. Against this, the Discussion disclaims causal inference, reports and discusses small-study bias, and notes that its abstinence finding contrasts with the Dunedin cohort and with another systematic review.

timeline.event: Grant et al. (ref. 52), the oldest included study; included studies span 1973 to 2017.
Pope et al. (ref. 101), monitored abstinence in people with long-term use: cited for deficits that diminish when abstinence is carefully monitored.

Grant et al. (ref. 23) and Schreiner and Dunn (2012, ref. 24), meta-analyses in adults: small effects, almost undetectable after a few days to weeks of abstinence; this review calls its own findings consistent with them.

The first author's meta-analysis of methamphetamine and cognition (ref. 35), cited with other drug meta-analyses as showing medium to large effects, the authors' argument that the tests are sensitive enough.

Meier et al. (ref. 102), Dunedin cohort: called the strongest evidence of dysfunction after adolescent-onset persistent heavy use, with the caveat that the subgroup was small; the abstinence finding is said to contrast with it.

Rogeberg (ref. 116) and Daly (ref. 115), letters arguing that socioeconomic status and personality may confound the Dunedin association, cited for the point that confounders are common in case-control studies of cannabis.
Ganzer et al. (ref. 25), systematic review of long-term effects in abstinent adolescents and adults, whose conclusions on persistence this review says it contradicts.

Jackson et al. (ref. 121), two longitudinal twin studies, cited with Meier et al. (2018, ref. 118, co-twin control) as large studies questioning cannabis as a cause of cognitive change once confounders and familial factors are accounted for.
Systematic review of 2004-2015 task-based studies in the project's Tier A list, not cited by this review.
Narrative review in the project's Tier A list, not cited by this review.
National Academies report (ref. 91), with which the authors say their findings converge: substantial uncertainty about deficits after sustained abstinence.
Scott et al. (ref. 16), the authors' own Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort analysis, the largest included sample (227 vs 3,401; no abstinence required).
This review (published online 18 April 2018).
Later tests in the project's lists, not appraised here: co-twin control analyses of cognitive functioning (Schaefer et al., 2022) and the Dunedin follow-up at 45 (Meier et al., 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of cognition restricted to young samples in the project's list; its headline is that cognitive differences in young people who use cannabis are small and fade with abstinence. The pooled differences are unadjusted cross-sectional associations of about a quarter of a standard deviation, possibly inflated by small-study effects; the abstinence result is a between-study association. Its conclusions on persistence rest on the same kind of evidence as the adult meta-analyses it cites, and on longitudinal and co-twin studies it discusses but did not pool (Meier et al., 2012, 2018; Jackson et al., 2016). Claims should cite it for the size and spread of cross-sectional differences by domain and for the study-level association with required abstinence, naming those limits; claims about recovery in people who stop need within-person studies.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that test cognition before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with biologically verified periods of abstinence, retested comparison groups to account for practice effects, and sibling or twin comparisons or adjustment for premorbid ability and other drug use, pooled as individual participant data; a within-person study of people who stop after frequent use, against people who continue and people who do not use, would test recovery directly.

domains.note: Population (sample mean age 26 or younger), exposure (heavy, frequent or problematic use), comparator (appropriate comparison group with minimal use) and outcome (standardized neurocognitive tests) stated (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st paragraph).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; only a priori inclusion criteria and predetermined moderators are described.
Only cross-sectional data, with the reason (too few, heterogeneous longitudinal studies) and baseline data taken from longitudinal studies (Methods › Study Eligibility, 2nd paragraph).

Four databases searched independently by two authors, an example PubMed strategy in the supplement (not read) and bibliographies of four qualitative reviews; but limited to English-language, peer-reviewed studies without a stated reason, with no grey literature, registries or experts consulted for further studies. Under item 4 as written (senior decision 21, 25 October 2026) an unexplained language or publication-type limit is judged no.
All identified articles reviewed independently by the same two authors (Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection).
Independent extraction by two researchers, discrepancies resolved by a third (Methods › Data Extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 counts full-text exclusions by reason (291 printed; the reasons sum to 289), but no list of excluded studies appears in the article, and none is among the supplement's listed contents (eMethods, eResults, eTables 1 and 2, eFigures 1 to 3; the supplement itself was not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The Table gives each sample's group sizes, domains tested, age range and required abstinence; exposure definitions, comparison-group characteristics, sex and setting are only in the supplement.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the included studies is reported; study features (abstinence, treatment seeking, alcohol matching) were examined only as moderators.

domains.note: Not reported.

The two-level multivariate model appropriately handles several effect sizes per study, with Hedges correction and inverse-variance weights. But the pooled values are unadjusted raw-score differences from non-randomized studies, pooled without a stated justification (the lack of adjustment is acknowledged only as a limitation), and rows that share a comparison group (seven publications with two rows each) enter the model as separate studies. A close call, since adjusted estimates are rarely reported in this literature.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Risk of bias was not assessed, so its impact was not analysed; the alcohol-matching moderator is the nearest analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion says the effects may be overestimates (small-study effects), that raw scores do not account for sociodemographic, psychiatric or substance-use confounders, that pre-existing deficits are not accounted for and that no causal conclusion can be drawn (Considerations for Interpretation, 4th and 5th paragraphs). The abstinence conclusions do not carry these caveats (see interpretation_gap).
Between-study variance reported and tested (0.070, P < .001) and explored with predetermined moderators; I-squared and prediction intervals are not reported.

Funnel plot, Egger test (t = 4.70, P < .001) and trim-and-fill, with their implications discussed (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and conflicts declared (Article information).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items fail (2, no protocol; 4, English-language and peer-reviewed limits without a reason; 7, no list of excluded studies; 9, no appraisal of the included studies; 11, unadjusted raw-score differences pooled without justification), so confidence is critically low under AMSTAR 2. This judges how far the pooled d can be trusted as an unbiased summary, not the review's usefulness: it models several outcomes per study properly, tests and discusses small-study effects, and states that it cannot address causation. In practice, the overall d of -0.25 is an unadjusted cross-sectional difference that small-study effects may inflate (trim-and-fill about -0.13), with wide spread between studies; the abstinence contrast is a comparison between studies, with about half of the more-than-72-hours group from studies by one research group, and cannot show recovery within people. Cite it for the size and spread of cross-sectional differences by domain and for the study-level association with required abstinence, with these caveats.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 2,562 records from databases and 30 from other sources; 1,324 after duplicates; 961 excluded on title and abstract; 363 full texts assessed; 74 articles met the criteria; 5 removed for overlapping samples, leaving 69 studies. Searches ran 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017 in PubMed, PsycINFO, Academic Search Premier and Scopus, limited to English-language peer-reviewed studies, run and screened independently by two authors.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Data Sources; Figure 1 (printed counts, read from the rendered image)

key_findings.finding: Full-text exclusions by reason: 67 no relevant neurocognitive testing, 48 no cannabis-only group, 35 outside the age range, 34 no appropriate comparison group, 29 measures only during neuroimaging, 19 reviews, 17 insufficient data, 16 participants with psychosis, 8 acute use, 7 prenatal exposure, 5 insufficient cannabis data, 3 IQ measures only, 1 intervention study.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (printed counts, read from the rendered image)
key_findings.note: The reasons sum to 289, while the box total reads 291 (see reporting issues). Studies reporting only IQ were excluded, as were longitudinal follow-ups (Methods › Study Eligibility, 2nd paragraph), so IQ cohorts such as Dunedin are outside the pool.

key_findings.finding: 69 studies with 8,727 participants: 2,152 in cannabis groups (mean age 20.6, SD 2.8; 68.1% male in the Results, 1,472 or 68.4% in the abstract; mean age at first use 15.2, SD 1.5) and 6,575 comparison participants with minimal cannabis use (mean age 20.8, SD 3.4; 55.8% male); 384 effect sizes; published 1973 to 2017. Required abstinence averaged 152.7 hours (SD 335.2): 22 studies (32%) none or unspecified, 32 (46%) 1 to 72 hours, 15 (22%) more than 72 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results; Table
key_findings.note: The Table's 69 rows come from 62 publications, and its columns sum to 2,188 and 6,573 participants (editors' arithmetic); the authors' own Philadelphia cohort study supplies 227 of the cannabis and 3,401 of the comparison participants.

key_findings.finding: Overall difference in neurocognitive performance, cannabis groups vs comparison groups (raw-score standardized mean differences, multivariate mixed-effects model): d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17); between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001), more than sampling error alone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: approximate 95% prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28 (normal random effects, treating the reported variance as the variance of study means).

key_findings.finding: Small-study effects: the funnel plot was asymmetric and Egger's test significant (t = 4.70, P < .001); Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill (univariate random effects, since no multivariate method exists) filled 44 effect sizes and reduced d from -0.206 (-0.24 to -0.16) to -0.128 (-0.17 to -0.09), about 37.9%, still significant; the authors advise caution about the exact reduction and say the effects may be overestimates.
key_findings.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: By domain (d, 95% CI): learning -0.33 (-0.42 to -0.24); executive abstraction/shifting -0.30 (-0.40 to -0.20); speed of information processing -0.26 (-0.38 to -0.15); delayed memory -0.26 (-0.35 to -0.16); executive inhibition -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13); executive updating/working memory -0.22 (-0.31 to -0.12); attention -0.21 (-0.31 to -0.12); verbal/language -0.14 (-0.27 to 0.001; P = .05); visuospatial -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.08; P = .53); motor -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.18; P = .83). Domains differed overall (chi-square 41.14, 9 df, P < .001), but learning, delayed memory, attention, speed and executive domains did not differ from one another after Bonferroni correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurocognitive Domains, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Numbers of studies and effect sizes per domain are only in the supplement (eResults, not read); Figure 2 is an image.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences in effect size by sample age category (adolescents vs adults), early vs late onset (cut-offs between 15 and 18, as each study defined), alcohol matching or period of publication; mean age, mean age at first use and the group difference in depression were not associated with effect size. Treatment-seeking samples (k = 12; n = 581) showed a larger difference, d -0.43 (-0.62 to -0.24), than others (k = 56; n = 8,146), d -0.22 (-0.29 to -0.14); chi-square 4.32, uncorrected P = .04.
key_findings.locator: Results › Follow-up Analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Study-level (ecological) comparisons; the age comparison is between samples with mean ages of 26 or less. Estimates for age, onset and alcohol matching are only in the supplement.

key_findings.finding: Abstinence: longer mean reported abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) went with smaller differences (beta 0.059; P = .04, uncorrected). Studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence (k = 15; n = 928) had d -0.08 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.07; P = .29), smaller than studies requiring 72 hours or less (k = 54; n = 7,799; d -0.30, -0.37 to -0.22); chi-square 6.36, P = .01. Figure 3 also plots studies requiring no abstinence (k = 22) and 1 to 72 hours (k = 32) separately, to show that the unknown or zero-abstinence studies do not drive the difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Follow-up Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Abstract › Results; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: A between-study comparison, not a within-person change. The more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25, which lies just outside it, so it does not exclude a difference of nearly the overall size. The -0.30 estimate for the other 54 studies is printed only in the Abstract. The authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). Figure 3 values were not extracted (axis not legible in the rendering). The unit of the beta for abstinence hours is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Composition of the more-than-72-hours subgroup (editors' reading of the Table and reference list): its 15 rows require 168 to 2,160 hours; 7 come from papers that list S. F. Tapert among their authors (refs 11, 54, 55, 61, 67, 78, 90) and an eighth (ref. 62) shares its first two authors with one of them; 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger; Fried et al. (2005) and Schweinsburg et al. (2010) each contribute one row to each abstinence subgroup, with a comparison group of the same size in both rows (apparently shared). The Table's rows for this subgroup sum to 947 participants against the reported 928.
key_findings.locator: Table (Minimum Required Abstinence Period column); reference list
key_findings.note: Editors' observation, not the authors'; it means the abstinence contrast may also reflect laboratory, sample and protocol differences.

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the association between length of abstinence and effect sizes as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons. Only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence. The authors read the abstinence result as suggesting that some deficits reflect residual effects of recent use or withdrawal rather than persistent change, and note that it contrasts with a large longitudinal study (Dunedin) and with a recent systematic review of abstinent adolescents and adults (Ganzer et al., 2016).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that effect sizes were computed mainly from raw scores and so do not account for sociodemographic, psychiatric or substance-use confounders; that results do not account for deficits that may have existed before use, so no causal conclusion can be drawn; that most included studies enrolled people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder, so findings may not apply to occasional use or to medical cannabinoids; and that longitudinal evidence conflicts, citing Dunedin as strong evidence for adolescent-onset persistent heavy use (small subgroup) and two large studies, including a co-twin study, that question a causal role.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: All domain effect sizes were below one-third of a standard deviation, which the authors take to argue against medium or large deficits, citing medium to large effects in meta-analyses of alcohol, methamphetamine, benzodiazepines and cocaine as evidence that the tests are sensitive.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Findings Across Cognitive Domains, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The statement holds for the domain estimates but not for the treatment-seeking subgroup (d -0.43); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: statistically significant but small associations; little evidence of more severe effects with use at earlier ages or in adolescence; longer abstinence associated with smaller group differences and with what the authors call restored cognitive functioning; very small, non-significant differences in studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence; large longitudinal studies needed.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Key Points › Meaning

key_findings.finding: Funding: US Department of Veterans Affairs Career Development Award IK2CX000772 (J. C. Scott); funders had no role. Conflicts: R. C. Gur reports royalties from the Brain Resource Center; no other disclosures.
key_findings.locator: Article information: Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor; Conflict of Interest Disclosures

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cannabis groups as 1,472 (68.4%) male, which matches 1,472 of 2,152; the Results give 68.1% male.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use 68.4%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results report 384 effect sizes from 69 studies with a mean (SD) of 9.46 (5.32) per study, range 1 to 17; 384 divided by 69 is 5.6 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the count of effect sizes or the mean per study is wrong, or the mean describes something else; the number of effect sizes behind the estimates cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 1 the box for excluded full texts reads 291, but its 13 reasons sum to 289; 363 minus 289 gives the 74 articles that met the criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic error in the flowchart; the flow is otherwise consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 derives 69 studies from 74 articles minus 5 with overlapping samples, but the Table's 69 rows cite 62 distinct publications: Cousijn 2013, Ehrenreich 1999, Filbey 2015, Fried 2005, Gruber 2012, Schweinsburg 2010 and Tait 2011 each contribute two rows with the same comparison-group size, and the two Tait rows are identical in every column.
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit called a study is a sample; rows sharing a comparison group enter the model as independent studies, count their comparison participants twice in the totals, and in two cases fall in opposite abstinence subgroups, so the subgroup test is not between independent sets.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's group sizes sum to 2,188 in cannabis groups and 6,573 in comparison groups (8,761 in all), against the reported 2,152, 6,575 and 8,727; its rows for studies requiring more than 72 hours sum to 947 and the rest to 7,814, against the reported 928 and 7,799 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Abstract › Results
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant counts cannot be reproduced from the Table; quote them as reported, with the caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment-seeking comparison counts 12 plus 56 = 68 studies, one short of 69, although its participant counts (581 plus 8,146) add up to the full 8,727.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: One study is unaccounted for in the study counts; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says all effect sizes in the study were below one-third of a standard deviation, while the Results report d -0.43 for treatment-seeking samples.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Findings Across Cognitive Domains, 1st paragraph; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The small-effects statement applies to the overall and domain means, not to every subgroup; claims about people in treatment should use the subgroup estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites eTable 1 for the tests in each domain and eTable 2 for the fuller per-study overview and the cannabis-use measures, while the supplement's listed contents name eTable 1 as the overview of the 69 studies and eTable 2 as the tests by domain.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data Extraction; Table footnote; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph; Supplementary Materials list
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-references to the supplement are swapped; a reader of the supplement must look in the other table.

reporting_issues.issue: Ganzer et al. (2016, ref. 25) is counted in the Introduction as one of three meta-analyses of adults and described in the Discussion as a systematic review of adolescents and adults, while the Introduction also states that no meta-analysis of adolescents or young adults existed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Overlap with earlier syntheses is described inconsistently; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The trim-and-fill starting value (d -0.206, -0.24 to -0.16) comes from a univariate random-effects model applied to the effect sizes, not from the main multivariate estimate (-0.247, -0.32 to -0.17), and its narrower interval suggests the 384 effect sizes were treated as independent; the Egger test probably likewise.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted estimate of -0.128 and the Egger P value are approximate, as the authors caution; the direction (inflation by small studies) is the usable result.
