design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-period within-participant crossover trial (NCT04201197) at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, January 2021 to March 2022. 18 healthy adults with past cannabis experience and no use for at least 30 days completed three 14-hour outpatient sessions at least one week apart, in an order set by a randomized Latin square, eating a brownie with placebo, a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) or a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD) (study conditions). In every session a cocktail of five cytochrome P450 probe drugs (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) was swallowed 30 minutes after the brownie, because the trial's primary aim was cannabinoid–drug interactions; this paper reports the secondary outcomes: THC pharmacokinetics and subjective, cognitive and cardiovascular effects over 24 hours.
can_establish: That in these conditions (oral extracts in a brownie, the probe cocktail given in every session, healthy adults who rarely use cannabis), the CBD-dominant extract produced higher plasma THC and much higher 11-OH-THC exposure, and stronger subjective, cognitive and heart-rate effects, than the THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose.
cannot_establish: The effect of CBD alone (no CBD-only condition) or of lower CBD doses, inhaled cannabis, regular cannabis use or CBD taken separately from THC; whether the stronger effects came only from altered THC metabolism rather than from the probe drugs (whose levels are not reported here) or from the extract's other cannabinoids; or that CBD increases anxiety or sleepiness compared with THC alone (these differences were not significant).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: media advertisements and word of mouth (Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18 to 50; body mass index 18 to 34; past experience with cannabis; no cannabis use in the 30 days before the first session; negative urine drug tests at screening and at the start of every session; not pregnant or nursing; no allergy to cannabinoids or study drugs; good health on blood tests, history and examination (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: 11 men and 7 women; mean age 30 (SD 7) years, weight 78 (SD 12) kg, BMI 25 (SD 2); 12 White, 3 Black and 3 Asian, all non-Hispanic; mean 124 (SD 80) days since last self-reported cannabis use, median 93, range 39 to 295 (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: 36 consented, 22 were randomized and 18 completed; participants who dropped out were replaced and only completers were analysed (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph). Reasons for dropping out and the conditions they had received are given only in the flow diagram (Figure 1), an image that was not viewable in this reading.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers with past but infrequent cannabis use, recruited by advertisement and willing to take a probe-drug cocktail in three long sessions; people with regular use, older adults, people with health problems and people on other medicines were not represented.

exposure.measurement: Supervised ingestion of a brownie prepared and dispensed by a pharmacist (participants and staff blinded); plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry at baseline and 0.25 to 24 hours after the cocktail (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Outcome Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one brownie per session, oral, after a standard low-fat breakfast: placebo (ethanol vehicle), THC-dominant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) or CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD); probe cocktail of caffeine 100 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, losartan 25 mg, dextromethorphan 30 mg and midazolam 2 mg 30 minutes later in every session; at least one week between sessions (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Extracts from the NIDA Drug Supply Program, decarboxylated, made under cGMP: the THC-dominant extract held 70% THC, 2.7% CBG, 1.5% CBN, under 1% THCV, CBC and Δ8-THC and no detectable CBD; the CBD-dominant extract held 59.3% CBD, 2.1% CBC, 2.0% THC, 1.1% CBG and under 1% CBN, THCV and Δ8-THC (Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs).
exposure.polysubstance: Urine drug tests negative at screening and before each session; participants were told to avoid cannabis and cannabinoid products, tobacco, caffeine, grapefruit and other fruit juices and not to change medicines or supplements throughout the study (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph). Alcohol testing is not mentioned. Within sessions, the probe drugs (including the sedative midazolam, dextromethorphan and caffeine) were taken with every brownie.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 days without cannabis before the first session by self-report (mean 124 days), with negative urine drug tests before every session; no THC metabolites were detectable after the placebo brownie (Methods › Participants; Results, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant had placebo, THC-dominant and CBD-dominant sessions, all with the probe cocktail. The key comparison for CBD is CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract at the same nominal THC dose.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person design).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person comparisons; anxiety-proneness and other traits that might change responses were not measured or analysed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in all conditions; the probe cocktail was identical across sessions.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH: Cmax, AUC (trapezoidal) and AUC ratios. Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100 visual analogue items: drug effect, pleasant, unpleasant, liking, sick, heart racing, anxious or nervous, relaxed, paranoid, sleepy, alert, irritable, restless, hungry, craving, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, memory, routine tasks and others). Digit symbol substitution task, modified paced serial addition task, divided attention task; heart rate and blood pressure. Ratings and vital signs at baseline and 0.25 to 24 hours, tasks at baseline and 0.5 to 24 hours after the cocktail (Methods › Outcome Measures, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The questionnaire and tasks are described as sensitive to acute THC and cannabis effects in the group's earlier studies; participants were trained on the tasks at screening to reduce practice effects (Methods › Outcome Measures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects are expressed as peak change from each session's baseline; comparisons between conditions are Tukey tests on peak change after two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (dose × time); pharmacokinetic comparisons are paired t tests between the two active conditions (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey adjustment across the three condition contrasts within each outcome; no adjustment across the 27 effect outcomes in the Table (21 questionnaire items, 3 tasks, 3 vital signs) and the 9 pharmacokinetic measures (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs; plasma analysed in a separate laboratory. THC's effects would make active sessions recognisable against placebo; the two active brownies held the same nominal THC dose.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pharmacokinetics, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD), units not printed in the text (Results, 2nd paragraph): THC Cmax 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), d = 1.4 (95% CI 0.4 to 2.4); 11-OH-THC Cmax 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), d = 3.1 (1.7 to 4.4); THC-COOH Cmax 118.6 (44.8) against 45.1 (18.5), d = 2.1 (0.9 to 3.3); THC AUC 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9), d = 2.2 (1.0 to 3.4); 11-OH-THC AUC 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4), d = 3.2 (1.8 to 4.6); THC-COOH AUC 1030.0 (456.4) against 445.7 (196.2), d = 2.8 (1.5 to 4.1); all P < .001. Editors' arithmetic from these means: THC Cmax about 1.8 times and AUC about 2.5 times higher, 11-OH-THC Cmax about 12 times and AUC about 10 times higher with the CBD-dominant extract. Effects, mean peak change from baseline (SD), placebo / THC-dominant / CBD-dominant (Table): drug effect 9.4 (27.8) / 59.2 (31.1) / 72.8 (25.9); unpleasant 4.1 (12.9) / 19.6 (23.4) / 38.6 (28.0); sick 3.4 (9.0) / 11.6 (18.9) / 26.1 (22.3); anxious or nervous 4.1 (14.8) / 13.3 (20.2) / 23.9 (29.1); paranoid -0.1 (8.0) / 12.0 (16.8) / 23.4 (28.8); sleepy or tired -12.9 (38.3) / 21.0 (42.9) / 42.6 (42.3); memory impairment 5.6 (10.0) / 27.4 (31.7) / 37.8 (32.6); difficulty with routine tasks 6.6 (13.4) / 30.3 (27.8) / 46.7 (30.3); paced serial addition -1.1 (14.2) / -6.6 (19.1) / -22.7 (24.6); divided attention -2.1 (9.4) / 15.9 (24.7) / 32.7 (39.2) (higher is worse); heart rate -4.4 (12.4) / 10.1 (14.1) / 25.4 (20.9) beats per minute. Many printed Cohen d values for effect outcomes do not match these means and SDs (see reporting issues), so the means, SDs and Tukey P values are the safer figures. Mean times of peak effect were later with the CBD-dominant extract for most ratings (for drug effect 2.9 h against 2.1 h, Table), not tested statistically.
analysis.covariates: None (within-person comparisons of change from each session's baseline).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04201197; the trial protocol is Supplement 2 (a PDF, not opened). The trial's primary outcome was losartan AUC (cannabinoid–drug interaction), to be reported elsewhere; the outcomes in this paper are secondary. The registry record was not read, so registered and reported secondary outcomes were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Probe-drug results, including midazolam and dextromethorphan exposure under each extract, are deferred to later papers although they bear on the effects reported here. The text and the Table disagree on several effect results (see reporting issues). All PD items are tabulated for all three conditions, which limits selective reporting within this paper.
analysis.power: Sample size set for the primary outcome (18 participants, 84% power for a 25% change in losartan AUC); for the effect outcomes the authors cite expected effect sizes of about 0.87 to 1.0 from their laboratory's earlier studies. Not powered for sex differences (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Limitations).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With the probe cocktail in every session, the CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD) gave higher plasma THC and far higher 11-OH-THC than the THC-dominant extract, and, against THC-dominant extract, higher ratings of drug effect, unpleasant, sick, red eyes, memory trouble and difficulty with routine tasks, worse paced serial addition and divided attention, and a larger rise in heart rate. Anxious or nervous, paranoid, sleepy, pleasant and liking ratings and the digit symbol task did not differ significantly between the two active extracts.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the CBD-dominant extract increased self-reported anxiety, sedation and memory difficulty compared with both THC-dominant extract and placebo (Abstract › Results); by the Table, anxiety and sleepiness differed from placebo only. The Key Points say the effects appear mediated by CBD inhibiting the metabolism of THC and 11-OH-THC, and the abstract's Conclusions and Relevance call this the likely mechanism; no mediation was tested, the CBD extract also carried other cannabinoids, and the probe drugs (including midazolam) were given in every session with their levels unreported, which the Limitations concede may have contributed to the effects. The abstract presents the result as contradicting common claims that CBD attenuates THC's adverse effects, from one high oral CBD dose in one product ratio.

timeline.event: Haney et al. (2016): oral CBD did not alter the subjective, reinforcing or cardiovascular effects of smoked cannabis (title from the project's BeforeDuring list; not read for this card).
Systematic review of how CBD influences the acute effects of THC in humans (on the project's BeforeDuring list, Tier A; not read for this card).
This trial: oral CBD-dominant extract raised THC and 11-OH-THC exposure and strengthened several effects compared with a THC-dominant extract at the same THC dose.
Chester et al. (2026): systematic review and meta-analysis of whether co-administered CBD changes plasma THC and its active metabolite (on the project's BeforeDuring list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper describes earlier laboratory findings on CBD with THC as equivocal (attenuation, potentiation or no change), mostly with inhaled or intravenous dosing (Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). It is the study in the project's map showing oral CBD raising THC levels and effects; a later meta-analysis of plasma THC with CBD (Chester et al., 2026) and further crossover trials are listed but not appraised here.

Three authors report fees or contract work from cannabis and cannabinoid companies, outside this work. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover trial without co-administered probe drugs that fixes the THC dose and varies the CBD dose (including amounts found in consumer products and a CBD-only condition), uses single-cannabinoid preparations to separate CBD from other cannabinoids, includes both infrequent and regular cannabis use, measures THC and 11-OH-THC, and pre-registers anxiety and paranoia as outcomes.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Condition order assigned by a randomized Latin square; a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs, keeping staff and participants blind. Each session had its own baseline.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: At least one week between sessions; no THC or metabolites were detectable after the placebo brownie, which argues against THC carry-over. Period effects and the balance of sequences among completers after replacement of dropouts are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Supervised dosing in the laboratory, double-blind. Active sessions are recognisable against placebo, but the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose. The probe cocktail was part of the protocol in every session, so it is a matter of applicability (and of mechanism) rather than a deviation.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: 4 of 22 randomized participants (18%) did not complete and were replaced; only completers were analysed, and the reasons and the conditions received before dropping out are only in an image that could not be viewed. If dropping out followed strong effects in one condition, differences between conditions could be under- or overstated.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Plasma assays and computerized tasks are objective; self-ratings were made under double-blind conditions (a pharmacist prepared and dispensed all study drugs); no check of blinding is reported, which matters little here because the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Registered trial whose primary outcome is reported elsewhere; the registry was not read here. Many outcomes without correction across outcomes; the abstract's summary of anxiety and sedation does not match the Table; many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with supervised dosing and objective pharmacokinetics: the large rise in THC and 11-OH-THC exposure with the CBD-dominant extract is credible for these conditions. Concerns are the completers-only analysis after replacing 4 of 22 randomized participants, the unreported probe-drug levels in a design that gave midazolam and dextromethorphan in every session, and inconsistent reporting of effect results. The card may be cited for: in 18 healthy adults with infrequent cannabis use, 20 mg oral THC taken in a CBD-dominant extract (640 mg CBD) produced higher THC and 11-OH-THC levels and stronger drug-effect, unpleasant, sick, memory, task, cognitive and heart-rate effects than the same nominal THC dose in a THC-dominant extract, with a probe-drug cocktail given in every session. It should not be cited for CBD increasing anxiety, paranoia or sleepiness compared with THC alone (not significant), for lower CBD doses, inhaled cannabis, regular use, or CBD on its own.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: randomized, double-blind, within-participant crossover; 18 of 22 randomized healthy adults (11 men, 7 women, mean age 30) with past cannabis experience and no use for at least 30 days completed three sessions at least one week apart, with brownies of placebo, THC-dominant extract (20 mg THC) or CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC + 640 mg CBD) (study conditions), each followed 30 minutes later by a five-drug CYP probe cocktail.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Interventions; Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Plasma exposure with the CBD-dominant against the THC-dominant extract: THC Cmax 14.8 (SD 5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), THC AUC 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC Cmax 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), AUC 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); THC-COOH Cmax 118.6 (44.8) against 45.1 (18.5), AUC 1030.0 (456.4) against 445.7 (196.2); all P < .001, n = 18. Higher 11-OH-THC:THC and lower THC-COOH:11-OH-THC AUC ratios (4.5 against 1.2; 3.1 against 14.4).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: Units are not printed in the text (eTable 1 in Supplement 1, a PDF, was not opened). Editors' arithmetic: THC Cmax about 1.8-fold, 11-OH-THC Cmax about 12-fold higher.

key_findings.finding: The placebo brownie with the probe cocktail produced no significant change in any effect measure over time.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against the THC-dominant extract, the CBD-dominant extract produced larger peak changes from baseline in ratings of drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), sick (26.1 against 11.6), dry or red eyes (28.8 against 15.9; 28.7 in the text), memory impairment (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty performing routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3) (Tukey P < .05).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table, rows marked c

key_findings.finding: No significant difference between the two active extracts in pleasant (57.9 against 55.9) or liking ratings, anxious or nervous (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0), sleepy or tired (42.6 against 21.0), heart racing or restless ratings; anxious or nervous, sleepy and paranoid were higher than placebo after the CBD-dominant extract.
key_findings.locator: Table (rows without the c marker); Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract states that anxiety and sedation were increased compared with both THC-dominant extract and placebo; the Table supports only the comparison with placebo.

key_findings.finding: Cognitive and cardiovascular effects: against the THC-dominant extract, the CBD-dominant extract gave fewer correct paced serial additions (-22.7 against -6.6, P = .049) and greater divided-attention tracking error (32.7 against 15.9, P = .04), and a larger rise in heart rate (25.4 against 10.1 beats per minute, P = .001); the digit symbol task did not differ significantly between the active extracts; blood pressure showed no effects.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table, Cognitive measures and Physiological measures rows

key_findings.finding: The CBD-dominant extract also contained 2.1% CBC and 1.1% CBG (THC-dominant extract: 2.7% CBG, 1.5% CBN, no detectable CBD), so the comparison is between two whole-plant extracts rather than THC with and without pure CBD.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: about 1.0 to 1.1 g of the CBD-dominant extract supplies the stated doses, bringing roughly 21 to 23 mg CBC and 11 to 12 mg CBG, against under 1 mg of each minor cannabinoid from the roughly 29 mg of THC-dominant extract.

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: a single dose of THC and of CBD, no CBD-only condition; outcomes measured with the CYP probe cocktail, which may have contributed to the behavioural effects in the active conditions; not powered to detect sex differences.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the CBD-dominant extract increased self-reported anxiety and sedation compared with both the THC-dominant extract and placebo, but the Table marks anxious or nervous (23.9 against 13.3) and sleepy or tired (42.6 against 21.0) as different from placebo only, not from the THC-dominant extract; the Results text names only unpleasant, sick and red-eye ratings among adverse items as higher than with THC alone.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Table; Results, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial does not show that CBD made the experience more anxious or sleepy than the same THC dose alone; the abstract should not be cited for that.

reporting_issues.issue: Days since last cannabis use are given as mean 86 (SD 66) in the abstract and mean 124 (SD 80), median 93, range 39 to 295, in the Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Results figure is the detailed one.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that the THC-dominant extract increased only dry mouth among the adverse ratings compared with placebo, while the Table marks unpleasant, paranoid, sleepy or tired, irritable, heart racing and throat irritation as significantly higher than placebo after the THC-dominant extract.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adverse effects of THC alone are understated in the text; use the Table.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed Cohen d values: for plasma Cmax and AUC (except THC-COOH AUC) and for drug effect they match a pooled-SD calculation from the printed means and SDs, but many others do not (editors' calculation): pleasant printed 1.7 and 2.4 (about 1.5 and 1.6), paranoid 2.4 (about 1.1), sleepy 0.7 (about 1.4), dry mouth 0.9 (about 1.7), heart rate against placebo 0.7 (about 1.7), THC-COOH AUC 2.8 (about 1.7). Pleasant and paranoid repeat the d and interval printed for drug effect; the unpleasant interval (0.4 to 2.1) is lopsided around 1.7; and several intervals include zero next to P < .001 (drug effect against THC alone, d 0.5, -0.5 to 1.4; THC-COOH:THC ratio, d -0.31, -1.2 to 0.6). Memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract also match (0.3 and 0.6), but two further contrasts against it do not: dry or red eyes, printed 1.0 (about 0.4), and paced serial addition, printed −0.5 (about −0.7); and intervals that include zero sit beside P < .05 against the THC-dominant extract for memory (0.3, −0.6 to 1.2, P = .03), routine tasks (0.6, −0.4 to 1.5, P = .02), paced serial addition (−0.5, −1.3 to 0.2, P = .049), divided attention (0.4, −0.4 to 1.5, P = .04) and heart rate (0.7, −0.1 to 1.8, P = .001) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed effect sizes and their intervals cannot be relied on for the effect outcomes; cite means, SDs and the Tukey or paired-test P values instead. The intervals appear not to reflect the within-person design.

reporting_issues.issue: Value slips between text and Table: the paced serial addition result against placebo is printed with SD 34.6 (Table and later text 24.6) and its comparator is labelled THC-dominant with the placebo value (-1.1, SD 14.2); dry mouth after THC-dominant extract is 35.9 in the text and 35.0 in the Table; dry or red eyes after CBD-dominant extract is 28.7 in the text and 28.8 in the Table; the drug-effect comparison of CBD-dominant extract with placebo carries two P values (P < .001; P = .003).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Table values are internally consistent and are preferred.

reporting_issues.issue: By the stated composition of the CBD-dominant extract (59.3% CBD, 2.0% THC), 640 mg CBD comes with about 21.6 mg THC, and 20 mg THC with about 593 mg CBD (editors' calculation); measured brownie contents are not reported, although periodic testing is described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Cannabis Extracts and Study Drugs)
reporting_issues.consequence: The THC dose in the CBD-dominant condition may have been up to about 8% higher than 20 mg; too small to explain an 1.8-fold THC Cmax difference, but the two conditions were not certainly matched for THC.

reporting_issues.issue: The levels of the probe drugs (including the sedative midazolam and dextromethorphan) under each extract are not reported in this paper, although CBD's inhibition of the same enzymes is the proposed mechanism and the authors note the cocktail may have contributed to the effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the extra sedation and impairment with the CBD-dominant extract could reflect higher probe-drug exposure; the attribution to THC and 11-OH-THC alone is not established by this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Peak times in the Table range from 0 to at most 6.0 hours for every measure in every condition, although ratings, tasks and vital signs were recorded up to 24 hours after the cocktail; the time course, and so how long the stronger effects lasted, is shown only in Figures 3 and 4, which were not viewable in either reading, and no test of peak time is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table; Methods › Outcome Measures, 1st paragraph; Figures 3 and 4)
reporting_issues.consequence: The card cannot state how long the effects lasted; the later mean peak with the CBD-dominant extract (2.9 against 2.1 hours for drug effect) is descriptive only.

disagreements.resolution: Recomputed with a pooled SD from the Table's means and SDs (dry or red eyes 0.44; paced serial addition −0.73; memory 0.32; routine tasks 0.56) and each interval read in Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; added.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (missed): peak-time ranges never exceed 6.0 h although measures ran to 24 h; how long the stronger effects lasted is shown only in Figures 3 and 4 (not viewable), so the card cannot state duration
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in the Table (every range ends at 6.0 h or earlier) and Methods › Outcome Measures, 1st paragraph (assessments to 24 h). Added as a reporting issue. The figures remain unread (deferred: figure images not viewable).

disagreements.field: risk_of_bias.domains[4].note (Bias in measurement of the outcome)
disagreements.first_pass: Plasma assays and computerized tasks are objective; self-ratings were made blind to condition.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 271 (agrees with the judgment, low): 'self-ratings were made blind to condition' rests on the double-blind procedure; the paper reports no check of blinding, which does not change the judgment because the two active brownies carried the same nominal THC dose
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph (pharmacist-prepared drugs; no blinding check reported anywhere in the text). Note reworded as a factual precision; the domain judgment (low) and the overall judgment (some concerns) are unchanged and agreed.

design_detail: Two prospective community twin cohorts analysed in parallel, with a co-twin control analysis. RFAB (Risk Factors for Antisocial Behavior, Los Angeles): 614 families of twins and triplets (1,241 children) enrolled at 9–10 in 2001; WASI Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design and Matrix Reasoning at 9–10 and again at 19–20. MTFS (Minnesota Twin Family Study): an original younger cohort (n=1,527, first assessed 1990–1996) and an Enrichment Study cohort (n=1,000, from 1999–2006) half of which was selected for disruptive behaviour and academic disengagement; WISC-R Vocabulary, Information, Block Design and Picture Arrangement at 11–12 and the WAIS-R versions at 17–19. Exposure: self-reported ever use of cannabis by follow-up; among people who used, 30 or more lifetime uses and daily use for 6 months or more. Mixed-effects models of change in age-standardized subtest scores (IQ metric), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort, with supplementary adjustment for binge drinking and other drug use; co-twin comparisons within MZ and DZ pairs discordant for ever use (RFAB 25 MZ and 54 DZ pairs; MTFS 112 MZ and 99 DZ pairs) and within 47 MTFS pairs discordant for heavy use.
can_establish: Whether adolescents who went on to use cannabis by 17–20 fell further behind age peers on vocabulary and other Wechsler subtests than those who did not, in two US twin cohorts, and whether the twin who used differed from the co-twin who did not, a comparison that removes confounding shared by twins (all genes in MZ pairs, about half in DZ pairs, and the shared family environment).
cannot_establish: That cannabis has no effect on IQ, because the co-twin estimates are imprecise (the MZ intervals in both cohorts include the between-family difference), exposure is mostly ever use with few people who used heavily or for long, recency of use is unknown, follow-up ends at 17–20, and in RFAB many twins lacked exposure data or follow-up testing; nor can it show anything about full-scale IQ, executive function or memory, which were not tested.

sample.recruitment: Community twin samples: RFAB from greater Los Angeles school districts, socioeconomically and ethnically diverse (Hispanic 37%, Caucasian 27%, mixed 17%, African American 14%, Asian 5%; 52% female; 46% MZ); MTFS from two population-based Minnesota twin samples recruited at 11 and followed about every 3 years (51% female, 63% MZ, 93% Caucasian), the later one enriched for externalizing problems (Methods › Participants and Procedure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Analytic samples: twins with a baseline IQ assessment and valid cannabis-use data, excluding those who reported use at baseline. RFAB 1,241, minus 24 without baseline IQ, 1 with use at baseline and 427 without cannabis data = 789; MTFS 2,527, minus 15, 15 and 220 = 2,277 (Table S1). For co-twin analyses the last-born of 14 triplet sets was excluded (RFAB 9, MTFS 5) (Methods › Statistical Analysis › Cotwin control).
sample.demographics: RFAB: age 9.6 at baseline in both groups and 19.5 (never used) against 20.0 (used) at follow-up; 43.9% against 46.7% male; MZ 51.1% against 40.7%. MTFS: 11.8 at baseline; 18.0 against 18.2 at follow-up; 44.6% against 55.0% male; SES percentile 52.1 against 48.6; Caucasian 95.3% against 88.9%. The cannabis group had far more other drug use (RFAB 38.3% against 1.6%; MTFS 39.4% against 6.6%) and heavier maximal drinking (Table 1).
sample.attrition: RFAB: 427 of 1,216 eligible twins (35%) lacked cannabis-use data and were excluded; of the 789 analysed, 323 did not complete follow-up IQ testing (466 tested), and their baseline scores were kept in maximum-likelihood models assuming data missing at random; follow-up n per subtest 438–459. MTFS: 220 of 2,497 (9%) excluded for missing cannabis data; follow-up attrition 10–20%; Information and Picture Arrangement were not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up (follow-up n 1,252 and 1,000) (Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 2nd paragraph; Tables S1–S3). The eligible totals, percentages and per-subtest follow-up totals are editors' arithmetic from Tables S1–S3.
sample.selection_effects: Twins without cannabis data had lower SES and baseline IQ in both cohorts and in RFAB were more often male, MZ and non-white (Table S2); the authors expect people with heavier use to be under-represented at later waves, biasing towards the null (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph). Half of the MTFS Enrichment sample was selected for disruptive behaviour and academic disengagement, which enriches MTFS for the confounders at issue; the two MTFS samples were combined with cohort as a covariate.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each wave, without biological verification. RFAB: a survey question on ever trying cannabis at each wave, and at wave 5 questions on daily use for at least 6 months and on 30 or more lifetime uses, completed in the laboratory or at home by mail or online. MTFS: structured interviews (DICA at 11 and 14; CIDI Substance Abuse Module at 17) and a computerized survey completed in private at 14 and 17 (and 11 for the Enrichment sample); ever use taken as the highest endorsement across instruments; agreement between survey and interview for ever use κ = 0.86 at 14 and 0.91 at 17, with 46 of 238 who reported use in the private survey (19%) denying it at interview (Methods › Assessment of marijuana use; Measurement of Marijuana Use in the Minnesota Twin Family Study, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Ever use on any occasion against never. Among people who used: 30 or more lifetime uses (RFAB 49.3%, MTFS 37.0%) and daily use for 6 months or more (20.8% and 22.6%) (Table 1). Recency, current against former use, route and potency were not measured; in MTFS the heaviest period of daily use most often began at 16 (Measurement of Marijuana Use in the Minnesota Twin Family Study, 5th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use (yes/no across 10 drug classes, plus nitrous oxide in RFAB) and maximal binge drinking (largest number of drinks in a day, log-transformed and winsorized) were measured. Primary models did not adjust for them, to maximize the chance of detecting an association with cannabis; supplementary models did (Tables S4 and S5). Binge-drinking data cover 270 and 421 RFAB twins (Table 1 footnote).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured; the authors state they could not separate current from former heavy use or acute from non-acute effects (Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Twins who reported never using cannabis by follow-up (RFAB 314; MTFS 1,455); in the co-twin analyses, the co-twin who never used.
comparison.matching: Co-twin control matches on everything twins share (all genes in MZ pairs, about half in DZ pairs; family environment); DZ models adjust for sex. Between-family models adjust for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES (RFAB: Hollingshead index percentile at baseline; MTFS: composite of income, both parents' education and parental occupation) and MTFS cohort.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline subtests were measured before use. Not adjusted: childhood conduct problems, attention problems and delinquency, parental monitoring and the other family-culture factors the authors propose as the confounders (Discussion › Are Developmentally Emerging IQ Deficits Found in Those Who Use Marijuana Widespread or Specific?, 2nd paragraph). Within pairs, factors that differ between co-twins (peers, individual behaviour problems) remain uncontrolled.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drug use was reported by 1.6% (RFAB) and 6.6% (MTFS) of the never-used group (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: RFAB: WASI Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design and Matrix Reasoning (the same test at both ages). MTFS: WISC-R Vocabulary, Information, Block Design and Picture Arrangement at 11–12, then the WAIS-R versions at 17–19 (Enrichment sample: Vocabulary and Block Design only). Scaled scores were age-standardized and converted to an IQ metric (mean 100, SD 15). WAIS-III Digit Span was given at 17–18 to 1,452 MTFS twins, at follow-up only (Methods › Assessment of intelligence; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard Wechsler norms. WISC-R and WAIS-R items differ, so only change in age-standardized scores, not raw scores, can be compared (Methods › Assessment of intelligence, 3rd paragraph). No full-scale IQ was computed.
outcomes.operationalization: Decline = a more negative change in the age-standardized score of the cannabis group than of the never-used group (time-by-group interaction), that is, falling behind age peers; in co-twin analyses, the within-pair difference in change. Vocabulary and Information are classed as crystallized ability, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Arrangement as fluid ability, and Similarities as both.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 6 subtests (4 per cohort; Vocabulary and Block Design in both) are each tested in the main models (8 cohort-subtest tests), the frequency models among people who used (16), the co-twin models by zygosity (16), the substance-adjusted supplementary models (24) and the heavy-use co-twin models (4): about 68 tests at P < 0.05 (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Difference in change, cannabis group minus never-used group, in IQ points (time-by-group interaction), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort (Table 3): Vocabulary RFAB −4.0 (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7), P = 0.001, and MTFS −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3), P < 0.001; Information (MTFS) −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7), P = 0.002; Similarities (RFAB) −0.1 (−2.8 to 2.5); Block Design RFAB 0.2 (−2.0 to 2.5) and MTFS −0.6 (−1.8 to 0.6); Matrix Reasoning (RFAB) 1.9 (−0.7 to 4.4); Picture Arrangement (MTFS) 0.4 (−1.6 to 2.4). With binge drinking and other drug use added (Table S4): Vocabulary RFAB −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5), P = 0.022, and MTFS −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), P = 0.244; Information −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9), P = 0.399. Vocabulary per year of age: RFAB +0.01 (never used) and −0.39 (used), difference 0.397 per year, about 4 points over 10 years; MTFS +0.12 and −0.45, difference 0.57, about 4 points over 7 years; difference between cohorts 0.176, P = 0.35. Within people who used (Table 4), Vocabulary: 30 or more uses RFAB −0.8 (−4.2 to 2.6) and MTFS −0.6 (−2.4 to 1.2); daily use RFAB −0.4 (−4.5 to 3.7) and MTFS −0.7 (−2.7 to 1.4); no subtest significant, also after substance adjustment (Table S5). Co-twin (Table 5), Vocabulary: RFAB MZ −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) and DZ −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2, 54 pairs); MTFS MZ −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs) and DZ 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3, 99 pairs); the only significant co-twin result was Matrix Reasoning in RFAB DZ pairs, 6.6 (0.6 to 12.7), P = 0.036, in favour of the twin who used. Pairs discordant for heavy use (MTFS, 47; Table S6): Vocabulary −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6), Information 0.2 (−5.1 to 5.6), Block Design −1.6 (−7.3 to 4.1), Picture Arrangement 5.2 (−4.1 to 14.6).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and MTFS cohort in the main models; maximal binge drinking and other drug use added in the supplementary models; sex in the DZ co-twin models.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan reported; three criteria for a causal effect (use precedes decline, dose-response, persistence after adjusting for genes and upbringing) are stated in the introduction (5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Every subtest is reported, including non-significant results, and the supplementary analyses are shown (Tables S1–S6). Not shown: the co-twin estimates pooled across MZ and DZ pairs, which the text says were not significant (Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 1st paragraph); and several printed co-twin P values do not match their intervals (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: No power analysis. The authors argue the larger MTFS gave the same conclusion (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences in IQ Be Attributed to a Possible Causal Effect of Marijuana Use?, 2nd paragraph); but the MZ co-twin intervals for Vocabulary (RFAB −11.2 to 0.5; MTFS −3.9 to 2.4) include the between-family differences of −4.0 and −3.4, so the co-twin analyses cannot tell no within-pair effect from one as large as the between-family association (editors' reading of Tables 3 and 5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In both cohorts, twins who had used cannabis by 17–20 changed 3.4 to 4.0 points less on Vocabulary than twins who had not (a difference in change: on the raw means those who used fell 1.8 and 2.5 points while those who did not rose 1.8 and 1.3) (and 2.0 points on Information in MTFS), with no difference on Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning or Picture Arrangement. In MTFS, future cannabis use already went with lower Vocabulary, Information and Block Design scores at 11–12, and the Vocabulary and Information differences in change shrank to non-significance after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (−0.8 and −0.7); in RFAB the Vocabulary difference did not (−3.7). Among people who used, 30 or more uses or daily use did not go with more change. Within discordant twin pairs no Vocabulary difference was significant; the RFAB MZ estimate was −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) and the MTFS MZ estimate −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the observed declines may not be a direct result of cannabis but attributable to familial factors, the significance statement that familial confounds underlie the association, and the conclusion that the deficits are attributable to confounding factors rather than a neurotoxic effect. Gaps: (1) non-significant within-pair differences are read as the absence of an effect, although the MZ intervals in both cohorts include the between-family association and the RFAB MZ point estimate (−5.4) is larger than the between-family estimate (−4.0), while the interval for the 99 MTFS DZ pairs (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family −3.4; (2) the conclusion counts baseline differences before use among its three grounds, but these were found only in MTFS, not in RFAB; (3) the discussion says the Vocabulary association was completely eliminated in MTFS after adjustment for other substances (Discussion › Are the Deficits in Crystallized Intelligence Specific to Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph), while the estimate fell to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), and drinking and other drug use may lie on a common pathway rather than only confound; (4) the absence of a dose-response rests on two binary contrasts among people who mostly used lightly, with RFAB intervals of about ±4 points; (5) the conclusion about intellectual decline in general rests on 6 subtests over adolescence, with no full-scale IQ, memory or executive measure; (6) the inference that family environment rather than genes is the source, because DZ estimates were not larger than MZ estimates (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences…, 1st paragraph), compares imprecise estimates without a test. The authors' limitations section concedes that effects of long-term or recent use cannot be ruled out.

timeline.event: Lyons et al. (Psychological Medicine): adult twins discordant for regular cannabis use differed little on tests, with one Block Design difference that its authors attributed to type 1 error; cited by Jackson et al. as concordant (Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences…, 2nd paragraph).

Fried, Watkinson & Gray (Neurotoxicology and Teratology): IQ declines in people currently using cannabis heavily but not in people who formerly used heavily, as cited in the introduction (3rd paragraph).
Meier et al. (Dunedin): IQ decline with persistent cannabis dependence, the study this paper sets out to test (card sc_meier_2012).

Rogeberg (PNAS): SES confounding as an explanation of the Dunedin result; Jackson et al. report no attenuation after adjusting for their SES composite (card sc_rogeberg_2013). The original authors' SES reanalysis (Moffitt et al., 2013; card sc_moffitt_2013) is not cited.

This study: two twin cohorts with parallel analyses; the Vocabulary association with ever use and the null co-twin estimates appear in both, while baseline differences and attenuation by other substance use appear only in MTFS.

Meier et al. (Addiction), a longitudinal co-twin control study of adolescent cannabis use and neuropsychological decline, in the project's Tier A list and carded in this round by another reader; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Within this paper the two cohorts agree on a between-family association of ever use with vocabulary decline of about 3.4 to 4.0 points over adolescence and on non-significant co-twin differences, and disagree on baseline differences and on attenuation by other substance use. The co-twin estimates are the most-cited result but are imprecise, and the exposure (mostly ever use by 17–20) is far lighter and shorter than the persistent dependence to 38 studied in Dunedin (Meier et al., 2012), so the two studies do not test the same contrast. Later co-twin studies in the project's lists (Meier et al., 2018; Schaefer et al., 2022) are needed for a claim about where the question stands; they are not read here.

funding.funder: National Institute of Mental Health Grant R01-MH58354 (RFAB) and NIH Grants DA 013240, DA 05147, DA036216 and AA 09367 (MTFS) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflict of interest." (Footnotes). PNAS Direct Submission; edited by Valerie F. Reyna (Cornell University), a guest editor invited by the Editorial Board; received 20 August 2015, accepted 14 December 2015 (author information).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the University of Southern California (RFAB), the University of Minnesota (MTFS), UCLA, Örebro University and the University of Pennsylvania; W.G.I., M.M., A.R. and L.A.B. designed the research, and N.J.J. and J.D.I. (equal contribution) analysed the data and wrote the paper.

what_would_settle_it: Co-twin or sibling studies with enough pairs discordant for heavy, persistent use (not ever use) followed into adulthood, with repeated full-scale IQ and memory and executive testing, biologically verified exposure and recency, and an equivalence margin stated in advance, so that a null within-pair estimate could be read as evidence of no effect rather than as an imprecise result.

domains.note: Judged for the co-twin estimates, which carry the paper's conclusion: they remove confounding shared by twins, but not factors that differ between co-twins (peers, individual conduct problems). The between-family estimates in Table 3 would be at high risk, as the paper's own baseline differences and attenuation by other substance use show.

Self-reported ever use, verified only by agreement between instruments in MTFS (κ 0.86–0.91); frequency as two binary measures; recency unknown; any misclassification of the never-using co-twin biases the co-twin estimates towards the null.
Community twin samples, but half of the MTFS Enrichment sample was selected for externalizing problems, and twins without cannabis data, who had lower SES and IQ, were excluded (see missing data).
None relevant.

RFAB: 35% of eligible twins excluded for missing cannabis data and 41% of the analysed twins without follow-up IQ, handled by maximum likelihood assuming data missing at random, although missingness went with lower SES and IQ and, the authors expect, heavier use. MTFS: 9% excluded and 10–20% attrition, with two subtests not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up (some concerns on its own).
Standardized Wechsler subtests, but no full-scale IQ, different item pools across WISC-R and WAIS-R in MTFS and a short form for the Enrichment sample; testers' blinding not reported.
About 68 tests without correction; pooled MZ and DZ co-twin estimates not shown; several printed P values do not match their intervals; but all subtests and supplementary models are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, here missing data in RFAB. The co-twin design is a real strength against confounding by family and genes, and the use of two cohorts adds a built-in replication. But the co-twin estimates are too imprecise to show the absence of an effect, exposure is mostly ever use within a few years of adolescence, and in RFAB missing data are large and related to SES and IQ. Citable for the between-family association of ever use with vocabulary and information decline, the MTFS baseline differences, the attenuation after adjustment for other substance use in MTFS, and the co-twin estimates with their intervals; not as evidence that cannabis does not affect IQ, nor for heavy, long-term or recent use.

key_findings.finding: Analytic samples: RFAB 789 twins from 436 families and MTFS 2,277 twins from 1,171 families; 427 RFAB and 220 MTFS twins were excluded for missing cannabis-use data, and these twins had lower SES and baseline IQ (for example RFAB Vocabulary 96.5 against 101.9; MTFS 97.6 against 100.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables S1 and S2

key_findings.finding: In RFAB, 323 of the 789 analysed twins did not complete follow-up IQ testing (466 tested); their baseline data were kept in maximum-likelihood models. MTFS follow-up attrition was 10–20%, and Information and Picture Arrangement were not given to the Enrichment sample at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 2nd paragraph; Table S3

key_findings.finding: 60% of RFAB twins (475 of 789) and 36% of MTFS twins (822 of 2,277), who were about 2 years younger at follow-up, had used cannabis; among them 49.3% and 37.0% had used it 30 or more times and 20.8% and 22.6% daily for 6 months or more.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of Analytic Sample, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Baseline scores, before any cannabis use: no differences in RFAB at 9–10; in MTFS at 11–12, future cannabis use went with lower Vocabulary (−1.9, P < 0.01), Information (−2.7, P < 0.001) and Block Design (−2.0, P < 0.01); no baseline differences in Similarities, Matrix Reasoning or Picture Arrangement.
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline Differences in IQ, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 2's MTFS Information means (97.9 against 101.2) give a raw difference of −3.3, not the −2.7 in the text; the other two differences match the table.

key_findings.finding: Difference in change, cannabis group minus never-used group, adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, SES and cohort: Vocabulary −4.0 points (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7) in RFAB and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3) in MTFS; Information −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7) in MTFS; Block Design, Similarities, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Arrangement not different (estimates −0.6 to 1.9, all intervals including 0).
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: A difference in change between groups: on the Table 2 means, Vocabulary in those who used fell 1.8 points (RFAB, 99.9 to 98.1) and 2.5 points (MTFS, 98.8 to 96.3), while in those who never used it rose 1.8 (100.2 to 102.0) and 1.3 (100.7 to 102.0), so about half of each gap is the comparison group's rise (editors' arithmetic). Fig. 1, named in the locator, was not inspected by the second reader or the adjudicator.

key_findings.finding: With maximal binge drinking and other drug use added, the Vocabulary difference was −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5, P = 0.022) in RFAB but −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6, P = 0.244) in MTFS, and the MTFS Information difference −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9); the authors suggest drinking may predict IQ decline less in the college-age RFAB sample.
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 1st paragraph; Table S4; Discussion › Are the Deficits in Crystallized Intelligence Specific to Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among people who used cannabis, 30 or more uses and daily use for 6 months or more were not associated with more change on any subtest (Vocabulary, 30 or more uses: RFAB −0.8, −4.2 to 2.6; MTFS −0.6, −2.4 to 1.2; daily use: RFAB −0.4, −4.5 to 3.7; MTFS −0.7, −2.7 to 1.4), also after substance adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Results › IQ Change Between Marijuana User Groups, 3rd paragraph; Tables 4 and S5
key_findings.note: The authors say their data do not allow a full examination of dose-dependent effects.

key_findings.finding: Vocabulary change per year of age: RFAB (n=785) +0.01 in the never-used group (P = 0.90) and −0.39 in the cannabis group (P < 0.001), a difference of 0.397 a year, or about a 4-point gap over 10 years; MTFS (n=2,271) +0.12 (P = 0.028) and −0.45 (P < 0.001), a difference of 0.57 a year, or 4.0 points over 7 years; the two cohorts did not differ (Δ0.176, P = 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Effect Size Between RFAB and MTFS, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Co-twin comparisons of twins discordant for ever use showed no significant difference in change for Vocabulary (RFAB MZ −5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs; DZ −2.8, −7.7 to 2.2, 54 pairs; MTFS MZ −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs; DZ 0.2, −2.8 to 3.3, 99 pairs), Similarities, Information, Block Design or Picture Arrangement; in RFAB DZ pairs the twin who used gained more on Matrix Reasoning (6.6, 0.6 to 12.7, P = 0.036). Pooling MZ and DZ pairs is said to leave all estimates non-significant (not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: The MZ intervals include the between-family Vocabulary differences (−4.0 RFAB, −3.4 MTFS), so these results are compatible with both no within-pair effect and an effect of that size. In the largest discordant group, the 99 MTFS non-identical pairs, the interval (−2.8 to 3.3) excludes the between-family difference of −3.4, so in that cohort the co-twin evidence leans towards a smaller within-pair effect.

key_findings.finding: In 47 MTFS pairs in which one twin never used and the other used frequently (more than 30 uses or a period of daily use), no subtest differed: Vocabulary −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6), Information 0.2 (−5.1 to 5.6), Block Design −1.6 (−7.3 to 4.1), Picture Arrangement 5.2 (−4.1 to 14.6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cotwin Control Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table S6

key_findings.finding: Digit Span (WAIS-III), given at 17–18 to 1,452 MTFS twins: mean 9.4 (SD 2.4) in the cannabis group against 9.2 (SD 2.4) in the never-used group; follow-up only, with no test reported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the absence of larger effects in DZ than in MZ pairs as pointing to family-wide environment rather than genes, and propose family-cultural factors (less parental monitoring, less emphasis on scholarship) rather than material SES as the confounders, noting that the deficits are specific to measures of acquired knowledge.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Can Within-Pair Differences in IQ Be Attributed to a Possible Causal Effect of Marijuana Use?, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Are Developmentally Emerging IQ Deficits Found in Those Who Use Marijuana Widespread or Specific?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: exposure was mostly measured as discrete categories without recency; participants were young adults at the last assessment, so effects of more prolonged use could not be ruled out, which they offer as a possible reason for the difference from Meier et al. (2012), whose participants were 38; current and former heavy use could not be separated; and attrition may have removed people who used more heavily.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

design_detail: Reply letter (PNAS 110(11):E980–E982, online 4 March 2013) by four authors of Meier et al. (2012), answering Rogeberg (2013) and a letter by Daly (2013, PNAS E979, not read). It reports new analyses of the Dunedin birth cohort: family SES (three classes by the breadwinner's occupation, illustrated by example occupations; the measure and the age at which it was assessed are not stated) as a predictor of adolescent-onset cannabis dependence and of IQ change; the 2012 linear-trend model of full-scale IQ change on waves of cannabis dependence with SES or childhood self-control added; and the same model restricted to the 553 members from middle-class families. Filed as prospective-cohort, the design of the data reanalysed, because its results are new individual-level analyses of that cohort; its argumentative passages are cited as the authors' position.
can_establish: Whether, in the Dunedin cohort, family SES as classified here and childhood self-control predicted adolescent-onset cannabis dependence or IQ change, and whether adding either to the 2012 model, or restricting it to middle-class families, changed the association between persistent cannabis dependence and IQ decline.
cannot_establish: That no confounding explains the association, because SES and self-control are each added alone to the sex-only model, never together or with the other-substance covariates of the 2012 multivariable model, and family, genetic and childhood behavioural factors beyond these two are not examined; nor does it report the pre-exposure IQ trajectory test that Rogeberg proposed.

sample.recruitment: Dunedin birth cohort (card sc_meier_2012): consecutive births in Dunedin, New Zealand, 1972–1973; the analyses use the 874 members of the 2012 analysis (Fig. 2 key).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in Meier et al. (2012). The middle-class restriction excludes families whose breadwinner had a low-skill occupation (foodpacker is the example given) or a professional one (dentist); middle class is illustrated by building inspector and aircraft mechanic (3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the letter; no table by SES class or by exposure group.
sample.attrition: Not reported in the letter; the analyses inherit the 2012 sample.
sample.selection_effects: As in the original cohort. The middle-class restriction keeps 553 of 874 (63%, editors' arithmetic) and leaves 8 to 32 people per cell in the age-of-onset comparison (Fig. 3B); 553 and the cell sizes are figure values read by the first reader only.

exposure.measurement: As in Meier et al. (2012): waves of DSM cannabis dependence between 18 and 38 (five-level exposure), and adolescent-onset dependence (dependence before 18).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As in Meier et al. (2012); not restated in the letter.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed in the new analyses: the SES- and self-control-adjusted models are compared with the sex-only model (β = −0.152, t = −4.45), not with the 2012 multivariable model that also adjusted for other dependence, recent use and schizophrenia (t = −2.20).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: As in Meier et al. (2012); not addressed.

comparison.controls: Cohort members who never used cannabis, in the full cohort or within the middle-class subsample (Fig. 2).
comparison.matching: None; SES or self-control is added as a covariate, or SES is held roughly constant by restriction to middle-class families.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family SES and childhood self-control, both measured before cannabis use, are now examined. Still not examined: family psychiatric history, genetic liability, parenting, childhood conduct or attention problems, and peers.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described.

outcomes.instruments: Full-scale IQ change from childhood (ages 7–13) to 38, as in 2012; for the SES trajectories, mean full-scale IQ at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 38 by SES class (Fig. 1); adolescent-onset dependence as the outcome of SES in one test.
outcomes.validity_norms: As in Meier et al. (2012).
outcomes.operationalization: Confounding is judged by (a) whether SES predicts adolescent-onset dependence, (b) whether SES or self-control correlates with IQ change, and (c) whether the trend coefficient changes when SES or self-control is added or when the sample is restricted to middle-class families.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; a handful of tests on two outcomes (full-scale IQ change and adolescent-onset dependence).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: SES and adolescent-onset dependence: χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56 (df not given; with three SES classes df = 2 reproduces P = 0.56, editors' check); 23% of the adolescents who used cannabis came from low-SES families (denominator and cohort share of low SES not given). SES and IQ change from adolescence to adulthood: r = −0.006, P = 0.86. Trend coefficient of IQ change on waves of dependence: β = −0.152 (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001) with sex only; β = −0.158 (t = −4.58, P < 0.0001) with SES added; β = −0.155 (t = −3.61, P = 0.0003) among the 553 from middle-class families (553 read from Fig. 2 by the first reader only). Childhood self-control and IQ decline: r = −0.034, P = 0.31; trend with self-control added β = −0.151 (t = −4.38, printed P = 0.0001). β is not defined (standardized or not) and no confidence intervals are given. Read approximately from the rendered Fig. 2: 3 or more waves of dependence about −0.38 SD in the full cohort and about −0.37 SD in the middle-class subsample; never used about +0.05 and +0.07.
analysis.covariates: Sex, as in 2012, plus SES or plus childhood self-control, one at a time.
analysis.selective_reporting: The tests were chosen to answer the two critiques. Not shown: the SES distribution of the cohort and of each exposure group, a model with SES, self-control and the other-substance covariates together, any test of the adolescent-onset contrast within the middle-class subsample (Fig. 3B shows bars only), and the data behind the statement that tests more susceptible to SES did not show more decline (3rd paragraph).
analysis.power: Not addressed; the middle-class age-of-onset cells hold 8 to 32 people (Fig. 3B, first reader's reading).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the Dunedin data, family SES class did not significantly predict adolescent-onset dependence and was unrelated to IQ change from adolescence to 38; adding SES or childhood self-control to the sex-adjusted model, or restricting to middle-class families, left the trend coefficient essentially unchanged (−0.152 against −0.158, −0.155 and −0.151).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title announces "No evidence that socioeconomic status or personality differences confound" the association, and the text says the data exclude SES as the explanation and that the tests exclude initial differences in conscientiousness. Gaps: (1) these are tests of two specific measures, each added alone to a sex-only model; they exclude these measures as explanations, not confounding in general; (2) the SES measure is three occupational classes, neither defined nor dated in the letter, and the 23% figure has no base rate; (3) the letter describes the within-individual change design as controlling for any and all childhood influences (5th paragraph), which holds for stable differences only, the point at issue in Rogeberg's critique; (4) the statement that SES-sensitive tests did not decline more is made without data; (5) personality is represented by childhood self-control, which the letter calls a precursor of conscientiousness. Against this, the tests are direct, use measures taken before cannabis use, and the letter acknowledges that observational studies cannot prove causation.

timeline.event: Meier et al. (Dunedin), the study defended (card sc_meier_2012).
Rogeberg (PNAS 110:4251–4254): simulation of SES confounding, answered here (card sc_rogeberg_2013).

Daly, letter proposing that conscientiousness may explain the association (PNAS 110:E979; not read). This reply says Daly's own test in the National Child Development Study did not confirm the idea and that its personality measure was taken at 50, after cannabis use (4th paragraph).
A rejoinder titled Reply to Moffitt et al.: Causal inference from observational data remains difficult (PNAS 110:E983), linked from this letter's page; not read.

Jackson et al., two US twin cohorts: adjustment for a composite SES measure did not attenuate the cannabis–vocabulary association, consistent with this reply on SES, but twins who used did not differ significantly from co-twins who did not, which the authors read as familial confounding other than SES (card sc_jackson_2016). Jackson et al. cite Rogeberg (2013) but not this reply.

Meier et al. (Addiction), a longitudinal co-twin control study of adolescent cannabis use and neuropsychological decline, in the project's Tier A list and carded in this round by another reader; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: On its narrow question the reply is direct and largely convincing: in Dunedin, family SES as classified did not predict adolescent-onset dependence or IQ change, and adding it or restricting to middle-class families left the association unchanged; Jackson et al. (2016) likewise found no attenuation by SES in two US cohorts. It does not settle the wider question of confounding: no joint model is reported, the pre-exposure trajectory test Rogeberg proposed is not reported, and within-family comparisons in other cohorts (Jackson et al., 2016; later co-twin studies in the project's lists, not read here) point to family factors beyond SES.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the letter; the funders of the 2012 study are on card sc_meier_2012.
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflict of interest." (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are authors of the study under criticism (M.H.M. first author; T.E.M. senior author), at Duke University, the Institute of Psychiatry at King's College London and the Dunedin unit of the University of Otago; all four designed, performed and analysed the new analyses and wrote the letter (author contributions). The letter defends the authors' own study, a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: One model of the Dunedin data adjusting jointly for family SES, childhood self-control, conduct problems, family psychiatric history and other substance dependence, reported with coefficients and intervals; the pre-exposure IQ trajectory test Rogeberg proposed (IQ from 7 to 13 by later exposure group); and within-family comparisons (twins or siblings discordant for persistent adolescent-onset dependence) followed into midlife.

domains.note: Adds family SES (three occupational classes) and childhood self-control, each alone, to a sex-only model; no joint model, and the other-substance covariates of the 2012 multivariable model are not carried over; genetic and family liability and childhood conduct problems remain uncontrolled. For the narrower question whether SES as classified explains the association, the tests are direct and at lower risk.
As in 2012: prospective structured diagnoses, self-reported and unverified.
Population birth cohort; the middle-class restriction is a deliberate analytic choice.
None relevant.
As in 2012 (874 of about 964 members assessed at 38); the numbers in each SES class and in the χ2 and correlation analyses are not given.
As in 2012: different Wechsler versions in childhood and at 38; testers' blinding not reported. The SES measure is not defined in the letter.
Analyses chosen to rebut two critiques; base rates, the joint model and the data behind the SES-sensitive-test statement are not shown; β is undefined and no intervals are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain. The reply addresses the two named confounders directly with measures taken before cannabis use, and on that narrow question it is informative: the coefficient barely moves. But each confounder is added alone, and other plausible confounders are not addressed, so the result does not lower the risk of confounding for the causal question as a whole. Citable for the SES and self-control tests and their coefficients, the middle-class restriction (n=553) and the SES trajectories in Fig. 1; not for the claim that confounding has been excluded in general.

key_findings.finding: Low family SES did not significantly predict adolescent-onset cannabis dependence (χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56); 23% of the adolescents who used cannabis came from low-SES families, defined by the breadwinner's low-skill occupation (foodpacker is the example).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Neither the share of low-SES families in the cohort nor the number of adolescents who used cannabis is given, so whether 23% is an over- or under-representation cannot be judged; the χ2 concerns adolescent-onset dependence, the 23% any adolescent cannabis use. The test is not significant in a small group (the 2012 paper's Fig. 2 shows 52 people with dependence before 18: 17 + 12 + 23, editors' sum), so it shows no significant association, not the absence of one.

key_findings.finding: IQ of children from low-SES families did not change from the beginning of schooling to adolescence or from adolescence to adulthood, and low SES was unrelated to adolescent-to-adult IQ decline (r = −0.006, P = 0.86). In Fig. 1, mean IQ by SES class at ages 7, 9, 11, 13 and 38 runs roughly flat: about 94 to 92 (low), 101 to 100 (middle) and 110 to 110 (high).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 values read approximately from the rendered figure by the first reader only; the second reader and the adjudicator could not view the image (deferred: figure image not viewable). key_findings.finding: Trend of full-scale IQ change on waves of cannabis dependence: β = −0.152 (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001) for the 2012 model, whose paper printed only the t; with SES added β = −0.158 (t = −4.58, P < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: β is not defined as standardized or unstandardized; the comparison model is the sex-only model, not the 2012 multivariable model (t = −2.20).

key_findings.finding: Restricted to the 553 members from middle-class families (excluding low-SES and high-SES families), the trend was β = −0.155 (t = −3.61, P = 0.0003), and the group means followed the full-cohort pattern (3 or more waves of dependence about −0.37 SD against about −0.38 in the full cohort of 874).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2 and its key
key_findings.note: The text confirms the restriction to middle-class families (low- and high-SES families left out) and β = −0.155, t = −3.61, P = 0.0003. The n of 553 and the bar values are printed only in Fig. 2 and were read by the first reader only; the second reader and the adjudicator could not view the image (deferred: figure image not viewable). A back-calculation from β and t (second reader) makes an n near 550 plausible. Group sizes within the middle-class subsample are not shown.

key_findings.finding: Fig. 3B restricts the age-of-onset analysis to middle-class families; its caption says it shows the same pattern as panel A (the full cohort). As read from the figure by the first reader: dependence before 18 against later onset at 1 wave n=9 against 32, at 2 waves n=8 against 10, at 3 or more waves n=17 against 8, with the largest decline (about −0.55 SD) in the adolescent-onset 3-or-more group and changes near zero for adult onset.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 3B and its legend
key_findings.note: Only the caption could be confirmed by the second reader and the adjudicator; the group sizes and bar heights are single-reader values from the figure (deferred: figure image not viewable). No p values or interaction test are given for panel B.

key_findings.finding: Childhood self-control, described as a precursor of conscientiousness and measured before cannabis use, was unrelated to IQ decline (r = −0.034, P = 0.31); with self-control added, the trend was β = −0.151 (t = −4.38, P = 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: For t = −4.38 with about 870 degrees of freedom the two-sided P is about 0.00001 (editors' calculation), so the printed P = 0.0001 should read P < 0.0001.

key_findings.finding: The reply's account of Daly's letter: Daly's own test in the National Child Development Study did not support his conscientiousness hypothesis; his exposure variable did not capture age of onset or persistence, and personality was measured at 50, after cannabis use.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: Daly (2013) was not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that observational studies cannot prove causation, list the strategies they used to approach causal inference (temporal order, dose-response, within-individual change, informant reports, exclusion of artefacts, testing rival explanations) and argue that statistical control for confounders needs a theoretical rationale, citing Meehl (1971).
