design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects (DerSimonian and Laird) meta-analysis of the dose-response association between level of cannabis use and psychosis-related outcomes. Within each study, people were ranked on that study's own ordinal cannabis measure and given an index from 0 (never used) to 1 (the most-exposed rank), people who had used being spread uniformly over bins sized by the group counts; individual-level data were then simulated from the published case and non-case counts at each level (the authors' earlier method, Vassos et al., 2012) and a logistic regression of outcome on the index was fitted. The pooled slope gives the odds ratio between the most-exposed rank and never use. Only crude counts were pooled. Search to 31 December 2013; 18 studies in the systematic review, 10 in the meta-analysis (6 prospective cohorts, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 case-control study), 66,816 individuals.
can_establish: Whether, in ten observational studies published up to 2013, people ranked higher on each study's own ordinal measure of cannabis use had higher crude odds of a psychosis-related outcome than people who never used cannabis, and the size and spread of that crude gradient on a common rank scale.
cannot_establish: Causation or its direction (no pooled estimate is adjusted for any confounder, and four of the ten studies are cross-sectional or case-control); the risk at any absolute frequency, amount, duration or potency of use, because the top of the rank scale is a different exposure in each study (more than 50 lifetime occasions among Swedish conscripts, daily use in the London case-control sample, regular use in nine Finnish adolescents); adjusted absolute risks (crude proportions by level can be computed from Table 1, for example admission with schizophrenia in 215 of 36,429 Swedish conscripts who had never used cannabis and 28 of 731 who had used it more than 50 times, about 6 and 38 in 1,000, editors' calculation, with follow-up not stated); or whether the gradient is linear, which the model assumes rather than tests.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 31 December 2013, combining dose-related terms (dose-response, daily use, duration, high frequency, heavy use) with psychosis or schizophrenia terms and cannabis or marijuana terms; reference lists of the included studies and of five earlier reviews were checked and experts were contacted (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The pooled primary studies are prospective cohorts from the USA, New Zealand, Sweden (1969 conscripts), Germany and England (two), cross-sectional surveys from Australia (two) and Finland (adolescents), and the London first-episode case-control sample of the Genetics and Psychosis (GAP) study (Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed cohort and cross-sectional studies that measured cannabis use with a dose criterion (frequency, amount or severity) before the onset of psychosis, classified it into at least three levels (never use plus two or more), and established psychosis-related outcomes with validated clinical measures; no language limit. Excluded: samples with mental illness before cannabis use or at ultra-high risk; studies of comorbidity between substance use disorders and psychosis; neuropsychological or schizoid-trait outcomes; studies of age at onset only (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph). For the meta-analysis, studies with continuous outcomes were left out, one of three reports on the Swedish conscripts was kept, one study with 10 cases was dropped, and the two published GAP reports were replaced by updated data supplied by the authors (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Not reported at review level. Table 1 gives only country, design, exposure measure, outcome and counts; no ages, sex or recruitment settings are given. The share of each pooled sample that had used cannabis ranges from 5.6% (Finnish adolescents) to 56.8% (London case-control sample) (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The electronic search required dose-related terms, and three of the four studies added by hand were reports of the Swedish conscript cohort (refs 15, 20, 29), which suggests the search was not sensitive (Results, 1st paragraph). Only peer-reviewed articles were sought, with no grey literature, and the search closed on 31 December 2013, about 25 months before online publication on 15 February 2016. Eight of the 18 systematic-review studies were not pooled and two of them are not identified. The London case-control data are the review team's own: the second author is first author of both published GAP reports (refs 16 and 31), and the pooled data were updated data on the same sample provided by the authors (Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used, always as an ordered variable (Table 1): lifetime frequency (US cohort, Swedish conscripts, Finnish adolescents, English cohort of Zammit 2011), frequency at baseline (Australian survey, German cohort), frequency in the past year with dependence as the top level (British survey of Wiles 2006), duration of use in years (Australian young adults of McGrath 2010), use more than three times a year at ages 18 and 15 (New Zealand) and frequency (London case-control study). The rank index gives never use 0 and spreads people who had used over bins of a uniform 0-1 scale sized by the group counts (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: The top category differs by study (Table 1): daily use (USA), weekly use (Australian survey), use more than three times a year by age 15 (New Zealand), more than 50 lifetime occasions (Sweden), almost daily use (Germany), cannabis dependence (British survey), regular use (Finland; 9 people), six or more years of use (Australian young adults), more than 60 occasions (English cohort) and everyday use (London). Potency and period of use were not considered (Discussion, 6th paragraph), and age at first use was not modelled as such, except that in the New Zealand cohort the ordered levels are themselves defined by age (use by 18, use by 15; Table 1); route was not considered.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. Crude counts were pooled, so tobacco, alcohol and other drug use are not adjusted for in any pooled estimate (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The authors state that they had no data on the time between regular cannabis use and illness onset (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

comparison.controls: The Methods state that people who had never used cannabis were the reference category (index 0) in every study (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph), but Table 1's reference rows read no cannabis within the last year (Wiles et al., British survey), no cannabis use at age 18 (Arseneault et al., New Zealand) and none or no use for frequency at baseline (Henquet et al., German cohort; Degenhardt and Hall, Australian survey); the reference is no use, as each study measured it.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. No adjustment of any kind: crude odds ratios were recomputed from the case and non-case counts at each exposure level even where a study had reported only adjusted odds ratios (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nothing premorbid enters the pooled estimates: family history of psychosis, childhood adversity, symptoms or functioning before first use, IQ, ethnicity, socioeconomic position and urbanicity are all unadjusted. The authors name ethnicity and socioeconomic status as possible confounders (Discussion, 6th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; people who never used cannabis may have used other drugs, and no pooled estimate separates cannabis from other substance use.

outcomes.instruments: Heterogeneous (Table 1): at least one psychotic symptom within one year of follow-up (DSM-III; USA); positive psychosis screener within one year (DSM-IV; Australian survey); schizophreniform disorder at age 26 (DSM-IV; New Zealand); inpatient admission for schizophrenia (ICD-8 and ICD-9; Swedish conscripts); two or more psychotic symptoms on the CIDI psychosis section (Germany); self-reported psychotic symptoms on the Psychosis Screening Questionnaire (British survey); prodromal symptoms on the PROD-screen (Finnish adolescents, where 1937 of 6298 were counted as cases); any CIDI hallucination (Australian young adults); self-reported severe psychotic experiences on the PLIKS questionnaire (English cohort); first-episode psychosis (ICD-10; London). Where a study reported several outcomes, the most severe was used (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies was done.
outcomes.operationalization: A psychosis-related outcome was either symptoms above each study's threshold or a diagnosis or admission. In the outcome subgroup analysis, eight studies are classed as psychotic symptoms and only two (Swedish admissions for schizophrenia; London first-episode psychosis) as diagnoses (Figure 3B).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five pooled estimates (overall; cohort; cross-sectional; psychotic symptoms; diagnosis), one meta-regression on study year and two small-study tests. The odds ratios for the median person who used cannabis and for the top 20% are transformations of the same pooled slope, not further tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Selection: one author identified studies and a second independently checked them for inclusion; extraction: two authors independently (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled log-odds slope b = 1.36 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68), I² = 82%, giving an odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34) between the most-exposed rank (index 1) and never use; model-based odds ratios of 1.97 (1.68 to 2.31) for the median person who used cannabis and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the median of the top 20% (Results, 3rd paragraph). Study estimates at index 1 (Figure 3): Tien 1990, 1.85 (1.33 to 2.57); Zammit 2002, 6.20 (4.19 to 9.17); Henquet 2005, 5.16 (3.13 to 8.50); Wiles 2006, 3.04 (1.41 to 6.59); Zammit 2011, 4.36 (2.38 to 7.99); Arseneault 2002, 4.29 (1.45 to 12.70); Degenhardt 2001, 7.45 (3.99 to 13.90); Miettunen 2008, 4.67 (3.66 to 5.96); McGrath 2010, 1.89 (1.32 to 2.69); GAP data 2012, 4.38 (3.30 to 5.81). Subgroups: cohort 3.83 (2.34 to 6.29); cross-sectional 3.99 (2.50 to 6.37); psychotic symptoms 3.59 (2.42 to 5.32); diagnosis 5.07 (3.62 to 7.09). Meta-regression on year p = .53; Egger p = .79; Begg p = .86 (Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs). Editors' calculation from the ten printed study estimates (DerSimonian and Laird; it reproduces the pooled 3.90 and I² of 82%): Q = 49.3 on 9 degrees of freedom, tau² = 0.19, 95% prediction interval for a new study's odds ratio at index 1 about 1.3 to 11.5; within-subgroup I² about 80% (cohort), 87% (cross-sectional), 82% (symptoms) and 50% (diagnosis, 2 studies).
analysis.covariates: None. Every pooled estimate is crude; adjusted estimates reported by primary studies were not used (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper states that the search followed the PRISMA statement (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Cochran's Q, tau², study weights, prediction intervals and subgroup heterogeneity are not reported, although the Methods say Q was used. The 18 systematic-review studies are not listed; two studies left out of the meta-analysis are not named, and the eight unpooled studies are not described beyond their exclusion reasons. The supplement (a Word file, not read) is described only as illustrating the simulation method with an example; no pooled result depends on it.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With ten studies, Egger's and Begg's tests have little power to detect small-study effects, which the paper does not mention; the diagnosis subgroup rests on two studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In ten observational studies (six cohorts, three cross-sectional surveys, one case-control study), crude odds of a psychosis-related outcome rose with rank on each study's own ordinal cannabis measure; the fitted odds ratio between the top rank and never use was 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34), with high heterogeneity (I² 82%; editors' 95% prediction interval about 1.3 to 11.5). The top of the rank scale is a different exposure in each study, and the category-level crude odds ratios in Table 1 do not rise steadily in several studies (for example 0.40 to 0.70 for the three lowest use categories in the London data). Nothing is adjusted for confounding.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that “high levels of cannabis use increase the risk of psychotic outcomes” and that the evidence confirms a dose-response relationship, and the conclusion calls the result “the most accurate estimate of the effect size” (Abstract; Discussion, 9th paragraph). Gaps: (1) a causal verb from crude observational data, in an abstract that also says a causal link cannot be established and does not say the estimates are unadjusted; (2) dose here is a within-study rank, not an amount, frequency or potency, so the gradient cannot be translated into any level of use, and linearity is assumed by the model (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); the consistent increase in every included study (Results, 3rd paragraph) describes the fitted lines of Figure 2, which rise by construction whenever the slope is positive, not the category-level data; (3) reverse causation is called unlikely because cohorts with symptomatic participants at baseline were excluded (Discussion, 1st paragraph), but four of the ten studies are cross-sectional or case-control; (4) the headline 3.90 is the odds ratio for the single most-exposed rank, and the authors themselves say that applying Moore et al.'s average 45% attenuation for adjustment to their top-20% estimate gives results comparable to Moore's 2.1 (Discussion, 7th paragraph), which the abstract does not mention; (5) the stronger association with hard outcomes (5.07) rests on two studies, one of them the authors' own data; (6) the conclusion's public-policy remarks about dose reduction and later onset are not tested by these data.

timeline.event: Earlier reviews by Henquet, Murray, Linszen and van Os (Schizophrenia Bulletin) and by Semple, McIntosh and Lawrie (Journal of Psychopharmacology), cited for an approximately two-fold risk of psychotic disorder in people who use cannabis (Introduction, 1st paragraph).

Moore et al. systematic review, whose pooled odds ratios this review gives as 1.4 for any use and 2.1 for the most frequent use; the authors argue their higher estimate reflects crude data, newer studies and the top-rank extrapolation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

Di Forti et al., an earlier report on high-potency cannabis from the London GAP case-control study (British Journal of Psychiatry); with the 2014 GAP report (Schizophrenia Bulletin), replaced in this meta-analysis by updated data on the same sample supplied by the authors.

Vassos et al., simulation method for meta-analysing an exposure gradient from grouped counts, first applied to urbanicity and schizophrenia; reused here (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).

Gage, Zammit and Hickman (F1000 Medicine Reports), a review titled as arguing that stronger evidence is needed before accepting an important role for cannabis in the aetiology of schizophrenia; used here only as a source of references, its arguments are not discussed.

Davis et al., US national survey (NESARC): adjusted odds ratio 3.69 (2.49 to 5.47) for a psychosis diagnosis with lifetime cannabis dependence, cited as remarkably similar to this review's estimate (Discussion, 7th paragraph; second-hand figure).

Di Forti et al. (Lancet Psychiatry), GAP case-control analysis of 410 cases and 370 controls from the same London study whose updated data are pooled here; not cited by this review (card sc_di_forti_2015). The two sources overlap and are not independent.
This review: random-effects meta-analysis of a crude rank-scale gradient in ten studies.

Di Forti et al. (EU-GEI, Lancet Psychiatry) cite this meta-analysis as showing a dose-response association with the highest odds in the heaviest use (Introduction, 1st paragraph; card sc_di_forti_2019).

replication.where_it_stands: Often cited as the dose-response meta-analysis for cannabis and psychosis. Its pooled figure is a crude odds ratio extrapolated to the top rank of ten different exposure scales and should only be cited with that description; it cannot give the risk at a stated frequency or potency. The review discusses no critique of a causal reading and no genetic (Mendelian randomization, polygenic score, co-relative) or quasi-experimental test. The London case-control data inside it overlap Di Forti et al. (2009, 2014 and 2015), and five of its six cohorts are the reports Moore et al. (2007) pooled (Tien and Anthony 1990, ECA; Arseneault et al. 2002, Dunedin; Zammit et al. 2002, Swedish conscripts; Henquet et al. 2005, EDSP; Wiles et al. 2006, NPMS; editors' cross-check of the two reference lists), so the two reviews are not independent replications.

funding.funder: Guy's and St Thomas Charity Grant (R080529); the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre for Mental Health at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London; the European Community's Seventh Framework Programme under the Marie Curie Industry-Academia Partnership and Pathways, grant agreement 286213 (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest in relation to the subject of the study (Acknowledgment section).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are at King's College London, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (Department of Psychosis Studies; MRC SGDP Centre). The second author is first author of both published GAP reports pooled here, and Marconi, Di Forti and Murray are also authors of the GAP case-control paper read for sc_di_forti_2015; Vassos, Murray and Lewis are authors of the simulation method used (ref 24). No procedure for appraising the authors' own study is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis of prospective cohorts that recorded frequency, amount and potency of cannabis use before any psychotic symptoms, harmonized onto an absolute scale (for example days of use per month and THC content), adjusted for family history, childhood adversity, other drug use and socioeconomic position, reporting absolute incidence by exposure level and testing rather than assuming a linear gradient.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (any), exposure (level of cannabis use measured with a dose criterion before psychosis, at least three levels), comparator (never use) and outcome (validated psychosis-related measures) are stated (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; the paper says only that the search followed PRISMA.
Cohort and cross-sectional designs were made eligible without explanation, and a case-control study was pooled although the criteria name only cohort and cross-sectional studies.

Three databases, the search terms, reference lists of included studies and five reviews, contact with experts, and no language limit. But the restriction to peer-reviewed articles is not justified, there was no grey-literature or registry search, and the search closed on 31 December 2013, about 25 months before online publication; the dose-term search missed three reports of the Swedish conscript cohort that were found only by hand. Under a reading of AMSTAR 2 that asks for justification of language restrictions only, the item would be partial yes (the project's reading of item 4 is decision p-amstar2-item4).

One author identified studies and a second independently checked them for inclusion (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph); the paper does not say that the second author screened the 571 records or the full texts, so exclusions by the first author were not duplicated. A close call.
Two authors extracted the data independently (Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives exclusion reasons by category (for example 53 for unsuitable outcome) and the text names five excluded reports (refs 17, 20, 29, 30, 36), but there is no list of excluded full texts with reasons, and two studies left out of the meta-analysis are not identified. The supplement, not read, is described only as illustrating the simulation method.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, design, exposure measure, outcome with diagnostic system, exposure levels and case and non-case counts for the ten pooled studies; it gives no ages, sex, recruitment setting or follow-up length beyond what the outcome column implies, and the eight systematic-review studies that were not pooled are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Crude odds ratios were recomputed from counts and pooled even where studies had reported adjusted estimates (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph); for non-randomized studies AMSTAR 2 asks for adequately adjusted estimates, or a justification for raw data when adjusted ones are unavailable. The rank-index method also assumes the same distribution of cannabis use across studies (5th paragraph), which the exposure categories in Table 1 contradict, and the case-control study is pooled with cohorts and surveys. Random-effects pooling itself is appropriate for I² of 82%.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact; subgroups by design and outcome type are not a test of study quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Bias in individual studies was never assessed. The discussion names confounding by ethnicity and socioeconomic status as a possible partial explanation and then sets it aside by citing two adjusted studies, and argues against reverse causation from an exclusion criterion that does not apply to the four cross-sectional and case-control studies; the abstract states that high levels of use increase the risk.

I² is reported (82%), subgroup analyses by design and outcome and a meta-regression on study year were run, and the discussion addresses the expected heterogeneity (Results, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph). Within-subgroup heterogeneity is not reported; the editors' recomputation from Figure 3 gives I² of 80% to 87% within the larger subgroups, so the subgroups explain little of it.

Egger's (p = .79) and Begg's (p = .86) tests were run and reported (Results, 5th paragraph). Their low power with ten studies is not mentioned and the discussion of possible publication bias is a single sentence; a close call.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are given; the paper does not flag that the London case-control data are the authors' own, updated and unpublished.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six of the seven critical items of AMSTAR 2 are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11 and 13); only item 15 is met, so confidence in the pooled numbers as an unbiased summary is critically low. Beyond the checklist, the main problem for claims is what the number means: an odds ratio between the top rank of ten different exposure scales and never use, from crude data, extrapolated by a linear model. The review may be cited for the existence and approximate shape of a crude gradient across the studies it pooled, for the study-level estimates and as a pointer to the primary studies; it should not be cited for a causal effect, an adjusted effect size, the risk at a stated frequency or potency, or for the absence of a safe level of use.

key_findings.finding: 571 records from the database search; 442 excluded on title or abstract; 129 full texts plus 4 studies from reference lists assessed; 115 excluded at full text (53 unsuitable outcome, 21 unsuitable cannabis data, 30 case-only or high-risk samples, 11 not primary studies); 18 studies entered the systematic review and 10 the meta-analysis. Three of the four studies found by hand were reports of the Swedish 1969 conscript cohort.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (flow diagram, an image read on screen)

key_findings.finding: The ten pooled studies include 66,816 individuals: six prospective cohorts (USA, New Zealand, Sweden, Germany, England twice), three cross-sectional surveys (Australia twice, Finland) and one London case-control sample (GAP). Editors' sum of Table 1: 4036 people with the outcome and 62,780 without.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' check of Table 1: every row total equals controls plus cases, every printed crude odds ratio is reproduced from the counts, and the totals sum to 66,816.

key_findings.finding: Pooled random-effects slope b = 1.36 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.68), corresponding to an odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34) for a psychosis-related outcome at the most-exposed rank of each study's cannabis scale compared with never use; heterogeneity I² = 82%. All data are crude.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 3.90 refers to the single highest rank (index 1) on a within-study rank scale, from a model that assumes a straight line in log odds; it is not the odds ratio of any reported exposure category.

key_findings.finding: From the same slope, the authors derive odds ratios of 1.97 (1.68 to 2.31) for the median person who had used cannabis (index 0.5) and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the median person in the top 20% of exposure (index 0.9).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' check: exp(1.36 × 0.5) = 1.97 and exp(1.36 × 0.9) = 3.40, so these are transformations of the pooled slope, not separate estimates.

key_findings.finding: Study odds ratios at the most-exposed rank: Tien 1990 (USA, cohort) 1.85 (1.33 to 2.57); Zammit 2002 (Sweden, cohort) 6.20 (4.19 to 9.17); Henquet 2005 (Germany, cohort) 5.16 (3.13 to 8.50); Wiles 2006 (England, cohort) 3.04 (1.41 to 6.59); Zammit 2011 (England, cohort) 4.36 (2.38 to 7.99); Arseneault 2002 (New Zealand, cohort) 4.29 (1.45 to 12.70); Degenhardt 2001 (Australia, cross-sectional) 7.45 (3.99 to 13.90); Miettunen 2008 (Finland, cross-sectional) 4.67 (3.66 to 5.96); McGrath 2010 (Australia, cross-sectional) 1.89 (1.32 to 2.69); GAP data 2012 (London, case-control) 4.38 (3.30 to 5.81).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3A (value labels, read on screen); Figure 2 shows the corresponding fitted curves
key_findings.note: Figure 3 is an image; the values are its printed labels. Every study's interval excludes 1.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: cross-sectional and case-control studies 3.99 (2.50 to 6.37), 4 studies; cohort studies 3.83 (2.34 to 6.29), 6 studies; psychotic symptoms 3.59 (2.42 to 5.32), 8 studies; diagnosis of schizophrenia or psychotic disorder 5.07 (3.62 to 7.09), 2 studies (Swedish conscript admissions 6.20; London first-episode data 4.38).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Figure 3A and 3B
key_findings.note: The diagnosis subgroup rests on two studies, one of them the authors' own data; the New Zealand schizophreniform-disorder outcome is plotted with the symptom studies (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Meta-regression on study year was not significant (p = .53); Egger's test p = .79 and Begg's test p = .86 for small-study effects.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the ten study estimates in Figure 3 (DerSimonian and Laird; it reproduces the pooled 3.90 [2.84 to 5.35] and I² of 82%): Q = 49.3 on 9 degrees of freedom, tau² = 0.19, and a 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio in a new comparable study of about 1.3 to 11.5. Within subgroups, I² is about 80% (cohort), 87% (cross-sectional), 82% (symptoms) and 50% (diagnosis, 2 studies).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3 (editors' calculation)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: standard errors derived from the printed 95% intervals on the log scale; prediction interval with t on 8 degrees of freedom. The paper reports none of these quantities.

key_findings.finding: The category-level crude odds ratios do not rise steadily in several studies: London case-control data 0.70 (once or twice), 0.40 (a few times a year), 0.65 (a few times a month), 1.24 (more than once a week), 3.51 (every day); Swedish conscripts 0.56 (1 occasion), 0.98 (2 to 4), 1.90 (5 to 10), 3.24 (11 to 50), 6.71 (more than 50), rising steadily across the exposed categories but below the never-use reference at the two lowest; US cohort 0.84 (moderate use), 2.17 (daily use); English cohort of Zammit 2011, 2.07, 3.11, 1.42 (1 case) and 5.69 (3 cases) across rising categories; Finnish adolescents 2.62 after a single use and 3.00 for regular use.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Method: never use is given index 0 and people who had used an index between 0 and 1 by rank, in bins whose widths follow the group counts; 1000 simulation iterations per study; studies weighted by the standard error of the slope and pooled “under the assumption of an equivalent distribution of cannabis use across studies”.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd to 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: In the London case-control sample, 473 of 798 participants are cases, and in the Finnish survey 31% are counted as cases, so their bins reflect the sampling or the screening threshold rather than the population's use (editors' observation from Table 1).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the estimates rest on unadjusted data and may be partly explained by confounders such as ethnicity or socioeconomic status, citing two studies that controlled for them (refs 16 and 19) as confirming the association; and that, because cohort studies enrolling people with symptoms at baseline were excluded, reverse causation is unlikely.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th and 1st paragraphs
key_findings.note: The reverse-causation argument applies at most to the six cohorts; three cross-sectional surveys and one case-control study measured exposure and outcome at the same time or retrospectively.

key_findings.finding: Compared with Moore et al. (2007), whose pooled odds ratios the authors give as 1.4 for any use and 2.1 for severe use, the authors say that applying Moore's average 45% attenuation for full adjustment to their top-20% estimate (3.4) would give comparable results; they also cite an adjusted odds ratio of 3.69 (2.49 to 5.47) for a psychosis diagnosis with lifetime cannabis dependence from a US national survey (Davis et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures: 1.4 and 2.1 from Moore et al. (2007), 3.69 from Davis et al. (2013). The attenuation calculation is not shown; reducing 3.4 by 45% gives about 1.9 on the odds-ratio scale or about 2.3 on the excess odds (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: The authors report having no data on cannabis potency, the period of use or the time between regular use and illness onset; they pooled different kinds of exposure measure (frequency, duration, diagnoses of use, abuse or dependence) because all were ordered, and outcomes ranging from self-reported psychotic experiences to admission for schizophrenia; their estimates assume a linear increase in risk with level of use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 cites reference 13 for the German prospective cohort (Henquet et al.), but reference 13 is a 2005 Schizophrenia Bulletin review by Henquet, Murray, Linszen and van Os on the environment and schizophrenia, not a cohort report; the primary cohort paper is not in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of one of the ten pooled studies cannot be identified from the paper; claim writers must not cite reference 13 as the German cohort.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 and the Results (2nd paragraph) list schizophreniform disorder at age 26 (New Zealand, Arseneault 2002) among the diagnostic outcomes, but Figure 3B plots this study in the psychotic-symptoms subgroup, leaving two studies in the diagnosis subgroup.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Figure 3B
reporting_issues.consequence: The stronger association for diagnosed disorder (5.07) rests on two studies, one being the authors' own; the classification of the New Zealand study is inconsistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility criteria name cohort and cross-sectional studies only, but a case-control study (GAP data) is pooled, and Figure 3A places it in the cross-sectional subgroup.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Figure 3A
reporting_issues.consequence: The cross-sectional subgroup mixes surveys and a case-control sample; the design comparison is less informative than presented.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria and abstract require cannabis use measured before the onset of psychosis, but three pooled studies are cross-sectional surveys in which use and symptoms were measured at the same time (Table 1).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Methods › Selection Criteria and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: For four of ten studies the temporal order is not established, which undercuts the discussion's argument against reverse causation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results cite two references (17, 36) for the exclusion of continuous-outcome studies, while Figure 1 reports three such exclusions, plus one study without the necessary data; two of the eight unpooled systematic-review studies are therefore not identified.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection of the pooled set cannot be fully reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q and I², but only I² is reported; Q, tau², study weights and subgroup heterogeneity are absent.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analysis, 5th paragraph; Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot judge the spread of true effects; the editors' recomputation (tau² 0.19, prediction interval about 1.3 to 11.5) is needed for any claim about consistency.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 2 speaks of an estimated risk ratio while its axis and all analyses are odds ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; with outcomes as common as 31% in the Finnish screen, odds ratios and risk ratios differ, so the quantities should not be described as risk ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference-list errors: reference 9 is given as 'Adverse health effects of medical cannabis use' (Lancet 2009), while the Hall and Degenhardt Lancet 2009 review held in this project (hall_2009) is titled 'Adverse health effects of non-medical cannabis use'; several entries carry implausible page fields (for example Arseneault 2002, BMJ 325:2; Degenhardt 2001, Psychol Med 31:10; Zammit 2011, Br J Psychiatry 199:6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Match cited studies by DOI rather than by the printed citation.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD42019126994, registered 28 February 2019, the day of the search) of human experimental studies that gave the same dose of THC by the same route with and without cannabidiol (CBD) and had a placebo or pre-drug baseline condition. Four databases searched on 28 February 2019, English-language peer-reviewed reports only. 23 articles reporting 16 studies (13 crossover, 3 parallel-group; 466 healthy volunteers in all), published 1974 to 2019. Table 1 lists the two experiments of Dalton et al. (1976) as separate studies, and groups several articles from one sample (for example Nadulski et al., 2005, with Juckel et al., 2007, Roser et al., 2008 and 2009, and Stadelmann et al., 2011). Narrative synthesis by outcome domain because outcomes were too heterogeneous to pool. Risk of bias rated with a Cochrane tool by two reviewers; Table 1 shows only an overall rating per study (domain judgments are in Appendix G, not in the file). Read as the journal pre-proof.
can_establish: What the published, English-language laboratory studies up to early 2019 reported when CBD was given with or at varying times before, a matched dose of THC to healthy volunteers, outcome by outcome, and how consistent those reports were across very different doses, routes, timings and THC: CBD ratios.
cannot_establish: How large any effect of CBD on THC's acute effects is (nothing was pooled and effect sizes are rarely given); whether it depends on dose, ratio or route (the authors found no consistent pattern, and the conditions tested rarely match each other); whether findings apply to clinical populations, people selected for previous adverse reactions or longer-term use (the review studied acute effects in screened healthy volunteers). Cannabis-use histories varied and included daily use; the review does not establish that most participants used only occasionally. It cannot establish whether the literature is free of reporting bias (no assessment beyond an informal statement).

sample.recruitment: Database search (MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus) on 28 February 2019 using terms for THC and CBD only, with Ovid filters for human studies and English, plus additional sources; four articles published after the search were added (pp. 10–12 of the journal pre-proof). Participants in the included studies were healthy volunteers in the UK, USA, Australia, Brazil and Germany (Table 1, pp. 65–71).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: a condition or group given acute THC; a matched condition or group given the same THC dose by the same route together with CBD under experimental conditions; a placebo condition or a no-drug pre-drug baseline; peer-reviewed; English. Excluded: conference abstracts, theses, reviews, supplements, letters and other non-peer-reviewed material; studies without a matched THC dose and route; repeated-dosing studies; studies whose analysis did not compare THC alone with THC plus CBD (or each with placebo); non-human studies (2.2, pp. 9–10).
sample.demographics: All 16 studies used healthy volunteers (3.2, p.15). Samples ranged from 4 to 155 participants; one parallel study and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell (pp.13–14). Table 1 gives heterogeneous cannabis-use histories: about half of Bird et al. used at least weekly; Haney et al. recruited people currently using cannabis; Hindocha/Morgan recruited 24 people who used cannabis daily and 24 who used it recreationally. Several other rows state only at least once, which does not establish occasional use. Two studies included people who had never used cannabis: 18 of 40 in Karniol et al. and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. Six experimental samples from five reports enrolled men only: the two Dalton experiments, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt and Karniol. Ages listed in Table 1 run from 18 to 70.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Table 1 records study-level losses, for example three of 14 not completing in Arkell et al. (2019), one of them discharged because of raised blood pressure and heart rate; failed cannulation in three of 48 in Englund et al. (2013); 19 further people withdrawn or excluded in Haney et al. (2016); 20 to 24 of 28 analysed in Nadulski et al. (2005), where three women had a panic attack (pp. 65, 67, 68, 70, 72).
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed reports only; no trial registries or grey literature. All participants were screened healthy volunteers. Applicability to clinical populations or people selected for previous adverse reactions is uncertain; the authors suggest studies may have excluded people at risk of adverse effects (4.3, p.34), but that is not a verified exclusion for every trial. Frequent use was represented in some samples, including people using cannabis daily. Two of the 16 studies (six of the 23 articles) were co-authored by review authors.

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration in each included study, as listed in Table 1 (pp.65–71). By the adjudicator's count of its 16 experimental rows, THC was oral in 5, intravenous in 3, smoked in 3, vaporised in 3 and oromucosal in 2. CBD was administered at the same time or as pre-treatment in five experiments. Table 1's Intervention column gives pre-treatment between 480 and 5 minutes before THC, but some timing entries disagree with the text or another column (see reporting issues). The review's route and dose summary on p.15 also differs from Table 1.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as printed in Table 1 and the text: THC 1.25 to 2 mg intravenously; 8 to 13.75 mg vaporised; about 42 mg or 0.025 mg/kg smoked; 10 to 30 mg, 0.215 mg/kg or 0.5 mg/kg orally; 10 to 15 mg by oromucosal spray. CBD from 5 mg intravenously to 1500 mg orally in three divided doses (Hunt et al., 1981), with THC: CBD ratios varying widely between studies. Acute matched-THC comparisons; repeated-dosing studies were excluded by the review, although Hunt used three CBD pre-treatment doses within the experimental regimen.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. Abstinence rules before sessions differed between studies (Table 1); the review names participants' own cannabis use outside the study as a possible source of residual effects (3.5, p. 16). In Arkell et al. (2019) the THC-alone condition contained less than 1.25 mg CBD and the placebo less than 1.25 mg THC and CBD (Table 1, p. 65).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied by study (Table 1): not reported in Dalton et al. (1976) and Hollister and Gillespie (1975); 12 hours without cannabis, alcohol or tobacco in Haney et al. (2016); 24 hours without alcohol or illicit drugs in the two UCL studies; 48 hours on site in Hunt et al. (1981); 15 days in Zuardi et al. (1982); 30 days or one month in Guy and Robson (2003), Nicholson et al. (2004) and Nadulski et al. (2005); urine or oral-fluid screens in several.

comparison.controls: Within each study, the same THC dose by the same route without CBD (or after placebo pre-treatment), and a placebo condition or a pre-drug baseline. The review's Treatment characteristics text says the five pre-treatment designs used baseline measures rather than a pure placebo condition (p.15). This is the review's description, not independent verification of the five primary protocols; Table 1 also describes these designs as placebo-controlled.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Thirteen within-person crossover studies and three parallel-group studies. Bird and Englund are described as randomly assigned; Karniol's groups are described as balanced for age and weight, without an explicit random-allocation statement in Table 1. Allocation procedures were not uniformly documented.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (experimental comparisons). Participant characteristics the authors say can change THC's acute effects (cannabis history, potency and frequency of use, psychosis-proneness, sex, genetic factors) were not assessed in most studies (4, 2nd paragraph, pp. 31–32).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in the crossover designs; abstinence rules varied between studies (see exposure).

outcomes.instruments: As used by the primary studies (Table 1; section 3.6): plasma THC and metabolites; pulse and blood pressure; visual analogue scales of intoxication, the ARCI-Ma and a modified Cornell Medical Index; anxiety ratings and the STAI, and the graded symptom scale of Karniol and Carlini; PANSS, BPRS, Psychotomimetic States Inventory and State Social Paranoia Scale; memory and attention tasks (HVLT-R, prose recall, N-back, digit span, DSST, divided attention, PASAT, time production, verbal fluency); auditory event-related potentials (mismatch negativity, P300); emotion-recognition and effort-for-reward tasks; fMRI; psychomotor and simulated-driving tasks; sleep measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study risk of bias was rated by two reviewers with a Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, named as RoB 2 but cited to the 2011 tool (2.6, p. 12) and to Higgins et al. (2016) in the limitations (p. 37); only one overall rating per study is shown (Table 1).
outcomes.operationalization: An influence of CBD was any reported difference between THC alone and THC with CBD on any outcome; the review planned to report all such comparisons (2.8, p. 12). Table 1 codes each finding as CBD increasing, decreasing or not changing THC's effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable at review level: no statistical tests were run; ten outcome domains are synthesized narratively (3.6.1 to 3.6.10). The authors note that not all primary studies corrected for multiple analyses (4.7, p. 38).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts, and then full texts, were each screened independently by two reviewers with a third for disagreements; two reviewers extracted data, a third resolved discrepancies and checked a random subset (2.4, 2.5, p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; the synthesis is narrative because heterogeneity of outcomes precluded meta-analysis (3.6, p. 17). No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. The text gives counts of studies, sample sizes and a few raw values, for example a mean fall in systolic blood pressure at 3 hours of 10.3 mmHg after THC 10 mg alone, 4.4 mmHg with CBD 10 mg and 5.1 mmHg after placebo (Guy and Robson, 2003; p. 20); Grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 participants after oral THC 30 mg alone and in 3 of 15 when oral CBD 15 to 60 mg was added (Karniol et al., 1974; p. 22); THC clearance of 17 and 20.9 ml/min/kg without and with CBD in 4 participants (Hunt et al., 1981; p. 18).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019126994, registered 28 February 2019, the date of the search (2.1, p. 9); PRISMA checklist in Appendix A and protocol in Appendix B, neither in the file. Whether the protocol specified the narrative synthesis, and whether there were deviations, cannot be checked from the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review planned an inclusive approach covering all comparisons of THC with and without CBD; nothing is pooled. Completeness cannot be independently established from the article without the primary reports and protocol appendices. Several counts and study descriptions in the text disagree with Table 1 (see reporting issues). The informal publication-bias judgment (3.5, p.16) does not rule out reporting bias.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level. The authors note that six studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell and that some studies may have been underpowered (pp. 13–14, 38).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 small laboratory studies of healthy volunteers (466 people in all; six studies with 4 to 8 per cell), CBD given with or before a matched THC dose mostly did not change THC's pharmacokinetics, heart rate, subjective intoxication (seven of nine studies found no difference) or psychomotor and driving impairment. Lower anxiety or psychosis-like effects with CBD were reported on selected outcomes: oral THC 30 mg in groups of 5 (Karniol et al., 1974; Grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 versus 3 of 15, no test reported in the review), intravenous THC 1.25 mg in 6 people (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010), and intravenous THC 1.5 mg in a 48-person parallel trial in which the mean PANSS increase did not differ but fewer people given CBD had a clinically significant rise (Englund et al., 2013); Zuardi et al. (1982; n=8) found a smaller STAI rise. With inhaled cannabis, Morgan et al. (2018; n=48) found no difference in psychotomimetic effects, and Arkell et al. (2019; n=14) found anxiety raised in both conditions at 15 minutes and still raised only without CBD at one hour. One study found higher peak plasma THC with CBD (Arkell et al., 2019). Results on memory, attention and emotion processing went both ways.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion are hedged (findings mixed; some evidence that CBD may reduce some effects; no dose-response). Gaps: (1) the discussion says three studies showed “significantly fewer participants” with extreme anxiety and psychotic-like effects (4.3, p. 33), but for two of them the review gives only counts in groups of 5 and 6 without a test, and the third found no difference in the mean; (2) the highlights and discussion call the risk of bias “typically low” (pp. 2, 31), while the limitations list inadequately described randomisation, allocation blinding and unexamined order effects (pp. 37–38), and Table 1 rates as low risk a pseudo-randomised study (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010) and one in which randomisation is not indicated (Nicholson et al., 2004); (3) the highlights say CBD did not alter subjective intoxication, while two of nine studies reported a reduction; (4) the harm-reduction section links these single-dose laboratory findings to consumer education and regulation (4.6, pp. 36–37) without any dose-response or route-specific result to support it.

timeline.event: Karniol et al.: oral CBD with oral THC 30 mg in parallel groups of 5; described in the review as the first report that CBD blocks THC's anxiety-provoking effects (included).
Bhattacharyya et al.: intravenous CBD before intravenous THC in 6 volunteers (included).
Englund et al.: oral CBD 600 mg before intravenous THC 1.5 mg, 48-person parallel trial (included).
Morgan et al.: vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg in 48 people; no difference in psychotomimetic effects and none by frequency of use or trait schizotypy (included).
Arkell et al.: vaporised cannabis with THC 13.75 mg, with and without CBD 13.75 mg, in 14 people; added after the search (included).
This review: the first systematic review of the question by the authors' account; narrative synthesis, nothing pooled.
Same first author and group: pooled analysis of four of the group's own crossover studies of THC versus placebo (CBD conditions not analysed), on frequency of use and schizotypy as moderators.
Zamarripa et al.: randomized clinical trial of oral THC co-administered with CBD on THC pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in healthy adults (to be appraised from the full text).
Chester et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of whether co-administered CBD changes plasma THC and its active metabolite (on the reading list; to be appraised from the full text).

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of the question at the time and the one usually cited, but it pooled nothing, its three positive studies on anxiety and psychosis-like effects are small and mostly used oral or intravenous THC, and its pre-proof text and table disagree in several places. Later randomized studies of THC with and without CBD on the encyclopedia's reading list (Arkell et al., 2020, driving; Lawn et al., 2023, adults and adolescents; Zamarripa et al., 2023, oral THC) and the 2026 meta-analysis of CBD and plasma THC (Chester et al., 2026) should be read before any claim that CBD does or does not change THC's acute effects.

funding.funder: No specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (p. 38 of the journal pre-proof).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: none (p. 38).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit and the Centre for Outcomes, Research and Effectiveness, University College London; University of Bath; King's College London (p. 1). Review authors T. P. Freeman, C. Hindocha, H. V. Curran and C. Mokrysz are co-authors of six of the 23 included articles (Hindocha et al., 2015 and 2019; Morgan et al., 2018; Lawn et al., 2016; T. P. Freeman et al., 2018; Wall et al., 2019; reference list), from two of the 16 studies, both rated at low risk of bias; C. Hindocha was the third reviewer for extraction and risk-of-bias disagreements (p. 11). This is not declared as a conflict. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered randomized crossover trial in people who use cannabis regularly, comparing inhaled THC alone, THC with two or more CBD doses and placebo under identical routes and timing, with plasma THC measured and prespecified outcomes (anxiety, psychotomimetic states, memory, intoxication); or an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing crossover trials.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Humans given acute THC; THC with CBD versus a matched THC dose and route; placebo or baseline control; all acute outcomes (2.2, 2.8).

PROSPERO CRD42019126994 registered on the day of the search (p. 9); the protocol (Appendix B) is not in the file, so whether it specified the synthesis plan and whether there were deviations cannot be checked.
Inclusion of acute experimental studies with a matched THC dose and route and a placebo or baseline control is justified, as is the exclusion of repeated dosing (pp. 9–10, 37).

Four relevant databases with a sensitive intervention-only strategy (Appendix C, not read) and a search within months of acceptance; but English-language and peer-reviewed-only restrictions without justification (English acknowledged only as a limitation, p. 16), grey literature excluded by design, no trial registries, and no reference-list searching reported.
Titles and abstracts, then full texts, screened independently by two reviewers, a third resolving disagreements (2.4, p. 11).
Two reviewers extracted data; discrepancies resolved with a third, who also checked a random subset (2.5, p. 11).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: a table of excluded studies is said to be in Appendix E and the flow diagram with reasons in Appendix F (p. 13); neither is in the file read, so whether each full-text exclusion is listed with a reason cannot be checked.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, aims, participants (number, sex, age, cannabis experience, abstinence rules), design, conditions with doses, routes and pre-treatment timing, outcomes, findings and risk of bias; the timing of outcome measurement is mostly absent, and several entries contradict the text (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A Cochrane risk-of-bias tool applied independently by two reviewers, but the version is unclear (RoB 2 named, 2011 tool cited), only an overall rating per study is shown (domains in Appendix G, not read), and two low ratings sit awkwardly with the tool: pseudo-randomisation (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010) and randomisation not indicated (Nicholson et al., 2004).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Only two industry-funded studies are named (Guy and Robson, 2003; Nicholson et al., 2004; p. 16); funding of the others is not reported.
Narrative synthesis; meta-analysis judged precluded by heterogeneity of outcomes (p. 17).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Each results subsection names the studies with some concerns, but the discussion and conclusions do not weigh them: the anxiety conclusion rests on three studies, two rated some concerns or unclear (Karniol et al., 1974; Zuardi et al., 1982), and the discussion calls risk of bias typically low. A close call.

Doses, routes, THC:CBD ratios, low oral CBD bioavailability, small samples and participant factors (cannabis history, psychosis-proneness, sex, genetics) are discussed as reasons for inconsistent findings (pp. 31–32).

No quantitative synthesis. The review nonetheless asserts a low risk of publication bias because many studies reported a mix of significant and non-significant findings (p. 16), which is not a method of detecting it.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No specific funding and no interests declared (p. 38); the review does not flag that four authors co-wrote six included articles.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from Appendix E, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because two critical items are not met: the search was restricted to English-language peer-reviewed reports without justification (item 4), and risk of bias was not weighed in the interpretation (item 13, a close call; if it were judged met, the rating would be low confidence). Items 2 and 9 are only partly met. This rates how far the review's summary can be trusted, not its usefulness: it is registered, transparent about its narrative approach, and its Table 1 is a usable map of the 16 studies. It may be cited for what each included study reported, with the study named, and for the absence of a consistent effect of CBD on THC's subjective intoxication, heart rate and pharmacokinetics in these laboratory studies; it should not be cited on its own for a general claim that CBD protects against THC-induced anxiety or psychosis-like effects.

key_findings.finding: The search on 28 February 2019 found 1808 records; 601 duplicates were removed and four articles published after the search were added; 1211 titles and abstracts were screened and 47 full texts assessed; 23 articles reporting 16 studies were included.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: All 16 studies were human laboratory experiments; three used parallel groups and the rest crossover designs. Sample sizes ranged from 4 to 155, with 466 participants in total; one parallel and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell, and two studies were designed for safety and pharmacokinetics and were not powered to detect effects.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text names the third parallel study as Karniol and Carlini (1974), a different reference in the list; Table 1 and the rest of the text use Karniol et al. (1974). The total of 466 is reproduced from Table 1 if Bird et al. (1980) counts 155 and the Nadulski study 24 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: All studies enrolled healthy volunteers, and all but two (Karniol et al., 1974; Zuardi et al., 1982) included only people with previous cannabis use. Table 1 shows 18 of 40 participants in Karniol et al. (1974) and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. (1982) had never used cannabis, and one study recruited 24 people using cannabis daily and 24 using it recreationally.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Participants (p. 15); Table 1, Participants column (Hindocha et al., 2015, row on p. 68; Karniol et al., 1974, row on p. 69; Zuardi et al., 1982, row on p. 71)

key_findings.finding: Ten studies were rated at low risk of bias and six at some concerns; none at high risk. The domain-level table is in Appendix G (not in the file); Table 1 gives one overall rating per study, with both Dalton et al. (1976) experiments rated low, which completes the ten (the text names nine).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Risk of bias within studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1, Risk of Bias column (pp. 65–71)

key_findings.finding: The review judged the risk of publication bias low because many studies reported a mixture of significant and non-significant findings, and named as further across-study biases the English-language restriction, industry funding of two studies (Guy and Robson, 2003; Nicholson et al., 2004), residual effects of participants' own cannabis use, and recognition of the placebo condition.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Risk of bias across studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eight studies measured pharmacokinetics; most found that CBD did not significantly change THC's pharmacokinetic profile. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): peak plasma THC was significantly higher after vaporised THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg than after THC alone (area under the curve over 0–3 hours higher but not significantly). Nadulski et al. (2005; n=24): oral CBD 5.4 mg partly inhibited the hydroxylation of oral THC 10 mg, with wide variability. Guy and Robson (2003; n=24): later time to peak THC with CBD 10 mg (oromucosal spray). Hunt et al. (1981; n=4): 1500 mg oral CBD in three doses before intravenous THC 2 mg had no significant effect (clearance 17 versus 20.9 ml/min/kg). No significant differences in Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; n=6) or Englund et al. (2013; n=36). Hollister and Gillespie (n=15) reported higher urinary metabolites with CBD, attributed by the authors to CBD's presence rather than altered THC metabolism. Roser et al. (2009) reported higher 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH in women than men after THC with CBD, but not after THC alone. The discussion treats Nadulski as a possible second peak-THC increase; the Results describe a possible metabolic explanation, rather than a clearly demonstrated second peak-concentration increase.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.1 Pharmacokinetic effects, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Ten studies measured pulse: eight found that THC raised pulse with or without CBD, with no difference between the two; Nicholson et al. (2004; n=8) found no difference over 30 minutes; Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group) described a further rise with oral CBD 15 mg and a smaller rise with 30 or 60 mg added to oral THC 30 mg. Three studies measured blood pressure: Guy and Robson (2003) reported mean systolic falls at 3 hours of 10.3 mmHg after THC 10 mg alone, 4.4 mmHg with CBD 10 mg and 5.1 mmHg after placebo; T. P. Freeman et al. (2018; n=17) found diastolic pressure raised after THC 8 mg alone but not with CBD 10 mg; Haney et al. (2016; n=31) found no differences after oral CBD 200, 400 or 800 mg before smoked THC (about 42 mg).
key_findings.locator: 3.6.2.1 Pulse rate, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 3.6.2.2 Blood pressure

key_findings.finding: Of nine studies of subjective intoxication, two reported that CBD reduced it: Dalton et al. (1976; n=15 in the text), smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with smoked CBD 0.150 mg/kg, and Zuardi et al. (1982; n=8), oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with oral CBD 1 mg/kg (ARCI-Ma). Seven found no evidence that CBD changed intoxication. The discussion concludes that participants mostly experienced intoxication similarly with and without CBD.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.3 Subjective intoxicating effects; 4.2 Subjective intoxication
key_findings.note: Dalton et al. (1976) appears on both sides in the text; Table 1 (pp. 66–67) shows two experiments: CBD smoked with THC reduced feeling high (16 enrolled, one withdrew), while oral CBD 30 minutes before smoked THC (8 men) altered no measure.

key_findings.finding: Three studies measured anxiety, two of them rated at some concerns or unclear risk. Karniol et al. (1974; parallel groups of 5): Grade 4 effects on the authors' 0–4 symptom scale (panic, an intense feeling of being watched, racing thoughts) in 4 of 5 participants after oral THC 30 mg alone, against 3 of 15 when oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg was added, and none at the highest CBD dose; no statistical test is reported in the review. Zuardi et al. (1982; crossover, n=8): oral CBD 1 mg/kg attenuated the STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD 13.75 mg raised anxiety ratings and STAI at 15 minutes; only THC without CBD still raised them after an hour.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.4 Anxiety, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three studies of psychotomimetic effects, none with risk-of-bias concerns. Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; pseudo-randomised crossover, n=6): intravenous THC 1.25 mg produced psychosis-like PANSS effects in 3 of 6, and intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand prevented them (Table 1: in all three). Englund et al. (2013; parallel, n=48): after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, the mean PANSS increase did not differ between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo pre-treatment, but fewer people given CBD had a clinically significant rise in positive symptoms (at least 3 points) and paranoia (SSPS) was lower. Morgan et al. (2018; crossover, n=48): vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg did not differ in psychotomimetic effects; both raised BPRS negative symptoms and PSI scores, and the effects did not differ by frequency of cannabis use or trait schizotypy.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.5 Psychotomimetic and psychosis-like experiences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1, Bhattacharyya et al. (2010) row

key_findings.finding: THC alone impaired episodic memory in five studies. Englund et al. (2013; n=48): with oral CBD 600 mg beforehand, immediate recall after intravenous THC 1.5 mg was equally impaired but the delayed-recall impairment was lessened, and CBD did not seem to change THC's working-memory impairment, including forward and backward digit span. Morgan et al. (2018; n=48): prose recall was impaired to the same level and N-back working memory was impaired after vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg. Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group): the speeding of time production after oral THC 30 mg was absent with CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): DSST was impaired 20 minutes after THC 13.75 mg alone but not with CBD 13.75 mg, while divided attention was more impaired with CBD than after THC alone or placebo.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.6.1 Episodic memory; 3.6.6.2 Attention and working memory

key_findings.finding: Hindocha et al. (2015; n=48): vaporised THC 8 mg impaired recognition of facial emotions, and the impairment was absent when CBD 16 mg was added. Lawn et al. (2016; n=17): THC 8 mg increased sensitivity to the probability and size of rewards relative to both placebo and THC with CBD 10 mg; in the same study (T. P. Freeman et al., 2018) THC alone dampened brain responses to music, which did not differ from placebo when CBD was added.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.7 Emotion and reward processing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor performance and driving: Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD 13.75 mg increased lane weaving in a simulated car-following task; Bird et al. (1980): oral CBD 0.320 mg/kg did not modify the impairment of standing steadiness and psychomotor coordination by oral THC 0.215 mg/kg; Dalton et al. (1976; n=16): smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg impaired standing steadiness, hand-eye coordination and dexterity with and without CBD 0.150 mg/kg; Roser et al. (2009; n=24): right-hand tapping was slower after oral THC 10 mg with CBD 5.4 mg but not after THC alone. In the same Roser experiment, THC alone impaired left-hand tapping in two of five sessions, associated with higher 11-OH-THC.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.8 Psychomotor performance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: One sleep study (Nicholson et al., 2004; n=8; oromucosal THC 15 mg with or without CBD 15 mg). The text says THC with CBD increased wakefulness and stage 3 sleep and THC alone increased sleepiness 30 minutes after waking; Table 1 says THC with CBD, but not THC alone, decreased stage 3 sleep and increased time awake, and that both conditions increased sleepiness after waking.
key_findings.locator: 3.6.9 Sleep; Table 1, Nicholson et al. (2004) row
key_findings.note: The text and the table disagree on the direction of the stage 3 sleep finding and on sleepiness; the primary paper is needed before either is cited.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events visible in Table 1: in Arkell et al. (2019) one of 14 participants was discharged because of raised blood pressure and heart rate; in the Nadulski et al. (2005) sample three women had a panic attack (28 recruited, 20 to 24 analysed). The conditions in which these events happened are not stated.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Arkell et al. (2019) row (p. 65) and Nadulski et al. (2005) row (p. 70); Table 1 note d (p. 72)

key_findings.finding: The authors found no consistent pattern across routes, doses and THC:CBD ratios and could not determine a dose-response relation; they caution that oral CBD has low bioavailability (13–19%, cited from another source), so studies with low oral CBD doses (from 5.4 mg) should be read with caution. Conclusion: some evidence that CBD may reduce some effects of THC, with substantial variability between and within studies.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph; 4.8 Conclusions

key_findings.finding: The discussion states that three studies showed significantly fewer participants with extreme anxiety and psychotic-like effects when CBD was added, and proposes that CBD may act only when THC's effects are extreme, since in Englund et al. (2013) CBD reduced clinically significant increases but not the mean increase.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Anxiety and psychosis-like experiences

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the combined condition of Arkell et al. (2019) as vaporised THC 3.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg (Intervention column, p. 65), while the text gives THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg throughout (pp. 17, 22, 25, 26, 29). Table 1 also shows that the THC-alone condition contained less than 1.25 mg CBD.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table value looks like a typing error, but claims about this study's dose ratio or plasma THC finding should be checked against the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Nicholson et al. (2004) is described inconsistently: the pulse section gives sublingual drops of THC 10 mg with or without CBD 10 mg (p. 19), while the sleep section and Table 1 give oromucosal spray with 15 mg each (pp. 30, 71); the text says THC with CBD increased stage 3 sleep (p. 30) where Table 1 says it decreased it (p. 71); and Table 1 rates the study at low risk of bias although its design entry says randomisation was not indicated.
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim about CBD and sleep, or about this study's doses, can rest on the review; the direction of the sleep finding is unknown from this source.

reporting_issues.issue: The size of Bird et al. (1980) appears three ways: 161 recruited with six excluded in Table 1 (p. 66), which matches the stated maximum sample of 155 (p. 13) and the total of 466; 166 divided into 16 groups in Table 1 note a (p. 72); and n=116 in the text (p. 29).
reporting_issues.consequence: 155 reproduces the review's stated maximum and total when the other Table 1 sample counts are used (adjudicator's arithmetic). The inconsistent figures remain unresolved without the primary report; this calculation does not independently establish the primary study's correct denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The group sizes of Englund et al. (2013) are reversed between the body of Table 1 (26 placebo, 22 CBD; p. 67) and its note b (22 placebo, 26 CBD; p. 72); the text uses n=36 for the plasma comparison (p. 19) and n=48 elsewhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Arm sizes must be checked in the primary paper. The plasma-comparison n=36 may be an outcome-specific subset; its difference from 48 is not by itself proof of a reporting error.

reporting_issues.issue: Dalton et al. (1976) contributed two experiments, listed separately in Table 1 (pp.66–67). Counting both makes ten low-risk experiments from nine named reports (p.16) and explains why Dalton appears among both the reducing and non-reducing subjective-intoxication results (p.21). The co-administration experiment enrolled 16 and had one withdrawal, which can explain the text's 15 versus 16. The pre-treatment experiment's CBD route remains inconsistent: smoked in the text (p.15), oral in Table 1 (p.66).
reporting_issues.consequence: Name the experiment when citing a Dalton finding. Distinguish enrolment from analysed samples; the pre-treatment route needs primary-source verification.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary of routes and doses (Treatment characteristics, p. 15) does not match Table 1: it counts two vaporised-THC studies at 8 mg and six oral, where Table 1 has three vaporised (including Arkell et al., 2019, at 13.75 mg) and five oral; its CBD route counts add to 15, not 16; its vaporised CBD range starts at 4 mg, a dose no study in Table 1 used (10, 13.75 and 16 mg); and its smoked CBD range reaches 0.320 mg/kg, which is the oral dose of Bird et al. (1980). Counts are the editors' from Table 1. The summary's oral THC range reaches 40 mg, whereas the highest fixed oral THC dose printed in Table 1 is 30 mg and Hollister's 40 mg is CBD. However, Table 1 also gives weight-based oral THC doses; the review does not establish the origin of the 40 mg endpoint.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dose and route descriptions need trial-specific checking. Table 1 itself contains discrepancies (including Arkell and Nicholson), so neither its entries nor the summary paragraph establish corrected primary regimens on their own.

reporting_issues.issue: Wall et al. (2019) is listed in two different study rows of Table 1, with the 48-person study (p. 68) and with the 17-person study (p. 70), while the text places it with the 17-person music-fMRI study (p. 28); Hindocha et al. (2019), the 48-person genetics analysis, is not named in Table 1, and the list of included articles under Study characteristics (p. 13) omits it and Wall et al. (2019) (editors' count: 21 of the 23 articles named).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which sample an article belongs to must be checked before treating findings as independent; the two UCL studies contribute six articles between them.

reporting_issues.issue: The risk-of-bias tool is named as RoB 2 but cited to Higgins et al. (2011) in the methods (p. 12) and to Higgins et al. (2016) in the limitations (p. 37); the anxiety section calls two studies unclear risk (p. 21) where Table 1 says some concerns; and Table 1 rates as low risk a study described as pseudo-randomised (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010; p. 65).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's low-risk ratings cannot be taken at face value for randomisation; the domain table (Appendix G) would be needed.

reporting_issues.issue: In the genetics paragraph, CC and A carriers are said to differ after THC with CBD, introduced as a contrast to a difference after THC alone. A missing negation is one possible explanation, but cannot be established from the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this genetic finding cannot be cited from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Bhattacharyya row gives intravenous CBD pre-treatment as T−5 minutes in Intervention and T−210 minutes in Main findings; the text describes intravenous pre-treatment immediately before THC.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precise pre-treatment interval is unresolved from the review; use the primary report before citing it.

reporting_issues.issue: Hunt pre-treatment is described as eight, six and two hours before THC in the text, but Table 1 lists 480 minutes, 300 minutes and 120 minutes; six hours is 360 minutes, not 300.
reporting_issues.consequence: The middle interval remains unresolved; do not choose a corrected regimen without the primary report.

reporting_issues.issue: The review repeatedly gives Arkell n=14, while Table 1 says three of 14 did not complete, including one withdrawal, one non-compliance and one discharge for elevated blood pressure and heart rate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review-level n=14 is not a verified analysis denominator for each outcome; do not silently replace it with 11.

reporting_issues.issue: For Arkell anxiety at one hour and DSST at 20 minutes, the review reports a significant difference from placebo for THC alone but not for THC with CBD. Those separate significance statements do not by themselves demonstrate a difference between the two active conditions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Retain the reported comparisons without treating a difference in significance as a significant treatment interaction. The divided-attention comparison is explicitly between active conditions.
