disagreements.first_pass: How large any effect of CBD on THC's acute effects is (nothing was pooled and effect sizes are rarely given); whether it depends on dose, ratio or route (the authors found no consistent pattern, and the conditions tested rarely match each other); whether findings apply to people with psychiatric vulnerability, frequent use or past bad reactions (all participants were screened healthy volunteers, mostly with occasional use, and two studies included people who had never used cannabis); or whether the literature is free of reporting bias (no assessment beyond an informal statement).
disagreements.reviewer: The review includes weekly/current/people using cannabis daily; occasional use is not established for most samples.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 407 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): How large any effect of CBD on THC's acute effects is (nothing was pooled and effect sizes are rarely given); whether it depends on dose, ratio or route (the authors found no consistent pattern, and the conditions tested rarely match each other); whether findings apply to clinical populations, people selected for previous adverse reactions or longer-term use (the review studied acute effects in screened healthy volunteers). Cannabis-use histories varied and included daily use; the review does not establish that most participants used only occasionally. It cannot establish whether the literature is free of reporting bias (no assessment beyond an informal statement). Source: Participants p.15; Table 1 pp.66–70; Discussion pp.33–34.

disagreements.first_pass: All 16 studies used healthy volunteers (3.2, p. 15). Samples ranged from 4 to 155 participants; one parallel study and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell (pp. 13–14). All but two studies required previous cannabis use; Table 1 shows that 18 of 40 participants in Karniol et al. (1974) and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. (1982) had never used cannabis, and that most other samples had used occasionally (for example at least once but never regularly, or at most 2 to 3 times a week); one study recruited 24 people using cannabis daily and 24 using it recreationally (Hindocha et al., 2015, with Morgan et al., 2018). Five studies enrolled men only (Dalton, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt, Karniol). Ages in Table 1 run from 18 to 70.
disagreements.reviewer: Count experiments consistently and do not infer frequency from at least once.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 407 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): All 16 studies used healthy volunteers (3.2, p.15). Samples ranged from 4 to 155 participants; one parallel study and five crossover studies had 4 to 8 participants per treatment cell (pp.13–14). Table 1 gives heterogeneous cannabis-use histories: about half of Bird et al. used at least weekly; Haney et al. recruited people currently using cannabis; Hindocha/Morgan recruited 24 people who used cannabis daily and 24 who used it recreationally. Several other rows state only at least once, which does not establish occasional use. Two studies included people who had never used cannabis: 18 of 40 in Karniol et al. and 3 of 8 in Zuardi et al. Six experimental samples from five reports enrolled men only: the two Dalton experiments, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt and Karniol. Ages listed in Table 1 run from 18 to 70. Source: Table 1 and notes pp.65–72; independent row count.

disagreements.first_pass: English-language, peer-reviewed reports only; no trial registries or grey literature. Two of the 16 studies (six of the 23 articles) were co-authored by review authors.
disagreements.reviewer: Do not equate healthy volunteer selection with absence of frequent cannabis use or establish every trial exclusion from author speculation.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 407 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): English-language, peer-reviewed reports only; no trial registries or grey literature. disagreements.first_pass: In 16 small laboratory studies of healthy volunteers (466 people in all; six studies with 4 to 8 per cell), CBD given with or before a matched THC dose mostly did not change THC's pharmacokinetics, heart rate, subjective intoxication (seven of nine studies found no difference) or psychomotor and driving impairment. Lower anxiety or psychosis-like effects with CBD were reported in three studies: oral THC 30 mg in groups of 5 (Karniol et al., 1974; Grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 versus 3 of 15, no test reported in the review), intravenous THC 1.25 mg in 6 people (Bhattacharyya et al., 2010), and intravenous THC 1.5 mg in a 48-person parallel trial in which the mean PANSS increase did not differ but fewer people given CBD had a clinically significant rise (Englund et al., 2013); Zuardi et al. (1982; n=8) also found a smaller STAI rise. With inhaled cannabis, Morgan et al. (2018; n=48) found no difference in psychotomimetic effects, and Arkell et al. (2019; n=14) found anxiety raised in both conditions at 15 minutes and still raised only without CBD at one hour. One study found higher peak plasma THC with CBD (Arkell et al., 2019). Results on memory, attention and emotion processing went both ways.
disagreements.reviewer: The original list named three studies and then a fourth; retain the results without an inconsistent count.

disagreements.first_pass: Eight studies measured pharmacokinetics; most found that CBD did not significantly change THC's pharmacokinetic profile. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): peak plasma THC was significantly higher after vaporised THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg than after THC alone (area under the curve over 0–3 hours higher but not significantly). Nadulski et al. (2005; n=24): oral CBD 5.4 mg partly inhibited the hydroxylation of oral THC 10 mg, with wide variability. Guy and Robson (2003; n=24): later time to peak THC with CBD 10 mg (oromucosal spray). Hunt et al. (1981; n=4): 1500 mg oral CBD in three doses before intravenous THC 2 mg had no significant effect (clearance 17 versus 20.9 ml/min/kg). No significant differences in Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; n=6) or Englund et al. (2013; n=36).
disagreements.reviewer: Add omitted findings and separate the discussion inference from demonstrated peak results.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 407 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): Eight studies measured pharmacokinetics; most found that CBD did not significantly change THC's pharmacokinetic profile. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): peak plasma THC was significantly higher after vaporised THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg than after THC alone (area under the curve over 0–3 hours higher but not significantly). Nadulski et al. (2005; n=24): oral CBD 5.4 mg partly inhibited the hydroxylation of oral THC 10 mg, with wide variability. Guy and Robson (2003; n=24): later time to peak THC with CBD 10 mg (oromucosal spray). Hunt et al. (1981; n=4): 1500 mg oral CBD in three doses before intravenous THC 2 mg had no significant effect (clearance 17 versus 20.9 ml/min/kg). No significant differences in Bhattacharyya et al. (2010; n=6) or Englund et al. (2013; n=36). Hollister and Gillespie (n=15) reported higher urinary metabolites with CBD, attributed by the authors to CBD's presence rather than altered THC metabolism. Roser et al. (2009) reported higher 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH in women than men after THC with CBD, but not after THC alone. The discussion treats Nadulski as a possible second peak-THC increase; the Results describe a possible metabolic explanation, rather than a clearly demonstrated second peak-concentration increase. Source: Pharmacokinetic effects pp.17–19; Discussion pp.32, 36.

disagreements.first_pass: THC alone impaired episodic memory in five studies. Englund et al. (2013; n=48): with oral CBD 600 mg beforehand, immediate recall after intravenous THC 1.5 mg was equally impaired but the delayed-recall impairment was lessened, and digit span was unchanged. Morgan et al. (2018; n=48): prose recall and N-back working memory were impaired equally after vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg. Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group): the speeding of time production after oral THC 30 mg was absent with CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): DSST was impaired 20 minutes after THC 13.75 mg alone but not with CBD 13.75 mg, while divided attention was more impaired with CBD than after THC alone or placebo.
disagreements.reviewer: Unchanged could be read as no THC impairment rather than no CBD modification.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 407 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): THC alone impaired episodic memory in five studies. Englund et al. (2013; n=48): with oral CBD 600 mg beforehand, immediate recall after intravenous THC 1.5 mg was equally impaired but the delayed-recall impairment was lessened, and CBD did not seem to change THC's working-memory impairment, including forward and backward digit span. Morgan et al. (2018; n=48): prose recall and N-back working memory were impaired equally after vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg. Karniol et al. (1974; n=40, 5 per group): the speeding of time production after oral THC 30 mg was absent with CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg. Arkell et al. (2019; n=14): DSST was impaired 20 minutes after THC 13.75 mg alone but not with CBD 13.75 mg, while divided attention was more impaired with CBD than after THC alone or placebo. Source: Attention and working memory p.25.

design_detail: Narrative review by three forensic medicine authors (Monash University and the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine) of published case reports of cardiovascular presentations to hospital temporally linked to cannabis (31 reports, 35 people; Table 1), of published deaths linked to cannabis (6 publications, 13 men; Table 2) and of 12 epidemiological studies of cannabis use and cardiovascular disease (Table 3), with background on THC and CBD pharmacology and a discussion of when a death should be attributed to cannabis in death investigation. Search in PubMed and Scopus with listed keywords, English only, plus reference-chasing; no dates, counts, screening or appraisal reported; synthesis limited to counts and medians from the case tables. Synthetic cannabinoids were excluded.
can_establish: That published case reports describe cardiovascular emergencies and 13 deaths shortly after cannabis use, many in men with coronary disease, which epidemiological studies existed by early 2019, and how three forensic medicine authors proposed that deaths be attributed to cannabis.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis caused any of the deaths described, how often cannabis contributes to sudden cardiac death in the population, or whether deaths involving cannabis are under- or over-counted: the case reports have no comparison or denominator and are not appraised, and the review gives no data on how often THC is present in sudden deaths not attributed to it.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). English-language publications found in PubMed and Scopus with keywords (marijuana or cannabis with fatality, death, poisoning, arrhythmias, heart, myocardial infarction) and by following citations (p. 299, §2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: publications in which cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular or related event, or to have contributed to or caused a death; epidemiological studies designed to examine a link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease. Excluded: synthetic cannabinoids; non-English publications (p. 299, §2). The tables are titled as summaries of selected publications, and Table 1 summarizes 31 of what the text calls numerous reports, without saying how they were chosen (pp. 300–301).
sample.demographics: Hospital reports: 35 people aged 15–53, 5 of them women (p. 301). Deaths: 13 men aged 17–52 (p. 301; Table 2, p. 302).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports are chosen by their authors for a suspected link; deaths in which cannabis was present but judged irrelevant are not published, so the reports cannot show how often a link is real or how often THC is found in sudden deaths generally. The review's case set is smaller than that of a systematic review it cites (81 case reports with 116 people; p. 302). The 9 deaths among French addictovigilance notifications in Table 3 (p. 303) are not added to the count of 13.

exposure.measurement: In the case reports, cannabis use comes from history, urine cannabinoid screens or, in 8 of the 13 deaths, THC measured in blood; specimen site and interval from death to sampling are not given (Tables 1–2, pp. 300–302). In the epidemiological studies, use is mostly self-reported or taken from hospital coding, with urine testing in a few (Table 3, p. 303).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mostly smoked cannabis in the case reports, with frequency and timing recorded unevenly; not used on this card.
exposure.polysubstance: The text says other drugs were excluded as far as possible by history or testing and that none were implicated (pp. 301–302), but the tables record alcohol, sildenafil, LSD, tobacco and, in one hospital case, a synthetic cannabinoid in the past week, and alcohol in two of the deaths (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%) (pp. 300–302).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Time since last use is given in some case reports (from minutes to the previous evening) and unknown in others; for the deaths, the interval from death to post-mortem sampling is not reported.

comparison.controls: None for the case reports. The epidemiological studies used their own comparisons (control periods in a case-crossover design, people not using cannabis in cohorts and hospital databases), as summarized in Table 3 (p. 303).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In the case reports, pre-existing coronary disease (significant atherosclerosis or other pathology in 8 of the 13 deaths), channelopathies, tobacco smoking and other risk factors are recorded unevenly and not weighed case by case.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Hospital presentations: acute myocardial infarction confirmed by creatine kinase or troponin, arrhythmias, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, Brugada pattern, myocarditis. Deaths: autopsy findings where an autopsy was done, and the cause of death as given by the case authors or, in one case, a coroner.
outcomes.validity_norms: No causality assessment is applied to the case reports, and the review's own criteria for attributing a death to a drug (below) are not applied to the 13 deaths it counts.
outcomes.operationalization: A cannabis-associated death is a published death that the case authors (or a coroner) linked to recent cannabis use, with or without THC measured in blood.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling. From the case tables: 35 people with hospital presentations (median age printed 25), 24 without evidence of coronary artery disease, 18 with confirmed acute myocardial infarction; 13 deaths, blood THC 1.9–22 ng/mL in 8. Relayed from Table 3 (p. 303): AMI risk 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis and 1.7 (0.6–5.1) in the second hour (Mittleman et al., case-crossover); after MI, mortality hazard 4.2 (1.2–14) for weekly use and 2.5 (0.9–7.3) for less than weekly use (Mukamal et al.); 29% higher long-term mortality, not significant (Frost et al.); acute ischaemic stroke adjusted RR 1.17 (1.15–1.20) (Rumalla et al.); cardiovascular mortality adjusted HR 2.22 (printed as 90% CI 1.27–3.70) in young adults with MI (DeFilippis et al.); no association of lifetime or recent use with cardiovascular mortality in CARDIA (Reis et al.).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection among the case reports is not explained; the French notification series' 9 deaths are not counted; the text's summaries of the case tables and of Table 3 differ from the tables in several places (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Thirty-one case reports describe 35 people with cardiovascular emergencies during or soon after cannabis use, and six publications describe 13 men aged 17–52 whose deaths case authors or a coroner linked to recent cannabis use. Of the 13, 8 had significant coronary atherosclerosis or other pathology; THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), the other 5 resting on urine cannabinoids or history, one with no THC found in blood; alcohol was present in 2; two died days after admission and one had no autopsy. Of 12 epidemiological studies tabulated, several report associations with myocardial infarction or stroke, one long cohort found no association with cardiovascular mortality and a large hospital-database study is described in the text as showing no increase in overall mortality, and two systematic reviews disagree. The authors themselves write that the evidence for a link with increased risk of cardiovascular death is not clear and the risk probably rare (p. 304).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says at least 13 deaths from a cardiovascular mechanism have been reported from use of the drug, and that this is “very likely to be an under-estimate” (p. 298), but presents no data on under-ascertainment. It recommends that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible cardiac or cerebrovascular cause, cannabis should be considered at least a contributory cause of sudden or unexpected death (p. 298), and the conclusion says inclusion of cannabis as cause or contributor “in appropriate cases is to be encouraged” (p. 304). These recommendations rest on case reports without comparison groups, in which coronary disease and alcohol were often present; 5 of the 13 deaths counted would fail the review's own requirement of a blood THC test (p. 304); its general rule that a drug must be present at a concentration capable of causing death is not given an operational THC threshold in this review; the authors say a minimum concentration may not be possible to provide (p. 304), so attribution would rest on THC being present plus circumstances. Post-mortem changes in THC concentration are not discussed. Applied in certification, the recommendation would raise counts of deaths attributed to cannabis without evidence on how often THC is present in sudden cardiac deaths that cannabis did not cause.

timeline.event: Bachs and Mørland: six deaths of men aged 17–43 attributed to cannabis, blood THC 2–22 ng/mL, most with coronary artery disease (as summarized in Table 2, p. 302).

Mittleman et al., case-crossover in 3882 people with acute MI: risk 4.8 times baseline in the hour after smoking cannabis (as summarized, pp. 302–303); the AHA 2020 statement, as recorded on its card, relays this estimate as resting on 9 people who had used cannabis within an hour of presenting with AMI.

Tormey: a coroner's court case with no THC in blood in which cannabis was found a secondary cause of death, and a discussion advising that cannabis be considered contributory only with use within 2 h of the arrest and ideally with blood THC confirmed (as summarized, pp. 302, 304).
Hartung et al.: two sudden deaths of young men with blood THC 5.2 and 1.9 ng/mL (as summarized in Table 2, p. 302); on the deaths reading list to be read with this review.

Jouanjus et al., systematic review (81 case reports, 29 observational studies): association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke; Reis et al. (CARDIA, 5113 young adults, over 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality (as summarized, pp. 302–303).
Ravi et al., systematic review: no compelling evidence linking cannabis use with mortality, including from AMI (as summarized, p. 302).
AHA scientific statement on cannabis and cardiovascular health: the evidence on adverse cardiovascular outcomes is still inconclusive (as recorded on its card).
Rock et al., characteristics of deaths following cannabis use in England, 1998–2020: on the deaths reading list, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: Case reports show that sudden cardiovascular deaths shortly after cannabis use have been attributed to cannabis by case authors and coroners. Whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death has not been measured in any controlled study read here; the cohort and review evidence summarized in this paper, and the AHA 2020 statement, call it unclear or inconclusive. The paper is cited mainly as the forensic argument for counting cannabis as a contributory cause, and its recommendation should be shown with that evidence base.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement. The Declaration covers only originality and approval by the authors (p. 305).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Forensic Medicine, Monash University, and the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, that is, from the death-investigation setting whose certification practice the review addresses; the acknowledgments thank the Institute, the Department and Professor Stephen Cordner (p. 305). Received 28 November 2018, accepted 7 March 2019.

what_would_settle_it: A population-based study of sudden cardiac deaths with complete toxicology (blood THC with the interval from death to sampling) compared with suitable controls, such as deaths from external causes or living people from the same population, with coronary disease, tobacco and alcohol measured, to estimate whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and how often THC is present in such deaths without having contributed.

domains.note: Databases and keywords are named, but no dates, counts, screening or flow; the tables are explicitly selections, and the case set is smaller than that of a systematic review the authors cite.

The case reports on which the conclusions rest are not appraised for causality or alternative causes; Table 3 has a comments column listing limitations of the epidemiological studies, but the text's summary does not use it.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The cases and epidemiological studies are by others; the authors' own work is cited only for background on driving.
The discussion hedges (arguably, conceivably, at least in theory), but the abstract states 13 deaths from use of the drug and an under-estimate without data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against cannabis as a cause of cardiovascular death
domains.note: The text counts 11 of 12 epidemiological studies as showing increased risk, although Table 3 includes a null cardiovascular-mortality cohort, no increased overall mortality in the Desai text summary, and a study finding less atherosclerosis; coronary disease, alcohol and tobacco in the fatal cases are not weighed; the denominator (THC in deaths not attributed to cannabis) is not considered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The search and selection are undocumented, the case reports are not appraised, and the text's summaries of its own tables lean towards a causal reading. The discussion is more cautious than the abstract. Citable for: what the published case reports describe (counts, ages, findings, toxicology, as in Tables 1–2); the epidemiological estimates as relayed, pointing to the primary studies; the authors' proposed criteria and recommendations for attributing death to cannabis, presented as their position; their qualified statement that it may not be possible to provide a minimum post-mortem THC concentration that might be regarded as causal. Not citable for: cannabis having caused any of these deaths; the size of any cardiovascular risk; undercounting of cannabis-related deaths.

key_findings.finding: Methods: English-language publications on deaths attributed to cannabis (synthetic cannabinoids excluded) were searched in PubMed and Scopus with keywords and by following citations; included were reports in which cannabis was believed to have contributed to an emergency admission for a cardiovascular or related event or to a death, and epidemiological studies designed to examine a link with cardiovascular disease. No search dates, numbers screened or appraisal method are given.
key_findings.locator: §2 Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Hospital presentations (Table 1): Thirty-one case reports describe 35 people aged 15–53 (median printed as 25), 5 of them women; cannabis use was not always confirmed by testing and, when tested, usually by urine cannabinoids; most had chest pain, arrhythmia or coronary thrombus; 24 had no evidence of coronary artery disease and 18 had acute myocardial infarction confirmed by creatine kinase or troponin; there were 5 strokes or transient ischaemic attacks secondary to a cardiovascular event, 3 possible Brugada syndromes and 1 myocarditis.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (pp. 300–301); §5, 1st–4th paragraphs (p. 301)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: median age 26 overall and 35 for the five women (printed 33).

key_findings.finding: Deaths (Table 2): six publications describe 13 men aged 17–52 (median 37) whose deaths the case authors or a coroner linked to recent cannabis use; in eight there was significant coronary atherosclerosis and/or other pathology (three with superimposed thrombus, two with enlarged hearts, at least three diagnosed with AMI); five are described as having little obvious pathology (aged 17–42, mean 31).
key_findings.locator: §6, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology of the thirteen deaths as tabulated: THC in blood in 8 (Bachs and Mørland's six men: 22, 4, 2, 5, 3 and 7 ng/mL; Hartung et al.'s two: 5.2 and 1.9 ng/mL); the other five rested on urine cannabinoids (Tormey; Casier et al., two cases; Orsini et al.) or history with urine confirmation (Dines et al.). In Tormey's case no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death. Blood alcohol was 0.04% in one of Bachs and Mørland's cases and 0.119% in Orsini et al.'s; one of Casier et al.'s cases had a history of alcohol problems.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: The text (§6, 5th paragraph) summarizes this as 8 blood-positive (2–22 ng/mL, median 4), 4 urine-positive and 1 with no cannabinoid measurement; see reporting issues. Editors' calculation from Table 2: median of the 8 blood values 4.5 ng/mL.

key_findings.finding: Circumstances of the thirteen deaths (Table 2): two of Casier et al.'s cases died days after admission (fatal ventricular tachycardia 3 days later; multiple organ failure a few days later); Dines et al.'s case had no autopsy, with rhythm disturbance only possible; one of Bachs and Mørland's cases had a previous MI and widespread coronary disease; Orsini et al.'s case had an extensive MI with hypertensive and atherosclerotic heart disease.
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: Epidemiological studies as relayed (Table 3): case-crossover study of 3882 people with acute MI (1258 women), risk 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) within 1 h of smoking cannabis and 1.7 (0.6–5.1) in the second hour as described in the text (Table 3 labels this within 2 h), without toxicology; cohort of 1913 people after MI, mortality HR 4.2 (1.2–14) for weekly use and 2.5 (0.9–7.3) for less than weekly use; 3886 people followed 18 years (519 deaths, 22 reporting cannabis use), mortality 29% higher, not significant; national inpatient data, acute ischaemic stroke adjusted RR 1.17 (1.15–1.20); 2097 people with MI before age 51, cannabis use in 6.0%, cardiovascular mortality adjusted HR 2.22 (printed 90%CI 1.27–3.70); CARDIA, 5113 young adults followed over 25 years (84% reported cannabis use), no association with cardiovascular mortality; French addictovigilance 2006–10, 35 (1.8%) cannabis-related notifications cardiovascular, 9 deaths. In the text's Desai summary, over 2 million US AMI admissions showed no increase in overall mortality with cannabis use; Table 3 describes 2.45 million admissions and an AMI association, not that mortality null. These are different outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Mittleman, Mukamal, Frost, Rumalla, DeFilippis, Reis, Jouanjus; section 7, 4th paragraph (p. 302, Desai mortality summary)
key_findings.note: Second-hand estimates; cite the primary studies. The AHA 2020 statement (card sc_page_2020) relays the 2.22 hazard ratio as for people who used cocaine and marijuana, without saying whether the exposures were combined.

key_findings.finding: The authors say eleven of the twelve epidemiological studies showed trends to increased mortality or significant associations with increased risk; they also summarize two systematic reviews that disagree: one (81 case reports with 116 people, 29 observational studies, 3 clinical trials, 2 experimental studies) found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke; the other found no compelling evidence linking cannabis with any mortality, including from AMI.
key_findings.locator: §7, 2nd, 5th and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The count of 11 does not match Table 3 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the Discussion the authors state that the larger retrospective studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and increased risk of cardiovascular death unclear; that the symptoms and diseases described may have other causes (rhythm disturbance, undiagnosed channelopathies, tobacco smoking); that a small number of susceptible people with other morbidities could still be harmed; and that the risk is probably rare.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Proposed criteria for attributing death to a drug: with no clear evidence from the scene, pathologists should exclude other reasonable explanations and establish that the drug can cause death by an understood mechanism, is present at a concentration capable of doing so, and fits the circumstances. For THC, the authors say it may not be possible to provide a minimum blood concentration that might be regarded as causal, because of delays from death to sampling; most laboratories detect 1–2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood, and they suggest lower values may reflect use days earlier; if THC is quantified and the case fits the criteria, they argue this could suffice to list cannabis as causal or contributory. They require a blood THC test, not urine cannabinoids or history alone, to link a death to recent use, and cite Tormey's advice that cannabis be considered contributory only with use within 2 h of the arrest, ideally with blood THC confirmed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th–12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Counting recommendations: the authors write that, ideally, the presence of cannabis (as THC) should be recorded in death statistics so as not to underestimate cannabis-associated mortality, and conclude that including cannabis as a cause or contributor in appropriate cases is to be encouraged so that global burden of disease estimates reflect its harm; the abstract adds that the 13 reported deaths are very likely an under-estimate.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 298); Discussion, 7th and 16th (last) paragraphs (p. 304)

key_findings.finding: Background stated in the review (citing earlier pharmacokinetic studies): after smoking, blood THC falls below 10% of its peak within an hour and below 5 ng/mL within a few hours; oral use gives lower peak THC concentrations, usually under 5 ng/mL, with an active metabolite (11-hydroxy-THC) formed in larger amounts.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 298, continues p. 299)

key_findings.finding: The review also mentions, without detail, well over 50 published reports of arteritis with long-term heavy cannabis use, many leading to limb amputation, and deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (four references).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Ages in Table 1 give a median of 26 for the 35 people and 35 for the five women (24, 33, 35, 36, 45); the text prints 25 and 33 (editors' calculation; the one age given as 40s lies above the median and does not affect it).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite ages from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The 28-year-old in Hartung et al.'s report is described with histological signs of single-cell necrosis in the heart in Table 2 and on p. 301, but on p. 302 as having no histopathological evidence of cellular necrosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Contradiction about the one death the review presents as an acute ischaemic event without structural heart disease.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 8 deaths had THC in blood (2–22 ng/mL, median 4), 4 had urine cannabinoids and 1 had no cannabinoid measurement (p. 302). Table 2 shows 8 blood values of 1.9–22 ng/mL (median 4.5, editors' calculation) and 5 cases confirmed only by urine, one of them (Tormey) with no THC found in blood, and no case without any cannabinoid test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Five of the 13 deaths lack blood THC confirmation, which the review itself requires to link a death to recent use (p. 304); one had a negative blood THC.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says no other drugs were implicated in the hospital cases or the deaths (pp. 301–302), and the Methods exclude synthetic cannabinoids (p. 299), but the tables record alcohol in two deaths (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%) and a history of alcohol problems in a third, and among hospital cases heavy alcohol use, alcohol with cannabis, sildenafil 36 h earlier, LSD 2 days earlier and a synthetic cannabinoid within the past week (Table 1, cases 6, 12, 16, 26, 29).
reporting_issues.consequence: Co-exposures were present and not weighed; the case set includes one exposure the Methods say was excluded. Co-exposure or an earlier history does not by itself show that another drug caused the event; the concern is unweighed alternative contributions and selection consistency, not proof that all co-exposures were causal.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 11 of the 12 epidemiological studies showed trends to increased mortality or significant associations with increased risk (p. 302), but in Table 3 Reis et al. (CARDIA) found no association with cardiovascular mortality, Lee et al. found less angiographic atherosclerosis in people who used cannabis, and Jouanjus et al. and Dines et al. are descriptive series without a comparison group (p. 303). The text also lists Frost et al. among studies that found an increased risk (p. 302), while Table 3 reports its 29% excess as not significant. The section 7 text also describes Desai as finding no increase in overall mortality, although its Table 3 row reports an association with AMI; an association with AMI is not itself an increase in deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count overstates the epidemiological support; by the editors' reading of Table 3, at most 8 rows report a raised risk estimate, some of them non-significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints the Petronis and Anthony interval as 95% CI 1555–3.25 and the DeFilippis et al. interval as a 90% CI; the Mittleman et al. interval (4.8, 95% CI 2.9–9.5) is not symmetric around the estimate on the log scale (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one printed interval is plainly malformed (1555–3.25); no corrected value is inferred. disagreements.first_pass: Proposed criteria for attributing death to a drug: with no clear evidence from the scene, pathologists should exclude other reasonable explanations and establish that the drug can cause death by an understood mechanism, is present at a concentration capable of doing so, and fits the circumstances. For THC, the authors say no minimum blood concentration can be given that might indicate cause, because of delays from death to sampling; most laboratories detect 1–2 ng/mL in post-mortem blood, and they suggest lower values may reflect use days earlier; if THC is quantified and the case fits the criteria, they argue this could suffice to list cannabis as causal or contributory. They require a blood THC test, not urine cannabinoids or history alone, to link a death to recent use, and cite Tormey's advice that cannabis be considered contributory only with use within 2 h of the arrest, ideally with blood THC confirmed.
disagreements.reviewer: Second reader 331: preserve the authors' hedge.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says at least 13 deaths from a cardiovascular mechanism have been reported from use of the drug, and that this is “very likely to be an under-estimate” (p. 298), but presents no data on under-ascertainment. It recommends that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible cardiac or cerebrovascular cause, cannabis should be considered at least a contributory cause of sudden or unexpected death (p. 298), and the conclusion says inclusion of cannabis as cause or contributor “in appropriate cases is to be encouraged” (p. 304). These recommendations rest on case reports without comparison groups, in which coronary disease and alcohol were often present; 5 of the 13 deaths counted would fail the review's own requirement of a blood THC test (p. 304); its general rule that a drug must be present at a concentration capable of causing death cannot be applied to THC, for which the authors say no minimum concentration can be given (p. 304), so attribution would rest on THC being present plus circumstances. Post-mortem changes in THC concentration are not discussed. Applied in certification, the recommendation would raise counts of deaths attributed to cannabis without evidence on how often THC is present in sudden cardiac deaths that cannabis did not cause.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of wave 1 (2001–2002) of the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC), a US national multistage probability survey of civilian non-institutionalized adults living in households and group quarters, interviewed face to face by Census Bureau interviewers with the AUDADIS-IV (response 81%). Of 43,093 respondents, the 3,297 with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis use disorder (abuse, dependence or both; 2,080 men and 1,217 women) were compared by gender on sociodemographic characteristics, lifetime psychiatric disorders, the course of the disorder (recalled ages at first use, heavy use, onset and remission; criteria; episodes) and help seeking. Weighted percentages and means with design-based standard errors (SUDAAN); comorbidity also modelled in the whole sample with gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder and their interaction. A general-population sample, not a treatment sample.
can_establish: How US adults who had ever met DSM-IV criteria for cannabis abuse or dependence by 2001–2002 differed by gender in their recalled ages at first use and onset, lifetime comorbidity, criteria met, recalled remission and ever seeking help.
cannot_establish: Whether women progress to cannabis use disorder faster than men in any general sense (the comparison is among people who already had the disorder, unadjusted for current age, from ages recalled at one interview); whether the disorder causes or follows the comorbid disorders (cross-sectional); or how remission relates to treatment (remission is not defined and not crossed with help seeking).

sample.recruitment: General-population sample: NESARC 2001–2002, US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 and older living in households and group quarters (shelters and group homes included, per the Discussion); Black and Hispanic people and young adults (18–24) oversampled; data weighted for oversampling and non-response and to the 2000 census; response rate 81% (PDF p. 2, 2.1 Sample; PDF p. 6, Discussion, 9th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse, dependence or both by AUDADIS-IV (PDF p. 2, 2.1 Sample). How many had dependence and how many abuse only is not reported.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (PDF p. 3), men vs women with the disorder, weighted %: aged 18–29 29.19 vs 35.82; 30–44 42.15 vs 43.05; over 45 28.66 vs 21.13; White 77.13 vs 78.54; Black 9.90 vs 9.10; Hispanic 7.67 vs 6.99; college education 55.51 vs 64.18; personal income under $20,000 35.74 vs 58.74; employed 81.15 vs 69.34; married 54.74 vs 52.98; widowed or divorced 14.17 vs 19.26.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). Item-level missing data are not reported; Tables 2 to 4 print the full group sizes for every row, including rows that apply only to subgroups (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: General-population survey; people in institutions and homeless people outside shelters are not sampled, which the authors note may miss some people with the disorder (PDF p. 6). The comparison is restricted to people who had the disorder, so the time from first use to onset says nothing about the chance of developing it, which the authors cite as about twice as high in men (11.8% vs 5.4% lifetime, from Stinson et al., 2006; PDF p. 2). Women with the disorder were younger (Table 1), and younger respondents can only report short intervals between first use and onset.

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are men and women (the paper uses 'gender' and does not separate biological sex from social roles). Ages at first cannabis use, at heavy use (daily, or more than 20 days a month), at onset of the disorder and at remission were self-reported at the single interview; nothing was recorded as it happened (PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average joints a day during the period of heaviest use: men 3.38 (SE 0.12) vs women 2.54 (0.12); duration of the longest episode 40.43 (2.09) vs 31.01 (2.10) months (Table 3, PDF p. 4). Other routes not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use disorders are reported as comorbidities (Table 2, PDF p. 4): any other substance use disorder 92.22% of men vs 88.39% of women, alcohol use disorder 84.97 vs 74.56%, any other drug use disorder 41.60 vs 37.34%, nicotine dependence 50.93 vs 52.73%. None was adjusted for in the course, remission or help-seeking comparisons.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women among people with the disorder; for comorbidity, people without the disorder in the whole NESARC sample also enter the interaction models.
comparison.matching: None. Course, remission and help-seeking comparisons are unadjusted (weighted means and percentages with Wald F tests or odds ratios); comorbidity models adjusted for ethnicity, nativity, age, education, personal income, employment, marital status, urbanicity and region (Table 2, footnote c, PDF p. 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, childhood adversity, the timing of the comorbid disorders and other drug use before cannabis were not used; conduct problems appear only as lifetime conduct disorder. Current age was not adjusted for in the course comparisons although women with the disorder were younger.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable to the gender comparison; see polysubstance.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV: DSM-IV cannabis abuse criteria rated independently of dependence; mood, anxiety and personality disorders. Course questions: ages at first use, heavy use, onset and remission; number of episodes; criteria met; duration of the longest episode; joints a day. Help seeking grouped as professional treatment (outpatient visits; inpatient detoxification or rehabilitation unit or hospital ward; emergency department) or help from human service professionals (clergy, employee assistance programmes, family or social services, halfway houses, therapeutic communities, crisis centres, self-help groups); reasons for not seeking help in four groups (PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite well-documented reliability and validity of AUDADIS substance use disorder diagnoses and fair-to-good test-retest reliability (κ 0.40–0.62) of the mood, anxiety and personality diagnoses (PDF p. 2). The reliability of the recalled ages is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping = recalled time from first cannabis use to onset of CUD among people with lifetime abuse, dependence or both. The paper does not specify whether onset means first abuse or first dependence; their proportions are not reported. Remission is undefined, and whether help-seeking questions asked specifically about cannabis is not stated (PDF p. 2,2.2 Measures).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: No multiplicity correction stated. Editors count 52 outcome rows in Tables 2–4:30 comorbidity rows with two odds ratios each, 12 course rows and 10 help-seeking rows, giving about 82 tests. Table 1 has 10 sociodemographic characteristics with 21 non-reference category contrasts. Counts distinguish outcomes from tests; this is not a single prespecified comparison.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (lay interviewers knew respondents' gender).

analysis.effect_sizes: Course (Table 3, PDF p. 4), men vs women, weighted means (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), Wald F 0.02, p 0.8768; age at heavy use 18.15 (0.16) vs 18.28 (0.25), p 0.6676; age at onset 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), F 2.73, p 0.1035; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F 5.20, p 0.0259; abuse criteria 1.62 vs 1.49, p 0.0005; dependence criteria 4.23 vs 4.20, p 0.7982; longest episode 40.43 vs 31.01 months, p 0.0009; age at remission 25.32 vs 23.08, F 48.45, p < 0.0001; remitted 77.83% vs 82.10%, OR 0.77 (0.62–0.95). Help seeking (Table 4, PDF p. 5): any 14.20% vs 12.43%, OR 1.17 (0.92–1.48); no type of help or reason for not seeking help differed. Comorbidity (Table 2): see key findings. Editors' calculation: the difference in time to onset is 0.40 years (about 5 months), approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72 years from the printed SEs (ignoring covariance); this is a conditional normal interval ignoring covariance and survey design. The printed WaldF implies a somewhat larger SE and, with about 65 design degrees of freedom, its p-value is compatible with 0.0259; neither calculation supplies an exact corrected interval. No SD is printed for a standardized difference.
analysis.covariates: None for the course, remission and help-seeking comparisons. Comorbidity models: gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder, their interaction, ethnicity, nativity, age, education, personal income, employment status, marital status, urbanicity and region (Table 2, footnote c).
analysis.selective_reporting: The proportions with abuse only and with dependence are not reported; the analysed numbers for Table 3 rows that apply to subgroups are not given; the model behind the 'gender main effect' column is explained only in footnotes, and the within-disorder gender odds ratios the text describes are not shown.
analysis.power: Not reported. 1,217 women and 2,080 men in the overall comparison; analytic bases and survey design effects for reasons-for-no-help rows are not supplied.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in 2001–2002, men and women had started cannabis at the same age (16.7 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.3 vs 19.0 years, p = 0.10); the recalled interval from first use to onset was 0.40 years shorter in women (2.24 vs 2.64 years, p = 0.026, unadjusted). Men met more abuse criteria, used more joints a day, had longer episodes and were older at remission; more women than men reported remission (82.1 vs 77.8%). About one in seven had ever sought help, with no gender difference. Among people with the disorder, men more often had other substance use disorders and antisocial personality disorder and women more often mood and anxiety disorders; some psychiatric disorder was nearly universal in both (95.6 vs 94.1%), largely because other substance use disorders, including nicotine dependence, were counted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that men with the disorder were more likely than women to have any psychiatric disorder, that after adjustment women with the disorder were at greater risk for externalizing disorders, and that "Women experienced telescoping to CUD" (PDF p. 1); the Discussion calls this evidence for the telescoping phenomenon, suggests gender-specific pathways (PDF p. 6), and reads the remission figures as possibly showing that the disorder remits naturally for a high proportion of people (PDF p. 6). Gaps: (1) by the table footnotes, the 'gender main effect' odds ratios that the text gives for men vs women with the disorder come from a whole-sample model with an interaction term; multiplied by the interaction odds ratios they reproduce the crude odds ratios among people with the disorder (editors' check), and among people with the disorder the difference in any psychiatric disorder is not significant by the printed SEs; (2) interaction odds ratios below 1 mean that the male excess in these disorders is smaller among people with the disorder than among people without it, not that women with the disorder had them more often: men with the disorder had the higher percentages of other substance use disorders, alcohol use disorder, pathological gambling and antisocial personality disorder; (3) telescoping rests on a 5-month difference, unadjusted for current age although women were younger, conditional on having the disorder, from recalled ages, among 52 outcome rows with multiple tests per comorbidity row and no multiplicity correction, while the age at onset itself did not differ; (4) remission is undefined and not related to help seeking, so it cannot show remission without treatment. The limitations paragraph names self-report and the cross-sectional design, but not the recall of ages or the lack of age adjustment.

timeline.event: Project MATCH alcohol treatment sample, cited by the authors as clinical evidence of telescoping (read in this round: shorter recalled intervals in women for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, mainly in older participants).

Hernandez-Avila, Rounsaville and Kranzler: women entering treatment for opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence progressed faster to treatment; one of the two earlier, small studies of telescoping in cannabis dependence cited by the authors (PDF p. 2).
Ehlers et al., San Francisco Family Study: the other earlier study of telescoping in cannabis dependence cited by the authors (PDF p. 2).
The authors' group's general-population analysis of alcohol dependence, cited as indicating that telescoping may not occur in general-population samples (PDF p. 6).
This study: NESARC general-population sample; recalled time from first cannabis use to onset 0.40 years shorter in women, unadjusted, among people with the disorder.

Critique describes this study as finding a time from first cannabis use to the disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (as recorded on the library's card sc_marks_2018); the primary paper gives 2.64 vs 2.24 years, a difference of 0.40 years.

replication.where_it_stands: This is the general-population cannabis analysis that later reviews cite for telescoping. Read in full, it shows a small (0.40-year) unadjusted difference in the recalled time from first use to onset among people who had the disorder, with no difference in the age at onset itself; the same research group's alcohol analysis of two national surveys (keyes_2010) did not find the full pattern. The description of this study as a 2.5-year difference (Marks and Clark, as recorded on sc_marks_2018) does not match the paper. No re-analysis adjusting for age or birth cohort, or separating the chance of developing the disorder from the speed, is cited here.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first cannabis use, with use, criteria and help seeking recorded as they happen, analysed so as to separate the chance of developing the disorder from the speed of developing it and adjusted for age and birth cohort; and a re-analysis of the NESARC data with survival methods that censor at current age.

domains.note: National probability frame of civilian non-institutionalized adults, including group quarters; institutions and homeless people outside shelters are not covered.
Multistage probability sampling with oversampling and weights; design-based standard errors (SUDAAN).

3,297 people with the disorder, 1,217 women. Reasons-for-no-help rows have larger standard errors and an unreported analytic base; simple binomial effective-size calculations about100–180 do not establish actual subgroup counts under a weighted survey design.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives the sociodemographic profile by gender; the survey design is described by reference.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Item missingness not reported; full group sizes printed for rows that apply only to subgroups.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV diagnoses by a structured interview with cited reliability; but the course measures behind the telescoping and remission findings are recalled ages, and remission is not defined.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same interview for all respondents.

Weighted, design-based analyses are appropriate, but the course comparisons are unadjusted for current age although women were younger, there is no correction for multiple comparisons, and the comorbidity odds ratios are presented as within-disorder differences although they come from a whole-sample interaction model.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 81%, with weights for non-response.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is moderate risk. The weighted percentages and means by gender among people with the disorder (Tables 1 to 4) come from a large national probability sample with good response and a standard interview, and can be cited as descriptions of US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in 2001–2002. The analytic statements are weaker: the telescoping finding is a 5-month unadjusted difference among people who already had the disorder, from recalled ages; remission is undefined; and the text's gender odds ratios for comorbidity describe people without the disorder. Cite the paper for the percentages, for the absence of differences in ages at first use and onset, for the small difference in recalled interval, and for low and similar rates of help seeking; do not cite it as showing that women progress faster to cannabis use disorder, that women with the disorder have more externalizing disorders than men with it, or that the disorder remits without treatment.

key_findings.finding: NESARC 2001–2002: face-to-face Census Bureau interviews with 43,093 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 and older in households and group quarters, response rate 81%, oversampling of Black and Hispanic people and young adults, weighted to the 2000 census. The study sample was the 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse, dependence or both (AUDADIS-IV).
key_findings.page: PDF p. 2 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Sample; 2.2 Measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Women with the disorder were younger than men with it (aged 18–29: 35.82% vs 29.19%; over 45: 21.13% vs 28.66%; OR for men 1.66, 95% CI 1.34–2.06 for over 45 vs 18–29), more often had a college education (64.18% vs 55.51%), more often had an income under $20,000 (58.74% vs 35.74%), and were less often employed (69.34% vs 81.15%).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–3 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Sociodemographic characteristics, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Table 1 (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Men and women with the disorder did not differ in recalled age at first cannabis use (16.71, SE 0.10, vs 16.73, SE 0.12; Wald F 0.02, p 0.8768), at heavy use (18.15 vs 18.28; p 0.6676) or at onset of the disorder (19.34, SE 0.13, vs 18.98, SE 0.16; F 2.73, p 0.1035). The recalled time from first use to onset was 2.64 years (SE 0.10) in men and 2.24 (SE 0.13) in women (F 5.20, p 0.0259), which the authors present as evidence of telescoping. Editors' calculation: difference 0.40 years, about 5 months (approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72), unadjusted for current age or anything else.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Clinical characteristics and course, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: All ages recalled at one interview; comparison restricted to people with the disorder and unadjusted for current age. Non-significant age comparisons are not equivalence tests. The 0.08–0.72 interval is an approximate normal calculation ignoring covariance/design, not the paper’s interval.

key_findings.finding: Men with the disorder met more abuse criteria (mean 1.62 vs 1.49; F 13.66, p 0.0005), smoked more joints a day during their heaviest use (3.38 vs 2.54; F 30.84, p < 0.0001) and had longer episodes (40.43 vs 31.01 months; F 12.04, p 0.0009); dependence criteria (4.23 vs 4.20) and numbers of episodes did not differ.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Clinical characteristics and course, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Remission was reported by 77.83% (SE 1.13) of men and 82.10% (1.28) of women (OR for men 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.95); mean age at remission was 25.32 vs 23.08 years (F 48.45, p < 0.0001). Remission is not defined in the paper, the window is lifetime to the interview, and remission is not reported by help seeking.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 2); 3.3, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Help seeking was low and similar: any treatment 14.20% (SE 0.98) of men vs 12.43% (1.03) of women (OR 1.17, 0.92–1.48); professional treatment 12.45% vs 11.16%; outpatient 9.53% vs 9.66%; inpatient 9.27% vs 7.03% (OR 1.35, 0.98–1.86); emergency room 3.11% vs 2.95%; human service professionals 11.44% vs 9.57%. Reasons for not seeking help, men vs women: lack of motivation 75.92% vs 75.88%, stigma 40.05% vs 44.01%, logistical barriers 39.55% vs 38.92%, decreased perceived need (stopped alone or with help from friends or family) 20.26% vs 22.88%; none differed.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 4–5 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Treatment-seeking behaviors, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 4 and footnotes (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: Whether help was specifically for cannabis is not stated. The reasons-for-no-help rows have larger standard errors and an unreported analytic denominator. Effective sample size inferred from a simple binomial formula is not proof that the actual subgroup was small: survey design and weighting can also affect precision.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime disorders among people with cannabis use disorder, men vs women (weighted %): any psychiatric disorder 95.57 vs 94.14; any other substance use disorder 92.22 vs 88.39; alcohol use disorder 84.97 vs 74.56; any other drug use disorder 41.60 vs 37.34; nicotine dependence 50.93 vs 52.73; any mood disorder 30.58 vs 49.47; major depressive disorder 17.35 vs 28.12; any anxiety disorder 25.67 vs 40.16; antisocial personality disorder 21.10 vs 14.36; conduct disorder 1.92 vs 2.49; pathological gambling 1.58 vs 1.26.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: Table 2, percentage columns

key_findings.finding: The 'gender main effect' adjusted odds ratios (for example any psychiatric disorder 1.25, 95% CI 1.19–1.31; any other substance use disorder 2.18; alcohol use disorder 2.90; antisocial personality disorder 2.99; any mood disorder 0.49) come, by the table footnotes, from a whole-sample model containing gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder, their interaction and sociodemographic covariates, with women without the disorder as the reference; the text presents them as differences between men and women with the disorder. Editors' check: each main-effect odds ratio multiplied by its interaction odds ratio reproduces the crude odds ratio from the percentages among people with the disorder (any psychiatric disorder 1.25 × 1.08 = 1.35 vs 1.34; alcohol use disorder 2.90 × 0.67 = 1.94 vs 1.93; antisocial personality disorder 2.99 × 0.53 = 1.58 vs 1.59), so the main effects describe men and women without the disorder. Among people with the disorder, 95.57% vs 94.14% (SEs 0.53 and 0.85) is not a significant difference (z about 1.4, ignoring covariance).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Psychiatric comorbidity, 1st paragraph (starting PDF p. 2); Table 2 and footnotes a–c (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Gender × disorder interaction odds ratios were below 1 for any other substance use disorder (0.71, 0.54–0.94), alcohol use disorder (0.67, 0.53–0.83), nicotine dependence (0.77, 0.63–0.93), bipolar I and II (0.74, 0.58–0.95), conduct disorder (0.29, 0.15–0.58), pathological gambling (0.41, 0.17–0.96) and antisocial personality disorder (0.53, 0.40–0.71). The authors read these as women with the disorder being more likely than men to have these disorders (externalizing disorders in the abstract). In the editors' reading they mean the male excess seen in people without the disorder is smaller, on the odds scale, among people with it; among people with the disorder, men still had the higher percentages of other substance use disorders, alcohol use disorder, pathological gambling and antisocial personality disorder (Table 2).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Psychiatric comorbidity, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that their group's general-population analysis of alcohol dependence (Keyes et al., 2010) indicated that telescoping may not occur in general-population samples, and suggest sample- and substance-specific aspects of telescoping; they offer gender differences in reinforcement or the role of comorbidity as possible causes, untested here.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 6 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-report not confirmed by other informants; cross-sectional design; household surveys may miss some people with the disorder (shelters and group homes were sampled); some disorders, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder, not assessed.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 6 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The 'gender main effect' odds ratios in Table 2 are, by footnotes a–c, from a whole-sample model with a gender × disorder interaction, so they compare men and women without the disorder; the Results (3.2, 1st paragraph) and the abstract present them as differences between men and women with the disorder.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 1–4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that men with the disorder were more likely than women to have any psychiatric disorder is not supported by the within-disorder percentages (95.57% vs 94.14%); cite the percentages, not the main-effect odds ratios, for gender differences among people with the disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Interaction odds ratios below 1 are described as women with the disorder being more likely than men to have the disorders concerned (PDF p. 3) and as women being at greater risk for externalizing disorders (PDF p. 1), although the within-disorder percentages are higher in men for most of these disorders (Table 2).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 1, 3–4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding should be cited as a stronger association of cannabis use disorder with these disorders in women than in men on the odds scale, not as more frequent disorders in women with cannabis use disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Every row of Table 3 carries the full group sizes (2,080 and 1,217), although age at remission applies only to people who remitted and the episode and criteria counts apply to people with abuse or with dependence; footnote b (among people with abuse or dependence) also differs from the Methods (abuse criteria among people with abuse, dependence criteria among people with dependence).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 2, 4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed numbers for these rows are unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote d of Table 4 gives the base for the reasons for not seeking help as everyone who did not seek treatment (about 1,785 men and 1,066 women, editors' arithmetic), but the standard errors of these percentages (2.98 to 4.85 points) are three to five times those of the help-seeking rates (0.95 to 1.03), implying an effective base of only about 100 to 180 people per sex (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 5 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The actual analytic denominator and design effects for these rows are not reported. The standard errors imply less effective information than a simple unweighted full-base calculation, but do not establish an unreported small actual subgroup.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion supports natural remission, and remission taking several years, by citing Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), whose title in the reference list concerns transition from first use to dependence, not remission.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 6–7 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The cited reference title concerns transition to dependence rather than remission. Its full text was not read here, so the title alone cannot establish whether it contains any remission analysis. Do not treat the citation as independently verified support for natural remission.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor reporting points in this in-press version: Table 1 lists a 'Northwest' region alongside Midwest, South and West; Table 2 reports histrionic personality disorder, psychotic disorder, conduct disorder and pathological gambling, which the Methods list of assessed disorders does not mention; one Discussion sentence on alcohol telescoping is garbled.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 2–3, 4, 6 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the version of record (not read) may differ.

Gaps: (1) by the table footnotes, the 'gender main effect' odds ratios that the text gives for men vs women with the disorder come from a whole-sample model with an interaction term; multiplied by the interaction odds ratios they reproduce the crude odds ratios among people with the disorder (editors' check), and among people with the disorder the difference in any psychiatric disorder is not significant by the printed SEs; (2) interaction odds ratios below 1 mean that the male excess in these disorders is smaller among people with the disorder than among people without it, not that women with the disorder had them more often: men with the disorder had the higher percentages of other substance use disorders, alcohol use disorder, pathological gambling and antisocial personality disorder; (3) telescoping rests on a 5-month difference, unadjusted for current age although women were younger, conditional on having the disorder, from recalled ages, among about 50 comparisons without correction, while the age at onset itself did not differ; (4) remission is undefined and not related to help seeking, so it cannot show remission without treatment.
