design_detail: Co-twin control analysis within a cross-sectional telephone diagnostic interview (1996–2000; the Semi-Structured Assessment for the Genetics of Alcoholism adapted for telephone use and DSM-IV) of the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; median age 30, range 24–36). The analysis uses 311 same-sex pairs (136 monozygotic, 175 dizygotic) in which one twin reported first cannabis use before age 17 and the co-twin did not (234 co-twins started at 17 or later, 77 never used cannabis). Outcomes: lifetime nonmedical use of sedatives, hallucinogens, cocaine/other stimulants and opioids; abuse/dependence on cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, opioids or any of them (modified criteria); DSM-IV alcohol dependence. Conditional logistic regression, unadjusted and adjusted for within-pair differences in covariates kept by backward stepwise selection; repeated in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis.
can_establish: Within these Australian twin pairs, the twin recalling cannabis use before 17 more often reported later use of other drugs and met the study’s modified drug-problem criteria or full DSM-IV alcohol-dependence criteria at some point in life. The pair design controls shared rearing, while pooled fraternal pairs retain genetic differences. The study did not date problem onset, so alcohol dependence or drug-problem criteria are not established as later than cannabis initiation.
cannot_establish: Whether early cannabis use caused later outcomes. Peer affiliation and temperament are not described as measured covariates in this paper; some other within-pair differences were assessed retrospectively and selected stepwise. Published estimates pool identical and fraternal pairs, with no separate identical-pair estimates shown. Ages at first use were recalled in adulthood and ages at onset of problems were unavailable.

sample.recruitment: Registry: young-adult cohort of the Australian Twin Register, a volunteer twin panel (pairs enrolled 1980–1982); a single telephone interview in 1996–2000 (p. 428, Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Same-sex pairs discordant for first cannabis use before 17: 311 of the 861 twins who started before 17 had such a co-twin. Seventeen individuals who reported starting sedatives (3), hallucinogens (6), stimulants (5) or opioids (3) before cannabis were excluded from the analyses (p. 428, Methods, 2nd paragraph; p. 430, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: 306 men (62 monozygotic and 91 dizygotic pairs) and 316 women (74 and 84 pairs); median age 30 (range 24–36). Early tobacco use (smoking at least weekly for 3 weeks or more before 17) in 36.6%; early regular drinking (at least monthly for 6 months or more before 17) in 11.6% (pp. 428–429).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); of 4,010 traceable pairs, both twins were interviewed in 2,765 (69% pairwise response) and one twin in another 735 (78% individual response) (p. 428, Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteer twin register with 69% pairwise response; the discordant pairs are a selected subset (311 pairs from 2,765 complete pairs); the concordance analysis lists more discordant same-sex pairs (407) than were analysed, unexplained (see reporting issues); handling of missing data is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported age at first cannabis use, asked earlier in the interview than drug problems to limit recall bias (p. 431, Comment, 2nd paragraph); early use = first use before 17. Zygosity from standard questions on physical similarity and confusion of the twins, which in earlier studies agreed with genotyping in more than 95% of pairs (p. 428).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured for the exposure: any use before 17, which the authors call a crude measure (p. 432, Comment, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Early tobacco and early regular alcohol use were measured and offered as covariates; people who started another illicit drug before cannabis were excluded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The co-twin from the same pair, who had not used cannabis before 17 (234 started later, 77 never used it).
comparison.matching: Matched by pair: same rearing household, sex and age for all pairs; all genes for monozygotic pairs and about half for dizygotic pairs. Within-pair covariate differences adjusted when retained by backward stepwise selection (P<.10).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Factors that differ between co-twins were measured only as lifetime conduct disorder, major depression, social anxiety, early tobacco and alcohol use (and, per the abstract, parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse), all recalled at about 30, without establishing that they came before cannabis use; peer affiliation and temperament are not described as measured covariates in this paper.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Most co-twins (234 of 311) used cannabis after 17; Table 3 repeats the analysis in pairs in which both twins used cannabis.

outcomes.instruments: Telephone-adapted Semi-Structured Assessment for the Genetics of Alcoholism (DSM-IV): lifetime nonmedical use of each drug class; for classes used at least monthly, abuse (either of 2 abuse symptoms) and dependence (2 or more of 4 dependence symptoms), modified rather than formal DSM-IV criteria; alcohol dependence by full DSM-IV criteria (pp. 428–429).
outcomes.validity_norms: The modified cannabis dependence criteria had sensitivity 96.7% and specificity 94.6% against DSM-IV in an earlier analysis of this sample (p. 429).
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime outcomes reported at a median age of 30; drug classes combined for abuse/dependence because of low prevalence. Ages at onset of problems were not collected, so lifetime alcohol dependence and drug-problem criteria do not establish temporal order relative to cannabis initiation. Drug criteria were modified symptom counts, not formal DSM-IV diagnoses.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 95% confidence intervals for 10 outcomes in two samples; power was computed at the .01 level (pp. 429–430).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; whether interviewers knew the co-twin's answers is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Conditional odds ratios, twin who started cannabis before 17 against co-twin (311 pairs, Table 2): unadjusted 2.83 (95% CI 1.66–4.85) sedative use, 5.15 (2.85–9.33) hallucinogen use, 4.19 (2.60–6.75) cocaine/stimulant use, 2.57 (1.39–4.77) opioid use; 2.13 (1.45–3.13) cannabis, 2.67 (0.71–10.05) sedative, 4.13 (1.91–8.93) cocaine/stimulant, 3.67 (1.02–13.14) opioid and 2.24 (1.52–3.30) any drug abuse/dependence; 2.17 (1.46–3.24) alcohol dependence. Adjusted: 2.28, 5.15, 4.06, 2.34; 1.96, 2.67, 3.98, 3.67, 1.98; 1.85. Absolute differences in lifetime prevalence (editors' calculation from Table 2): cocaine/stimulant use 47.9% against 26.4% (21.5 points), hallucinogen use 17.4 points, any drug abuse/dependence 14.8 points, alcohol dependence 13.2 points, opioid use 7.1 points. Editors' reconstruction of the discordant pairs from the printed prevalences reproduces every unadjusted odds ratio and interval (for example 67 against 13 pairs for hallucinogen use; 8 against 3 for sedative abuse/dependence).
analysis.covariates: Within-pair differences in early regular tobacco use, early regular alcohol use, conduct disorder, major depression and social anxiety (and, per the abstract, parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse), retained by backward stepwise selection at P<.10 with early cannabis use forced in (p. 429, Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 2 footnote).
analysis.selective_reporting: Separate monozygotic and dizygotic analyses and alternative cut-offs (before 15, 16 and 18) are described only as confirming the conclusions, without estimates; the zygosity and sex interactions are reported only as P>.10 (p. 429; p. 431, Subsidiary Analyses).
analysis.power: By simulation at the .01 level: 80% or more for odds ratios above 1.7 for five outcomes and above 2.5 for sedative use, opioid use and cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence; low for sedative and opioid abuse/dependence (pp. 429–430). The printed formula for the minimum odds ratio is not an odds ratio (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within 311 same-sex pairs, the twin who recalled starting cannabis before 17 more often reported later use of each other drug class (conditional odds ratios 2.6 to 5.2), drug abuse/dependence (2.1 to 4.1; sedatives not significant) and alcohol dependence (2.2) than the co-twin. Adjusting for within-pair differences in measured covariates lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (to 1.9–5.2). In the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis the unadjusted odds ratios were 1.6 to 6.0, and after adjustment cannabis abuse/dependence (P=.06) and sedative abuse/dependence were no longer significant. No identical-pair estimates are shown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the associations cannot be explained solely by shared genetic or environmental predisposition and suggests that they may arise from the peer and social context in which cannabis is used and obtained, lowering perceived barriers to and giving access to other drugs (p. 427); the Comment says the results are consistent with a causal role and that heritable factors cannot explain the association because identical pairs share their genes (p. 431). The shared-environment conclusion is supported; the genetic one rests on identical pairs whose separate estimates are not reported (only a non-significant interaction, with 136 identical pairs), while more than half of the pairs analysed are fraternal. Factors that differ between co-twins are judged less plausible rather than measured. The abstract calls the effect of adjustment 'negligible', though the odds ratios fell by up to about a fifth. The proposed mechanisms (peer context, lowered perceived risk, access through dealers, pharmacological sensitization) are not tested. The Comment itself says strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from these associations alone (p. 432).

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence behind the gateway question (see that card).

Grant & Dawson, US national survey: earlier age at first drug use went with DSM-IV drug abuse and dependence; cited here among non-twin studies reporting early onset as a risk factor (card written in the same round).

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a model with a shared propensity and no gateway effect reproduces the population-level gateway phenomena; it does not address comparisons within twin pairs (see that card).

Wagner & Anthony: in US household surveys, marijuana use went with an earlier first chance to try cocaine and with starting it once offered, in line with the access mechanism proposed here (see that card).
This study, with an editorial (JAMA 289(4):482–483; PubMed 12533129) and, later in 2003, four letters with the authors' reply (JAMA 290(3):329–332; PubMed 12865366–12865369), none read for this card.

Irons, Iacono & McGue, Minnesota twins: drinking by 14 went with more drug classes used at 24 within identical pairs discordant for early drinking, a co-twin result for alcohol rather than cannabis (as recorded on that card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication of this co-twin result for cannabis appears in the sources read for this card, and the editorial and letters were not available; later studies were not searched by this reader. The authors note that the association with early cannabis use had been reported in prospective non-twin studies (references 16–19, not read). Among the gateway papers of this round it is the design that best controls shared family factors; the reading list notes that no study separates the causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective twin study that records cannabis use, peer affiliation and behaviour problems in both twins from before first use through adolescence, reports identical-pair estimates separately with enough discordant identical pairs to be precise, and dates later drug use; replicated in another country with different cannabis availability.

domains.note: The pair design removes shared rearing environment and, in identical pairs, genes; but the reported estimates pool fraternal pairs (56% of pairs) without separate identical-pair estimates, and the paper does not describe measuring peer affiliation or temperament as within-pair covariates, with the covariates used recalled at about 30 and chosen by stepwise selection, some possibly consequences rather than causes of early use.

Age at first cannabis use recalled at a median age of 30 with a cut-off at 17; 234 of 311 co-twins also used cannabis, so many pairs may differ by a year or two near the cut-off; recall could be shaped by later drug involvement.
Volunteer register with 69% pairwise response; 311 discordant pairs analysed against 407 listed in the concordance analysis, unexplained.
None relevant.
Missing answers and the handling of the 17 people excluded for using another drug before cannabis are not described; the table percentages use all 311 (234) pairs.
Lifetime outcomes self-reported in the same interview as the exposure, using modified abuse/dependence criteria for drugs; interviewer blinding not reported.
All 10 outcomes are reported unadjusted and adjusted, but identical-pair and alternative cut-off analyses are summarized without estimates, and one adjusted row of Table 3 duplicates Table 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The co-twin comparison holds constant everything co-twins share in their upbringing and, for identical pairs, their genes, which none of the other gateway designs of this round can do, so it is the strongest of them on confounding. It still cannot exclude factors that differ between co-twins, the estimates pool fraternal pairs with no identical-pair results shown, and early use was recalled in adulthood. Citable for the within-pair associations (Table 2) as evidence that shared family environment does not account for the link between early cannabis use and later drug use in this Australian cohort; not as proof that early cannabis use causes later drug use, and not for the mechanisms proposed.

key_findings.finding: Of 4,010 traceable pairs, both twins were interviewed in 2,765 (69% pairwise response) and one twin in 735 (78% individual response), 6,265 people in all; 3,772 had used cannabis, 861 (13.7%) before 17; 311 of these (36.1%) had a same-sex co-twin who had not used cannabis before 17 (234 started later, 77 never), giving 622 twins.
key_findings.locator: Figure; Methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 311 discordant pairs comprised 74 female and 62 male identical pairs and 84 female and 91 male same-sex fraternal pairs; median age 30 (range 24–36).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In the full interview sample, concordance for cannabis use before 17 was higher in identical than fraternal pairs: men 65 concordant and 88 discordant identical pairs against 59 and 110 fraternal (chi-square 7.92, 1 df, P=.005); women 61 and 98 against 44 and 111 (chi-square 7.80, P=.005); the authors read this as heritable influence on age at first cannabis use.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 429); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 430)
key_findings.note: The test is a Breslow-Day comparison whose full counts (pairs concordant for no early use) are not printed, so it cannot be recomputed; the discordant counts here exceed the 311 pairs analysed (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime prevalence, twin who started cannabis before 17 against co-twin: sedative use 19.0% against 8.4%; hallucinogen use 35.4% against 18.0%; cocaine/stimulant use 47.9% against 26.4%; opioid use 13.5% against 6.4%; cannabis abuse/dependence 45.7% against 31.8%; cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence 12.5% against 4.5%; any drug abuse/dependence 47.6% against 32.8%; alcohol dependence 42.8% against 29.6%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, lifetime prevalence columns
key_findings.note: Absolute differences (editors' calculation): 21.5 points for cocaine/stimulant use, 17.4 for hallucinogens, 14.8 for any drug abuse/dependence, 13.2 for alcohol dependence, 7.1 for opioid use.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted conditional odds ratios (311 pairs): sedative use 2.83 (95% CI 1.66–4.85), hallucinogen use 5.15 (2.85–9.33), cocaine/stimulant use 4.19 (2.60–6.75), opioid use 2.57 (1.39–4.77); cannabis abuse/dependence 2.13 (1.45–3.13), sedative 2.67 (0.71–10.05), cocaine/stimulant 4.13 (1.91–8.93), opioid 3.67 (1.02–13.14), any drug 2.24 (1.52–3.30); alcohol dependence 2.17 (1.46–3.24). All but sedative abuse/dependence were significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, unadjusted conditional OR column; Results, items 1 and 2
key_findings.note: Editors' reconstruction from the printed prevalences (pairs in which only the early-use twin, or only the co-twin, had the outcome) reproduces each odds ratio and interval, for example 67 against 13 pairs for hallucinogen use, 88 against 21 for cocaine/stimulant use, 83 against 37 for any drug abuse/dependence and 8 against 3 for sedative abuse/dependence. This is an arithmetic reconstruction consistent with the printed results, not access to independently reported joint outcome data; marginals alone do not identify the discordant-outcome counts.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for within-pair differences in the covariates retained (P<.10): sedative use 2.28 (1.20–4.31), hallucinogen use 5.15 (2.85–9.33, no covariate retained), cocaine/stimulant use 4.06 (2.30–7.17), opioid use 2.34 (1.13–4.85); cannabis abuse/dependence 1.96 (1.25–3.09), sedative 2.67 (0.71–10.05), cocaine/stimulant 3.98 (1.73–9.17), opioid 3.67 (1.02–13.14), any drug 1.98 (1.26–3.10); alcohol dependence 1.85 (1.21–2.83). Early regular tobacco and alcohol use were the covariates most often retained; 9 of 10 outcomes remained significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, adjusted columns and footnote; Results, item 3 and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis (54 female and 53 male identical, 56 female and 71 male fraternal), unadjusted odds ratios were 3.00 (1.60–5.62) sedative use, 3.92 (2.13–7.21) hallucinogen use, 3.00 (1.83–4.92) cocaine/stimulant use, 2.33 (1.19–4.59) opioid use; 1.58 (1.05–2.37) cannabis, 6.00 (0.72–49.83) sedative, 4.29 (1.88–9.76) cocaine/stimulant, 5.00 (1.10–22.82) opioid and 1.75 (1.16–2.64) any drug abuse/dependence; 2.03 (1.30–3.17) alcohol dependence. After adjustment, cannabis abuse/dependence was 1.57 (0.98–2.52; P=.06) and sedative abuse/dependence was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Analyses Restricted to Those Reporting Lifetime Cannabis Use (p. 430, continuing p. 431); Table 3 (p. 431)

key_findings.finding: Interactions of early cannabis use with zygosity and with sex were not significant (P>.10 in all cases), so the data were pooled; separate identical- and fraternal-pair analyses with early use defined as before 15, 16 or 18 are said to confirm the conclusions, without estimates.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 429); Subsidiary Analyses (p. 431)

key_findings.finding: Abuse/dependence by sex in the 622 twins: cannabis 50.0% of men and 27.9% of women; any illicit drug 51.3% and 29.4%; cocaine/stimulants 11.8% and 5.4%; alcohol dependence 44.8% and 27.9%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Lifetime Alcohol Dependence

key_findings.finding: The modified cannabis dependence criteria had sensitivity 96.7% and specificity 94.6% against DSM-IV in an earlier analysis of this sample; 36.6% of twins in the discordant pairs reported early tobacco use and 11.6% early regular drinking.
key_findings.locator: Lifetime Drug Abuse/Dependence; Family, Social, and Individual Factors › Early Tobacco Use; Early Regular Alcohol Use

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the results consistent with early cannabis use having a causal role, consider unshared environmental influences less plausible because co-twins grew up in the same household, and argue that family background or heritable factors cannot explain the association.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations and counter-arguments given by the authors: reliance on retrospective self-report and no data on ages at progression to frequent use or problems; age at first use was asked before drug problems; under-reporting by one twin is judged implausible because some cannabis use was normative in this cohort; delayed onset in co-twins is judged unlikely because more than 95% of people in the sample who used cannabis had started by 24.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 431, continues p. 432)

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms proposed if the association is causal, none tested here: pharmacological sensitization from cited laboratory research, pleasurable early experiences, lower perceived legal risk and access through dealers. Only the cross-tolerance discussion expressly identifies rats; the species of the cited dopamine experiment is not stated in this paper. Authors say laboratory exposures exceed those near the start of drug use and state that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from these associations alone.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd–8th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 (234 pairs) the adjusted odds ratio for alcohol dependence, 1.85 (1.21–2.83) with covariates 3 and 4, is identical to the Table 2 value (311 pairs), although the samples and the unadjusted odds ratios differ (2.03 against 2.17).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably duplicated in error; the adjusted alcohol-dependence estimate for the restricted sample is unknown and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The power calculation defines the minimum odds ratio as pE(1−pE)/pU(1−pU), which is not an odds ratio. With the stated pE = 12.5% and pU = 4.5% it gives 2.5 (editors' calculation), the threshold the paper reports for cocaine/stimulant abuse/dependence, whereas the odds ratio for those prevalences is 3.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: The power statements may refer to a misdefined quantity, so the power to detect the stated odds ratios is uncertain; the main results are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The concordance analysis lists 407 same-sex pairs discordant for cannabis use before 17 (88 + 110 male, 98 + 111 female, 186 of them identical), whereas the analysis uses 311 pairs (136 identical); the difference is not explained. The same concordance counts imply 229 pairs concordant for early use and 407 discordant pairs: 2×229+407=865 early starters, exceeding the 861 early starters reported for the entire interviewed sample before singletons or opposite-sex pairs. The counts cannot all describe the same sample as printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: About a quarter of the discordant pairs, including 50 identical pairs, are missing from the analysis for unstated reasons, which could matter for the identical-pair argument.

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators: the 17 people who started another drug before cannabis are said to be excluded, yet the prevalences in Tables 2 and 3 use all 311 and 234 pairs; the sex-specific prevalences of use in the Methods imply slightly smaller denominators than 306 men and 316 women; and the 24.8% described as twins in discordant pairs who never used cannabis is 77 of the 311 co-twins (12.4% of the 622 twins).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; which analyses excluded the 17 people is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment's ranges (2.3- to 3.9-fold for other drug use, 1.6- to 6.0-fold for alcohol dependence and drug abuse/dependence) come from the unadjusted odds ratios of the restricted sample (Table 3), include the non-significant sedative abuse/dependence estimate (6.00, 0.72–49.83), and are said to hold whether or not pairs were identical, though no identical-pair estimates are shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use the Table 2 estimates; the statement about identical pairs rests on a non-significant interaction test, not on shown estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists parental conflict/separation and childhood sexual abuse among the covariates controlled, and the Methods say the family-environment and abuse measures are described below, but the covariate section describes only psychiatric disorders, social anxiety, early tobacco use and early regular alcohol use.
reporting_issues.consequence: How those two covariates were measured and entered is not described in this paper; they were never retained by the stepwise selection.

design_detail: 'For Debate' article (Addiction 97(12):1493–1504; three commentaries and the authors' reply follow in the same issue and were not read). A Monte Carlo model of adolescent drug initiation: each simulated person gets a standard-normal 'drug use propensity' that brings forward the ages of the first opportunity to use marijuana and to use hard drugs (heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens) through a gamma frailty term, and raises the yearly chance of first use once an opportunity has occurred; given propensity, marijuana opportunity and use have no influence on hard drugs, so the model contains no gateway effect by construction. Parameters were set from the pooled 1982–1994-A US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse (58,846 respondents aged 12–25, birth cohorts 1964–1982, weighted). One million simulated people were compared with survey estimates of three phenomena cited for a gateway effect (relative risk, ordering, dose–response); a further exercise adds noisy indicators of propensity as covariates to show how much association survives adjustment. Filed as modelling: the evidence is a simulation calibrated to survey margins, not a test of the gateway effect against data.
can_establish: That a model with no causal link from marijuana to hard drugs, in which one shared propensity governs both opportunities and use, can produce a strong marijuana–hard-drug relative risk, an order of first use in which hard drugs rarely come first, and a hazard of hard-drug initiation that rises with marijuana frequency, under its stated assumptions and US parameters for 1982–94; and that adjusting for imperfect proxies of such a propensity leaves large residual associations.
cannot_establish: That the shared propensity rather than a gateway effect explains the real associations: no model with a gateway effect was fitted for comparison, the propensity parameters were fitted to correlations in data that may themselves contain such an effect, the paper prints 157 versus 24 but may not use identical order definitions for those quantities, and its dose–response match depends on a correlation chosen without data.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (simulation). Inputs come from the National Household Survey on Drug Abuse, a probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population aged 12 and over, 1982 through 1994-A (p. 1497, Parameter estimation › Data source).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Survey respondents aged 12–25 from birth cohorts 1964–1982; the relative-risk comparison uses respondents aged 22 or older (p. 1497, Data source; p. 1499, Estimation of the relative risk effect).
sample.demographics: Not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The calibration data are self-reports in household surveys, which miss people without a fixed address or in institutions (not discussed). Pooling the birth cohorts rests on preliminary analyses that are not shown (p. 1497, Data source).

exposure.measurement: Simulated. In the survey data: self-reported ages of the first opportunity to use and of first use of marijuana, heroin, cocaine and hallucinogens, and past-year marijuana frequency (pp. 1497–1498, Data source).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Past-year marijuana frequency in five bands (none, 1–2, 3–11, 12–51, 52 or more times), drawn for each simulated person from the survey distribution by age and years since starting, through a random effect whose correlation with propensity was set at 0 to 1 because no data exist to estimate it (p. 1497, Marijuana use frequency).
exposure.polysubstance: 'Hard drugs' pool heroin, cocaine and hallucinogens (earliest reported age); alcohol and tobacco are not modelled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Simulated people who had not started marijuana by 21 (relative risk) or had not used it in the past year (dose–response), compared with the corresponding survey estimates.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The model's driver is assumed rather than measured: no information exists on how a drug use propensity is distributed among adolescents, so a standard normal distribution was used (p. 1496, Drug use propensity, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Simulated survival functions; relative risk of starting a hard drug by 21 for people who had and had not started marijuana by 21; share of people starting a hard drug at least a year before marijuana; hazard ratios of hard-drug initiation by past-year marijuana frequency (complementary log-log model on 30,000 simulated cases, ages 12–21); odds ratios from a logistic model that adjusts for a propensity indicator of chosen reliability (pp. 1499–1502).
outcomes.validity_norms: Fit to the survey judged only on the marginal survival functions (within 0.009 at every age); no goodness-of-fit for the joint distribution of the four ages.
outcomes.operationalization: A phenomenon counts as 'reproduced' if the model produces it in the same direction and of similar or greater size than the survey estimate (pp. 1500–1501).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; no intervals for simulated or survey quantities.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Model against survey: reported relative risk 157 in the model against 24 in the survey; the survey compares hard-drug use by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21, without requiring cannabis to precede the other drug. The model’s results also use prior-initiation language, so the quantities may differ; for starting marijuana by 15 against later, 3.44 against 1.60; share starting a hard drug at least a year before marijuana, 0.011 against 0.016 (11 against 16 per 1,000); hazard ratios of hard-drug initiation rising with past-year marijuana frequency at every assumed correlation, the heaviest group above 10 even at zero correlation, with the survey hazard ratios near the r=0.4 curve at low frequencies and between r=0.4 and r=0.8 at the highest (pp. 1500–1501; Fig. 3). Read from the log-scale Fig. 3 by the first reader only: survey hazard ratios about 7.5, 12, 23 and 39 for 1–2, 3–11, 12–51 and 52 or more uses against none. Adjustment exercise (Fig. 4): odds ratio of starting a hard drug by 22 after marijuana use 297 with no propensity indicator, 178 at correlation 0.6, 82 at correlation 0.8, 32 at correlation 0.9, 12 at about 0.95, 2 at 0.99 and 1 at 1.0. No uncertainty intervals anywhere. Figure 4 calls its abscissa reliability, but the text defines it as indicator–propensity correlation;0.8 corresponds to 64% of variance in the simple linear interpretation (editors’ calculation,0.8²), not 80%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; in the Fig. 4 exercise, a simulated indicator of propensity.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only one specification of the model is shown; parameter values other than β1 (3.22) are not printed and no code is provided; the dose–response result is shown for four assumed correlations.
analysis.power: Not applicable. With one million simulated people Monte Carlo error is small, but uncertainty in the survey inputs is not carried into the model outputs.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under its assumptions, a propensity-only model calibrated to US survey margins produces all three gateway phenomena: it prints a larger relative risk (157 against 24, possibly with a different order definition) and stronger ordering (11 against 16 per 1,000 with hard drugs first), and matches the dose–response only for some values of an unmeasured correlation. It shows that these phenomena cannot by themselves distinguish a gateway effect from a shared propensity.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Introduction says the primary evidence for a marijuana gateway effect can be explained completely by the order of opportunities and a non-specific liability (p. 1493), and the abstract that no gateway effect is required and that the common-factor model has policy implications that differ significantly from the gateway model (p. 1493). The Discussion concludes that marijuana policies would have little effect on hard drug use except through propensity or the availability of hard drugs (p. 1503). The same pages state that the model does not disprove a gateway effect, that something like one probably exists through contact with the black market, and that its validity must remain uncertain until compared directly with the common-factor model (pp. 1502–1503). The demonstration shows that the phenomena do not identify the cause; the policy conclusion assumes that the common-factor model is the true one, which the paper does not test. The printed 157/24 difference,whose order definitions may differ,is attributed to slight imprecision in a small denominator (p. 1500); the printed figures imply that the survey denominator was itself only about 0.013 to 0.015 (editors' calculation), so the 'slight' difference invoked is almost all of it.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the ordering phenomenon modelled here (see that card).
Wagner & Anthony: in US household surveys of 1991–94 (overlapping this model's calibration years), earlier drug use went with earlier opportunities and with starting once offered (see that card).
This model; three commentaries (Addiction 97(12):1505–1507; PubMed 12472630–12472632) and the authors' reply (PubMed 12472633) appeared in the same issue, not read for this card.

Lynskey et al.: early cannabis use went with later other drug use within same-sex twin pairs, a within-pair comparison accounting for shared rearing and, with identical and fraternal twins pooled, only part of genetic confounding, which this model does not address (see that card).
Degenhardt et al., 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys, cite this model for the common-cause explanation (as recorded on that card).
Vanyukov et al.: narrative review by proponents of common liability cites this model in support (as recorded on that card).

Irons, Iacono & McGue, Minnesota twins: drinking by 14 went with more drug classes used at 24 within identical pairs discordant for early drinking, which a liability shared by co-twins cannot by itself produce (as recorded on that card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no re-analysis or independent replication of the model appears in the sources read for this card, and the commentaries and reply published with it were not available. The model stands as the standard demonstration that the relative-risk, ordering and dose–response phenomena do not by themselves identify a gateway effect. Designs that hold shared factors constant, such as co-twin comparisons (Lynskey et al., 2003; Irons et al., 2015, for early drinking), found within-pair associations that a liability shared by co-twins cannot produce, although a propensity that differs between co-twins remains possible. Later studies were not searched by this reader.

what_would_settle_it: Fit both a common-factor model and a model that adds a gateway effect (for example through access to drug markets) to the same individual-level longitudinal data with measured opportunities and propensity indicators recorded before any use, and compare how well each reproduces the joint distribution, including associations within twin pairs; or study a natural experiment that changes access to marijuana without changing propensity, such as a policy that separates cannabis from hard-drug markets, and measure later hard-drug initiation.

domains.domain: Model assumptions and their empirical support
domains.note: The core assumptions (a normally distributed propensity, a gamma frailty for opportunities, one shared β2 for both drugs, no effect of marijuana given propensity) are not tested; the propensity parameters were fitted to correlations in survey data that may contain a real gateway effect, which the model would then absorb into propensity; the dose–response result needs a correlation for which, as the authors say, no data exist.

domains.domain: Calibration and comparison with the target data
domains.note: Only the marginal survival functions are calibrated (within 0.009); of the three phenomena, the printed relative risks differ (157 against 24), with a possible mismatch in their order definitions, the early-onset relative risk about twofold (3.44 against 1.60), and the ordering is stronger than observed (0.011 against 0.016), all without intervals.
No model with a gateway effect was fitted to the same data, so the paper cannot show that the data favour either explanation.
Parameter values other than β1 are not printed, no code is given, and the printed equations contain notation errors (see reporting issues), so the model cannot be rebuilt exactly from the paper.

No intervals for survey estimates or simulated quantities, and sampling error in the survey inputs is not carried into the outputs; the authors themselves call the survey dose–response estimate inaccurate (p. 1499).

domains.domain: Balance (between the common-factor and gateway explanations)
domains.note: The authors acknowledge that a gateway effect may exist, probably through black-market contact, and that the model does not disprove it; but the abstract, Introduction and policy paragraph state the common-factor reading more firmly than a non-identification result supports, and the gateway side (for example access to markets) is not modelled.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a simulation (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to a modelling study, as on card sc_rogeberg_2013, and the overall is no milder than the worst domain. The model legitimately shows that a shared propensity plus the order of opportunities could produce the phenomena usually cited for a gateway effect, and its adjustment exercise shows why controlling for imperfect proxies cannot rule a shared factor out. It does not show that a shared factor is the actual explanation: it was not compared with a gateway model, the printed 157/24 comparison does not establish matched joint-data fit and may compare different order definitions, and its parameters could absorb a real gateway effect. Citable for the argument that the gateway phenomena do not identify a causal effect and for the size of residual association left by imperfect adjustment within the model; not as evidence that the gateway effect is zero or that marijuana policy cannot affect hard-drug use.

key_findings.finding: In the model, one standard-normal propensity per person brings forward the first opportunities to use marijuana and hard drugs and raises the yearly chance of first use once offered; given propensity, opportunity to use and use of marijuana are independent of opportunity to use and use of hard drugs, so the model excludes any causal gateway effect by design.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 1495); Methods › Model specification (pp. 1495–1497); Figure 1 (p. 1497)

key_findings.finding: Calibration data: all 58,846 survey respondents aged 12–25 from birth cohorts 1964–1982, pooled from the 1982 through 1994-A National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse with sample weights; 'hard drugs' means the earliest reported heroin, cocaine or hallucinogen. The questions on opportunities were dropped from later surveys.
key_findings.locator: Parameter estimation › Data source

key_findings.finding: β1 = 3.22, the maximum-likelihood estimate from a 5% random sample of the survey data stratified by survey year and birth cohort, sets the correlation between ages of first opportunity for the two drug groups; β2 was chosen by simulation (10,000 cases per trial value) to match the survey correlation between the opportunity-to-use lags for marijuana and hard drugs among people who used both by 22; the remaining parameters make the model's marginal probabilities match the survey.
key_findings.locator: Statistical methods › Estimation of β1; Estimation of β2; Estimation of ψ*

key_findings.finding: Survey survival curves: by age 22, about 77% had had an opportunity to use marijuana, about 46% an opportunity to use a hard drug, about 54% had used marijuana and about 23% a hard drug.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi crop of Fig. 2 by the first reader (proportions surviving at 22 of about 0.23, 0.54, 0.46 and 0.77); approximate.

key_findings.finding: Modelled marijuana and hard-drug initiation survival rates differed from the survey's by 0.009 or less at every age.
key_findings.locator: Model Results › Model precision

key_findings.finding: The paper reports a relative risk 157 in the model and 24 in survey respondents aged 22 or older. The survey compares other-drug use by 21 between people reporting cannabis use by 21 and those not reporting it,without imposing an order;the model also uses prior-initiation wording,so exact comparability is unresolved. The authors attribute the gap to imprecision in the small denominator: if the survey's probability of starting a hard drug by 22 without marijuana by 21 were lower by as little as 0.013, the relative risk could exceed 190.
key_findings.locator: Model Results › Gateway effects › Relative risk, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with a survey ratio of 24, a reduction of 0.013 can raise it above 190 only if the survey denominator lay between about 0.013 and 0.015, so the 'slight' imprecision invoked would be most of the estimate. This calculation holds the numerator fixed while changing only the denominator; the report’s shifting by 21/by 22 and prior-use wording mean it is a conditional reconstruction, not recovered raw survey data.

key_findings.finding: Starting marijuana by 15, against later, went with 1.60 times the risk of using a hard drug by 22 in the survey and 3.44 times in the model.
key_findings.locator: Model Results › Gateway effects › Relative risk, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Starting a hard drug at least a year before marijuana (before 22): 0.011 of simulated people against 0.016 in the survey (11 against 16 per 1,000); the authors attribute the order to opportunities for marijuana usually coming before opportunities for hard drugs, often by many years.
key_findings.locator: Model Results › Gateway effects › Ordering (p. 1500); Discussion › Adolescent drug use initiation, 3rd paragraph (p. 1501)

key_findings.finding: Hazard ratios of hard-drug initiation rose with past-year marijuana frequency under every assumed correlation (0, 0.4, 0.8, 1) between marijuana intensity and propensity; even at zero correlation the heaviest group had more than 10 times the hazard of people with no past-year use. The survey estimates lay close to the r=0.4 curve for the two lowest frequencies and between r=0.4 and r=0.8 at the highest.
key_findings.locator: Model Results › Gateway effects › Dose–response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1500); Figure 3 (p. 1501)
key_findings.note: Read from the log-scale Fig. 3 at 300 dpi by the first reader only: survey hazard ratios about 7.5, 12, 23 and 39 for 1–2, 3–11, 12–51 and 52 or more uses; model at zero correlation about 6, 8, 9 and 12. The authors call their survey dose–response estimate inaccurate, because frequency can change after hard-drug initiation in the same year; proportional hazards are a separate modelling assumption that the paper later acknowledges may be wrong (p. 1499).

key_findings.finding: Adjusting a logistic model of hard-drug initiation by 22 for a simulated propensity indicator: the odds ratio for marijuana use was 297 with an indicator of reliability 0, 285 at 0.2, 245 at 0.4, 178 at 0.6, 82 at 0.8, 32 at 0.9, 12 at about 0.95, 2 at 0.99 and 1 at 1.0; the authors conclude that covariates used in earlier studies are very unlikely to be reliable enough to remove the association. The source uses reliability for indicator–propensity correlation, not the usual variance share; correlation 0.8 corresponds to 0.64 (editors’ squared-correlation calculation).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Exhibiting gateway effects by controlling for common factors, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 4 (p. 1502)
key_findings.note: Values printed beside the points in Fig. 4; the abscissa of the 12 is read as about 0.95.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: untested assumptions (normal propensity, frailty model); parameters specific to US youth of the survey period, so results may not generalize to other places or times; response bias could create the phenomena, so propensity is defined as the likelihood of reporting drug use; and the model excludes a gateway effect regardless of parameter values.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Model limitations, 1st–4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the analyses do not disprove a gateway effect, that something like one probably exists because marijuana purchases bring people into contact with a black market that also sells hard drugs, and that a real effect could be too small to matter or offset by effects in the opposite direction in other people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › The status of the marijuana gateway effect, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Policy conclusion: marijuana policies would have little effect on hard drug use except insofar as they changed propensity to use any drug or made hard drugs less available or available later; the validity of the gateway effect is held to be uncertain until it is compared directly with the common-factor model.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › The status of the marijuana gateway effect, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Figures cited from other studies to frame the three phenomena (second-hand, not this paper's data): a relative risk of 85 in one US report; 3 of 1,265 New Zealand youths using hard drugs before marijuana against about 124 expected if the two were independent; hazards more than 140 times greater for 50 or more past-year cannabis uses.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd–4th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Equation 3 sets the survival function for marijuana initiation to 0 when the first opportunity comes after age t, which would mean everyone without an opportunity has already started; it should be 1. The same equation uses F(ψ*−θ) as the yearly probability of not starting, while the text (pp. 1496, 1499) equates its expectation with the yearly probability of starting.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model cannot be rebuilt exactly from the printed equations; whether the code shared these slips cannot be checked, as no code or full parameter list is published.

reporting_issues.issue: The ordering statistic is defined as hard-drug initiation preceding marijuana initiation 'only if' YH < YM, which in the paper's notation are the ages of first opportunity, not of first use (ZH < ZM).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a notation slip, but as printed the ordering result (0.011) would describe opportunities rather than initiation; it cannot be confirmed from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The explanation of the relative-risk gap (157 in the model against 24 in the survey) relies on an imprecision of 0.013 in the survey denominator; the printed numbers imply that denominator was about 0.013 to 0.015 (editors' calculation), and no interval is given for it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overshoot is not shown to be within sampling error; the model's propensity may produce stronger associations than the data, which would also make the adjustment exercise (starting from an odds ratio of 297) more extreme than the observed data.

reporting_issues.issue: Parameter values other than β1 (β2, πM, πH and the yearly ψ* values) are not printed, and the preliminary analyses that justified pooling birth cohorts are not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The calibration cannot be checked or reproduced from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Reliability' of the propensity indicator in Fig. 4 is used for the correlation between indicator and propensity: a reliability of 0.99 is said to leave 2% of the variance uncaptured, whereas reliability usually denotes the share of variance captured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; on the usual definition the threshold described corresponds to a reliability of about 0.98.

design_detail: Prospective birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study): 1265 children born in mid-1977 in the Christchurch urban region, New Zealand, followed to age 25. Frequency of cannabis use and use of other illicit drugs were reported for each year from 14–15 to 24–25 at interviews at ages 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25, so from 16 on each year was recalled over an interval of 2–4 years. The analyses relate cannabis frequency (four levels) to other illicit drug use, DSM abuse/dependence and the number of drug classes used in the same year, with prior other illicit drug use, age and a cannabis × age term in every model: random-effects models adjusted for 23 fixed and 18 time-varying measured covariates (editors' count from the Table 3 footnotes), and fixed-effects (within-person conditional logistic and Poisson) models adjusted for the time-varying covariates and for stable differences between people whose effects are constant over ages 14–25 and do not combine with cannabis use (pp. 558, 567). Yearly analysis samples 953–1025; about 900 in adjusted models.
can_establish: That in this New Zealand birth cohort, years in which a person used cannabis more often were years in which the same person was more likely to use other illicit drugs, to meet DSM criteria for abuse or dependence on them and to use more kinds, after removing stable differences between people whose effects did not change with age or combine with cannabis use, and adjusting for measured time-varying factors, that this association weakened steeply between mid-adolescence and 25, and how often cannabis use came before the first use of other illicit drugs.
cannot_establish: That cannabis use causes later use of other drugs: cannabis and other drug use were measured over the same years, so their order within a year is unknown; influences that change over time and were not measured (such as access to drugs or involvement in drug-using social settings, an explanation the authors themselves raise) are not removed; some adjusted factors may lie on the causal path; and the results describe one city's cohort born in 1977, whose other illicit drugs were mostly hallucinogens.

sample.recruitment: Population birth cohort: 1265 children born in the Christchurch (New Zealand) urban region in mid-1977, studied at birth, 4 months, 1 year, every year to 16, and at 18, 21 and 25, using parent interviews, teacher reports, self-reports, psychometric tests and records (p. 558, Method, 1st paragraph). A general-population sample, not a treatment sample.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Each year's analysis used members with complete data on cannabis and other illicit drug use for that year (953–1025, 75–81% of the cohort); missing covariates reduced the adjusted analyses to about 900, with listwise deletion (p. 561).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated. Covariate descriptions give 24.9% with parental illicit drug use (assessed at 11), 12.4% with parental offending and 11.9% with parental alcohol abuse/dependence (assessed at 15), and 4.6% who left school before the legal leaving age (pp. 559–560). The sex distribution is not reported in this paper. The years of age 14–25 were about 1991–2002 (editors' calculation from the birth year).
sample.attrition: Yearly samples were 75–81% of the cohort. Compared on birth measures with the remaining members, they under-represented people from disadvantaged backgrounds (low parental education, low socio-economic status, single parenthood; P < 0.01). Re-analyses weighted for this (method of Carlin et al.) are said to give essentially the same pattern; the weighted results are not shown (p. 561).
sample.selection_effects: Losses were greater among disadvantaged families, in whom both cannabis and other drug use may differ; the authors' weighted analyses are not shown. One city and one birth year, so era-specific drug availability applies.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at ages 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25 of cannabis use since the previous interview, giving a frequency for each year from 14–15 to 24–25; no biological verification (p. 558, Method › Cannabis use). From 16 on, yearly values were therefore recalled over intervals of 2–4 years (16–18, 18–21, 21–25). Age at first use of other illicit drugs is the first year in which use was reported. No early-onset group is defined: age enters the models as a linear interaction with cannabis frequency.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Yearly frequency classed as no use; less than monthly (1–11 times in the year); at least monthly (12–50 times); at least weekly (more than 50 times), entered in the models as a linear four-level score (pp. 558, 561). Amounts, potency and route were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Other illicit drug use is the outcome. Tobacco and alcohol enter as covariates: smoking and alcohol frequency at 14 (fixed), and previous cigarette smoking, previous alcohol use and alcohol abuse/dependence each year (time-varying) (p. 560; Table 3 footnotes, p. 563).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The reference category is no cannabis use in a year. Random-effects models compare between and within people; fixed-effects models compare each person's years at a given frequency with that same person's years of no use, so the odds ratios in Table 4 are within-person contrasts although the text describes them as comparisons with people who did not use cannabis (p. 563). In conditional (fixed-effects) logistic models only people whose outcome changed across the years contribute; the paper does not report how many did.
comparison.matching: Not applicable; adjustment as under analysis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Fixed-effects models remove stable factors such as genes and family background only to the extent that their effects are constant across ages 14–25, which the authors acknowledge (pp. 558, 567). Childhood sexual abuse and physical punishment were recalled at 18 and 21, after the period of interest had begun (p. 559).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Other illicit drug use in a year: any use of solvents (glue, petrol, paint), stimulants including methamphetamine, barbiturates, illicitly obtained prescription medicines, opiates (heroin, morphine), cocaine, hallucinogens (ecstasy, LSD, PCP) or other substances, mainly plant extracts such as mushrooms and datura. Abuse/dependence: custom items for DSM-III-R criteria at 15 and 16, Composite International Diagnostic Interview items for DSM-IV at 18, 21 and 25. Diversity: number of these classes used in the year (p. 559).
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report throughout; for the abuse/dependence outcome, the diagnostic method changed between 16 and 18 (custom DSM-III-R items, then CIDI DSM-IV items), during the ages over which the association is said to decline; the questions on any use of other illicit drugs are not described as changing (p. 559).
outcomes.operationalization: Use in a year means at least one occasion of any listed class; abuse/dependence means meeting the DSM criteria in that year. The outcome is any use in the year, with prior other illicit drug use as a covariate, not first onset.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every printed main effect is P < 0.0001.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report interviews).

analysis.effect_sizes: Log-odds per step of the four-level cannabis frequency score, with age centred at 19–20: unadjusted random-effects B = 1.45 (SE 0.06), previous other illicit drug use 1.63 (0.11), age 0.50 (0.06), cannabis × age −0.12 (0.01) (Table 2, p. 563); adjusted random-effects B = 1.12 (0.07), fixed-effects B = 0.93 (0.07), both with cannabis × age −0.10 (0.02), all P < 0.0001 (Table 3, p. 563). Fixed-effects odds ratios against years of no use (Table 4, p. 564): at 14–15, 4.1 (95% CI 3.1–5.3) less than monthly, 16.4 (9.5–28.5) at least monthly, 66.7 (29.4–151.4) at least weekly; at 17–18, 3.1 (2.5–3.7), 9.3 (6.4–13.5), 28.5 (16.3–49.4); at 20–21, 2.3 (2.0–2.6), 5.3 (4.0–7.0), 12.2 (8.0–18.4); at 24–25, 1.6 (1.3–1.9), 2.5 (1.7–3.6), 3.9 (2.2–7.0). Abuse/dependence: random 1.57 (0.20), fixed 1.16 (0.17); diversity: random 0.90 (0.04), fixed 0.74 (0.04) (Table 5, p. 564). Editors' calculation: per frequency step at age 19–20, odds ratios of about 4.3 unadjusted, 3.1 random-effects adjusted and 2.5 fixed-effects.
analysis.covariates: Counts are the editors', from the Table 3 footnotes. Random-effects models: 23 fixed covariates, mostly measured before 15 (some up to 16; childhood sexual abuse and physical punishment recalled at 18 and 21): maternal age and education, socio-economic status at birth, living standards 0–10, family changes to 15, parental offending, alcohol problems and illicit drug use, parental attachment at 14, childhood sexual and physical abuse, gender, novelty seeking, neuroticism at 14, self-esteem at 15, conduct problems at 14 and at 7–9, attention problems at 7–9, IQ, grade point average 11–13, smoking and alcohol use at 14, leaving school without qualifications. Both models: 18 time-varying factors: prior other illicit drug use, stressful life events, cohabitation, dependent children, unemployment, paid employment, student status, previous smoking, previous alcohol use, alcohol abuse/dependence, previous cannabis use, conduct problems, peer substance use, peer offending, partner substance use, partner offending, anxiety, depression (Table 3 footnotes, p. 563).
analysis.selective_reporting: The weighted analyses for attrition are described but not shown (p. 561). Odds ratios are given at four ages only. No model is shown without the time-varying covariates that could themselves be consequences of cannabis use (peer and partner substance use, depression, unemployment), so their influence on the estimates cannot be judged.
analysis.power: Not reported; large overall, but at 14–15 only 7 people used cannabis weekly and 12 monthly (Table 1, p. 562), so the youngest odds ratios rest on the linear form of the model.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A strong same-year association between how often a person used cannabis and his or her use of other illicit drugs, which shrank but persisted in within-person models (per frequency step, fixed-effects B 0.93 against 1.45 unadjusted) and fell steeply with age (weekly use: odds ratio 66.7 at 14–15, a model-based figure resting on 7 people using weekly that year, to 3.9 at 24–25). Among those who used other illicit drugs, cannabis had been used at least a year earlier in 86% and by the same year in 98%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the findings may support a general causal model such as the gateway hypothesis while mechanisms remain unclear (p. 556). The discussion goes further: the findings are consistent with a cause-and-effect association (p. 564), the evidence is “relatively compelling” that cannabis plays a causal role (p. 565; a judgment they introduce by noting that causal conclusions from correlational designs are always open to uncertainty and debate), and it clearly favours the view that cannabis encourages other illicit drug use (p. 566). The same discussion offers an explanation without a causal step from cannabis, involvement in youth and drug culture as a time-varying common cause (p. 566), which the models capture only through peer and partner substance use, and the limitations concede that omitted time-varying confounders, or fixed confounders whose effects change with age, could lead to overestimation (p. 567). The abstract's annual assessments were five interviews with year-by-year recall (pp. 556, 558), and the captions of Tables 2 and 3 speak of later risk for same-year associations (pp. 561, 563).

timeline.event: Fergusson & Horwood (Addiction 95: 505–520), same cohort: fewer than 1% of those using both used other illicit drugs before cannabis, and weekly cannabis use went with 59 times the likelihood of other illicit drug use (as cited here, pp. 556–557); not in the library.

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a simulation with one common factor (drug-use propensity) reproduced the sequencing and the associations, provided opportunities to use cannabis were more plentiful than for other drugs (as summarized here, p. 557)

Lynskey et al.: discordant-twin design; cannabis use went with 2.1–5.2 times the risk of other illicit drug use after common genes and environment were taken into account (as cited here, pp. 557, 565)

van Ours (Journal of Health Economics 22: 539–554): bivariate duration models; adjustment for unobserved factors explained much of the cannabis–cocaine association but a significant part remained (as cited here, p. 565); not in the library.

Three published comments with a discussion in the same issue (Addiction 101(4): 470–474, discussion 474–476; PMIDs 16548924, 16548925 and 16548926 per the project's search log); not among the files and not read.
Degenhardt et al., WHO World Mental Health surveys: described in the project's reading list as showing that the order of initiation varies between countries; to be appraised from its own card

replication.where_it_stands: An association that survives adjustment for stable differences between people is reported here and, by this paper's account, in a co-twin study (Lynskey 2003). A common-factor model (Morral 2002) explains the same pattern without a causal step from cannabis. Exposure-opportunity analyses (Wagner & Anthony 2002, on the project's reading list) found that young people who had used marijuana more often had an opportunity to try cocaine and more often used it once they had one; such access is one of this paper's own routes from cannabis use (differential association, p. 566), though it could also reflect the common cause the authors raise, involvement in drug culture (p. 566). This design cannot decide between a causal step, a shared liability and drug-using social settings; the commentaries published with the paper are summarized on their own cards (sc_kandel_2006, sc_hall_2006, sc_maccoun_2006, and the authors' reply sc_fergusson_2006b), read on 12 November 2026.

funding.funder: Grants from the Health Research Council of New Zealand, the National Child Health Research Foundation, the Canterbury Medical Research Foundation and the New Zealand Lottery Grants Board (p. 567, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests printed in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors: Christchurch School of Medicine and Health Sciences, New Zealand (p. 556); the cohort is the authors' own study, and several of the supporting analyses cited are by the same group (for example Fergusson & Horwood, 2000).

what_would_settle_it: A design that separates a causal step from cannabis, a shared liability and drug-using social settings: for example, cohort data with finely dated first use of each drug and measured access to drugs and social networks; natural experiments that change access to cannabis without changing access to other drugs; and genetically informed designs (co-twin, Mendelian randomization) tested against an explicit common-liability model in the same sample.

domains.note: Fixed-effects models remove stable confounders with constant effects and adjust for 18 measured time-varying factors. Not removed: unmeasured time-varying influences (the authors' own alternative, involvement in youth and drug culture, is measured only through peer and partner substance use), fixed factors whose effects change with age (acknowledged, p. 567), and influence of other drug use on cannabis use within the same year. Several adjusted time-varying factors (peer and partner substance use, depression, unemployment) could be consequences of cannabis use, which would bias towards the null; the net direction is uncertain.
Self-reported yearly frequency recalled over 1–4 years, in four broad classes, without verification; errors may be shared with the outcome reported in the same interview.
Population birth cohort; restriction to complete data is assessed under missing data.
No interventions; treatment for drug problems is not considered in the analyses.
19–25% missing each year and about 29% in adjusted models, with listwise deletion; losses greater among disadvantaged families; weighted results said to be similar but not shown.

Self-reported use of a broad class (including solvents and plant extracts) in the same interview as the exposure; for the abuse/dependence outcome only, the diagnostic method changed between 16 and 18 (custom DSM-III-R items, then CIDI DSM-IV items), during the ages over which the association declines; the questions on any use are not described as changing (p. 559).
No protocol; linear coding of frequency and of the age interaction with no alternatives reported; weighted analyses not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large population cohort followed for 25 years, analysed within persons, is a strong design against stable confounding, and the association it reports is large and consistent across three outcomes. As evidence that cannabis use causes other illicit drug use it remains at high risk of bias: cannabis and other drug use are measured over the same years, unmeasured time-varying influences such as drug-using social settings and access are not removed, and adjustment for possible mediators leaves the direction of the net bias uncertain. Citable for: the size and age gradient of the within-person association in this cohort, the temporal order of first use, and the authors' list of explanations. Not citable alone for: a causal gateway effect or its mechanism.

key_findings.finding: By age 25, 42% of the cohort had used illicit drugs other than cannabis. Of these, 82% had used hallucinogens (ecstasy, LSD), 62% stimulants including methamphetamine, barbiturates or illicitly obtained prescription medicines, 39% substances such as mushrooms and datura, 20% cocaine, 11% solvents and 9% opiates including heroin and morphine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Usage of other illicit drugs

key_findings.finding: Among those who used other illicit drugs, cannabis had been used in the same year or earlier in 98% and at least 1 year earlier in 86%; the authors treat these as the upper and lower bounds of the share in which cannabis came first (at most 98%, at least 86%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between frequency of cannabis use and other illicit drug use, 1st paragraph (p. 562); Discussion, list item 1 (pp. 564–565)
key_findings.note: The number of people with other illicit drug use behind these percentages is not given.

key_findings.finding: In every year from 14–15 to 24–25, the share using other illicit drugs rose with cannabis frequency (Mantel–Haenszel test for trend, P < 0.0001 each year): at 14–15, 0.2% of those with no cannabis use (n = 881), 6.2% less than monthly (n = 65), 50.0% at least monthly (n = 12) and 71.4% at least weekly (n = 7); at 24–25, 5.7% (n = 559), 31.5% (n = 232), 53.9% (n = 76) and 61.8% (n = 136).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Associations…, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Use of other illicit drugs among people with no cannabis use in the year rose from 0.0–0.3% at 14–20 to 5.7% at 24–25. Two cells (17–18: 0.1% of 598; 19–20: 0.3% of 506) cannot be produced by a whole number of people; immaterial.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted random-effects model (log-odds of other illicit drug use in a year): cannabis frequency B = 1.45 (SE 0.06), previous other illicit drug use 1.63 (0.11), age 0.50 (0.06), cannabis × age −0.12 (0.01), all P < 0.0001.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 563); Results › Associations…, list items 1–3 (pp. 562–563)
key_findings.note: The text gives SE = 0.05 for the cannabis effect; Table 2 gives 0.06.

key_findings.finding: After adjustment, the cannabis frequency effect was B = 1.12 (SE 0.07) in the random-effects model (fixed and time-varying covariates; editors' count from the Table 3 footnotes: 23 and 18) and B = 0.93 (SE 0.07) in the fixed-effects model (stable differences between people plus the time-varying covariates); cannabis × age was −0.10 (0.02) in both; all P < 0.0001. Editors' calculation: odds ratios per frequency step at age 19–20 of about 4.3 unadjusted, 3.1 and 2.5.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Control for confounding factors, list items 1–2

key_findings.finding: Fixed-effects odds ratios of other illicit drug use, against years of no cannabis use: at 14–15, 4.1 (3.1–5.3) less than monthly, 16.4 (9.5–28.5) at least monthly, 66.7 (29.4–151.4) at least weekly; at 17–18, 3.1, 9.3, 28.5; at 20–21, 2.3, 5.3, 12.2; at 24–25, 1.6 (1.3–1.9), 2.5 (1.7–3.6), 3.9 (2.2–7.0). The authors summarize weekly use as over 60 times the odds at 15, falling to 3.9 by 25.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 564); Results › Effect size, list item 2 (p. 563)
key_findings.note: Editors' check: the log odds ratio per frequency step implied by Table 4 is about 1.40, 1.12, 0.83 and 0.46 at the four ages, which fits B = 0.93 at 19–20 and a decline of about 0.095 a year; the odds ratios are therefore read off the linear model, and the one at 14–15 rests on 7 people using weekly and 12 monthly that year (Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Abuse/dependence on other illicit drugs: cannabis frequency B = 1.57 (SE 0.20) random-effects and 1.16 (0.17) fixed-effects, cannabis × age −0.22 (0.05) and −0.14 (0.04; P < 0.05). Number of drug classes used: B = 0.90 (0.04) and 0.74 (0.04), cannabis × age −0.11 (0.01) in both. Other effects P < 0.0001.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; Results › Cannabis use and other illicit drug abuse/dependence and drug diversity, list items 1–2

key_findings.finding: Yearly analysis samples were 953–1025 (75–81% of 1265) and about 900 in covariate-adjusted analyses (listwise deletion); the samples under-represented socially disadvantaged backgrounds (P < 0.01), and weighted re-analyses are said to give essentially the same pattern.
key_findings.locator: Sample size and sample bias, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cannabis and other illicit drug use were reported at interviews at ages 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25 for each year since the previous interview; cannabis frequency was classed as none, under monthly (1–11 times), at least monthly (12–50) or at least weekly (over 50 times) a year.
key_findings.locator: Method › Cannabis use (p. 558); Outcome measures › Other illicit drug use (p. 559)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the findings are consistent with a cause-and-effect association and, noting that causal conclusions from correlational designs are always open to uncertainty and debate, say they believe the study provides relatively compelling evidence to suggest that cannabis plays a causal role, citing temporal order, dose–response, size of association and resistance to statistical control.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph and list items 1–4 (pp. 564–565); What is responsible for the cannabis gateway effect?, 1st paragraph (p. 565)

key_findings.finding: The authors list possible pathways (changes in brain responsiveness, which they say remain possible but fail to explain some findings in humans; individual learning, for which they say there is little direct evidence; contact with drug markets and drug culture), add that the association may instead reflect involvement in youth and drug culture as a time-varying common cause, or a reciprocal relation, say which (if any) applies is unclear, and note that the explanations point in opposite directions for cannabis law.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › What is responsible for the cannabis gateway effect?, list items 1–3 (pp. 565–566; item 3 ends with two indented paragraphs on p. 566) and the paragraph beginning At the present time (p. 566)

key_findings.finding: For the decline with age the authors offer social maturity, biological maturity, and a recruitment effect (people most susceptible to other illicit drug use tend to take up cannabis early, so later starters would on average be less predisposed), and say which (if any) applies is unclear.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Developmental trends, 1st paragraph (p. 566) and list items 1–3 with the following paragraph (p. 567)

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: the models only approximate a complex process; all variables are self-reported; omitted time-varying confounders could lead to overestimating the causal link; fixed confounders whose effects vary with age are not controlled and could do the same.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st–4th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The standard error of the unadjusted cannabis effect is 0.05 in the text but 0.06 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the estimate (1.45) and its significance are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The Effect size paragraph introduces Table 4 and then says Table 2 shows the results that follow, which are those of Table 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling slip; readers should take the age-specific odds ratios from Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes annual assessments of cannabis use from 14 to 25, but interviews were at 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25, with year-by-year frequencies recalled since the previous interview.
reporting_issues.consequence: For ages 18–25, yearly exposure and outcome were recalled over 3–4 years, adding error that may be shared between them.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2 and 3 describe the association with later risk of other illicit drug use, but the models relate cannabis use in a year to other illicit drug use in the same year (p. 561, Statistical methods, item 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The models do not establish that cannabis use preceded the other drug use within the year; only the separate first-use tabulation (86% and 98%) speaks to order.

reporting_issues.issue: The Method section says the analysis examines the onset of other illicit drug use, but the outcome is any use in a given year, with prior use entered as a covariate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Estimates mix starting and continuing use of other drugs; they are not hazards of first use.

reporting_issues.issue: The first model is called a random-effects generalized estimating equation model, but generalized estimating equations give population-averaged estimates and random-effects models subject-specific ones; which was fitted is not clear.
reporting_issues.consequence: If population-averaged, the drop from the random-effects to the fixed-effects coefficient (1.12 to 0.93) mixes two scales and cannot be read simply as the share explained by unobserved stable confounders.

reporting_issues.issue: The weighted analyses that address under-representation of disadvantaged families are reported only as giving essentially the same pattern.
reporting_issues.consequence: The robustness to attrition cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Two Table 1 percentages cannot be produced by a whole number of people (17–18, no cannabis use: 0.1% of 598; 19–20: 0.3% of 506).
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial rounding or transcription slips in very small cells.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 1 and 4 label the reference column 'Never', but by the Method the category is no cannabis use in that year (p. 558), which can include people who used cannabis in other years.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference group is years without cannabis use, not people who never used it; in Table 4 (fixed effects) these are the same person's years without use.

disagreements.first_pass: can_establish: That in this New Zealand birth cohort, years in which a person used cannabis more often were years in which the same person was more likely to use other illicit drugs, to meet DSM criteria for abuse or dependence on them and to use more kinds, after removing all stable differences between people and adjusting for measured time-varying factors, that this association weakened steeply between mid-adolescence and 25, and how often cannabis use came before the first use of other illicit drugs. | design_detail: Prospective birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study): 1265 children born in mid-1977 in the Christchurch urban region, New Zealand, followed to age 25. Frequency of cannabis use and use of other illicit drugs were reported for each year from 14–15 to 24–25 at interviews at ages 15, 16, 18, 21 and 25, so from 16 on each year was recalled over an interval of 2–4 years. The analyses relate cannabis frequency (four levels) to other illicit drug use, DSM abuse/dependence and the number of drug classes used in the same year, with prior other illicit drug use, age and a cannabis × age term in every model: random-effects models adjusted for 23 fixed and 18 time-varying measured covariates (editors' count from the Table 3 footnotes), and fixed-effects (within-person conditional logistic and Poisson) models adjusted for the time-varying covariates and for all stable differences between people. Yearly analysis samples 953–1025; about 900 in adjusted models.

disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 558, Introduction, paragraph before Method (fixed effects do not control (a) fixed factors whose effects vary with age, (b) fixed factors interacting with cannabis use, (c) time-dynamic factors) and p. 567, Limitations, 4th paragraph.
