disagreements.first_pass: An association that survives adjustment for stable differences between people is reported here and, by this paper's account, in a co-twin study (Lynskey 2003); a common-factor model (Morral 2002) and exposure-opportunity analyses (Wagner & Anthony 2002, on the project's reading list) explain the same pattern without a causal step from cannabis. This design cannot decide between those explanations; the commentaries published with the paper are summarized on their own cards (sc_kandel_2006, sc_hall_2006, sc_maccoun_2006, and the authors' reply sc_fergusson_2006b), read on 12 November 2026.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 448 (round-2 check): missed (outside this PDF, not checked by the reviewer); exposure opportunity (Wagner & Anthony 2002) can itself be a route from cannabis use, as this paper's differential-association pathway says (p. 566); 'without a causal step from cannabis' should be checked against that card.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes after reading this paper, p. 566 (differential association; drug culture as a common cause), and the Wagner & Anthony (2002) PDF, Am J Epidemiol 155, p. 918 (abstract) and p. 923 (Discussion): they describe opportunity as a mechanism linking marijuana to cocaine use. Only Morral (2002) is now described as non-causal; the opportunity finding is stated with both readings.

design_detail: Research letter (2 pages). Policy evaluation using pooled repeated cross-sectional surveys: the national and state Youth Risk Behavior Surveys of US high school students (grades 9–12), 1993–2017, N=1,414,826. Unweighted logistic regressions with state and year indicators (a generalized difference-in-differences design, in the editors' description: the letter names no design, though it invokes the parallel trends assumption), with standard errors clustered by state, estimate the association of state medical marijuana laws (MML) and recreational marijuana laws (RML) with any marijuana use in the past 30 days and frequent use (at least 10 times in the past 30 days), first with state and year indicators only, then adding individual and state covariates; an event study (leads and lags) is shown for medical laws only.
can_establish: Whether, across US states and survey years from 1993 to 2017, the odds of past-month and frequent marijuana use among high school students changed after a state's medical or recreational marijuana law took effect, relative to changes in other states over the same years.
cannot_establish: That the laws caused any change (laws were not assigned at random, pre-law trends were checked only for medical laws, and recreational laws contribute few states and few post-law years); how many fewer teenagers used marijuana (only odds ratios from unweighted models are printed, with no prevalence or absolute change); effects after retail sales had been running for years; or why use changed (the dispensary explanation the authors offer was not measured).

sample.recruitment: Secondary analysis of the national and state Youth Risk Behavior Surveys, given every two years to US high school students (grades 9–12) and used by government agencies to track health behaviours, pooled from 1993 to 2017 following the authors' earlier work (ref. 5); data analysis began in December 2018 (p. E1, Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All respondents in the pooled surveys from 1993 to 2017; exclusions and the handling of missing answers are not described.
sample.demographics: Not reported (age, sex, grade and race or ethnicity were used as covariates but are not described).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (repeated cross-sections). Item non-response and the number of respondents dropped are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: School-based surveys miss young people who are not in school or are absent on the survey day. Which states and years contributed, how the state surveys were combined with the national survey, and response rates are not described in the letter. The estimates are unweighted (Table, footnote a), so they describe the pooled respondents rather than the population of US high school students. The recreational-law estimate rests on 7 states with survey data before and after the law (p. E1).

exposure.measurement: State law indicators for medical and recreational marijuana laws. The source of the law dates is not given, nor whether recreational laws were coded from the date possession became legal or the date retail sales began; the event study counts years since the medical law came into effect (pp. E1–E2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (policy exposure). The outcomes are the survey items on any use in the past 30 days and use at least 10 times in the past 30 days.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. State covariates included decriminalization of marijuana use and possession, a 0.08 blood alcohol concentration law, the state beer tax, income per capita and the unemployment rate (Table, footnote c, p. E1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: State-years without the law (states before adoption and states that never adopted), compared through state and year indicators: the difference-in-differences logic (the editors' description; the letter does not use the term).
comparison.matching: None; state indicators absorb fixed differences between states and year indicators absorb national trends; individual covariates (age, sex, grade, race or ethnicity) and state covariates are added in the fully adjusted models.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time-varying state differences not in the model (attitudes, policing, prevention programmes, other drug, alcohol or tobacco policies) and trends specific to the states that legalized recreational use; the pre-law trend check was done only for medical laws.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported survey items: any marijuana use in the past 30 days; frequent use, defined as at least 10 times in the past 30 days (p. E1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed in the letter. Self-report in school surveys, whose accuracy could change when use becomes legal.
outcomes.operationalization: Binary outcomes; associations reported as odds ratios.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 8 table estimates (2 laws × 2 outcomes × 2 covariate sets) plus 14 event-study coefficients, each judged at P<.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (survey self-report; how the surveys were administered is not described in the letter).

analysis.effect_sizes: Odds ratios (95% CI), state and year indicators only: medical laws, past-30-day use 0.95 (0.90–1.00) and frequent use 0.93 (0.86–1.00), both marked P<.05; recreational laws 0.91 (0.85–0.98) and 0.91 (0.83–0.99). Fully adjusted: medical laws 0.95 (0.89–1.01) and 0.94 (0.87–1.03), not significant; recreational laws 0.92 (0.87–0.96) and 0.91 (0.84–0.98), which the authors describe as decreases of 8% and 9% in the odds (Table and Results, p. E1). Event study for medical laws (Figure, p. E2): no evidence of an association before the law; after it, coefficients not significant with one exception, which the text does not identify; in the Figure it is past-30-day use 3 years after the law, OR about 0.89 (about 0.81 to 0.96) (read from a 300-dpi rendering, approximate). Average marginal effects are said to be qualitatively similar but are not shown; no prevalence or absolute change is given.
analysis.covariates: Fully adjusted models: age, sex, grade, race or ethnicity; decriminalization of marijuana use and possession; a 0.08 blood alcohol concentration law; the state beer tax; state income per capita; state unemployment rate; indicators for 50 states and 12 years (Table, footnote c, p. E1).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the analysis follows the authors' earlier paper on medical laws (ref. 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: Both outcomes and both covariate sets are shown. The event study is shown for medical laws only (recreational laws omitted for lack of post-law data); average marginal effects are mentioned (as qualitatively similar to the odds ratios) but not shown, and no weighted estimates are mentioned (all estimates are unweighted: Table, footnote a; Figure legend); the text reports the fully adjusted null for medical laws but not that the state-and-year models gave significant odds ratios below 1.
analysis.power: Not reported. The sample is very large, but the information on recreational laws comes from 7 states with short post-law periods, and the intervals allow for clustering by state.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among about 1.4 million survey responses, medical marijuana laws were not associated with teen marijuana use in the fully adjusted models (OR 0.95 and 0.94) and were associated with more use in no model. Recreational laws were associated with modestly lower odds of past-month use (OR 0.92, 0.87 to 0.96) and of frequent use (OR 0.91, 0.84 to 0.98), based on 7 states with data before and after the law and without a check of pre-law trends.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion says there was no evidence that medical laws encourage youth use, which matches the data, and that youth use “may actually decline after legalization for recreational purposes” (p. E2). It offers as consistent the argument that licensed dispensaries requiring proof of age make marijuana harder for teenagers to obtain, citing a 2012 Huffington Post article on a legalization campaign's arguments (ref. 6), not data from this study. The text says that the lack of pre-law trends suggests the medical-law lag estimates can be interpreted causally (p. E1); there is no such check for recreational laws. A headline that legalization cut teen use by 8% would overstate: 8% is a relative change in odds, not in the share of teenagers who use, no prevalence or absolute change is reported, the models are unweighted, and the result rests on 7 states in the first years after the law.

timeline.event: Anderson, Hansen and Rees: earlier analysis of medical marijuana laws and teen use with the Youth Risk Behavior Surveys, whose pooling this letter follows (ref. 5); not read.

Cerdá et al. (Monitoring the Future): marijuana use rose among 8th and 10th graders in Washington State after recreational legalization, with no evidence of an association in Colorado (as summarized by this letter); not read.
Sarvet et al. meta-analysis: earlier studies do not support medical laws increasing youth use, while evidence on recreational laws is mixed (as summarized by this letter); not read.
Dilley et al. (Washington Healthy Youth Survey): use among 8th and 10th graders fell after recreational legalization in Washington State (as summarized by this letter); not read.
This letter: recreational laws associated with modestly lower odds of teen use in 7 states; medical laws not associated.

Later analyses on the project's cannabis list, not read for this card: Anderson et al. (2024, recreational laws and teen use, 1993–2021); Coley et al. (2024, legalization, retail sales and adolescent substance use through 2021); O'Grady et al. (rapid systematic review on youth, online 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: When this letter was written, the evidence on recreational laws and teen use was mixed (in one survey, a rise in Washington State and no evidence of an association in Colorado; in another, a fall in Washington State; as the letter summarizes it). The letter adds a multi-state estimate pointing to slightly lower use, from few states and short follow-up. The later analyses on the project's list should be read before any claim is made about the longer-term direction.

funding.funder: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development of the National Institutes of Health (research infrastructure grant R24 HD042828 to the Center for Studies in Demography and Ecology at the University of Washington, where Dr Anderson was a fellow) and the Center for Health Economics & Policy Studies at San Diego State University, including grant funding from the Charles Koch Foundation to Dr Sabia; the funders had no role in the design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or decision to submit (p. E2).
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported (p. E2).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from departments of economics at Montana State University, the University of Oregon, the University of Colorado Denver and San Diego State University. The private foundation grant to one author is recorded exactly as printed, as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-state analysis with many years after recreational legalization and after retail sales began, using estimators suited to laws adopted in different years, survey weights and pre-law trend checks for recreational laws, reporting prevalence and absolute changes, and measuring where young people obtain cannabis to test the dispensary explanation.

domains.note: State and year indicators plus time-varying state covariates. Pre-law trends were flat for medical laws (event study) but were not checked for recreational laws, whose estimate rests on 7 states with short post-law periods; other changes in the same states and years are not modelled. With laws adopted in different years, two-way fixed-effects estimates can be biased when effects change over time (editors' methodological note).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: School-based surveys; contributing states, years and response rates are not reported; national and state surveys pooled without weights.
Law dates and their source are not given; recreational laws are one indicator that does not separate legal possession from the start of retail sales; medical laws of differing scope are combined.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: How the laws were implemented (dispensary and shop openings, enforcement) varies between states and over time and is not measured.
Missing answers and exclusions are not reported.
Self-reported use; willingness to report use may change when it becomes legal, in a direction that is unknown.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; both outcomes and both covariate sets are reported, but there is no event study for recreational laws, and average marginal effects are described (as qualitatively similar to the odds ratios) without being shown; no weighted estimates are mentioned (all estimates are unweighted).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the letter estimates the effect of state laws (interventions) from non-randomized variation between states and years. The recreational-law estimate is at serious risk of bias from confounding (no pre-trend check, 7 states, short follow-up); the other domains add moderate concerns, and missing data cannot be judged. Cite it for: in pooled US high school surveys from 1993 to 2017, medical marijuana laws were not followed by more teen use, and recreational laws were followed by modestly lower odds of past-month and frequent use (OR 0.92 and 0.91) in the 7 states with data. Do not cite it for: legalization reducing teen use as a causal effect, the size of any change in the share of teenagers who use, or the dispensary explanation.

key_findings.finding: The letter pooled the national and state Youth Risk Behavior Surveys of US high school students from 1993 to 2017 (final sample 1,414,826); 27 states and Washington, DC contributed survey data before and after adopting a medical marijuana law, and 7 states before and after adopting a recreational law.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports that medical laws were not associated with use in the fully adjusted models but does not mention that the state-and-year models gave statistically significant odds ratios below 1 (0.95, 0.90–1.00; 0.93, 0.86–1.00), whose printed upper limits of 1.00 sit at the edge of significance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The medical-law result depends on the covariate set; neither model suggests more use after medical laws.

reporting_issues.issue: The one significant event-study coefficient is not identified in the text; in the Figure it is lower odds of past-30-day use 3 years after a medical law took effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only post-law signal for medical laws points to less use, not more; it is one of eight post-law coefficients across the two outcomes and may be chance.

reporting_issues.issue: No prevalence, absolute change or weighted estimate is reported; the associations are given only as odds ratios from unweighted models (Table, footnote a).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 8% and 9% figures are relative changes in odds among pooled respondents; they cannot be turned into a number or share of teenagers without the baseline prevalence, which the letter does not give.

reporting_issues.issue: How the national and state surveys were combined (overlapping respondents, state identification of national respondents) and which states and years contributed are not described; the letter refers to the authors' earlier paper (ref. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample cannot be reconstructed from the letter.

reporting_issues.issue: The law dates and their coding are not given; for recreational laws it is not stated whether the indicator starts when possession became legal or when retail sales began.
reporting_issues.consequence: The short post-law period for recreational laws may include little retail availability; what the estimate measures depends on this coding.

design_detail: Multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02091375), funded and designed by GW Pharmaceuticals, at 23 centres in the United States and Europe. 120 children and young people aged 2 to 18 with Dravet syndrome whose convulsive seizures were not controlled by their antiepileptic drugs were randomized 1:1 to add-on cannabidiol oral solution or matching placebo: 4-week baseline, 14-week treatment period (2 weeks of dose escalation, 12 of maintenance), 10-day taper and 4-week safety follow-up. Primary end point: percentage change per 28 days in convulsive-seizure frequency, recorded daily by patients or caregivers, over the treatment period compared with baseline.
can_establish: That, in children and young people with Dravet syndrome whose convulsive seizures were not controlled by their antiepileptic drugs, adding this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution at the trial's dose to their usual antiepileptic drugs reduced convulsive seizures, recorded daily by patients or their caregivers, over 14 weeks more than placebo, and how often adverse events occurred in each arm.
cannot_establish: Effects beyond 14 weeks; effects of other cannabidiol products (such as unregulated products of unknown content), of lower doses, in adults or in other epilepsies; how far the effect depends on interactions with clobazam or valproate (efficacy by co-medication was a prespecified subgroup analysis but is reported in neither the article nor its appendix); or effects on seizure freedom, quality of life, behaviour or sleep, which did not differ significantly and for which the trial was not powered.

sample.recruitment: Patients at 23 centres in the United States and Europe: 177 screened, 57 did not meet the inclusion criteria or met exclusion criteria, 120 randomized (p. 2014, Results › Trial Population; Figure 1, p. 2015). The appendix's study-group list names investigators at three French, two Polish, four British and ten US institutions, members of the Epilepsy Study Consortium and five GW Pharmaceuticals staff, besides the authors; it gives no count of patients by centre (Supplementary Appendix p. 2, Supplementary Material S1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Established diagnosis of Dravet syndrome (diagnosis and seizure classification re-checked for each patient by an independent panel appointed by the Epilepsy Study Consortium), age 2 to 18, taking one or more antiepileptic drugs, and four or more convulsive seizures during the 28-day baseline; all epilepsy treatments, including ketogenic diet and vagus-nerve stimulation, stable for 4 weeks before screening and to remain unchanged during the trial (p. 2012). The final protocol (version 8, 29 May 2015) adds that the four or more convulsive seizures had to occur in the first 28 days of the baseline period, that the telephone diary had to be completed on at least 25 baseline days, and that antiepileptic doses had to be stable for at least 4 weeks, the ketogenic diet and vagus-nerve stimulation not counting as antiepileptic drugs. Exclusions included clinically significant unstable illness other than epilepsy, clinically significant laboratory or ECG abnormalities, alcohol or other substance-use problems in the past two years, recreational or medicinal cannabis or cannabinoid medicines in the 3 months before entry or unwillingness to abstain during the trial, symptoms of postural hypotension, felbamate taken for less than a year, another investigational product in the previous 6 months, markedly impaired liver function, suicidal behaviour or serious suicidal ideation on the C-SSRS at screening, planned travel abroad and earlier randomization in the dose-ranging part (Protocol PDF pp. 148–151, final protocol §6.2–6.3, pp. 49–52 of 128).
sample.demographics: Mean age 9.8 years (range 2.3–18.4); 62 male (52%) and 58 female: 35 of 61 (57%) male with cannabidiol vs 27 of 59 (46%) with placebo; 72 (60%) from the United States. Previously tried a median of 4.0 antiepileptic drugs (range 0–26) and taking a median of 3.0 (range 1–5): clobazam 65%, valproate 59%, stiripentol 42%, levetiracetam 28%, topiramate 26%; ketogenic diet 8%, vagus-nerve stimulation 12%. Baseline convulsive seizures median 13.0 a month (range 3.7–1717); developmental delay in 114 of 118 children with data, severe or profound in 56 (pp. 2014, 2016; Table 1).
sample.attrition: 108 of 120 (90%) completed the treatment period: 52 of 61 (85%) with cannabidiol and 56 of 59 (95%) with placebo. Withdrawals with cannabidiol: 8 for adverse events and 1 by an investigator on day 43 for non-adherence, a patient who had had seven serious adverse events by day 32 that led to stopping the trial agent; with placebo: 1 for an adverse event, 1 by a parent or guardian, 1 lost to follow-up. All 120 were in the intention-to-treat and safety analysis sets; 105 of the 108 completers entered an open-label extension (p. 2014; Figure 1 and legend, p. 2015). The appendix adds that at the end of double-blind treatment 26 patients given cannabidiol and 30 given placebo went straight into the extension and 29 and 26 began the 10-day taper; 5 and 4 left the taper early to join the extension, 1 patient given cannabidiol withdrew from the taper because of an adverse event, and 18 and 22 joined at the end of the taper, so that by the editors' addition 49 of the 52 cannabidiol completers and all 56 placebo completers entered the extension (Supplementary Appendix p. 3, Supplementary Material S2).
sample.selection_effects: Specialist-centre patients with severe Dravet syndrome whose seizures were not controlled by their current antiepileptic drugs and whose families accepted a placebo-controlled trial; the authors note that interest in cannabidiol for epilepsy was generated by media reports (p. 2012). Chance baseline differences: more males (57% vs 46%) and more stiripentol use (49% vs 36%) in the cannabidiol arm, and a lower median baseline frequency (12.4 vs 14.9 convulsive seizures a month) (Tables 1 and 2, p. 2016). The protocol also required the telephone diary to be completed on at least 25 baseline days, which selects families able to keep daily records (Protocol PDF p. 149, final protocol §6.2.9).

exposure.measurement: Randomized assignment. Adherence to the daily voice-response seizure diary was 97% (cannabidiol) and 96% (placebo) during treatment; the mean number of days with a missed dose was 0.6 in both arms (SD 2.1 and 2.9) (p. 2014). Blood levels of cannabidiol or of the other antiepileptic drugs are not reported in the article. Blood levels of the other antiepileptic drugs were added to the protocol by amendment 7 (29 May 2015), but by the time the new assessments were in place most patients had completed the trial, so the levels were to be listed only (Protocol PDF pp. 394, 396, statistical analysis plan §5.7.2 and §5.8). Urine THC screens at screening, randomization and the end of treatment, the last to confirm that no cannabis was taken during the trial, were planned (Protocol PDF p. 161, final protocol §9.1.8); their results are not reported in the article or the appendix.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: cannabidiol oral solution (100 mg per mL) or matching placebo, escalated over 14 days to 20 mg per kg of body weight per day (or the same volume of placebo), given in two daily doses for 14 weeks, then tapered by 10% a day over 10 days. This target was the highest dose that an independent data and safety monitoring committee judged safe after a dose-ranging pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation of 5, 10 and 20 mg per kg per day (pp. 2012–2013). Adverse events led to dose reductions in 10 patients given cannabidiol (p. 2018). In the protocol, the cannabidiol was extracted from Cannabis sativa plants and purified to more than 95% cannabidiol, typically with less than 0.5% (w/w) THC, and the solution (25 or 100 mg/mL) also contained sesame oil, anhydrous ethanol (79 mg/mL), sucralose (0.5 mg/mL) and strawberry flavouring (0.2 mg/mL) (Protocol PDF p. 138, final protocol §3.2; PDF p. 145, §5.1, Table 5.1-1).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients continued their antiepileptic drugs (median 3); there were few dose adjustments of these during the trial (p. 2018). Efficacy by co-medication (for example with or without clobazam or valproate) is reported in neither the article nor its appendix, although subgroup analyses by clobazam, valproate and stiripentol use were prespecified (Protocol PDF pp. 387–388, statistical analysis plan §5.5.5); adverse events are linked to co-medication only for somnolence (clobazam) and raised liver enzymes (valproate) (p. 2018). Recreational or medicinal cannabis and cannabinoid medicines were excluded for 3 months before entry and prohibited during the trial (Protocol PDF pp. 150, 155, final protocol §6.3.7–6.3.8 and §8.3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Matching placebo solution, identical except for the absence of cannabidiol, added to the same stable antiepileptic regimens (p. 2012). In the protocol both solutions contain the same excipients (sesame oil, anhydrous ethanol, sucralose and strawberry flavouring) and come in the same 100-mL amber glass bottles with child-resistant caps, as pre-packed numbered packs (Protocol PDF p. 145, final protocol §5.1–5.3.1; PDF p. 152, §7.1); the protocol says nothing about matching colour, smell or taste, and caregivers more often rated the cannabidiol solution as not liked at all (9 of 56 vs 1 of 57; Supplementary Appendix p. 6, Table S1).
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1, performed and assigned independently and held centrally; the trial groups are described as similar (p. 2014; Table 1). The protocol specifies a schedule produced by an independent statistician, stratified by age group (2–5, 6–12 and 13–18 years) and not divulged until database lock and authorized unblinding (Protocol PDF p. 152, final protocol §7.2); the stratification is absent from the original protocol and was added by amendment 5 (30 March 2015), carried into version 8 (Protocol PDF p. 359).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; the chance imbalances are listed under selection effects.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same background antiepileptic drugs by design: clobazam 64% and valproate 58% in the placebo arm vs 66% and 61% with cannabidiol (Table 1, p. 2016).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: percentage change per 28 days in convulsive seizures (tonic, clonic, tonic–clonic or atonic), counted daily by patients or caregivers through an interactive voice-response system, over the 14-week treatment period compared with the 4-week baseline. Secondary: Caregiver Global Impression of Change (7 points); reductions of at least 25%, 50% (the key secondary end point), 75% and 100%; total and nonconvulsive seizures; caregiver-rated change in seizure duration; sleep disruption (0–10); Epworth Sleepiness Scale; Quality of Life in Childhood Epilepsy; Vineland-II; hospitalizations for epilepsy; new seizure types; rescue medication. Safety: adverse events (MedDRA 17.0), Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (age 6 and over), vital signs, ECG, physical examination and laboratory tests at baseline and weeks 2, 4, 8 and 14 (p. 2013).
outcomes.validity_norms: Caregiver-counted seizure frequency is the usual primary end point in such trials, but the authors call it partially subjective and note that side effects could unblind caregivers (p. 2019); they also note that parents may not reliably count nonconvulsive seizures in developmentally delayed children and that the suicidality scale's applicability in this population is unclear (p. 2019).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy = percentage change from baseline in seizure frequency per 28 days; response = at least a 25, 50, 75 or 100% reduction; global impression = the caregiver's rating of the child's overall change.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for secondary end points (p. 2014; Table 3, footnote). The count of 21 is the primary end point plus the 20 secondary end points in Table 3; rescue medication and new seizure types were also secondary end points. The protocol states that with a single primary end point no adjustment is required (Protocol PDF p. 195, final protocol §13.6). The statistical analysis plan names the at-least-50% responder rate as the key secondary end point, following advice from the European Medicines Agency and without a protocol change, and provides hierarchical testing of the secondary end points for European regulatory submissions only (Protocol PDF p. 368, statistical analysis plan §3.3.2; PDF p. 396, §5.8).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind: the allocation was held centrally and not divulged to anyone involved until database lock, and the placebo was identical except for cannabidiol (pp. 2012–2013). Neither the original protocol, the final protocol nor the statistical analysis plan provides for any assessment of blinding (such as asking caregivers or investigators to guess the assignment), and none is reported; emergency unblinding by code-break envelope or voice-response system was allowed when needed for medical management, and the number of unblindings is not reported (Protocol PDF pp. 156–157, final protocol §8.5; PDF pp. 401–410, statistical analysis plan list of outputs). Caregivers' end-of-treatment palatability ratings differed mainly in the extreme category: not liked at all 9 of 56 with cannabidiol vs 1 of 57 with placebo; by the editors' addition, not liked or not liked at all 17 of 56 (30.4%) vs 9 of 57 (15.8%) (Supplementary Appendix p. 6, Table S1); the authors say this could have affected blinding in a small number of patients (p. 2019). In a post hoc analysis, the median reduction in convulsive seizures with cannabidiol was 38.41% in the 22 children with somnolence and 38.94% in those without (estimated difference 3.63%, 95% CI −28.9 to 22.25; P=0.74) (Supplementary Appendix p. 3, Supplementary Material S3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: median monthly convulsive seizures 12.4 (range 3.9–1717) at baseline to 5.9 (0.0–2159) with cannabidiol, median change −38.9% (interquartile range −69.5 to −4.8), vs 14.9 (3.7–718) to 14.1 (0.9–709) with placebo, −13.3% (−52.5 to 20.2); Hodges–Lehmann median difference −22.8 percentage points (95% CI −41.1 to −5.4), P=0.01 (Wilcoxon rank-sum). First month of maintenance: 12.4 to 5.0 vs 14.9 to 13.0 (P=0.002). Responders: at least 25% reduction 38/61 vs 26/59, OR 2.10 (1.01 to 4.35), P=0.05; at least 50% (key secondary) 26/61 (43%) vs 16/59 (27%), OR 2.00 (0.93 to 4.30), P=0.08; at least 75% 14/61 vs 7/59, OR 2.21 (0.82 to 5.95), P=0.11; free of convulsive seizures (Table 3: a 100% reduction; the text says free of seizures) 3/61 vs 0/59, difference 4.9 percentage points (−0.5 to 10.3), P=0.08. Total seizures: median 24.0 to 13.7 vs 41.5 to 31.1, median difference −19.20 points (−39.25 to −1.17), P=0.03; nonconvulsive seizures 0.00 (−21.36 to 31.59), P=0.88. Caregiver global impression improved in 37/60 (62%) vs 20/58 (34%), P=0.02. No significant difference in seizure duration, sleep disruption (−0.4, −1.5 to 0.7), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (1.5, −0.2 to 3.2, P=0.08), Quality of Life in Childhood Epilepsy (1.5, −3.8 to 6.8), Vineland-II (−2.6, −6.8 to 1.6) or hospitalizations. Editors' calculation of absolute differences: at least 50% response 15.5 percentage points (26/61 vs 16/59; Wald 95% CI about −1.3 to 32.3), about 6.5 patients treated for each extra responder; because that interval includes no difference, the interval for this number runs from about 3.1 treated per extra responder, through no difference, to about 76 treated per responder fewer; somnolence 25.9 points; serious adverse events 11.3 points. Sensitivity analyses of the primary end point (Supplementary Appendix p. 4, Figure S1; Hodges–Lehmann differences for Wilcoxon analyses, least-squares mean differences for ANCOVAs): per protocol −25.99 (−44.79 to −8.94; P=0.0037); rank ANCOVA −15.6 (−27.7 to −3.5; P=0.0117); ANCOVA on percentage change −21.99 (−45.20 to 1.22; P=0.0631); unreported diary days imputed −22.98 (−42.20 to −4.87; P=0.0134); maintenance period −26.06 (−45.07 to −8.24; P=0.0052), with weeks 1–4 −29.69 (−48.75 to −11.23; P=0.0020), weeks 5–8 −25.21 (−44.76 to −8.33; P=0.0055) and weeks 9–12 −19.96 (−40.74 to 1.25; P=0.0756). By seizure type, only tonic–clonic seizures differed significantly: −22.01 (−42.52 to −2.11; P=0.0254) (Supplementary Appendix p. 7, Table S2).
analysis.covariates: None for the primary analysis: the statistical analysis plan specifies an unadjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a Hodges–Lehmann estimate (Protocol PDF p. 377, statistical analysis plan §5.5.2), so the article's label adjusted (p. 2014) is not explained by the plan. Responder rates by Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group (Protocol PDF p. 380, §5.5.3.1.1); continuous secondary outcomes by ANCOVA with baseline and age group as covariates (Protocol PDF p. 382, §5.5.3.2.6); the global impression by ANCOVA with age group (Protocol PDF p. 387, §5.5.3.2.11). The protocol's ANCOVA alternative for the primary end point (baseline and age group as covariates) is reported only as a sensitivity analysis (Protocol PDF p. 196, final protocol §13.6.2; Supplementary Appendix p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02091375; EudraCT 2014-000995-24; protocol GWEP1332, of which this trial is Part B, after a dose-ranging Part A (Protocol PDF pp. 3, 141). The protocol supplement (original protocol of 24 March 2014, final protocol version 8 of 29 May 2015, table of amendments, final statistical analysis plan of 22 February 2016) was read; the registry record was not. The primary end point kept its measure (percentage change from baseline in convulsive-seizure frequency, worded as a mean percentage change in the protocol) but changed its window and analysis: the original protocol planned the last 28 days of a 12-week treatment period, analysed by a mixed model for repeated measures, with 60 patients (Protocol PDF pp. 74, 77); amendment 1 (20 June 2014) lengthened treatment to 14 weeks, moved the window to the maintenance period, added non-parametric testing and raised the size to 80; amendment 5 (30 March 2015, not implemented itself but carried into version 8) made an ANCOVA primary, with a Wilcoxon test if the data were not normally distributed, added age-stratified randomization and raised the size to 100; amendment 7 (29 May 2015) moved the window to the whole 14-week treatment period, defined baseline and added the 25-day diary criterion (Protocol PDF pp. 356–360). On blinded review the data were judged not normally distributed, and the statistical analysis plan, approved after a blinded data review meeting on 12 February 2016 and before unblinding, made the Wilcoxon test primary and, on advice from the European Medicines Agency, the at-least-50% responder rate the key secondary end point (Protocol PDF pp. 369, 396). The reported primary analysis follows this plan; the deviations are in secondary and sensitivity analyses (see selective reporting). The plan states that most patients had already completed the trial by the time the assessments added by amendment 7 were in place (Protocol PDF p. 396); the dates of first and last enrolment are given in none of the documents read, so how far enrolment had progressed when the window was changed cannot be determined, but every change preceded unblinding.
analysis.selective_reporting: The primary and key secondary end points are reported as designated in the statistical analysis plan, with the other secondary end points in Table 3 and individual and new seizure types in Table S2 (Supplementary Appendix p. 7). Prespecified in the plan but reported in neither the article nor the appendix: subgroup analyses of the primary end point and of responders by age group, sex, region, clobazam, valproate and stiripentol use, baseline frequency, numbers of current and previous antiepileptic drugs and SCN1A status (§5.5.5); time to reach the baseline seizure count (§5.5.4.1); the log-transformed ANCOVA and the multiple-imputation (missing not at random, tipping-point) sensitivity analyses, which Figure S1 says are not included; and adverse events of special interest for abuse liability (plan Appendix 1) (Protocol PDF pp. 377–379, 387–388, 397; Supplementary Appendix p. 4). For the global impression, the original protocol planned ordinal logistic regression (Protocol PDF p. 78), the final protocol and the plan an ANCOVA, with ordinal logistic regression at each visit as a further analysis (Protocol PDF pp. 199, 387), the article's Methods name ordinal logistic regression (p. 2013), and Table 3 reports a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a Hodges–Lehmann difference (p. 2017), which none of the plans names. The rescue-medication counts in the Results (p. 2014) come from data the plan describes as inconsistently collected and not to be analysed (Protocol PDF p. 396, §5.8).
analysis.power: 100 patients were planned for 80% power to detect an absolute difference of 32 percentage points (SD 56%, two-sided 5%); 120 were randomized, with no reason given for exceeding the plan (pp. 2013–2014). The observed difference (−22.8 points) was smaller than the planning difference, and the trial was not powered for responder or seizure-freedom outcomes. The protocol shows the planned size rising from 60 (original protocol: assumed placebo reduction 10%, difference 50 points, SD 68%) to 80 (amendment 1) and to 100 (amendment 5, carried into version 8: assumed placebo reduction 18%, difference 32 points, SD 56%) (Protocol PDF pp. 74, 193, 356, 359); screening failures were to be replaced until the target was reached (Protocol PDF p. 143), and none of the documents read explains the 20 patients beyond the target.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 14 weeks, convulsive seizures fell more with cannabidiol than with placebo (median −38.9% vs −13.3%; difference −22.8 percentage points, 95% CI −41.1 to −5.4), and 62% vs 34% of caregivers rated their child's overall condition improved. The key secondary outcome, at least halving seizures, was not significantly more frequent (43% vs 27%; OR 2.00, 0.93 to 4.30), and freedom from convulsive seizures (a 100% reduction) was rare (3 of 61 vs 0 of 59). Adverse events were more common with cannabidiol (93% vs 75%), including serious events (16% vs 5%), withdrawals for adverse events (8 vs 1), somnolence (36% vs 10%; 18 of the 22 were also taking clobazam), decreased appetite (28% vs 5%), diarrhea (31% vs 10%) and raised liver enzymes (12 vs 1, all taking valproate).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion matches the data: a greater reduction in convulsive seizures and more adverse events. The discussion goes further in places: (1) the authors write that the caregiver global impression suggests the reduction was meaningful as caregivers assessed it (p. 2019), but caregivers made the rating, could have been partly unblinded by side effects and palatability, no assessment of blinding was planned or reported, and the test reported for the global impression (Wilcoxon) is not the analysis the statistical analysis plan prespecified (ANCOVA); (2) non-significant sleep scores are read as “suggesting that there was no negative effect of cannabidiol on sleep” (p. 2015), although somnolence was the most common adverse event (36% vs 10%) and the Epworth difference leaned towards more sleepiness with cannabidiol (1.5, −0.2 to 3.2); (3) the statement that cannabidiol lacks the psychoactivity of THC (p. 2019) was not tested in this trial; (4) the sponsor designed the trial and ran the data and statistical analyses (p. 2012). (5) The article says the prespecified sensitivity analyses supported the primary analysis (p. 2014); in Figure S1 all nine shown favour cannabidiol, but the ANCOVA on percentage change, the analysis the protocol would have used for normally distributed data (−21.99, −45.20 to 1.22; P=0.063), and the last 4 weeks of maintenance (−19.96, −40.74 to 1.25; P=0.076) do not exclude no difference, and two prespecified analyses, including the one for data missing because of withdrawal, are not shown (Supplementary Appendix p. 4). (6) The post hoc analysis is said to show no relationship between somnolence and the treatment effect (p. 2019); the appendix gives similar medians (38.41% vs 38.94%) but an interval for the difference from −28.9 to 22.25 points, within the cannabidiol arm only, which cannot exclude a sizeable relationship (Supplementary Appendix p. 3). (7) The statement that the screening criteria ensured drug-resistant epilepsy as the International League against Epilepsy defines it (p. 2018) is not borne out by the protocol, whose criteria require only seizures not completely controlled by current antiepileptic drugs and at least one such drug (Protocol PDF p. 149). A headline that CBD halves or stops seizures would overstate: the median fall was 38.9% against 13.3% with placebo, halving was not significantly more common, freedom from convulsive seizures was 3 of 61, and the product was a pharmaceutical solution at a weight-based dose added to other medicines in a rare, severe childhood epilepsy, not an over-the-counter CBD product.

timeline.event: The earliest of four small trials of cannabidiol in epilepsy (refs 2–5, 1978–1990), which the authors describe as giving mixed results; not read.

Devinsky et al. open-label trial of a standardized cannabidiol oral solution in 214 children and young adults with treatment-resistant epilepsy (Lancet Neurology; ref. 7), whose adverse-event profile the authors call similar; not read.
This trial; 105 of the 108 completers entered an uncontrolled long-term open-label extension.

Miller et al. (JAMA Neurology; PMID 32119035, as identified by AI reader 534, round-2 check): a later randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial of add-on cannabidiol in Dravet syndrome; not on the project's lists and not read, so its results are not recorded here.

replication.where_it_stands: Replication status is not judged on this card. A later randomized, placebo-controlled trial of add-on cannabidiol in Dravet syndrome exists (Miller et al., 2020), but it is not on the project's lists and has not been read here, so whether this trial's result held is not judged; the open-label extension cannot replicate a placebo-controlled result. Set the status when that trial has been read. Update, 13 November 2026: the second placebo-controlled trial (Miller et al., 2020; card sc_miller_2020) is now read: both of its dose levels reduced convulsive seizures more than placebo, and at least halving was significant there, unlike here; the two trials share a sponsor and some authors.

funding.affiliations_note: An employee of the sponsor is an author and the sponsor ran the analyses; the authors state that they vouch for the accuracy and completeness of the data and analyses (p. 2012). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Independent, longer placebo-controlled trials in Dravet syndrome that ask caregivers to guess the arm, report results by clobazam and valproate use with drug levels, compare several doses, and are powered for seizure freedom, quality of life and development.

domains.note: 1:1 randomization performed and assigned independently, held centrally and not divulged until database lock (p. 2013). Baseline differences in sex (57% vs 46% male), stiripentol use (49% vs 36%) and median baseline frequency (12.4 vs 14.9 a month) are compatible with chance in a trial of 120. The protocol adds that an independent statistician produced the schedule, stratified by age group (Protocol PDF p. 152).

Double-blind with an identical placebo; background treatments held stable, with few dose adjustments; everyone randomized was analysed (intention to treat). Possible unblinding through side effects bears mainly on the caregiver-reported outcomes (fourth domain). Emergency unblinding was allowed for medical management; the number of unblindings is not reported (Protocol PDF pp. 156–157).

Primary-outcome data for all 120: each patient's seizure rate over the days reported in the voice-response diary, up to withdrawal for the 12 who withdrew (9 with cannabidiol, 3 with placebo), as the statistical analysis plan specifies (Protocol PDF pp. 370, 376); diary completion on at least 25 baseline days was an entry criterion. Imputing unreported diary days by the worst of three rules gave −22.98 (−42.20 to −4.87), and the per-protocol analysis −25.99 (−44.79 to −8.94) (Supplementary Appendix p. 4); the prespecified multiple-imputation analysis for data missing not at random, the one addressing the withdrawals, is not shown. Global impression missing for 1 patient per arm.

Seizures were counted daily by caregivers (partially subjective, as the authors say) and the global impression was rated by caregivers. Side effects (somnolence 36% vs 10%, decreased appetite, diarrhea) and palatability (not liked at all 9 of 56 vs 1 of 57; Table S1) could have revealed the assignment, and no assessment of blinding was planned in the protocol or statistical analysis plan or reported. The post hoc analysis found similar seizure reductions with and without somnolence (38.41% vs 38.94%), but its interval is wide (−28.9 to 22.25) and it covers the cannabidiol arm only (Supplementary Appendix pp. 3, 6; Protocol PDF pp. 156–157, 401–410).

For the primary result: the statistical analysis plan was approved after a blinded data review meeting (12 February 2016) and before unblinding, and the reported analysis (Wilcoxon rank-sum test over the whole treatment period) follows it; the choice of the Wilcoxon test over the ANCOVA was made on blinded data under a rule in the final protocol, and the ANCOVA result is reported (P=0.063). The window of the primary end point changed by amendment (last 28 days, then the maintenance period, then the whole treatment period), all before unblinding, and the maintenance-period result is reported too (Protocol PDF pp. 196, 356–360, 369, 396; Supplementary Appendix p. 4). Secondary results carry more risk: the test reported for the global impression is not the prespecified one, and prespecified subgroup and two sensitivity analyses are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A centrally randomized, placebo-controlled trial that analysed everyone randomized. The primary analysis follows a statistical analysis plan approved before unblinding, though the end point's window and analysis were changed by protocol amendments in 2014 and 2015, all before unblinding. The concerns are caregiver-reported outcomes with possible functional unblinding (no assessment of blinding was planned or reported), a sponsor that designed the trial and ran the analyses, a registry record not checked here, and secondary results (the global impression, co-medication subgroups) whose reported or missing analyses depart from the plan. Cite it for: in 120 children and young people with Dravet syndrome whose convulsive seizures were not controlled by their antiepileptic drugs, adding the trial's pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution to existing antiepileptic drugs reduced convulsive seizures, recorded daily by patients or caregivers, more than placebo over 14 weeks (median −38.9% vs −13.3%; difference −22.8 points, −41.1 to −5.4), with more somnolence, appetite loss, diarrhea and raised liver enzymes (all 12 cases in patients taking valproate). Do not cite it for: seizure freedom, halving of seizures, long-term benefit, over-the-counter CBD products, other doses, adults or other epilepsies.

key_findings.finding: 120 of 177 screened patients were randomized at 23 centres (61 cannabidiol, 59 placebo); mean age 9.8 years (2.3–18.4); a median of 4.0 antiepileptic drugs tried before and 3.0 being taken (clobazam 65%, valproate 59%); baseline median 13.0 convulsive seizures a month (3.7–1717).
key_findings.locator: Results › Trial Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1 (p. 2015); Table 1 (p. 2016)

key_findings.finding: Primary end point: median monthly convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with cannabidiol (median change −38.9%, interquartile range −69.5 to −4.8) and from 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo (−13.3%, −52.5 to 20.2); Hodges–Lehmann median difference −22.8 percentage points (95% CI −41.1 to −5.4), P=0.01.
key_findings.locator: Results › Seizure Frequency (p. 2014); Table 2 (p. 2016)
key_findings.note: Figure S1 gives the same estimate to two decimals, −22.79 (−41.06 to −5.43), P=0.0123, as the intention-to-treat Wilcoxon rank-sum analysis; the statistical analysis plan specifies no covariate adjustment for it (Supplementary Appendix p. 4; Protocol PDF p. 377, statistical analysis plan §5.5.2).

key_findings.finding: The difference was already present in the first month of maintenance: median monthly convulsive seizures 12.4 to 5.0 with cannabidiol vs 14.9 to 13.0 with placebo (P=0.002).
key_findings.locator: Results › Seizure Frequency

key_findings.finding: At least a 50% reduction (key secondary end point): 26 of 61 (43%) vs 16 of 59 (27%), OR 2.00 (0.93 to 4.30), P=0.08; at least 25%: 38 vs 26 patients, OR 2.10 (1.01 to 4.35), P=0.05; at least 75%: 14 vs 7, OR 2.21 (0.82 to 5.95), P=0.11.
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 2014); Table 3 and its footnotes (p. 2017)

key_findings.finding: Free of seizures over the whole treatment period (in Table 3, a 100% reduction in convulsive seizures): 3 of 61 with cannabidiol vs 0 of 59 with placebo (difference 4.9 percentage points, −0.5 to 10.3; P=0.08). Four more patients were seizure-free during the maintenance period, but three of them withdrew early.
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 2014); Table 3, 100% reduction row and footnote ¶ (p. 2017); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 2018, continuing on p. 2019)

key_findings.finding: Total seizures (all types): median 24.0 to 13.7 a month with cannabidiol vs 41.5 to 31.1 with placebo; median difference −19.20 percentage points (−39.25 to −1.17), P=0.03. Nonconvulsive seizures: no significant difference (0.00, −21.36 to 31.59; P=0.88; 37 and 41 patients).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary End Points, 1st paragraph (p. 2014); Table 3 (p. 2017)

key_findings.finding: Caregivers judged their child's overall condition improved in 37 of 60 (62%) with cannabidiol vs 20 of 58 (34%) with placebo (P=0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary End Points, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The P value comes from a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Table 3, p. 2017). No plan names that test for this end point: the final protocol specifies an ANCOVA of the final rating (Protocol PDF p. 199) and the statistical analysis plan an ANCOVA with age group, plus ordinal logistic regression at each visit (PDF p. 387). The plan's general rule is to use non-parametric techniques when parametric assumptions fail and then to present the parametric test as a sensitivity analysis (PDF p. 376, §5.5.1); no ANCOVA result is reported.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences in sleep disruption (−0.4, −1.5 to 0.7), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (1.5, −0.2 to 3.2; P=0.08; positive values numerically favour placebo), Quality of Life in Childhood Epilepsy (1.5, −3.8 to 6.8), Vineland-II (−2.6, −6.8 to 1.6) or hospitalizations for epilepsy; rescue medication was used by 36 (59%) vs 41 (69%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Secondary End Points (pp. 2014–2015); Table 3 and footnotes (p. 2017)
key_findings.note: The statistical analysis plan dropped the planned efficacy analysis of change in rescue-medication usage because of inconsistencies in collecting these data (Protocol PDF p. 396, §5.8), but kept count summaries of concomitant rescue medications (PDF p. 394, §5.7.1); the article does not say which data its counts come from.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events in 93% with cannabidiol vs 75% with placebo (mild or moderate in 84% and 95% of those with events; judged related to the trial agent in 75% and 36% of those with events); serious adverse events in 10 vs 3 patients (16% vs 5%); withdrawals for adverse events 8 vs 1; status epilepticus 3 vs 3, none judged related; no deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph (p. 2016, continuing on p. 2018) and 2nd paragraph (p. 2018); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 2019)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events with cannabidiol vs placebo (Table 4): somnolence 22 (36%) vs 6 (10%), with 18 of the 22 also taking clobazam (5 of 6 with placebo); diarrhea 19 (31%) vs 6 (10%); decreased appetite 17 (28%) vs 3 (5%); fatigue 12 (20%) vs 2 (3%); vomiting 9 (15%) vs 3 (5%); pyrexia 9 (15%) vs 5 (8%); lethargy 8 (13%) vs 3 (5%); convulsion 7 (11%) vs 3 (5%); upper respiratory tract infection 7 (11%) vs 5 (8%). Adverse events led to dose reduction in 10 patients given cannabidiol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph (continued from p. 2016); Table 4

key_findings.finding: Raised liver aminotransferase levels occurred in 12 patients with cannabidiol vs 1 with placebo, all of them taking valproate; levels above 3 times the upper limit of normal led to withdrawal of 3 vs 1; in the 9 who continued, levels returned to normal while still receiving cannabidiol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No suicidal ideation was recorded on the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale in the 77 patients who completed it; the authors note that the scale's applicability is unclear because most patients have cognitive impairment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph (p. 2018); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 2019)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses of the primary end point (differences, cannabidiol minus placebo, with 95% CI; in percentage points except for the rank ANCOVA, which analysed ranks of the percentage change, so its difference is on the rank scale): intention-to-treat Wilcoxon (the primary analysis) −22.79 (−41.06 to −5.43; P=0.0123); per protocol −25.99 (−44.79 to −8.94; P=0.0037); rank ANCOVA −15.6 (−27.7 to −3.5; P=0.0117); ANCOVA on percentage change −21.99 (−45.20 to 1.22; P=0.0631); unreported diary days imputed by the worst of three rules −22.98 (−42.20 to −4.87; P=0.0134); maintenance period −26.06 (−45.07 to −8.24; P=0.0052), its weeks 1–4 −29.69 (−48.75 to −11.23; P=0.0020), weeks 5–8 −25.21 (−44.76 to −8.33; P=0.0055) and weeks 9–12 −19.96 (−40.74 to 1.25; P=0.0756). The log-transformed ANCOVA and the multiple-imputation analysis for data missing not at random were prespecified but are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Figure S1, its footnotes and the list of prespecified sensitivity analyses below it (file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF pp. 5–7)
key_findings.note: Wilcoxon rows give Hodges–Lehmann median differences and ANCOVA rows least-squares mean differences (Figure S1 footnote). The weekly-block analyses include only patients with at least 7 diary days in the block (Protocol PDF p. 377, statistical analysis plan §5.5.2.1).

key_findings.finding: Post hoc analysis within the cannabidiol group: median reduction in convulsive seizures 38.41% in the 22 patients who reported somnolence and 38.94% in those who did not (39 by the editors' subtraction); estimated difference 3.63% (95% CI −28.9 to 22.25; P=0.74).
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Material S3 (file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: The direction of the estimated difference is not defined, and it differs from the difference between the two medians (0.53 points, editors' arithmetic), as a Hodges–Lehmann estimate can; the interval is wide.

key_findings.finding: Caregivers' end-of-treatment rating of how acceptable the child found the trial medication, cannabidiol vs placebo: liked it a lot 6 (10.7%) vs 6 (10.5%); liked it 13 (23.2%) vs 16 (28.1%); neither liked nor disliked 20 (35.7%) vs 26 (45.6%); did not like it 8 (14.3%) vs 8 (14.0%); did not like it at all 9 (16.1%) vs 1 (1.8%). By the editors' addition, 17 of 56 (30.4%) vs 9 of 57 (15.8%) did not like it or did not like it at all.
key_findings.locator: Table S1 and the paragraph below it (file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Percentages are of 56 and 57 respondents, not the 61 and 59 in the table heading; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Percentage change by seizure type, cannabidiol vs placebo (Hodges–Lehmann median differences, 95% CI): tonic–clonic −22.01 (−42.52 to −2.11; P=0.0254; 55 vs 52 patients); tonic −13.19 (−52.63 to 48.47; P=0.6719); clonic 2.38 (−29.48 to 40.63; P=0.6199); atonic −1.04 (−124.95 to 96.42; P=1.0000); myoclonic 3.48 (−34.18 to 53.46; P=0.7572); countable partial −40.68 (−101.50 to 5.36; P=0.0964); other partial −63.64 (−543.53 to 47.55; P=0.2118); absence 2.74 (−19.98 to 29.67; P=0.7137). Seizure types not seen at baseline emerged in 0 to 3 patients per type with cannabidiol and 0 to 4 with placebo, for example tonic seizures in 1 (1.6%) vs 4 (6.8%) and myoclonic seizures in 3 (4.9%) vs 1 (1.7%).
key_findings.locator: Table S2 (file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The primary end point kept its measure but changed its window and analysis by protocol amendment before unblinding: the original protocol (24 March 2014) planned the mean percentage change in the last 28 days of a 12-week treatment period, analysed by a mixed model for repeated measures, in 60 patients; amendment 1 (20 June 2014) lengthened treatment to 14 weeks, moved the window to the maintenance period, added non-parametric testing and raised the size to 80; amendment 5 (30 March 2015) made an ANCOVA primary with a Wilcoxon test if the data were not normal, stratified randomization by age and raised the size to 100; amendment 7 (29 May 2015; final protocol version 8) moved the window to the whole treatment period, titration included, and added a diary-completion criterion of at least 25 baseline days.
key_findings.locator: Original protocol §13.6.2 (p. 75 of 97); table of protocol amendments, amendments 1, 5 and 7 (file Devinsky_2017_Protocol.pdf)

key_findings.finding: The statistical analysis plan (version 2, 22 February 2016), approved after a blinded data review meeting on 12 February 2016 and before unblinding, records that on blinded review the seizure data were judged not normally distributed, so the Wilcoxon analysis became primary as the protocol allowed; that the at-least-50% responder rate became the key secondary end point on advice from the European Medicines Agency, without a protocol change; and that planned analyses of long seizures (status epilepticus) and of rescue medication were dropped, for too few events and inconsistently collected data.
key_findings.locator: Statistical analysis plan, title page; §4, Blinded Data Review Meeting (p. 9 of 50); §5.8, Changes in the Conduct of the Study or Planned Analysis (p. 36 of 50) (file Devinsky_2017_Protocol.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Neither the original protocol, the final protocol nor the statistical analysis plan provides for an assessment of blinding; the protocol allows emergency unblinding by code-break envelope or voice-response system when needed for medical management, and the number of unblindings is not reported. Both solutions contain the same excipients and come in the same 100-mL amber glass bottles; nothing is said about matching appearance, smell or taste.
key_findings.locator: Final protocol §5.1–5.3.1 (p. 46 of 128) and §8.5 (pp. 57–58 of 128); statistical analysis plan list of tables, listings and figures (pp. 41–50 of 50), which contains no blinding assessment (file Devinsky_2017_Protocol.pdf)
key_findings.note: A finding of absence, from searching the whole protocol supplement for blinding, guessing, appearance and taste terms; the only acceptability measure is the palatability question (Supplementary Appendix p. 6).

key_findings.finding: At the end of double-blind treatment, 26 patients given cannabidiol and 30 given placebo went straight into the open-label extension and 29 and 26 began the taper; 5 and 4 ended the taper early to join the extension, 1 patient given cannabidiol withdrew from the taper because of an adverse event, and 18 and 22 joined at the end of the taper: by the editors' addition 49 and 56 patients, 105 in all.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Material S2 (file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The investigational product was cannabidiol extracted from Cannabis sativa plants and purified to more than 95% cannabidiol, typically with less than 0.5% (w/w) THC, dissolved at 25 or 100 mg/mL in sesame oil with anhydrous ethanol (79 mg/mL), sucralose (0.5 mg/mL) and strawberry flavouring (0.2 mg/mL). The appendix's support statement says the findings are specific to this formulation and cannot be extrapolated to other cannabidiol products.
key_findings.page: Protocol PDF pp. 138, 145; Supplementary Appendix p. 7
key_findings.locator: Final protocol §3.2 (p. 39 of 128) and §5.1, Table 5.1-1 (p. 46 of 128) (file Devinsky_2017_Protocol.pdf); Support Statement (Supplementary Appendix p. 7, file Devinsky_2017_Appendix.pdf, PDF p. 8)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's footnotes contradict each other on Vineland-II: higher scores mean better adaptive behaviour (first footnote), yet the last footnote says negative differences favour cannabidiol for Vineland-II, as for the sleep scores.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the non-significant Vineland-II difference (−2.6) cannot be read with certainty; do not cite it as favouring either arm.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the global impression was analysed with ordinal logistic regression (p. 2013), but Table 3 gives a Hodges–Lehmann median difference of −1.0 (−1.0 to 0.0) with a Wilcoxon rank-sum P of 0.02; the interval reaches 0 although P is 0.02, and 60 and 58 caregivers are counted rather than the 61 and 59 of the intention-to-treat set. The protocol supplement names others: the original protocol planned ordinal logistic regression of the final rating (Protocol PDF p. 78), the final protocol an ANCOVA of the final rating (PDF p. 199), and the statistical analysis plan an ANCOVA of the end-of-treatment score with age group as covariate, with ordinal logistic regression at each visit as a further analysis (PDF p. 387). None names the Wilcoxon test for this end point, though the plan's general approach is to switch to non-parametric techniques if parametric assumptions are violated and then to present the parametric test as a sensitivity analysis (PDF p. 376, §5.5.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Wilcoxon test may fall under the plan's general rule, but no check of assumptions is reported and the prespecified ANCOVA, which that rule would keep as a sensitivity analysis, is not reported; the proportions improved (62% vs 34%) remain the clearest summary. Reason: the first-pass text gave the age-group covariate and visit-wise ordinal regression to the final protocol, which names only an ANCOVA of the final rating (PDF p. 199); and it omitted the plan's general rule (§5.5.1).

reporting_issues.issue: The primary median difference (−22.8, Hodges–Lehmann) is called adjusted without saying for what, and for total seizures the adjusted reductions of 28.6% and 9.0% (medians 24.0 to 13.7 and 41.5 to 31.1) are not defined. By the editors' arithmetic, the simple difference between the two median changes is −25.6 points, and the printed medians for total seizures fall by about 43% and 25%. The statistical analysis plan specifies an unadjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a Hodges–Lehmann estimate for the primary end point and analyses total seizures in the same way (Protocol PDF pp. 377, 381), and Figure S1 labels the same estimate (−22.79) as the Wilcoxon analysis (Supplementary Appendix p. 4), so no adjustment was planned for either.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 2013–2014, 2016; Protocol PDF pp. 377, 381; Supplementary Appendix p. 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Hodges–Lehmann differences with their intervals; the word adjusted is not explained by the plan, and the adjusted reduction percentages for total seizures still cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion required four or more convulsive seizures in the 28-day baseline (p. 2012), but baseline frequencies go down to 3.7 (placebo) and 3.9 (cannabidiol) seizures a month (Table 2; p. 2014). The protocol explains it: only convulsive seizures in the first 28 days of the baseline period counted towards eligibility, the baseline period lasted at least 28 days, and the reported baseline frequency used all diary days before the first dose, averaged per 28 days (Protocol PDF pp. 149, 357, 360, 371; final protocol §6.2.5, amendments 3 and 7, statistical analysis plan §5.1.3.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Resolved by the protocol: a baseline longer than 28 days, averaged per 28 days, can fall below 4 in a patient who had 4 or more seizures in the first 28 days; the article's description of a 28-day baseline simplifies this.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that all patients met the International League against Epilepsy definition of drug-resistant epilepsy (p. 2018), but the printed criteria require only one or more current antiepileptic drugs, and the number of drugs previously tried ranges from 0 (p. 2014). The protocol's criteria do not require it either: a documented history of Dravet syndrome not completely controlled by current antiepileptic drugs and one or more antiepileptic drugs at a stable dose (Protocol PDF p. 149, final protocol §6.2.4–6.2.6); the independent diagnostic review checked the diagnosis and that seizures were not adequately controlled (Protocol PDF p. 414).
reporting_issues.consequence: The eligibility criteria did not ensure drug resistance as the ILAE defines it; the discussion's statement rests on something other than the criteria and cannot be checked; describe the population as having seizures not controlled by their current antiepileptic drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: One withdrawal with cannabidiol is counted as an investigator withdrawal for non-adherence, although the Figure 1 legend says this patient had seven serious adverse events by day 32 that led to stopping the trial agent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Withdrawals related to adverse events with cannabidiol can be read as 8 (as in the text) or 9.

reporting_issues.issue: Developmental delay: 56 (48%) severe or profound and 58 (50%) mild or moderate, of 118 with data. By the editors' arithmetic, 56 of 118 is 47% and 58 of 118 is 49%, and the two printed percentages sum to 98% while 114 of 118 is 97%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding slip; trivial.

reporting_issues.issue: Table S1 is headed n=61 (cannabidiol) and n=59 (placebo), but by the editors' addition its counts sum to 56 and 57, the denominators of its percentages; the 5 and 2 caregivers without a rating are not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; palatability ratings are missing for 8% of the cannabidiol group and 3% of the placebo group (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Supplementary Material S2 counts 55 cannabidiol patients at the end of double-blind treatment (26 straight into the extension, 29 into the taper) against 52 cannabidiol completers, and 111 in all against 108; the article's Figure 1 legend accounts for the 3: the 29 who tapered included 3 patients withdrawn during the treatment period, and 2 of the 5 who completed the taper but did not enter the extension were ineligible because they had been withdrawn.
reporting_issues.consequence: Resolved by the article; the extension totals (49 and 56, 105 in all) agree. Reason: the first-pass text says the extra 3 are not explained, but the Figure 1 legend (p. 2015, checked on the rendered page) explains them.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results report rescue medication used by 36 (59%) vs 41 (69%) patients among the secondary end points, although the statistical analysis plan dropped the planned efficacy analysis of change in rescue-medication usage because of inconsistencies in collecting these data (§5.8); the plan kept count summaries of concomitant rescue medications (§5.7.1), and the article does not say which data its counts come from.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read the counts as descriptive; do not cite them as an efficacy outcome. Reason: statistical analysis plan §5.7.1 (Protocol PDF p. 394) plans counts and percentages of concomitant rescue medications, so the first-pass claim that the counts rest on the dropped data is not established.

disagreements.first_pass: 1:1 randomization performed and assigned independently, held centrally and not divulged until database lock, with an interactive voice-response system. Baseline differences in sex (57% vs 46% male), stiripentol use (49% vs 36%) and median baseline frequency (12.4 vs 14.9 a month) are compatible with chance in a trial of 120.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 534 (round-2 check): agree with RCT, RoB 2 and some concerns overall; fix the note: the article does not say randomization used the voice-response system, which served the seizure diary.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 2013, Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (randomization performed and assigned independently, held centrally, not divulged until database lock), p. 2012, Trial Design and Oversight, 2nd paragraph (the voice-response system listed among services) and p. 2013, Procedures, 2nd paragraph (used for the daily seizure records): nothing links it to randomization. disagreements.first_pass: Seizures were counted daily by caregivers (partially subjective, as the authors say) and the global impression was rated by caregivers. Side effects (somnolence 36% vs 10%, decreased appetite, diarrhea) and different palatability ratings could have revealed the assignment, and blinding was not measured; the post hoc somnolence analysis is only in the supplement (not read).

disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 2019, Discussion, 5th paragraph: the authors discuss possible unblinding through side effects and palatability and a post hoc somnolence analysis, but report no assessment of blinding; the supplement was not read, so not measured cannot be asserted. Reworded; judgment (some concerns) unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: (1) the caregiver global impression is taken to show that the reduction was meaningful (p. 2019),
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 534 (round-2 check): agree minor; in item (1) the authors say the findings suggest the reduction was meaningful as caregivers assessed it; the card's wording drops that hedge.

Item (1) reworded to keep the hedge; the caveats (caregiver rating, possible unblinding) still apply, so the gap assessment (minor) is unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 534 (round-2 check): not-attempted is not established: a later placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial of adjunctive cannabidiol in Dravet syndrome exists (Miller et al., 2020, JAMA Neurology, PMID 32119035; not read here). Set the status after it is read.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes (not settled from this PDF: the later trial is not on file and was not read, and its PubMed record could not be fetched here): not-attempted is dropped. The schema has no value for a trial that exists but is unread, so the status is n/a and where_it_stands says replication is not judged on this card (as on sc_daly_2018); a 2020 timeline entry names the trial without its results.
