design_detail: Systematic review with a two-stage random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019130055) of observational studies reporting mean THC and/or CBD concentration (% by weight) in cannabis samples at three or more annual time points. Stage 1: within each study, the inverse-variance weighted mean difference of each year from the study's first year was regressed on calendar year (random-effects meta-regression, linear trend), giving an annual change in percentage points of THC or CBD by weight (the paper writes, for example, 0.29% each year). Stage 2: these study-level annual changes were pooled across studies (random effects, inverse variance), separately for all herbal cannabis, sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and resin (THC) and for herbal cannabis and resin (CBD). 12 studies: USA 5, Netherlands 2, UK, France, Denmark, Italy and New Zealand 1 each; samples from 1970 to 2017. Two Dutch studies bought samples at random from retail outlets; the other 10 used non-random samples, mostly seizures of illicit material.
can_establish: The average linear annual change in mean THC and CBD concentration of seized or purchased cannabis samples within studies from seven countries between 1970 and 2017, and how much these trends differ between studies, countries, periods and product types.
cannot_establish: How much THC people actually took in (concentration is not intake; the authors cite evidence that people only partly adjust their use to potency), trends in whole markets or worldwide (10 of 12 studies used non-random, mostly seized samples, and the herbal pool is weighted to the USA), whether the herbal rise came from a shift in market share toward sinsemilla (market share was not measured), trends in legal markets or in concentrates (not analysed), or any health consequence (no health outcome was analysed).

sample.recruitment: Database search from inception to 27 March 2019 (Embase; MEDLINE with Epub Ahead of Print, In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations and Daily; Global Health; PsycINFO; Scopus), limited to peer-reviewed papers, with no language or date limits. 5,131 records from databases and 1 from another source; 3,893 after removal of duplicates; 122 full texts assessed; 12 studies included (PDF p. 3, Information sources and search; Figure 1). Corresponding authors were asked for missing data, and seven people are thanked for supplying additional data (PDF p. 4; p. 8, Acknowledgements).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies giving mean THC and/or CBD concentration in cannabis at three or more annual time points within the same study (two time points were planned at first and raised to three to allow within-study meta-regression). Excluded: studies without original data, and studies for which the mean, SD and sample size per year and product could not be obtained. The 110 full-text exclusions (Figure 1): fewer than three time points 32; non-observational or cultivation studies 21; methods of cannabinoid detection or quantification 16; full text not accessible 15; insufficient data 11; no original data 8; botanical studies 2; human specimens 2; same data in a later article 3 (PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (samples of cannabis, not people). Study periods (Figures 3 and 5, PDF pp. 6–7): UK 1975–1989; New Zealand 1979–1996; USA 1970–1994, 1993–2007, 1995–2007, 1996–2008 and 2008–2017; Netherlands 2000–2004 and 2005–2015; France 1992–2016; Denmark 2000–2017; Italy 2010–2013. Four US studies drew on the same federal (Drug Enforcement Agency) seizure source; for overlapping years only the most recently published study's data were used (PDF p. 4, Study characteristics).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Data for overlapping years from US studies using the same seizure source were omitted from all but the most recent study (PDF p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Ten of 12 studies used non-random samples, mostly seizures, whose make-up depends on what enforcement agencies seized; only the two Dutch studies bought samples at random from retail outlets (PDF p. 4; p. 7, Risk of bias). The search excluded reports that were not peer-reviewed, such as agency monitoring reports, and 15 full texts could not be obtained, including early abstracts published before 1980 (PDF p. 3; Figure 1), so the early decades are thin: in Figure 2 the years 1970–1974 rest on one US series, joined by the UK series from 1975 and New Zealand from 1979. Four of the seven herbal studies are from the USA and carry about 62% of the random-effects weight (editors' sum of the Figure 3 weights). Legal markets were not included because their data series were too short (PDF p. 8).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The time variable is calendar year; the measured quantity is each primary study's mean THC or CBD concentration (% by weight) per year and product, from that study's own laboratory analyses, which the review's main text does not describe (study characteristics are in Supplementary Tables S2–S3, not read). Consistency of the analytical protocol over time within each study was rated: consistent in all, except one study rated unclear (PDF p. 7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. The authors convert the pooled annual changes into about 2.9 mg more THC per gram of herbal cannabis and 5.7 mg more per gram of resin each year, and compare these with a proposed standard THC unit of 5 mg, a proposal by the first author and a colleague (ref. 54) (PDF p. 7, Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (product samples). Only herbal cannabis (unspecified herbal cannabis, sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and products such as ditchweed) and resin or hashish were analysed; concentrates and edibles were not (PDF p. 4, Data analysis).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Within each study, every later year is compared with that study's first year; the fitted slope over years is the study's annual change. There is no external comparison.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to product samples. The analogous unmeasured factors are changes over time in what was seized (enforcement priorities), the age and storage of samples before analysis (the title of one included study, Sevigny, ref. 43, asks whether today's cannabis is more potent simply because it is fresher), and differences in what each laboratory measured. The review's risk-of-bias tool assessed none of these except consistency of method within a study.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Mean THC and CBD concentration (% by weight) per year and product, as reported by each primary study. Per-study means with standard errors are plotted for all herbal cannabis (Figure 2) and resin (Figure 4); the other strata are in supplementary figures (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: A review-specific risk-of-bias tool, designed because no existing tool suited observational studies of non-human samples, with four criteria rated for each cannabinoid and product: sampling method (random low risk, non-random high risk); at least 19 samples per measurement (based on a power calculation in one included study, ref. 40); consistent sampling location; consistent analytical protocol. It was applied by a single researcher; item-level ratings are in Supplementary Figure S9 (not read) (PDF p. 4, Risk of bias).
outcomes.operationalization: Annual change = slope in percentage points of THC or CBD by weight per year from a within-study linear meta-regression; non-linear trends were not estimated; for CBD, means and standard errors were used although the two Dutch studies reported medians (PDF pp. 4, 8).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (six pooled estimates).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening (titles first, then titles and abstracts, then full texts) and data extraction were done by two independent reviewers; risk of bias by one researcher (PDF pp. 3–4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled annual change in percentage points of THC or CBD by weight (95% CI): THC, all herbal cannabis 0.29 (0.11 to 0.47), P<0.001 as printed, 7 studies, 66,747 samples, 1970–2017, I2 94.2%; THC, sinsemilla 0.26 (−0.09 to 0.61), P=0.141, 5 studies, 15,882 samples, 1986–2017, I2 89.4%; THC, traditional herbal cannabis 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.36), P=0.079, 5 studies, 28,418 samples, 1986–2017, I2 48.1%; THC, resin 0.57 (0.10 to 1.03), P=0.017, 8 studies entered as 10 series, 17,371 samples, 1975–2017, I2 79.1%; CBD, herbal cannabis −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), P=0.280, 5 studies, 49,434 samples, 1995–2017, I2 66.0%; CBD, resin 0.03 (−0.11 to 0.18), P=0.651, 6 studies, 11,382 samples, 1992–2017, I2 82.6%. Study-level slopes, all herbal cannabis (Figure 3): UK 1975–1989 0.04 (−0.09 to 0.17); New Zealand 1979–1996 0.01 (−0.06 to 0.08); USA 1970–1994 0.17 (0.13 to 0.22); USA 1995–2007 0.47 (0.39 to 0.56); USA 1996–2008 0.66 (0.49 to 0.84); USA 2008–2017 0.59 (0.02 to 1.16); Italy 2010–2013 1.66 (−0.59 to 3.91). Resin (Figure 5): UK 1975–1989 −0.03 (−0.35 to 0.28); Netherlands 2000–2004, imported 1.77 (−1.97 to 5.51) and Dutch-produced 8.15 (−0.25 to 16.56); USA 1993–2007 1.58 (0.87 to 2.30); Italy 2010–2013 1.41 (−5.92 to 8.74); Netherlands 2005–2015, imported −0.01 (−0.50 to 0.49) and Dutch-produced −0.69 (−2.08 to 0.69); France 1992–2016 0.62 (0.45 to 0.79); USA 2008–2017 0.03 (−2.58 to 2.64); Denmark 2000–2017 1.27 (0.81 to 1.72). No tau-squared or prediction intervals are reported.
analysis.covariates: None; no moderator analysis beyond stratification by product type.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019130055, reported to PRISMA (checklist in Supplementary Table S1, not read). One deviation is stated with its reason: the minimum number of annual time points was raised from two to three to allow within-study meta-regression (PDF p. 2, Eligibility criteria). The PROSPERO record was not read, so whether the review-specific risk-of-bias tool and the two-stage model were planned in advance could not be checked.
analysis.selective_reporting: All six pooled estimates are reported, but the forest plots for sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and both CBD analyses are only in supplementary figures (not read). No sensitivity analysis (for example, restricted to the two randomly sampled studies), no assessment of publication bias and no prediction intervals.
analysis.power: Not addressed for the pooled analyses: five to eight studies per stratum with I2 from 48% to 94%; the authors note that with few studies and unbalanced sample sizes the heterogeneity statistics may be biased (PDF p. 8). Within studies, adequacy was defined as at least 19 samples per year; four studies fell short for at least one product, and one more for CBD (PDF p. 7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across seven studies of herbal cannabis (mostly seizures; four of them from the USA), mean THC rose on average by 0.29 percentage points a year (0.11 to 0.47), with very high heterogeneity (I2 94.2%): only the four US series rose clearly (0.17 to 0.66 points a year), while the two older non-US series (UK 1975–1989, New Zealand 1979–1996) were flat and the four-year Italian series was too imprecise to tell (1.66, −0.59 to 3.91). Resin THC rose on average by 0.57 points a year (0.10 to 1.03), driven by the US 1993–2007, French and Danish series, while the UK series and the Dutch 2005–2015 imported-resin series were flat and the other five series were imprecise. No test compared the resin and herbal averages, and the resin interval contains the herbal estimate. CBD showed no detectable trend in herbal cannabis (−0.01, −0.02 to 0.01) or resin (0.03, −0.11 to 0.18). Within sinsemilla (0.26, −0.09 to 0.61) and traditional herbal cannabis (0.17, −0.02 to 0.36) the pooled trends were not statistically significant, but their point estimates are close to the all-herbal estimate.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that THC rose in international cannabis markets while CBD stayed stable, that the increases were greater in resin than in herbal cannabis, and, as a finding, that the herbal rise was “attributable to an increased market share of high-THC sinsemilla” (PDF p. 1); the Discussion's closing paragraph repeats both of the last two as findings (PDF p. 8). Gaps: (1) market share was not measured; the attribution rests on non-significant within-type trends whose point estimates (0.26 and 0.17) are similar to the all-herbal 0.29 and come from a partly different set of studies (only three studies, refs 35, 37 and 42 by the pools' citations, are in both the all-herbal and the within-type pools), so absence of significance is read as absence of a within-type rise; the Discussion's 3rd paragraph words this as a suggestion (PDF pp. 7–8), but its closing paragraph calls the herbal rise primarily attributable to market share (PDF p. 8). (2) Greater in resin: no test compared the two pooled slopes; the resin interval (0.10 to 1.03) contains the herbal 0.29, and by the editors' approximate calculation from the two printed intervals, treating them as independent, the difference of 0.28 points a year has z of about 1.1 and P of about 0.27. (3) International markets: 10 of 12 studies used non-random, mostly seized samples; in herbal cannabis only the four US series rose clearly (the UK, New Zealand and Italian intervals include zero; Figure 3, PDF p. 6), and the Discussion itself says the estimates should not be read as globally representative (PDF p. 8). (4) The abstract calls risk of bias low apart from non-random sampling, but non-random sampling is the main threat to any statement about markets, and the review's tool did not assess sample age or storage. (5) Stable CBD is precise for herbal cannabis, but the resin interval (−0.11 to 0.18 points a year) is compatible with meaningful change. (6) The closing statement on health implications and the conversion to 2.9 and 5.7 mg of THC per gram per year are not tested here: no intake or health outcome was analysed. A headline that today's cannabis is many times stronger than in the 1970s would go beyond this paper: it reports average annual changes, not fold-changes, and the lowest early values come from a single US series of seized samples.

timeline.event: Cascini, Aiello and Di Tanna meta-analysis of herbal cannabis, data 1970–2009 (as summarized in this review's introduction): THC rose by 0.21% a year (95% CI 0.16 to 0.27); herbal cannabis only, no resin or CBD estimates; not read.
Di Forti et al. south London case-control study of high-potency cannabis and first-episode psychosis, cited by this review as background for why potency matters (ref. 14)

Smart et al. (2017) and Caulkins et al. (2018): Washington State legal-market data, cited by this review as documenting substantial THC rises in legal markets (refs 58–59); not part of the meta-analysis; not read.
This review published online (journal issue 2021); the authors describe it as the second meta-analysis of THC trends, the first of CBD trends and the first stratified by product type.
Petrilli et al. systematic review of the association of cannabis potency with mental ill health and addiction (on the project's list; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: With the earlier herbal-only meta-analysis (Cascini et al., 2012, as summarized here), this is the main pooled estimate of THC trends in seized and sampled cannabis up to 2017. Its numbers describe products, not what people take in or any harm. Primary series inside it (for example ElSohly et al., 2016; Chandra et al., 2019; the Dutch monitoring studies) must not be cited beside it as independent support. Legal markets and years after 2017 are outside it.

funding.funder: Senior Academic Fellowship from the Society for the Study of Addiction awarded to T. P. Freeman; the funder had no role in study design, data analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (PDF p. 8, Acknowledgements; p. 9, Declaration of interests).
funding.declared_conflicts: No authors report any declarations of interest (PDF pp. 8–9).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Bath, King's College London, the University of Sydney and the University of Mississippi. Two review authors are authors of included primary studies: M. ElSohly of refs 35 and 37, and T. P. Freeman of ref. 35 (reference list, PDF p. 10); the author lists of refs 38 and 45 end in et al., so further overlap cannot be checked from the article; the article describes no procedure for review authors appraising their own studies. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated, randomly sampled test purchases across outlets and regions (including legal markets and concentrates), analysed with one protocol that reports THC and CBD and records sample age and storage, together with sales-weighted market shares by product type; and studies that measure how much THC people actually take in as product potency changes.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adapted to product samples: cannabis samples by product type, calendar time as the comparison, mean THC and CBD as outcomes, observational designs with three or more annual time points.

PROSPERO CRD42019130055 with PRISMA reporting; one deviation (two to three time points) is stated with its reason. The record was not read, so whether the review-specific risk-of-bias tool, designed after no suitable tool was found, and the two-stage model were planned in advance cannot be checked.
Observational studies with at least three time points from the same study, justified as giving more reliable within-study estimates (same region, sampling method and analytical protocol).

Five databases, key words given and no language limit, but the search was limited to peer-reviewed papers without a stated reason, so agency monitoring reports were excluded; no reference-list or registry searching is described (one record came from another source); 15 full texts could not be obtained. Judged as written (decision p-amstar2-item4, decided 25 October 2026).
Two independent reviewers at the title, title-and-abstract and full-text stages, with discrepancies resolved by consensus (PDF p. 3).
Two researchers extracted independently with a standardised, pre-piloted template (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons are counted in the PRISMA figure, but no list of excluded full-text studies is given, and none of the listed supplementary items (Tables S1–S3, Figures S1–S9) is such a list.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Country, years, product type, number of samples and sampling source are given in the text and figures; per-study characteristics are in Supplementary Tables S2–S3 (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A review-specific four-criterion tool covering sampling (selection) and consistency of location and analytical protocol, applied by one researcher; it does not cover sample age or storage, differences between laboratories, or selective reporting.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the article.

A justified two-stage approach with inverse-variance random-effects weighting at both stages and stratification by product. Weaknesses not scored by this item: the within-study differences all share the first year as reference, so they are correlated; two Dutch studies each enter the resin pool as two series; only linear trends were fitted; means and standard errors were used where two studies reported medians.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis restricted to the two randomly sampled studies and no stratification by risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion names non-random sampling as a common source of bias and warns that the estimates are not globally representative, but does not discuss how seizure-based sampling could bias the trends, and the abstract calls risk of bias low apart from non-random sampling; a close call.

I2 is reported for every pool and discussed, including, for sinsemilla, one Dutch study (ref. 40) whose large increase contrasted with the other studies, and the possible bias of I2 with few studies; stratification by product type addresses one source; no meta-regression across studies.
Not assessed or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a nil declaration of interests are reported; that two review authors wrote included studies is not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because four critical items are not met (4: search limited to peer-reviewed papers without a reason; 7: no list of excluded studies; 13: the likely effect of seizure-based sampling on the trends is not discussed; 15: publication bias not addressed), with items 2 and 9 only partly met. AMSTAR 2 was built for reviews of health interventions and fits a review of product samples imperfectly; publication bias, for example, matters less for monitoring series than for effect estimates. The rating says how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not that the review is careless: it is registered, duplicates selection and extraction, stratifies by product and states its main limitation. Cite it for: average annual rises in mean THC in seized and sampled herbal cannabis (0.29 percentage points a year) and resin (0.57) in seven countries from the 1970s to 2017, with no detectable change in CBD, and for the large differences between countries and periods. Do not cite it for: market-wide or global potency, how much THC people take in, health effects, the cause of the herbal rise, a faster rise in resin than in herbal cannabis (not tested), or legal-market trends.

key_findings.finding: 12 studies were included after screening 3,893 records and assessing 122 full texts: USA 5, Netherlands 2, UK, France, Denmark, Italy and New Zealand 1 each, with samples from 1970 to 2017. All 12 gave THC data. Ten used non-random samples, mostly seizures of illicit material; two Dutch studies bought samples from retail outlets by random sampling.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (PDF p. 3); Results › Study selection; Study characteristics, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Herbal cannabis (all types): mean THC rose on average by 0.29 percentage points of THC by weight per year (95% CI 0.11 to 0.47; P<0.001 as printed), from 66,747 samples in 7 studies, 1970–2017, with very high heterogeneity (I2 94.2%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in THC concentrations over time › All herbal cannabis; Figure 3 (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: The abstract (PDF p. 1) says eight studies; the Results text and Figures 2–3 show seven. By the editors' calculation from the printed interval (normal approximation), P is about 0.002.

key_findings.locator: Figure 3
key_findings.note: The values are printed inside the figure, which is an image without a text layer; they were read from a 300-dpi rendering, where they are legible. By the editors' sum, the four US studies together carry about 62% of the weight. The p = 0.000 printed beside I-squared in the overall row belongs to the heterogeneity statistic, not to the pooled change: Figure 5 prints the same beside a pooled resin change whose P is 0.017 in the text (PDF p. 5).

key_findings.finding: Resin: mean THC rose on average by 0.57 percentage points a year (0.10 to 1.03), P=0.017, from 17,371 samples in 8 studies entered as 10 series, 1975–2017 (I2 79.1%). Rising (interval above zero): USA 1993–2007 1.58 (0.87 to 2.30), Denmark 2000–2017 1.27 (0.81 to 1.72), France 1992–2016 0.62 (0.45 to 0.79). Flat, with narrow intervals: UK 1975–1989 −0.03 (−0.35 to 0.28) and Netherlands 2005–2015, imported −0.01 (−0.50 to 0.49). Wide intervals including zero: Netherlands 2005–2015, Dutch-produced −0.69 (−2.08 to 0.69); Netherlands 2000–2004, imported 1.77 (−1.97 to 5.51) and Dutch-produced 8.15 (−0.25 to 16.56); Italy 2010–2013 1.41 (−5.92 to 8.74); USA 2008–2017 0.03 (−2.58 to 2.64).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis resin (PDF p. 5); Figure 5 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: The series values are printed inside Figure 5, an image without a text layer; they were read from a 300-dpi rendering, where they are legible. As in Figure 3, the p = 0.000 printed beside I-squared in the overall row belongs to the heterogeneity statistic, not to the pooled change, whose P the text gives as 0.017 (PDF p. 5).

key_findings.finding: Within types of herbal cannabis, no significant trend: sinsemilla 0.26 percentage points a year (−0.09 to 0.61), P=0.141, 15,882 samples, 5 studies, 1986–2017, I2 89.4%, with one Dutch study (2000–2004) rising by 3.11 a year (2.06 to 4.17); traditional herbal cannabis 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.36), P=0.079, 28,418 samples, 5 studies, 1986–2017, I2 48.1%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in THC concentrations over time › Sinsemilla; Traditional herbal cannabis

key_findings.finding: CBD showed no detectable change: herbal cannabis −0.01 percentage points a year (−0.02 to 0.01), P=0.280, 49,434 samples (47,622 all herbal, 1,510 sinsemilla, 302 traditional) from 5 studies, 1995–2017, I2 66.0%; resin 0.03 (−0.11 to 0.18), P=0.651, 11,382 samples from 6 studies, 1992–2017, I2 82.6%. The authors describe CBD as very low in herbal cannabis and generally higher in resin, without figures in the main text.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in CBD concentrations over time (PDF pp. 5–7); Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Mean THC levels by series, read from Figure 2: the earliest US seized samples averaged below about 1.2% from 1970 to 1978; UK samples about 3.4–6.3% in 1975–1989; the US series end at about 9.6% (1995–2007 series), 11.8% (1996–2008 series) and about 13.6% in 2017 (2008–2017 series).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi rendering of the figure, approximate; the review prints no levels in its text. The 2008–2017 US series starts at about 6.0% in 2008, below the about 9.6% at the end of the 1995–2007 series from the same federal seizure source, and its 2017 point (about 13.6%) is far above 2016 (about 7.7%); neither is discussed.

key_findings.finding: The authors translate the pooled slopes into about 2.9 mg more THC per gram of herbal cannabis and 5.7 mg more per gram of resin each year, which they compare with a proposed standard THC unit of 5 mg (ref. 54, co-written by the first author).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: only the two Dutch studies with random retail sampling (refs 39, 40) were rated low on all four criteria, which the text qualifies “for any product category”; this can only mean for at least one product, since both are among the four studies (refs 39–42) that averaged fewer than 19 samples a year for at least one product (ref. 45 also fell short, for CBD only). All other studies used non-random sampling, such as law-enforcement seizures. The analytical protocol was rated consistent over time in every study except ref. 34 (not reported, so unclear); sampling location was consistent in all.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias

key_findings.finding: The authors attribute the herbal THC rise to a growing market share of high-THC sinsemilla relative to traditional herbal cannabis, rather than to rises within types, because neither within-type pool changed significantly; market share was not measured.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 7, continuing on p. 8); abstract, Conclusions (PDF p. 1)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: non-random, mostly law-enforcement sampling; estimates not globally representative, with more samples from the USA; means and standard errors used for CBD although two Dutch studies reported medians; only linear trends; moderate to substantial heterogeneity; legal markets not included for lack of long enough data, while initial studies show substantial THC rises there.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives eight studies for the all-herbal THC analysis (PDF p. 1); the Results text gives seven (PDF p. 5), and Figures 2 and 3 show seven series.
reporting_issues.consequence: Seven is supported by the text and both figures; cite seven.

reporting_issues.issue: Study characteristics say five studies (refs 34–37 and 45) gave eligible CBD data (PDF p. 4), but the CBD analyses use refs 34, 35, 37, 39 and 40 for herbal cannabis and refs 35, 36, 38, 39, 40 and 45 for resin (PDF pp. 6–7): eight different studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of studies contributing CBD data cannot be stated with certainty; use the analyses' own counts (five for herbal cannabis, six for resin).

reporting_issues.issue: The PRISMA counts in Figure 1 (an image; read on the rendered page) do not add up. By the editors' arithmetic: 3,893 titles screened minus 3,673 excluded leaves 220, but 58 + 159 = 217 go forward; and 58 + (159 − 98) = 119, while 122 full texts were assessed. The 110 listed full-text exclusions do match 122 − 12.
reporting_issues.consequence: A count of 61 instead of 58 would reconcile both steps; minor, with no effect on the included studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The all-herbal estimate 0.29 (0.11 to 0.47) is printed with P<0.001; by the editors' calculation (normal approximation), the printed interval implies z of about 3.2 and P of about 0.002.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the estimate remains statistically significant at conventional levels.

reporting_issues.issue: The resin pool enters 10 series from 8 studies as separate units: the two Dutch studies each contribute an imported-resin and a Dutch-produced series (Figure 5), without comment in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Series from the same study share sampling and laboratory methods, so the pooled interval may be slightly too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: Study labels differ between figures and the reference list: Sevigny (2012) in Figure 3 but 2013 in ref. 43; Zamengo et al. (2014) in Figures 3 and 5 but 2015 in ref. 44; Dujordy and Besacier (2017) in Figure 5 but Dujourdy in Figure 4 and ref. 36.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; take primary-study years and spellings from the reference list.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 2, two US series from the same federal seizure source do not join: the 1995–2007 series ends at about 9.6% and the 2008–2017 series starts at about 6.0% (values read from the figure); the 2008–2017 series then jumps from about 7.7% in 2016 to about 13.6% in 2017. Neither feature is discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Levels depend heavily on each study's definitions and sampling; the 2008–2017 US slope (0.59, 0.02 to 1.16) appears to rest largely on the single 2017 point (editors' reading of the figure).

reporting_issues.issue: Study characteristics say three studies (refs 35, 37 and 40) gave THC data for sinsemilla, traditional herbal cannabis and all herbal cannabis (PDF p. 4), but ref. 40 is not in the all-herbal pool, whose seven studies are refs 34, 35, 37, 41, 42, 43 and 44 (PDF p. 5; Figures 2 and 3 show no Dutch series), while ref. 42 is in all three herbal pools (PDF p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the citation should read 42 or ref. 40's all-herbal data were not used; by the pools' own citations, refs 35, 37 and 42 are the three studies in all three herbal pools. Whether this bears on the abstract's eight studies (first reporting issue) cannot be told from the article.

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from the longitudinal arm of the CannTeen study (Greater London), with two between-group factors: cannabis vs control, and adolescents (16–17) vs adults (26–29). 274 participants: 76 adolescents and 71 adults who used cannabis 1–7 days a week over the past 3 months, and 63 adolescent and 64 adult controls matched on gender and age group (fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses). Outcomes: anhedonia (Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale), apathy (Apathy Evaluation Scale), effort-based decision-making for reward (Physical Effort task) and wanting and liking of real rewards (Real Reward Pleasure task: a favourite song, chocolate or candy, a 1-pound coin), the tasks in a subsample of 139. Pre-registered hypotheses and analyses; 2×2 analyses of covariance with prespecified covariates; post hoc Bayesian t tests for null results.
can_establish: Whether, in this London community sample tested at least 12 hours after last cannabis use, people who used cannabis about 4 days a week differed from matched controls on self-reported anhedonia and apathy and on two laboratory reward tasks, and whether any difference was larger in adolescents than in adults.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes or prevents apathy or anhedonia (single time point, no measurement before use began, and the authors note that people more prone to seek pleasure may be more likely to use cannabis); effects of daily or heavier use, of intoxication itself or of many years of use; effects on motivation in daily life such as school or work (not measured); or results in people with recent mental health treatment, daily psychotropic medication or frequent other drug use, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Community recruitment in the Greater London area through school assemblies, posters and flyers, and social media advertisements; baseline sessions of the longitudinal arm of the CannTeen study (p. 11, Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cannabis groups: use on 1–7 days a week on average over the past 3 months; adults were excluded if they had used cannabis regularly before age 18. Controls: had used cannabis or tobacco at least once, fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses, no cannabis use in the month before baseline. Everyone: no daily psychotropic medication, no treatment for a mental health condition (including cannabis dependence) in the past month, no use of any one illicit drug more than twice a month over the past 3 months. Full criteria are in supplemental Table 1 and the study protocol (not read) (p. 11).
sample.demographics: Analysed sample of 268 (Table 1, p. 14): mean age 17.09 and 17.12 in the adolescent groups, 27.63 and 27.41 in the adult groups; female 51% (adolescents who use cannabis), 44% (adults who use cannabis), 52% and 52% (controls); White 63–68%. Depression scores (Beck Depression Inventory) higher in adolescents (means 12.77 and 10.03) than adults (7.75 and 6.97); risk-taking higher in the cannabis groups; tobacco use 2.24 and 1.35 days a week in the cannabis groups vs 0.52 and 0.45 in controls; monthly use of another illicit drug in 59% of adolescents and 25% of adults who used cannabis vs 3% and 2% of controls; premorbid intelligence (Wechsler Test of Adult Reading) means 107.25–111.81.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single assessment). Of 274, 268 entered at least one analysis (reasons in supplemental Table 2, not read). Anhedonia was analysed in 268 and apathy in 211 (215 completed the apathy scale; why fewer than 274 is not explained in the main text). Of the 139 in the task subsample, analyses used 137 (effort acceptances), 112 (reward sensitivity), 103 (effort sensitivity) and 135 (wanting and liking), after excluding people with reward- or effort-sensitivity scores of 0 or below (p. 12; Figure 1 legend, p. 13).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited through schools and advertising to obtain frequent cannabis use and matched controls; the authors state the sample does not represent the UK or people who use cannabis at large (p. 17). Excluding people with recent mental health treatment, daily psychotropic medication or frequent other drug use removes, from both groups, people more likely to have high apathy or anhedonia, which may make differences harder to detect. Most people in the cannabis groups mainly used strong herbal cannabis (skunk; 91% of adolescents, 84% of adults), and 56 adolescents (74.7%) and 33 adults (48.5%) met the CUDIT-R cut-off for at least mild cannabis use disorder (Table 2 and Discussion, p. 15).

exposure.measurement: Timeline follow-back for cannabis, alcohol, tobacco and other drug use; at the start of each session recent use was checked by an instant saliva drug test, a breathalyser and self-report (p. 12).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, as recorded by the study (Table 2, p. 15), adolescents vs adults who used cannabis: days a week of use 3.74 (SD 1.97; range 0.83–6.92) vs 4.17 (SD 1.90; 0.75–6.92); grams on a day of use 1.05 vs 0.62; age at first use 14.61 vs 18.01 and at first weekly use 15.65 vs 22.25; CUDIT-R score 15.40 vs 11.87. Route of use and THC content were not reported; the authors chose not to analyse quantity or cannabinoid content (p. 17).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was common in the cannabis groups (monthly use of another illicit drug: 59% of adolescents, 25% of adults) and rare in controls; frequency of alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use was a covariate in every model (p. 12; Table 1, p. 14).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 12 hours for cannabis and alcohol and 48 hours for other illicit drugs, checked by saliva test, breathalyser and self-report; sessions were rescheduled otherwise (p. 12). Last cannabis use a mean 2.41 days (adolescents) and 2.56 days (adults) before the baseline session (Table 2, p. 15); the authors describe abstinence as typically about 2 days (p. 15).

comparison.controls: Adolescent (n=63) and adult (n=64) controls from the same recruitment, with fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses and none in the past month; 87% of adolescent and 97% of adult controls had ever used cannabis (Table 2, p. 15).
comparison.matching: Gender and age group; the adolescent and adult cannabis groups were matched on frequency of use (p. 11; Table 2). Covariates chosen in advance: depression (Beck Depression Inventory), risk-taking (RT-18), maternal education, and frequency of alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use (pp. 11–12).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measurement before cannabis use began; motivation, reward sensitivity and personality in childhood were not measured. Premorbid intelligence was measured but not used as a covariate. Depression and other drug use, which cannabis use could itself influence, were adjusted for, which may remove part of any effect.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls rarely used other illicit drugs monthly (2 adolescents, 1 adult) and used tobacco on fewer days than the cannabis groups (Table 1, p. 14).

outcomes.instruments: Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (anhedonia; Cronbach's alpha .83); Apathy Evaluation Scale (apathy; alpha .75; item 4 was omitted for everyone by experimenter error and imputed, with results unchanged when it was left out); Physical Effort task (accept or reject offers of button-pressing at 3 effort and 3 reward levels for points later exchanged for chocolates or sweets; outputs: total acceptances, reward sensitivity, effort sensitivity); Real Reward Pleasure task (wanting and liking ratings of 30 seconds of a favourite song, a piece of chocolate or candy and a 1-pound coin) (pp. 11–12).
outcomes.validity_norms: The questionnaires are described as reliable and valid in adults and adolescents; the two tasks' formal reliability and validity have not yet been confirmed (authors, p. 17). Depression was negatively related to effort acceptances, reward sensitivity and reward liking, which the authors take as evidence that the tasks work (p. 16).
outcomes.operationalization: Higher questionnaire scores mean more anhedonia or apathy; reward sensitivity = acceptances at the highest minus the lowest reward level; effort sensitivity = acceptances at the lowest minus the highest effort level. Motivation was not measured in daily life (school, work) or by others' reports.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the seven analyses of covariance (21 effects); only the exploratory correlations between outcomes were corrected (p. 12).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to self-report; whether testers knew participants' group is not stated. The authors raise the possibility that people who use cannabis, sensing that others such as the researcher see them as demotivated, want to appear more motivated in psychological studies (p. 15).

analysis.effect_sizes: Anhedonia (n=268): cannabis vs control F(1,258)=5.35, P=.02, partial eta-squared .02, controls higher (unadjusted difference 0.55 points); adolescents vs adults F(1,258)=17.98, P<.001, partial eta-squared .065 (adolescents 3.84 points higher); interaction F(1,258)=1.01, P=.32, partial eta-squared .004. Apathy (n=211): cannabis vs control F(1,201)=0.05, P=.82, partial eta-squared <.001; adolescents 4.05 points higher, F(1,201)=13.89, P<.001, partial eta-squared .065; interaction F(1,201)=0.39, P=.54, partial eta-squared .002; Bayes factor 6.48 for no cannabis–control difference. Physical Effort and Real Reward Pleasure tasks: no significant group, age-group or interaction effects (statistics in supplemental Tables 7–8, not read); Bayes factors for no cannabis–control difference: acceptances 3.78, reward sensitivity 3.58, effort sensitivity 1.89, liking 5.16, wanting 2.78; for no difference between adults and adolescents who use cannabis (cannabis groups only): reward sensitivity 3.58, acceptances 2.60, effort sensitivity 1.09, wanting 3.69, liking 3.87; all from post hoc independent-samples t tests, not from the covariate-adjusted models (p. 12). Correlations with days a week of use, none significant: anhedonia r=.07, apathy r=.16, acceptances r=−.01, reward sensitivity r=.06, effort sensitivity r=.03, wanting r=−.18, liking r=−.18 (pp. 12–13).
analysis.covariates: Depression (Beck Depression Inventory), risk-taking (RT-18), maternal education, and frequency of alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use, chosen in advance (pp. 11–12).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Hypotheses and analyses pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (Skumlien et al., 2020; not read); study protocol published (Lawn et al., 2020; not read). The Bayesian tests are labelled post hoc. Whether excluding reward- or effort-sensitivity scores of 0 or below was planned is not stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: All seven outcomes are reported, nulls included, but full statistics for every model are in supplemental Tables 6–8 (not read). The main text gives the unadjusted anhedonia difference (0.55 points) without its significance, and no Bayes factor for anhedonia.
analysis.power: No power calculation in the article. The task subsample had about 35 per group (139 in all), and the cannabis–control Bayes factors for effort sensitivity (1.89) and reward wanting (2.78) were below the authors' threshold of 3, so those two nulls are inconclusive, as are the adult–adolescent comparisons for acceptances (2.60) and effort sensitivity (1.09).

interpretation_gap.results_show: People who used cannabis on average about 4 days a week, most of them mainly strong herbal cannabis, tested at least 12 hours after last use, did not report more apathy than matched controls and did not differ on effort-based choices or on wanting and liking of real rewards; controls reported slightly more anhedonia (0.55 points; partial eta-squared .02). Adolescents reported more anhedonia and apathy than adults (about 4 points on each scale) whether or not they used cannabis, and no cannabis–control difference was larger in adolescents. The evidence for no cannabis–control difference was substantial (Bayes factor at least 3) for apathy, effort acceptances, reward sensitivity and liking, but inconclusive for effort sensitivity and wanting; comparisons of adults with adolescents within the cannabis groups (not tests of the interaction) gave Bayes factors of at least 3 for reward sensitivity, wanting and liking but not for acceptances (2.60) or effort sensitivity (1.09).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that null findings “were supported by post hoc Bayesian analyses” (p. 10), but four of the eleven Bayes factors in the main text fall below the authors' own threshold of 3 (cannabis against control: effort sensitivity 1.89, wanting 2.78; adults against adolescents who use cannabis: acceptances 2.60, effort sensitivity 1.09; pp. 12–13), and all come from two-group t tests not described as adjusted for the covariates (p. 12). The Significance Statement says the study counters the lazy-stoner stereotype by showing that the groups did not differ on several measures of reward and motivation, and that adolescents were not more sensitive to a presumed harmful effect of cannabis (p. 10); the latter rests on non-significant interactions for apathy and anhedonia (P=.54 and .32), and the Bayesian support the Discussion adds for the lack of interactions (p. 16) comes from comparisons of adults with adolescents within the cannabis groups, two of five below 3. Non-significant differences and interactions in a cross-sectional study, with about 35 people per group for the tasks, show no detectable difference, not the absence of one. The limitations section is more careful: cross-sectional design, possible delayed effects, a non-representative sample, heavier use and younger people not studied, and tasks not yet validated (pp. 16–17). The anhedonia difference would not survive a correction for seven outcomes (P=.02 against .05/7, about .007; editors' calculation), and the authors themselves say it may not be clinically relevant. A headline that science shows cannabis does not make people lazy would overstate: the study measured self-rated apathy and anhedonia and two laboratory tasks with sweets, music and coins, at least 12 hours after last use, in volunteers using on average 4 days a week; it did not measure motivation at school or work, did not test daily heavy use or intoxication, and cannot rule out that people who use cannabis started out more reward-seeking.

timeline.event: Lane et al.: lower effort for reward in 14 adolescents who used cannabis than in 20 controls (as summarized by this paper, p. 10); not read.
Barnwell et al.: no significant relation between cannabis use and apathy (Apathy Evaluation Scale) in 487 adults (as summarized, p. 10); not read.
Lawn et al.: no difference in effort for reward between 40 adults who used cannabis and controls (as summarized, p. 10); not read.
Leventhal et al.: in 3394 adolescents followed over time, anhedonia at 14 predicted later cannabis use but not the reverse (as summarized, p. 10); not read.
Meier and White: informants rated people who used cannabis as more apathetic than controls, the only informant-rated study the authors know of (p. 15); not read.
Petrucci et al.: in 1168 young adults, apathy correlated weakly with quantity of use and problem use (largest r=.125 after adjustment) but not with frequency (as summarized, p. 10); not read.

Taylor and Filbey (2021), Vele et al. (2022) and Acuff et al. (2022): adults who used cannabis chose high-effort options more often than controls, or more with heavier use; Pacheco-Colón et al. (2021): no apathy association in 401 adolescents followed over time (as summarized, pp. 10, 15); not read.

Companion CannTeen analyses of the same participants (not independent replications): no age-by-cannabis interactions for depression, anxiety, psychotic-like symptoms or memory and inhibition (Lawn et al., 2022a, 2022b) and no cannabis-related differences in reward-system imaging (Skumlien et al., 2022) (p. 16); not read.

replication.where_it_stands: By the authors' own review, earlier findings on apathy and effort are mixed and mostly from small samples, while anhedonia in adolescents has the strongest earlier support, with longitudinal evidence that it may precede use. This study adds a larger null for apathy and reward tasks at moderate frequency of use, but it is cross-sectional, and the companion CannTeen papers use the same people. Daily heavy use, motivation rated by others or measured in daily life, and the longitudinal follow-up of this cohort remain the open questions.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal follow-up of adolescents from before regular use, with repeated self-rated, informant-rated and behavioural measures of motivation (including school and work outcomes), measured cannabis amount and potency, enough people using daily to test a dose-response, and depression treated as a possible pathway rather than adjusted away.

domains.note: Cross-sectional, with no measurement before use; the authors raise the possibility that people prone to seek pleasure are more likely to use cannabis (p. 13). Prespecified adjustment for depression, risk-taking, maternal education and alcohol, tobacco and other drug use, but depression and other drug use may themselves be influenced by cannabis use, so adjusting for them can mask an effect, and other drug use barely overlaps between groups (59% vs 3% in adolescents), so its adjustment relies on the model.

Frequency over 3 months by timeline follow-back, with recent use checked biologically; the grouping (regular use vs fewer than 10 lifetime uses) is clear-cut, although at least one person in each cannabis group averaged below the 1-day-a-week criterion (Table 2) and THC content was not measured.

Volunteers recruited through schools and advertising; excluding recent mental health treatment, daily psychotropic medication and frequent other drug use removes people with likely higher apathy or anhedonia from both groups, which may bias towards no difference.
People treated for a mental health condition (including cannabis dependence) in the past month were excluded; no interventions were given.

Questionnaire data were nearly complete for anhedonia (268 of 274) but apathy was analysed in 211 without an explanation in the main text, and one apathy item was imputed for everyone (sensitivity analysis unchanged). The task analyses excluded about 18% (reward sensitivity) and 25% (effort sensitivity) of those with task data for scores of 0 or below, a rule based on the outcome; exclusions by group are only in supplemental Table 2 (not read).

Self-report questionnaires with good internal consistency, but participants knew their own group and the study's topic (the authors raise self-presentation, p. 15); the tasks' reliability and validity are not established (p. 17).

Pre-registered hypotheses and analyses with all seven outcomes reported; but the registration was not read here, the outcome-based exclusion rule is not said to be pre-registered, and the task statistics are only in supplements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used because the study compares people who use cannabis with people who do not on outcomes that cannabis might affect. The overall judgment is high because, in a cross-sectional design, pre-existing differences cannot be separated from any effect of cannabis, and the covariate set may partly adjust an effect away; selection and outcome-based exclusions add some concerns, mostly in the direction of finding no difference. Cite it for: in this London community sample, regular cannabis use (about 4 days a week) was not associated with more self-rated apathy or with less effort for reward or less liking of rewards on two laboratory tasks, and cannabis–control differences were not larger in adolescents than in adults; controls reported slightly more anhedonia. Do not cite it for: cannabis having no effect on motivation, daily heavy use, intoxicated states, motivation in daily life, or adolescents being unaffected in the long term.

key_findings.finding: 274 participants: 76 adolescents (16–17) and 71 adults (26–29) who used cannabis on 1–7 days a week over the past 3 months, 63 adolescent and 64 adult controls; anhedonia completed by 274, apathy by 215, the tasks by a subsample of 139 (34 adolescents who used cannabis, 35 in each other group).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph (left column) and 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Cannabis use, adolescents vs adults who used cannabis: 3.74 vs 4.17 days a week; 68 (91%) vs 57 (84%) mainly used strong herbal cannabis (skunk); 1.05 vs 0.62 g on a day of use; last use 2.41 vs 2.56 days before the session; first weekly use at 15.65 vs 22.25 years; 56 adolescents (74.7%) and 33 adults (48.5%) met the CUDIT-R cut-off for at least mild cannabis use disorder.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Discussion › Anhedonia and Apathy, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Anhedonia: controls scored higher than the cannabis groups, F(1,258)=5.35, P=.02, partial eta-squared .02, an unadjusted difference of 0.55 points; adolescents scored 3.84 points higher than adults, F(1,258)=17.98, P<.001, partial eta-squared .065; no interaction, F(1,258)=1.01, P=.32; no correlation with days a week of use (r=.07, P=.40).
key_findings.locator: Results › Anhedonia and Apathy, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Apathy: no cannabis–control difference, F(1,201)=0.05, P=.82, partial eta-squared <.001, and no interaction, F(1,201)=0.39, P=.54; adolescents 4.05 points higher than adults, F(1,201)=13.89, P<.001; unchanged without the imputed item; Bayes factor 6.48 for no cannabis–control difference; no correlation with frequency (r=.16, P=.10).
key_findings.locator: Results › Anhedonia and Apathy, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Physical Effort task: no significant group, age-group or interaction effects on acceptances, reward sensitivity or effort sensitivity; Bayes factors for no cannabis–control difference 3.78 (acceptances), 3.58 (reward sensitivity) and 1.89 (effort sensitivity, inconclusive), and for no difference between adults and adolescents who use cannabis 3.58 (reward sensitivity), 2.60 (acceptances, inconclusive) and 1.09 (effort sensitivity, inconclusive); no correlation with frequency (r from −.01 to .06).
key_findings.locator: Results › Physical Effort Task
key_findings.note: Both reward-sensitivity Bayes factors are printed as 3.58. The adult–adolescent comparison includes people who use cannabis only, so it is not a test of the age-by-cannabis interaction; all Bayes factors come from post hoc independent-samples t tests (p. 12, Methods › Analyses › Statistical Models).

key_findings.finding: Real Reward Pleasure task: no significant group, age-group or interaction effects on wanting or liking of a song, chocolate or candy and a coin; Bayes factors for no cannabis–control difference 5.16 for liking and 2.78 for wanting (inconclusive), and for no difference between adults and adolescents who use cannabis 3.69 for wanting and 3.87 for liking; correlations with frequency r=−.18 (P=.15) for wanting and r=−.18 (P=.14) for liking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Real Reward Pleasure Task (p. 12, continuing on p. 13)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the anhedonia difference (under 1 point on the scale) small and possibly not clinically relevant, setting it against a 14-point difference between healthy people and people with depression in an earlier study; they suggest either that cannabis enhances some rewards or that people more prone to seek pleasure are more likely to use cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Anhedonia and Apathy, 1st paragraph (p. 13, continuing on p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Testing took place at least 12 hours after last cannabis use (typically about 2 days), with a saliva drug test, breathalyser and self-report at every session.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure (p. 12); Discussion › Anhedonia and Apathy, 3rd paragraph (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: The cannabis groups had higher risk-taking scores and more tobacco use and other illicit drug use (monthly use of another illicit drug in 59% of adolescents and 25% of adults who used cannabis vs 3% and 2% of controls); depression scores were higher in adolescents than adults (means 12.77 and 10.03 vs 7.75 and 6.97), with no cannabis–control difference marked.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion required cannabis use on 1–7 days a week (p. 11), but Table 2 gives minimum frequencies of 0.83 (adolescents) and 0.75 (adults) days a week.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one person in each cannabis group used less often than the stated minimum; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Controls were to have fewer than 10 lifetime cannabis uses (p. 11), but Table 2 gives ranges of 0–10 in both control groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one control appears to be at or over the limit; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Adults were excluded if they had used cannabis regularly before age 18 (p. 11), but in Table 2 adults' age at first weekly use ranges from 17.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either regular use is defined more strictly than weekly in the full criteria (supplemental Table 1, not read) or the exclusion was not applied strictly; the adult group may include some regular use that began in adolescence.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample sizes differ between places: the abstract gives n=274 for anhedonia, 215 for apathy and 137 for the reward-pleasure task (p. 9); the text says 139 completed the tasks (p. 11); the analyses used 268, 211, 137, 112, 103 and 135 (Figure 1 legend, p. 13).
reporting_issues.consequence: Completion and analysis numbers are mixed; cite the analysed numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: People with reward- or effort-sensitivity scores of 0 or below were dropped from those analyses (p. 12), a rule based on the outcome itself. By the editors' arithmetic from the Figure 1 legend (137, 112 and 103 analysed), 25 of 137 (18%) and 34 of 137 (25%) of those with task data were dropped.
reporting_issues.consequence: If exclusions differed by group, the sensitivity results could be biased; the breakdown is only in supplemental Table 2 (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract presents the null findings as supported by post hoc Bayesian analyses (p. 10), and the Discussion calls the lack of age-by-cannabis interactions supported by Bayesian analyses (p. 16, Age-Group Differences, 4th paragraph); but four of the eleven Bayes factors in the main text are below the authors' threshold of 3: for no cannabis–control difference, effort sensitivity (1.89) and reward wanting (2.78); for no difference between adults and adolescents who use cannabis, acceptances (2.60) and effort sensitivity (1.09) (pp. 12–13). The Discussion's opening paragraph calls the support broad (p. 13); the Significance Statement makes no Bayesian claim (p. 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: Those four nulls are inconclusive rather than evidence of no difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The significance footnote letters are swapped between the tables: in Table 1, a means P<.001 and b P<.05; in Table 2, a means P<.05 and b P<.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; read each table with its own footnote.

reporting_issues.issue: The Bayesian follow-ups were post hoc independent-samples t tests of cannabis against control groups and of adults against adolescents within the cannabis groups (p. 12, Methods › Analyses › Statistical Models): two-group comparisons, not described as including the ANCOVA covariates, and the comparison of adults with adolescents who use cannabis leaves out the controls, so it does not test the age-by-cannabis interaction. The Discussion's Bayesian support for the lack of interactions (p. 16) therefore rests on an indirect comparison, given in the main text only for the five task outcomes, two of them below 3 (pp. 12–13).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Bayes factors describe unadjusted two-group differences; the absence of larger effects in adolescents rests on the non-significant interaction tests, not on Bayesian evidence.

design_detail: Research letter (JAMA 2017;318(17):1708-1709) reporting a laboratory analysis of commercial products, not of people or cells (the schema has no design for a laboratory analysis of products; 'in-vitro' is the nearest, as for sc_vandrey_2015 and sc_mallock_2024). Internet searches between 12 September and 15 October 2016 (keywords CBD, cannabidiol, oil, tincture, vape) identified CBD extracts sold online in the USA with a CBD content on the packaging; every unique product was bought, excluding identical formulations under the same brand: 84 products from 31 companies (40 oils, 20 tinctures, 24 vaporization liquids). Within 2 weeks of receipt the labels were replaced with blinded study codes and the products were sent to an outside laboratory (Botanacor Services) for high-performance liquid chromatography, in triplicate, of six cannabinoids (CBD, CBDA, CBG, CBN, THC, THCA). Measured CBD was compared with the label using a plus or minus 10% rule. No one consumed any product, and no urine or blood was tested.
can_establish: How often the measured CBD content of 84 CBD extracts bought online in the USA in autumn 2016 was within 10% of the label, above it or below it, by product type, and how many of these products contained THC, CBDA or CBG and how much.
cannot_establish: The label accuracy of CBD products in other years, markets or shops, or of products without a CBD label (excluded); batch-to-batch variation (one purchase per product as far as stated); whether using any product would cause intoxication, impairment or a positive drug test (no one took a product and no urine was tested); or whether the shortfalls affect clinical response, which the Discussion infers without data.

sample.recruitment: Products, not people. Internet searches from 12 September to 15 October 2016 with the keywords CBD, cannabidiol, oil, tincture and vape, to find CBD products available for online retail purchase that gave a CBD content on the packaging; all unique CBD extracts meeting these criteria were bought (Methods, p. 1708). The search engine, the number of results screened and the number of products found or excluded are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: CBD extracts (oil, tincture or vaporization liquid) for online purchase with a CBD content on the packaging. Excluded: products with the same formulation as another product of the same brand (Methods, p. 1708). Products without a CBD content label were not eligible.
sample.demographics: Not applicable (products).
sample.attrition: None reported: all 84 products appear in Table 1 (p. 1708).
sample.selection_effects: Online products only, one search period in 2016, no weighting by sales, products without a CBD label excluded, and one purchase per product as far as stated. The letter says the online approach was used to maximize sampling and ensure representativeness of available products (p. 1708) and calls online-only buying a limitation while describing these products as the most readily available to US consumers (p. 1709); no sampling frame is described from which representativeness could be judged.

exposure.measurement: Six cannabinoids (cannabidiol, cannabidiolic acid, cannabigerol, cannabinol, delta-9-THC and delta-9-THC acid) measured by high-performance liquid chromatography in triplicate at Botanacor Services, which received the products under blinded study codes; lower limit of quantification given as 0.3170% wt/wt or less; a 10-point method validation procedure was used to choose sample preparation and method; triplicate results were averaged and reported by product weight (Methods, p. 1708). All results are presented in mg/mL; how weight-based results were converted to volume is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content, not doses. Measured CBD 0.10 to 655.27 mg/mL (median 9.45); labelled CBD 1.33 to 800.00 mg/mL (median 15.00) (Results, p. 1708). THC up to 6.43 mg/mL, CBDA up to 55.73 mg/mL, CBG up to 4.67 mg/mL; CBN and THCA not found in any product (Table 2, p. 1709). No one consumed the products.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (products). Only six cannabinoids were measured; other contents (for example solvents, pesticides, metals, terpenes or added drugs) were not.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (products).

comparison.controls: The CBD content printed on each label is the comparator. No reference material, second laboratory or comparison with products from dispensaries or shops.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a product analysis. Not described: how labels giving content per container or per serving were converted to mg/mL; how results by weight were converted to mg/mL; how long products were stored before analysis; whether any label declared THC.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: High-performance liquid chromatography at Botanacor Services (instrument, standards and conditions not described), in triplicate; labels read by the investigators.
outcomes.validity_norms: The 10% allowable variance is said to be consistent with other herbal products in the US Pharmacopeia and with emerging standards from medicinal cannabis industry leaders (Methods, p. 1708); no source is cited for either. Method validation is described only as a 10-point procedure, without results.
outcomes.operationalization: Accurately labelled: measured CBD 90% to 110% of the labelled value; underlabelled: more than 110% (the product holds more CBD than its label says); overlabelled: less than 90% (it holds less) (Methods; Table 1 footnotes a-c, p. 1708). Table 1 also gives the deviation of labelled from tested content in mg/mL and as a percentage, without defining whether it is absolute or signed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed: the only test is one chi-squared test of product type against the three accuracy categories; all other results are descriptive, with 95% intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Labels were replaced with blinded study codes before the products went to the laboratory (Methods, p. 1708).

analysis.effect_sizes: CBD label accuracy, all 84: 26 within 10% (30.95%; 95% CI 22.08%-41.49%), 36 with more CBD than labelled (42.85%; 32.82%-53.53%), 22 with less (26.19%; 17.98%-36.48%). By type, accurate / more / less: oils 18 / 10 / 12 of 40; tinctures 5 / 8 / 7 of 20; vaporization liquids 3 / 18 / 3 of 24. Product type and accuracy: chi-squared 16.75, printed with 1 degree of freedom, P = .002 (Results and Table 1, p. 1708). THC detected in 18 of 84 (21.43%; 14.01%-31.35%), CBDA in 13 (15.48%; 9.28%-24.70%), CBG in 2 (2.38%; 0.65%-8.27%) (pp. 1708-1709). Editors' calculation: the printed intervals reproduce as Wilson score intervals; the chi-squared statistic reproduces from Table 1 as 16.75 with 4 degrees of freedom (a 3 by 3 table), which gives P = 0.002, whereas 1 degree of freedom would give about P = 0.00004; no expected count is below 5; 58 of 84 products (69.0%; Wilson 95% interval 58.5% to 77.9%) were outside 10% of the label.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (a research letter).
analysis.selective_reporting: Results for single products and companies are not listed; THC-containing products are not broken down by type or by CBD label accuracy; deviation is not broken down by accuracy category.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 20 to 40 products per type.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 84 CBD extracts bought online in autumn 2016, about 3 in 10 held CBD within 10% of the label; about 4 in 10 held more than labelled and about 1 in 4 less. Vaporization liquids were least accurate (3 of 24 within 10%, 18 holding more than labelled), oils the most (18 of 40). THC was detected in 18 products (about 1 in 5), at up to 6.43 mg/mL.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says that the 26% of products holding less CBD than labelled could negate any potential clinical response, and that the THC observed may be sufficient to produce intoxication or impairment, especially among children (p. 1709): neither was measured, the second rests on one cited report of two children, and the letter gives no estimate of how much THC a person would take in from these products. That the overlabelling is similar in magnitude to levels that triggered FDA warning letters (CBD negligible or below 1% of the label) cannot be checked, because the letter gives no count of products with negligible CBD. That underlabelling is less concerning because CBD lacks abuse liability and serious adverse effects at high doses rests on two citations. A headline that most CBD products are fake would overstate the letter: the commonest error was more CBD than labelled. A headline that CBD makes people fail drug tests would go beyond it: about one in five products contained THC, but no urine was tested.

timeline.event: Vandrey et al. (2015), label accuracy of edible cannabis products from medical dispensaries, cited by this letter as an example of inaccurate labelling (reference 2, p. 1709).
US Food and Drug Administration warning letters and test results for CBD products, 2015-2016, described by this letter as sent to 14 businesses (reference 3, p. 1709); not read for this card.
Products identified and bought online, 12 September to 15 October 2016.
This research letter (accepted 7 August 2017; JAMA, 7 November 2017).

replication.where_it_stands: A single, one-period sample of online products from 2016. The authors call for monitoring of changes over time and comparison with dispensary products (p. 1709). No repetition is reported in the letter, and later product surveys were not read for this card, so the figures describe what could be bought online then, not CBD products in general or today.

funding.funder: Not reported: the letter has no funding statement; the author contributions credit Dr Bonn-Miller with obtaining funding (Author Contributions, p. 1709).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 1709): Drs Bonn-Miller, Thomas and Vandrey reported serving as unpaid board members of the Institute for Research on Cannabinoids. Dr Bonn-Miller reported personal fees from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, the Lambert Center for the Study of Medicinal Cannabis and Hemp, the Realm of Caring Foundation, Tilray, CW Botanicals, Insys Therapeutics, International Cannabis and Cannabinoids Institute, the Medical Cannabis Institute and Aphria. Dr Vandrey reported personal fees from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, CW Hemp, Battelle Memorial Institute and Insys Pharmaceuticals. No other disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine (Bonn-Miller), VA San Diego Health Care System (Loflin), RTI International (Thomas), Americans for Safe Access (Marcu), Palo Alto University (Hyke) and Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Vandrey) (p. 1709). The letter does not say what the organizations named in the disclosures do, or whether any of them made products in the sample; the editors have not added this from other sources. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results; the measurements were made by an outside laboratory that received the products under blinded codes.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated, sales-weighted sampling of CBD products online and in shops over several years, several batches per product, analysed blind by independent accredited laboratories that report analyte-specific limits and recovery and state how label and result units were aligned; and, for the drug-test question, controlled studies of urine after use of products with measured THC content.

domains.note: Every unique labelled CBD extract found by keyword searches in five weeks of 2016 was bought (a strength), but the search method and the numbers found and excluded are not reported, there is no sales weighting, products without a CBD label were excluded, and online products only were sampled. Describes what was found online then, not the market.

Triplicate chromatography at an outside laboratory blind to the labels, after a stated method validation (strengths); but no recovery, precision or analyte-specific limits are reported, the quantification limit is given only as 0.3170% wt/wt or less, results reported by weight are presented in mg/mL without a stated conversion, and storage time before analysis is unclear.

A clear 10% rule, but how labels stated per container or per serving were converted to mg/mL is not described, and the deviation measures in Table 1 are not defined. The terms are counter-intuitive (underlabelled means more CBD than stated) and need glossing when cited.

Shares are given with Wilson intervals (good); the single chi-squared test is printed with 1 degree of freedom where a 3 by 3 table has 4 (its P value matches 4); products are treated as independent although 84 came from 31 companies; mean percentage deviations are dominated by a few extreme products.

No funder is named. Two authors declare personal fees from several cannabinoid businesses and organizations, and three serve on the board of a cannabinoid research institute; the letter does not say whether any of these made products in the sample. Blind analysis by an outside laboratory limits the scope for influence on the measurements.

The Discussion's statements on clinical response and on intoxication or impairment, especially in children, are inferences without measurements; the comparison with FDA warning letters cannot be checked from the data shown; whether any of the 18 THC-containing products declared THC is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of commercial products (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design, as for sc_vandrey_2015; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The core counts are simple, internally consistent with Table 1 and come from blinded triplicate analysis, so they can be cited as what these 84 products held. Concerns are representativeness, undescribed unit conversions and method validation, an unnamed funder alongside industry ties, and a Discussion that goes beyond the measurements. Citable for: in 84 CBD extracts sold online in the USA in 2016, 31% were within 10% of the CBD label, 43% held more CBD and 26% less, and 21% contained THC (up to 6.43 mg/mL). Not citable for: CBD products in general or today, effects of the products on anyone, or positive drug tests.

key_findings.finding: Sample and method: internet searches from 12 September to 15 October 2016 (keywords CBD, cannabidiol, oil, tincture, vape) for CBD products sold online with a CBD content on the packaging; every unique product was bought, excluding identical formulations under the same brand: 84 products from 31 companies (40 oils, 20 tinctures, 24 vaporization liquids). Within 2 weeks of receipt, labels were replaced with blinded study codes and products were sent to Botanacor Services for high-performance liquid chromatography in triplicate (lower limit of quantification 0.3170% wt/wt or less; 10-point method validation), results averaged and reported by product weight.
key_findings.locator: Methods; Results; Table 1 column headings

key_findings.finding: Classification rule: accurately labelled, measured CBD 90% to 110% of the labelled value; underlabelled, more than 110% (more CBD than the label says); overlabelled, less than 90% (less CBD than the label says); the 10% variance is said to follow other herbal products in the US Pharmacopeia and emerging industry standards.
key_findings.locator: Methods (right column); Table 1 footnotes a-c

key_findings.finding: CBD against the label, all 84 products: 26 accurately labelled (30.95%; 95% CI 22.08%-41.49%), 36 underlabelled, holding more CBD than stated (42.85%; 32.82%-53.53%), and 22 overlabelled, holding less (26.19%; 17.98%-36.48%).

Accuracy depended on product type (chi-squared printed as 16.75 with 1 degree of freedom, P = .002): vaporization liquids were most often mislabelled (21 of 24, 87.50%; 95% CI 69.00%-95.66%) and oils most often accurate (45.00%; 30.71%-60.17%).

Labelled concentration by type, median (range): oils 22.26 (2.50-800.00), tinctures 8.33 (1.33-50.00), vaporization liquids 18.33 (2.00-160.00) mg/mL.

key_findings.finding: Cannabinoids not on the labels were generally low, but THC was detected in 18 of 84 products (21.43%; 95% CI 14.01%-31.35%), up to 6.43 mg/mL (mean 0.45, SD 1.18; median 0); cannabidiolic acid in 13 (15.48%; 9.28%-24.70%), up to 55.73 mg/mL; cannabigerol in 2 (2.38%; 0.65%-8.27%), up to 4.67 mg/mL; cannabinol and THC acid in none.

key_findings.finding: Aim stated in the introduction: to examine label accuracy of CBD products sold online, including identification of present but unlabelled cannabinoids, buying online to maximize sampling and ensure representativeness of available products.
key_findings.locator: Introductory paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: CBD concentrations varied widely, consistent with the lack of an accepted dose; 26% of products held less CBD than labelled, which the authors say could negate any potential clinical response; the overlabelling is described as similar in magnitude to levels that triggered FDA warning letters to 14 businesses in 2015-2016 (actual CBD negligible or below 1% of the label); underlabelling is called less concerning because CBD appears to have neither abuse liability nor serious adverse effects at high doses (two citations); the THC found may be enough to cause intoxication or impairment, especially among children (citing a report of two children). Online-only buying is named as a limitation; the authors call for monitoring over time, comparison with dispensary products, and manufacturing and testing standards and oversight.
key_findings.locator: Discussion; References 3-6
