reporting_issues.issue: The test of product type against label accuracy is printed as chi-squared(1) = 16.75, P = .002. A 3 by 3 table has 4 degrees of freedom; recomputed from Table 1, the statistic is 16.75 and with 4 degrees of freedom P = 0.002 (editors' calculation), whereas with 1 degree of freedom it would be about 0.00004.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error in the degrees of freedom; the statistic and P value are right and the conclusion stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say results were reported by product weight and give the quantification limit in % wt/wt (0.3170% or less), but every result is presented in mg/mL, with no stated density or conversion; nor is it said how labels giving content per container or per serving were turned into mg/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Products near the 10% limits could be classified differently under another conversion; the large deviations are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The quantification limit is given only as an upper bound (0.3170% wt/wt or less, about 3.2 mg/g by the editors' arithmetic), while measured CBD values as low as 0.10 mg/mL are reported and THC is counted as detected without a stated limit.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be checked whether the lowest values and the 18 THC detections lie above the laboratory's quantification limit for each product.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter presents THC as an unlabelled cannabinoid (Results) but does not say whether any of the 18 THC-containing products declared THC on the label, or how THC-containing products were distributed by type.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citations of the finding as unlabelled THC in about one in five products rest on the letter's framing rather than a stated count.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or role-of-funder statement is printed, although the author contributions credit Dr Bonn-Miller with obtaining funding.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of funding cannot be assessed; recorded as a flag, not a reason to discount.

design_detail: Controlled secondhand-smoke exposure experiment at Johns Hopkins (Baltimore, USA), Part I of a series (urine only). A sealed plexiglass chamber of 3.05 m x 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling (about 12 m2 of floor, editors' arithmetic). In each of three 1-hour sessions, held at weekly or longer intervals in a fixed order, six people who smoke cannabis daily or near-daily smoked cannabis cigarettes as they wished, seated in alternate seats around a table with six non-smoking participants. Session 1: 5.3% total THC, no ventilation; Session 2: 11.3% THC, no ventilation; Session 3: 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour. Each of the 18 non-smoking participants took part in one session only; eight different smoking participants took part across the sessions. Non-smoking participants' urine was collected about 1 hour before and for 34 hours after exposure and tested for the THC metabolite THCCOOH by GC-MS (confirmation cut-off 15 ng/mL) and by immunoassays at four laboratories at screening cut-offs of 20 and 50 ng/mL, with 75 and 100 ng/mL run on the CEDIA assay only, plus one assay at a fifth laboratory (Lab Corp, 50 ng/mL) that appears only in the Results. Blood, oral fluid, hair, vital signs, subjective and cognitive results were to be reported elsewhere (p. 4). Design recorded as 'human-laboratory', the nearest schema design for a controlled exposure in volunteers. The investigators set the three conditions but ran them in a fixed order, neither randomized nor counterbalanced, with a different group of six non-smoking participants in each, so risk of bias is judged with ROBINS-I (non-randomized studies of interventions), as METHODS 5.3 provides when order is not randomized or counterbalanced (applied to fixed-order laboratory studies by the senior author's decision of 25 October 2026); it concerns the comparisons between the three conditions.
can_establish: How many urine specimens, and how many of six non-smoking adults per condition, exceeded each immunoassay screening cut-off and the GC-MS confirmation cut-off after one hour seated beside six people smoking cannabis in a small sealed or ventilated chamber, and how long THCCOOH stayed detectable under these three conditions.
cannot_establish: What happens after ordinary, longer or repeated real-world exposure, vaping or other distances (the exposure was deliberately brief, extreme and obvious); the separate effects of potency and ventilation (fixed order, different groups of six, and less cannabis smoked in Session 1 after eye irritation); or anything about blood, oral fluid, hair or impairment, which this paper does not report.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers recruited through newspaper advertisements, flyers on campus and community bulletin boards, and word of mouth (Experimental › Participants, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Smoking participants: self-reported cannabis use at least twice a week in the prior 90 days, not trying to quit, urine positive for cannabis (more than 50 ng/mL THCCOOH) and negative for other drugs and alcohol at screening and at each admission. Non-smoking participants: healthy volunteers with lifetime cannabis use but no cannabis or other illicit drug use in the previous 6 months by self-report, urine-negative at screening and at admission (pp. 2-3). Written informed consent; approved by the Johns Hopkins Medicine Institutional Review Board; participants were paid (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Only non- or minimal tobacco use; no tobacco during participation (p. 3). Each non-smoking participant took part in one session only; of the eight smoking participants, four took part in all three sessions, two in two sessions and two in one (Participants, 3rd paragraph, p. 3).
sample.demographics: Non-smoking participants: 9 women and 9 men; mean age 28 years (SD 7, range 20-45); weight 74 kg (SD 12, 55-98); BMI 24.7 (SD 3.6, 18.7-33.0); 12 White non-Hispanic, 3 African American, 2 Hispanic or Latino, 1 Asian. Smoking participants: 3 women and 5 men; mean age 29 (SD 6, 24-40); mean 12 years of cannabis smoking (SD 7, 2-25), 28 days of use in the past month (SD 2, 25-30), 1.5 g a day (SD 2, 0.4-5.2), all self-reported (Participants, 2nd paragraph, p. 3). Characteristics of the six non-smoking participants in each session are not reported.
sample.attrition: All 18 non-smoking participants completed their session and the supervised 34-hour stay. 2 of 252 scheduled urine specimens are missing, both from participant 8 in Session 2 (2 hours and 4-6 hours) (Table I, p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: Paid volunteers, not a population sample. The non-smoking participants had all used cannabis at some time (abstinent at least 6 months by self-report, urine-negative), so none was cannabis-naive. How non-smoking participants were allocated to sessions is not described and their characteristics by session are not given. The smoking participants were experienced daily or near-daily smokers; the authors suggest that people who smoke occasionally may produce more sidestream smoke because they inhale less often, but presume they would burn less cannabis overall (Discussion › Study limitations, 3rd paragraph, p. 11).

exposure.measurement: Exposure was the experimental condition; it was not measured at the non-smoking participants. Cannabis cigarettes were weighed before and after each session to give the amount the smoking participants consumed (Experimental cannabis exposure conditions, p. 3; Results, p. 5). Room-air THC was not measured. Smoke density was reported from observation (heavy in Sessions 1 and 2; visible but greatly reduced in Session 3) and shown in one photograph of Session 2 (Figure 2, p. 5). Staff observed that no non-smoking participant tried to inhale the smoke actively (p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, not doses for any person. One 1-hour session per non-smoking participant, seated in alternate seats with six smoking participants; all wore disposable paper clothing and booties, washed hands and face afterwards and moved to a cannabis-free area (pp. 3-4). Cigarettes from the US federal research supply: lower potency 0.92 g each (SD 0.06), 5.3% total THC (SD 0.48%), 0.01% CBD, 0.35% CBN; higher potency 1.0 g each (SD 0.04), 11.3% total THC (SD 0.29%), 0.08% CBD, 0.76% CBN (Cannabis cigarettes, p. 3). Cannabis consumed in the room: 10.3 g (Session 1), 14.4 g (Session 2), 16.5 g (Session 3) (Results, p. 5). Editors' arithmetic from these figures: total THC in the cannabis consumed was about 0.55 g, 1.63 g and 1.86 g, so Session 2 burned about three times as much THC as Session 1. Session 3 ventilation: 11.2 air changes per hour, described as comparable to home air-conditioning (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Non-smoking participants were urine-negative for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA, opioids, PCP and alcohol at screening and at admission; no tobacco was allowed during the study (pp. 2-3). They could not eat or drink during the session or until the first oral fluid specimen afterwards (p. 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Non-smoking participants: no cannabis in the previous 6 months by self-report; every pre-exposure urine specimen was negative by GC-MS (below 0.75 ng/mL) and by immunoassay (Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, 1st paragraph, p. 5; Table I, pp. 6-9).

comparison.controls: No unexposed control group. Each non-smoking participant's pre-exposure specimen is his or her own baseline; the three conditions are compared with one another, each with a different group of six non-smoking participants tested in a different week.
comparison.matching: None reported between the three session groups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a premorbid question. Not measured or not reported: room-air THC; each non-smoking participant's distance from each smoking participant beyond alternate seating; breathing or activity during the session; the session groups' characteristics; whether the smoking participants knew the potency; urine dilution adjustment (creatinine and specific gravity were measured but results were not normalized).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Non-smoking participants were urine-negative for other drugs and alcohol at admission (p. 3).

outcomes.instruments: Urinary THCCOOH after alkaline hydrolysis by GC-MS at Clinical Reference Laboratory: limit of detection and of quantification 0.75 ng/mL, upper limit of linearity 600 ng/mL, single-point calibration at 15 ng/mL, four controls per batch (Analytical methods, p. 4). Immunoassays: Microgenics DRI at Clinical Reference Laboratory on bottle A (CRL1) and again on bottle B (CRL2), 20 and 50 ng/mL; KIMS at MEDTOX, 20 and 50 ng/mL; EMIT II Plus at MetroLab-Legacy, 20 and 50 ng/mL; CEDIA at One Source, 20, 50, 75 and 100 ng/mL (p. 4); and EMIT II 5B3 at Lab Corp, 50 ng/mL, which appears in the Results and Table III but not in the Methods (pp. 5, 11). Volume, creatinine, specific gravity and pH were recorded for every specimen (Table I).
outcomes.validity_norms: The confirmation cut-off of 15 ng/mL THCCOOH is the one in the SAMHSA Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs; the Discussion calls 50 ng/mL the screening cut-off those guidelines recommend and says some private, non-regulated programmes screen at 20 ng/mL (pp. 4, 10).
outcomes.operationalization: A presumptive (screening) positive was an immunoassay response at or above the cut-off; for confirmation, GC-MS THCCOOH at least 15 ng/mL. Each immunoassay result was classed as a true or false positive or negative against GC-MS at 15 ng/mL, giving sensitivity, specificity and agreement (Sensitivity, specificity and agreement, pp. 4-5). Concentrations were not adjusted for urine dilution.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests are reported; all results are counts and concentrations, tabulated for every specimen (Table I). 14 = GC-MS THCCOOH plus the 13 immunoassay-by-cut-off columns of Table III.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the laboratories. The authors list non-blindness to the ventilation conditions as a limitation (p. 10). The outcomes are instrumental measurements.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only: no intervals or tests. Peak THCCOOH per non-smoking participant, mean/median: Session 1, 11.2/9.6 ng/mL (range 1.9-20.1); Session 2, 28.3/24.9 (5.5-57.5); Session 3, 7.5/8.5 (1.3-15.5) (Table II, p. 10). Specimens at or above 15 ng/mL: 3, 22 and 2 by session, 27 of 250 (10.8%) (pp. 5, 10). Screening positives at 20 ng/mL by session (DRI, KIMS, EMIT II, CEDIA): 12, 6, 12, 6; 22, 8, 22, 12; 0, 0, 1, 0 specimens (p. 9). At 50 ng/mL: 1 of 250 specimens, on 1 of 5 laboratories' assays; none at 75 or 100 ng/mL, cut-offs run on CEDIA only (pp. 4-5; Table III, p. 11). Editors' recount of Table I (minus signs read from the rendered pages) reproduces every per-session count and every true-positive, false-positive and false-negative count of Table III, and shows that the 250 specimens include the 18 taken before exposure: 27 of 232 post-exposure specimens (11.6%; Wilson 95% interval 8.1% to 16.4%) reached 15 ng/mL, from 7 of 18 non-smoking participants (Wilson 95% interval 20% to 61%); 12 of 18 (44% to 84%) had at least one screening positive at 20 ng/mL on some assay (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All urine results are tabulated for every specimen, which allows the counts to be checked. Other outcomes (blood, oral fluid, hair, vital signs, subjective and cognitive measures) are deferred to other reports (p. 4). The EMIT II 5B3 assay at Lab Corp, the only assay positive at 50 ng/mL, is not described in the Methods.
analysis.power: Not addressed; six non-smoking participants per condition and one session per condition.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After one hour in about 12 m2 of floor space beside six people smoking cannabis freely, every non-smoking participant had detectable THCCOOH in urine within 0.25-3 hours, and 12 of 18 still did at 30-34 hours. At the 50 ng/mL federal workplace screening cut-off, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive, on one laboratory's assay (the other four called it negative); none did at 75 or 100 ng/mL, cut-offs run on the CEDIA assay only. At a 20 ng/mL screen, 5 of 6 participants in Session 1, all 6 in Session 2 and 1 of 6 in the ventilated Session 3 had at least one positive on some assay (editors' count); 27 specimens from 7 participants reached the 15 ng/mL confirmation level, 22 of them in the unventilated high-potency session.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that extreme exposure can produce positive urine tests at commonly used cut-offs, but that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure, and confined to circumstances where exposure is obvious (p. 1). 'Rare' fits the 50 ng/mL screen (1 of 250 specimens, on 1 of 5 assays) but not a 20 ng/mL screen, at which 12 of 18 people screened positive at least once and 3 to 7 of 18, depending on the assay, would have had a confirmed positive (editors' count). 'Limited to the hours immediately post-exposure' is loose: screening positives continued for 2-22 hours after the first (p. 9), one EMIT II screen was positive in the 26-30-hour pool and that specimen held 15.6 ng/mL (participant 37, Table I, p. 7). 'Only where exposure is obvious' was not tested, because only obvious exposure was studied. That THCCOOH rose with potency and fell with ventilation rests on three fixed-order sessions of six different people, and Session 1 burned about a third as much THC as Session 2 after eye irritation cut smoking short (p. 5; editors' arithmetic). The authors do say the conditions were extreme and can only partially be extrapolated (p. 11). A headline that secondhand smoke can make you fail a drug test overstates the paper for the federal workplace screen; a headline that it cannot overstates it for 20 ng/mL screening.

timeline.event: Earlier passive-exposure experiments in unventilated rooms and cars with cannabis of 2.8% THC or less (Perez-Reyes et al., 1983; Law et al., 1984; Morland et al., 1985; Cone & Johnson, 1986; Mule et al., 1988; and others), listed in this paper's Introduction (p. 2); not read for this card.

Cone et al. (1987): 1-hour exposures to 2.8% THC smoke on six consecutive days gave only suggestive evidence of accumulation or higher positivity rates, as described by this paper (p. 11); not read for this card.
Niedbala et al. (2005): four non-smoking participants with four smoking participants in an unventilated van, 5.4% or 10.4% THC cannabis (as described, p. 2); not read for this card.
Rohrich et al. (2010): eight non-smoking participants spent 3 hours in a ventilated Dutch coffee shop (as described, p. 2); not read for this card.
This paper published online (Advance Access, 17 October 2014; issue 39(1), 2015), as Part I; blood, oral fluid, hair and effect results announced for other reports (p. 4).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper says its results are not unlike those of the earlier passive-exposure studies it cites, most at lower potency, in which non-smoking participants also had THC and metabolites in their urine (pp. 2, 10); those studies were not read for this card, so 'partially replicated' rests on the authors' account. No repetition of these exact conditions is reported, and later studies were not read. The results describe one brief, extreme, obvious exposure in a small room at the potencies used; longer, repeated, ordinary or vaping exposures are untested here.

funding.funder: SAMHSA provided financial support for the study; NIDA provided material support (the cannabis) and financial support for Dr Herrmann's participation (T32-DA07209) (Funding, p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement as such. The Acknowledgments state that E.J.C. is a consultant to the Division of Workplace Programs of SAMHSA and holds an adjunct professorship at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine; R.V., G.E.B. and E.S.H. are with Johns Hopkins School of Medicine; J.M.M. is an employee of RTI International; C.L. and R.F. are employees of SAMHSA (p. 11).
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors work for SAMHSA's Division of Workplace Programs, the office whose federal workplace testing cut-offs the study evaluates, and the first author consults for it; RTI International characterized and rolled the cigarettes (p. 3). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized or counterbalanced exposure study with larger groups and measured room-air THC, covering ordinary ventilation, distances, repeated and longer exposures and vaping, in cannabis-naive as well as previously exposed volunteers, with dilution-normalized urine results at both the 50/15 ng/mL federal cut-offs and lower private screening cut-offs.

domains.note: Each condition had a different group of six non-smoking participants; how they were allocated to sessions is not described, their characteristics by session are not reported and nothing was adjusted. Each condition is also tied to its session's week, order and smoking group (8 people across 18 places), so potency and ventilation cannot be separated from these session-level differences.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Every non-smoking participant who entered a session was followed for 34 hours and analysed; selection into the study did not depend on anything after exposure.
The conditions were set by the investigators and recorded at the time: assayed cigarette potency (5.3% and 11.3% total THC) and measured ventilation (11.2 air changes per hour) (p. 3).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Exposure differed between sessions in ways the design did not intend: in Session 1, after eye irritation, some smoking participants reported stopping early, to avoid adding smoke or because of social pressure, so 10.3 g was consumed against 14.4 g and 16.5 g (about one third of the THC burned in Session 2, editors' arithmetic), and goggle use changed after Session 1 (p. 5). The door was opened for bathroom breaks of about 5 minutes in Sessions 2 and 3 (p. 3). No one was blind to ventilation (p. 10). The potency contrast is the most affected; the ventilation contrast is, if anything, conservative, because more cannabis was burned in Session 3.

250 of 252 scheduled specimens analysed; all 18 non-smoking participants completed. The two missing specimens (participant 8, 2 hours and 4-6 hours) fall in the window when others peaked, so that participant's peak may be understated.

GC-MS is objective and validated (limit of quantification 0.75 ng/mL), with single-point calibration at 15 ng/mL. Concerns: the assay that gave the only 50 ng/mL positive (Lab Corp EMIT II 5B3) is not described in the Methods; repeating DRI on bottle B turned 7 true positives into false negatives, so results near the 20 ng/mL cut-off varied between runs; laboratory blinding is not reported; concentrations were not normalized for urine dilution.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol, but every specimen's GC-MS and four 20 ng/mL immunoassay results are tabulated (Table I), and the paper's counts can be reproduced from them. Non-urine outcomes are openly deferred to other reports.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the investigators set the three conditions but ran them in a fixed order, neither randomized nor counterbalanced, with a different group of six non-smoking participants in each (METHODS 5.3; the senior author's decision of 25 October 2026 on fixed-order laboratory studies); RoB 2, used in the first pass, applies to randomized or counterbalanced comparisons. The overall judgment, serious, follows the worst domains and concerns the comparisons between conditions: fixed order, a different small group in each session and an unplanned drop in smoking in Session 1. The within-condition results are another matter: urine concentrations and positivity counts are objective, complete and fully tabulated, so they can be cited as what happened to these six people per condition; their limits are small numbers and deliberately extreme, obvious exposure (indirectness), not bias. Citable for: after 1 hour beside six people smoking 5.3% or 11.3% THC cannabis in a sealed 12 m2 chamber, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive at 50 ng/mL, many did at 20 ng/mL, and some reached the 15 ng/mL confirmation level, mostly without ventilation. Not citable for: how often ordinary secondhand exposure causes positive workplace tests, or the size of potency or ventilation effects.

key_findings.finding: Design and conditions: 18 non-smoking participants, 6 per session, each in one 1-hour session seated in alternate seats with 6 smoking participants (8 different people across the sessions), in a sealed chamber of 3.05 m x 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling. Session 1: 5.3% total THC cigarettes, no ventilation; Session 2: 11.3%, no ventilation; Session 3: 11.3% with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour. Sessions at weekly or longer intervals in this fixed order; smoking was ad libitum. Urine: about 1 hour before, then at 0.25, 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours and in pools to 34 hours.
key_findings.locator: Experimental › Participants, 3rd paragraph; Chamber construction and layout, 1st paragraph; Experimental cannabis exposure conditions (p. 3); Urine collections, 1st paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Participants: non-smoking participants were 9 women and 9 men, mean age 28 (range 20-45), all with lifetime cannabis use but none in the previous 6 months by self-report, urine-negative for cannabis and other drugs at screening and admission, with no or minimal tobacco use. Smoking participants (3 women, 5 men) reported a mean 12 years of cannabis smoking, 28 days of use in the past month and 1.5 g a day.
key_findings.locator: Experimental › Participants, 1st paragraph (pp. 2-3) and 2nd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Cannabis consumed in the room by the six smoking participants: 10.3 g in Session 1 (5.3% THC), 14.4 g in Session 2 and 16.5 g in Session 3 (11.3% THC); per person mean 1.7 g (range 1.1-2.5), 2.4 g (1.6-2.9) and 2.8 g (2.1-3.4). In Session 1 most participants did not wear goggles at first and then had substantial eye irritation; some smoking participants reported stopping earlier than they otherwise would have, to avoid adding smoke to the room, and others reported stopping because they felt social pressure after others had stopped; after Session 1 everyone wore goggles part-time or full-time. Smoke accumulated heavily in Sessions 1 and 2 and was visible but greatly reduced in Session 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis use and reported smoke effects, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: about 0.55 g, 1.63 g and 1.86 g of total THC in the cannabis consumed, so the Session 1 to Session 2 contrast is about threefold in THC burned, not only a difference in potency.

key_findings.finding: Every pre-exposure specimen was negative by GC-MS and immunoassay. After exposure THCCOOH became detectable (at least 0.75 ng/mL) in all 18 non-smoking participants within 0.25 to 3 hours, peaked 2-11 hours after exposure, and was still detectable in the 30-34-hour pool in 12 of 18 (67%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Peak urinary THCCOOH per non-smoking participant (ng/mL): Session 1: 7, 6.8, 19.3, 12.2, 1.9, 20.1 (mean 11.2, median 9.6); Session 2: 10.8, 57.5, 46.3, 20.1, 5.5, 29.7 (mean 28.3, median 24.9); Session 3: 2.4, 8.7, 8.2, 9, 1.3, 15.5 (mean 7.5, median 8.5). The last detectable specimen came at a mean of 28.8, 31.3 and 25.3 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table II
key_findings.note: Time to peak for the sixth participant in Sessions 2 and 3 does not match Table I (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 27 specimens reached the 15 ng/mL GC-MS confirmation cut-off of the federal workplace guidelines: 3 in Session 1 (participants 13 and 16), 22 in Session 2 (participants 23, 37, 38 and 41) and 2 in Session 3 (participant 36). 17 specimens exceeded 20 ng/mL, 16 of them in Session 2, excreted 2-22 hours after exposure; none in Session 3 exceeded 20 ng/mL. The paper gives the 27 as 10.8% of 250 specimens.
key_findings.locator: Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 10)
key_findings.note: Editors' recount of Table I: the 250 include the 18 pre-exposure specimens, so 27 of 232 post-exposure specimens (11.6%) reached 15 ng/mL; they came from 7 of 18 participants (2 of 6, 4 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session).

key_findings.finding: No specimen screened positive at 100 or 75 ng/mL, cut-offs at which only the CEDIA assay was run. At 50 ng/mL, the screening cut-off of the federal guidelines, one specimen of 250 (0.4%) screened positive, and only on one assay (Lab Corp EMIT II 5B3): participant 37, 4 hours after Session 2, a 24-year-old woman of 98.1 kg (BMI 29.9), whose specimen held 46.3 ng/mL THCCOOH, creatinine 149.7 mg/dL, specific gravity 1.0218. The other four laboratories reported it negative at 50 ng/mL and all reported it positive at 20 ng/mL. At 50 ng/mL the other five assay columns of Table III detected none of the 27 specimens at or above 15 ng/mL (sensitivity 0); the Lab Corp assay detected 1 (3.7%).
key_findings.locator: Experimental › Analytical methods, 3rd paragraph (p. 4); Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 5); Table III, upper panel (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: At a 20 ng/mL screening cut-off, which the authors say some private, non-regulated programmes use, positive specimens by session and assay (DRI, KIMS, EMIT II, CEDIA) were: Session 1, 12, 6, 12, 6; Session 2, 22, 8, 22, 12; Session 3, 0, 0, 1, 0. The first presumptive positives came in specimens collected 1-4 hours after exposure, and individuals then continued to test positive for 2-22 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, last paragraph (begins on p. 5, continues at the top of p. 9); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 10)
key_findings.note: Editors' recount of Table I reproduces these counts, counting a response at or above the cut-off as positive. Participants with at least one 20 ng/mL screening positive on any assay: 5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session (12 of 18). Participant 36's only positive was EMIT II in the 4-6-hour pool, and participant 37 had an EMIT II positive in the 26-30-hour pool.

key_findings.finding: Against GC-MS at 15 ng/mL, at the 20 ng/mL cut-off (250 specimens each): CEDIA 15 true positives, 3 false positives, 12 false negatives (sensitivity 55.6%, specificity 98.7%); DRI on bottle A 23, 11, 4 (85.2%, 95.1%); DRI on bottle B 16, 9, 11 (59.3%, 96.0%); KIMS 10, 4, 17 (37.0%, 98.2%); EMIT II Plus 25, 10, 2 (92.6%, 95.5%). Repeating DRI on bottle B turned 2 false positives into true negatives and 7 true positives into false negatives. The authors say the differences between assays were likely due to differences in cross-reactivity with THCCOOH glucuronide, which package inserts appear to report only for EMIT II (79%) and KIMS (44.1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity of immunoassays, 2nd paragraph (p. 9); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 10); Table III, lower panel (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: The 27 specimens at or above 15 ng/mL that the 50 ng/mL screens missed had mean THCCOOH 24.6 ng/mL (range 15.0-57.5) and mean creatinine 102.6 mg/dL (19.7-175.6); 22 (81.5%) came from Session 2, 3 (11.1%) from Session 1 and 2 (7.4%) from Session 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity of immunoassays, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table I: in a two-step programme screening at 20 ng/mL and confirming at 15 ng/mL, the non-smoking participants with at least one specimen reported positive would have numbered 3 of 18 with KIMS, 6 of 18 with DRI (bottle A) or CEDIA, and 7 of 18 with EMIT II Plus, all from the unventilated sessions except participant 36 (Session 3, EMIT II only). Table I gives only 20 ng/mL results; from the Results text and Table III, at the federal 50 and 15 ng/mL cut-offs 1 of 18 would have been positive with the Lab Corp assay and none with the other assays.
key_findings.locator: Table I (pp. 6-9; editors' count; true positives as defined on pp. 4-5); for the 50 ng/mL clause, Results › Urinalyses of non-smoker specimens, 4th paragraph (p. 5) and Table III, upper panel (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Authors' summary: extreme exposure can produce positive urine tests at commonly used cut-offs, but positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure, and to occur only where exposure is obvious; THCCOOH generally rose with potency and ventilation substantially reduced exposure. The Conclusions add that exposure produced positives at a 20 ng/mL screen but only a single positive at 50 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Conclusions (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: fixed order of conditions, no blinding to ventilation, a single session and few participants per condition, possible social influences among the smoking participants; distance from the smoke and duration matter; results are most representative of short-term extreme exposure and can only partially be extrapolated to other conditions. An earlier six-day study at 2.8% THC gave only suggestive evidence of accumulation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Study limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding and ties as printed: SAMHSA funded the study; NIDA supplied the cannabis and funded Dr Herrmann (T32-DA07209). E.J.C. consults for SAMHSA's Division of Workplace Programs; C.L. and R.F. are SAMHSA employees; J.M.M. is an employee of RTI International.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Funding

reporting_issues.issue: The denominator of 250 specimens (14 per participant, 2 missing) includes the 18 specimens taken before exposure, which all tested negative. The 10.8% at the confirmation level, the 0.4% positivity at 50 ng/mL, the 99.6% negative and the true-negative, specificity and agreement figures of Table III all use it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small but systematic: among the 232 post-exposure specimens, 11.6% reached 15 ng/mL (editors' recount), and specificities at 20 ng/mL are 94.6% (DRI bottle A), 98.0% (KIMS), 95.1% (EMIT II Plus) and 98.5% (CEDIA) instead of 95.1%, 98.2%, 95.5% and 98.7%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name four laboratories (Clinical Reference Laboratory and three others, p. 4), but the only positive at 50 ng/mL came from a fifth, Lab Corp (EMIT II 5B3), which appears only in the Results and Table III. The Results also say all five laboratories reported that specimen positive at 20 ng/mL, yet no 20 ng/mL result from Lab Corp is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: The assay, specimen bottle and timing behind the single positive at the federal screening cut-off cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table II gives the time to peak as 4 hours for the sixth participant of Session 2 (participant 41) and of Session 3 (participant 36), but their peak values (29.7 and 15.5 ng/mL) are from the 4-6-hour pools in Table I, which the table's footnote dates at the 5-hour midpoint (the 4-hour specimens held 29.1 and 15.0 ng/mL).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: with 5 hours, the Session 2 and 3 mean times to peak would be 3.8 and 5.8 hours instead of 3.7 and 5.7 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says six experienced smokers smoked in the sessions; the Methods describe eight different smoking participants, four in all three sessions, two in two and two in one. The Methods also say a 'non-smoker smoker' took a bathroom break of about 5 minutes in Session 2, without saying whether a non-smoking participant left the chamber.
reporting_issues.consequence: The smoke-producing group changed between sessions, one more difference between conditions; if a non-smoking participant left, that person's exposure was shortened.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says THCCOOH generally increased with THC potency, and the Conclusions say potency and ventilation were demonstrated to be two major factors (pp. 1, 11), but Session 1 differed from Session 2 not only in potency: less cannabis was smoked (10.3 g against 14.4 g) after eye irritation and, by the smoking participants' own reports, social pressure; goggle use changed; and different people took part, in a fixed order.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Session 1 to 2 difference reflects about three times as much THC burned (editors' arithmetic), not potency alone; the potency effect cannot be separated.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say first presumptive positives appeared 1-4 hours after exposure and positivity lasted 2-22 hours, but participant 36's only positive came from the 4-6-hour pool and participant 37 screened positive on EMIT II again in the 26-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL by GC-MS).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the time window of positives is slightly longer than the text and abstract suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists four immunoassays at cut-offs of 20, 50, 75 and 100 ng/mL and reports no positives at 100 and 75 ng/mL, and the Results say all specimens screened negative at these cut-offs for all screening assays (pp. 1, 5); but the Methods and Table III show that only the CEDIA assay was run at 75 and 100 ng/mL (p. 4; p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of positives at 75 and 100 ng/mL rests on one assay, while at 50 ng/mL the assays disagreed (one positive, on one of six assay columns).

design_detail: Multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (GWPCARE2; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02224703), funded by GW Research Ltd, which was responsible for its design and conduct, at 38 enrolling centres (of 43) in the United States, Spain, Poland, the Netherlands, Australia and Israel, recruiting from 13 April 2015 to 10 November 2017. 199 children and adolescents aged 2 to 18 with Dravet syndrome, taking at least one antiepileptic drug and having at least 4 convulsive seizures in a 4-week baseline, were randomized 2:2:1:1 to add-on cannabidiol oral solution at 10 mg/kg/d or 20 mg/kg/d, or to placebo at the volume of either dose (the two placebo groups pooled): 4-week baseline, 14-week treatment period (2 weeks of dose escalation, 12 of maintenance), taper of up to 10 days and 4-week safety follow-up. Primary end point: change from baseline in convulsive-seizure frequency over the 14-week treatment period, counted daily by caregivers and analysed by negative binomial regression.
can_establish: That, in children and adolescents with Dravet syndrome whose convulsive seizures were not controlled by their antiepileptic drugs, adding this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution at 10 or at 20 mg/kg/d reduced caregiver-recorded convulsive seizures over 14 weeks more than placebo, and how often adverse events occurred in each of the three groups.
cannot_establish: Whether 10 and 20 mg/kg/d differ in efficacy (neither the protocol nor the statistical analysis plan specified a test of one dose against the other: the protocol named each dose against placebo as the major comparisons and said the dose response would be explored, and the plan's eight hierarchical tests all compare a dose with placebo; the sample-size calculation assumed the same response at both doses, and caregivers and investigators knew each child's dose level; Supplement 1 pp. 80, 116 and 126 of 167); whether raising the dose from 10 to 20 mg/kg/d helps a child who has not responded (the protocol kept each child at the dose level assigned at randomization, allowing the dose to be suspended or reduced for poor tolerability and brought back towards the target, with no provision for going above it; the statistical analysis plan says that 4 children randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level, 2 given cannabidiol and 2 placebo by Figure 1, received higher doses incorrectly, without giving a reason, and they stayed in their randomized groups for efficacy; Supplement 1 pp. 41–42 and 122 of 167); effects beyond 14 weeks, of doses below 10 mg/kg/d, of other cannabidiol products, in adults or in other epilepsies; or whether the effect depends on clobazam (the interaction test was prespecified in the statistical analysis plan, Supplement 1 p. 140 of 167, but its P value is not given).

sample.recruitment: Patients at 38 enrolling centres of 43 (United States 23, Spain 7, Poland 3, Netherlands 2, Australia 2, Israel 1), recruited from 13 April 2015 to 10 November 2017, follow-up completed 9 April 2018. 285 were screened and 86 excluded (52 did not meet the eligibility criteria, 29 for another reason, 5 withdrew or were withdrawn by a parent or guardian, 3 by investigator decision; 3 had more than one reason); 199 were randomized (abstract, PDF p. 1; Methods › Trial Design, PDF p. 2; Figure 1 and legend, PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 2 to 18 (inclusive); confirmed diagnosis of Dravet syndrome, with the diagnosis and seizure types verified by the independent Epilepsy Study Consortium; seizures incompletely controlled by current antiepileptic drugs; taking at least 1 antiepileptic drug; at least 4 convulsive seizures in the 4-week baseline; epilepsy medicines and non-drug treatments (ketogenic diet, vagus-nerve stimulation) stable for 4 weeks before screening and throughout. Excluded: a clinically significant unstable illness other than epilepsy in the 4 weeks before screening, alcohol or other substance-use problems, recreational or medicinal cannabis in the previous 3 months, and felbamate taken for less than 1 year (Methods › Patients and Procedures, PDF p. 2). Protocol amendment 5 (29 June 2015) added a minimum number of days of voice-response diary entries during baseline as a condition of eligibility (Supplement 1 p. 107 of 167, Table 1.1.1-1); eTable 1 sets it at 25 days of the baseline period, children below it being ineligible, and counts the 4 convulsive seizures over the first 28 days of the baseline period (Supplement 2 p. 2, inclusion criteria 5 and 9). The full criteria (eTable 1, Supplement 2 pp. 2–3) also exclude, among others: a history or presence of alcohol or substance abuse (the criterion's wording) in the previous 2 years, or daily consumption of 5 or more alcohol-containing drinks; any use of recreational or medicinal cannabis or of synthetic cannabinoid medicines (including Sativex) in the 3 months before entry, or unwillingness to abstain during the trial; known or suspected hypersensitivity to cannabinoids or to the excipients (eg, sesame oil); another investigational product in the previous 6 months; clinically significant abnormal laboratory values or ECG; significantly impaired liver function at screening or randomization (ALT or AST above 5 times the upper limit of normal, or above 3 times together with raised bilirubin or INR or with symptoms), children later found to meet this criterion being withdrawn; and any history of suicidal behaviour or suicidal ideation of type 4 or 5 on the C-SSRS at screening.
sample.demographics: ITT set of 198: mean age 9.3 years (SD 4.4); 104 female (52.5%) and 94 male (47.5%); 176 (88.9%) white; 93 (47.0%) from the United States. A median of 4 antiepileptic drugs tried before (range 0–19) and 3 being taken (range 1–5): valproate 139 (70.2%), clobazam 126 (63.6%); by the editors' addition of Table 1, stiripentol 71 (35.9%), levetiracetam 54 and topiramate 46. Ketogenic diet 17 (8.6%); vagus-nerve stimulator 27 (13.6%). Commonest seizure types at screening: generalized tonic–clonic 150 (75.8%), myoclonic 100 (50.5%), absence of any type 83 (41.9%), complex partial 80 (40.4%). Median 12 convulsive seizures in the 4-week baseline (IQR 6–33) (Results › Patients, PDF p. 4; Table 1, PDF p. 5).
sample.attrition: 9 of 199 did not complete treatment: 3 randomized to 10 mg/kg/d (1 never treated and withdrawn by the investigator, randomized in error according to the statistical analysis plan, Supplement 1 pp. 121–122 of 167, 2 for other reasons) and 6 given 20 mg/kg/d (5 for adverse events, 1 withdrew or was withdrawn by a parent or guardian); none in the placebo group. 190 completed treatment (64, 61 and 65) and 186 of them (97.9%) entered the open-label extension (63, 58 and 65). Efficacy (ITT) sets 66, 67 and 65; safety sets 64, 69 and 65, because 2 patients randomized to 10 mg/kg/d, described in the article as titrated above the target dose, were counted with 20 mg/kg/d for all safety analyses (Figure 1, PDF p. 3; Results › Patients, PDF p. 4; Table 2 footnote b, PDF p. 7). According to the statistical analysis plan, a blinded data review found that 4 patients randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (cannabidiol or its placebo volume; 2 and 2 in Figure 1) had incorrectly received up to 20 mg/kg/d (for placebo, the equivalent volume), 1 of them up to 50 mg/kg/d, the plan not saying in which arm; they were assigned to the 20 mg/kg/d groups for safety reporting and analysed as randomized for efficacy (Supplement 1 p. 122 of 167, SAP §5.2.1–5.2.2).
sample.selection_effects: Specialist-centre children with severe, treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome whose families accepted a placebo-controlled trial; 88.9% were white, which the authors list as limiting generalizability (Limitations, PDF p. 7). 29 of the 86 screen failures were excluded for an unspecified other reason (Figure 1). Chance imbalance: the pooled placebo group had a higher median baseline frequency of convulsive seizures (17 vs 14 and 9 per 28 days) and of all seizures (46 vs 35 and 26) (Table 1, PDF p. 5), which the authors offer, with high patient and caregiver expectations of efficacy, as a possible partial explanation of the large placebo response (Discussion, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 7). Recruitment continued until November 2017, after the first Dravet trial of this product had been published (Devinsky et al., 2017; reference 19).

exposure.measurement: Randomized assignment. Caregivers counted seizures daily by interactive voice-response system after instruction on countable seizure types; use of trial medication, concomitant medicines and adverse events were recorded in a paper diary (Methods › Procedures, PDF pp. 2–3). Dosing adherence, diary completion and blood levels of cannabidiol or of the other antiepileptic drugs are not reported in the article, although the statistical analysis plan provided for summaries of treatment compliance, of unreported voice-response diary days and of plasma levels of the concomitant antiepileptic drugs (Supplement 1 pp. 141 and 149–151 of 167). Blood samples for cannabidiol and its major metabolites were taken in this trial (added by amendment 3, limited by amendment 5 to children weighing at least 20 kg; Supplement 1 pp. 106–107 of 167), but the statistical analysis plan left their analysis out of its scope (p. 115) and the article reports no cannabidiol levels; urine cannabinoid analyses were not done because no consented patient could give a urine sample (p. 109).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: plant-derived, highly purified cannabidiol oral solution, 100 mg/mL (Epidiolex in the United States, Epidyolex in the European Union), or matching placebo solution (excipients only), supplied in identical 100-mL amber glass bottles; target 10 or 20 mg/kg/d (or the equivalent volume of placebo) in two equal daily doses for 14 weeks, escalated from 2.5 mg/kg/d over the first 2 weeks, then tapered over up to 10 days. Two patients randomized to 10 mg/kg/d, and two in the placebo group assigned the 10 mg/kg/d volume, received more than that dose or volume (Figure 1). The original protocol (version 1, July 2014) defined the lower dose as half the higher one, the higher to be set by the data safety monitoring committee of Part A of the sponsor's earlier Dravet study GWEP1332 at no more than 20 mg/kg/d (amendment 5, June 2015, named them 20 and 10 mg/kg/d); each child was to stay at the assigned target dose level throughout maintenance, the investigator could suspend dosing during titration or reduce the dose for poor tolerability, with a return to the target encouraged, and the protocol made no provision for going above the target (Supplement 1 pp. 31–32, 41–42 and 107 of 167). The statistical analysis plan calls the higher doses received at the 10 mg/kg/d level incorrect (p. 122). Investigators were to keep the doses of other medicines unchanged, with adjustments allowed for adverse events (Methods › Procedures, PDF pp. 2–3). No purity figure is given; the authors state that other cannabidiol formulations vary in purity, excipients and consistency (Discussion, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 6).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients continued their antiepileptic drugs (median 3). Across all groups, clobazam dosage was adjusted in 20 of the 126 patients taking it (15.9%) and valproate dosage in 19 of 139 (13.7%); one patient given 10 mg/kg/d started clobazam because of prolonged seizures and one given 20 mg/kg/d started valproate after a serious adverse event of status epilepticus; changes in other antiepileptic drugs were infrequent (Results › Adverse Events, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 6). In eTable 3 (safety set, no tests), somnolence, fatigue, lethargy or sedation occurred in 29.3%, 43.2% and 57.1% of the children taking clobazam (placebo, 10 and 20 mg/kg/d) and in 16.7%, 10.0% and 18.5% of those not taking it; clobazam dose was adjusted in 1, 8 and 11 children and valproate dose in 4, 4 and 11, mostly decreases in the cannabidiol groups (Supplement 2 p. 6). Recreational or medicinal cannabis in the previous 3 months was an exclusion criterion (PDF p. 2). The original protocol ended a child's evaluable period the day before a relevant change in antiepileptic or prohibited medicines (Supplement 1 p. 81 of 167); the statistical analysis plan uses the term evaluable period without defining it (p. 117), its treatment period runs from Day 1 to Day 99 or the last dose with no rule on medicine changes (p. 121), and its blinded data review was to assess changes in concomitant antiepileptic drugs (p. 118); amendment 6 (February 2017) allowed antiepileptic-drug adjustments for suspected drug–drug interactions after discussion with the sponsor's medical monitor (p. 108). How the clobazam and valproate dose changes were handled in the efficacy analysis is not stated.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Placebo solution containing the excipients only, in identical bottles, given at the volume of the 10 mg/kg/d dose (32 patients) or of the 20 mg/kg/d dose (33 patients); the two placebo groups were pooled for efficacy and safety (Methods › Procedures, PDF pp. 2–3; Figure 1 and legend, PDF p. 3). In the protocol, the placebo solution contained the active solution's excipients at the same concentrations (sesame oil to volume, anhydrous ethanol 79 mg/mL, sucralose 0.5 mg/mL, strawberry flavouring 0.2 mg/mL) without cannabidiol, and both were supplied in 100-mL amber glass bottles with child-resistant caps, dispensed by pack number assigned through the voice-response system (Supplement 1 pp. 34 and 40 of 167, Tables 5.1-1 and 5.2-1); the protocol describes no test of whether the two solutions could be told apart by appearance, taste or smell.
comparison.matching: Randomization 2:2:1:1 in blocks of 6, stratified by age group (2–5, 6–12, 13–18 years); schedule computer-generated by an independent statistician and held centrally; allocation by interactive web response system (Methods › Procedures, PDF p. 3). Demographics are described as similar; baseline seizure frequency was higher in the placebo group (Table 1, PDF p. 5). The randomization schedule was produced by an independent statistician and was to be withheld from everyone involved in the trial until database lock and authorized unblinding; stratification by age group was added by amendment 3 (20 March 2015), before recruitment began on 13 April 2015 (Supplement 1 pp. 40 and 105 of 167; abstract, PDF p. 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; the chance imbalance in baseline seizure frequency is listed under selection effects.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same background antiepileptic drugs by design: placebo group valproate 74%, clobazam 63%, stiripentol 37%; 10 mg/kg/d group 67%, 68% and 38%; 20 mg/kg/d group 70%, 60% and 33% (Table 1, PDF p. 5).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: change from baseline in convulsive-seizure frequency (tonic–clonic, tonic, clonic or atonic) over the 14-week treatment period, counted daily by caregivers by voice-response system. Key secondary, tested in a fixed order: change in total (all types) seizure frequency; at least a 50% reduction in convulsive seizures; Caregiver Global Impression of Change (CGIC) in overall condition. Other secondary: worsening or improvement in convulsive seizures; at least 25%, 75% and 100% reduction; nonconvulsive seizures (myoclonic, partial or absence); individual seizure types; CGIC in seizure duration; sleep disruption; Epworth Sleepiness Scale; Quality of Life in Childhood Epilepsy; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales II. Safety: adverse events and laboratory tests, with clinic visits at weeks 2, 4, 8 and 14 and safety calls at weeks 6 and 10, after the taper and 4 weeks after the last dose; an adjudication committee for possible signals of abuse liability (Methods › Procedures and Outcome Measures, PDF p. 3). Prespecification (Supplement 1): in the original protocol (version 1, 22 July 2014) the primary end point was the mean percentage change in convulsive-seizure frequency over the 12-week maintenance period (Day 15 onwards) and no key secondary outcomes were named; amendment 5 (29 June 2015) extended the primary and secondary analyses to the whole 14-week treatment period, amendment 7 (6 September 2018) removed the words percentage change from the end point, and the three key secondary outcomes and their testing order were first defined in the statistical analysis plan of 5 October 2018, before unblinding on 16 November 2018 (Supplement 1 p. 3 of 175; pp. 32, 106–108, 110, 117 and 152 of 167; article PDF p. 4). The cognitive function the article mentions was measured with the protocol's cognitive assessment battery: for the child, WPPSI-4 or WASI-2 vocabulary and matrix reasoning with Wechsler digit span, coding and bug search subtests, D-KEFS Trail Making, the Expressive One-Word Picture Vocabulary Test (4th edition), NEPSY-2 word generation or F-A-S and animal fluency, the Developmental Test of Visual Motor Integration (6th edition) and the Purdue Pegboard; rated by parents and teachers, the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function, an ADHD checklist, the BASC-2 and a behaviour report form; given at Visit 2 and at the end of treatment by psychometricians at sites with the expertise (Supplement 1 pp. 51, 105 and 137–139 of 167).
outcomes.validity_norms: Caregiver-counted seizure frequency is the usual primary end point in such trials; the article does not discuss its validity. The authors note that few patients completed the adaptive-behaviour and cognitive measures, which limits their interpretation (Results › Other Secondary Outcomes, PDF p. 5); eTable 2 shows the Vineland composite analysed for 37, 32 and 27 children (96 of 198, 48%, editors' calculation) and the quality-of-life score for 49, 57 and 53, and gives no number for the cognitive measures (Supplement 2 p. 5). Adverse-event severity was judged by the investigators and not independently adjudicated (Table 2 footnote a, PDF p. 7). The protocol expected that a number of children would complete only part of the cognitive battery and some none of it, and amendment 1 restricted it to sites able to administer it (Supplement 1 pp. 51 and 105 of 167). The voice-response diary accepted at most 99 seizures of one type per day; where caregivers did not supply the true count, 99 was kept, and one placebo-group entry of 99 tonic–clonic seizures (Day 37) may have been a mistyped 9 (pp. 109 and 127).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy = percentage reduction from a negative binomial regression on the summed convulsive-seizure counts: the ratio of treatment-period to baseline rates in each group, and the ratio of each cannabidiol group to placebo, each expressed as (1 − ratio) × 100 (Methods › Statistical Analysis, PDF p. 4). Response = at least a 25, 50, 75 or 100% reduction; CGIC = proportion of caregivers rating the overall condition slightly, much or very much improved at the last visit.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The statistical analysis plan (5 October 2018) controls type I error for the primary and the three key secondary outcomes with a fixed sequence of eight two-sided tests at the 0.05 level, each dose against placebo, 20 mg/kg/d before 10 mg/kg/d at every step (primary outcome, total seizures, at least 50% reduction, CGIC), testing to stop at the first non-significant result (Supplement 1 p. 126 of 167, SAP §5.5.1 and Table 3). The plan has no Hochberg step, although the article cites Hochberg's sharper Bonferroni procedure for this testing (PDF p. 4, reference 25; see reporting issues). By the editors' check of the article's P values in the plan's order (.03, .01, .03, <.001, .007, .03, .03, <.001), every test in the sequence was reached and met the 0.05 level. The key secondary outcomes and the hierarchy were not in the protocol and were added in the plan before unblinding (p. 152); the original protocol (July 2014) had planned no adjustment for multiple outcomes or for the three-group comparisons, relying on an overall test across groups (p. 80). Other secondary outcomes were not adjusted (p. 117); P values for the 75% responder analysis were withheld for that reason (Methods › Statistical Analysis, PDF p. 4; Figure 3 legend, PDF p. 6). The plan also specifies two exploratory outcomes with tests (time to baseline seizure frequency; convulsive-seizure-free days) and effect-modifier analyses (13 factors by the editors' count), with no adjustment described (pp. 139–141). The count of 13 outcomes refers to those named in the article's Methods (1 primary, 3 key secondary and 9 other secondary, some with several parts), each tested for two doses against placebo.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Patients, caregivers, investigators, those assessing the data and the sponsor did not know whether a patient received cannabidiol or placebo until trial completion, but they were not blinded to the volume each patient received, and so to the dose level (Methods › Procedures, PDF p. 3); the abstract says only that all were blinded to group assignment (PDF p. 1). No assessment of blinding is reported. Neither the protocol nor the statistical analysis plan includes an assessment of blinding, such as asking caregivers or investigators to guess the assignment; the plan has caregivers rate at the end of treatment how acceptable the child found the medication, summarized by group, which the article does not report (Supplement 1 pp. 52 and 150 of 167). Emergency unblinding through the voice-response system was allowed only when the assignment was essential for medical care, with the reason documented (pp. 43–44); the article does not say whether any occurred.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary, model-based reduction from baseline in convulsive seizures over 14 weeks: 48.7% (10 mg/kg/d), 45.7% (20 mg/kg/d), 26.9% (placebo); reduction relative to placebo 29.8% (95% CI 8.4 to 46.2; P=.01) and 25.7% (2.9 to 43.2; P=.03). Maintenance period: 49.2%, 48.6% and 28.6%; ratio to placebo in the first 4 weeks of maintenance 0.63 (0.47 to 0.84) and 0.70 (0.52 to 0.94). Total seizures: 56.4%, 47.3% and 29.7%; relative to placebo 38.0% (20.1 to 51.9; P<.001) and 25.1% (3.5 to 41.9; P=.03). At least 50% reduction: 29/66 (43.9%; OR 2.21, 1.06 to 4.62; P=.03) and 33/67 (49.3%; OR 2.74, 1.32 to 5.70; P=.007) vs 17/65 (26.2%). At least 75% reduction: 20/66 (30.3%; OR 6.63, 2.12 to 20.73) and 12/67 (17.9%; OR 3.33, printed interval 1.10 to 10.92) vs 4/65 (6.2%), without P values. CGIC improved: 45/66 (P<.001) and 40/66 (P=.03) vs 27/65. Freedom from convulsive seizures over the 14 weeks, among completers: 2, 2 and 1. No statistical comparison between the two doses is reported. Editors' calculations (Wald intervals from the printed counts): at least 50% reduction, 17.8 percentage points (1.7 to 33.8) for 10 mg/kg/d and 23.1 (7.1 to 39.1) for 20 mg/kg/d, that is about 5.6 (3.0 to 58) and 4.3 (2.6 to 14) patients treated for one extra responder; CGIC improvement 68.2% and 60.6% vs 41.5%, differences 26.6 (10.2 to 43.1) and 19.1 (2.3 to 35.9) points; serious adverse events 20.3% and 24.6% vs 15.4%. Sensitivity analyses of the primary end point (eFigure 2a, Supplement 2 p. 8): every estimate favours cannabidiol, but the 95% intervals include no difference at 10 mg/kg/d with the rank-sum test (Hodges–Lehmann median difference in percentage change −15.74 points, 95% CI −31.27 to 3.68), rank ANCOVA (−16.9, −36.3 to 2.4) and ANCOVA (−15.20, −41.17 to 10.77), at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days (ratio to placebo 0.798, 0.616 to 1.033), and in maintenance weeks 5–8 at both doses (0.802, 0.592 to 1.087, and 0.757, 0.554 to 1.035) and weeks 9–12 at 20 mg/kg/d (0.755, 0.565 to 1.009). Caregiver global impression of change by ordinal logistic regression of the 7-point rating: odds ratios 2.93 (1.56 to 5.53; P=0.0009) and 2.02 (1.08 to 3.78; P=0.0279) (eFigure 4, Supplement 2 p. 12).
analysis.covariates: The statistical analysis plan specifies the primary model: a negative binomial mixed model of convulsive-seizure counts in the baseline and treatment periods, with age stratum (2–5, 6–12, 13–18 years), period, treatment arm and the treatment-by-period interaction as fixed effects, patient as a random effect and, as offset, the log number of days "in which seizures were reported"; baseline counts enter as the model's first period rather than as a covariate, and no other covariates are included (Supplement 1 p. 127 of 167, SAP §5.5.2). The responder outcomes (at least 25, 50, 75 or 100% reduction) were to be analysed by a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, with differences in proportions and odds ratios with 95% CIs (pp. 130–131); the printed odds ratios for at least 50% and 75% reduction, and three of the four intervals, equal crude values computed from the printed counts (editors' calculation), so the odds ratios appear unstratified, and the article does not say whether its P values come from the stratified test. The CGIC was to be analysed by ordinal (proportional-odds) logistic regression of the 7-point rating at the last visit, with treatment as the only factor (p. 131); the article reports the proportions improved and does not say which analysis produced its P values. Supplement 2 repeats the primary model's terms (eFigure 2 footnote a, p. 9) and states a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, expressed as an estimated odds ratio, for the categories of change and the responder outcomes; ordinal logistic regression for the CGIC, with age group as a factor for seizure duration only; and ANCOVA with baseline and age group for sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness and quality of life (eMethods, p. 13; eTable 2 footnotes, p. 5). All six responder odds ratios in eTable 2 (at least 25%, 75% and 100% reduction) equal crude values with Wald intervals (editors' calculation), so the printed odds ratios appear not to be the stratified estimates the eMethods describe. eFigure 4 gives the CGIC odds ratios from the ordinal model, whose P values match those in the article (p. 12).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02224703 (abstract, PDF p. 1); EudraCT 2014-002939-34 on the protocol (Supplement 1 p. 3 of 175). The registry record was not read. Supplement 1 holds the original protocol (version 1, 22 July 2014), a table of seven amendments (amendment 4 never implemented) and the statistical analysis plan of 5 October 2018, based on protocol version 8 of 6 September 2018 (Supplement 1 p. 3 of 175; pp. 105–110 and 115 of 167). Recruitment ran from 13 April 2015 to 10 November 2017 and follow-up ended on 9 April 2018 (abstract, PDF p. 1). Changes to the planned primary analysis: maintenance period and mixed model for repeated measures (version 1); statistical methods amended and the sample raised to 150 (amendment 3, 20 March 2015, before recruitment); analysis extended to the whole treatment period (amendment 5, 29 June 2015, after recruitment had begun); nonparametric analysis and 186 patients (amendment 6, 23 February 2017); negative binomial regression in place of the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which became a sensitivity analysis, and the words percentage change removed from the end point (amendment 7, 6 September 2018, after follow-up had ended). The key secondary outcomes and the testing hierarchy were added in the plan, which states that it was to be approved before the blind was broken; a blinded data review met on 21 September 2018, and the article dates unblinding to 16 November 2018 (Supplement 1 pp. 106–108, 119, 122 and 152 of 167; article PDF p. 4). All changes thus preceded unblinding, but the article's text describes none of them; the amendment table attributes them to requirements identified by the FDA and/or the sponsor and gives no further reasons, and the plan's own amendment table lists no changes (p. 153). Recorded as registered with deviations because the reported primary analysis differs from the one first planned, through documented amendments made before unblinding.
analysis.selective_reporting: The primary and all three key secondary outcomes are reported for both doses, as the statistical analysis plan specifies. The other secondary outcomes are summarized in the text and tabulated in eTable 2 (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5): categories of change, responders, nonconvulsive seizures, individual seizure types, CGIC in seizure duration, sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness, quality of life and the Vineland composite (not its domains, although the eMethods describe domain analyses, p. 13). eTable 2 has no cognitive outcome, although the article cites it for cognitive function; the plan provided only descriptive summaries for the cognitive battery (Supplement 1 pp. 138–139 of 167). The article's text does not mention that countable partial seizures increased relative to placebo at 20 mg/kg/d in eTable 2 (an exploratory, unadjusted result). Prespecified in the plan but reported neither in the article nor in Supplement 2: growth and development (height, weight, IGF-1, Tanner staging), the exploratory time to baseline seizure frequency and convulsive-seizure-free days, the effect-modifier analyses other than a statement on clobazam, caregiver-rated palatability, treatment and diary compliance, plasma levels of concomitant antiepileptic drugs, and per-protocol analyses of the second and third key secondary outcomes (Supplement 1 pp. 117, 130, 139–141, 149–151 and 158 of 167; the article mentions per-protocol analyses for the primary and first key secondary outcomes only, PDF p. 4). Listed in the eMethods but without results in Supplement 2: the multiple-imputation analysis under a missing-not-at-random assumption and the three sensitivity analyses of the CGIC (caregiver only, end-of-treatment scores, per-protocol set) (Supplement 2 p. 14). Before unblinding, the planned analyses of seizures lasting over 30 minutes and of epilepsy-related hospitalizations were dropped for too few patients, and rescue-medication use was not analysed because it had been collected inconsistently (Supplement 1 pp. 108–109 and 152 of 167). Not reported in the article or in Supplements 1 and 2: the results of the abuse-liability adjudication, dosing adherence and voice-response diary completion, the P value of the clobazam interaction test (whose method is in the plan, Supplement 1 p. 140 of 167), and P values for the 75% responder analysis.
analysis.power: Planned sample size and basis (Supplement 1): the original protocol (July 2014) planned 120 patients (40 per group, the placebo group split 20 and 20) to detect a 40-point difference in mean percentage reduction in convulsive seizures (10% with placebo, 50% with cannabidiol), with an SD of 63%, a two-sided 5% level and 80% power (p. 78 of 167). Amendment 3 (20 March 2015) raised this to 150 (50 per group) with an assumed placebo reduction of 18%; amendment 6 (23 February 2017) to 186 (62 per group), with nonparametric analysis of seizure data; amendment 7 (6 September 2018) switched the primary analysis to negative binomial regression without changing the sample size (pp. 106–108). The plan's basis for 62 per group: at least 80% power for a two-sided Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test at the 0.05 level, with gamma distributions fitted by maximum likelihood to data from Part B of the sponsor's earlier Dravet study GWEP1332 (cannabidiol: scale 65.614, shape 1.0886; placebo: scale 40.887, shape 2.3059), one distribution serving for both cannabidiol groups (p. 116); the eMethods repeat these values and identify GWEP1332 Part B as GWPCARE1, the first Dravet trial (Supplement 2 p. 13). The plan does not name the variable these distributions describe or state the expected difference, and the calculation refers to the rank test, not to the negative binomial model used. 199 patients were randomized against 186 planned; neither document explains the difference. 66 and 67 patients were analysed in the cannabidiol groups and 65 in the pooled placebo group. The trial was not designed or powered to compare the two doses with each other.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 14 weeks, convulsive seizures fell more with cannabidiol at either dose than with placebo (model-based reductions relative to placebo of 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), at least halving of convulsive seizures was more frequent (43.9% and 49.3% vs 26.2%), and so was caregiver-rated improvement (45 of 66 and 40 of 66 vs 27 of 65); freedom from convulsive seizures was rare (2, 2 and 1 among completers), and the placebo group's seizures fell by 26.9%. Adverse events were about equally frequent in all three groups (87.5%, 89.9% and 89.2%), but with 20 mg/kg/d there were more withdrawals for adverse events (5 vs 0 and 0), more serious adverse events (17 of 69 vs 13 of 64 and 10 of 65), more decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue and vomiting, and more transaminase rises above 3 times the upper limit (13 vs 3, all in children taking valproate; none with placebo). In the sensitivity analyses every estimate favoured cannabidiol, but the intervals included no difference at 10 mg/kg/d in the rank-based and ANCOVA analyses of percentage change, at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days, and in maintenance weeks 5–8 at both doses and weeks 9–12 at 20 mg/kg/d; tonic–clonic seizures taken alone were not clearly reduced at either dose (exploratory; Supplement 2 pp. 4 and 8).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract concludes that both doses led to similar clinically relevant reductions (PDF p. 1), and the discussion that efficacy was similar, with no appreciable difference between the doses (PDF pp. 6, 8); no comparison between the doses is reported, nor was one specified (Supplement 1 pp. 80 and 126 of 167), their intervals against placebo are wide and overlap almost entirely, and neither the protocol nor the statistical analysis plan defines a clinically relevant difference (the original power calculation assumed a 40-point difference in mean percentage reduction; Supplement 1 p. 78 of 167). (2) The better safety and tolerability profile claimed for 10 mg/kg/d (PDF pp. 1, 6) rests on descriptive counts without a test, in a trial whose caregivers and investigators knew each child's dose level; it agrees with the counts of withdrawals, transaminase rises and several common adverse events. (3) The abstract advises that increases above 10 mg/kg/d be tailored to individual efficacy and safety, and the conclusions that, because individual responses vary, escalation to 20 mg/kg/d may still be warranted for children who need better seizure control if safety and tolerability allow (PDF pp. 1, 8); children were randomized to fixed doses in parallel groups, the protocol made no provision for raising a dose above the level assigned at randomization (Supplement 1 pp. 31 and 41–42 of 167), and the 4 children randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (2 given cannabidiol and 2 placebo, by Figure 1) who received more did so incorrectly, by the plan's account (p. 122), so the trial did not test escalation after a poor response. (4) The placebo response is compared with 13% in the first Dravet trial (PDF p. 7), but that figure was the median of individual percentage changes analysed by a rank test (Devinsky et al., 2017, pp. 2013–2014), whereas 26.9% is a model-based estimate from negative binomial regression, so the two are not directly comparable. (5) A non-significant clobazam interaction is read as suggesting that clobazam use did not significantly affect the outcome (PDF p. 6), but its P value is not given (the statistical analysis plan prespecified the test as an effect-by-period-by-treatment interaction in the negative binomial model, one of 13 effect modifiers (editors' count) prespecified without any described adjustment for multiplicity; Supplement 1 pp. 140–141 of 167), and a non-significant interaction in groups of 65 to 67 cannot show that there is no effect modification. (6) The 20 mg/kg/d dose and valproate are called independent risk factors for transaminase rises, as in prior studies (PDF p. 7), but no multivariable analysis is reported in this article. (7) The article says that the sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary analysis and that the difference from placebo was maintained for the duration of treatment (PDF p. 4); in eFigure 2a all estimates favour cannabidiol, but the intervals include no difference at 10 mg/kg/d in the rank-sum analysis (the primary analysis planned until amendment 7), the rank ANCOVA and the ANCOVA, at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days, and in maintenance weeks 5–8 at both doses and weeks 9–12 at 20 mg/kg/d (Supplement 2 p. 8). (8) The article cites eTable 2 for no notable difference in cognitive function (PDF p. 5), but eTable 2 contains no cognitive outcome (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5). The authors themselves caution against extrapolating the results to other cannabidiol-containing products (PDF p. 6).

timeline.event: First placebo-controlled trial of this cannabidiol solution in Dravet syndrome (GWPCARE1), 20 mg/kg/d only, 120 patients: median change in monthly convulsive seizures −38.9% vs −13.3% with placebo, Hodges–Lehmann difference −22.8 percentage points (95% CI −41.1 to −5.4); at least halving of convulsive seizures 43% vs 27% (P=0.08).

Two placebo-controlled trials of the same product at 10 and 20 mg/kg/d in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (GWPCARE3, Devinsky et al., 2018; GWPCARE4, Thiele et al., 2018), cited by the authors as consistent with this trial (references 20 and 21); not read.

This trial (GWPCARE2): both 10 and 20 mg/kg/d reduced convulsive seizures more than placebo; the first test of 10 mg/kg/d in Dravet syndrome. The authors report that a meta-analysis of the clobazam subgroups of this and three earlier GW-sponsored trials is under way (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, PDF pp. 6–7); not read.

replication.where_it_stands: Two placebo-controlled trials of this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution in Dravet syndrome, both sponsored by its manufacturer, agree that 20 mg/kg/d added to existing antiepileptic drugs reduces convulsive seizures more than placebo over 14 weeks; at least halving of convulsive seizures was significant here but not in the first trial (P=0.08). The 10 mg/kg/d result has no second trial in Dravet syndrome among the sources read, and within this trial its interval included no difference in the rank-based sensitivity analyses (Supplement 2 p. 8); no trial independent of the manufacturer has been read. The sizes of effect are not directly comparable between the two trials, because the first analysed medians of individual percentage changes and this one a negative binomial model.
