funding.affiliations_note: Three authors are affiliated with GW Research Ltd (Checketts, who had full access to the data, takes responsibility for the data analysis and did the statistical analysis) or Greenwich Biosciences Inc (Dunayevich, Knappertz); no disclosures are listed for them (Author Affiliations and Contributions, PDF p. 8). Staff of Greenwich Biosciences and GW Research contributed to the study design and managed the study, and medical writing support came from employees of both companies (Additional Contributions, PDF p. 9). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A blinded trial that randomizes children who respond poorly to 10 mg/kg/d either to stay on it or to move to 20 mg/kg/d, or a parallel trial powered to compare the two doses directly with the dose level concealed; run independently of the manufacturer, longer than 14 weeks, with caregivers asked to guess the assignment, results reported separately for children taking and not taking clobazam and valproate, and drug levels measured.

domains.note: Computer-generated schedule by an independent statistician, held centrally, with allocation by interactive web response system, in blocks of 6 stratified by age group (PDF p. 3). The placebo group's higher baseline seizure frequency (median 17 vs 14 and 9 convulsive seizures per 28 days) is compatible with chance but may have added to the placebo response, as the authors suggest.

Patients, caregivers and investigators did not know whether the solution was active, and the analysis followed intention to treat (198 of 199; the one excluded was never treated). Two children randomized to 10 mg/kg/d, and 2 at the matching placebo volume, received more than their assigned dose, in error according to the statistical analysis plan (up to 20 mg/kg/d, 1 of the 4 up to 50 mg/kg/d), and stayed in their randomized groups for efficacy (Supplement 1 p. 122 of 167); the protocol made no provision for going above the assigned dose level (pp. 41–42). The dose level (volume) was known, which bears on comparisons between the doses rather than on comparisons with placebo.

190 of the 198 treated completed treatment; data up to withdrawal were used without imputation; the 9 withdrawals were 3 and 6 in the cannabidiol groups and none with placebo. Unreported diary days were left out of the seizure-rate denominators (rates computed over reported days and scaled to 28 days; the log number of days with seizure reports as the model's offset) rather than imputed, which assumes that seizures on unreported days resemble those on reported days; how many days went unreported is not reported, although the plan provided for a summary (Supplement 1 pp. 120, 126–130 and 151 of 167). Supplement 2 shows that the prespecified worst-case imputation of unreported days (for each child, the highest of last observation carried forward, next observation carried backward and the mean daily count) keeps the 10 mg/kg/d result (ratio to placebo 0.729, 95% CI 0.563 to 0.943) but not the 20 mg/kg/d result (0.798, 0.616 to 1.033); the multiple-imputation analysis under a missing-not-at-random assumption is described but not shown (eFigure 2a, Supplement 2 p. 8; eMethods, p. 14). The per-protocol and safety-set analyses agree with the primary result (p. 8).

Seizures were counted and the global impression rated by caregivers, who knew the dose level; somnolence (25% and 23% vs 14%) and, at 20 mg/kg/d, decreased appetite and diarrhoea could have revealed the assignment, the authors cite high caregiver expectations of efficacy, and no assessment of blinding is reported or was planned (none appears in the protocol or the statistical analysis plan, Supplement 1).

The protocol, its amendments and the statistical analysis plan are on file (Supplement 1). The primary end point and its analysis were changed during the trial (maintenance to whole treatment period in June 2015, after recruitment had begun; nonparametric analysis in February 2017; Wilcoxon rank-sum test to negative binomial regression on 6 September 2018, after follow-up had ended), and the key secondary outcomes and testing order were first defined in the plan of 5 October 2018; all of this preceded unblinding on 16 November 2018 (Supplement 1 pp. 106–108, 110 and 152 of 167; article PDF p. 4). The reported analyses follow that plan, the replaced rank test was kept as a sensitivity analysis (p. 127), and the plan's testing order never stopped. Supplement 2 shows that the rank test does not agree at 10 mg/kg/d: the Hodges–Lehmann median difference in percentage change is −15.74 points (95% CI −31.27 to 3.68), against −19.88 (−33.92 to −5.29) at 20 mg/kg/d (eFigure 2a, Supplement 2 p. 8), so the choice between the two analyses, made after follow-up ended, determines whether the 10 mg/kg/d interval excludes no difference. Because the switch was documented before unblinding, when results by group were not available, the judgment stays low under RoB 2; the reasons for the amendments are not given, and the registry record was not seen.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A centrally randomized, placebo-controlled trial analysed by intention to treat, with a fixed testing order for the primary and key secondary outcomes. The concerns are caregiver-reported outcomes with possible functional unblinding and no assessment of blinding (none was planned), missing diary data (unreported days were not imputed in the primary analysis, their number is not reported, and the 20 mg/kg/d result does not survive the prespecified worst-case imputation; Supplement 2 p. 8), and a sponsor that designed the trial and ran the analyses. The protocol and statistical analysis plan (Supplement 1) account for the difference between the planned rank test and the reported negative binomial analysis: a documented amendment made after follow-up ended but before unblinding, with the rank test kept as a sensitivity analysis, in which the 10 mg/kg/d interval includes no difference (Supplement 2 p. 8). Comparisons between the two doses carry more risk than comparisons with placebo: the dose level was known to caregivers and investigators, and no statistical comparison between the doses was specified or made. Cite it for: in 198 children and adolescents with Dravet syndrome and uncontrolled convulsive seizures, adding this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution at 10 or 20 mg/kg/d to existing antiepileptic drugs reduced caregiver-recorded convulsive seizures more than placebo over 14 weeks in the prespecified analysis (model-based reductions relative to placebo 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), with the qualification that the 10 mg/kg/d result depends on the analysis model and the 20 mg/kg/d result on the handling of missing diary days, and with more withdrawals for adverse events, more serious adverse events and more transaminase rises at 20 mg/kg/d (the transaminase rises all in children taking valproate). Do not cite it for: equal efficacy of the two doses, benefit from raising the dose in a child who has not responded, seizure freedom, effects on cognition (no cognitive data or test is reported), long-term effects, other cannabidiol products, doses below 10 mg/kg/d, adults or other epilepsies.

key_findings.finding: 199 of 285 screened patients were randomized at 38 centres in six countries: 67 to 10 mg/kg/d, 67 to 20 mg/kg/d and 65 to placebo (32 at the 10 mg/kg/d volume and 33 at the 20 mg/kg/d volume, pooled). One patient randomized to 10 mg/kg/d was never treated, leaving 198 in the ITT set (66, 67 and 65); mean age 9.3 years (SD 4.4); 104 female (52.5%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Figure 1 and legend (PDF p. 3); Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Median baseline convulsive seizures per 28 days were 17 (IQR 7–51) with placebo, 14 (6–31) with 10 mg/kg/d and 9 (6–21) with 20 mg/kg/d (overall 12, IQR 6–33); all seizures 46 (16–217), 35 (10–104) and 26 (10–194).
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4, right column); Table 1 (PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Primary end point: model-based reduction from baseline in convulsive-seizure frequency over the 14-week treatment period of 48.7% with 10 mg/kg/d, 45.7% with 20 mg/kg/d and 26.9% with placebo; reduction relative to placebo 29.8% (95% CI 8.4 to 46.2; P=.01) and 25.7% (2.9 to 43.2; P=.03). The article says that the sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary analysis (eFigure 2 in Supplement 2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome; also the abstract (PDF p. 1) and the Figure 2 legend (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: In eFigure 2a (Supplement 2 p. 8) all estimates favour cannabidiol, but the intervals include no difference at 10 mg/kg/d in the rank-sum, rank ANCOVA and ANCOVA analyses and at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days; see the eFigure 2a finding and reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Over the 12-week maintenance period the reductions were 49.2%, 48.6% and 28.6%; the difference from placebo was present in the first 4 weeks of maintenance (ratio to placebo 0.63, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.84, with 10 mg/kg/d and 0.70, 0.52 to 0.94, with 20 mg/kg/d) and is said to have been maintained for the duration of treatment (eFigure 2A in Supplement 2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary Outcome
key_findings.note: The 4-weekly ratios in eFigure 2a (Supplement 2 p. 8) all favour cannabidiol, but their intervals include no difference in weeks 5–8 at both doses and in weeks 9–12 at 20 mg/kg/d (see the eFigure 2a maintenance finding).

key_findings.finding: Key secondary, total seizures: reductions from baseline of 56.4%, 47.3% and 29.7%; relative to placebo 38.0% (95% CI 20.1 to 51.9; P<.001) with 10 mg/kg/d and 25.1% (3.5 to 41.9; P=.03) with 20 mg/kg/d.
key_findings.locator: Results › Key Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 2 legend (PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Key secondary, at least a 50% reduction in convulsive seizures: 29 of 66 (43.9%; P=.03) with 10 mg/kg/d and 33 of 67 (49.3%; P=.007) with 20 mg/kg/d vs 17 of 65 (26.2%) with placebo; odds ratios 2.21 (95% CI 1.06 to 4.62) and 2.74 (1.32 to 5.70).
key_findings.locator: Results › Key Secondary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 3 legend (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: The statistical analysis plan specifies a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group for this outcome (Supplement 1 p. 130 of 167); the printed odds ratios equal crude values from the counts (editors' calculation; see analysis.covariates). The eMethods also state a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, expressed as an estimated odds ratio (Supplement 2 p. 13); all six responder odds ratios in eTable 2 likewise equal crude values with Wald intervals (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: At least a 75% reduction (another secondary outcome, without P values): 20 of 66 (30.3%) and 12 of 67 (17.9%) vs 4 of 65 (6.2%); odds ratios 6.63 (95% CI 2.12 to 20.73) and 3.33 (printed interval 1.10 to 10.92).
key_findings.locator: Results › Key Secondary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 3 legend (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed counts gives a crude Wald interval of 1.01 to 10.92 around 3.33; see reporting issues. eTable 2 prints the interval as 1.01 to 10.92 (Supplement 2 p. 4), which confirms the transposition.

key_findings.finding: Key secondary, Caregiver Global Impression of Change: overall condition slightly, much or very much improved at the last visit in 45 of 66 (P<.001) with 10 mg/kg/d and 40 of 66 (P=.03) with 20 mg/kg/d vs 27 of 65 with placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results › Key Secondary Outcomes, 3rd paragraph (top of the left column)
key_findings.note: eFigure 4 (Supplement 2 p. 12) gives the ordinal logistic regression of the whole 7-point rating: odds ratio 2.93 (95% CI 1.56 to 5.53; P=0.0009) for 10 mg/kg/d and 2.02 (1.08 to 3.78; P=0.0279) for 20 mg/kg/d, matching the article's P values, which therefore refer to the whole scale rather than to the proportions improved; one child in the 20 mg/kg/d group had no rating at the last visit, hence 40 of 66.

key_findings.finding: Freedom from convulsive seizures, among those who completed the trial: during the 12-week maintenance period 2 (10 mg/kg/d), 3 (20 mg/kg/d) and 1 (placebo); during the whole 14-week treatment period 2, 2 and 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: eTable 2 (Supplement 2 p. 4), in the ITT set, counts a 100% reduction in convulsive seizures over the treatment period in 1 of 65, 2 of 66 and 3 of 67; the article's count of 2 at 20 mg/kg/d is among completers, so the third child in eTable 2 may be one who did not complete; the article does not reconcile the two.

key_findings.finding: No notable difference between either dose and placebo in sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness, quality of life, adaptive behaviour or cognitive function (the article cites eTable 2 in Supplement 2); the authors note that few patients completed the adaptive-behaviour and cognitive measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other Secondary Outcomes, 1st paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: eTable 2 (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5) reports sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness, quality of life and the Vineland composite, all with intervals including no difference (see the eTable 2 finding), but contains no cognitive outcome, and the eMethods describe no cognitive analysis (p. 13). The statistical analysis plan provided only descriptive summaries for the cognitive battery (Supplement 1 pp. 138–139 of 167). The statement of no notable difference in cognitive function therefore rests on no data or test shown in the article or in Supplements 1 and 2.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events occurred in 58 of 65 (89.2%) with placebo, 56 of 64 (87.5%) with 10 mg/kg/d and 62 of 69 (89.9%) with 20 mg/kg/d (safety sets); of the 176 patients with events, 98 had mild, 64 moderate and 14 severe events at worst. Serious adverse events in 10, 13 and 17 patients; withdrawals for adverse events 0, 0 and 5; no deaths. Events had resolved by the end of the trial in 61 of 118 patients with events given cannabidiol (51.7%) and 35 of 58 given placebo (60.3%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Figure 1 (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Common adverse events, placebo vs 10 vs 20 mg/kg/d: decreased appetite 11 (17%), 11 (17%), 20 (29%); diarrhoea 8 (12%), 11 (17%), 18 (26%); somnolence 9 (14%), 16 (25%), 16 (23%); pyrexia 11 (17%), 15 (23%), 15 (22%); fatigue 7 (11%), 5 (8%), 15 (22%); vomiting 4 (6%), 4 (6%), 11 (16%); status epilepticus 9 (14%), 5 (8%), 7 (10%); ALT increased 0, 3 (5%), 9 (13%); AST increased 0, 3 (5%), 8 (12%). Two patients randomized to 10 mg/kg/d who were titrated above it are counted with 20 mg/kg/d.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnotes a–c
key_findings.note: The article says these 2 children titrated above the target dose (Table 2 footnote b); the statistical analysis plan states that 4 patients randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (cannabidiol or placebo; 2 and 2 in Figure 1, PDF p. 3) incorrectly received up to 20 mg/kg/d, 1 of the 4 up to 50 mg/kg/d (Supplement 1 p. 122 of 167); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Transaminase rises above 3 times the upper limit of the reference range occurred in 16 of 133 patients given cannabidiol (12.0%): 3 of 44 (6.8%) with 10 mg/kg/d and 13 of 47 (27.7%) with 20 mg/kg/d, the denominators being the children taking valproate; all 16 were taking valproate, and none of the placebo group had such a rise. All resolved: after leaving the trial (1 and 2 patients), spontaneously (1 and 3), after lowering valproate and/or clobazam (3, all at 20 mg/kg/d), after lowering cannabidiol (1, at 20 mg/kg/d) or after entering the extension (1 and 4); none met Hy's law criteria.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 6); Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Somnolence, rash and pneumonia were more frequent in children also taking clobazam (eTable 3 in Supplement 2; its counts are in the eTable 3 finding). Across groups, clobazam dosage was adjusted in 20 of 126 patients (15.9%) and valproate dosage in 19 of 139 (13.7%). The authors report the interaction P value for clobazam use as not statistically significant, without giving it.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the placebo response (26.9%) was higher than the 13% of the first Dravet trial; they call the reason unclear and suggest as possible reasons the placebo group's numerically higher median baseline frequency of convulsive and total seizures, high patient and caregiver expectations of efficacy, and the rise in placebo responses in epilepsy trials over two decades.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors caution that the results should not be extrapolated to other cannabidiol-containing products, which vary in purity, excipients and consistency; that the efficacy of doses below 10 mg/kg/d and long-term effects remain unknown; and that, with children only and 88.9% white participants, generalizability to adults and other ethnic groups is limited, as is any assessment of specific drug combinations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 6); Limitations (PDF pp. 7–8)

key_findings.finding: Patients, caregivers, investigators, those assessing the data and the sponsor were unaware of cannabidiol versus placebo until trial completion but were not blinded to the volume each patient received, and so to the dose level.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph (starting on PDF p. 2, right column; the blinding statement is on PDF p. 3, left column)

key_findings.finding: As first written (protocol version 1, dated 22 July 2014), the trial was to randomize 120 patients 1:1:1 (40 per group, the placebo group split 20 and 20 between the two dose volumes), and its primary end point was the mean percentage change from baseline in convulsive-seizure frequency over the maintenance period (Day 15 to the end of the evaluable period), to be analysed with a mixed model for repeated measures if the data were normally distributed and with nonparametric tests (Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank) otherwise; the evaluable period was to end the day before a relevant change in antiepileptic or prohibited medicines. No key secondary outcomes were named.
key_findings.page: Supplement 1 p. 3 of 175; pp. 32, 78 and 80–81 of 167
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Original Trial Protocol: header and Investigator Agreement (p. 3); §4.1 Study Design and §4.1.1 Primary Endpoint (p. 32); §13.1 Sample Size, Power and Significance Levels (p. 78); §13.6.1 Evaluable Period and §13.6.2 Primary Endpoint(s) (pp. 80–81)

key_findings.finding: The protocol was amended seven times (amendment 4 never implemented). Amendment 3 (20 March 2015) added stratification by age, amended the statistical methods for the primary and secondary end points, raised the sample to 150 (50 per group) and the assumed placebo reduction from 10% to 18%, and added the felbamate exclusion; amendment 5 (29 June 2015) extended the primary and secondary analyses to the whole treatment period (titration plus maintenance) and named the doses 20 and 10 mg/kg/d; amendment 6 (23 February 2017) raised the sample to 186 (62 per group) and switched seizure analyses to nonparametric methods; amendment 7 (6 September 2018, non-substantial) replaced the Wilcoxon rank-sum primary analysis with negative binomial regression, kept the rank test as a sensitivity analysis, removed the words percentage change from the end point, restated the allocation as 2:2:1:1 to four groups and left the sample size unchanged.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Amendments to the Original Protocol, §1.1.1 Changes in the Conduct of the Trial, Table 1.1.1-1

key_findings.finding: The statistical analysis plan, dated 5 October 2018 and based on protocol version 8 (6 September 2018), defines the primary end point as the change in convulsive-seizure frequency over the treatment period (Day 1 to Day 99 or the last dose) compared with baseline, and three key secondary end points: change in total seizure frequency, at least a 50% reduction in convulsive seizures, and the CGIC score. The key secondary end points and the hierarchical testing were not in the protocol and were added in the plan before unblinding; a blinded data review meeting was held on 21 September 2018, and the article gives 16 November 2018 as the date of unblinding.
key_findings.page: Supplement 1 pp. 110, 115, 117, 121–122 and 152 of 167; article PDF p. 4
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan: title page (p. 110); §1 Introduction (p. 115); §3.3.1–3.3.2 (p. 117); §5.1.3.3 Treatment Period (p. 121); §5.2.3 (p. 122); §5.8 Changes in the Conduct of the Study or Planned Analysis (p. 152); article Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Testing hierarchy in the plan: eight comparisons in a fixed order, each two-sided at the 0.05 level and tested only if the previous one was significant: the primary end point, then total seizures, then at least 50% reduction, then the CGIC, each with 20 mg/kg/d against placebo before 10 mg/kg/d against placebo. The primary null hypothesis concerns 20 mg/kg/d against placebo. Every end point has two comparisons, both against placebo; no comparison of the two doses with each other is specified, although the objectives say that the dose response will be explored. Other secondary end points are not adjusted for multiplicity.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §2.1 Primary objective (p. 115); §3.3.2 Secondary Efficacy Endpoints (p. 117); §5.5.1 General Approach and Table 3 Hierarchy for Analysis (p. 126)

key_findings.finding: Sample size in the plan: 186 patients randomized 2:2:1:1 (cannabidiol 10 or 20 mg/kg/d, placebo at either volume), stratified by age group (2–5, 6–12, 13–18 years), the placebo groups pooled for efficacy; 62 per group gives at least 80% power for a two-sided Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test at the 0.05 level, assuming gamma distributions with scale 65.614 and shape 1.0886 for the cannabidiol groups and scale 40.887 and shape 2.3059 for placebo, estimated by maximum likelihood from data of Part B of the sponsor's study GWEP1332.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §3.2 Definition of Sample Size
key_findings.note: The plan does not name the variable the gamma distributions describe or state the difference to be detected; one distribution serves for both cannabidiol groups. The eMethods repeat these values and identify GWEP1332 Part B as GWPCARE1, the first Dravet trial (Supplement 2 p. 13).

key_findings.finding: Dosing rules in the original protocol: each child titrated over 2 weeks to the assigned target dose level and was to stay at that level throughout the maintenance period; during titration the investigator could suspend or amend dosing for an unacceptable adverse event, and during maintenance could reduce the dose temporarily or permanently if it was poorly tolerated, with a return to the target encouraged where possible; maintenance doses were capped at 20 mg/kg/d. The protocol contains no provision for raising a dose above the assigned level. Amendment 3 (March 2015) let dosing suspended for an adverse event resume before full recovery if the event was well tolerated.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Original Trial Protocol §3.3.1 Selection of Study Dose (p. 31); §8.1.2 Dose Escalation, Dose Adjustments and Down-Titration (pp. 41–42); Amendments, Table 1.1.1-1, amendment 3 (pp. 105–106)

key_findings.finding: At a blinded review of the data, 1 randomized patient was found never to have received study medication (excluded from the safety and ITT sets), and 4 patients randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (cannabidiol or placebo) were found to have incorrectly received up to 20 mg/kg/d during treatment, 1 of them up to 50 mg/kg/d; these 4 were assigned to the 20 mg/kg/d groups (cannabidiol or placebo) for safety reporting, while the ITT set analyses patients as randomized.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §5.2.1 Safety Analysis Set and §5.2.2 Intention to Treat Analysis Set
key_findings.note: The plan does not say in which arm the patient given up to 50 mg/kg/d (or its volume) was; the article's Figure 1 (PDF p. 3) shows 2 cannabidiol and 2 placebo patients at the 10 mg/kg/d level with a dose above it.

key_findings.finding: Placebo and blinding in the protocol: the placebo solution contained the active solution's excipients at the same concentrations (anhydrous ethanol 79 mg/mL, sucralose 0.5 mg/mL, strawberry flavouring 0.2 mg/mL, sesame oil to volume) without cannabidiol (100 mg/mL in the active solution); both were supplied in 100-mL amber glass bottles with child-resistant caps and dispensed by pack number through the voice-response system; the randomization schedule, produced by an independent statistician, was held centrally and withheld from everyone involved until database lock; emergency unblinding through the voice-response system was permitted only when the assignment was essential for medical care, with the reason documented. Neither the protocol nor the statistical analysis plan includes any assessment of blinding; a caregiver rating (5-point scale) of how acceptable the child found the medication at the end of treatment was to be summarized by group.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Original Trial Protocol §5.1–5.3.1 and Tables 5.1-1, 5.2-1 (p. 34); §7.1–7.2 (p. 40); §8.5 Access to Blinded Treatment Assignment (pp. 43–44); §9.1.11.8 Caregiver Impression of IMP Palatability (p. 52); Statistical Analysis Plan §5.7.3 (p. 150)

key_findings.finding: Missing data in the plan: seizure frequencies are computed from reported diary days only (seizures in the period divided by reported days, times 28), and the negative binomial model is offset by the log number of days with seizure reports, so unreported days are not imputed in the primary analysis; for a patient who withdrew, all data before withdrawal are used. Prespecified sensitivity analyses: the primary analysis with intermittent unreported days in the treatment period imputed by the worst (highest) of last observation carried forward, next observation carried backward and the patient's mean daily count rounded up; a Wilcoxon rank-sum analysis after 100 multiple imputations under two missing-not-at-random scenarios (data missing after discontinuation for adverse events, or for any reason, in the cannabidiol groups); per-protocol and safety-set analyses; maintenance-period and 4-weekly analyses limited to patients with at least 7 days of seizure data. A summary of unreported diary days by group was planned.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §5.1.1.1 (p. 120); §5.5.2 Primary Efficacy Endpoint (pp. 126–127); §5.5.2.1 Sensitivity Analyses and §5.5.2.1.1 Sensitivity Analysis of Missing Data (pp. 127–130); §5.7.8 IVRS Compliance (p. 151)
key_findings.note: Results in Supplement 2: the worst-case imputation is shown (ratio to placebo 0.729, 95% CI 0.563 to 0.943, and 0.798, 0.616 to 1.033; eFigure 2a, p. 8), the multiple-imputation analysis is described in the eMethods but not shown (p. 14); see the eFigure 2a finding.

key_findings.finding: Primary model in the plan: a negative binomial mixed model of convulsive-seizure counts in the baseline and treatment periods, with age stratum, period, treatment arm and treatment-by-period interaction as fixed effects, patient as a random effect and the log number of days with seizure reports as offset; for each arm the ratio of treatment-period to baseline rates, and for each cannabidiol group its ratio to placebo, are presented with 95% CIs and converted to percentage reductions as (1 − ratio) × 100. If the model fails to converge, a sequence of fallbacks ends with a log-normal rate model.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §5.5.2 Primary Efficacy Endpoint

key_findings.finding: Changes recorded in the statistical analysis plan before unblinding: analyses of seizures lasting more than 30 minutes and of epilepsy-related hospitalizations were dropped because too few patients had them, and no analysis of rescue-medication use was proposed because the data had been collected inconsistently. The voice-response diary accepted at most 99 seizures of one type per day (for a period of the trial, according to the plan); a log for higher counts was added to the case report form, but at many sites caregivers did not supply the true counts, and entries of 99 were kept. The amendments section, which names the patient's randomized group and so was written after unblinding, reports that only 1 patient, randomized to placebo, entered 99 for a convulsive seizure type (99 tonic–clonic seizures on Day 37; the patient's diary profile suggests 9, which could not be confirmed) and concludes that the process did not change the interpretation of the primary endpoint.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Amendments to the Original Protocol, §1.1.2 Changes in the Planned Analyses (pp. 108–109); Statistical Analysis Plan §5.8 (p. 152)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation: Day 37 lies within the treatment period; if the true count was 9, the placebo group's treatment-period count is overstated by 90 convulsive seizures, which would favour cannabidiol slightly; the effect on the estimates is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Effect-modifier analyses were prespecified for the primary end point (negative binomial model with an effect-by-period-by-treatment interaction test) and the 50% responder end point (logistic regression with an effect-by-treatment interaction test), each effect in a separate model: age group, sex, region (United States or elsewhere), clobazam, valproate, stiripentol, clobazam with stiripentol, levetiracetam, topiramate, baseline convulsive-seizure tertile, and the numbers of concurrent, prior, and prior plus concurrent antiepileptic drugs; no adjustment for multiplicity is described (the editors' count: 13 effects).
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement1.pdf, Statistical Analysis Plan §5.5.5 Subgroup Analyses

key_findings.finding: The cognitive assessment battery (for the child: WPPSI-4 or WASI-2 vocabulary and matrix reasoning with Wechsler digit span, coding and bug search subtests; D-KEFS Trail Making; Expressive One-Word Picture Vocabulary Test, 4th edition; NEPSY-2 word generation or F-A-S and animal fluency; Developmental Test of Visual Motor Integration, 6th edition; Purdue Pegboard; rated by parents and teachers: Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function, ADHD checklist, BASC-2, behaviour report form) was to be given at Visit 2 and at the end of treatment by an experienced psychometrician at a subgroup of sites with the expertise; the protocol expected that a number of children would complete only part of it and some none of it. The plan provides only descriptive summaries (scores and change from baseline by group), with no statistical test.

Caregiver impression of change in seizure duration, odds ratio: tonic–clonic 3.27 (1.48 to 7.24) and 1.68 (0.78 to 3.62); absence 4.44 (1.13 to 17.39) and 3.01 (0.88 to 10.30); the other types' intervals include 1.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events of special interest by clobazam use (safety set; placebo, 10 and 20 mg/kg/d; no tests): with clobazam (41, 44 and 42 children), somnolence, fatigue, lethargy or sedation 12 (29.3%), 19 (43.2%) and 24 (57.1%); rash 1 (2.4%), 6 (13.6%) and 3 (7.1%); pneumonia 1 (2.4%), 6 (13.6%) and 3 (7.1%); aggression or irritability 2 (4.9%), 3 (6.8%) and 5 (11.9%). Without clobazam (24, 20 and 27), somnolence, fatigue, lethargy or sedation 4 (16.7%), 2 (10.0%) and 5 (18.5%); rash 0, 0 and 1 (3.7%); pneumonia 1 (4.2%), 0 and 1 (3.7%); aggression or irritability 1 (4.2%), 0 and 4 (14.8%). Clobazam dose adjusted in 1, 8 and 11 children (1 increase; 7 decreases and 1 start; 8 decreases, 1 temporary decrease, 1 increase and 1 stop) and valproate dose in 4, 4 and 11 (1 increase, 1 decrease/increase and 2 decreases; 3 decreases and 1 decrease/increase; 8 decreases, 1 increase, 1 interruption and 1 initiation/increase, as printed).

key_findings.note: Rash and pneumonia are any MedDRA preferred term containing the word. The groups with and without clobazam sum to 127 and 71 (198), against 126 taking clobazam in the article's Table 1; the extra child may be the one who started clobazam during the trial (not stated). Without clobazam, sedation-type events were about as frequent with cannabidiol as with placebo (10.0% and 18.5% against 16.7%); with clobazam they rose with dose. The groups are small and no test is reported.

key_findings.finding: Caregiver Global Impression of Change in overall condition at the last visit, placebo (65), 10 mg/kg/d (66) and 20 mg/kg/d (66): very much worse 0, 0 and 1; much worse 2, 1 and 3; slightly worse 4, 2 and 5; no change 32, 18 and 17; slightly improved 18, 21 and 19; much improved 8, 11 and 10; very much improved 1, 13 and 11. Ordinal logistic regression, ITT: odds ratio 2.93 (95% CI 1.56 to 5.53; P=0.0009) at 10 mg/kg/d and 2.02 (1.08 to 3.78; P=0.0279) at 20 mg/kg/d. One child in the 20 mg/kg/d group had no rating at the last visit.

Editors' calculation: some worsening in 6 of 65 (9.2%), 3 of 66 (4.5%) and 9 of 66 (13.6%); much or very much improved in 9 (13.8%), 24 (36.4%) and 21 (31.8%).

key_findings.finding: Methods in the eMethods: categories of change and responder outcomes analysed by a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, expressed as estimated odds ratios; percentage change in total, nonconvulsive and individual seizure types as for the primary outcome; CGIC by ordinal logistic regression (age group as a factor for seizure duration only); sleep disruption, Epworth and quality of life by ANCOVA with baseline and age group; Vineland-II domains by ANCOVA or ordinal logistic regression with baseline adaptive level. No analysis of the cognitive measures is described. Prespecified sensitivity analyses: per-protocol and safety sets, the maintenance period and each 4-week block, the rank-sum test with Hodges–Lehmann median difference, parametric analyses after transformation, and imputation of unreported diary days by the worst of LOCF, NOCB or the mean daily count and by multiple imputation under a missing-not-at-random assumption; for the CGIC, analysis by caregiver only, with end-of-treatment scores and in the per-protocol set.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement2.pdf, eMethods (Other secondary outcomes; Sensitivity analyses)

key_findings.finding: Full eligibility criteria: aged 2 to 18; a documented history of Dravet syndrome not completely controlled by current antiepileptic drugs; 4 or more convulsive seizures during the first 28 days of the baseline period; 1 or more antiepileptic drugs at doses stable for at least 4 weeks; the telephone diary completed on at least 25 days of the baseline period. Among the 22 exclusion criteria: alcohol or substance abuse (as worded) within 2 years or daily consumption of 5 or more alcohol-containing drinks; recreational or medicinal cannabis or synthetic cannabinoid medicines in the 3 months before entry; hypersensitivity to cannabinoids or the excipients; felbamate for less than 1 year; impaired liver function at screening or randomization, children later found to meet it being withdrawn; any history of suicidal behaviour or C-SSRS suicidal ideation of type 4 or 5 at screening.
key_findings.locator: file Miller_2020_Supplement2.pdf, eTable 1 (inclusion criteria 3–6 and 9; exclusion criteria 6, 7, 11, 15, 17 and 22)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 66 patients were randomized to 10 mg/kg/d, but Figure 1 shows 67 randomized to that dose, 1 of whom was never treated; 66 is the number in the ITT set.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: 199 were randomized and the ITT denominators (66, 67 and 65) are correct.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all patients, caregivers, investigators and data assessors were blinded to group assignment; the Methods say they were not blinded to the volume received, that is, to the dose level (10 or 20 mg/kg/d).
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the comparison of cannabidiol with placebo was blinded; comparisons between the two doses, including the safety and tolerability comparison behind the abstract's conclusion, were made with the dose level known.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample size was calculated for a two-sided Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, but the primary outcome was analysed by negative binomial regression; the article does not explain the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Supplement 1 explains it: amendment 7 (6 September 2018, protocol version 8), after follow-up had ended and before unblinding on 16 November 2018, replaced the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with negative binomial regression, kept the rank test as a sensitivity analysis and left the sample size unchanged (Supplement 1 p. 108 of 167; article PDF p. 4). The power calculation therefore refers to the rank test that was the planned primary analysis until then; the article names the rank test as the basis of the calculation but does not say that it was the planned primary analysis or that the analysis was changed.

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratio for at least a 75% reduction with 20 mg/kg/d is printed as 3.33 (95% CI 1.10 to 10.92). By the editors' calculation from the printed counts (12 of 67 vs 4 of 65), the crude odds ratio is 3.33 with a Wald interval of 1.01 to 10.92; the other three printed responder odds ratios and intervals equal the crude values to two decimals, and 1.10 to 10.92 is not symmetric around 3.33 on the log scale (3.33 squared is 11.1; 1.10 × 10.92 is 12.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: eTable 2 prints the interval as 1.01 to 10.92 (Supplement 2 p. 4), confirming a transposition in the article; the interval only just excludes 1, and the outcome was exploratory, with no P value shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give transaminase rises as 3 of 44 (6.8%) in the 10 mg/kg/d group and 13 of 47 (27.7%) in the 20 mg/kg/d group, as if 44 and 47 were group sizes; they are the numbers taking valproate in the ITT groups (Table 1), as the Discussion makes clear, whereas the safety sets were 64 and 69 after 2 patients were moved from the 10 to the 20 mg/kg/d group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read 6.8% and 27.7% as rates among children taking valproate; it is not stated whether the denominators follow the ITT or the safety assignment.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results report no notable difference in cognitive function (eTable 2), but no cognitive measure is listed among the outcomes or named anywhere in the Methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Supplement 1 names the battery and its timing (Visit 2 and the end of treatment, at sites with the expertise) and shows that only descriptive summaries were planned (pp. 51 and 137–139 of 167): eTable 2, to which the article refers, contains no cognitive outcome (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5) and the eMethods describe no cognitive analysis (p. 13), so no cognitive data, number tested or test is reported in the article or in Supplements 1 and 2, and the statement cannot be cited as evidence that cannabidiol does not affect cognition.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 footnote b: one patient in the 20 mg/kg/d group was later found to be taking felbamate, carbamazepine and levetiracetam besides the stiripentol, clobazam and topiramate recorded at database lock; Table 1 uses the database at lock, in which concomitant antiepileptic drugs in this group range from 1 to 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the counts; this patient took six antiepileptic drugs, and the duration of felbamate use, an exclusion criterion if under a year, is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: The article attributes its hierarchical gatekeeping to Hochberg's sharper Bonferroni procedure (reference 25), but the statistical analysis plan it cites describes a plain fixed-sequence procedure: eight comparisons in a set order, each at the full two-sided 0.05 level, with no Hochberg step (Supplement 1 p. 126 of 167, SAP §5.5.1 and Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the conclusions: all eight P values are below .05 (editors' check), so testing never stopped; but the citation misdescribes the procedure, and readers should not infer a Hochberg-type adjustment of the dose comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The article says 2 children randomized to 10 mg/kg/d titrated above the target dose (Table 2 footnote b), as if this were part of the titration; the statistical analysis plan states that 4 children randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (cannabidiol or placebo) incorrectly received up to 20 mg/kg/d, 1 of them up to 50 mg/kg/d, and the protocol made no provision for going above the assigned dose (Supplement 1 pp. 41–42 and 122 of 167).
reporting_issues.consequence: The plan calls these doses incorrect, that is, departures from the protocol's dosing rules rather than part of the planned titration; neither the plan nor the article says how they arose. The article does not mention the child given up to 50 mg/kg/d, and the plan does not say whether that child was in the cannabidiol or the placebo group; the 2 cannabidiol children's adverse events are counted under 20 mg/kg/d, while the efficacy analysis kept all 4 in their randomized groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The article says that the sensitivity analyses of the primary end point were consistent with the primary analysis and that the difference from placebo was maintained for the duration of treatment (PDF p. 4). In eFigure 2a every estimate favours cannabidiol, but the 95% intervals include no difference at 10 mg/kg/d in the rank-sum (Hodges–Lehmann), rank ANCOVA and ANCOVA analyses, at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days, and in maintenance weeks 5–8 (both doses) and weeks 9–12 (20 mg/kg/d).
reporting_issues.consequence: Consistent holds for direction, not for excluding no difference: the 10 mg/kg/d result depends on the model (its interval includes no difference under the rank-sum analysis, the planned primary analysis until amendment 7), the 20 mg/kg/d result depends on how unreported diary days are handled, and the 4-weekly blocks are too imprecise to show either maintenance or waning clearly.

reporting_issues.issue: The eMethods list a multiple-imputation analysis of unreported diary days under a missing-not-at-random assumption and three sensitivity analyses of the CGIC (caregiver only, end-of-treatment scores, per-protocol set), but Supplement 2 shows no result for any of them (eFigure 2a, eFigure 4). The statistical analysis plan described the multiple imputation as applying to data missing after withdrawal (Supplement 1 pp. 127–130 of 167), the eMethods to unreported days.
reporting_issues.consequence: Four prespecified sensitivity analyses are unreported, among them the one meant to test the missing-at-random assumption behind the primary analysis, whose worst-case alternative already changed the 20 mg/kg/d result.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to eTable 3 says that in cannabidiol-treated patients the antiepileptic dose adjustments were due primarily to adverse events (15 of 19 patients for valproate, 14 of 20 for clobazam), but 19 and 20 are the numbers of valproate and clobazam adjustments across all three groups (4 + 4 + 11 and 1 + 8 + 11), whereas the cannabidiol groups account for 15 valproate and 19 clobazam adjustments (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: How many of the cannabidiol-group adjustments were made because of adverse events cannot be read; the article gives the overall counts (20 of 126 and 19 of 139), the reasons for two starts (clobazam for prolonged seizures at 10 mg/kg/d; valproate after status epilepticus at 20 mg/kg/d) and, without counts, that somnolence led to clobazam dose reductions more often in the cannabidiol groups (PDF p. 6).

reporting_issues.issue: eTable 2 counts a 100% reduction in convulsive seizures over the treatment period in 1 of 65, 2 of 66 and 3 of 67 (ITT), whereas the article reports freedom from convulsive seizures over the 14-week treatment period in 1, 2 and 2 completers, and 1, 2 and 3 over the maintenance period.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the definitions differ (ITT against completers) and a child who did not complete may explain the third case at 20 mg/kg/d, but neither source says so; seizure freedom was rare in every group either way.

Excluded: a clinically significant unstable illness other than epilepsy in the 4 weeks before screening, alcohol or other substance-use problems, recreational or medicinal cannabis in the previous 3 months, and felbamate taken for less than 1 year. The full criteria are in eTable 1 of Supplement 2, which was not on file (Methods › Patients and Procedures, PDF p. 2).

disagreements.first_pass: Study conditions: plant-derived, highly purified cannabidiol oral solution, 100 mg/mL (Epidiolex in the United States, Epidyolex in the European Union), or matching placebo solution (excipients only), supplied in identical 100-mL amber glass bottles; target 10 or 20 mg/kg/d (or the equivalent volume of placebo) in two equal daily doses for 14 weeks, escalated from 2.5 mg/kg/d over the first 2 weeks, then tapered over up to 10 days. Two patients randomized to 10 mg/kg/d, and two in the placebo group assigned the 10 mg/kg/d volume, received more than that dose or volume (Figure 1). Investigators were to keep the doses of other medicines unchanged, with adjustments allowed for adverse events (Methods › Procedures, PDF pp. 2–3). No purity figure is given; the authors state that other cannabidiol formulations vary in purity, excipients and consistency (Discussion, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 6).

Key secondary, tested in a fixed order: change in total (all types) seizure frequency; at least a 50% reduction in convulsive seizures; Caregiver Global Impression of Change (CGIC) in overall condition. Other secondary: worsening or improvement in convulsive seizures; at least 25%, 75% and 100% reduction; nonconvulsive seizures (myoclonic, partial or absence); individual seizure types; CGIC in seizure duration; sleep disruption; Epworth Sleepiness Scale; Quality of Life in Childhood Epilepsy; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales II. Safety: adverse events and laboratory tests, with clinic visits at weeks 2, 4, 8 and 14 and safety calls at weeks 6 and 10, after the taper and 4 weeks after the last dose; an adjudication committee for possible signals of abuse liability (Methods › Procedures and Outcome Measures, PDF p. 3).

disagreements.first_pass: (1) The abstract concludes that both doses led to similar clinically relevant reductions (PDF p. 1), and the discussion that efficacy was similar, with no appreciable difference between the doses (PDF pp. 6, 8); no comparison between the doses is reported, their intervals against placebo are wide and overlap almost entirely, and no threshold for clinical relevance was set. (2) The better safety and tolerability profile claimed for 10 mg/kg/d (PDF pp. 1, 6) rests on descriptive counts without a test, in a trial whose caregivers and investigators knew each child's dose level; it agrees with the counts of withdrawals, transaminase rises and several common adverse events. (3) The abstract advises that increases above 10 mg/kg/d be tailored to individual efficacy and safety, and the conclusions that escalation to 20 mg/kg/d may be warranted for children who need better seizure control (PDF pp. 1, 8); children were randomized to fixed doses in parallel groups and none who responded poorly to 10 mg/kg/d was escalated, so the trial did not test this. (4) The placebo response is compared with 13% in the first Dravet trial (PDF p. 7), but that figure was the median of individual percentage changes analysed by a rank test (Devinsky et al., 2017, pp. 2013–2014), whereas 26.9% is a model-based estimate from negative binomial regression, so the two are not directly comparable. (5) A non-significant clobazam interaction is read as showing that clobazam use did not significantly affect the outcome (PDF p. 6), but the test is not described and its P value is not given, and a non-significant interaction in groups of 65 to 67 cannot show that there is no effect modification. (6) The 20 mg/kg/d dose and valproate are called independent risk factors for transaminase rises, as in prior studies (PDF p. 7), but no multivariable analysis is reported in this article. The authors themselves caution against extrapolating the results to other cannabidiol-containing products (PDF p. 6).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 613 (update): items (1), (3) and (5): no between-dose comparison was planned and no clinically relevant difference is defined; the protocol made no provision for escalation above the assigned dose and the higher doses were errors; the clobazam interaction test is prespecified in the plan.

disagreements.first_pass: A centrally randomized, placebo-controlled trial analysed by intention to treat, with a fixed testing order for the primary and key secondary outcomes. The concerns are caregiver-reported outcomes with possible functional unblinding and no assessment of blinding, an unexplained difference between the planned (rank-test) and the reported (negative binomial) analysis that the unread protocol might settle, and a sponsor that designed the trial and ran the analyses. Comparisons between the two doses carry more risk than comparisons with placebo: the dose level was known to caregivers and investigators, and no statistical comparison between the doses was made. Cite it for: in 198 children and adolescents with Dravet syndrome and uncontrolled convulsive seizures, adding this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution at 10 or 20 mg/kg/d to existing antiepileptic drugs reduced caregiver-recorded convulsive seizures more than placebo over 14 weeks (model-based reductions relative to placebo 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), with more withdrawals for adverse events, more serious adverse events and more transaminase rises at 20 mg/kg/d (the transaminase rises all in children taking valproate). Do not cite it for: equal efficacy of the two doses, benefit from raising the dose in a child who has not responded, seizure freedom, long-term effects, other cannabidiol products, doses below 10 mg/kg/d, adults or other epilepsies.

disagreements.first_pass: Primary, model-based reduction from baseline in convulsive seizures over 14 weeks: 48.7% (10 mg/kg/d), 45.7% (20 mg/kg/d), 26.9% (placebo); reduction relative to placebo 29.8% (95% CI 8.4 to 46.2; P=.01) and 25.7% (2.9 to 43.2; P=.03). Maintenance period: 49.2%, 48.6% and 28.6%; ratio to placebo in the first 4 weeks of maintenance 0.63 (0.47 to 0.84) and 0.70 (0.52 to 0.94). Total seizures: 56.4%, 47.3% and 29.7%; relative to placebo 38.0% (20.1 to 51.9; P<.001) and 25.1% (3.5 to 41.9; P=.03). At least 50% reduction: 29/66 (43.9%; OR 2.21, 1.06 to 4.62; P=.03) and 33/67 (49.3%; OR 2.74, 1.32 to 5.70; P=.007) vs 17/65 (26.2%). At least 75% reduction: 20/66 (30.3%; OR 6.63, 2.12 to 20.73) and 12/67 (17.9%; OR 3.33, printed interval 1.10 to 10.92) vs 4/65 (6.2%), without P values. CGIC improved: 45/66 (P<.001) and 40/66 (P=.03) vs 27/65. Freedom from convulsive seizures over the 14 weeks, among completers: 2, 2 and 1. No statistical comparison between the two doses is reported. Editors' calculations (Wald intervals from the printed counts): at least 50% reduction, 17.8 percentage points (1.7 to 33.8) for 10 mg/kg/d and 23.1 (7.1 to 39.1) for 20 mg/kg/d, that is about 5.6 (3.0 to 58) and 4.3 (2.6 to 14) patients treated for one extra responder; CGIC improvement 68.2% and 60.6% vs 41.5%, differences 26.6 (10.2 to 43.1) and 19.1 (2.3 to 35.9) points; serious adverse events 20.3% and 24.6% vs 15.4%.

disagreements.first_pass: The statistical analysis plan specifies the primary model: a negative binomial mixed model of convulsive-seizure counts in the baseline and treatment periods, with age stratum (2–5, 6–12, 13–18 years), period, treatment arm and the treatment-by-period interaction as fixed effects, patient as a random effect and, as offset, the log number of days "in which seizures were reported"; baseline counts enter as the model's first period rather than as a covariate, and no other covariates are included (Supplement 1 p. 127 of 167, SAP §5.5.2). The responder outcomes (at least 25, 50, 75 or 100% reduction) were to be analysed by a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, with differences in proportions and odds ratios with 95% CIs (pp. 130–131); the printed odds ratios for at least 50% and 75% reduction, and three of the four intervals, equal crude values computed from the printed counts (editors' calculation), so the odds ratios appear unstratified, and the article does not say whether its P values come from the stratified test. The CGIC was to be analysed by ordinal (proportional-odds) logistic regression of the 7-point rating at the last visit, with treatment as the only factor (p. 131); the article reports the proportions improved and does not say which analysis produced its P values.

disagreements.first_pass: The primary and all three key secondary outcomes are reported for both doses, as the statistical analysis plan specifies. The other secondary outcomes (sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness, quality of life, adaptive behaviour, CGIC in seizure duration, individual seizure types, nonconvulsive seizures) are only summarized in the text or deferred to eTable 2, which was not on file. The text also reports cognitive-function results, although no cognitive measure is named in the Methods; the plan provided only descriptive summaries for the cognitive battery (Supplement 1 pp. 138–139 of 167). Prespecified in the plan but not mentioned in the article (some may be in Supplement 2, not on file): growth and development (height, weight, IGF-1, Tanner staging), the exploratory time to baseline seizure frequency and convulsive-seizure-free days, the effect-modifier analyses other than a statement on clobazam, caregiver-rated palatability, treatment and diary compliance, plasma levels of concomitant antiepileptic drugs, and per-protocol analyses of the second and third key secondary outcomes (pp. 117, 130, 139–141, 149–151 and 158; the article mentions per-protocol analyses for the primary and first key secondary outcomes only, PDF p. 4). Before unblinding, the planned analyses of seizures lasting over 30 minutes and of epilepsy-related hospitalizations were dropped for too few patients, and rescue-medication use was not analysed because it had been collected inconsistently (pp. 108–109 and 152). Not reported in the article: the results of the abuse-liability adjudication, dosing adherence and voice-response diary completion, the P value of the clobazam interaction test (whose method is in the plan, p. 140), and P values for the 75% responder analysis.

disagreements.first_pass: Planned sample size and basis (Supplement 1): the original protocol (July 2014) planned 120 patients (40 per group, the placebo group split 20 and 20) to detect a 40-point difference in mean percentage reduction in convulsive seizures (10% with placebo, 50% with cannabidiol), with an SD of 63%, a two-sided 5% level and 80% power (p. 78 of 167). Amendment 3 (20 March 2015) raised this to 150 (50 per group) with an assumed placebo reduction of 18%; amendment 6 (23 February 2017) to 186 (62 per group), with nonparametric analysis of seizure data; amendment 7 (6 September 2018) switched the primary analysis to negative binomial regression without changing the sample size (pp. 106–108). The plan's basis for 62 per group: at least 80% power for a two-sided Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test at the 0.05 level, with gamma distributions fitted by maximum likelihood to data from Part B of the sponsor's earlier Dravet study GWEP1332 (cannabidiol: scale 65.614, shape 1.0886; placebo: scale 40.887, shape 2.3059), one distribution serving for both cannabidiol groups (p. 116). The plan does not name the variable these distributions describe or state the expected difference, and the calculation refers to the rank test, not to the negative binomial model used. 199 patients were randomized against 186 planned; neither document explains the difference. 66 and 67 patients were analysed in the cannabidiol groups and 65 in the pooled placebo group. The trial was not designed or powered to compare the two doses with each other.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 625 (update): the eMethods identify the source of the sample-size distributions, GWEP1332 Part B, as GWPCARE1.
disagreements.resolution: Changed after reading Miller_2020_Supplement2.pdf, p. 13, eMethods (Sample size): clause added.

disagreements.first_pass: Over 14 weeks, convulsive seizures fell more with cannabidiol at either dose than with placebo (model-based reductions relative to placebo of 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), at least halving of convulsive seizures was more frequent (43.9% and 49.3% vs 26.2%), and so was caregiver-rated improvement (45 of 66 and 40 of 66 vs 27 of 65); freedom from convulsive seizures was rare (2, 2 and 1 among completers), and the placebo group's seizures fell by 26.9%. Adverse events were about equally frequent in all three groups (87.5%, 89.9% and 89.2%), but with 20 mg/kg/d there were more withdrawals for adverse events (5 vs 0 and 0), more serious adverse events (17 of 69 vs 13 of 64 and 10 of 65), more decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue and vomiting, and more transaminase rises above 3 times the upper limit (13 vs 3, all in children taking valproate; none with placebo).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 625 (update): the sensitivity analyses and the seizure-type results qualify the robustness of the primary result.
disagreements.resolution: Changed after reading Miller_2020_Supplement2.pdf, p. 8 (eFigure 2a) and p. 4 (eTable 2, tonic–clonic row): sentence appended.

disagreements.first_pass: (1) The abstract concludes that both doses led to similar clinically relevant reductions (PDF p. 1), and the discussion that efficacy was similar, with no appreciable difference between the doses (PDF pp. 6, 8); no comparison between the doses is reported, nor was one specified (Supplement 1 pp. 80 and 126 of 167), their intervals against placebo are wide and overlap almost entirely, and neither the protocol nor the statistical analysis plan defines a clinically relevant difference (the original power calculation assumed a 40-point difference in mean percentage reduction; Supplement 1 p. 78 of 167). (2) The better safety and tolerability profile claimed for 10 mg/kg/d (PDF pp. 1, 6) rests on descriptive counts without a test, in a trial whose caregivers and investigators knew each child's dose level; it agrees with the counts of withdrawals, transaminase rises and several common adverse events. (3) The abstract advises that increases above 10 mg/kg/d be tailored to individual efficacy and safety, and the conclusions that, because individual responses vary, escalation to 20 mg/kg/d may still be warranted for children who need better seizure control if safety and tolerability allow (PDF pp. 1, 8); children were randomized to fixed doses in parallel groups, the protocol made no provision for raising a dose above the level assigned at randomization (Supplement 1 pp. 31 and 41–42 of 167), and the 4 children randomized to the 10 mg/kg/d level (2 given cannabidiol and 2 placebo, by Figure 1) who received more did so incorrectly, by the plan's account (p. 122), so the trial did not test escalation after a poor response. (4) The placebo response is compared with 13% in the first Dravet trial (PDF p. 7), but that figure was the median of individual percentage changes analysed by a rank test (Devinsky et al., 2017, pp. 2013–2014), whereas 26.9% is a model-based estimate from negative binomial regression, so the two are not directly comparable. (5) A non-significant clobazam interaction is read as suggesting that clobazam use did not significantly affect the outcome (PDF p. 6), but its P value is not given (the statistical analysis plan prespecified the test as an effect-by-period-by-treatment interaction in the negative binomial model, one of 13 effect modifiers (editors' count) prespecified without any described adjustment for multiplicity; Supplement 1 pp. 140–141 of 167), and a non-significant interaction in groups of 65 to 67 cannot show that there is no effect modification. (6) The 20 mg/kg/d dose and valproate are called independent risk factors for transaminase rises, as in prior studies (PDF p. 7), but no multivariable analysis is reported in this article. The authors themselves caution against extrapolating the results to other cannabidiol-containing products (PDF p. 6).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 625 (update): the article's statements on consistent sensitivity analyses, a maintained effect and cognitive function are not borne out by the supplement it cites.
disagreements.resolution: Changed after reading Miller_2020_Supplement2.pdf, p. 8 (eFigure 2a) and pp. 4–5 (eTable 2), compared with the article (PDF pp. 4–5): items (7) and (8) added.

disagreements.first_pass: Two placebo-controlled trials of this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution in Dravet syndrome, both sponsored by its manufacturer, agree that 20 mg/kg/d added to existing antiepileptic drugs reduces convulsive seizures more than placebo over 14 weeks; at least halving of convulsive seizures was significant here but not in the first trial (P=0.08). The 10 mg/kg/d result has no second trial in Dravet syndrome among the sources read, and no trial independent of the manufacturer has been read. The sizes of effect are not directly comparable between the two trials, because the first analysed medians of individual percentage changes and this one a negative binomial model.

disagreements.first_pass: A centrally randomized, placebo-controlled trial analysed by intention to treat, with a fixed testing order for the primary and key secondary outcomes. The concerns are caregiver-reported outcomes with possible functional unblinding and no assessment of blinding (none was planned), and a sponsor that designed the trial and ran the analyses. The protocol and statistical analysis plan (Supplement 1) account for the difference between the planned rank test and the reported negative binomial analysis: a documented amendment made after follow-up ended but before unblinding, with the rank test kept as a sensitivity analysis. Comparisons between the two doses carry more risk than comparisons with placebo: the dose level was known to caregivers and investigators, and no statistical comparison between the doses was specified or made. Cite it for: in 198 children and adolescents with Dravet syndrome and uncontrolled convulsive seizures, adding this pharmaceutical cannabidiol solution at 10 or 20 mg/kg/d to existing antiepileptic drugs reduced caregiver-recorded convulsive seizures more than placebo over 14 weeks (model-based reductions relative to placebo 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), with more withdrawals for adverse events, more serious adverse events and more transaminase rises at 20 mg/kg/d (the transaminase rises all in children taking valproate). Do not cite it for: equal efficacy of the two doses, benefit from raising the dose in a child who has not responded, seizure freedom, long-term effects, other cannabidiol products, doses below 10 mg/kg/d, adults or other epilepsies.

disagreements.first_pass: The statistical analysis plan specifies the primary model: a negative binomial mixed model of convulsive-seizure counts in the baseline and treatment periods, with age stratum (2–5, 6–12, 13–18 years), period, treatment arm and the treatment-by-period interaction as fixed effects, patient as a random effect and, as offset, the log number of days "in which seizures were reported"; baseline counts enter as the model's first period rather than as a covariate, and no other covariates are included (Supplement 1 p. 127 of 167, SAP §5.5.2). The responder outcomes (at least 25, 50, 75 or 100% reduction) were to be analysed by a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, with differences in proportions and odds ratios with 95% CIs (pp. 130–131); the printed odds ratios for at least 50% and 75% reduction, and three of the four intervals, equal crude values computed from the printed counts (editors' calculation), so the odds ratios appear unstratified, and the article does not say whether its P values come from the stratified test. The CGIC was to be analysed by ordinal (proportional-odds) logistic regression of the 7-point rating at the last visit, with treatment as the only factor (p. 131); the article reports the proportions improved and does not say which analysis produced its P values. Supplement 2 repeats the primary model's terms (eFigure 2 footnote a, p. 9) and states a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test stratified by age group, expressed as an estimated odds ratio, for the categories of change and the responder outcomes; ordinal logistic regression for the CGIC, with age group as a factor for seizure duration only; and ANCOVA with baseline and age group for sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness and quality of life (eMethods, p. 13; eTable 2 footnotes, p. 5). All six responder odds ratios in eTable 2 (at least 25%, 75% and 100% reduction) equal crude values with Wald intervals (editors' calculation), so the printed odds ratios are not the stratified estimates the eMethods describe. eFigure 4 gives the CGIC odds ratios from the ordinal model, whose P values match those in the article (p. 12).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 635 (round-2 check): corrected at the source. Six crude Wald matches recomputed and confirmed; the conclusion is an inference and should stay hedged, as the field's own earlier sentence ('appear unstratified') is.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted by the AI co-editor (adjudication, 13 November 2026).

disagreements.first_pass: The primary and all three key secondary outcomes are reported for both doses, as the statistical analysis plan specifies. The other secondary outcomes are summarized in the text and tabulated in eTable 2 (Supplement 2 pp. 4–5): categories of change, responders, nonconvulsive seizures, individual seizure types, CGIC in seizure duration, sleep disruption, daytime sleepiness, quality of life and the Vineland composite (not its domains, although the eMethods describe domain analyses, p. 13). eTable 2 has no cognitive outcome, although the article cites it for cognitive function; the plan provided only descriptive summaries for the cognitive battery (Supplement 1 pp. 138–139 of 167). The article's text does not mention that countable partial seizures increased relative to placebo at 20 mg/kg/d in eTable 2 (an exploratory, unadjusted result). Prespecified in the plan but reported neither in the article nor in Supplement 2: growth and development (height, weight, IGF-1, Tanner staging), the exploratory time to baseline seizure frequency and convulsive-seizure-free days, the effect-modifier analyses other than a statement on clobazam, caregiver-rated palatability, treatment and diary compliance, plasma levels of concomitant antiepileptic drugs, and per-protocol analyses of the second and third key secondary outcomes (Supplement 1 pp. 117, 130, 139–141, 149–151 and 158 of 167; the article mentions per-protocol analyses for the primary and first key secondary outcomes only, PDF p. 4). Listed in the eMethods but without results in Supplement 2: the multiple-imputation analysis under a missing-not-at-random assumption and the three sensitivity analyses of the CGIC (caregiver only, end-of-treatment scores, per-protocol set) (Supplement 2 p. 14). Before unblinding, the planned analyses of seizures lasting over 30 minutes and of epilepsy-related hospitalizations were dropped for too few patients, and rescue-medication use was not analysed because it had been collected inconsistently (Supplement 1 pp. 108–109 and 152 of 167). Not reported in the article or its supplements: the results of the abuse-liability adjudication, dosing adherence and voice-response diary completion, the P value of the clobazam interaction test (whose method is in the plan, Supplement 1 p. 140 of 167), and P values for the 75% responder analysis.

disagreements.first_pass: Over 14 weeks, convulsive seizures fell more with cannabidiol at either dose than with placebo (model-based reductions relative to placebo of 29.8%, 95% CI 8.4 to 46.2, and 25.7%, 2.9 to 43.2), at least halving of convulsive seizures was more frequent (43.9% and 49.3% vs 26.2%), and so was caregiver-rated improvement (45 of 66 and 40 of 66 vs 27 of 65); freedom from convulsive seizures was rare (2, 2 and 1 among completers), and the placebo group's seizures fell by 26.9%. Adverse events were about equally frequent in all three groups (87.5%, 89.9% and 89.2%), but with 20 mg/kg/d there were more withdrawals for adverse events (5 vs 0 and 0), more serious adverse events (17 of 69 vs 13 of 64 and 10 of 65), more decreased appetite, diarrhoea, fatigue and vomiting, and more transaminase rises above 3 times the upper limit (13 vs 3, all in children taking valproate; none with placebo). In the sensitivity analyses every estimate favoured cannabidiol, but the intervals included no difference at 10 mg/kg/d in the rank-based and ANCOVA analyses of percentage change and at 20 mg/kg/d with worst-case imputation of unreported diary days; tonic–clonic seizures taken alone were not clearly reduced at either dose (exploratory; Supplement 2 pp. 4 and 8).

design_detail: Scoping review and evidence map (Joanna Briggs Institute and Cochrane scoping methods; reported to PRISMA-ScR), commissioned under Colorado House Bill 21-1317 to inform whether the THC concentration of cannabis products should be regulated. Seven databases searched in October 2021 and updated in July 2022; English language and human studies only; human studies of any epidemiological design that reported a THC concentration or a known high-concentration product. Artificial-intelligence-assisted title and abstract screening in DistillerSR; one reviewer extracted data, checked by senior reviewers; no risk-of-bias assessment, by design; no synthesis of results. The output is counts of studies by exposure, outcome and design, plus a public interactive evidence map (Tableau, not opened) of the 452 included studies. It is an inventory of what has been studied, not a summary of what was found.
can_establish: How much human research exists in which a THC concentration or a high-concentration product is reported: how many studies, of which designs, in which countries and with which outcomes; how they report exposure (concentration, frequency, duration, route); how many study concentrates (54 of 452) or THC concentration (189) directly and how many give data that could be pooled; how the strengths studied compare with market strengths the authors cite from other sources; and who funded the studies and how often interests were declared. It supports the statement that direct evidence on high-concentration products and health outcomes is limited and hard to combine.
cannot_establish: What any strength or product does to health: no study results are extracted, pooled or appraised, so nothing here says which outcomes concentrates raise or lower. Whether the 54 studies on concentrates, or the 189 on THC concentration, are good studies (no risk-of-bias assessment) or what they found. Dose or exposure: the authors state that THC concentration is not the same as dose. Completeness: searching was English-only and designed to be sensitive rather than specific, screening was AI-assisted with no recall figure, and one reviewer extracted each study, so studies may be missed or mis-coded. The market strengths quoted come from other sources (a 2018 seven-state survey and a Colorado market report), not from this review’s data. The Appendix (search strategy, study characteristics table), the evidence map and the protocol were not opened.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (a literature search). Seven databases, designed by a medical information specialist with controlled vocabulary and keywords and peer-reviewed against the PRESS checklist; initial search October 2021, update July 2022; English language and human studies only; no date limit; comments, editorials, interviews, news articles and letters excluded (Methods › Data Sources and Searches).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies of any epidemiological design, in any country, age group, health status or outcome, on recreational or medicinal cannabis, that reported a THC concentration in any unit or described a product from which a high concentration could be inferred (for example a high-potency concentrate or dab). Excluded: animal, laboratory and simulation studies; studies reporting only a THC:CBD ratio; CBD-only or cannabinol-only products; dronabinol, nabilone and similar medicines (Methods › Study Selection Criteria).
sample.demographics: Included studies (452): 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports, 34 case series; earliest 1971, 60% (269) published 2017 to 2022; United States 220 (49%), United Kingdom 46 (10%), Canada 45 (10%) and 27 other countries; purpose of cannabis use medicinal 39%, recreational 15%, unintentional 4%, other 35%, not reported 19%; participants from newborns to adults over 65; 48 studies (11%) included any health-equity analysis and none analysed structural racism (Results › Characteristics of Included Studies).
sample.attrition: 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports, 452 included studies (Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1, an image, not read). Reasons for excluding full-text reports were recorded (Methods › Study Selection › Full-text screening).
sample.selection_effects: English-only; searches sensitive rather than specific, and the authors say relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening (Limitations). By design only studies that report a THC concentration or a known high-concentration product are included, so research on cannabis use in general lies outside the map. Most included studies concern generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study reported, extracted as written. THC concentration as a percentage in 172 studies (38%; 349 exposures) or in milligrams in 113 studies (25%; 143 exposures); route in 393 (87%); frequency of intake in 384 (85%); duration in 371 (82%). Units and indices vary (range, threshold, exact value, mean). The authors write that most studies did not capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose (Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route: inhalation 279 studies (62%), ingestion 174 (38%), sublingual 39 (9%), topical 31 (7%); a study can report more than one. THC as a percentage: median 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%). THC in milligrams: median 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Median reported THC was below 50 mg or 25% for every outcome domain. Frequency most often daily (177 studies, 39%) (Results › Exposures; Results › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use is not among the extracted data items listed in the Methods, and no analysis of it is reported (Methods › Data Collection).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Of the 452 studies, 212 (47%) had a control group; the review extracted details of the comparison exposure where there was one but does not compare outcomes between exposure groups.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the confounding in the included studies was not assessed. The authors note that key populations, for example racial and ethnic minority groups, may be missing from the studies and that generalisability cannot be gauged without specific information on who uses which products (Discussion › Populations Studied).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes were extracted as written in each study and sorted by the reviewers into 16 domains based on earlier reports on cannabis: mental health, neurologic, pain, cardiometabolic, gastrointestinal, psychosocial, sleep, substance use or dependence, respiratory, cancer, ocular, injury and death, immunity, sexual and reproductive health, pregnancy-related outcomes (mother), and pre-, peri- and neonatal outcomes (Methods › Study Selection Criteria › Health outcomes).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assessment of the validity of outcome measures in the included studies. The extraction form was piloted; one reviewer extracted each study and senior reviewers checked it.
outcomes.operationalization: Counts of studies by outcome domain (mental health 180, 40%; neurologic 134, 30%; pain 133, 29%; cardiometabolic 110, 24%; gastrointestinal 101, 22%; psychosocial 98, 22%; sleep 94, 21%) and by whether a study examined concentrates or THC concentration directly (54 and 189) or indirectly (62 and 114). The authors note that outcome domains are broad and that even a single outcome such as depression was measured in different ways (Results › Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The results are counts and percentages of studies. Of 452 studies, 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome, 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome, 114 (25%) an indirect association between THC concentration and outcomes and 62 (14%) an indirect association between concentrates and outcomes; 212 (47%) had a control group; outcomes were reported with effect estimates in 184 (41%), measures of precision in 274 (61%), significance tests in 335 (74%), sample size in 349 (77%) and raw data in 232 (51%) (Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A protocol was published on OSF Registries in 2021 (reference 16) and the Methods point to it for detail; the Methods say three authors were added because of their contributions after the protocol was published. The protocol itself was not opened, so deviations were not checked. A risk-of-bias assessment was not planned, as scoping methods allow (Methods › Data Collection, last paragraph).
