analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) against never, for lifetime but not past 6 months, past 6 months but not past 30 days, 1 to 2 days in the past 30, and 3 or more days in the past 30 (sociodemographic model; full model). CANNABIS VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84); full 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96), 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56), 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47), 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.06 (0.65 to 1.73), 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00), 1.76 (0.96 to 3.13), 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36); full 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 0.95 (0.63 to 1.44), 1.35 (1.04 to 1.75), 1.67 (0.98 to 2.86), 1.67 (1.09 to 2.53); full 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). NICOTINE VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.35 (0.92 to 1.97), 1.18 (0.79 to 1.78), 1.48 (0.97 to 2.21), 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41); full 1.21 (0.76 to 1.93), 0.82 (0.50 to 1.32), 1.13 (0.71 to 1.81), 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.13 (0.74 to 1.71), 1.55 (1.04 to 2.32), 1.27 (0.81 to 1.99), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96); full 0.96 (0.58 to 1.59), 1.06 (0.66 to 1.71), 0.99 (0.59 to 1.65), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 1.20 (0.85 to 1.71), 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), 1.64 (1.14 to 2.36), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full 1.03 (0.68 to 1.57), 1.10 (0.73 to 1.67), 1.31 (0.86 to 1.99), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Overall 17.5% (384 of 2194) reported bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2396) wheeze and 20.4% (488 of 2389) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis, against 61.6% of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data (Table 2 and Results). Editors' rough calculation, not in the paper: if people with missing outcome data were spread evenly across vaping groups, unadjusted bronchitic-symptom rates would be about 14% in people who never vaped cannabis and about 27% to 31% in those who vaped it in the past 30 days; the paper says missing respiratory data were commoner in people who vaped nicotine or smoked, so the true gap may be larger. Odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common (13% to 20%).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, personal financial status, body mass index; the full model adds the other vaping variable, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. No adjustment for asthma, secondhand smoke, air quality or tobacco co-use in cannabis. The number of people in each model is not given: Table 3 headings show 2194, 2396 and 2389, the counts with outcome data, but the full models also need cannabis vaping, financial status and body mass index.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All three outcomes and both exposures are shown in Table 3, with sociodemographic and full models. The abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3 and the Results text (reporting issue 1). The stated multiple-testing correction is not shown. The headline emphasises the cannabis vaping results in the full model; the nicotine vaping associations seen in the sociodemographic model, which became null on full adjustment, are reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The nicotine and cannabis vaping top bands are small (400 and 155 people), and the cannabis vaping intervals at 1 to 2 and 3 or more days are wide (1.42 to 5.47; 1.18 to 4.06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 2553 young adults in one Southern California school-based cohort, people who reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs had higher odds than people who never had of reporting bronchitic symptoms in the past year at every level of recency and frequency (full-model adjusted odds ratios 1.6 to 2.8, adjusting for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis), higher odds of wheeze only in the top band (3 or more days in the past 30, 2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and no reliable difference in shortness of breath. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with bronchitic symptoms, wheeze and shortness of breath after sociodemographic adjustment only (1.45 to 1.78), and with none of them after full adjustment (0.85 to 0.96).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say cannabis vaping is associated with increased risk of bronchitic symptoms and wheeze, independent of nicotine vaping and smoking combustible products, and that nicotine and cannabis vaping warrant consideration in patient care and public health policy. Key Points say cannabis vaping may be associated with bronchitic symptoms beyond the consequences of other drug use. Gaps: (1) risk language comes from one cross-sectional survey, with no information on what came first; (2) independence rests on adjustment with coarse five-level bands for the other exposures, and combustible cannabis includes blunts with unrecorded tobacco, so residual confounding is plausible; (3) odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people who had last vaped cannabis more than 6 months earlier (1.73), about as raised as in those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79), which does not fit an effect of recent vaping alone and is not discussed; (4) the Discussion's mechanisms (vitamin E acetate, higher exposure from deeper puffs and concentrates) were not measured, and the statement that vitamin E acetate vaping has virtually disappeared is made without a source; (5) the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; (6) symptoms are self-reported and unconfirmed. The Limitations section does state the cross-sectional design, the single region and the need for longitudinal work.

timeline.event: McConnell et al. (cited, not read) linked nicotine vaping to respiratory symptoms in adolescents; Wills et al. (2019) did the same in adults, per the authors' introduction (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

This survey, which the authors describe as new evidence for an independent association of cannabis vaping with bronchitic symptoms, with nicotine vaping and smoking adjusted at the same time; they note longitudinal work on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Limitations).

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional survey from one cohort. No second study of cannabis vaping and respiratory symptoms was read for this card, and the authors say longitudinal research on this question is lacking. Evidence on smoked cannabis and symptoms, cited by the authors, is not read here.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health: grants U54CA180905 (all authors; principal investigator Leventhal), R01CA229617-01 (Barrington-Trimis, Leventhal) and K24DA048160 (Leventhal). The paper states the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young adults with repeated symptom reports and lung function tests before and after people start vaping cannabis, recording product type (cartridge, dry-herb, concentrate), source, device and puffing, tobacco co-use, and biomarker confirmation of use, with separate groups who only vape cannabis, only smoke it, do both, or neither, and a registered analysis plan with the multiple-testing correction shown.

domains.note: One time point, so reverse causation and shared causes cannot be separated. Adjustment is for sociodemographics and for the other exposures in five coarse bands; tobacco in joints or blunts, secondhand smoke, air quality, asthma and allergy are not measured. Raised odds in people who last vaped cannabis more than 6 months before the survey (1.73) point to residual confounding or to an exposure measure that captures more than recent vaping.

Self-reported recency and days of use, not verified; the cannabis vaping variable merges THC or hash oil devices with dabs, and no product, device or amount is recorded. Misclassification is probably not related to symptoms, which would bias towards no association.

A school-based Southern California cohort, 75% participation in this wave; people without respiratory data were more likely to have vaped nicotine or smoked cigarettes; not representative of other regions or of people who left school.
Not an issue for a single-time survey of exposure and symptoms.

Outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms) and 6% (wheeze, shortness of breath), with missingness related to vaping and smoking; 110 people have no cannabis vaping data; handling is not described and the number analysed in each model is not given.

Self-reported symptoms from questions used in earlier cohort studies, with no spirometry or clinician; the bronchitic composite counts any of four broad items; the same person reported exposure and outcome.

No protocol or registration; the stated Benjamini-Hochberg correction is not shown; the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; all outcomes and both models are shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain; confounding is judged high because a single cross-sectional survey with coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures and from reverse causation, and the pattern of raised odds in people who last vaped long before the survey suggests residual confounding. The study is sizeable for a vaping survey, adjusts at once for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis, reports both an unadjusted-to-sociodemographic and a fully adjusted model, and shows its null results. It may be cited for the association between self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil or dabs and self-reported bronchitic symptoms (and, in the top band, wheeze) in these young adults, and for the loss of the nicotine vaping association on full adjustment. It may not be cited for causation, for the effect of any particular product, for lung function, for absolute risk in a vaping group, or for older people.

key_findings.finding: 2553 young adults (mean age 19.3, SD 0.79; 57.9% women; 47.3% Hispanic) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered a survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2396 (wheeze) and 2389 (shortness of breath).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Analytic Sample, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Of the 2553, 1095 (42.9%) reported ever vaping nicotine. Of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data, 939 (38.4%) reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs: 204 (8.4%) only in their lifetime, 490 (20.1%) in the past 6 months but not the past 30 days, 90 (3.7%) on 1 or 2 days and 155 (6.3%) on 3 or more days in the past 30; 110 people had no cannabis vaping data. Smoked cannabis on 3 or more days in the past 30: 517 (20.3%); cigarettes on 3 or more days: 98 (3.8%).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's fully adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms with cannabis vaping (1.83, 1.08 to 3.10; 1.58, 1.02 to 2.46; 2.83, 1.46 to 5.50; 2.14, 1.16 to 3.92) differ from Table 3 and the Results text (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96; 1.63, 1.04 to 2.56; 2.79, 1.42 to 5.47; 2.19, 1.18 to 4.06). The wheeze value (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37) is the same in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract appears to quote an earlier version of the model. Table 3 is used for every figure; the direction and the conclusion are unchanged, but the abstract values must not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 204 of 2553 (8.4%) for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and 939 of 2553 (38.4%) for any, but 8.4% and 38.4% are shares of the 2443 people with cannabis vaping data (204 of 2553 is 8.0%, as in Table 2; 939 of 2553 is 36.8%). The abstract also says lifetime but not in the past '60 months'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mixed denominators and a typing error (6 months); the 110 people with no cannabis vaping data are the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on nicotine vaping and bronchitic symptoms in the fully adjusted model gives 'aORs range from 1.63-2.79 [95% CI, 1.01-5.47]', which are the cannabis vaping figures. Table 3 gives 0.82 to 1.21 for nicotine vaping.
reporting_issues.consequence: A copy error; the table shows no reliable nicotine vaping association with bronchitic symptoms on full adjustment, consistent with the sentence's claim of no significant association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is headed 'Prevalence of each respiratory outcome', but the percentages are column percentages (the share of people with each outcome who fell in each vaping group), not symptom rates within each vaping group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper never gives the percentage of each vaping group with symptoms; do not read the 48.2% of cases who never vaped cannabis as the rate in that group.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 headings give n = 2194, 2396 and 2389 (people with outcome data), but the fully adjusted models also need cannabis vaping (110 missing), financial status (161 missing), body mass index and the smoking variables. The Methods also say 2553 provided complete data on lifetime, 6-month and 30-day vaping while 110 have no cannabis vaping data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 headings; Methods › Analytic Sample; Table 2 footnote f
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people in each model is not stated; complete-case loss may be larger than 14%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values corrected for multiple tests; no adjusted P value or adjusted interval is shown. Several fully adjusted lower bounds are close to 1 (1.01 for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and bronchitic symptoms; 1.04 and 1.02 elsewhere).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the weaker associations survive the stated correction cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The pattern of odds in Table 3 is not discussed: people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey had raised odds of bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), similar to those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79).
reporting_issues.consequence: The data do not show a clear gradient with recency, which argues for caution about an effect of current vaping and for residual confounding.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7756238 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3 and author notes read as text; the Supplement, with eTable 1, eTable 2 and the questionnaire, is a PDF and was not opened)

design_detail: Population-based cohort of 49,321 Swedish men conscripted for military service in 1969–70 at age 18 to 20. Cannabis, tobacco and alcohol use were self-reported once, at conscription, in non-anonymous questionnaires; lung cancer was taken from national registers by record linkage (inpatient Patient Register to the end of 2009, Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006). Cox regression of time to lung cancer by lifetime cannabis use (ever against never; never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times), crude, tobacco-adjusted and fully adjusted. Exposure was recorded before the outcome, but the study is a historical record-linkage analysis of data collected for conscription.
can_establish: Whether men who reported more cannabis use by age 18 to 20 were diagnosed with lung cancer more often over the next 40 years than men who reported none, after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory illness and occupation as recorded at that time.
cannot_establish: That smoking cannabis causes lung cancer, or the risk in men who never smoked tobacco (too few to analyse), in women, above about age 60 or with later patterns of use and products: use after conscription, how cannabis was smoked, how much and whether tobacco was mixed in were never recorded, and the number of cancers in each cannabis group is not given in the text or tables.

sample.recruitment: Registry/conscription: all men conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–70 (born 1949–51), which the authors say covered more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, 2–3% being excused for disqualifying mental or physical conditions (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men conscripted in 1969–70 at age 18 to 20. The models are complete-case analyses: men without cannabis answers (3,768 for ever use, 3,800 for frequency) or with other missing predictors were left out, and 10 of the 189 lung cancers were excluded for missing predictor information.
sample.demographics: Men only, aged 18 to 20 at baseline. At conscription 41.4% did not smoke tobacco, 11.2% smoked 1–5 cigarettes a day, 20.7% 6–10, 23.1% 11–20 and 3.6% more than 20; 10.5% had ever used cannabis and 1.7% more than 50 times; physician-diagnosed respiratory conditions about 2% in every cannabis group; occupation from the 1970 census, about half manual skilled or unskilled (Table 1).
sample.attrition: During follow-up 2,958 men (6.0%) died of causes other than lung cancer and 930 (1.9%) emigrated, both censored; 44,257 to 44,285 men entered the adjusted models (about 90% of the cohort).
sample.selection_effects: Population-based and nearly complete for Swedish men of that age, so selection into the cohort is not the concern. Limits to generalising: men only, Swedish cannabis and tobacco use of 1969–70, and follow-up ending at about age 60. The men who did not answer the cannabis questions (about 7.6%) had a lower lung cancer risk than men who reported never using cannabis (fully adjusted HR 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so non-responders differed in some way the paper does not explain.

exposure.measurement: Non-anonymous self-report at conscription: ever against never use of cannabis, and lifetime frequency in six bands (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50, more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort, and this paper calls more than 50 times 'heavy' use. No biological verification; the authors cite a validation study of self-reported drug use in this cohort as showing reasonable accuracy.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime number of uses by age 18 to 20 only. No quantity, potency, duration, method of smoking (joint or pipe) or tobacco mixed in, and no measure of cannabis use at any time after conscription over the 40 years; smoking is assumed as the route.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco (cigarettes a day at conscription, five answers collapsed into three bands: none, 1–10, more than 10) and alcohol (grams a week from five questions, four levels) were adjusted for, each measured once. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 756 (91.0%) also smoked tobacco and 514 (61.8%) more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 54.7% and 23.2% of the men who reported never using cannabis (editors' arithmetic from Table 1). Other drug use was collected at conscription but not used in the analysis. Whether tobacco was mixed into cannabis is unknown.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (registry outcomes decades later).

comparison.controls: Men who reported never using cannabis at conscription (40,397; 44.8% did not smoke tobacco, 31.5% smoked 1–10 cigarettes a day and 23.2% more than 10).
comparison.matching: None. Cox models adjusted for tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status (occupation in the 1970 census).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tobacco and cannabis use after conscription; how much tobacco was smoked within the coarse bands (the top band runs from 11 to more than 20 a day); occupational and environmental exposures, diet and family history of lung cancer; use of other drugs. None was adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; 54.7% of the men who reported never using cannabis smoked tobacco (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Lung cancer coded ICD-8/9 162 or ICD-10 C33–C34 in any diagnostic position in the Swedish Patient Register (inpatient care) from conscription to the end of 2009, or as the underlying cause in the National Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006; emigration from the Total Population Register. The Swedish Cancer Register was not used.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between lung cancer records in the Patient Register and the Cause-of-Death or Cancer Registers, and sensitivities of about 80% to 95% for administrative lung cancer codes in studies elsewhere. Of the 189 cases, 95 were in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only and 6 in the death register only.
outcomes.operationalization: Time to a first lung cancer record, censored at death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009; person-time from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men who died in 1969), about 1.9 million person-years per line of analysis. Proportional hazards checked with log survival plots.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: one outcome, but ever use and five frequency bands were each tested in three models, with p < 0.05 as the threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes came from national registers, independent of the conscription questionnaire.

analysis.effect_sizes: Hazard ratios with 95% CIs (Tables 2–4). Lifetime frequency against never (crude; tobacco-adjusted; fully adjusted): once 2.07 (1.06–4.06); 1.48 (0.75–2.91); 1.52 (0.77–3.01). 2–4 times 0.95 (0.39–2.33); 0.65 (0.26–1.58); 0.66 (0.27–1.62). 5–10 times 1.02 (0.32–3.20); 0.66 (0.21–2.09); 0.68 (0.21–2.16). 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26–5.74); 1.68 (0.78–3.62); 1.68 (0.77–3.66). More than 50 times 3.72 (1.96–7.06); 2.24 (1.17–4.29); 2.12 (1.08–4.14). Ever against never: 1.90 (1.30–2.75); 1.25 (0.85–1.83); 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco against none, fully adjusted: 1–10 a day 2.34 (1.47–3.70), more than 10 a day 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Missing cannabis answers against never, fully adjusted: 0.41 (0.17–0.99) and 0.40 (0.16–0.98). No absolute risks by group are given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 men (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by the end of 2009, about 9 per 100,000 person-years in the analysed cohort (179 cases over about 1.9 million person-years).
analysis.covariates: Tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions at conscription and socioeconomic status (occupation, 1970 census), all measured once at baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The frequency bands, including 'more than 50 times', follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort (Zammit et al., 2002, cited for consistency); the label heavy is this paper's.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports only the more-than-50 band, the one band significant after adjustment, and omits the null ever-use result after tobacco adjustment, the lack of a gradient across bands and the crude and tobacco-only estimates (all in the Results and tables). Tobacco-stratified analyses are in Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, described as unstable or inestimable; the supplement was not available to this reader.
analysis.power: 179 cases in the models; the number among the 831 men in the heaviest band is not given in the text or tables (Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, was not extracted); too few men used cannabis without tobacco for stratified analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Men who reported more than 50 lifetime uses at age 18 to 20 had about twice the hazard of a lung cancer record by about age 60 (fully adjusted 2.12, 1.08 to 4.14), with an interval reaching close to 1; the estimate fell from 3.72 unadjusted to 2.24 with a three-band tobacco adjustment, ever use was not associated after tobacco adjustment (1.25, 0.84 to 1.87), and the lower bands showed no gradient. Of the heaviest band 91% also smoked tobacco, and no estimate could be made for men who did not.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports 'more than a twofold risk' for heavy use 'even after statistical adjustment for baseline tobacco use' and concludes that the study provides 'initial longitudinal evidence that cannabis use might elevate the risk of lung cancer' (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the conclusion adds that the finding requires further replication (p. 8). The Discussion proposes that the findings be integrated into drug-prevention programmes as initial evidence of the risks of marijuana smoking for lung cancer (p. 7), and argues that unmeasured changes in use after conscription would bias the estimate toward the null (p. 8). Gaps: the label 'heavy' for more than 50 lifetime uses by age 20; an abstract silent on the null ever-use result, the missing gradient and the near-1 lower limit; and a one-sided bias argument, since later tobacco smoking, more common in men who used cannabis, could bias the estimate away from the null, which the authors cover only as residual confounding by tobacco. The conclusion itself is hedged ('might', 'requiring further replication') and the limitations are stated candidly.

timeline.event: Sidney et al.: Kaiser Permanente cohort in California, no association between cannabis smoking and lung cancer; this paper notes its members were followed only to a mean age of 42 (as cited).
Hashibe et al.: population-based case-control study in Los Angeles, no association (as cited).
This cohort: HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription, no gradient below that band, no association for ever use after tobacco adjustment.

Zhang et al.: pooled analysis of six case-control studies in the International Lung Cancer Consortium, habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (0.66–1.38), known here only through the National Academies committee's account.

National Academies committee: 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and lung cancer, naming this cohort as a study outside the pooled analysis that points to an increased risk.
Muheriwa-Matemba et al., systematic review by route: the reviews it included did not conclusively link cannabis smoking and lung cancer.

replication.where_it_stands: The only cohort with follow-up of decades among the sources read. Its raised estimate in the heaviest band stands against the null pooled case-control analysis and has not been repeated in another cohort in the sources read; it rests on one baseline report of cannabis and tobacco use, with 91% tobacco co-use in that band, and on follow-up that ends before the ages at which most lung cancers are diagnosed.

funding.funder: Supported indirectly by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (salary support for R. C. Callaghan), and by a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611 to P. Allebeck; salary support for A. Sidorchuk). The paper states that the funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, manuscript preparation or approval to publish, and that the views are not necessarily the Ministry's.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Northern British Columbia, University of Toronto and CAMH (Callaghan); Karolinska Institutet (Allebeck, Sidorchuk); North-Western State Medical University, Saint Petersburg (Sidorchuk). No cannabis- or tobacco-industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort, or pooled cohorts, that records cannabis and tobacco use repeatedly through adult life (including how cannabis is smoked, how much and whether tobacco is mixed in), includes enough people who smoke cannabis but never tobacco, follows them with cancer-register outcomes into the ages at which most lung cancers occur, and reports absolute risks by group.

domains.note: Tobacco, the main confounder, was measured once at age 18 to 20 in three coarse bands; 91% of the heaviest cannabis band smoked tobacco and 61.8% more than 10 a day, against 23.2% of the never group. Adjustment for these bands alone cut the ever-use estimate from 1.90 to 1.25 and the heaviest band from 3.72 to 2.24, so residual confounding by tobacco amount within bands and by smoking after conscription is plausible and would run away from the null. Occupational exposures, diet, family history and other drugs were not adjusted for, and estimates among men who did not smoke tobacco could not be made.

A single non-anonymous self-report of lifetime frequency at age 18 to 20 stands for 40 years of exposure: no use after conscription, no method, amount, potency or tobacco mixing. The authors expect under-reporting from non-anonymity and report anecdotal over-reporting to avoid military training; with several bands and a confounded exposure, the direction of the resulting bias is not certain.
Population-based cohort covering more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, followed through national registers from baseline; only 1.9% emigrated.
No intervention after exposure is described that would differ by cannabis use.

About 7.6% lacked cannabis answers and 10 of 189 cancers were dropped for missing predictors (complete-case analysis). The men without cannabis answers had a lower lung cancer risk than the never group (fully adjusted 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so missingness was related to the outcome; the effect on the heavy-against-never contrast is unclear.

Register-based lung cancer records, independent of the exposure report; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%. Inpatient and death records rather than the cancer register, and death records only to 2006, may miss some cases, but not in a way linked to cannabis answers given decades earlier.

No registered protocol; the frequency bands were taken from an earlier paper on this cohort, which limits the choice of cut-off, but ever use and five bands were each tested in three models without correction, and the abstract reports only the one significant band.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because confounding by tobacco and the single baseline measure of exposure could each change the estimate materially, and the remaining tobacco confounding most plausibly biases away from the null. The design's strengths are real: a near-complete national cohort, outcomes from registers and 40 years of follow-up. The study may be cited for the adjusted association between reporting more than 50 lifetime cannabis uses at age 18 to 20 and a lung cancer record by about age 60, with its crude and tobacco-adjusted versions, the null ever-use result and the absent gradient; not for an effect of smoking cannabis, for people who never smoked tobacco, for women, for later or current patterns of use and products, or for risk at older ages.

key_findings.finding: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Materials and methods › Data sources; Swedish male conscripts' files

key_findings.finding: Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the cohort, and this paper labels more than 50 times heavy use. 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Materials and methods › Measurement of cannabis use

key_findings.finding: Tobacco was measured once, at conscription, by cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Confounders adjusted: tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders

key_findings.finding: Table 1: of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) had no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 192 (23.1%) against 918 (2.3%). Respiratory conditions: 18 (2.2%) against 747 (1.9%). The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
key_findings.note: 756 of 831 is 91.0% (92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer); editors' arithmetic.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each line of analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register in any diagnostic position to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register as underlying cause to the end of 2006; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%, and sensitivity of administrative codes about 80% to 95% elsewhere.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses

key_findings.finding: 189 incident lung cancers (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only); 2,958 men (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cases were excluded for missing predictor information, leaving 179 in the analyses. Cases by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Tables 2-4 (n = 179 in the titles)
key_findings.note: Figure 1's values were not extracted, so no absolute risk by cannabis group is given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) by the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: More than 50 lifetime uses against never (Table 4, 44,257 men, 179 cancers): crude HR 3.72 (95% CI 1.96 to 7.06), tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17 to 4.29), fully adjusted 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), described by the authors as more than a twofold risk even after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (more than 50 times row; footnotes a and b)

key_findings.finding: Ever against never use (Table 3, 44,285 men, 179 cancers): crude 1.90 (1.30 to 2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84 to 1.87); the authors say tobacco adjustment greatly attenuated the risk and further adjustment did not change it.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Lower frequency bands, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). The authors state that the results did not show a clear dose–response relationship.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Tobacco against none, with cannabis and the other covariates in the model: 1–10 cigarettes a day 2.34 (1.48 to 3.71) and more than 10 a day 5.06 (3.25 to 7.86) with ever use; 2.34 (1.47 to 3.70) and 5.03 (3.23 to 7.81) with cannabis frequency; crude 2.29 (1.48 to 3.57) and 5.16 (3.45 to 7.73). The authors call this a strong dose–response relation.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Men without cannabis answers (3,768 on ever use, 7.64%; 3,800 on frequency, 7.70%) were not more likely to develop lung cancer than men reporting never using cannabis: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06), 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 5th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4

key_findings.finding: Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) did not give compelling results: there were too few people who used cannabis but not tobacco and too few lung cancers, even when men smoking 5 or fewer cigarettes a day were grouped with those who did not smoke.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph (continued on p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on use before conscription and none on tobacco or cannabis use after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the men in the heavy band also reported tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have inflated their use to be exempted from military training. They argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70; their cohort was followed for 40 years from age 18 to 20.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the authors call their primary finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise the risk of lung cancer; the Discussion proposes that the findings be used in drug-prevention programmes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions

No conflicts of interest declared.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: Heavy use is defined as more than 50 lifetime uses in the Methods, Results and Table 4, but as at least 50 uses in the first paragraph of the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysis uses the more-than-50 band (Table 4), which is the definition to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives n = 44,284 for the Cox analyses that produced HR 2.12, but Table 3 (ever use) gives 44,285 and Tables 2 and 4 (frequency, the source of 2.12) give 44,257.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 44,257 with the heavy-use estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say approximately 91% and the Discussion more than 91% of the heaviest band reported tobacco use; Table 1 gives 756 of 831 (91.0%), or 92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; about 91% is the figure to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of lung cancers in each cannabis group is given only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, and not in the text or tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: No absolute risk can be stated for the heavy-use group from the text or tables; only the cohort's overall base rate (189 of 49,321) is available.

verification.source_read: PDF, online-first version (published online 12 July 2013) without printed page numbers, 10 pages (PDFs/Cannabis/Callaghan_2013_LungCancerCohort.pdf); text extracted once with pdftotext -layout: all text, Tables 1 to 4 with footnotes, the Figure 1 legend (the stacked bar chart, viewed on a rendered page, was not extracted), acknowledgments (funding), conflict statement and reference list. The electronic supplementary material (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2) was not available and was not read. The printed article (reference record) is pp. 1811–1820; page references here are to the PDF's own pages 1 to 10.

design_detail: Descriptive laboratory analysis of product samples, with no comparison group. The Wadsworth Center (the New York State Department of Health public health laboratory) analysed 38 samples of residual fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) for whom cartridges were obtained (the laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019), and six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners. Untargeted screening by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and high-resolution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS/MS), then targeted measurement of 11 natural cannabinoids (HPLC with photodiode array), five mycotoxins, vitamin E acetate (VEA; GC-MS), the fungicide myclobutanil and the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide (PBO; LC-MS/MS), a screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites, and a screen for synthetic cannabinoids and 150 synthetic opioid compounds; nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) for the commercial products. Results are counts and percentages by mass; no statistical tests or intervals are given. Version read: the PMC full text of the Toxics article (2020;8(1):8).
can_establish: What was in the residual fluid of vaporizer cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI in 2019: of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, 23 (64%) contained VEA, at 16 to 58% by mass; 14 or 15 contained medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil; most also held pesticide residues; some had unusually high delta-8-THC; none had synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins above the stated limits. It also shows that three of six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners were essentially pure VEA, so VEA was on sale for this use.
cannot_establish: That VEA, or any other substance in the fluid, caused the lung injury: there are no fluids from people who vaped without injury, no dose or timing data and no result per patient. It cannot show what share of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge (13 of the 36 fluids had none), how common VEA was in cartridges in general in 2019, what the patients inhaled other than the residue left in the cartridge, or how these cartridges differ from legally sold ones (that contrast rests on the laboratory's earlier work with New York medical products, not on data shown here). The aerosol was not analysed; products formed when VEA is heated are mentioned from initial experiments that are not shown.

sample.recruitment: Cartridges and devices were obtained through New York Poison Control Centers and health care providers. Medical staff of the Department of Health's Center for Environmental Health reviewed each reported case's medical record for consistency with the CDC clinical description of EVALI; when case-associated cartridges were available they were sent to the Wadsworth Center (Methods 2.1). The six commercial products were bought on the internet by the Department of Health (Results 3.4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Fluids from the first 10 New York EVALI cases for which cartridges were obtained. Cartridges with little fluid were centrifuged to recover it and run at adjusted dilution; sample 38 had too little material for the PBO test (Table 2). Whether any cartridge was excluded is not stated. How each cartridge was judged to be illicit is not described: the Methods call them case-associated and say that packing and markings were noted, but report neither.
sample.demographics: Not reported for the 10 patients (no age, sex, dates or hospital course). The only patient information is that, of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories (the number who provided one is not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing products (Discussion 4.3, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Thirty-eight samples are analysed from 10 patients, about 3.8 per patient on average; the number per patient is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Only cartridges that patients, families or clinicians handed over, from 10 patients in one state, are analysed; who handed over cartridges and who did not is not described. The fluid is what was left in the cartridge at recovery, which may differ from what was inhaled earlier. No sample of cartridges from the wider market was taken, so the shares apply to these cartridges, not to cartridges in general.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis of residual fluid, about 10 mg weighed into acetonitrile. VEA: GC-MS with a deuterated internal standard, calibration 0.039 to 2.5 micrograms per mL, analytical range 1 to 100% by mass; identity confirmed against an analytical standard by retention time, library mass spectrum and accurate mass (Results 3.1). Cannabinoids: HPLC with photodiode array, the method the laboratory has used for New York medical marijuana products since December 2015. MCT oil was estimated roughly (3 to 24% by mass) by comparing four peak areas with a commercial MCT oil, because standards for the individual components are not available. Pesticides: myclobutanil and PBO by LC-MS/MS; a wider screen with a cut-off of 1 microgram per gram. Synthetic cannabinoids and opioids: detection to 0.05% by mass.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. The paper gives no information on how much each patient vaped, for how long, which cartridge they used when, or how the cartridges were obtained. The statement that vaping heats fluids to 250 to 350 degrees Celsius is made without a source.
exposure.polysubstance: Two of the 38 fluids held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16); 36 held cannabinoids. Of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories, 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (product analysis).

comparison.controls: None within the study. The authors contrast the fluids with vaporizer products of New York State's medical marijuana program that the same laboratory has tested ('thousands of samples'): free of additives and 80 to 90% total cannabinoids (Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph). No data from those products are shown here. No fluids from people who vaped without injury, and none from legal retail in 2019, are analysed.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Which cartridge each patient used and when; how many cartridges each of the 10 patients contributed; where and how each was obtained; whether patients whose cartridges held no VEA (13 of 36 fluids) also used a cartridge that did.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS untargeted screens; HPLC with photodiode array for 11 natural cannabinoids; LC-MS/MS for five mycotoxins (aflatoxins B1, B2, G1, G2 and ochratoxin A), myclobutanil and PBO; GC-MS for VEA; Q-Orbitrap screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites; NMR, GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS for the six commercial products.
outcomes.validity_norms: The cannabinoid, mycotoxin, myclobutanil and PBO methods are ones the New York laboratory has validated and had certified or accredited for medical marijuana products; they were adapted here (a scaled-down mycotoxin extraction because of small samples; cannabinoid samples run without the usual surrogate spike). The VEA method was developed for this work. Whether the methods perform the same in illicit fluids was not tested in the text read. Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 (supplement) were not opened.
outcomes.operationalization: VEA 'found' means measured at 1% by mass or more; lower values are printed as below 1.0. A fluid is cannabinoid-containing if any of the 11 natural cannabinoids was quantified. The paper's 64% is 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, not 23 of 38 fluids and not a share of patients.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (instrumental analysis); not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cannabinoid-containing fluids (36): VEA in 23 (64%), 16.4 to 57.6% by mass, median 38.4% among the 23 (editors' calculation from Table 1); no detectable VEA in 13, of which 12 held MCT oil. MCT oil: 15 in the text, 14 marked in Table 1 (editors' count); both VEA and MCT in 2 fluids (samples 7 and 14); neither in 1 (sample 27). Delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass, median 29.6%; sum of quantified cannabinoids 23 to 73%, under 50% in 27 of 36 (editors' calculation; the paper gives no totals). Delta-8-THC quantified in 8, higher than delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count). At least one pesticide (myclobutanil in 22, PBO in 18, other pesticides above 1 microgram per gram in 26 fluids) in 31 of the 36 (editors' count from Table 2); none in the other 5. Mycotoxins below 4.8 ng/g and synthetic cannabinoids and opioids below 0.05% by mass in all 38. Commercial products: three of six (two diluents, one thickener) essentially pure VEA, two squalane-based, one alpha-bisabolol-based. Update to 12 December 2019 given in the Conclusions without methods: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 containing THC and 59 nicotine; 101 of the 147 (69%) contained VEA. Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals, treating fluids as independent (they come from 10 and 61 patients, so these are too narrow): 23 of 36, 46% to 79%; 101 of 147, 61% to 76%.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not registered; a public health laboratory response analysed as samples arrived. The paper says the laboratory had no prior expectation of what the cartridges held (Results 3.1).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 38 samples are shown in Tables 1 and 2 and the six commercial products in Table 3. The untargeted screens are reported only for the additives and contaminants the authors discuss; other compounds seen are not tabulated in the text read. The extended series (206 fluids) and the heating experiments are reported as statements with no data.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI, 23 (64%) held VEA at 16 to 58% by mass, 13 held none, 14 or 15 held MCT oil, 31 held at least one pesticide, and no synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins were found; cannabinoid content was mostly under 50% by mass; three of six commercial diluent and thickener products were essentially pure VEA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title names VEA as a major diluent, and the abstract says the cause of EVALI is unknown. The Discussion says it is possible that VEA is causative or contributes, offers lipoid pneumonia and heating products as mechanisms, and states that there is no evidence that vaping large amounts of VEA, squalane or other diluents is safe. The Conclusions add that there is additional evidence of a strong association of VEA with EVALI (101 of 147 fluids and 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples in a CDC report) and that in vitro and in vivo studies will be required to establish cause. Gaps: (1) this paper has no comparison fluids, so the association is not tested within it; (2) 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; (3) the contrast with legal products rests on unpublished laboratory experience; (4) the market timeline for VEA diluents (introduced in 2018, sales up in spring 2019) is sourced to trade-press articles on a cannabis-industry website, not peer-reviewed work; (5) heating products of VEA and the claim that pesticide contamination is 'intermittent and random' are inferences without data shown.

timeline.event: The laboratory shared its VEA findings with CDC, FDA and state health officials on 19 August and the New York State Department of Health announced them on 5 September (the authors' account; the announcement was not read).

The authors cite the FDA, Utah and Minnesota as later finding VEA in case-associated fluids; Blount et al. quote FDA testing that found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples. These reports were not read; the proportions differ from this study's 64% and from the New York update's 69%.
CDC reported vitamin E acetate in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients with EVALI and in none of 99 healthy volunteers (the New York laboratory cites an earlier CDC report of 28 of 28).
CDC update on the outbreak: 2,668 hospitalized patients by 14 January 2020, most who reported product use having used THC-containing products.

replication.where_it_stands: Several agencies are cited as finding VEA in case-associated products or lung fluid, and the New York figures overlap one another, so they are not independent replications. The proportions differ between reports. Whether VEA alone causes the injury is stated by the authors to need laboratory and animal studies.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial or other conflicts of interest (Conflicts of Interest section).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors work at the Wadsworth Center and the Center for Environmental Health of the New York State Department of Health, the University at Albany School of Public Health and Albany Medical Center. The Wadsworth laboratory also tests the state's medical marijuana products, which the paper uses as the comparison for the illicit fluids. A government health laboratory, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; no industry tie is declared.

what_would_settle_it: Testing every cartridge each patient used, by laboratories blind to case status, alongside cartridges from people of similar age and product use who vaped without injury and from legal retail in the same months, with the number of cartridges per patient and their source reported; plus experiments on the aerosol of VEA, with and without THC, at realistic temperatures.

domains.domain: Selection and provenance of the samples
domains.note: Cartridges from 10 patients in one state, handed over for analysis; the number per patient, the dates, the source of each cartridge and the basis for calling them illicit are not reported.

Mass-spectrometric identification confirmed against standards, validated or certified methods for most analytes, and detection limits stated. MCT oil is only roughly estimated, the VEA method is new, performance in this fluid type was not tested in the text read, and the supplement was not opened.

No fluids from people who vaped without injury or from legal retail; the contrast with New York medical products is the laboratory's experience and is not shown. The share with VEA cannot be read as higher or lower than other cartridges.

domains.domain: Link between the analysed product and the patient's illness
domains.note: Results are not given per patient; 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; the residue in a recovered cartridge may not be what a patient inhaled earlier.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The findings are described as findings and cause is called unknown, but the Discussion's mechanisms, the safety statement about large amounts, the market timeline from trade press and the 'strong association' wording go beyond the data shown.

The text counts 15 fluids with MCT oil where Table 1 marks 14; the VEA ceiling is 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; the extended series of 206 fluids has no methods or table; no per-sample MCT amounts are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a laboratory analysis of case-associated products (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for product analysis. The overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The chemistry is careful and the findings are clearly tabulated, and the authors keep the cause open. The paper may be cited for what was in the fluid of 38 cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, for the VEA content of three commercial diluent and thickener products, and for the absence of the named synthetic compounds and mycotoxins. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for how common VEA was in cartridges in general, for a difference from legal products, or for what any patient inhaled.

key_findings.finding: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained were analysed; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16) and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019 and chose untargeted analysis because it had no prior information on what they held.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: VEA was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; the Discussion says as much as 58%); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: MCT oil was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14 with a plus sign, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without VEA held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 4th paragraph; Table 1 (MCT column)

key_findings.finding: Cannabinoid content was lower than the laboratory's usual medical products: delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass (median 29.6%, editors' calculation) in the 36; the authors say illicit fluids are usually under 50% cannabinoids against 80 to 90% in New York's medical program products (27 of 36 under 50% by the editors' sum of the quantified cannabinoids). Delta-8-THC was quantified in 8 fluids and exceeded delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Discussion 4.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The medical-program comparison is the laboratory's account; no data are shown. Table 1 units are not printed in the text read; per cent by mass is taken from the surrounding text.

key_findings.finding: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), PBO in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 26; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and say EVALI is not due to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 5th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure VEA, one diluent was mostly squalane with MCT and triethyl citrate, one thickener was squalane, and one thickener was alpha-bisabolol with a little isophytol. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4; Table 3; Discussion 4.2, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the first 10 New York cases who provided product-use histories (number not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products. The two nicotine-containing fluids held no unusual compounds of concern.
key_findings.locator: Discussion 4.3, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Update to 12 December 2019 (Conclusions, no methods or table): 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held VEA. Editors' calculation, exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. The authors also cite 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples with VEA in an early CDC report, and CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions
key_findings.note: National and lung-fluid figures are the authors' citations of a CDC web page and an MMWR report, not read here.

key_findings.finding: The authors' timeline for the diluents rests on articles from a cannabis-industry news site: VEA-based diluents appeared on the market in 2018, sales greatly increased in spring 2019, and they were touted as tasteless, odourless and miscible with cannabis oil in all proportions. The authors also say cutting product with cheaper material the customer cannot detect is long-standing practice in illegal drug markets.
key_findings.locator: Discussion 4.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; references 20 to 22
key_findings.note: Trade-press sources, not peer-reviewed; not read.

key_findings.finding: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; VEA is high-molecular-mass, lipophilic and similar to oils known to cause lipoid pneumonia, so it is possible that it is causative or contributes; initial experiments (not shown) indicate compounds including duroquinone form when VEA is vaped; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish cause.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Discussion 4.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Funding: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors are employees of the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Center and Center for Environmental Health, with academic affiliations at the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MCT oil was detected in 15 fluids; Table 1 marks 14 fluids with a plus sign (samples 3, 7, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 and 34).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which fluid is the fifteenth is not clear, and the 3 to 24% range cannot be checked because per-sample MCT amounts are not tabulated.

reporting_issues.issue: The basis for calling the cartridges illicit is not stated. The title, abstract and Discussion say illicit or street products; the Methods say only that case-associated cartridges were collected and that packaging and markings were noted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The label may be an inference from the contents, the cartridges' look or the patients' accounts; the shares cannot be applied to 'illicit' cartridges as a class.

reporting_issues.issue: The extended series (206 fluids from 61 cases; 101 of 147 with VEA) appears only in the Conclusions, with no methods, no table and no statement of whether the first 38 are included.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 69% cannot be checked and overlaps the 64% from the first 10 cases; the two should not be counted as independent.

reporting_issues.issue: The upper VEA value is given as 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; Table 1 units are not printed in the text read.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion 4.1
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding only; the units are inferred from the surrounding text.

reporting_issues.issue: Results are not given per patient: the 38 fluids are listed by sample number only.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be seen how many of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge, or whether the 13 fluids without VEA came from patients who also had one that did.

reporting_issues.issue: Claims that the lab's medical-program products are 80 to 90% cannabinoids and free of additives, that heating VEA forms compounds including duroquinone, and that the extended series found more VEA are given without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are the authors' account and are not checkable from the paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7151740 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure captions, funding and conflict statements, author affiliations and reference list read as text; Figures 1 to 5 were not viewed as images; the supplementary PDF with Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 was not opened)

design_detail: Narrative review comparing cannabis flower, concentrates and edibles on prevalence of use (mainly US samples), methods of consumption and cannabis use disorder (CUD) outcomes. PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract, plus backward and forward citation searches; 27 articles included (Figure 1), 72 references listed. No eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no search dates, no appraisal of the included studies; the authors scored their own review 12 of 12 on SANRA, a scale for the quality of narrative reviews. Published online 26 October 2024; issue dated 2026.
can_establish: What a 2024 narrative reading of mostly US survey studies says about which forms of cannabis people use and about CUD by form, and which comparisons the authors found missing (form-specific longitudinal data, CUD with edibles, flower by mode of use).
cannot_establish: Whether concentrates, flower or edibles differ in CUD risk, or by how much: there is no systematic search, no appraisal and no pooling, and the CUD evidence it cites is cross-sectional.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed searches combining 'cannabis' with a form, a method of consumption or CUD terms; studies kept if the title or abstract mentioned both the form and the outcome or method; further studies from reference lists and PubMed's Cited By feature (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 4; Figure 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Relevance to a form of cannabis and its prevalence, method of consumption or CUD outcomes; 3,861 articles excluded on title or abstract and 196 at relevance review (Figure 1). No dates, languages, designs or quality thresholds are stated, and who screened is not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited samples are mostly from the US: national adult surveys, college students, high-school students in Colorado and Los Angeles, web-based and Twitter-based samples of people who use concentrates, and medical cannabis patients.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: One database and no stated search dates. The reference list does not include the 2022 systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli et al., 2022) or the UK and multinational survey studies of potency and dependence that it covers (editors' check of the 72 references). The prevalence part is restricted to US samples by design; the CUD part draws on US college, high-school, web and national samples.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: self-reported form and frequency of use in surveys; no measured THC.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Forms as the authors define them: flower (raw plant material), concentrates (material extracted from the plant to increase potency; typically about three times the THC content of flower or more, as cited), and edibles (products for oral ingestion). Product content as cited only.
exposure.polysubstance: Blunts (cannabis rolled in a tobacco wrap) are flagged as a confounder of flower findings because they add tobacco; otherwise not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Comparisons across forms within the cited surveys (frequent concentrate use against frequent flower use or no concentrate use; one form against several; inhaled forms against edibles); none with people who do not use cannabis.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. The authors note that people who frequently use concentrates may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor of CUD across forms, both of which bear on any comparison by form.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed except tobacco in blunts.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies (CUD symptom counts and severity, problematic use, tolerance and withdrawal, worry about one's use); the review does not name the instruments.
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the cited studies; the SANRA score is the authors' own rating of their review.
outcomes.operationalization: CUD outcomes are described as types such as symptom count, severity and problematic use (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative review).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None for CUD comparisons. Prevalence percentages are reported as cited, for example US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003): past-year flower smoking 12.9%, vaporizing 4.7%, concentrates 1.9% and edibles 6%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Null findings on concentrates and CUD reported elsewhere (a US sample of 156 in the 2022 systematic review) are not cited; the cited survey of 191 people is described as showing heightened CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use, a difference the 2022 systematic review reports as not statistically significant.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The CUD evidence by form that the review cites is a handful of cross-sectional US surveys: one of 191 people comparing frequent concentrate with frequent flower use (Bidwell et al., 2018), surveys of dab or butane hash oil use in web and college samples (Sagar et al., 2018; Meier, 2017), surveys linking more frequent use of the inhaled forms but not edibles to problematic use (Steeger et al., 2021) and high-frequency use of all three forms to more CUD than high-frequency flower-only use (Gunn et al., 2020), a college survey linking flower potency to CUD symptom count (Piercey et al., 2024), and a US study linking average potency to a first CUD symptom (Arterberry et al., 2019). For edibles it finds no CUD data and argues by analogy from studies of slower-acting formulations of other drugs. It finds no form-specific longitudinal data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Results state that concentrate use has consistently been associated with increased CUD risk compared with other forms, and the Highlights state as a fact that concentrate use "is associated with more severe cannabis use disorder outcomes"; the Abstract says only that it may be. Gaps: (1) 'consistently' rests mainly on one cross-sectional survey of 191 people, which the 2022 systematic review reports as showing no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use (editors' comparison; the primary paper was not read), plus surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates rather than by form; (2) the Discussion's own conclusions, that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor across forms and that causal roles of quantity and potency are not established, are not carried into the Highlights; (3) case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use are called alarming; (4) the 12 of 12 SANRA score, including for the literature search, is self-assigned. Against this, the Abstract and Conclusion say plainly that comparisons across forms are scarce and form-specific longitudinal data are lacking, and the edibles section says the CUD risk is unknown.

timeline.event: Bidwell et al. (2018), a US cross-sectional study of 191 people buying concentrates and flower on the legal market (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004), the main source of this review's statement on concentrates and CUD; not read here.
Meta-analysis of the prevalence of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis (not cited by this review)
Systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction, which reports the same 191-person study as showing no significant difference (not cited by this review)
This narrative review, online 26 October 2024 (issue 2026).

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative review that adds no new evidence on CUD by form. Its statement on concentrates traces mainly to one cross-sectional survey that the 2022 systematic review describes differently, and it omits that review. It is useful for the gaps it names (edibles, form-specific longitudinal data, mode of flower use) and for US prevalence figures as cited; claims should trace any CUD figure to the primary studies.

funding.funder: No funding associated with the preparation of the review (Funding, p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest reported by the authors (Disclosure statement, p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: Oregon State University (Department of Integrative Biology; School of Psychological Science). No study by the authors is among the cited sources for the CUD findings (editors' check of the reference list). No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry ties are printed.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use cannabis that record each form used, its labelled or tested THC content, and how much and how often it is used, and that measure DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by interview over years, analysed with frequency and amount as possible confounders or mediators and including enough people who mainly use edibles.

domains.note: PubMed only, no dates, no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, screening by unstated reviewers; the main systematic review on potency and addiction (2022) and the survey studies it covers are missing from the 72 references.
No appraisal. Designs are sometimes named (survey, case reports), but no study's limits are weighed, and 'consistently' rests on one cross-sectional study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No study by the authors is cited for the review's findings (editors' check of the reference list).

Hedged in the Abstract and Conclusions ('may', 'suggest'), but the Highlights state the concentrate association without a hedge, and the edibles argument by analogy from formulations of other drugs sits beside the data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a higher CUD risk with concentrates (evidence of no difference under-represented)
domains.note: A null comparison of concentrates with herbal cannabis (US sample of 156) is not cited, and the cited 191-person survey's non-significant difference is presented as heightened symptoms; the review does note that frequency predicts CUD across forms and that potency's causal role is not established.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The selection is unsystematic and misses the main systematic review, the cited studies are not appraised, and the concentrate statement in the Results and Highlights is stronger than its main cross-sectional source; on the other hand the review is explicit that comparisons by form and longitudinal data are lacking. It may be cited for what it says, for the gaps it names and for US prevalence figures as cited; its statement on concentrates and CUD should be traced to the primary studies, and it is not evidence of a CUD difference by form.

key_findings.finding: Methods: PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract; 4,077 articles found, 3,861 excluded, 216 reviewed for relevance, 196 excluded, 20 included, 7 added from reference lists and citing articles, 27 in the review. The authors rated their own review on SANRA and scored it 2 of 2 in all six areas (12 of 12).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 4-5); Figure 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Flower: among US adults (n = 9,003), 12.9% reported past-year flower smoking, more than edibles and concentrates combined; 94.6% of college-age people who used cannabis in the past year (n = 1,390) had ever used flower; among Colorado high-school students who currently used cannabis (n = 4,637), 76.1% had used flower in the past 30 days and 53.1% named it their usual form. Flower potency is cited as having risen from about 4% THC in 1995 to over 12% in 2014 and commonly 20% or more by 2020, with dispensary flower testing at 13% to 36%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis flower, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Concentrates: among US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003), 4.7% reported vaporizing cannabis, 1.9% concentrates and 6% edibles in the past year; 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates; among the Colorado high-school students, 47.1% had used concentrates in the past 30 days and 17.4% named them their usual form (edibles 9.5%); in web-based studies with over 600 participants each, 13% of people who used concentrates did so daily or near daily. Concentrates are described as typically about three times the THC of flower or more, from 50-60% to over 90% THC, as cited. The authors note a lack of recent nationally representative data on concentrate use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 6-7)

key_findings.finding: Edibles: 6% of US adults reported past-year edible use; among Los Angeles high-school students (n = 2,163), 17.5% had ever used edibles against 25.8% flower; among the Colorado high-school students, 34.3% had used edibles in the past 30 days and 9.5% named them their usual form.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flower and CUD: a cross-sectional survey of Colorado college students (n = 617; ref. 36) found flower potency positively associated with CUD symptom count and severity; bong use (refs 18, 20-22) and blunt frequency (refs 26-28) are cited as associated with more frequent use, problematic symptoms, tolerance or CUD. The authors say the literature lacks CUD data for flower compared with other forms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis flower › Methods of consumption, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5); Results › Cannabis flower › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Concentrates and CUD: the review states that concentrate use has consistently been associated with higher CUD risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more CUD symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and report fewer positive effects from concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, a 2021 review); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). Longitudinal studies of long-term concentrate use are called for. No effect sizes are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates › CUD outcomes, paragraph; references 37, 40, 42 and 43 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Edibles and CUD: there is limited information specific to the CUD potential of edibles.
