The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, on formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often naming edibles as their primary form. The section concludes that the CUD outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles › CUD outcomes, paragraph; Results › Cannabis edibles › Conclusion, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across forms, the Discussion describes the literature on problematic use as small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and CUD risk (ref. 52), more CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more CUD with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it states, without a citation, that inhalation is generally associated with a higher CUD risk than ingestion. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of CUD risk across all forms and that further causal factors, such as quantity and THC potency, have yet to be firmly established.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › CUD outcomes, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other harms, as cited: smoking flower linked to asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but not reported as a significant contributor to lung cancer or irreversible airway changes (refs 54-58); case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use (refs 62-64); edibles commonly associated with hospital visits for accidental ingestion or over-intoxication (ref. 65), while in a survey of 172 people who had an uncomfortable experience with edibles, 95.2% reported no medical problem from it (ref. 66).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Other acute and chronic health complications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Abstract and Highlights: concentrate use may be associated with a greater CUD risk (Abstract); concentrate use is associated with more severe CUD outcomes, and edible CUD risk is unclear (Highlights). Conclusion: few single studies report all three forms, and form-specific long-term data are lacking.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Highlights (p. 3); Conclusion, paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: No funding; no potential conflict of interest reported.
key_findings.locator: Disclosure statement; Funding

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence on dry herb vaping is garbled as printed: after lower plasma carbon monoxide, the next sentence reads as a fragment comparing respiratory toxicity with flower smoke at comparable plasma THC, so what ref. 30 found cannot be told from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis of the review's suggestion that dry herb vaping may be a safer alternative for people who use cannabis chronically cannot be checked from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 44, titled as a cross-sectional study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain, is cited for statements about non-medical use (people new to it or using it infrequently naming edibles as their main form; flower and concentrates being more popular among people who use cannabis non-medically) and for vaporization having risen to a prevalence comparable to smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements may not rest on samples of non-medical use; the primary paper was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates, which is only 20% less than the number who had ever used edibles, without giving the edible figure for that sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the gap is relative or in percentage points cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 191-person survey (Bidwell et al., 2018) is described here as showing heightened CUD symptoms in people who frequently use concentrates, while the 2022 systematic review reports no significant difference (means 2.1 and 1.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's main source for concentrates and CUD is reported differently by two reviews; the primary paper (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004) should be read before either description is used.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 3-13 (PDFs/Cannabis/Inman_2026_FlowerConcentratesEdiblesCUD.pdf; version of record, online 26 October 2024): all text, Figure 1 (read from the page image), the 72 references, disclosure and funding statements; no supplementary material

design_detail: National passive surveillance report (CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 24 January 2020, with state and local health departments and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists) on e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) as of 14 January 2020. States and jurisdictions voluntarily reported confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased patients to CDC each week using CDC case definitions and a national case report form (linked documents, not read). The report describes 2,668 hospitalized patients (age, sex, race and ethnicity, case status), the substances they reported using in vaping products in the 3 months before symptom onset (limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance), weekly hospital admissions, and trends in possible EVALI-related emergency department visits from the National Syndromic Surveillance Program (a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit; about 70% of emergency visits nationwide). No product or patient samples are tested in this report, and there is no comparison group.
can_establish: How many people had been reported to CDC as hospitalized with this lung injury by 14 January 2020, who they were, what they said they had vaped, and when weekly admissions and related emergency visits rose and fell between August 2019 and January 2020.
cannot_establish: What caused the injury (nothing was tested in this report; it relies on other work for vitamin E acetate); how many people were affected out of all who vape, or out of all who vape cannabis (no denominator); how severe the illnesses were or how many people died (not reported here); whether what patients said they vaped was what was in the device; whether every reported case was EVALI (the authors say the case definition favored sensitivity over specificity); and the full size of the outbreak (voluntary reporting; product information missing for a quarter of patients).

sample.recruitment: Not a sample: all cases reported by the 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico as of 14 January 2020, by voluntary weekly reporting using CDC case definitions (main text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased EVALI patients meeting the CDC surveillance case definition (not reproduced in the report). Substance-use percentages are limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset (Table footnotes).
sample.demographics: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); age groups 13 to 17 years 404 (15%), 18 to 24 979 (37%), 25 to 34 631 (24%), 35 to 44 335 (13%), 45 to 64 223 (9%), 65 and over 47 (2%) of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 with sex (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 1,360 (73%) non-Hispanic white, 64 (3%) Black, 12 (1%) American Indian or Alaska Native, 38 (2%) Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, 97 (5%) other, and 285 (15%) Hispanic.
sample.attrition: Product-use information was missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668; editors' count), and many patients were not interviewed because of loss to follow-up, refusal, or lack of resources (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Race and ethnicity were missing for about 30% (812 of 2,668; editors' count). The admissions figure shows 2,398 patients, so 270 reported patients are not in it (editors' count; the report gives no reason).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are those clinicians recognized, hospitals admitted, health departments classified and states chose to report; about half (47%) are 'probable' rather than 'confirmed'. The authors say the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). People with milder illness who were not hospitalized are outside the report.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported by patients (interview or case report form; who interviewed and how is not described) as substances used in e-cigarette, or vaping, products in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product, any nicotine-containing product, both, exclusive THC, exclusive nicotine, neither. No laboratory confirmation of the products or of the patients' exposures in this report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: no product type (cartridge or other), brand, source, amount, frequency or duration. The report says vaping or dabbing and that CDC advises against products from informal sources, but gives no numbers on sources.
exposure.polysubstance: Nicotine and THC product use were recorded together as categories: both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither reported 44 (2%) among the 2,022 with information. Other substances, additives and contaminants cannot be captured by self-report; the authors say patients may not know the content of what they vaped.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None in this report. For context, the report notes a low but long-standing background rate of emergency visits related to vaping products before the outbreak, which could reflect chemicals of concern in nicotine products or sporadic cases from the same substances that later spread (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: There is no denominator of people who vape THC or nicotine products, no comparison with people who vape and were not ill, no information on source, device, additive or amount, and no testing in this report, so the share of patients who used THC products says nothing about the risk to a person who does.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: CDC surveillance case definitions (confirmed, probable; not reproduced); weekly count of hospital admissions by week of admission (Figure 1, an image); National Syndromic Surveillance Program rate of possible EVALI-related emergency visits per million (Figure 2, an image), using a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit, excluding injuries such as device explosions and accidental ingestion of e-liquid but not acute THC intoxication or nicotine poisoning.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say the exposure query in the emergency data may have been affected by public and clinical awareness of the outbreak, and that coverage of the system is uneven across and within states and changes over time (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Severity beyond hospitalization (intensive care, ventilation, death) is not reported in this update; the report speaks of hospitalized or deceased patients but gives no count of deaths.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive report).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive. 2,668 hospitalized patients; among 2,022 with substance information (76% of cases), any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%), any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%), both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither 44 (2%). Editors' calculation: 1,650 of all 2,668 patients (62%) is the least that reported any THC-containing product, if none of the 646 with no information had. Weekly hospital admissions peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since. Possible EVALI-related emergency visits rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) between 11 August and 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, which is still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; surveillance report.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report is a descriptive update that cites earlier CDC updates (October and November 2019, and a January 2020 product and demographic update) for other characteristics; deaths, intensive care use and product sources are not given here.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By 14 January 2020, 2,668 people in every US state, Washington DC and two territories had been reported as hospitalized with this lung injury; they were young (median 24, three quarters under 35), two thirds male and mostly non-Hispanic white. Among the 76% with substance information, 82% said they had used a THC-containing vaping product (33% only THC products) and 57% a nicotine-containing product (14% only nicotine products). Weekly admissions and related emergency visits peaked in September 2019 and fell steadily afterwards.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report concludes that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to the outbreak (a conclusion drawn from another paper, not shown here), that the evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases, and that the decline might be multifactorial (public awareness, removal of vitamin E acetate from products, enforcement). CDC's recommendation to avoid THC vaping products, especially from informal sources, and its advice to adults who vape instead of smoking are statements of advice, not findings of this report. Gaps: (1) the abstract's and the Summary box's percentages are of patients with information, stated as 'of EVALI patients', without the 24% with no information; (2) the exclusive categories do not add up with the 'any' categories (reporting issue 1); (3) the reasons offered for the decline are not tested, and the suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from products cites two news articles; (4) no number is given for deaths or for how people obtained products. The report is open about its limits and about the unexplained 14% who reported only nicotine products.

timeline.event: Earlier CDC updates in October and November 2019 (Moritz et al.; Chatham-Stephens et al.; cited in this report's reference list, not read) described patients in the same outbreak.
Laboratory analysis of lung fluid from patients, cited here for the link with vitamin E acetate
This update: 2,668 hospitalized patients and the decline in cases after September 2019.

replication.where_it_stands: A cumulative surveillance snapshot, not a study that can be replicated. Its counts are firmer than its product-use shares, which are self-reported and missing for a quarter of patients. Deaths and the later course of the outbreak are not covered by this update.

funding.funder: Not stated as a grant. Authors are staff of CDC centers (injury, immunization and respiratory diseases, chronic disease, surveillance, birth defects, minority health, environmental health, toxic substances) and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, with a task force of state health department staff; the report is a CDC publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE disclosure form and no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are the agency that ran the investigation and issued the public recommendations discussed; the report describes its own surveillance. A government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry.

what_would_settle_it: A case-control or cohort study of people with and without lung injury, interviewed with the devices in hand, with products tested for contents and source, with the denominator of people who vape and which products they used, and with outcomes (intensive care, ventilation, death, recovery) followed for months.

domains.note: Voluntary reporting by states; 47% of cases are 'probable'; the authors say the sensitive definition lowered specificity and may include people without EVALI. Counts of hospitalized patients are probably an undercount of all lung injury and may include some other illnesses.
Missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668); many were not interviewed; the 2,022 with data may differ from those without. Race and ethnicity are missing for about 30%.

Patients may not know or may not report what was in a device, and the authors say so; no sample was tested in this report; the 14% who reported only nicotine products are explained by misreporting, misclassification or true exclusive nicotine use without telling which.

domains.domain: Separation of surveillance findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The report states that its evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals and that reasons for the decline might be multifactorial, but the vitamin E acetate link and the effects of awareness, product removal and enforcement are not tested here; advice is mixed with findings.
The exclusive and any product categories do not reconcile; the abstract's shares are of patients with data; the under-35 share is 76% in the text and 76.9% from the table counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a national surveillance case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for surveillance counts. The report is a clear description of who was reported as hospitalized and when, by an agency with access to the case reports, and the counts of patients and their age and sex are reasonably firm descriptions of reported cases. Its product-use shares are self-reported and incomplete and cannot show what was in any product. It may be cited for the number and characteristics of hospitalized patients reported to CDC by 14 January 2020, the share who said they had used THC-containing or nicotine-containing products among those asked, and the timing of the September 2019 peak. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for the risk to any person who vapes, for the proportion of patients who used illicit or informally sourced products, for deaths, or for what the decline was due to.

key_findings.finding: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)

key_findings.finding: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic. The text says 76% were under 35 (404 + 979 + 631 = 2,014 of 2,619 is 76.9%, editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)

key_findings.finding: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668): any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); exclusive THC 669 (33%); exclusive nicotine 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
key_findings.note: The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022, and 1,650 minus 834 is 816, not 669 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since (Figure 1 is titled N = 2,398 patients, 270 fewer than the 2,668 reported, with no reason given; values not extracted from the image).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title

key_findings.finding: Possible EVALI-related emergency visits (National Syndromic Surveillance Program) rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) from 11 August to 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, and fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 title

key_findings.finding: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by patients (citing the lung fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped, some cases may be misclassified because the case definition was sensitive rather than specific, or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract and Discussion state the vitamin E acetate link; the data behind it are in the cited paper, not in this report.

key_findings.finding: Possible reasons for the decline after mid-September 2019 given by the authors (not tested): public awareness and actions by people who vape, removal of vitamin E acetate from THC products after the link was identified (supported by two news articles in footnotes), and enforcement affecting supply from informal sources. Also noted: it is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury, and long-term consequences need long-term follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; footnotes ¶ and **

key_findings.finding: Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system is uneven and changes over time.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's mutually exclusive categories (exclusive THC 669, exclusive nicotine 274, both 834, neither 44) add to 1,821 of the 2,022 patients with information; and 'any THC' (1,650) minus 'both' (834) is 816, not 669, while 'any nicotine' (1,162) minus 'both' is 328, not 274.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 201 patients (10%) are in none of the four categories; the report does not say who they are (for example, THC use reported but nicotine unknown). The 'exclusive' shares should not be summed with 'both' to get 'any'.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 82% of EVALI patients used any THC-containing product and 57% any nicotine-containing product, but these are shares of the 2,022 with information (76%), not of the 2,668 reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: A share 'of EVALI patients' overstates what is known; the least that is known is 62% (1,650 of 2,668) for THC (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 76% of patients were under 35, while the table counts give 2,014 of 2,619 (76.9%); the 76% is the sum of the rounded table percentages (15 + 37 + 24).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Age group)
reporting_issues.consequence: A rounding artefact of 1 percentage point; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from THC products and so contributed to the decline is supported by two news articles (footnotes ¶ and **), a state recall report and FDA statements; no data on product contents after the outbreak are presented.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the explanations for the decline as the authors' conjecture.

reporting_issues.issue: Race and ethnicity are available for 1,856 of 2,668 patients (70%), sex for 2,606, age for 2,619, and the figure for 2,398; percentages use these differing denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The race composition rests on 70% of cases and may differ for the rest.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7367698 (all sections, the Table, figure titles, footnotes and reference list read as text; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; the linked CDC case definition and case report form were not opened)

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of proportions (PROSPERO CRD42019133166) estimating the prevalence and risk of cannabis use disorder (CUD), cannabis abuse (CA) and cannabis dependence (CD), by DSM or ICD criteria from structured interviews, among people in general-population samples who had used cannabis. Cohorts were sought in PubMed and cross-sectional surveys in the Global Burden of Disease data input sources (studies published from January 2009; searched February 2019, updated April 2020); 21 studies gave 153 data points. Subgroups by design and by recall period of use (lifetime, past year or month, weekly or daily); meta-regression on year of data collection, tool and country adjusted for age, sex and recall period. Read from the journal pre-proof (accepted manuscript).
can_establish: The average share of people who had used cannabis who met DSM criteria for cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence in general-population studies from high-income countries published 2009 to 2020, and how it differed by design and by how often people had used.
cannot_establish: The risk for any one product, form or strength (no included study estimated risk by potency), the risk outside high-income countries, or a precise lifetime risk of developing a disorder, because lifetime, past-year and past-month measures are pooled together and the included studies were not appraised.

sample.recruitment: PubMed (MeSH 'marijuana abuse' AND 'cohort studies', with title and abstract synonyms) for longitudinal studies and the Global Burden of Disease data input sources for cross-sectional studies, searched in February 2019 for papers from January 2009; supplemented by reference lists, key population surveys, drug monitoring agency publications, references forwarded by experts, the authors' collection and a search for new publications in April 2020 (Method › Search strategy, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Observational general-population studies reporting DSM or ICD cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence ascertained by structured clinical interviews; high-risk or sub-populations such as prisoners or ethnic minorities excluded, as were unvalidated scales, self-reported problems and studies published before 2009 (Method › Selection criteria; Search strategy, pp. 5-6). Full texts excluded: 9 not observational general-population studies, 48 without data on the disorders, 31 without estimates among people who had used cannabis, 21 duplicating data in another included study (Results › Study selection, p. 8).
sample.demographics: Samples from the US (over half of the studies), the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 11 studies sampled adolescents or young adults, one older adults and the rest broad age ranges such as 12 or older or 18 or older (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st paragraph, p. 8; Discussion, 12th paragraph, p. 15). Table 1 gives no sample size for any study.
sample.attrition: Not reported for the included cohorts.
sample.selection_effects: General-population surveys from high-income countries only. Definitions of a person who uses cannabis range from having tried it once to daily use: nine studies counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required more than a few occasions, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 2nd paragraph, p. 8). Excluding studies published before 2009 leaves out the early-1990s survey behind the widely cited one-in-ten dependence figure, which the review discusses separately (Introduction, p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use in each survey, recorded as ever used, number of times used, past-year, past-month, or weekly or daily use (Method › Data extraction, p. 7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only through these recall categories; no data on potency, form or route. The authors found no population study that estimated cannabis use disorder risk by the potency of products used (Discussion, 11th paragraph, p. 15).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; other substance use disorders are named only as a topic for future research (Discussion, 14th paragraph, p. 16).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None; proportions among people who had used cannabis.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a pooled prevalence; age and sex differences and age of first use are summarised from the studies that reported them.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Structured diagnostic interviews: CIDI and M-CIDI, AUDADIS-IV and AUDADIS-5, SCID and DIGS, and DSM-IV criteria-based tools in the US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (Table 1). One study used DSM-III-R and one DSM-5; the rest used DSM-IV, in which cannabis use disorder means abuse or dependence (Discussion, 13th paragraph, p. 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the included studies is reported. A Canadian study using the Severity of Dependence Scale was excluded for not using a structured interview; it classed 10.5% of adolescents who used cannabis in the past year as dependent (p. 16).
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence over the lifetime, the past 3 years, the past year or the past month, or incidence at follow-up, of cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis as each study defined use; several data points per study by sex, age, survey year or recall period (Method › Data extraction, p. 7; Table 1 footnote).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; three outcome pools, each with subgroups and a meta-regression.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled proportions with 95% CI (Table 2, p. 28). Cannabis use disorder: overall 0.22 (0.18 to 0.26); longitudinal, lifetime use 0.27 (0.25 to 0.28), recent use 0.22 (0.20 to 0.24); cross-sectional, lifetime 0.28 (0.10 to 0.48), recent 0.17 (0.12 to 0.23), regular (weekly or daily) 0.22 (0.17 to 0.28). Abuse: overall 0.13 (0.08 to 0.18); longitudinal recent 0.17 (0.14 to 0.20); cross-sectional lifetime 0.20 (0.14 to 0.26), recent 0.10 (0.03 to 0.19), regular 0.08 (0.02 to 0.16). Dependence: overall 0.13 (0.10 to 0.15); longitudinal lifetime 0.12 (0.07 to 0.18), recent 0.09 (0.01 to 0.19), regular 0.33 (0.22 to 0.44); cross-sectional lifetime 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15), recent 0.08 (0.06 to 0.10), regular 0.18 (0.12 to 0.24). Q, I2 and the studies in each pool are in S4 (not read). Meta-regression: year of data collection moderated cannabis use disorder (B = -0.01, p = 0.049) and abuse (B = -0.01, p = 0.017), not dependence (B = 0.00, p = 0.270); age, sex, recall period, assessment tool and country did not (p. 12).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression adjusted for study-level age, sex and recall period.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019133166, described as an a priori protocol; PRISMA checklist in S1 (p. 5). Separate analyses for each DSM version were planned (Method › Selection criteria, 2nd paragraph, p. 6) but are not reported, and the main pools combine DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-5 estimates. The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Heterogeneity statistics, forest plots and the studies in each pool are only in the supplement; Table 1 gives no sample sizes; the abstract and conclusions report the overall pools and the cohort figure for regular use, not the lower cross-sectional figure for daily use.
analysis.power: The authors state they had limited power to detect moderators other than year of data collection (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 14).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (153 data points), the pooled share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria was 22% (18 to 26) for cannabis use disorder, 13% (8 to 18) for abuse and 13% (10 to 15) for dependence. Single-study estimates of use disorder ranged from 4.5% (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1% (Australian 21-year-olds), and of dependence from 3.5% (young adults in Ireland) to 40.9% (daily use in an Australian adolescent cohort). Dependence was 33% (22 to 44) in two longitudinal studies of young people who used weekly or daily, and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. No study estimated risk by potency.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions present the pooled shares as risks (1 in 5 for use disorder, 1 in 8 for abuse or dependence) and extend the cohort figure to people who use cannabis weekly or more often (1 in 3); the Discussion says closer to 1 in 8 people who have used cannabis will develop dependence and that clinicians "can have confidence in using this updated figure". Gaps: (1) the pools mix lifetime, past-3-year, past-year and past-month prevalence with incidence, so they are not a lifetime risk of developing a disorder, as the authors themselves caution (Discussion, 9th paragraph); (2) the 1 in 3 figure comes from two cohorts of young people in Australia and the Netherlands, while cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18%; (3) confidence is claimed without heterogeneity statistics in the main text and without any appraisal of the pooled studies; (4) the abstract's message on early initiation does not mention that two of four studies found no association with dependence; (5) the Introduction and Conclusions point to more potent products, but no study in the review measured potency. Against this, the Discussion names the heterogeneity, the reliance on cross-sectional surveys, the different recall periods, the high-income samples and the lack of potency data.

timeline.event: US National Comorbidity Survey (1990-92): 9.1% of people who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), the one-in-ten figure this review sets out to update
US NESARC analysis of transition from first use to dependence, one of the 21 included studies; the encyclopedia's card of it gives a lifetime cumulative probability of 8.9% for cannabis
This review: by its authors' account, the first meta-analysis of epidemiological studies of the prevalence and risk of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis.
Systematic review of cannabis potency and mental ill health and addiction, which cites this review's 22% in its Introduction

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent pooled general-population figures read for the encyclopedia: about 22 in 100 people who had used cannabis met criteria for a use disorder and about 13 in 100 for dependence, in high-income countries, mostly by DSM-IV. They update the older one-in-ten figure but pool recall periods and DSM versions without appraising the studies; the stratified figures (lifetime, recent, regular use; cohort or survey) are more informative for a base rate than the overall pool. No figure is available by potency or form. The NESARC estimate in Table 1 should be checked against the primary paper (see reporting issues).

funding.funder: JL: University of Queensland development fellowship. LH: NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship. The Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research and the Lives Lived Well group are supported by Commonwealth funding from the Australian Government under the Drug and Alcohol Program. The funding bodies had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Role of Funding Sources, pp. 28-29).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest (Conflict of Interest, p. 29).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Queensland: School of Psychology, Lives Lived Well Group, and the Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated general-population cohorts that record when people start using cannabis, how often they use it, which products and how much THC, and that measure DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by interview over time, reporting cumulative incidence by frequency, product strength and form, in high-income and low- and middle-income countries.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people in general-population samples who had used cannabis), outcomes (DSM or ICD cannabis use disorder, abuse and dependence from structured interviews) and designs (observational) are stated; a prevalence question needs no comparator (Method › Selection criteria, p. 5).

PROSPERO CRD42019133166, described as an a priori protocol, with a PRISMA checklist in S1 (p. 5). The registry record was not read; separate analyses by DSM version were planned (p. 6) but are not reported, and the change is not explained.
Cross-sectional surveys were included alongside cohorts because there were too few cohorts, with the consequence discussed (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 14).

PubMed for cohorts (MeSH terms named, full terms in S3a, not read) and the Global Burden of Disease data input sources for cross-sectional surveys, supplemented by reference lists, key population surveys, drug monitoring agency publications, references from experts, the authors' collection and an update in April 2020 (p. 6). The restriction to studies published from 2009 is explained by the aim; language limits are not stated; only one bibliographic database was searched, with a narrow strategy for cohorts.
Who screened titles, abstracts and full texts is not stated, and no duplicate screening is reported (Method › Study selection, p. 6).
Who extracted the data is not stated beyond the contributors' roles (two authors acquired and analysed the data); no duplicate extraction is reported (pp. 7, 29).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for the 109 full-text exclusions are counted in the text (9, 48, 31 and 21; p. 8); the flowchart is in S1 and examples of excluded studies in S3c, which were not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, study name, years and design, ages, the definition of use, the outcome definition, the diagnostic tool, the percentage and sex and age differences, but no sample size or response rate for any study (pp. 24-27).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No assessment of the risk of bias or quality of the included studies is reported.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of proportions, but several data points per study (by sex, age, survey year or recall period) were extracted as separate data points (p. 7) with no stated handling of their dependence, the method for pooling proportions is not stated, and the overall pools combine lifetime, past-year and past-month prevalence with incidence; forest plots are in S4 (not read). Judged from the main text.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias, which was not assessed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Without an appraisal of the included studies, the interpretation could not account for their risk of bias; the Discussion considers recall bias in cross-sectional surveys and stratifies by design (p. 14), which concerns designs, not the studies pooled.

Subgroups by design and recall period and meta-regression on year of data collection, assessment tool and country (adjusted for age, sex and recall period) investigated heterogeneity, and the Discussion names it as a limitation (pp. 11-12, 14); I2 values are only in S4.
Not investigated or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the authors' conflicts are declared (pp. 28-29).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from supplements S1 and S3c, which were not read. Four critical items fail (9, no appraisal of the included studies; 11, several dependent data points per study pooled across recall periods without stated handling; 13; 15), so confidence is critically low whatever item 7 shows. This is a judgment on how far the pooled percentages can be trusted as a precise summary, not on the usefulness of the review: it is registered, restricted to structured diagnostic interviews in general-population samples, stratifies by design and recall period, and its stratified figures broadly agree (about 17 to 28 in 100 for use disorder, about 8 to 12 in 100 for dependence among people who had used, higher with regular use). Cite it for the order of size and the spread, with the recall periods and populations named; take single-study figures from the primary papers where possible.

key_findings.finding: 1,383 records identified, 1,264 unique titles screened, 130 full texts assessed, 109 excluded (9 not observational general-population studies, 48 without data on the disorders, 31 without estimates among people who had used cannabis, 21 duplicating data), leaving 21 studies with 153 data points and 255,010, 28,951 and 58,661 observations for cannabis use disorder, abuse and dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study selection, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Samples from the US, the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 15 studies gave cross-sectional and 9 longitudinal data; 11 sampled adolescents or young adults and one older adults. Nine studies counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required use more than a few times, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use; three cohorts reported incidence in people without a disorder at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: One study used DSM-5 (lifetime probability of transition to cannabis use disorder after use 27%), one DSM-III-R (26.4%, 20.9 to 32.0, given lifetime use), the rest DSM-IV (for example 23.7%, 19.7 to 27.7, in a Dutch cohort). In a US survey that approximated DSM-5 with DSM-IV-based criteria, 16.8% (15.9 to 17.7) of adults who had used cannabis in the past year, and 36.8% (34.4 to 39.3) of those who used it daily or near daily, met two or more criteria.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Single-study extremes: cannabis use disorder from 4.5% (1.8 to 7.3) in US adults aged 50 or more who used in the past year (2005-06) to 41.1% (38.4 to 43.8), lifetime, in an Australian cohort of 21-year-olds; abuse from 2.9% (2.5 to 3.3) in US adults in 2017 to 28.4% (25.8 to 30.9) in a 2001-02 US survey; dependence from 3.5% (0.1 to 7.0) in young adults in Ireland to 40.9% (29.0 to 52.8) among people using daily in an Australian adolescent cohort (22.6%, 15.2 to 29.9, with weekly use); past-year dependence 14.7% (13.0 to 16.5) among US adults using daily or near daily in 2017.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 4th to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Most of the ten studies that reported sex differences found higher risk in males; US studies consistently found higher risk at younger ages. Earlier first use went with higher risk of use disorder and abuse in the studies that examined it, while for dependence two studies found higher risk with earlier use and two did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pooled shares: cannabis use disorder 22% (18 to 26); longitudinal lifetime 27% (25 to 28) and recent 22% (20 to 24); cross-sectional lifetime 28% (10 to 48), past year 17% (12 to 23), daily or near daily 22% (17 to 28). Abuse 13% (8 to 18). Dependence 13% (10 to 15); longitudinal lifetime 12% (7 to 18) and recent 9% (1 to 19); cross-sectional lifetime 11% (7 to 15) and recent 8% (6 to 10); weekly or daily use 33% (22 to 44) in cohorts and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-analysis results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 11); Table 2 (p. 28)

key_findings.finding: Year of data collection moderated the pooled prevalence of cannabis use disorder (B = -0.01, p = 0.049) and abuse (B = -0.01, p = 0.017) but not dependence (B = 0.00, p = 0.270), an effect the authors attribute to lower prevalence over time in the one US survey reported across years; age, sex, recall period, tool and country did not moderate the estimates.
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-regression, paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion says the 13% for dependence is slightly higher than the one-in-ten figure, that closer to 1 in 8 people who have used cannabis will develop dependence, and that clinicians, researchers and policymakers can have confidence in the updated figure. The 33% for weekly or daily use comes from two cohorts of young people (Australia and the Netherlands); cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18% (12 to 24). In one US study, dependence was 10.6% (7.1 to 14.1) among everyone who had ever used and 18.1% (12.4 to 23.8) among those who had used more than six times.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: heterogeneity, with estimates possibly too different to pool and limited power to detect moderators; 60% of estimates from cross-sectional surveys open to recall bias; past-year and lifetime estimates that mean different things (past-year use disorder 15.4% among 18 to 25-year-olds who used that year against 9.8% among those who had ever used, in one US survey).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th to 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: No population study estimated the risk of cannabis use disorder by the potency of the cannabis used; the authors mention, without a reference, a Michigan study of high-risk families in which people who used higher-potency products had higher risks of developing use-disorder symptoms. All included studies were from high-income countries and over half from the US.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: people who use cannabis have a 1 in 5 risk of a use disorder (abuse or dependence) and a 1 in 8 risk of abuse or dependence, rising to 1 in 3 for dependence among people who use weekly or more often; these risks may rise if people use more often and use more potent products after legalisation.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funding: University of Queensland development fellowship (JL); NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (LH); Australian Government Drug and Alcohol Program funding of the authors' centre and group; funders had no role. All authors declare no conflicts of interest.
key_findings.locator: Role of Funding Sources; Contributors; Conflict of Interest

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the same odds ratio and interval, 2.20 (1.37 to 3.52), for two different variables in a study of older adults: the number of joints smoked at peak use and the frequency of use.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is probably a copying error; neither can be used without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: A Michigan study of high-risk families, said to show higher risks of use-disorder symptoms with higher-potency products, is described without any reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only potency finding in the review cannot be traced from it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the NESARC-III analysis of 2012-13 (Feingold 2020) longitudinal and the analysis of the same survey wave by Hasin (2015) cross-sectional. The only Table 1 rows labelled longitudinal that give lifetime use disorder are Feingold (27.0%), Kirisci (26.4%) and Prince van Leeuwen (23.7%), so the longitudinal lifetime pool of 27% (25 to 28) appears to rest on them (editors' reading; the studies in each pool are listed only in S4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The longitudinal lifetime figure for use disorder may rest largely on a single-wave survey; quote it with that caution.

reporting_issues.issue: For the NESARC cohort (Lopez-Quintero 2011), Table 1 gives 7.2% (6.6 to 7.7) 'past year' dependence among people who had ever used cannabis, and the text says 70% of people with lifetime dependence started before 14. The encyclopedia's card of that paper (sc_lopez_quintero_2011, read in full by another reader) gives a lifetime cumulative probability of dependence of 8.9% for cannabis, does not list 7.2%, and records that onset before 14 predicted cannabis dependence only before adjustment, reversing after it (hazard ratio 0.63).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's figure for this study and its use of it for early onset need checking against the primary paper; the base rate should not lean on this row.

reporting_issues.issue: Separate analyses for each DSM version were planned but are not reported, and the pools combine DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-5 estimates; Table 1 gives no sample size for any study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weight of each study in a pool cannot be judged from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: A review article about one cohort (Coffey & Patton 2016, on the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort Study) is an included data source, although the selection criteria say reviews were used only to find references; and the Introduction's description of the 2007 Australian survey is garbled (risk if people had used cannabis five times or in their lives).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the cohort's figures come second-hand through that review.

verification.source_read: PDF, journal pre-proof (accepted manuscript), manuscript pp. 1-29 (PDFs/Cannabis/Leung_2020_CUDPrevalenceMA.pdf): all text, Tables 1 and 2, highlights, references, funding, contributors and conflict statement read; pages are the pre-proof's own; supplementary material S1 to S6 (flowchart, search terms, forest plots with heterogeneity statistics, meta-regression) not read; not the version of record

design_detail: Retrospective chart review of emergency department (ED) visits at one academic hospital in Colorado (University of Colorado Hospital: urban, about 100,000 visits a year, more than 97% adults), 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016. The unit is the visit, not the person. Visits carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code were read by trained research assistants, who judged whether the visit was at least partly attributable to cannabis, the route (edible or inhaled), the dose when written down, and the symptoms. Edible-attributed and inhaled-attributed visits were then compared for symptoms, who attended and what happened to them. A second analysis set the share of attributable visits that involved edibles against the share of THC sold as edibles in Colorado in 2014 to 2016, using state sales data and assumed THC contents. There is no group of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital, and none of people who do not use cannabis.
can_establish: What clinicians at this one emergency department recorded as the reasons for visits they linked to cannabis, and how the mix of recorded reasons differed between visits recorded as edible and visits recorded as inhaled (or, where no route was written down, presumed inhaled), with differences in percentage points and 95% confidence intervals (Table 2). That serious cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) occurred in both groups, although the paper gives no counts (Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph). A rough size of the gap between edibles’ share of attributable visits and their share of THC sold, under stated assumptions about product strength.
cannot_establish: How often a visit follows each form, per person or per occasion: only people who reached this department are counted, with no count of people who took each form and did not attend, so the percentages are shares among visits, not risks. Whether the form itself caused the different mix of reasons: the two groups differed (more women and more people living outside Colorado among edible-attributed visits), the amount taken was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits (5.1%), product strength was not measured, route was presumed inhaled when not documented (135 visits), and the paper reports no adjustment for age, sex, residence, previous experience, alcohol, tobacco or other drugs. What happens in other hospitals or states, to people treated elsewhere or to people who did not seek care. The sales comparison rests on assumed THC content (20% of flower weight, 10 mg per edible unit), leaves out home-grown and illicit supply, and sets one hospital against statewide sales, so it cannot show how much more likely an edible is to lead to a visit than the same amount of THC taken another way. The edible group (238 visits) is small beside the inhaled group (2,329).

sample.recruitment: No one was recruited. All ED visits at the hospital in the five years were eligible (449,031). Visits with a cannabis-related ICD code (9,973) were abstracted by hand, and 2,567 (25.7%) were classed as at least partly attributable to cannabis if the ED provider named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or the inpatient provider did after admission, or the urine drug screen was positive with a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Attribution is a clinician judgment recorded in the chart.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with an ED visit carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code (Appendix Table lists the codes), and within them the attributable visits as defined above. Visits without such a code were not abstracted, so visits in which cannabis mattered but was not coded would be missed: a check of 4,800 randomly chosen records found 26 with a mention of cannabis that the code search had not captured (all in 2015 to 2016, the ICD-10 period; medical shorthand in consultants’ notes, polypharmacy ingestions), none judged attributable (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability).
sample.demographics: Attributable visits (n = 2,567): median age 30 (interquartile range 24 to 41); 65.2% male; 43.4% White, 36.6% Black, 17.8% Hispanic; 90.2% Colorado residents and 9.8% (252) from other states; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths (Table 1). Pregnant: 46 patients (under 2%). Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%, living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%, admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (range 0 to 121); age said to be similar, no figures (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a chart review. Route was recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 attributable visits (94.7%); for the 135 visits with insufficient documentation, inhalation was assumed. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%).
sample.selection_effects: Strong. Only people who came to this hospital’s ED, were coded with a cannabis-related diagnosis and were judged by a clinician to be affected by cannabis are in the data; people who took cannabis without harm, or were harmed and did not attend, are absent, so the paper cannot say who tends to choose which form or how many came to no harm. Attribution depends on what patients said and what clinicians asked and wrote down. The authors note that this department has the second-highest number of visits a year in the state and sits in an area of high cannabis availability, which they say likely raises its rates of attributable visits (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Visitors from outside Colorado are 9.8% of attributable visits and 40.8% of edible-attributed visits (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Route and dose as written in the chart: the drug-use section of the standard nursing assessment questionnaire and the medical providers’ notes (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Self-report, not verified; no blood levels. Route was assumed to be inhalation when not documented, because that is the most common route in Colorado (Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph); the authors say this could have biased the comparison toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Product strength and content were not measured. The paper reports two groups only, edible and inhaled; no breakdown of the inhaled group by product (for example flower, vaporized oil or concentrates) appears in the text or tables.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route: edible or inhaled (inhaled includes anything documented as smoked or inhaled and every undocumented route). A dose was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits; among edible-attributed visits it was written down in 80, and in 19 of those it was 50 mg of THC or more (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Frequency and duration of use before the visit are not reported. Time between exposure and the visit is not reported, apart from the 24-hour link used in one attribution criterion.
exposure.polysubstance: Not examined. The paper does not describe alcohol, tobacco or other drugs taken at the same time, and no comparison accounts for them. One attribution criterion rests on a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis; the screen does not show which form was taken. Tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (emergency presentation).

comparison.controls: No group of people who do not use cannabis, and none of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital. The comparison is inside the attributable visits: edible-attributed (238) against inhaled-attributed (2,329, of which 135 presumed). The sales analysis sets the edible share of attributable visits (10.7%, 2014 to 2016) against the edible share of THC sold by weight (0.32%).
comparison.matching: None. Crude percentages, chi-square tests and absolute differences in percentage points with 95% confidence intervals; no adjustment (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: previous experience with cannabis (the authors suggest inexperience among visitors as one explanation, without testing it: Discussion, 7th paragraph), usual frequency and amount of use, tolerance, mental-health and heart history (only partly seen in the reasons ‘acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease’ and ‘chronic psychiatric condition’), other substances, and which product was taken.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described.

outcomes.instruments: Manual chart abstraction by four trained research assistants who were blinded to the study hypothesis, after an ICD code search; no clinical scales. Variables: attribution to cannabis, route, dose when available, clinical and presenting symptoms (not mutually exclusive), length of stay, disposition. A medical toxicologist abstracted a random 10% for reliability and arbitrated questionable attributions; 1,111 visits were abstracted twice (Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Inter-rater agreement kappa 0.79 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.83), described as good (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability). The symptom groups in Table 2 are the authors’ own groupings; the Appendix Table gives the codes used to find visits, not definitions of the symptom groups.
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Attributable to cannabis’: the ED provider, or the inpatient provider after admission, named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours plus a condition known to be associated with cannabis. ‘Edible’ or ‘inhalable’: the route as documented, with inhalation presumed when not documented. Reasons: gastrointestinal symptoms (including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome), intoxication, psychiatric symptoms (acute symptoms such as acute anxiety or acute psychosis, acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease, chronic psychiatric condition such as depression, schizophrenia or psychosis) and cardiovascular symptoms. The outcome is the share of each group’s visits carrying each reason, not an event rate.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eight symptom groups (some nested within others) are compared in Table 2, plus age, sex, residence, admission and length of stay in the text; P values and 95% confidence intervals are given at the usual level without adjustment. Among the differences that carry the paper’s message, the intervals for cardiovascular symptoms (1.4 to 8.4 percentage points) and acute psychiatric symptoms (2.1 to 12.1) come closest to zero.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Research assistants were blinded to the study hypothesis, not to the route, which they coded in the same pass as attribution and symptoms.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentage of visits with each reason, edible (n = 238) against inhaled (n = 2,329), with the absolute difference (edible minus inhaled, percentage points) and 95% CI (Table 2): gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1% vs 32.3%, −17.2 (−22.1 to −12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% vs 18.0%, −9.6 (−13.5 to −5.7); intoxication 48.3% vs 27.8%, 20.5 (13.9 to 27.1); any psychiatric symptom 26.1% vs 24.5%, 1.6 (−4.2 to 7.4); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0% vs 10.9%, 7.1 (2.1 to 12.1); acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease 0.4% vs 4.0%, −3.6 (−4.7 to −2.5); chronic psychiatric condition 0.4% vs 4.3%, −3.9 (−5.0 to −2.8); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0% vs 3.1%, 4.9 (1.4 to 8.4). Recalculating from the printed counts with a standard formula reproduces these intervals to within 0.1 point. Sales (Table 3; Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure): 309 times more THC sold as flower than as edibles (range 279 to 325); 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits in 2014 to 2016, so 10.7% edible, against 0.32% of THC sold; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the two routes were equally toxic.
analysis.covariates: None. There is no multivariable model; visits are not adjusted for age, sex, residence, experience, dose, other substances or year.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The paper says the protocol was approved by the local institutional review board (Methods › Study Design and Population, 2nd paragraph). The comparison of edible against inhaled visits is the stated objective, but no analysis plan is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: All eight symptom groups in Table 2 are shown, including those with fewer edible visits, and several favour the inhaled group, so there is no sign of one-sided reporting. Not reported: counts of the severe cardiovascular events, any breakdown of the 135 presumed-inhalation visits, doses in table form, and whether the symptom groups were fixed before the data were seen.
analysis.power: A sample of 2,000 was calculated to estimate a five-fold higher rate of ED visits for edible against inhaled exposure, assuming a 1:9 ratio of edible to inhaled exposures (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph). The edible group is small for the rarer reasons (one visit each for acute exacerbation and for chronic psychiatric condition), where the percentages are near zero and an approximate interval is less reliable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among visits to one Colorado emergency department that clinicians linked to cannabis, those recorded as edible (238) more often carried intoxication (48.3% vs 27.8%), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% vs 10.9%) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% vs 3.1%) than visits recorded as inhaled (2,329), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% vs 32.3%, mostly cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, 8.4% vs 18.0%) or admission (18.9% vs 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% vs 24.5%). Severe heart events occurred in both groups. Most visits for every reason, including intoxication (647 of 762), acute psychiatric symptoms (254 of 297) and cardiovascular symptoms (73 of 92), were inhaled-attributed, because edibles made up 9.3% of attributable visits. In 2014 to 2016 edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits and 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents. No count of people taking each form, a dose recorded in 5.1% of visits, no adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract concludes that visits attributable to inhaled cannabis are more frequent than those attributable to edibles, although edibles are “associated with” more acute psychiatric visits and more visits than expected. The Discussion goes further: its first sentence says edible products “lead to” more acute psychiatric events and cardiovascular symptoms than inhaled exposure (a causal verb for shares of visits in one department); it treats the 33-fold ratio as evidence that edibles have greater toxicity per unit of cannabis sold, while saying that careful interpretation is required; it explains the higher admission rate in the inhaled group by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome without analysing it; it cites three deaths linked to edibles, taken from news reports (references 10 to 12), none from this hospital’s data (Table 1 records no deaths); and it recommends limiting edibles to medical use, stronger regulatory oversight and education, which the results do not test. It also states that the main public-health effect may come from the inhaled products, which account for most visits and most admissions. The authors list their main limits (retrospective, single centre, self-report, little dose data, no community comparison group).

timeline.event: Same hospital group: cyclic vomiting presentations after marijuana liberalisation in Colorado (Kim et al., Acad Emerg Med; cited as reference 31, not read).

Label testing of edible medicinal cannabis products in three US cities (Vandrey et al.), cited in the Discussion for inconsistent dosing (reference 33). Not yet readable for this library; will be added.

Poison-centre reports of edible exposures across the United States (Cao et al., Clin Toxicol; cited as reference 6, not read); and a letter on marijuana tourism and ED visits in Colorado from the same hospital group (Kim et al., N Engl J Med; reference 32, not read).

Overview of edibles in this batch, citing a 2015 viewpoint by Monte and colleagues (JAMA, reference 13 here) for the statement that edible products are responsible for most health care visits due to cannabis intoxication; in this study’s counts, edible-attributed visits were 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%).

Same hospital group: mental-health-related ED visits associated with cannabis in Colorado (Hall et al., Acad Emerg Med; reference 19, not read); the authors say such studies did not stratify visits by route of exposure (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
This chart review: visits by route of exposure at one academic ED, 2012 to 2016.

replication.where_it_stands: No second dataset that splits cannabis-related emergency visits by route was read for this batch. The authors say earlier visit studies did not stratify by route and ask for studies that do, with counts of how many people are exposed to each form (Discussion, 2nd and 8th paragraphs). Related papers from the same hospital group cover cannabis-related visits without the route comparison; poison-centre reports use a different kind of data. Treat the edible-against-inhaled differences as one hospital’s record of who attended and why.

funding.funder: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), through a competitive grant programme (project titled “The Adverse Health Effects of Edible Cannabis Products”). The paper states that CDPHE was not involved in study design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination (Methods › Role of the Funding Source; Grant Support).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Monte received support from NIH K23 GM110516, NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082 and CDPHE 17 FHHA 96950 (Grant Support), reports grants from CDPHE during the study and sits on the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee, a group of clinicians and scientists reviewing the literature on the public health effects of cannabis (Disclosures); Saben reports CDPHE grants; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. No cannabis-industry, tobacco-industry or advocacy funding or ties are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Colorado School of Medicine; Rocky Mountain Poison & Drug Center, Denver Health. The funder is a state health department that monitors the legal cannabis market and convenes the advisory committee on which Monte sits and whose literature review the authors searched (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); it is neither industry nor an advocacy body. Several related papers cited (Kim, Hall, Wang) come from the same group, so the surrounding literature is not wholly independent of the authors. Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that counts the people at risk: a prospective cohort or linked health-records study of people who eat cannabis products, people who inhale cannabis and people who do not use cannabis, followed for emergency visits and admissions, with amount and product content measured (tested products or recorded labels), time since exposure, other substances, age, sex, residence and previous experience recorded, across several hospitals and states. For the sales comparison, person-level purchase or use data in place of weight of THC sold.

domains.note: No adjustment. Edible-attributed and inhaled-attributed visits differ in sex (51.3% vs 33.1% women) and residence (40.8% vs 6.6% from outside Colorado), probably also in experience with cannabis and in amounts taken, none of which enters the comparison; other substances are not described. Reasons such as cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, concentrated in the inhaled group, shape the comparison of shares.

Route from chart notes and a nursing questionnaire, self-reported and unverified; 135 visits (5.3% of 2,567) with no route written down were counted as inhaled; dose recorded in 5.1%; no product testing; edible and inhaled are the only categories.

Only visits to one academic ED in an area of high availability, coded with a cannabis diagnosis and judged cannabis-attributable by a clinician; everyone in the data has the outcome (an ED visit), and people taking each form who did not attend are absent, so shares of visits cannot be read as risks.
Not an issue for a record of emergency presentations; treatment during the visit does not define the groups.
Route undocumented for 135 visits and dose for 94.9%; handling of other missing values is not described; the check of 4,800 charts found 26 uncaptured mentions, none attributable.

Trained abstractors blinded to the hypothesis, double abstraction of 1,111 visits and kappa 0.79 are reassuring; but attribution is a clinician judgment, symptom groups overlap and are not defined in full, and route and attribution were coded in one pass, so attribution was not blind to route.

No protocol or registration cited; all eight symptom groups are shown, including those favouring the inhaled group, without correction for multiple comparisons; text and Table 1 contain numerical slips (see reporting issues); the 33-fold figure depends on one choice of denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is applied as the closest tool for a chart-review comparison. Confounding, exposure measurement and selection are each judged high (no adjustment, route presumed when undocumented, every participant selected by an emergency visit), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Against that, the chart abstraction is careful and reported with reliability figures, the results table shows every symptom group including those that run against the headline, and the Abstract qualifies the main finding. The study can be cited for what clinicians at this hospital recorded as the reasons for visits, by route, and for the size of those differences as shares of visits; it cannot be cited for how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and the Discussion’s causal wording and the 33-fold ratio go beyond what it supports.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6788289 (author manuscript; abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, Tables 1 to 3, the Appendix Table of ICD codes, reference list, grant support and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; no supplementary files)

key_findings.finding: Over five years 449,031 emergency visits were eligible; 9,973 carried a cannabis-related code and 2,567 (25.7%) were judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3%) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image not extracted).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Abstract
key_findings.note: Visits, not people.

key_findings.finding: Attributable visits (n = 2,567): median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% (252) living outside Colorado; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, third column

key_findings.finding: Reasons across the 2,567 visits (not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%; 301 people accounted for 440 visits, 1 to 17 visits per person per year); intoxication 762 (29.7%); psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%: 297 acute, 94 acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease, 100 chronic psychiatric conditions); cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Reasons for Cannabis-Attributable ED Visits, paragraph; Table 2, last column

key_findings.finding: Edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329) visits, percentage of visits (difference in points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3% vs 27.8% (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0% vs 10.9% (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0% vs 3.1% (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1% vs 24.5% (1.6; −4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1% vs 32.3% (−17.2; −22.1 to −12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% vs 18.0% (−9.6; −13.5 to −5.7).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
key_findings.note: Shares of each group’s visits, not rates. Editors’ arithmetic from the Table 2 counts: edible-attributed visits were 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%), 43 of 297 acute psychiatric visits (14.5%) and 19 of 92 cardiovascular visits (20.7%), so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed.

key_findings.finding: Edible-attributed visits against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%; admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (range 0 to 121); age similar (no figures).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; this is not analysed (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Severe adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular dysrhythmia, occurred in both the edible and the inhaled groups; no counts are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Colorado sales, 2014 to 2016: 219 edible-attributed and 1,819 inhaled-attributed visits, so edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits, while edibles were 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC, giving 65,598 kg; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each, giving 212 kg; ratio 309, range 279 to 325). The authors call the visit share about 33 times the share expected if the two routes were equally toxic and list the limits: assumed THC content, one hospital against statewide sales, no home-grown or illicit supply, sales not geocoded.
key_findings.locator: Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure; Table 3; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: THC by weight is one denominator among several, and none counts people or occasions of use. The overview by Barrus and colleagues (this batch) cites a 2014 Colorado report in which edible units were about 45 percent of total cannabis sales, a different measure that would give a very different ratio.

key_findings.finding: A dose was written down in 80 edible-attributed visits, and in 19 of them it was 50 mg of THC or more. The authors say they were surprised by the low doses reported and note that a typical Colorado joint contains about 100 mg of THC.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Doses are as written in the chart, not tested; 94.9% of the 2,567 visits have no dose.

key_findings.finding: Reliability and capture: kappa 0.79 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.83) between abstractors; 4,800 random records checked, no uncaptured cannabis mentions in 2012 to 2014 and 26 in 2015 to 2016 (medical shorthand in consultants’ notes; polypharmacy ingestions, no urine screen), none judged attributable.
key_findings.locator: Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability; Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design; exposure mostly self-reported; no community comparison cohort; people attending an ED differ from people who use cannabis in general, most of whom may have no adverse effect; doses not verified; route presumed inhaled when undocumented; one hospital in an area of high availability. They call for a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Abstract (Limitation)
