key_findings.finding: The Discussion summarises timing as described in a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): after inhalation, effects within 10 minutes, a blood peak at 30 to 90 minutes and clearance within 4 hours; after oral THC, no significant blood level until at least 30 minutes, a peak at about 3 hours and clearance at about 12 hours. It adds that people report longer-lasting and more intense effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reports from a consumer survey and a Twitter analysis, not read).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Not measured in this study; no times were recorded.

reporting_issues.issue: Results and Table 2 print 94 acute exacerbations of underlying chronic disease as 14.1% of the 633 psychiatric visits; 94 of 633 is 14.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small numerical slip; the count (94, from 1 + 93 in Table 2) is consistent. This card uses counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: in the two cannabis columns the insurance percentages do not match the counts and add to more than 100% (112.2% for the 9,973 coded visits and 107.7% for the 2,567 attributable visits). For example 1,190 Medicaid visits of 2,567 is 46.4%, printed 50.6%; 4,225 of 9,973 is 42.4%, printed 48.6%. The counts themselves add to the group totals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The insurance mix should be recomputed from counts. It does not affect the comparison by route.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity check puts the 26 uncaptured cannabis mentions at 0.01% of total records; 26 of the 4,800 records checked is 0.54%, and 26 of all 449,031 visits is 0.006%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is unclear, so the likely number of uncaptured mentions across 2015 to 2016 visits cannot be judged; none was attributable.

reporting_issues.issue: The unit of analysis is the visit. 301 people account for 440 visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (up to 17 visits a year), and the chi-square tests and confidence intervals treat visits as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intervals are probably narrower than the data justify, and counts of visits overstate counts of people.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract does not say that 135 visits with no route written down (5.3% of attributable visits) were counted as inhaled; its list of limitations omits it (Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the Abstract alone would not know that the inhaled group includes visits with no documented route.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute psychiatric symptoms are reported at P < 0.001; recalculating a chi-square test from the printed counts (43 of 238 against 254 of 2,329) gives P of about 0.0010 without continuity correction and 0.0015 with it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial to the direction of the finding; this is the difference nearest the threshold among those reported as P < 0.001.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, and that the higher edible share of cardiovascular visits seems to have translated into more cardiovascular events; neither is analysed in the Results (no admission by reason, no counts of events).
reporting_issues.consequence: These are the authors’ readings, not findings; counts of severe cardiovascular events are not given.

design_detail: An original laboratory screening study, not a review (the reading list describes it as a review). Liquid from 38 THC-containing cartridges the authors call counterfeit or patient-provided, 4 CBD-containing cartridges and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; one is described as the reference), obtained from local vape shops and from patients or other people who vaped them, in what the authors call a particular region of New York State, were screened by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) with identification by library match; the liquids of counterfeit and CBD cartridges were screened for 50 elements by ICP-MS; and aerosol from counterfeit cartridges (10 puffs over 10 minutes per cartridge, collected in one-litre vacuum bottles) was sent to a commercial laboratory for volatile-compound analysis by EPA method TO-15 plus library search. The authors hypothesised beforehand that constituents other than vitamin E acetate (VEA) might contribute. Descriptive: no counts per compound, no statistical tests. Version read: the PMC full text of the Toxics article (2020;8(2):25).
can_establish: That a library-matched GC-MS screen of cartridge liquids found hundreds of chemicals (more than 500 across all cartridges), with Table 1 listing 47 entries said to be commonly present in the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges and not in the others (13 for CBD cartridges, 15 for medical-grade), among them VEA, silicon-containing compounds, terpenes and MCT-type triglycerides; that Table 2 lists 53 volatile compounds for aerosol from counterfeit cartridges (three of them look like laboratory standards), seven on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; and that silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in those cartridges' liquid. These are leads for further work.
cannot_establish: Which compounds are truly present (identifications are library matches without reference standards, the method is described as qualitative screening, and some entries look like laboratory standards or reaction products); how often any compound occurred (no counts, and 'commonly present' is not defined; the paper does not say how many of the 38 cartridges held VEA); whether counterfeit cartridges differ from CBD or medical-grade ones in the vapor phase or metals (those were not measured or not shown for the comparison cartridges); how many of the 38 came from patients with EVALI; the exposure a person would receive; or whether any named compound contributes to lung injury.

sample.recruitment: Cartridges were obtained from local vape shops and from individuals or patients (Methods 2.2). The counterfeit brands are said to have been recovered from patients with EVALI and are cited to a published case series (reference 4); hospital staff supplied information on patients' cartridges (Acknowledgments). The paper does not say how many of the 38 came from patients with EVALI and how many from shops or other individuals, when they were collected, or how they were judged counterfeit. Medical-grade cartridges came from a named New York supplier; the number is not stated and the text speaks of one cartridge as the reference.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not described. No manufacturer details were printed on the counterfeit cartridges or packaging. Cannabis oil variants tested were sativa, indica and hybrid.
sample.demographics: Not reported (no patient information).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The number of cartridges used for vapor-phase analysis and for metals is not stated; the ranges in Table 2 imply at least two cartridges for some compounds.
sample.selection_effects: Convenience samples from one region of New York State (the authors say other regions may differ). The counterfeit group mixes cartridges from patients, individuals and shops. The comparison groups are very small (4 CBD cartridges; medical-grade number not stated) against 38.

exposure.measurement: GC-MS of cartridge rinsates (interior flushed five times with 100 microlitres of methanol) and of neat liquids diluted 100-fold in methanol, mass range 50 to 550, identification by search of the NIST library; no reference standards are described. Vapor phase: aerosol sampled into one-litre vacuum bottles (10 puffs over 10 minutes per cartridge), shipped to a commercial laboratory, analysed by EPA TO-15 for a standard suite of volatile compounds and by library search for 'tentatively identified' compounds; the authors note that any VEA in the aerosol would have condensed on the canister walls before analysis. Elements: ICP-MS with external standards (50 elements at 20 parts per billion). Total volatile organic compounds and particles were measured with a handheld monitor and a particle monitor, described only in the Discussion.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to people. Aerosol was generated at common voltages (3.5 to 5.5 V, per the Discussion) with a device that the Methods do not name; vapor-phase figures are air concentrations in a one-litre canister, which depend on puff volume and dilution that are not given.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (product analysis).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: CBD-containing cartridges (4) and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; a named New York supplier; formulated in coconut oil according to the Discussion). Table 1 lists only compounds 'commonly found' in one category and not in the others, so compounds shared by categories are not shown. Vapor-phase results (Table 2) are for counterfeit cartridges only; metals are reported for counterfeit cartridges only. A separate comparison of total volatile compounds and particles uses pure MCT oil, mineral oil and VEA as the comparators (Discussion).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: How many of the 38 counterfeit cartridges came from patients; the number of cartridges in each analysis; the device used; the age of cartridges and storage before analysis; which chemicals arise from heating, from the device or from preparation in methanol rather than from the liquid.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS (Agilent 7890A with 5975 detector, NIST library); EPA TO-15 volatile compound analysis by a commercial laboratory; ICP-MS (PerkinElmer NexION 2000); handheld volatile-compound and particle monitors (Discussion only).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors describe the GC-MS method as a preliminary screen with a qualitative result. No reference standards, detection limits, blanks or replicate runs are described for the GC-MS work. Table 2 lists three compounds that are laboratory surrogate or tuning standards of the EPA volatile-compound method (toluene-d8, 1,2-dichloroethane-d4 and bromofluorobenzene, each with a very narrow range) as if they were vapor-phase constituents (editors' note from general analytical chemistry, to be confirmed by a chemist).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Commonly present' is not defined (no number or share of cartridges). Compounds are sorted into groups by the authors' use categories (terpenes, silicon compounds, pesticide constituents, flavour additives, cannabinoids, plasticizers and others, humectants and oils, vitamins, miscellaneous); the same compound (hexadecanoic acid methyl ester) appears under two categories.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Table 1 entries (editors' count): 47 for counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges (46 distinct), 13 for CBD, 15 for medical-grade; by category for counterfeit: 13 terpenes, 12 silicon compounds, 7 plasticizers, drugs and manufacturing agents, 3 each flavour additives, cannabinoids and humectants or oils, 2 pesticide constituents (fatty acid methyl esters), 2 vitamins and conjugates (including VEA), 2 miscellaneous. Table 2 (vapor phase of counterfeit cartridges): 53 entries, 51 with concentrations, from 44 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre; highest listed ranges for isoprene (8,400 to 360,000), propene (1,500 to 300,000), 2-methylpropene (2,600 to 290,000), acrolein (350 to 150,000) and 1,3-butadiene (98 to 85,000). Metals: silicon, copper, nickel and lead most abundant, very variable between cartridges, up to 600 parts per million (which element is not stated). Total volatile compounds in aerosol, mean with standard error (number of replicates not given): counterfeit cartridges 20.03 (0.59) parts per million against MCT oil 10.33, mineral oil 7.33 and VEA 9.67.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; the authors state a hypothesis in the Introduction (other constituents may act alone or together with VEA).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 shows only compounds specific to one category, which cannot show what the categories share. Results for metals in CBD cartridges and for the vapor phase of CBD and medical-grade cartridges are not shown although the Methods describe metals screening of CBD liquids and the Conclusion contrasts counterfeit with CBD and medical products. Particle data and the monitors' methods are not given.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A qualitative, library-matched screen listed many compounds in the liquids of 38 counterfeit or patient-provided THC cartridges, including VEA in an unstated number, silicon-containing compounds, terpenes and MCT-type triglycerides; the aerosol of counterfeit cartridges held 51 compounds with listed concentrations, seven of which are on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; and silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in their liquid. Comparison cartridges were few (4 CBD; medical-grade number not stated), and neither the vapor phase nor the metals are shown for them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the study provides additional insights into the chemicals associated with EVALI cartridges and may contribute to the disease mechanism. The conclusion says numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in the medical or CBD products; that symptoms in EVALI are similar to what can be anticipated from inhaling the compounds detected; and that exposure to a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute along with VEA, as opposed to a single cause. Gaps: (1) vapor-phase and metals data are not shown for CBD or medical-grade cartridges, so 'not present' is not tested for them; (2) the list is of library matches with no counts, so presence in any given cartridge is unknown; (3) compound-by-compound toxicity is taken from general toxicology without exposure levels, and the authors themselves say the effect depends on concentration and duration; (4) the symptom match is general; (5) combinations were not tested.

timeline.event: A New York State Department of Health laboratory analysed 38 case-associated fluids with targeted and untargeted methods and found VEA, MCT oil and pesticide residues; it did not report the silicon compounds, hydrocarbons or metals this study highlights.
CDC reported VEA in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients with EVALI and in none of 99 healthy volunteers; its panel was targeted and did not include the compounds this study highlights.

replication.where_it_stands: The presence of VEA and MCT oil in some cartridges is also reported by the other laboratory studies read, with counts; the study's own distinctive claims (silicon compounds, solvent-derived hydrocarbons, metals, vapor-phase toxicants and their role) were not tested by any other source read here. The authors say they are investigating these in models.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no actual, potential or perceived competing financial interests (Conflicts of Interest section).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors work at the University of Rochester Medical Center (Environmental Medicine; Pediatric Pulmonology), The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo. Universities and a state agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; no industry tie is declared.

what_would_settle_it: A repeat with reference standards for each named compound, equal numbers of cartridges of each type with counts per compound reported, the same liquid, aerosol and metals analyses on every type, a named device and defined puffing, provenance recorded (patient, shop, date), and exposure experiments at realistic concentrations to test whether any compound contributes to injury alone or with VEA.

domains.note: 38 counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges from shops, individuals and patients (split not stated), 4 CBD, medical-grade number not stated, vapor-phase and metals numbers not stated; one region.

Library matching without reference standards; described by the authors as qualitative preliminary screening; surrogate standards listed as constituents; some named compounds (acetyl chloride, tetramethyl silicate, 2,2-dimethoxybutane) can react with, or be formed from, methanol, the dilution solvent, so may be preparation artefacts (editors' chemistry note); vapor samples stored and shipped before analysis.

Unequal numbers (38 against 4 and an unstated number); Table 1 lists only compounds exclusive to a category, so longer lists for the larger group are expected; vapor phase and metals not shown for the comparison cartridges.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: Compound-by-compound toxicity is inferred from general toxicology (for example 'paralytic agents', silicon dioxide formation) without exposure levels or patient data; the conclusion contrasts counterfeit with medical and CBD products for phases not measured in those products.

No count of cartridges with VEA; compounds named in the text (decane, naphthalene, benzene and aflatoxin B1 in medical-grade cartridges) are absent from the tables or have no method; stated range of 140 to 360,000 against 44 as the lowest in Table 2; methods for volatile-compound and particle monitors missing; one compound in two categories.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a laboratory screening of products (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for product analysis. The overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The paper is open about being a preliminary qualitative screen and that the cause may involve more than VEA, and the hypothesis was stated in advance, but the identifications, counts and comparisons are too incomplete to carry the conclusion about toxicants absent from other products. It may be cited as hypothesis-generating: that a screening of counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges reported chemicals other than VEA, and which kinds. It may not be cited for how many cartridges held any compound, for VEA prevalence, for differences from CBD or medical-grade cartridges in the vapor phase or metals, for the exposure of any person, or for the cause of EVALI.

key_findings.finding: The study screened liquid from 38 cartridges described as counterfeit or patient-provided (THC-containing), 4 CBD-containing cartridges and medical-grade cartridges (number not stated), obtained from local vape shops and from patients or other people who vaped them, in one region of New York State, to test the hypothesis that constituents other than VEA, alone or with VEA, might injure the lung. It is a laboratory study, not a review.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Methods 2.2 and 2.3

key_findings.finding: More than 500 chemicals were found across the tested cartridges, mostly terpenes and silicon compounds. Chemicals described as specific to the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges include 2,2-dimethoxybutane, tetramethyl silicate, methyl and ethyl esters, siloxanes, acetates including VEA, benzophenone, glycerol tricaprylate and THC derivatives. Table 1 lists 47 entries for these cartridges, 13 for CBD and 15 for medical-grade (editors' count). No count of cartridges containing VEA is given.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Vapor phase of counterfeit cartridges: over 50 chemicals with concentrations listed (Table 2 has 53 entries, 51 with concentrations, 44 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre), mostly volatile hydrocarbons and solvents; seven are on the FDA list of harmful or potentially harmful constituents of tobacco products and smoke (isoprene, acetaldehyde, ethylbenzene, toluene, acrolein, 1,3-butadiene, benzene). VEA was not found in the vapor phase, which the authors suggest may be due to condensation before analysis.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2.4; Results 3.2; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Elements in the liquid of counterfeit patient cartridges: silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant, very variable between cartridges, up to 600 parts per million. The Methods say CBD cartridges' liquids were screened too; no results are given for them.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2.5; Results 3.3

key_findings.finding: The authors say they detected VEA in many EVALI-associated liquids but not in all, and that this does not mean the other cartridges patients used earlier lacked it, since only what was provided was tested. Medical-grade cartridges held retinol (vitamin A) acetate rather than VEA, and fewer contaminants than counterfeit cartridges, though some harmful chemicals were still identified in them.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Total volatile compounds in aerosol were higher from counterfeit patient cartridges (20.03, standard error 0.59, parts per million) than from MCT oil (10.33), mineral oil (7.33) or VEA (9.67), and particle concentrations were also higher; the comparators are pure oils, the numbers of replicates are not given and the monitors are not described in the Methods.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: the GC-MS method was a preliminary screen and the findings are qualitative; samples came from one region of New York State; the effect of any constituent depends on concentration and duration; susceptibility factors and use of other vaping products may contribute because not all people who used THC cartridges were hospitalised; legal restrictions limit toxicology research on cannabis products.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph (concentration and duration) and 10th and 11th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Context quoted from other sources (second-hand): over 2,500 hospitalised patients by December 2019, most men younger than 35; most patients report vaping THC-containing counterfeit street products; VEA is described as a key agent, though inhaled VEA is not a proven cause of lung damage, and animal studies cited by the authors suggest VEA may protect against effects of cigarette smoke and bacterial toxin; a cited study found no VEA in licit UK e-cigarette products; EVALI has been seen almost only in North America.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: None of the cited sources was read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion as written: numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in the medical or CBD vape products; a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute to EVALI together with VEA rather than a single agent; the authors are investigating this in models.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 12th paragraph (Conclusion)

key_findings.finding: Funding: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors are at the University of Rochester Medical Center, The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says VEA was in many but not all counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges and gives no count; the share of the 38 containing VEA, MCT oil or any other named compound is not reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.1; Discussion, 6th paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The study cannot be cited for how common VEA or any other compound was; for VEA prevalence a counted source (duffy_2020) is needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists toluene-d8, 1,2-dichloroethane-d4 and bromofluorobenzene as vapor-phase constituents, each with a very narrow range (510 to 516, 391 to 395 and 556 to 561 micrograms per cubic metre). These are deuterated or halogenated compounds that the EPA volatile-compound method uses as laboratory surrogate or tuning standards, and a deuterated compound is not expected in a cartridge.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of over 50 vapor-phase chemicals may include laboratory standards (editors' note from general analytical chemistry, to be confirmed by a chemist); the true count would be 50 or fewer.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the vapor-phase range as 140 to 360,000 micrograms per cubic metre; Table 2 lists lower values (n-hexane from 44, 2-butanone from 94, benzene from 97, 1,3-butadiene from 98).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated range does not match the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says respiratory toxicants in both phases were not present in the medical or CBD products. Vapor-phase results (Table 2) are for counterfeit cartridges only, and metals results are for counterfeit cartridges only.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.2 and 3.3; Discussion, 12th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: For the vapor phase and metals the claimed contrast has no data shown for the comparison products.

reporting_issues.issue: Compounds named in the text as found are not in the tables or have no method: decane and naphthalene (the Conclusion calls them semi-volatile hydrocarbons; Table 1 lists undecane and no naphthalene), and benzene and aflatoxin B1 in medical-grade cartridges (benzene is in Table 2 for counterfeit cartridges only; the Methods describe no test for aflatoxin).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.1; Discussion, 3rd, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: These specific claims cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Hexadecanoic acid methyl ester is listed for counterfeit cartridges both as a pesticide constituent and as a plasticizer or manufacturing agent; fatty acid methyl esters are the only 'pesticide constituents' listed, and no targeted pesticide analysis was done.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pesticide finding here is a category label from a library match; targeted pesticide measurements are in duffy_2020.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods for the volatile-compound monitor and the particle monitor, the device and its settings, the number of cartridges in the vapor-phase and metals work, and the replicate numbers behind the means with standard errors are not given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods 2.4 and 2.5; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The aerosol comparisons cannot be reproduced or weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: The reading list describes this paper as a review; it is an original laboratory study.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is treated here as primary (low-grade) laboratory evidence, not as a summary of other work.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7355865 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, funding and conflict statements, author affiliations and reference list read as text; no supplementary files were opened)

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021226447) of observational studies comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis, as each study defined potency, for psychosis or psychosis-like symptoms, anxiety, depression and cannabis use disorder. MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 14 January 2021, plus reference lists. 20 articles met the criteria; by the editors' count they report 16 distinct studies (the GAP case-control study in four articles, EU-GEI in two): 2 case-control studies, 1 prospective cohort, 9 cross-sectional studies (one of them in people using medical cannabis) and 4 naturalistic or repeated-measures studies in people using medical cannabis. Narrative synthesis by outcome; risk of bias with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
can_establish: Which observational studies up to January 2021 compared higher- with lower-potency cannabis on psychosis, anxiety, depression and cannabis use disorder, in which designs and samples, how the reviewers rated their quality, and the direction and adjusted size of each study's association as the review reports it.
cannot_establish: A pooled size of any association (no meta-analysis was possible), whether higher potency causes any of these outcomes (all studies observational, most cross-sectional, potency taken from what people said they used), the THC dose people actually took, or much about concentrates, which were studied only in four cross-sectional samples and one small clinical sample.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE (from 1 January 1966), Embase (from 1 January 1974) and PsycINFO (from 1597), all to 14 January 2021, with terms for cannabis, potency and the four outcomes, no date or language limits but English terms only, and reference lists of identified articles (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph, p. 736). The included studies sampled patients with first-episode psychosis and local population controls (UK; 17 catchment areas in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil), patients followed after psychosis onset (UK), respondents to online drug surveys (20 countries, n = 181,870; 175 countries, n = 55,240; UK, n = 2,514), a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24 with childhood measures, US convenience samples (156, 191 and 574 people), 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, and people using medical cannabis in the Netherlands, Canada and the US (Tables 1 to 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of humans with quantitative data on cannabis potency as a direct or indirect comparison of higher- with lower-potency products (as each study defined them, so read in relative terms), quantitative data on symptoms, diagnosis or relapse of depression, anxiety, psychosis, or cannabis use disorder, dependence or misuse, and an association between the two. Excluded: conference abstracts, editorials, correspondence, and experimental studies (Methods, 2nd paragraph, pp. 736-737). At full text 69 of 89 articles were excluded: 44 conference abstracts, editorials or correspondence, 10 not observational, 7 without lower-potency cannabis as the comparator, 6 without higher-potency cannabis as the exposure, 2 without an outcome of interest (Figure, p. 737).
sample.demographics: Mean ages in the included samples range from 24 years (UK online survey; UK sample of 1,087) to 52.8 years (Dutch medical cannabis study); women make up 16.9% (Japanese patients) to 53% (EU-GEI controls; one Canadian medical sample). Countries, by the editors' count of the 16 studies: UK 4, US 5, Canada 2, the Netherlands 1, Japan 1, multinational 3 (Tables 1 to 4).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the one cohort is not reported in the review.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases with English terms; no grey literature, registries or experts; conference abstracts excluded; the search ended in January 2021 and the review was published online in July 2022. Most included samples are self-selected (online drug surveys with pictorial aids, US convenience samples, people using medical cannabis) or clinical (first-episode psychosis, cannabis-related disorders). The review's senior author is an author of at least five included studies and another review author is first author of one (see funding); no procedure for selecting or appraising the authors' own studies is described.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in every study (with pictorial aids in the online surveys and an optional photo upload in one US study): product type (skunk or sinsemilla against hash, grass or resin; butane hash oil or concentrates against herbal cannabis; liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis) or a stated THC band (typically 10% or more against under 10%; labelled percentages in the medical cannabis studies). No included study measured THC in the cannabis people used or THC intake; the authors call the exposure a highly simplified measure of THC content (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 748).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency of use was adjusted for in some studies, combined with potency into one variable in others (for example daily use of higher-potency cannabis) and not considered in others; amount used was adjusted for in only one study (the 175-country survey); route was not analysed (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 748; Tables 1 to 4). Strength bands are study definitions only.
exposure.polysubstance: Only as each study adjusted: tobacco, alcohol and other drugs in the two case-control studies; alcohol, other illicit drugs and cigarettes in the cohort; other substance use in the 20-country survey; tobacco added to cannabis in the 175-country survey; no adjustment listed in four smaller cross-sectional studies (Tables 1 to 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; exposure windows ranged from current use or the past 12 months to lifetime use and were not specified in several studies (Tables 1 to 4).

comparison.controls: Lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it (hash-type, grass or resin, herbal cannabis, under 10% THC, dry herbal), or never-use of cannabis in the two case-control studies and former use in the cohort, in which case the comparison of higher with lower potency is indirect (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 748).
comparison.matching: EU-GEI controls were sampled to represent the catchment population by age, gender and ethnicity, and GAP controls came from the same area (Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs, p. 740); no matching in the other studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Reasons for choosing stronger products (the authors name self-medication by people with poorer mental health as possible reverse causation), earlier mental health outside a few studies, family history and socio-economic position outside one UK sample; the authors state there is no agreement on which confounders matter (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 748).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Adjusted in the case-control studies, the cohort and two surveys; not in the smaller US and Japanese samples (Tables 1 to 4).

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis: first-episode psychosis by the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry or ICD-10, relapse as psychiatric admission, self-reported lifetime diagnosis, the DSM-5 cross-cutting symptom measure, ICD-10 clinical interview, a semi-structured interview or a self-report scale for psychosis-like experiences. Cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156), ICD-10 clinical interview (Japanese patients). Anxiety and depression: self-reported lifetime diagnosis, the Clinical Interview Schedule-revised, the DSM-5 cross-cutting measure, a mental-health self-report scale, and visual analogue or symptom scales in the medical cannabis studies (Tables 1 to 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Two reviewers rated each study independently on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and categorised it as good, fair or poor (details in appendix p 6, not read). None was rated good: by the editors' count of Tables 1 to 4, 5 of the 16 distinct studies were rated fair (the two case-control studies, the cohort, the UK sample of 1,087 and one Dutch medical cannabis study) and 11 poor, with scores from 0 to 8; the same study could score differently by outcome.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Higher' and 'lower' potency are relative within each study: the authors state that the exposure can be read only in relative terms within a study, not in absolute terms across studies (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 748).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcome domains, with more than 50 study-level estimates printed across Tables 1 to 4 (editors' count); the review gives no rule for when a set of findings counts as consistent.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, full-text selection, extraction and risk-of-bias rating were done by two reviewers independently, with disagreements resolved with the senior author (Methods; Contributors, p. 749).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Study-level estimates as the review prints them (odds ratios with 95% CI unless stated). Psychosis: GAP (UK) skunk-type use against never-use 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30), earlier onset hazard ratio 1.68 (1.08 to 2.63); EU-GEI types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5), daily 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6), positive symptoms 0.22 (0.02 to 0.29) against 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.28); relapse cohort 3.28 (1.22 to 9.18) against 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); 20-country survey higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.28 (1.07 to 1.53), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46); US sample of 156 concentrates r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), higher-potency herbal -0.27 (-0.45 to -0.06); Japanese patients 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735); psychosis-like experiences 1.29 (0.67 to 2.50) and Cohen's d 0.12 (fewer with concentrates). Cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale b 0.254 (0.161 to 0.357) per extra day a month of higher-potency use, grass 0.020 (-0.029 to 0.070), resin 0.025 (-0.019 to 0.067); b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209) and 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337) for the higher-potency classes in the 175-country survey; recent problems 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81); dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145); US sample of 156 r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30) and -0.05 (printed -0.35 to -0.26); US sample of 191 means 2.1 against 1.3, not significant. Anxiety: generalised anxiety disorder 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32); butane hash oil 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01) and 1.72 (1.55 to 1.91); higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12); US samples null. Depression: 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25), butane hash oil 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) and 1.15 (1.03 to 1.25); major depression 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32); US samples null. Medical cannabis studies: varied, several without intervals or statistical tests.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; estimates were extracted from each study's fully adjusted model, with covariates listed per study in Tables 1 to 4.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021226447, described as prospectively registered (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 737); PRISMA followed. The registry record was not read, so planned and reported analyses could not be compared; the paper explains why no meta-analysis was done (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 748).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four outcomes are reported, with the medical cannabis studies separated. Several estimates are printed without intervals ('95% CI NS'), and several numbers differ between the text and the tables (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable; no pooling. Several included samples are small (71, 102, 156 and 191 people).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Psychosis: in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair, stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) was associated with first-episode psychosis compared with never-use (adjusted odds ratios 2.91 and 1.6; 5.40 and 4.8 with daily use) while lower-potency use was not (0.83; 1.1), although daily lower-potency use was in EU-GEI (2.2); continued daily use of stronger cannabis was associated with relapse (3.28) and stronger cannabis with earlier onset (hazard ratio 1.68). Cross-sectional findings for psychosis were mixed, including no association for concentrates in two samples and an inverse one in a clinical sample. Cannabis use disorder: four of six cross-sectional studies (one fair, three poor) found more dependence severity, problems or dependence with higher potency, and the two comparing concentrates with herbal cannabis found no significant difference. Anxiety: one fair study and the butane hash oil comparison in one large survey found associations, others did not. Depression: small associations in one large survey only. No study was rated good, and none measured THC.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says higher-potency use "was associated with an increased risk of psychosis and CUD" and that evidence varied for depression and anxiety, which matches the results. Gaps: (1) the Discussion calls the association with cannabis use disorder consistent, but two of the six studies found no significant association and all six were cross-sectional, five rated poor; (2) 'risk' wording comes from mostly cross-sectional data, which the authors themselves say cannot establish direction; (3) the Conclusion draws recommendations for education, clinical management and THC-based regulation without a certainty rating of the evidence; (4) the psychosis evidence concerns skunk-type cannabis or types of 10% THC or more, not concentrates as a separate form, while the Introduction motivates the review with concentrated extracts, and the studies of concentrates themselves were few, cross-sectional and mostly null; (5) several printed numbers disagree between text and tables. Against this, the Discussion is explicit about self-reported exposure, proxies, reverse causation, the lack of agreement on confounders and why no meta-analysis was possible, and argues that titration would bias associations toward the null.

timeline.event: First GAP article (Di Forti et al., 2009): in a preliminary analysis of 454, patients with first-episode psychosis more often used higher-potency cannabis than controls (as summarised in this review).
Full GAP sample (Di Forti et al., 2015) and a UK online survey of potency and dependence severity (Freeman & Winstock, 2015), both included here.
UK cohort of relapse after a first episode of psychosis (Schoeler et al., 2016), the only prospective cohort included.
20-country online survey of butane hash oil (Chan et al., 2017), the largest included sample and the main source on concentrates.
EU-GEI case-control study across six countries (Di Forti et al., 2019), described by the review as replicating GAP; it shares its first author with the GAP articles.
Meta-analysis of the prevalence of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis, cited in this review's Introduction for its 22% estimate
This review: the first systematic review of cannabis potency and mental health and addiction, by its authors' account.
Narrative review of flower, concentrates and edibles and cannabis use disorder (online 2024, issue 2026), which does not cite this review

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review on this question read for the encyclopedia. It pools nothing, so its weight is that of its studies: the psychosis conclusion rests on two case-control studies sharing a first author and one cohort, all rated fair; the cannabis use disorder conclusion rests on six cross-sectional studies, three of the four positive ones co-authored by the review's senior author. Claims must count the GAP study's four articles and EU-GEI's two articles once each, must not count the review's own authors' surveys as independent of the review, and should quote numbers from the tables, which differ from the text in places.

The funder had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Acknowledgments, p. 749).
funding.declared_conflicts: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing work unrelated to this project; KP, SO, LH, SA and TPF declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests, p. 749).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Universities of Bath, Bristol and Birmingham and University College London. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of at least five included studies (EU-GEI 2019, Freeman & Winstock 2015, Chan et al. 2017, Hines et al. 2020 and Craft et al. 2020) and L Hines as first author of Hines et al. 2020; these supply the fair-quality anxiety and cannabis use disorder findings, three of the four positive cannabis use disorder findings and the main concentrate data. The review also recommends measurement tools (the iCannToolkit and the standard THC unit) developed with its authors' involvement. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed. Recorded as reasons to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use cannabis, recruited before problems begin, that record the products used and THC exposure (tested or labelled content in standard THC units, with frequency and amount), measure cannabis use disorder and psychosis by diagnostic interview over years, adjust for earlier mental health and reasons for use, and are run by groups other than those that produced most current studies; for concentrates, the same design in places where they are widely sold.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Observational human studies; exposure higher-potency cannabis; comparator lower-potency cannabis, both as each study defined them; outcomes depression, anxiety, psychosis and cannabis use disorder (Methods, 2nd paragraph, pp. 736-737).

Described as prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021226447) and done to PRISMA (Methods, 1st and 3rd paragraphs). The registry record was not read, and the paper does not say whether a meta-analysis was planned or whether anything changed from the protocol.
Experimental studies were excluded for a stated reason: the authors wanted real-world exposure to the potency and amount used (Methods, 2nd paragraph).

Three databases from inception to 14 January 2021 with key terms given and the strategy in the appendix, plus reference lists, and no formal date or language limit; but English search terms only and the exclusion of conference abstracts, editorials and correspondence (44 of the 69 full-text exclusions) are not justified, and no grey literature, registries or experts were searched. Judged as AMSTAR 2 item 4 is written, as for the batch 3 cards; the senior author decides the project's reading of this item (decision p-amstar2-item4).
KP and SO screened titles, titles and abstracts, and full texts independently (agreement 96.2%, 89.9% and 89.9%), with disagreements resolved with TPF (Methods, 3rd paragraph; Contributors).
KP and SO extracted independently into a spreadsheet, cross-checked by KP (Data analysis; Contributors).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flowchart gives reasons for the 69 full-text exclusions as counts, and the text says the specific exclusions are reported in appendix p 5, which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1 to 4 give for each study the design, location and years, participants with sample size, age and sex, exposure and comparator, how exposure was collected, the timing of exposure and outcome, the outcome measure, the confounders adjusted for, the main findings and the quality score.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was applied by two reviewers independently per outcome, covering selection, comparability (confounding) and exposure and outcome measurement; the modifications and domain scores are in appendix p 6 (not read); selective reporting of results is not assessed, and the summary into good, fair or poor hides which domain failed in which study, although the text names the main shortfalls.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for any included study.
No meta-analysis; the reasons are given (self-reported exposure, no precise measure of THC exposure, differing definitions of higher and lower potency; Discussion, 7th paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion states that no study was rated good and discusses self-reported exposure, product type as a proxy, titration, cross-sectional designs and confounding (5th to 9th paragraphs). The Conclusion and the sentence calling the cannabis use disorder association consistent do not carry these limits through.

Differences in how studies defined higher and lower potency, and in direct against indirect comparisons, are discussed as the reason results can be read only within studies and could not be pooled (Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs); inconsistent findings are partly explained (few symptoms in one sample, low rates of psychosis and a self-reported outcome in another, a small clinical sample).
No meta-analysis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and author interests are declared (p. 749); the paper does not flag that its authors wrote several included studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from appendix p 5, which was not read. One critical item fails (item 4: English search terms and the exclusion of conference abstracts without justification, no grey literature, registries or experts), which gives low confidence; if item 7 also failed the rating would be critically low. Items 2 and 9 are partly met and item 13 is met; items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because nothing was pooled. The review is registered, screened, extracted and appraised in duplicate and describes its studies in full tables; the main weakness for readers lies in its evidence rather than its conduct: no study rated good, mostly cross-sectional designs, self-reported potency, and a Discussion sentence calling the cannabis use disorder association consistent when two of six studies found none. Cite it for which studies exist and what each found as reported, preferring the tables where text and tables differ.

key_findings.finding: MEDLINE (from 1966), Embase (from 1974) and PsycINFO (from 1597) were searched to 14 January 2021 with English terms for cannabis, potency and the four outcomes (no date or language limits), plus reference lists. 6,389 records, 2,218 duplicates, 4,171 titles screened, 89 full texts assessed and 69 excluded (44 conference abstracts, editorials or correspondence; 10 not observational; 7 without lower-potency cannabis as comparator; 6 without higher-potency cannabis as exposure; 2 without an outcome of interest), leaving 20. Two reviewers screened and assessed independently (agreement 96.2%, 89.9% and 89.9%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure (PRISMA flowchart, p. 737)

key_findings.finding: 20 articles, printed as 20 studies with 119,581 participants: 8 on psychosis or psychosis-like symptoms, 8 on anxiety, 7 on depression and 6 on cannabis use disorder. By the editors' count the tables hold 16 distinct studies (the GAP study in four articles, EU-GEI in two): 2 case-control, 1 prospective cohort, 9 cross-sectional (one in people using medical cannabis) and 4 naturalistic or repeated-measures studies in people using medical cannabis. None was rated good; 5 were rated fair and 11 poor (editors' count from the risk-of-bias column).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 4 (risk-of-bias column)
key_findings.note: The printed participant total is smaller than the sample of one included survey (181,870); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: GAP case-control study (UK, 2005-10; 410 patients with first-episode psychosis and 370 controls from the same area; rated fair): in a preliminary analysis of 454, patients more often used higher-potency cannabis than controls (adjusted odds ratio 6.8, 95% CI 2.6 to 25.4); in the full sample of 780, skunk-type use against never-use 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30), with daily lower-potency use not associated. EU-GEI case-control study (17 catchment areas in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil, 2010-15; 901 patients and 1,237 population controls; rated fair): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) after adjustment for daily use, under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) for higher and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6) for lower potency. Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 740); Table 1 (p. 738)

key_findings.finding: Earlier onset of psychosis by about 4 years with higher-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63; GAP, adjusted for gender and frequency). Positive symptoms in 901 first-episode patients: higher-potency use against no use 0.22 (0.02 to 0.29), lower potency 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.28). Relapse within 2 years of onset in a UK cohort of 256 patients (rated fair): 58% of those who used higher-potency cannabis daily against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18), lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75), adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. Cross-sectional, all rated poor: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis in a 20-country online survey of 181,870, higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.28 (1.07 to 1.53), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46) and against higher-potency herbal 0.89 (0.69 to 1.09); psychosis symptoms in 156 US adults, concentrates r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), higher-potency herbal -0.27 (-0.45 to -0.06); residual or late-onset psychotic disorder in 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin against dry herbal 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th to 8th paragraphs (pp. 740-742); Table 1 (pp. 738-740)

key_findings.finding: Psychosis-like experiences: in a within-person comparison of 574 US adults who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently, means were 1.2 when using herbal cannabis and 1.1 when using concentrates on a 0 to 10 scale (Cohen's d 0.12; rated poor); in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24, higher- against lower-potency use 1.29 (0.67 to 2.50) after adjustment for frequency, sex, childhood socio-economic position and psychotic experiences at 12 (rated fair).
key_findings.locator: Results, 9th paragraph (pp. 742-744); Table 1 (p. 740)

key_findings.finding: Six cross-sectional studies of cannabis use disorder, one rated fair and five poor, with limits in the exposure measure in all six and in outcome measures, sample selection and confounder adjustment in the poor ones. Outcomes: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample of 1,087), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156) and an ICD-10 clinical interview (71 Japanese patients).
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (p. 744); Table 2 (pp. 741-742)

key_findings.finding: Four studies found more cannabis use disorder signs with higher potency. UK online survey 2009-10 (2,514; skunk against grass and resin; adjusted for gender and age; poor): each extra day a month of higher-potency use went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.254 higher (0.161 to 0.357), with no association for grass (0.020, -0.029 to 0.070) or resin (0.025, -0.019 to 0.067). Survey of 55,240 people in 175 countries 2017-18 (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added; poor): classes using sinsemilla and herbal, b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209), and hashish and herbal, b 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337), against herbal only. UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (Cannabis Abuse Screening Test; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, age at first use and frequency; fair): recent cannabis problems, odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (ICD-10 interview; no adjustment listed; poor): liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145).
key_findings.locator: Results, 11th paragraph (p. 744); Table 2 (pp. 741-742)
key_findings.note: The text gives 6.9 (1.19 to 25.15) for the Japanese study and 0.161 to 0.3578 for the UK survey; Table 2 values are used here.

key_findings.finding: Two studies found no clear difference. US sample of 156 (self-report questionnaire; no adjustment listed; poor): higher-potency herbal use and symptoms of cannabis use disorder r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30); for concentrates the review prints -0.05 (-0.35 to -0.26) and the text reads it as fewer symptoms. US sample of 191 (MINI cannabis screening test; no adjustment listed; poor): people who frequently used concentrates did not endorse significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3); the review notes that the sample endorsed few symptoms overall.
key_findings.locator: Results, 12th and 13th paragraphs (pp. 744-746); Table 2 (p. 741)
key_findings.note: The printed interval for the concentrate estimate does not contain the estimate; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder in the UK sample of 1,087, higher- against lower-potency use 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32), adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; in the 20-country survey, self-reported anxiety diagnosis with butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01) and against higher-potency herbal 1.72 (1.55 to 1.91), higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12); no association in 156 US adults (concentrates r 0.21, -0.10 to 0.49; higher-potency herbal 0.03, -0.18 to 0.24) and no difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use in 191 (means 1.1 and 0.66). Four studies of people using medical cannabis (one fair) gave varied results, some without intervals or statistical tests.
key_findings.locator: Results, 14th to 19th paragraphs (pp. 746-747); Table 3 (pp. 743-744)

key_findings.finding: Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): in the 20-country survey, self-reported depression diagnosis with higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) and against higher-potency herbal 1.15 (1.03 to 1.25); major depression in the UK sample of 1,087, 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32); no difference in the US sample of 191 (means 0.72 and 0.76) and no association in the US sample of 156 (concentrates r 0.17, -0.15 to 0.45; higher-potency herbal 0.02, -0.19 to 0.23). Three studies of people using medical cannabis (all poor) found greater relief with higher THC in one, the greatest reduction with the lowest THC in another, and differences not tested in the third.
key_findings.locator: Results, 20th to 24th paragraphs (p. 747); Table 4 (pp. 745-746)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that higher-potency use is associated with an increased risk of psychosis, higher in people who use daily, and with earlier onset, more symptoms and relapse; that the evidence does not suggest an association with psychosis-like symptoms; that higher potency was consistently associated with an increased risk of cannabis use disorder, recent problems and dependence severity, citing animal self-administration studies and a link between rising potency and treatment entry; and that there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: most studies used self-reported product type, an approximate proxy for THC content; studies did not account for THC intake as opposed to content, which can differ through titration, which they say evidence suggests is partial and would be expected to weaken rather than inflate associations; dichotomous potency categories; some studies compared higher with lower potency directly and others each with no use, so results can be read only within each study; no meta-analysis was possible; cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction (people with poorer mental health might choose stronger cannabis as self-medication); there is no agreement on confounders, amount used was adjusted for in only one study, and frequency may be a confounder or a mediator. Other cannabinoids such as cannabidiol were not considered.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th to 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Conclusion draws recommendations for education tools, clinical management and regulation by THC concentration (limits or taxes) from these findings; no certainty rating of the evidence is given.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 11th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funding: ESRC South West Doctoral Training Partnership studentship (KP); Cancer Research UK fellowship C56067/A21330 and project award PPRCPJT\100023 (GT); Wellcome Trust 209158/Z/17/Z (LH); the funder had no role. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing unrelated work; the other authors declare none. The reference list shows the senior author as an author of at least five included studies and another review author as first author of one.
key_findings.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 15, 22, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 20 studies with 119,581 participants, but one included survey alone has 181,870 participants (Tables 1, 3 and 4), and the samples printed in Tables 1 to 4 sum to about 249,000 across the 16 distinct studies (editors' arithmetic, counting each study once).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed participant total cannot be used; any claim should give the samples of the individual studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline count of 20 'studies' counts articles: the GAP study appears in four articles and EU-GEI in two, so the tables hold 16 distinct studies (editors' count), while the per-outcome counts (8, 8, 7, 6) count each of GAP and EU-GEI once.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must not count the GAP or EU-GEI articles as separate studies.

reporting_issues.issue: For the Japanese patients, the text gives dependence syndrome odds ratio 6.9 (95% CI 1.19 to 25.15) and Table 2 gives 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower limit differs; the table value is used, and the study is small (71) with no adjustment listed either way.

reporting_issues.issue: For concentrates in the US sample of 156, the review prints r -0.05 with 95% CI -0.35 to -0.26 (text and Table 2), an interval that does not contain its own estimate, and the text reads it as concentrate use associated with fewer symptoms of cannabis use disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is probably a sign error (0.26); read as no association, as for the herbal estimate in the same study. Not checked against the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs differ between text and tables: the text prints the herbal anxiety estimate in the US sample of 156 as 0.03 (-0.18 to -0.24) and Table 3 as 0.03 (-0.18 to 0.24); the herbal depression estimate as 0.02 (0.19 to 0.23) in the text and 0.02 (-0.19 to 0.23) in Table 4; the medical cannabis anxiety coefficients (Stith 2020) as b 0.618 and 0.599 in the text and -0.618 and -0.599 in Table 3. The text also gives that US sample as 151 people for depression, against 156 in Table 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table values; the substantive reading (no association; symptom relief) is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the Japanese chronic psychosis result 'No association' although its odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735) excludes 1; the text describes fewer residual and late-onset psychotic disorders with higher potency.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimate is an inverse association in a small clinical sample; the table label understates it.

reporting_issues.issue: The EU-GEI positive-symptom estimate is labelled an unstandardised coefficient b in Table 1 and a standardised coefficient beta in the text (0.22, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.29, an interval asymmetric around its estimate); the GAP odds ratio 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60) and the EU-GEI daily-use odds ratio 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) sit near the upper ends of their intervals on the ratio scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible misprints carried from or into the review; the primary papers were not read, so these figures are quoted as the review prints them.

reporting_issues.issue: In one medical cannabis study (Wan 2017) Table 3 lists the strength bands compared as 25-28%, 20-23% and 0.1-0.8% THC, while its findings column and text report 21-24%, 25-28% and 15-18%; the text cites table 4 for the quality ratings of the medical anxiety studies, which are in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the medical cannabis findings are not used for claims.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 736-750 (PDFs/Cannabis/Petrilli_2022_PotencySR.pdf): all text, the PRISMA figure and Tables 1 to 4 (the rotated tables read from page images at 110 dpi and checked against the text layer), references, contributors, declaration of interests and acknowledgments; the online appendix (search strategy, list of excluded studies, risk-of-bias scoring) was not read

design_detail: Randomized, counterbalanced, within-person crossover laboratory trial (Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, Baltimore; June 2016 to January 2017) in 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least a month. Each person completed six 8.5-hour outpatient sessions at least a week apart: cannabis flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg of THC, either smoked in a small handheld pipe or heated in a desktop vaporizer (Volcano Medic) and inhaled from a balloon, over a 10-minute period. The three sessions of one method were run together; method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method. Described as double-blind, but no double-dummy was used, so people could tell smoke from vapor. Outcomes: ratings of drug effects (Drug Effect Questionnaire), three computerized performance tasks, heart rate and blood pressure, and whole-blood THC, at baseline and up to 8 hours after dosing. Registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03676166) after the study ended; the record was read.
can_establish: In 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis, in single laboratory sessions with one type of flower, one pipe and one desktop vaporizer, how ratings of drug effects, task performance, heart rate and whole-blood THC differed between smoked and vaporized cannabis containing the same THC in the material loaded, each person serving as their own comparison.
cannot_establish: How the two ways of inhaling compare when people pace and adjust their own use, in people who use cannabis regularly, or with joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates or tobacco mixed in; how much THC actually reached the body (only the THC in the material loaded was set, not the amount delivered); anything about the lungs, repeated use or harm over time; differences by sex or between individuals (17 people); and, for most outcomes, whether a difference between the two methods is more than chance (only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected across the 32 outcomes, and no interval is given for any of them).

sample.recruitment: Advertisements and word of mouth. Judged healthy by medical history, electrocardiogram, blood tests and physical examination; denied cannabis or other illicit drug use in the month before (timeline follow-back); urine toxicology negative for cannabis, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cocaine, MDMA, opioids and phencyclidine at screening and before every session (Methods › Participants). Participants were paid. The registry record adds age 18 to 45, body mass index 19 to 36 and exclusion of non-medical use of psychoactive drugs other than nicotine, alcohol or caffeine in the 3 months before screening.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As above. The paper defines infrequent use as no use in the past 30 days with a negative urine test; it does not state any minimum or typical earlier use beyond self-reported prior use of cannabis (Methods › Participants; Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: 9 men and 8 women; mean age 27.3 years (SD 5.7); mean weight 77.9 kg (SD 15.5), body mass index 26.2 (SD 3.3); 10 white non-Hispanic, 3 other or Hispanic, 3 black non-Hispanic, 1 white Hispanic. Mean 398 days (SD 437) since last self-reported cannabis use; median 365, range 30 to 1,825. How often or how much people had used before that is not reported.
sample.attrition: The text says 17 people completed the study and gives no count of people screened, enrolled or lost; the CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image and was not extracted. The registry record gives actual enrolment as 18, so one person may be unaccounted for in the text.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers willing to inhale cannabis in a laboratory, abstinent for at least a month (a median of about a year) and screened for drug use before each session. People who use cannabis regularly, who may respond very differently because of tolerance, were excluded by design. Tiny sample; education, income, tobacco use and earlier patterns of cannabis use are not reported.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Cannabis flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply: batch 1 contained 13.4% delta-9-THC, 0.08% delta-8-THC, 0.03% cannabidiol and 0.8% cannabinol; the placebo batch contained under 0.01% THC with no detectable other cannabinoids. Target THC was set by weighing: 186.6 mg of placebo material for 0 mg, 74.6 mg of batch 1 mixed with 112 mg of placebo material for 10 mg, and 186.6 mg of batch 1 for 25 mg (the same amount of plant material in every session). Whole-blood THC was measured by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (limit of quantitation 0.5 ng/mL). Heart rate and blood pressure were measured seated with an automated monitor. Methods › Study Design and Procedure; Study Drug; Blood Specimens.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 0, 10 or 25 mg THC in the plant material loaded; inhaled over a 10-minute period (smoked in a small handheld pipe prefilled and lit by the participant, with a metal top to hide the plant material and limit side-stream loss; or heated in a Volcano Medic desktop vaporizer at one fixed temperature, vapor collected in a balloon and inhaled until empty, three balloons for the 25-mg condition). Six single-dose sessions at least a week apart. Research pharmacy staff checked the pipe contents to confirm the whole dose was used; nothing was measured to show how much THC was delivered from either device (no puff, residue or exhaled-breath measure).
exposure.polysubstance: No cannabis or other illicit drug in the month before the study and a negative urine test and alcohol breath test before each session. Tobacco, nicotine and caffeine use are not reported. The pipe held only the study cannabis (no tobacco is mentioned).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 days by self-report at screening, mean 398 days; urine drug screens (rapid enzyme immunoassay) negative before each session. Blood THC before dosing is not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant had all six conditions, including placebo cannabis (under 0.01% THC) smoked and vaporized, so every active condition is compared with the same person's placebo session of the same method, and the two methods with each other at the same THC content.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Method order counterbalanced across people; dose order randomized within each method; the method of generating or concealing the sequence is not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Earlier frequency and amount of cannabis use, tobacco or nicotine use, expectancy about what each method would do, sleep, food and caffeine before sessions, and genetics (the authors say the sample was too small to examine such characteristics) were not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants in every condition; no illicit drug use in the month before and negative urine tests before each session.

outcomes.instruments: Drug Effect Questionnaire: 20 items rated on a 100-mm line from not at all to extremely (drug effect, pleasant, unpleasant, sick, heart racing, anxious or nervous, relaxed, paranoid, sleepy, alert, irritable, vigorous or motivated, restless, hungry, craving, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, memory impairment, throat irritation or coughing, difficulty performing routine tasks). Digit Symbol Substitution Task (number attempted, number correct, percent correct in 90 seconds), Divided Attention Task (time tracking the central stimulus, mean distance from it, peripheral stimuli correct out of 24) and Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task (correct out of 90, reaction time for correct and incorrect answers). Heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Whole-blood THC. Assessments at baseline and 0.17, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 hours after dosing (tasks not at 0.17 hours). Training on the tasks at screening.
outcomes.validity_norms: The tasks are described as sensitive to cannabis and relevant to workplace performance and driving, with references to earlier laboratory work (Methods › Outcome Measures); no norms or cut-offs for impairment are given. The authors conclude from this and other studies that blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects and impairment are the peak change from each session's own baseline, compared with the placebo session of the same method (planned contrasts), and between methods at each active dose. No clinical, legal or safety threshold for impairment is set.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. The two contrasts against placebo within each method used a threshold of P below .025; the two smoked-versus-vaporized contrasts per outcome (10 and 25 mg) were treated as orthogonal and tested at P below .05 with no correction; nothing was corrected across the 32 outcomes in the Table (up to 192 planned contrasts: 4 against placebo and 2 between methods for each), and Holm-Bonferroni was used for the correlations only.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and staff were blinded to dose but not in practice to method: no double-dummy procedure was used, and an opaque bag over the balloons and a metal top on the pipe were used to hide vapor and plant material. Research pharmacy staff who checked the pipe contents were unblinded. Task scores, blood pressure and heart rate are automated; drug-effect ratings are self-report.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean (SD) peak change from each session's baseline, smoked and then vaporized. Drug-effect rating (0 to 100): placebo 11.2 (15.9) and 2.1 (5.2); 10 mg 45.7 (26.4) and 69.5 (26.4); 25 mg 66.4 (28.6) and 77.5 (23.4). Heart rate (beats/min): placebo -3.7 (8.5) and -4.3 (6.1); 10 mg 11.3 (10.4) and 23.3 (11.8); 25 mg 19.1 (17.1) and 26.8 (16.6). Peak whole-blood THC (ng/mL), no placebo values given: 10 mg 3.8 (5.9) and 7.5 (5.5); 25 mg 10.2 (12.4) and 14.4 (9.4). Digit Symbol Substitution, number correct: placebo -3.2 (12.3) and +4.9 (8.9); 10 mg +3.4 (4.4) and -8.3 (11.3); 25 mg -7.0 (14.3) and -13.8 (14.9). Paced Auditory Serial Addition, reaction time for correct answers (ms): placebo -38.7 (107) and -43.8 (80.8); 10 mg +80.3 (119) and +86.9 (104); 25 mg +84.9 (90.8) and +85.4 (162). Between-method contrasts flagged at P below .05 in the Table: drug effect, dry mouth, dry or red eyes, vigorous or motivated, heart rate and Divided Attention mean distance at 10 mg; paranoid, vigorous or motivated, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg; also two Divided Attention outcomes in the 0-mg sessions. No interval or exact P value is given for any contrast. Editors' calculation (vaporized minus smoked difference in group mean peak changes; unpaired normal-theory 95% interval with t of 2.04, n = 17 per condition; conservative because it ignores the within-person pairing, whose correlation is not reported): drug effect at 10 mg +23.8 points (5.4 to 42.2; standardized difference about 0.9) and at 25 mg +11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4; 0.4); heart rate at 10 mg +12.0 beats/min (4.2 to 19.8; 1.1) and at 25 mg +7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5; 0.5); peak blood THC at 10 mg +3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7; 0.65; ratio of means 2.0) and at 25 mg +4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9; 0.4; ratio 1.4). The paper itself reports no test of the blood THC difference.
analysis.covariates: Repeated-measures regression (first-order autoregressive covariance) with time, dose and method; no covariates, no period effect and no sex term reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03676166 was first submitted on 16 September 2018 and posted on 18 September 2018, about 20 months after the last session (17 January 2017, actual completion) and about two weeks before the paper was accepted (28 September 2018): a retrospective registration, so it cannot show what was planned. Registered primary outcome: quantity of THC in blood by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry, 8 hours after exposure. Registered secondary outcomes: Drug Effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention scores. The paper states no primary outcome; its headline findings are the ratings and task scores, with blood THC reported without a test of the method difference. Heart rate, blood pressure and the other 19 rating items are reported but not registered as outcomes. The record's summary also mentions oral fluid and urine, which this paper does not report. The trial protocol (Supplement 1, a PDF) was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: 32 outcomes in one Table with no correction across outcomes; the main text names the significant ones and reports the rest only in the Table; the sample-size reasoning is not about cannabis. Oral fluid and urine measures named in the registry summary are not in the paper. Adverse events are described in one sentence, with no counts for placebo or 10-mg sessions.
analysis.power: The authors justify 17 participants by a 1996 meta-analysis of six drug-administration studies of anti-anxiety medicines (about 14 participants each, effect sizes 0.87 to 1.0) published as a chapter in a government volume titled Problems of Drug Dependence (Methods › Statistical Analysis; reference 24). It concerns another drug class and other comparisons, and is not a power calculation for a smoked-versus-vaporized contrast or for blood THC, the registered primary outcome.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for a month or more, cannabis flower with 10 or 25 mg THC, smoked or vaporized, raised ratings of drug effect and heart rate and slowed or worsened some task scores in dose-ordered fashion, and effects outlasted blood THC (blood THC back to zero by 4 hours, heart rate by 3 hours, drug-effect ratings still above baseline 6 hours after the 25-mg conditions).
